Blissful and funky... but watch out for bad port and performance!
On paper this game should be boring and as uninteresting as playing Simon Says, from which Space Channel 5 series essentially takes one of important game mechanics. Ulala, your character and a space reporter for the title TV station is forced to rescue hostages and save the day by the power of dancing moves. For the player that mostly means repeating the exact button combinations that the game prompts you to do. This Simon however adds a crucial element of the rhythm and timing to the ongoing music. Memorize all those inputs if you want, but without any sense of flow and pacing you will be fired like a Buzzfeed “journalist” failing their daily clickbait quota.
The visual and musical mash-up consists of jazz-o-funky tunes, colorful graphics, extremely satisfying feedback on every action, and the absolute insanity of things happening on the screen. All of this makes for one of the most purely satisfying gameplay experiences I had. Color me surprised when I realized how often I saw myself coming back to this game. I simply cannot stop recognizing how much those simple mechanics and absolutely amazing music can create such mesmerizing and hypnotizing pleasure. When you start performing well enough, you will feel like you could touch all of that funky flow with your bare hands at the press of a button.
To get to this level though, there are some sacrifices required. First off, Space Channel 5 firmly goes by the old SEGA’s school of game design, where playing well is extremely rewarded, but to gain that skill you need to fail a few times and learn the game first. This is not a hard game by a long shot, but I could clearly imagine people without any sort of rhythm feel to fall flat on their face even on easiest sequences. This will result with frequent game overs early on, but if you aren’t afraid of a little challenge and getting your inner flow strings straighten you should be fine.
Unfortunately, in terms of PC port and the game’s performance, I got nothing good to say about it. I was quite lucky that I was only hit with fixable “game not saving” issue, but there are numerous reports that game somehow fails to maintain proper framerate, which is extremely crucial for the game’s logic and mechanics. When the music gets desynchronized, you will screw every possible dance move. There is no way to predict if you will be hit with this problem. To add insult to injury, configuration options are barebones and the game did not receive any significant graphical upgrade, which is what you would want for this PS2 era title. I also feel that it’s important to note that the game is quite short, especially if you are good at the genre.
I NEED to recommend this game, but I cannot turn a blind eye on its problems. I would suggest you to still get it and refund it on the slightest sign of trouble (it should be apparent right away). If you like rhythm, musical games, or other titles that require great input execution skills, then you are making yourself a disservice not playing Space Channel 5.
Oh yeah… and there’s Michael Jackson in this game.

I am a FPS gamer and mainly stick to the tactical and competative shooter genre. I've never liked or played MOBAs, RPGs,  RTSs, simulators and survival crafting games just wear out after a few hours of playtime. However, Rimworld could be considered an RTS, RPG survival, crafting, game all-in-one and I have dumped 66 hours into it after owning it for 5 days. The most similar game I can compare this to is Dwarf Fortress, but Rimworld is modernized and has a slick coat of paint. This game is very complex and has many different layers and facets to it. It has an active developer who is awesome and each uppdate adds another layer of gameplay. I should also mention that this game has two setting. The "have a laugh and a good time" difficulty settings and the "will kick your♥♥♥♥♥through the roof" difficulty settings. Literally anything, and I mean anything can destroy your colony and ruin your day. This game is also really good at getting you attached to the low-res cartoon Russian nesting dolls that are your colonists. My first successful colony (my third try) lasted four in-game years and then everyone was killed by an insect hive that spawned in my storage room. I almost cried because so much effort had gone into the colony and I wanted to keep on playing with those characters. The bottom line is that this game should go down as one of the greatest indie games ever. BUY IT RIGHT NOW

If you enjoy rhythm games, or quirky games in general, I seriously can't recommend Space Channel 5: Part 2 enough.  I've played it for more than two dozen hours on PS2, and I bought it anyway on Steam just because.  The animation and choreography are a joy to watch, the music is catchy and varied, the controls are tight, and the port is perfect.  Gameplay is basically Simon Says to music, so it's pretty much accessible to anyone, and the crazy settings and situations keep things fresh, funny, and entertaining from start to finish.  It also comes loaded with extras (costumes, microphones, survival, and 2-player), so there are a ton of ways to really get the most out of your Channel 5 experience. I just wish it included the first one.

I have not used a floor planner 'game' in a long time.
I use the word 'game' loosely, but it does not bother me.
This program allowed me to design a few rooms in under a few hours and fill it in with everything I needed.
(Some objects did not exist that I could have used, floor fans, standing fans, etc.), but it was easy to use a placeholder and scale an object to signify where it was meant to go. There really is a good chunk of items to choose from.
It is not super advanced, but from what I had used of this program a long while ago (8+ months).
It has been polished some and is more user friendly than what I did remember. It got the job done for me.
The biggest Pro to this program is that it has a nice "walk around" (3d+visit) mode, so you can see what you have made in a first person view. You only have VERY minor interaction with objects (re-texture) in this mode. And I must say 2d mode was super great with some information, it gives measurements of how far what you are working with is from walls and other objects, which allows for tight and super uniform placement of objects. 3d+Aerial is very helpful for scaling objects height.

Divekick is built on the premise of what some of your button mashing jump kicking friends use to do in regular fighting games. The stuff that would irritate you because you would somehow always get kicked by them constantly even when you knew how to fight in the game.
Each character has a humorous storyline to go through in single player mode which can bring some laughs. The game is played with only using two buttons and whoever gets the higher kick or faster kick wins the match. There are some who say the game has a lot of strategy but I just don’t see it that way.
There’s also an online mode and local mode to play but I didn’t bother with either since I didn’t care much for the single player portion. I wasn’t really fond of the game when it was announced and that feeling didn’t change after playing it. It’s a novelty game making fun of players who would constantly jump kick through the whole fight. Some of the character designs were funny along with their names but that only last for a short time.
Only way I could recommend this game is if you got it for free or dirt cheap. Its novelty wears off fast and reading around it sounds like the online has pretty much died.

OK, so first off this is not a game. It's not meant to be a game and if you want a game then try something else.
If you want to redesign your kitchen, plan an extension or create a fantasy home then this program does the job. It's pretty easy to use and has a range of furniture and decor so you can complete your look. I created my entire house in this app on the iPad and used it to plan redecorating and other home improvement projects.
Recently I have purchsaed the PC version and imported my ipad plans. I have then used it to plan out an extension and new kitchen - although we still needed to hire a professional to draw up the plans for the extension I was able to run through a lot of ideas myself before we got him in and it helped to communicate what we wanted. It also helped plan the kitchen units with my wife.
One problem is that this app appears to be tailored towards the US appliances and building standards. Furniture common in the UK is not always available and sizes are not UK standards. It would be fantastic if there was a B&Q, Homebase or Ikea catalogue download.
Also the last ipad version I used allowed you to set wall height and I have not located this option on the PC. As most post war built houses in the UK have a ceiling of 2.3m rathere than the app standard 2.5m this can make rooms look very different expecially when placing taller or wall mounted furniture. Also you can't build an upstairs.
All that said, for under £10 this application is well worth it for any home improvement enthusiast looking for a way to plan and preview before starting a project.

Divekick is a two button fighting game. Just two buttons. No joystick, no d-pad, no other buttons, just two. One for jump and one for kick. Each hit in Divekick is a one-hit-Knockout, so games go pretty quick. The game has a roster of 13 characters which all play surprisingly differently. At least I was surprised how much character variety can be had with a two button game.
Because there’s only two buttons, Divekick is also very accessible; there’s no memorizing combos or movesets, so anyone can jump right in and start playing. The game also has a very ridiculous sense of humor. There’s lots of poking fun at other fighting games, pop-culture references and internet humor references. There’s a character in the game who just quotes Will Smith lines from all of his movies. It’s quite silly.
Overall though, I’d say there’s probably not a whole lot of depth or replayability with Divekick. It’s a fun novelty to have in your game collection, but it’s probably not going to hold anyone’s attention for very long.

This was one of my favorite games to play when I was growing up and it is still fun today. Many of the puzzles are still difficult to complete once you get up into the more difficult settings. I wish there was a way to customize the journey to start out with the more difficult level since it basically was no challenge for me for the first couple hours of play.
For me the game was worth getting just for the nostalgia of playing it but I'd still recommend the game to others that didn''t grow up with it. It's great for kids and adults alike. If you are an adult and want to try out playing the puzzles on the more difficult level but don't want to play the game to reach it the game has a "practice" function where you can change the difficulty and play any puzzle you want. Most likely after playing through the game once all the way through when I return to it in the future I'll just "practice" the puzzles I like the most and likely won't ever play a full game again.

I've just completed this game. For the first time, despite having played it as far as at least 9 years ago.
Why? Because the plot is just... let's just say it's so bad it's just irrelevant to any sane player. Don't even bother following it. The setting/vibe is kinda nice, reminds me of old-school RPG games, that's M&M alright.
However, the gameplay is absolutely fantastic. This game is over 10 years old and it still has one of the best combat systems I've ever seen. That's why most people who bother to play it never get to the ending. They don't have to, simply because they have what is best right from the beginning: combat.
How is it remarkable? I'd explain, but I think a video - which wasn't made by me - is gonna be more expressive than a thousand words uttered by me:
Oh, and if you're worried this game has aged too much for you to bother with it - no, it hasn't. Trust me.
By 2017 standards, my rating is:
-graphics: 5/10 (that has aged, indeed, although they aren't offputting)
-sounds: 7/10 (voice acting is kinda mediocre, and once you hear Leanna, you'll want to plug your ears with something... although Xana is just as obnoxious with her "edgy" commentaries)
-gameplay: 9/10 (plotwise, your choices don't make much sense, there is very little character development, but less is more, if it's polished - and it is, if you ask me)
OVERALL: 7,5/10
One con: be prepared for crashes while loading the game. I mean, some people report that this game crashes on other occassions, too, but I only had crashes while reloading savegames for any reason.
Oh, and multiplayer is dead. Which really does suck. But it's still worth it.

I'm back in Elementary School. The graphics look a bit better and it plays well on the Mac. It also gets difficult rather quickly, despite being what should be a comparatively simple puzzle game. I'm only on the second difficulty in some areas and that's pretty tough. Maybe I just never saw this, but I don't remember there being a specified number of zoombinis you had to rescue from their first home, as in there are like 400, I think, to start with, and every saved bunch decreases that number until, presumably, 0. I remember the part where you can see how many zoombinis you save and there's a limited number you travel with for each journey, but I don't remember it having an end goal of rescuing ALL the zoombinis. I seem to recall it was just an infinite number of them. So I like that change. I don't know what happens when you've rescued them all. Probably just game complete. They also - from what I can recall - added some minor animation in Zoombiniville. As you rescue more zoombinis, you can see buildings appear. More huts show up. I think they also added some brand new buildings.
I have found a bug. The crystal chamber glitches out sometimes - I can't pick up new zoombinis, although I can pick up new crystals and I can move to the next area, leaving behind the zoombinis I haven't tried to help. And even when the whole zoombini side isn't frozen, it's a pain to try and pick them up off the shelf.
I do think that the "help" option is kind of silly. I understand the "help" of repeating what the narrator says so you can look at it, since that does occasionally give you a clue for what you're doing, but for most of the puzzles it is completely useless. The rock puzzle is essentially just keep guessing until you figure it out.  The hotel puzzle makes no sense whatsoever outside of easy difficulty, and gives you the least margin for learning error of all the puzzles in the game. There are no clues that I can find, whatever the help says about "you have all the information you need to solve the puzzle".
There are a few UI issues. I don't think you can change the difficulty manually, like I remember doing when this was a CD game, which is incredibly frustrating. I like the puzzles outside of the hotel puzzle, and if I could just lower the difficulty for that one to bypass it, I would use that route. As it is, I avoid the route entirely. I also don't see a way to skip through the mini cinematic stuff, like when a zoombini gets knocked off something when you screw up and they recover. You have to wait until they finish moving and whatever interacted with them finishes talking. This is incredibly frustrating on the rock troll puzzle, where you have to sit through dialogue after nearly every single move. There's also no way to know how many tries left you have on the rock troll puzzle. I have yet to lose any of my zoombinis on that, even on the hardest difficulty, so maybe it doesn't matter, but it's one of two puzzles where you can't visually tell how many tries you have left off the bat (the other being the boat puzzle). Tecnhically that's four, but you can learn how many tries you have on the pizza puzzle pretty easily, and the same is true for the other one.
I also have no idea what was behind making a rock troll in a game for Elementary School students say "move it toots" to what essentially a blue pebble with legs of some kind. It's the only problematic dialogue I can think of in the game and it is so incredibly random.
Overall it's a nice nostalgia trip. Maybe a nice puzzle game for children. Wait till it's on sale, though.

I played this, or rather, the original game, Logical Journey of the Zoombinis, when I was very young, and I can remember absolutely adoring every moment of it. I still have the CD! I tried to install it on Windows 7 and you can only get so far before the graphics card just errors out and displays everything in inverted colours or worse.
This remake, while close to what a Zoombinis game ought to be, is not what I had hoped it would be.
While the graphics have been updated to a very high degree and the animations have been redrawn etc for all the characters, and allowed for proper resolutions higher than 640 x 480, the charm of that delightful original game has sadly been lost, and that's really what I wanted to see again. It's a shame because the graphical update is simply fantastic, and the inclusion of the ridiculously enthusiastic announcer and other voice and musical content from the original game is spot-on. However, there's just no charm to it any more.
The Zoombinis themselves move at the pace of a crippled snail - it's become a chore just to watch them move to the next place - and there's no sound for their footsteps like in the original. Zoombinis with feet would have steps, the wheels would make engine noises, springs... spring noises. When they ride the rollercoaster in the crystal caverns, they would yell out 'wahey' or 'yippee' on a successful run, and it just felt so lively and excitable.
The issue with the charm of the graphical update is that the Zoombinis themselves suffer from the TV Tropes entry "Conspicuously Light Patch". This is where, because of their drawn style, they stand out way too much from the beautifully drawn backgrounds, as the obviously only animated figures, whereas in the original, they had lighter outlines and shades to match the background, like they were meant to be there. Here they stand out so much it's almost painful to look at.
What's ACTUALLY painful to look at is when the Zoombinis walk over a patch of the background that's actually in the foreground. In the original game, at the Crystal Caverns, it was possible to see the mine-cart Zoombini travel behind the supporting struts of the track. In this release, the characters are always, without fail, on the topmost layer of the foreground. It's particularly noticeable because of the way they stand out so much from the background, too.
The worst thing about the game is the hotspots. Good luck trying to enter your name on the very first screen of the game. I couldn't until I restarted the game in windowed mode. Perhaps resolution plays into it too. I'm not sure. I just know that you will have issues clicking on certain things.
At least Mudball Wall survived. ... well, partially. As I said, the Zoombinis' walking speed cripples the pace of the game when you have to wait 20 seconds each for them to get into position. Maybe I'm being nitpicky. The puzzles are sound and, well - puzzling! Especially on the harder difficulties. It's a decent game; I do recommend Zoombinis. But I personally wouldn't recommend this specific remake. If you can find a copy of the original and install it without issues, do that instead.

Highly recommended! It’s a thoughtful, usually slow-paced ride through history and philosophy.
The story begins with you waking up. God - Elohim - greets you. Elohim tells you to explore the garden He has made for you, but warns you to not climb the tower, as this is forbidden.
Whether you listen to Elohim or not is up to you.
In the meantime, enjoy the beautiful scenery, the clever and sometimes mind-bending first-person puzzles for you to solve, the lessons on history and quotes from major figures, and getting into philosophical debates with the being in the library’s databanks.  I could have done without the sudden shift to a timed mission at one point, but it was thematically appropriate, so I can’t complain too much.
One thing that stuck with me was this. I kind of saw where the story was going early on and decided to play my character in a particular manner, but… I found a secret that I viscerally felt my character react to at one point which changed how I played the game. It gets high marks from me just for that moment alone - when a game makes you feel like that, you know you’ve got a good one.
The Talos Principle is one of those games where saying too much about it kind of spoils the experience, so, in closing: if you’re like me and dig weird arty games, this is very much worth looking into.

I was quickly frustrated when I started playing Sora. The game isn't unfair, it just does an incredibly poor job of communicating it's boss mechanics. You'll have no idea what you're supposed to be doing the first time in a fight, maybe even the second and third. Sora expects you to figure things out on your own, which can be extremely frustrating. If you're interested in playing this game, I suggest patience. If you persist, it's quite enjoyable.
Unlike other shmups, in Sora, you can't just hold down the fire button. When you attack, you are forced to stand still for a brief period, and are left vulnerable. You can cancel out of these attacks, but I found the sudden change in momentum jarring at first. It takes a while to get used to if you've played other shmups before. But, I think this unique mechanic is the only real edge Sora has.
You can equip 3 weapons before each stage. Generally, a rifle, a rocket and a melee weapon, although there are some exceptions, such as mines. The melee weapons are very high risk/reward and add a bit more variety to the combat.
I'm not a big fan of Sora's artstyle, but it isn't objectively bad. I think the hand-drawn characters have a certain cute charm to them, even if I don't really appreciate it. However, The combination of the playable character and bosses as 2-D sprites with the 3-D enemies and backgrounds certainly put me off. They don't feel like they belong in the same game, but the problem is mostly ignorable after the first few minutes of gameplay.
The music isn't as great as other soundtracks I've heard recently, but I still enjoyed it. I especially liked the track that plays in Stage 7, however ironically. The Engrish vocals are just too good for me to ignore, I smile every time.
Sora lacks an overall level of polish. The visuals look a bit off, the gameplay isn't as smooth as it should be, and there are a lot strange design choices. I have no idea how the weapon unlock system works, they seem to randomly appear after stages every now and then, regardless of how well I performed. Is it simply tied to how many stages I've played? Are there secret tasks you have to perform? I have no idea.
I don't think Sora is a brilliant example of bullet-hells, and I don't feel like I'm really in the intended audience, but I still had a lot of fun with it. It's interesting enough to set it apart from it's competition, so if you're really itching for something new, I'd recommend picking it up. There are probably better options out there to sate your bullet-hell fix, but I wouldn't ignore Sora entirely.

Following the success of Serious Sam 3 Croatian developers Croteam toyed with the idea of expanding on the shoot on sight style of gameplay by mixing in puzzle elements. Penned initially as a tech demo for the Serious Engine 4, Croteam saw potential in their newly developed puzzle format and eventually went on to spearhead the release of their new engine with The Talos Principle.
Given the first-person puzzle genre had been dominated by Valve heavyweight Portal, The Talos Principle stands up well providing the player with with a myriad of surprisingly challenging puzzles, none of which are frustrating in the slightest. Never does the game cheat you with artificial difficulty and cheap filler material puzzles. The controls feel almost exactly the same as the Serious Sam series and makes for a comfortable gaming experience.
The story is centered heavily on the philosophy of human life, challenging what it means to be a human, free will and the human psyche. You awaken in a garden and are guided by the voice of Elohim, creator of the worlds who tells you that your purpose is to seek sigils through solving puzzles and attain eternal life. Although not put so bluntly the player is left to draw their own conclusion about what is going on. Through the use of in-game text files and audio logs found on computer terminals scattered across the worlds, you begin to learn about your surroundings and about who you are in this world, deciphering information given by others with their own unique motivations, desires and purposes. The ultimatum towards the latter part of the game really challenges your mind, forcing you to decide whether to disobey the word of Elohim and ascend the mysterious tower or giving into the temptation of eternal life.
The game's graphics are as equal a selling point as its gripping story and challenging puzzles. The visuals are quite simply incredible, complimented by its beautiful renditions of ancient Greek, Egyptian and Medievil setpieces. Damjan Mravunac heads up the soundtrack with peaceful melodic music which fits perfectly to the given level and even some times it is somewhat reminiscent of binaural beats. Inspired by minimalism, the music is also used to convey the deeper, darker undertones of the game whilst remaining soft to the ear. Each new song fitting perfectly with the level design and somehow tickling that unconscious desire to learn more about your true purpose, a true footnote to the somewhat melancholic undertone of the game.
This game to me really is a masterpiece. Acting as a window to your subconscious, serving as a perfect satisfaction for the infeasable human desire, the lifelong yearning of discovering why you are really here on this earth. Something we may never discover, so I leave you with a quote. 'How do you solve a problem that extends beyond your own lifespan?'.

Borderland is truly one of the most boring, bland, laziest, and uninspired AAA games in recent history. It is incredibly tedious and offers little challenge, even smaller reward, and almost no satisfaction from accomplishment. Its characters manage to be less than one-dimensional and are forgotten as soon as they are met. Not to mention that the colour palette comprises of little more than three hues; dull, monotonous, and ugly.
Basic expectations are not met when it comes to Borderlands, for example, character's mouths do not always move when they talk. Such a basic part of animation that has been a staple of gaming for decades, yet a game from 2009 can't bring itself to bother with something so trivial. Time and time again you will find yourself stuck on a piece of scenery, slightly raised higher off the ground than the rest of the mess strewn across Borderland's semi-expansive world, which gives it an excuse to snag a corner of your clothing, keeping you in place for a few short seconds. If you're lucky and want to take a shortcut you might even get stuck between a boulder and a cliff face or a fence and a post with no means of escape, all due to incompetent design. Hooray.
There will be times when you become so confused as to where you are that you'll travel in circles as everything and everywhere blends into one giant continuous blurry blob of colour before realising that, without the waypoint guiding you along, you have exactly no idea how you even got here in the first place. Never mind the fact that Borderlands absolutely loves reverting your video settings and keybindings once every few months, regardless of syncing them to Steam, just to keep you on your toes.
By the time any exciting variation comes along, in the form of scenery and enemies, it's almost over. One final boss battle that can be accurately summed up as throwing pebbles at a beached whale for 20 minutes until it explodes and you're done. Congratulations, you've just beaten the saddest excuse for a game in the 21st century. Now go do it again. Lovely.

Dungeonland is a typical 3-man dungeon crawler where players traverse one dungeon per game. The dungeon itself is always randomly generated and allows for a unique experience every time you play. The twist is that the 4th player plays as the "Dungeon Maestro" whose goal is to stop the other three players from completing the dungeon by spawning mobs and towers while also playing as mobs, elite mobs, and the final boss. The game itself is incredibly challenging and clearly built with 4 player cooperative play in mind. There are other formats to play with fewer friends and an AI Dungeon Maestro, but the game really shines when you have four people playing.
Honestly worth the $4 and honestly worth the almost 3k hours spent having it open.

Ah Lovecraft mods. No matter what game they managed to slither into they always makes for interesting stories. This is one such story.
The planet I ended up with was a desert with a large number of mountains and a huge ♥♥♥♥ing ocean. So I go the rich explorer and give myself a little boost in wood and cloth. I crash land into a tundra. There are pockets of rabbits and squirrels, along with some Elephants. So I build a little♥♥♥♥♥♥shack and get to work building into a nearby mountain. And after a few days my colonist (Wendy) suddenly runs off. I see her go towards this spooky lookin' monolith. She stands there for a second and then goes back to her room. She then makes an Occult Grimoir and takes a huge mood debuff. This is where things take a fun turn. I build into another mountain and mine out a giant church and occult research room. I get it all floored and lighted up and set to work. While researching weird symbols Wendy turns into a Cultist. Nice. She then names her cult the Esoteric Order of Dagon...fitting. I craft her up some robes and a Cthulhu mask. I then end up making an altar and sacrificing some rabbits for power. Then I get the message, two people join me in obsession of joining my cult... alrighty. I craft them up some robes and get them some beds in already mined out rooms.
Now we skip to season later. I've held off countless raids from the local tribes and even some Deep Ones. Wendy is now head cultist and everyone has a good life. My mountain base is now a fortress equipped with untold eldritch horrors trapped within the stone. I am now fairly well equipped with some guns and a many melee weapons. My colony is now 7 strong and has no signs of stopping. Sermons are held for Great Cthulhu and father Dagon. But life is kinda boring as while the Lovecraft storyteller can be brutal it doesn't really give you a ton of events to work with. So I gather my cultists find a nearby coastal village. So I caravan up and gather my most loyal followers and set to work. We arrive to what can only be described as a shanty town. I draw a rune and wait. Now when the first thing you research on, on the forbidden research table is figuring out what all those ♥♥♥♥ing symbols are. And when done researching you can then make a rune that attracts Deep Ones. They will defend the rune with their life until they are all dead. The towns people put up a fairly good fight and even managed to take down a Greater Deep One. But that was all for naught as they were then slaughtered by the eldritch tide. Mopping up the Deep Ones was easy for me as Harpoon-guns work wonders against them. I then take all the coastal towns♥♥♥♥♥♥and ♥♥♥♥ back off to my colony. A great first raid, and there were still so many more to come. And while raiding coastal towns was fun for a little bit I got bored, but it was mostly because I killed all the coastal towns in my area. But something did come my way as one of the local tribes tried raiding me again, but this time...with an army. My guard of Deep Ones could only hold off the tide for so long before they got overwhelmed. My turrets did most of the killing, along with the more...unstable part of my colony. But they did♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, they killed the co-head cultist and Wendy's lover. Wendy fell into a deep depression and I had to straitjacket her so she wouldn't go off the rails and murder people. This lasted for some time, but Wendy did eventually get out of her stopper and started leading sermons and daily sacrifices once more. But she was out for revenge and as it turns out the tribe responsible for killing Wendy's lover was also the biggest tribe in the world. And thus began the war. It was easy at first as my tide of Deep Ones did most of the work for me, but the farther I pushed into their territory the harder the raids would get...and the wounded count would also get higher. Lucky was I that my underground farms has reaped a bountiful harvest this season and I had a plenty herbal medicine in stock. It did get tricky when a plague of insanity swept through my lands and rendered most of my colony null. It wasn't until Wendy herself died in battle that I was on a real disadvantage. She was there the longest and was friends with most people there. She also had some REALLY good stats. She did die fighting however. Taking many tribal people on her way out. I built her a special place of rest, right beside her lover.
Fay the new Head Cultist took over and boy was she good with her social stats (it was the main reason I picked her). She was a non-violent soul however and would never engage in combat. This wasn't a huge problem, but I like a social leader more than one with a huge bloodlust. Our numbers grew greatly as we went from a mere 7 people to now 12, all of them cultists. I also had a pack of 4 people, all of them had the traits of, cannibal, psychopath (I forget what it's called correct me if I'm wrong), and bloodlust. I had them wear black goat heads and differing robes. I called them the Spawn of Dagon and they wrecked♥♥♥♥♥ All except for one used melee and the one who didn't was their leader. His name was Sven and he was a ♥♥♥♥ing monster in both ranged and melee. He also liked getting hurt so...that was a plus...I guess. But I used the Spawn for more "covert" operations. They did win me the war when we assailed their fortress of♥♥♥♥♥♥and mud. Well it was properly built for an NPC village, but the faction leader was there and blah blah blah. The final battle was to begin.
The best way to describe the fortress is a wooden castle. But that's...slightly inaccurate. I began the siege with drawing 5 runes outside the "walls". The first wave of Deep Ones got ♥♥♥♥ing obliterated. I didn't really anticipate the number of arrows they were packing...the short answer is...too many. As the waves of eldritch horrors crashed upon their walls my cultists waited for the right time to charge in. The Spawn of Dagon however took a differing route. They dug into the mountain for a flanking assault. We did get the jump on a few archers held up inside a little shack. And with that we gained a small, but valuable foothold within the fortress. And with that I constructed not 1, not 2, but 7 runes. The tide of Deep Ones was spooky, but it would be worth it as Deep Ones now streamed into the fortress taking out many archers and guards inside their humble abode. And with the storm gate open, but overflowing. The Deep Ones did end up dying, but the damage they caused was massive to the point where I just sent my army to deal with the rest. And with most the damage done I took who I could prisoner including the faction leader. And while the war was won a larger threat came to my colony and destroyed it. An avatar of great Cthulhu came in the night and just ♥♥♥♥ing ganked my colony to an early grave. And with that The Chosen were mushed into the dirt.
And thus ends our tale. I will be back with more tales in the future my friends, but for now. I bid you goodbye.

This is a really nice game.
Is it worth full price? I would say yes.
Your goal is to beat the waves that come at you by using your attack. There are different classes, and the attack is different for each one. There is only 1 attack per class, but each class has abililities and perks that can modify the class specific attack, which is very nice indeed. For instance, as a pyro, the base attack is a ball of fire, but as you level up you can improve the chance of instead of firing a ball of fire, you fire a meteor, or even fire the base ball of fire in multiple directions. There's all sort of crazy things you can do really.
As you beat waves, you go trough different areas. Those areas are different each time you play (they are somewhat randomly generated), and different areas have different traps and enemies. What i mean by "somewhat randomly generated" is that for instance the size of the area, the type of the enemies, and the type of traps you can expect in one area it's always the same, but they are placed in different locations each time, and some instances may or may not have some traps. That makes each play-trough unique, and you may have to adopt slightly different strategies each time.
Killing enemies gives you experience, which you use to level up. When you level up you are given points that you can spend on improving your stats. There are 4 stats in the game, those being Damage, Attack Speed, Armor and Health. Also, you receive points to improve/unlock abilities or the chances of your base attack do something different. It's also a rogue-like, in the sense that if you die on one wave, you're done and you have to start from the Wave 1 of the act all over again. Though, unless you're playing on Hardcore, you keep you character, its levels, points, abilities etc.. Part of the point of the game is level up so you're stronger the next time you play.
The game also features dungeons, that appear on the areas of the game. The dungeons sometimes are harder to beat than the normal waves, but they give you an item if you beat the dungeon, so it's more often than not worth the risk. Those special items, called "relics" are also given to you each time you beat an area, and they really improve you experience with the game. Those items do all sort of crazy things. Some give you base attack a chance of freezing/poison enemies, others give you homing missiles that are around you that fire automatically and help you killing the enemies, others "simply" improve your base stats etc... I say "simply" because even though "improve you base stats" may sound something boring, it can REALLY help you out making areas easier. These items are also wiped from you if you die, so you have to collect new items again each time you play. The game seems to have a finite number of these relics, but there's a large number of them and the items you find are also randomly generated.
As you kill enemies they drop gold, that you can spend on the store on thing like health potions, damage boost potions etc. Those boosts are also only valid for that specific play-trough, they reset if you die, as well as all the gold you happen to find. The game has also a rare currency, the crystals. These crystals are really hard to find, as far as i know there's only 2 ways to get them: crystal chests (chests that need a crystal key to be opened) or bosses that sometimes drop a few of them, very rare to happen though. With crystals you can buy cosmetic stuff, the possibility of have a skeleton pet the next time you play (that actually helps you fight the enemies), the possibility of starting with a relic on your next playtrough, crystal keys. You might be like "Hang on a minute..you say you can get crystals from crystal chests, but you have to spend crystals on crystal keys to open them, what?" I hadn't played any of the Might & Magic games prior to playing Dark Messiah and, in fact, had never heard about it until I came across a picture of Xana somewhere on the internet and, fueled by my short-sighted, knuckle-dragging masculine urges, wanted to find out where she was from. I found out about Dark Messiah, played the demo, and upon completing it, immediately wanted to buy it.
The first thing that I, as pretty much everyone else, will praise the game for is it's combat. The combat system is simple enough, but incredibly fine-tuned and responsive so that you feel like you have complete control over how you fight. Because of this, deaths rarely feel like they're anything but your own fault. Whether you didn't block on time or enough, didn't keep your distance, or missed the key window to unleash your power attack, most of the time I found that I died because of either poor decisions in the midst of a fight or my own lack of skill. That aside, the combat is incredibly satisfying and I never found myself bored or aggravated save for a few choice moments, which I'll go over further down.
I found the story to be fairly predictable, but engaging enough that you at least are motivated to see what happens next. The characters don't have much depth to them, save for your companion, Xana, who provides a coquettish and flirty personality that makes your long treks through spider-infested tunnels and orc camps feel more worthwhile. That's because, practically from the moment you meet her, she's quite clearly obsessed with your character, often going out of her way to tease or flatter him. She also will provide a few tips and try to help throughout the game, and while some of them may seem obvious, she can sometimes point out something that you totally overlook on your own. Without spoiling anything, the reason she acts in such a way becomes more clear later in the game. What's also great about her is that she's an incorporeal companion, so you don't have to worry about her getting in the way during gameplay.
The only point that I found truly frustrating or difficult about the game is a certain enemy that you begin to encounter later on in the game, in which a healthy dose of artificial difficulty combined with every fight involving no less than at least 3 of the little ♥♥♥♥♥ makes you start to dread hearing their raspy, heavy breathing. The orcs, which you fight for the majority of the second act of the game, can become rather annoying as well with repetitive dialogue and the fact that where they are found, they seem to be absolutely everywhere, so that you rarely get any time to stop and take a breather. Spiders and Zombies don't provide much of a challenge, but for God's sake ALWAYS KEEP AT LEAST ONE ANTIDOTE IN YOUR INVENTORY. I made the mistake of using my last antidote to cure my poison before I cleared the spider's tunnels and found myself poisoned for at least 2 hours straight, as I was unable to find another antidote for some time. Also, invest in your poison resistance skill very early on. It'll save you much headache later down the line.
All in all, Dark Messiah's shining example of First Person Melee Combat done right is easily it's primary strength, followed closely by the most charming companion character I've found in a game. The solid RPG mechanics backing up the gameplay allow for you to pick and choose how to go about combat, also providing some strong reply value. Some enemies can become frustrating, but with perseverence and patience, it's really not that bad. I'll likely find myself coming back for another playthrough later on.

Bullet hells are typically fairly formulaic in fashion, mostly being based around pure dodging in a vertically-oriented screen space with focused movement, small hitboxes allowing for grazing and oftentimes you have your standard bullet-cancelling scoring tricks. Orange Juice had subverted most of these tropes in Suguri, and continue to polish their style of danmaku gameplay in the sequel Sora.
The main nuance to this series is that instead of the standard focused movement, you can perform a dash that sends you flying quickly across the screen. This dash allows you to phase through bullets and standard lasers, but you are still susceptible to physical obstacles such as rockets, dashing also builds up your heat gauge which makes you take even more damage (up to 3 times more damage at 300%). This along with the dashing being used to cancel out shot inputs makes most of the depth in this game, as fighting becomes a visceral mix of shooting and dashing around enemy bullets and rockets, as you try to destroy everything as fast as possible. The potential of these mechanics are realized as each boss plays differently and demand different skills and understanding of mechanics from the player. For example, Tsih can temporarily go invisible meaning that you cannot lock-on to them during this time and you will have to use melee attacks against them, whereas Sham surrounds you with smaller swarming enemies which require switching your lock-on frequently.
Although you can phase through most projectiles, this game is in no way easy. If you are new or relatively new to the series like I was when starting this game, it will take you a while to get used to the fast pace of enemy attacks and the sheer density of projectiles at certain points. The game has quite a steep learning curve that will challenge those experienced with bullet hells along with a grading system at the end of each stage which makes the act of playing Sora feel rewarding and addictive.
Like its predecessor, Sora oftentimes feels like a blend between a fighting game and a shmup, especially due to the addition of swords and other melee weapons that you can use. The scoring system capitalises on this, as it rewards players who can play aggressively and take out hordes of enemies swiftly without taking damage. The addictive mechanics are topped off with an improved visual presentation from Suguri and a great trance-style soundtrack that succeeds in giving each boss a lasting impression.
All in all, Sora feels like an ideal sequel to suguri, as it further expands on the innovations made by suguri with new weapons, abilities, boss fights and certain balance changes. If you are at all a fan of the doujin circle Orange_Juice you would be doing yourself a great disservice by missing out on Sora.

I honestly never would have thought this game would come to steam.
This game, Sora, is the sequel to the game Suguri, which was published by Rockin' Android. You are Sora, an enhanced, basically mechanized superhuman fighting in a neverending war that seems to encompass all of Earth, and your goal is to make people stop fighting... by shooting rockets into their faces. Nobody said peacekeeping was easy!
Anyway, this is actually the second time the game has been localized. The first time was done by--I guess you can call them a person--called OmegaTH, who, bluntly speaking, screwed the pooch in localizing it. Horrific translations, Pointless name changes, terrible bugs, missing music I believe, game breaking DRM, the improper use of the word "Reploid" were just a few of the things that you could have expected from that localization.
It seemed the game was doomed to be stuck in a kind of limbo where it was basically as good as never released in the US.
At least until Fruitbat factory came outta nowhere and decided through the darkest of magic rituals to obtain the license to the game and give it the release it deserved.
The game has none of the aforementioned problems of the previous localization, integrates with the steam overlay without any flaws, seems to control flawlessly (I've read it "feels" off compared to the Japanese version, though I cannot confirm that), and just exudes a lot of the love and care put into it to make it a fine release. The only minor flaw I could think of is some slowdown during the more intense bossfights, though there are options to remove blur effects and the likes to mitigate it. Aside from that the game is as good as it can get.
They did the impossible
and should have the highest praise from everyone for just going where I would figure no one else would try to do.
Anyway, it's an awesome game that anyone who is a fan of great shmups,  good video game music, or just anyone looking for a fun challenge, should pick up.

You are Sora, a human who has been modified to fly and fight and is given a blaster, bazooka, and energy sword at the start of the mission but will get some as you progress *or die*. The people on earth have been fighting with each other for whatever reason. So basically you are a war asset and other things which I won't mention due to spoilers.
Gameplay
--------------
The game is very very challenging. It's not as difficult as Suguri (The first game, Sora is the Prequel) but still not that easy. Mission 1 took me 1 try, Mission 2 took me 2 tries but Mission 3... Took me 15 and the scale gets higher until I reached Mission 5 Where I beat it on my first but the rest soon took longer to finish. So yeah, not too easy and not too difficult but for most I think they'd say its hard. Enough about difficulty, tiem for the gametype, It's a Bullet-Hell. But instead of moving around the energy bullets you can pass through them if you were to Use your "Dash" ability. However, you cannot dash through live ammunition (Eg. Missiles) and as you dash, you gain Heat. Heat can reach up to 300% and that would mean if you were to get hit... You will take much more damage. Heat would take about 8 seconds to settle *But you need to keep dodging too* so it's really bad if you are careless.In each mission, there are enemies which pop up throughout the mission (henchmen?), followed by a mid-stage boss which is there to prepare you for the true boss and at the end, the actual boss with a name and health bar. As I said before, You unlock even more weapons as you progress so you can ditch your sword for an even bigger sword *After dying 100 Times* I really like arcade games so this was a treat for me. If you don't like Bullet-hell games then you should just ignore this game.
Art
-----
Sora is such a freakin adorable character <3 (and some others too but no one can beat Sora imo)
The character sprites are really well done and pretty (Atleast to my taste). The level design is like it's from a ps2 era game so nothing special. The missiles and lasers you blast out (and or shot at you) are also well animated which givest he game more life.
That's about the only thing I can think to describe this nice and wonderful game. I hope they make a 3rd Installment to the story.
My Overall score for Sora: 8.5/10 considering the price and maybe because I'm biased.

The Talos Principle's visuals and music are both very pleasant and relaxing, and several of its puzzles are nice brain-teasing exercises I enjoyed. The lore/story is largely conveyed by text files you read on in-game computer screens. They often seem irrelevant, though I figure some tie into the overarching storyline at some point. The only spoken dialog comes in the form of pretentious verbage from a seemingly self-deified figure. You play as a robot, and the game does not bother to conceal this fact. What twists and turns the story might take did intrigue me and fuel my efforts to press forward for as long as I could muster the resolve to go on, despite dissatisfaction with the game.
You will solve puzzles in first person, a la Portal, Quantum Conundrum, and The Turing Test. Movable technology jamming devices, hexahedrons (boxes/cubes), light-redirecting poles, keys for doors, and Tetris-shaped blocks you collect will all be used in solving puzzles. The game is entirely puzzles, which I loved about the aforementioned games; especially Portal and The Turing Test. Granted, the God-wannabe creator in this game did not appeal to me at all when compared to GLaDOS, the AI on The Turing Test, or John DeLancey on Quantum Conundrum, and he didn't say anything I found interesting or entertaining on any level.
On the puzzle topic, however, light-redirecting puzzles, despite having no problems with such puzzles in Ocarina of Time, Beyond Good & Evil, and so many other games out there, were more "brain-agitators" than brain teasers. I stumbled my way out of a few, but eventually, despite being fairly early in the game, these refraction puzzles became far too much for me. I spent 20 minutes on the last such one, wandering from section to section, applying logic to which refractory device was mandatory and could not be moved or repositioned, and simply could not come up with even a theoretical solution to try.
I could have used a walkthrough for the last one that stumped me, but each of these light refracting puzzles were often comparatively as messy as the last. This may not be as big an issue for some players. A very likely culprit for my dilemma could be ADD (attention deficit disorder), as I suffer from this and have great difficulty paying attention to simultaneous functioning parts in a game that are split apart. It's the reason RTS games often kick my butt (managing different units and buildings on opposite sides of a map at the same time), and Infinifactory, another puzzle game, whooped me because I had to make machines crank out parts on different sides in different directons out of synch, turning them to line up in synch further down the line while other factors are also at play. If you're easily able to pay attention to multiple "moving parts" in different areas at the same time in a game, then this might not be a problem for you, but for me, a massive part of the game became an exercise in futility and aggravation.
One issue is also that there are stars hidden in each area. A few seem very poorly hidden, while others are nearly impossible to find without a walkthrough (according to other players who have posted in the forums who claim to be experienced at the game (you can look through the forums by searching about the stars). These stars, apparently give you different endings to the game. Unless you're intending on using a walkthrough or are a deranged optimist who doesn't listen to people who have beaten the game and found the stars who testify to the difficulty in getting these stars without a guide, this means you will miss out on different endings if you can't find these often well-hidden stars. The light-refracting puzzles were that much more aggravating for me just knowing that I would undoubtedly be missing out on endings as well, serving as an ever-present nagging under-mining to any desire to complete the game.
Between the refractory puzzles being beyond my attention-based faculties and the knowledge of the hidden stars preventing me from getting to see all the endings if I
manage to limp my way through the game despite my aggravation and despair, I simply could not muster the willpower to play any further than I did, despite taking a few breaks to try and let my irritation subside.

Plays pretty similar to its predecessor, Suguri, being that you move horizontally and use your dash to phase through energy based attacks, while shooting enemies. So gameplay wise, if you enjoyed Suguri you'll definitely like Sora, especially with the latter's refinements over the original. For example, dash spamming has been nerfed in general--initiating a dash will boost your Heat by about 30%, thus making it more risky to turn on a dime. You also gain Heat from attack cancelling, making that riskier as well. The difficulty curve also feels less abrupt than in Suguri (I still have PTSD from that Kae fight), and scales more linearly. Furthermore, the weapons have been rebalanced making most of the worse weapons from Suguri more viable.
In terms of length, it took me around 9 hours or so to beat story mode (stages 1-7) on easy, so there's quite a bit of content, along with the fantastic OST. Even if you're not so good at these games like I am, you should be able to progress atleast on easy.

Borderland is truly one of the most boring, bland, laziest, and uninspired AAA games in recent history. It is incredibly tedious and offers little challenge, even smaller reward, and almost no satisfaction from accomplishment. Its characters manage to be less than one-dimensional and are forgotten as soon as they are met. Not to mention that the colour palette comprises of little more than three hues; dull, monotonous, and ugly.
Basic expectations are not met when it comes to Borderlands, for example, character's mouths do not always move when they talk. Such a basic part of animation that has been a staple of gaming for decades, yet a game from 2009 can't bring itself to bother with something so trivial. Time and time again you will find yourself stuck on a piece of scenery, slightly raised higher off the ground than the rest of the mess strewn across Borderland's semi-expansive world, which gives it an excuse to snag a corner of your clothing, keeping you in place for a few short seconds. If you're lucky and want to take a shortcut you might even get stuck between a boulder and a cliff face or a fence and a post with no means of escape, all due to incompetent design. Hooray.
There will be times when you become so confused as to where you are that you'll travel in circles as everything and everywhere blends into one giant continuous blurry blob of colour before realising that, without the waypoint guiding you along, you have exactly no idea how you even got here in the first place. Never mind the fact that Borderlands absolutely loves reverting your video settings and keybindings once every few months, regardless of syncing them to Steam, just to keep you on your toes.
By the time any exciting variation comes along, in the form of scenery and enemies, it's almost over. One final boss battle that can be accurately summed up as throwing pebbles at a beached whale for 20 minutes until it explodes and you're done. Congratulations, you've just beaten the saddest excuse for a game in the 21st century. Now go do it again. Lovely.

Allow me to tell you a grand tale, a tale of three colonists that made a thriving colony only to be ruined by malaria. I was proud of this little thriving community I had created, I had put my mainbase in the mountains surrounded by limestone and other non flammable materials and all was well the colony. I had created a thriving economy, with my three main colonists Lord, Engie and Hunter who all were very happy off. I took in about 5 other settlers and all was peaceful with the colony other than the occasional raid or siege which was dealt with brutality.
I had eventually harvested 5000 food with several indoor farms inside the base, life was great, medicine to last, animals breeding, a marriage even happened, and also food glorious food. Then disaster struck, Malaria, causing three of my colonists to die, one of them whom had a wife.I built sarcophgas' to honor the dead, but the pain was too much for my settlers and they began to wander aimlessly and die...
There was thing I had not tried yet and I had heard the rumors (via google) to open the forboding places... At first all was fine cryo tubes filled with people, I thought SLAVES for the GRAND EMPIRE..... Unfortunately one survived and she was integrated into our society. Luckily though I had another 5 cryo tubes who I managed to save all except 1... Yet that one was the ringleader for all of the Cryotube inhabitants and none of them wanted to stay with the EMPIRE... So I let them go after treating them... But then the widowed wife wander aimlessly depressed at the amount of death at the colony, and my great construction worker soon followed in suit... Not a problem right? Wrong... Just then the pirates who I have defended against on numerous occasions showed up and completely raided my camp and kidnapped my own slave.... Only one person remained... The pacifist, who had been watching in horror as his friends were blown to bits shot to death and kidnapped away. He went mad.... attacking my pet grizzly bears who even after he passed out after blood loss still rescued my pacifist gone mad... As he laid in bed, bleeding he remembered those that passed and their stories... Butler and his wild attempt at taming the muffalo, Engie and her wondrous engineering feats, Lumi and Lorde with their beautiful home and cooking, Hunter the precision shot able to gun down any bandit from a great distance away, Nichloes the scientist who had just finished researching medicine, and finally as he laid on the bed with his final breaths... Tiger the pacifist healer, his doctoring skills saved a numerous of colonists, but not those from malaria...
Who will carry the lives of these colonists? As you can see I am but a mere story teller... But one person did manage to survive the raid, a prisoner by the name of dweeb who had became friends with the colonists but would not join them... He will carry on the story, those of the Glitorians that were far from home... Yet built a lasting remembrance..

WARNING: I sum up a lot of Telltale games in this. If you want the sum just skip to the end. (Pardon grammer and spelling. I spend my days worrying about those writing stories at work, so I don't really fancy copy editing myself at home.)
I eagerly await the next episode. I will explain why in a break down of my experience with Telltale games.
I played a little Sam & Max and honestly just found them boring and lacking in any actual humor.
I really got introduced to them when they took the reins of Monkey Island. I was a long time fan of the series and have many child hood memories of playing The Curse of Monkey Island and very fond memories of Escape from Monkey Island. Escape was the first game I ever pulled an all-nighter to play. So when they took on the franchise I was very worried. Unfortunately Tales of Monkey Island was kind of a disappointment in my book. It seemed fake, forced and missed the mark on the charm of the former games. Left me with a sour tast for Telltale games.
When The Walking Dead game came out I was very slow on the draw and didn't get around to playing the first season until well after its release. When I finally  got around to it I was kicking myself. They did a good job of creating characters ; fictional characters you cared about. A success, because if you don't care then fiction is just a bunch of arbitrary crap.
Now to Game of Throne. In only the first episode I was stressed out and honestly just plain bored at some points. Alot of talking heads just chatting about politics. Thats fine in the show because you can just sit back and relax while watching it, you don't have to constantly be on edge in case a character suddenly wants your input on bargaining lumber.
Now... Borderlands.
I had fun. I was kind of confused at first honestly. Am I having fun with a franchise I stopped care about after beating the first game? I was having fun being part of this cast. I enjoy their character building conversations and throwing in my own spin on it when prompted. I love the Walking Dead fanchise, love Game of Throne, Monkey Island is my childhood, but a franchise I roll my eyes at every time I see another samey game release on steam. Thats the one I can't wait to see more of? It truely is a first would problem, having such conflicting emotions.
It's not stressful like The Walking Dead or Game of Thrones games. They just throw situations at you and you respond without having to worry about changing the course of Westeros history or whether you have enough cheese and crackers to feed all the zombie apocalypse survivors.

Though I already had a preexisting respect for Tell Tale Games due to their contributions of the revival of the Point & Click genre with Sam & Max, plus what little but exceptional experience I had with The Walking Dead Episode 1, I still couldn't help but be somewhat skeptical as to how an intriguing yet fully interactive story could be written about a series that, for the most part, relies almost COMPLETELY on the run and gun action gameplay to progress you further through the story...
Needless to say, I've been completely BLOWN AWAY.
Everything from the cinematography of the scenes, the structure of the story, the quirky and all suprisingly unique characters, to the iconic voices of Patrick Warburton, Nolan North, and Troy Baker turn the usually intense action packed world of Pandora into a quirky, edge of your seat, comical, action adventure heist story gone wrong, and all of that is just in the first Episode. Tales from The Borderlands is living evidence, just as Wolf Among Us is, that Tell Tale more than almost any other company in the industry have some of the best and most talented story writers, all capable of creating some of the most original characters in gaming, yet also capable of taking some of the best and most critcally acclaimed stories of our time and putting their own spin to them with equal greatness.
If you were to set the game to play on a certain set of player choices and remove all the UI elements from the dialogue choices and the Quick Time Events, I would feel as though I were watching a major motion picture adaption of the Borderlands franchise, and I'd gladly pay money to see it. Somebody hire these people to write some movies, dammit.

So, looking at the screenshots on display, this game looks, being completely honest, like SEGA's attempt at a spin-off crossed with a fanservice. The ideas of transforming into aeroplanes and boats, back into cars are all too good to be true, and levels that change every lap?! Oh my jeebus, shoot me down and call me Valve, and announce Half-Life3! It's just too good to be true, but it is very true.
Having played most every Sonic game you can think of (going all the way back to Sonic on the Genesis platform) SEGA definitely had its highs and its lows, but this... this is possibly the best Sonic game in the more recent years, not to mention Kart Racing, AND IT'S A PLATFORMER! Who knew a Platformer could be this good?
But to the actual game instead of the history then...
The mechanics are so fluent, there is very little to want (it would be cool if you would like enter slow-motion and then speed up once the transformation is done though :P) and they all offer a whole new game (literally). If you're strictly good at cars, well, you won't get very far with higher AIs. Aeroplanes and cars couldn't more different, instead of having two controls, (left and right) you now have this whole new demension of up and down and everything imbetween, which means that drifting just got over 9000x more difficult. Don't even get me started on boats (literally, they're so difficult to use!) Driving the boats in this game... what can I say, makes drifting in the air seem like cake. The controls can't even be explained, you just have to buy to find out what I mean.
The changing level dynamics of this game are some of the most reinvigorating aspects of any game I've played to date, and there's a good phew of them to play, as well! First lap, you may start with cars, but you may end up entirely on an aquatic level flopping all over the place. So for the first time you play any map, even after that to some extent, it's a new map every time, so if you went left at that one bend, I doubt you'll be able to do that again (on some maps, there are exceptions). And some maps are completely elitist skilled-based. Like, your first 20 times, you won't be able to come in qualifying positions.
All in all, this is the kind of game that with it's cartoonyness (if that's a word... well NOW IT IS!) and it's zealous mechanics, really does restore hope in a gaming community that is majoritively starting to become dark and gloomy. This is the kind of game that you sit down, have fun and♥♥♥♥♥♥around on for hour and hours, Hell I've only had the game for a few days, and I have this much to say about it! I would love to see some better server systems though, as lag-outs and DxCs happen all far too often.
If you want anything more, like a number rating; ⓴/⓴
Anything more? Oh come on, please, to put it bluntly, if you don't get this game, you're missing out on the Amnesia of Scary games, the Skyrim of Free-roam, the Kingdom Hearts of Stories, the Disney of Tales, the Dragon Ball Z of action, the Legend of Zelda of Experiences, the Mario of 8-bit, the Minecraft of creativity, the GMOD of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥around... PixelJunk Eden is one of those 'Arty" 'Indie' games, the kind you can't seem to describe. You play this little figure with floppy ears on its nose, hoping from one plant to plant in a giant garden, smashing into these drifting spores to create more plants, gathering amoebas to help stave off the timer while you look for five 'Spectras' in each garden. Its not a profound premise, but at least original.
Let's say it right now, this is a pretty game. When you find a rhythm you'll fall into a zen mode watching your character zip around on a dynamic and pleasing back drop, charmed by the smooth animations of the blossoming plants swaying slowly in an unfelt wind. Its accompanied by a minimalist electronic soundtrack done by graphic designer 'Baiyon'; I never heard of him either nor would I say his music is that memorable. But the rest of the design team must of been proud enough too give him top billing. But I think that is my biggest problem with the game.
Its too self indulgent...
Because of PixelJunk Eden's engrossing and viberate art style, actually playing the game can be very troublesome, very often, not to mention slow. The controls require careful study to ensure you've executed a jump successful, else you being falling a ways and starting you long climb again. The game will let you recover yourself, but the penalty too do so makes it seldom worthwhile. And if you fall all the way to the bottom of the garden, you come to understand how easy it is to get lost in a garden (but the menu is the worst for this, of all things), The game is also very unforgiving with its timer, too many times I'm desperately seeking out a batch of amoebas to spare my life; and yet the scant enemies in the game are a total pushover, requiring an intention bump to split them up and second strike to finish most of them. All in all it almost feels like the gameplay mechanics were an afterthought.
Oddly this game kindly reminds me alot of the Diddy Kong Racing remake for the Nintendo DS back in 2007. That otherwise stirling game was ruined by its♥♥♥♥♥♥poor impletation of the DS controls as much as PixelJunk Eden was hurt by its ruling design aesthetic. Perhaps if the games had a slightly less intrusive style I could come to grips with its gameplay. But like many other indie Magnum opus' out there, PixelJunk Eden is just too 'Arty' for its own good.

What I hate about the game?
If I had to critticize this game on anything its probably on just the way the mechanics are
There are a lot of dumb features in the game that accomplish nothing but raise an eyebrow.
The weapon design trifecta is incredibly arbitrary and at some points very two faced
So the design is supposed to be that you can:
Dash < Beam Attacks
Dodge or Destroy < Missile Projectiles
And your melee is just a melee
This annoys me on so many levels.
The training stage establishes this idea where the level/power of your beam attack holds a vital role in either over-riding other attacks or simply destroying their projectiles
Not only is it incredibly aggrevating trying to attack missiles with beam attacks to destroy their projects but you cannot target them. Which makes destroying projectiles guessing games at best.
Beam attacks are stupidly random, where certain beam attacks cannot be dashed past, but then they teach you you're supposed to dash vs beam attacks? Why even...?
Melee weapons are incredibly useless, their damage is laughable at best and only promote the idea of staying long range and keeping the highest priority to dodge stuff.
There's no reward for being risky with a melee weapon, and in various instances beam weapons seem to easily outdps projectile and melee attacks.
There are no base attack values or any form of attack damage calculations or functions which teach you in the game and makes the training stages tips about knowing the damage you inflict with weapons completely negligible
Beam attacks have a very... VERY slow rate of fire and usually promote animation cancelling as a way of life, instead of a quirky reward for being quick on controls.
Rocket Launchers are the same thing, however you're also inclined to suffer through their poor projectile speed which is so lazy any idea of even thinking their a threat to dodge is a joke. It makes the idea of simply destroying the projectiles as a strategy of minimizing threat a smart idea, but without any form of control/targetting onto missiles, the idea is hastily culled.
The last thing I want to mention is the boss design. They're all the same
They all have this rather lazy blink around, "ha you cant target me! wait until my boring invicibility frame has ended while I charge my ultimate attack!?!"
And well... it's pretty dull XD
Though it doesn't really impede on the game THAT much... the strategies used to fight bosses only differ around the idea of survivability which is one thing I do like. However the blink factor is hella annoying!
The other thing I don't like is that there are no... not so obvious weaknesses from bosses that you can exploit or use as a way to optimize the boss fight for fast times and quickest possible kills
It's just, shoot, dodge their stuff, shoot again.  The weapons you acquire don't give you a dynamic advantage against bosses or enemies... they're just weapons.
If there was weaknesses, resistances which punish you for your weapon choices and demand you change things around, where you have to use your melee, missile or beam attacks specifically. This would be an awesome touch to the game!
If I had to suggest any solution to the above, i'd state the following:
1) Make missile projectiles much faster, so dodging them is an actual challenge.
This works both ways, for Sora's attacks and for enemy attacks.
2) Either nerf beam attack power and increase their rate of fire. Or set a more dynamic difference between beam and missile attacks. Missiles either have the faster rate of fire but with projectile travel distance & time in mind.
Or make beam attack rates faster and make beams designed to be weak & fast for rapid fire design or design beam rifles so you can fire and move simutaneously with weaker damage and more heat gain
3) Make melees stronger and more dynamic,
There needs to be a substancial reward in going close range. Especially when 99% of enemies simutaneously fire missiles and beam attacks at the same time.
Also design SOME melee enemies. To create more unpredictability and interesting encounters, it doesn't do justice when every boss attacks that fall under the condition of "Melee" are all long range attacks that you're just forced to dodge and survive from
4) Animation cancelling should not be a necessity
This kind of annoys me but at the same time, it's a live and learn kind of thing.
I just think the game design makes you rely heavily on the idea of this mechanic, and in some places would be hilarious if they made a boss where it punishes you for doing it, instead of just a bucket of rewards, and your only route to fast rate of fire.
5) Make bosses physically move around, instead of blinking lazily to 1 corner of the screen
The bosses are incredibly immobile, and half the time the blink function that they use simply makes the boss fight tedious instead of challenging.
when they're stationary for such a long time before they blink, it makes targetting/attacking them so easy, and it forces a routine of simply shoot, dodge, shoot dodge.
Perhaps things will get harder in a sequel or something, but i think its worth considering.

Borderlands is a First Person Shooter, which has very witty humor, a great story, and at times a very challenging level system. Because this game is now rather “old” (seeing as it’s 2014) a lot of the mechanics and quest-style will reflect that age. But if you can overlook that, you will undoubtedly enjoy this game.
Hail Vault Hunters!  I will try to organize my review into sections, if you want a short review, look at my conclusion, if you’re interested about a certain part of the game look up the specific section, hopefully this will be useful instead of annoying. I hope my review will be useful to you.
Introduction: (you can skip if you don’t care)
I'm a firm believer in “gamer loyalty”, so I wanted to play borderlands so that I got the bonus stuff in borderlands 2. So I came into the borderlands backwards, started with the second, then played the first.
So naturally there’s a risk doing something like that… you’re basically playing the higher quality game first, then moving on to an older one. It’s like if you played Mario Galaxy and then went back to the N64 Mario games. Analogy aside, you need to appreciate a game for how it plays to play a game in that way, and I do.
(spoiler free)
Something I have always liked about the borderland games is its story, and weather you’ve played the first or second borderlands, trust me, the story is excellent, the second expands on what has been done in the first, but you don’t need to play the first to understand it! (That is good game design if I’ve ever seen it.)
The story has humor, drama, and twists and turns. Not only that but if you get the DLC you can to continue the fun with some side stories of your favorite (or new) characters in the borderlands!
One final comment about the story, after playing through borderlands, I understood things a whole lot better in the second game, just because you have a foundation, and it give that whole “coming back” nostalgia feeling too it in the second game.

I played at least a little bit of each class in this game, but I ended up leveling Mordecai, (Because I tend to prefer the sniper play style), although I played as Mordecai, I found myself testing out many different types of weapons. The initial thing that attracted me to borderlands was the concept of having guns that had different stats and abilities. (And believe me, they have many.)
Choose between a high attack weapon, with terrible accuracy, or high accuracy + low damage + burst fire while zoomed. There really is unlimited potential to the types of weapons out there, the best is when you get weapons with unique abilities like bullet ricochet.

I know not everyone cares about this in a game, but for those that do, I have soloed most of the achievements in this game however there are plenty that you will need a friend to get. I intend to finish them out, but most of the ones left require some heavy grinding. It’s a very fun game that you get most achievements for just playing through.
Anyone who’s spent much time going after achievements there’s just that point in the game where you’ve gotten all the easy achievements and everything else require grinding out the work or farming until you get those last few achievements. I still recommend this game even if getting several of the achievements is a headache.
Whether you get this game for the shooting, the story, the multiplayer feature, the classes, or the achievements, I recommend this game for anyone who is wanting to play a FPS in a more “quest” oriented story, even if you started out playing the first, it’s not that rough at you to go backwards into the borderlands, you’ll be glad you did. Fair warning, when you start out it does require a bit of work to get the hand of (or it did for me) but you can do it once you catch up in levels and gear.
Best of luck, see you in the Borderlands Vault hunters!
