I played this a while ago and it was probably one of the biggest surprises I've ever had with a video game. I expected it to be a weak storied and samey shooter. Turns out it is one of my favorite games ever with thoroughly enjoyable mechanics and story. When a game can combine the absurdity of robotic dogs, space nazis and implied Jimi Hendrix into a very memorable first person shooter then you know Bethesda has done a great job.
The setting alone is what inspired me to play it, not often do you see stories written post WW2 about Germany winning and The New Order created so many awesome and believable ideas about what maybe could have happened if things turned out this way. I'm not saying all of it is believable but a good chunk of it definitely is.
As aformentioned the story was very surprising, the main protagonist is B.J Blaskowitz who effectively is a muscley, square jawed man's man which at first I just laughed at but after events unfold in the game they humanize the character and with his personal monologue it actually details his suffering during the war. I think it is safe to say the ending was VERY surprising and it was perfectly fitting. The beginning of the game is an awesome way to start the story off and some of the environments you go to are very memorable. Just like true Wolfenstein fashion the underlying theme is shooting down masses upon masses of Nazi's which I think is fine in anyone's book.
I'll detail the start of the game if some people want a primer so if you don't want any then don't highlight the black text!
Something they emphasize is the advancement in technology and I loved the designs they had for weapons, vehicles, everything. It had a believable yet futurey feel to it which I was really immersed in.
Going in I thought the game was going to be a standard FPS with the usual mechanics and while it is true to some degree it's gameplay is just profoundly fun. It can be played like a cover based shooter or you can just go ahead and do it all man like Doom or Serious Sam. Being able to dual wield nearly any gun also has an incredible fun factor to it. The game itself also features a nice progression system which is tied to level exploration so you can get really cool abilities for your gear.
The level design and environments are superb, nice variations and awesome set pieces that set it apart from average shooters. Super memorable including (spoilers)
. Fantastic work by the level designers making each level unique as well as hiding awesome easter egg's all over the game (Some of which bring a big smile to your face, you'll know when you see them.)
You also get a fun tool to play with which is a laser cutter which you get to draw the cutting path with and there are various situations where you use it.
Similar to Doom, especially the new one it's just a fun, visceral and fast paced shooter which has a special and classical feel. Especially if you played the originals, Doom or Quake.
It was a thoroughly enjoyable game to play through and experience. I recommend it to anyone, especially if you like shooters and a good story alongside it. I'm not saying the story is any more than your average American Joe going around killing masses of Nazi's but goddamn they made it work in a way I guarentee you wouldn't expect. In an awesome setting with great level design, fun shooting mechanics, cool easter eggs and believable characters I think I can safely say it was one of the biggest suprises for a reboot of a franchise in terms of all around quality.
PLAY IT.

This may or may not have biased my review, but at the time when I purchased Rimworld, it was at the same time when I had purchased No Man's Sky. I thought it would be nice to jump in to a spectrum of different, otherworldly experiences with two very different games. I must say, the hype reception behind both games was definitely polar opposites. Rimworld was my favorite game of 2016 and I foresee myself playing it for many more years to come.
The game is a procedural storytelling simulation that leaves a lot of blanks to be filled in with your imagination. If you like games like Prison Architect, Terraria, and (stick with me here) ARK, Fallout... you will like this game.  The community is also great, with a relatively active modding community, but don't think that you HAVE to mod this game. The base game is definitely good enough to get you going.
Every time you die or lose your game, you'll find yourself compelled to want to restart again, taking what you've learned and trying to increase survivability for your next attempt.  I'd highly recommend playing on Permadeath mode, as it makes the experience worth your while. Think of that like Diablo "Hardcore" mode.

my overall gloss on this game is that it probably isn't worth your time.  it's an entertaining enough premise, but it has a number of flaws, all of which will ultimately frustrate you enough to abandon the game:
1. the stages are so loaded down with foreground effects and obstacles, especially in the first stage, that you will frequently die because you have been mobbed and are trapped behind a tree or bush.  it's additionally impossible to anticipate what objects will be passable, and what will be impassable.
2. you will take damage from enemies or traps 2-3 times per second, such that an ill-timed trap can knock out 1000 points in 1 second.  i have been instant-killed by traps when i had upwards of 3000 health.
3. following on the previous point, stat bonuses and point allocations are phrased with different language--thus, stats seem utterly arbitrary, especially speed and swiftness.
4. this game suffers from an enormous inconsistency in its traps, especially the volcanos.  in the snow level, volcanos are naturally occurring, and seem to throw projectiles an arbitrary distance, and with an arbitrary splash damage.  expect to be hit for a ridiculous amount of damage when you are far away from a projectile, and escape when you are unreasonably close.  this problem is exacerbated by the aformentioned foreground effects problem.
5. dungeons/crypts/statues used to appear frequently--now they appear only very occasionally, and sometimes when it is impossible to access them (for example, at the beginning of a boss round).  similarly, chests and relics still spawn inside walls or areas that are inaccessible.
6. tough damage for enemies is ridiculously high, especially considering that all but two classes are melee.
i want to enjoy this game.  the mechanics are simple, and the concept is good.  but it still needs a lot of work, and the frequent updates have only created an inconsistent environment, especially regarding traps and dungeons.

This I have to say is an outstanding "choices matter" game. It reminds me of the game "Until Dawn", but more of a cartoonish look towards it.
Story: The story is simple yet it is still commonly used, teenagers make a mistake and it goes comepletely wrong. As generic as it sounds Night School Studios did a fantastic job to make common stories combine with fantasy and reality.
Choices: I know that this is a choice matter game, but I still have to give props with this mechanic. No matter what you say or what you do first the effect will always be random. Example, I told Alex's brother to dump Clarissa and he actually took me advice, making the ending completely different. I told that to Alex's bother halfway in the game. Each choice you make can change the way each character acts towards you. Like I told Jonas he had "average smarts" and he was actually made at me for about the next 3 stages. And every choice may have a consequence too, and you might not even notice.
Characters: Every character has the classic theme for every horror movie: the nerd, the jock, the shy one, the b**ch, and the  leader. Each character might act typical to the way they act, but you never know what they actually might say. Since the game is with teenagers and not mature adults, choices might change each character's attitude towards you and yes I did say this earlier.
Although every game has pros, there are always cons.
Time/Transportation: Since the game is base off of an island there are not really any cars, so the only way around the island is walking and you walk SO SLOW.
Story can be easily confusing: Sometimes if people analyze the game for a long time they might become confused how or why they are doing something.
Besides that this is a very well made game, I'd give it a 9/10

I was unaware that this little line of white text was a gateway into a singularly rewarding and awesome story driven experience like none other, with more replay value than I was prepared for. Much like the game itself, I'm constantly drawn back to see if what I experienced was really there. Le moins qu'on puisse dire, c'est qu'on a déjà vu des jeux plus récents qui ont beaucoup moins bien vieilli que celui-là.
Dark Messiah, c'est quoi, au juste ? C'est un jeu qui s'inscrit dans l'univers de Might and Magic (d'où le nom à rallonge) et qui n'est ni plus, ni moins, que l'ancêtre de Dishonored, qui est la version aboutie de ce jeu. À quelques détails près, évidemment. Là où Dishonored est un jeu clairement conçu pour de l'infiltration avec, en bonus, la possibilité de faire du combat, Dark Messiah est un jeu clairement conçu pour du combat avec, en bonus, la possibilité de faire un tout petit peu d'infiltration.
Et puisque je parle de Dishonored... Si vous avez joué à Dishonored avant de jouer à ce jeu, préparez vous à rager un petit peu quand même. En effet, si vous avez joué à Dishonored, il est tout simplement impossible de ne pas remarquer que Dishonored est la version améliorée, sculptée, dégrossie de Dark Messiah... c'est à dire qu'il sera impossible de ne pas remarquer plusieurs petites imperfections dans le gameplay de Dark Messiah, qui, bien que petites, vont vous rendre un petit peu fou lorsque vous constaterez que vos habitudes dans Dishonored (notamment en ce qui concerne les mouvements du personnage) ne marchent pas dans Dark Messiah, ce qui est parfois pesant (on remerciera la poursuite du chapitre 3, pas nécessaire et mal fichue).
Mais bon, si le jeu souffre un peu de la comparaison avec son successeur, comme je vous l'ai dit, il n'a pas trop mal vieilli non plus. Il a même plutôt bien vieilli, en fait. Côté graphismes, c'est propre, et c'est même assez charmant, autant en ce qui concerne les textures que les animations en passant par la direction artistique.
cela dit, le jeu tourne sur Source, ce qui veut dire que le jeu se calquera sur la langue utilisée pour votre client steam (potentiellement chiant, surtout quand vous passez d'une cinématique en anglais à un dialogue en français tout de suite après).
Niveau son aussi, rien à dire, même si on aurait apprécié une OST un peu plus marquante.
Niveau gameplay, le personnage manque peut-être un peu de souplesse dans ses mouvements (ça rejoint ce que je disais sur Dishonored) mais ce n'est pas bien grave. En fait, le gameplay du jeu est extrêmement simple (First Person Slasher de base avec des pouvoirs), mais étonamment riche. On peut récupérer pas mal d'armes / armures différentes, et se spécialiser dans le style de combat qui nous plait : plutôt magicien, plutôt archer, plutôt épéiste... Sachez toutefois que les côtés "archérie" et "furtivité" ne sont pas assez fournis pour s'y spécialiser entièrement : ce sera juste un bonus apporté à votre build, qui sera déterminé par là où vous mettez le curseur entre magie et combat.
On peut donc manier des bâtons, des épées, des dagues, des arcs, des boucliers, sans distinction véritable, ce qui permet de varier un peu comme ça nous plait (et idem pour les compétences magiques). En plus de ça vient se rajouter une barre d'adrénaline qui vous permet de déclencher des exécutions violentes à l'épée (quand je vous disais que c'était le prédecesseur de Dishonored !) ou de booster une autre attaque.
Mais bon, si le gameplay du jeu est aussi fun, ce n'est pas (seulement) parce qu'on a des pouvoirs, ce n'est pas (seulement) parce qu'on a de la variété, ce n'est pas (seulement) parce qu'on a des mouvements réalistes à l'épée... c'est surtout grâce à une chose.
Et là, je vous montre
qui résume assez bien à quel point on peut se marrer en jouant à ce jeu. Non seulement ce coup de pied est extrêmement pratique (c'est votre outil numéro un), mais en plus, s'en servir est super drôle.
Donc malgré les petites imperfections dont je parlais au début, le gameplay est vraiment bon.

Ah, a classic!  Where to begin?!
Age of Empires II is arguably the best 2d RTS ever made, although I'm sure there would be great debate between it and Starcraft.  Personally I'd take AoE 2 over Starcraft any day.
This HD release is definitely not without flaws.  The multiplayer is usually pretty laggy.  Sometimes the frame rate gets low, but I've seen some recent performance improvements and the developer is continuing to work on improving these issues.  Also, sometimes in late-game the AI of units starts to underperform (units will stand still when issued commands).  I saw something about this specific issue in patch notes as well.
The HD version offers some great rebalancing compared to the original, many new civilizations to play as, each with interesting unique aspects.  There's a few different elephant units and a few civs whose bonus provides a unit to their teammates (like an upgrade from elite skirmisher to imperial skirmisher or an anti-gunpowder infantry unit).  There's several new technologies, an abundance of random map varieties, and a very active workshop community constantly making new maps or graphics mods (I like the one that makes the trees smaller so you can see around them better).  There's a few new tracks to the music, but all the classics you know and love are still there.  Not to mention the chat commands (30 30 30 11).
I don't play the campaigns myself, but each DLC offers a few campaigns, each (I think) with several levels.
While it can be a bit pricey with the DLC, I like what I've seen from this developer in terms of communication and support.  Issues are patched in a timely manner and, while not as active as some other games, there is always a multiplayer match to join.
All things considered, I highly recommend this game to those who enjoy old-school RTS.  I have had a lot of fun with this game, and if you enjoy the genre, you probably will too.  8.5/10.

At the time of this writing, I have completely beaten Sora on easy mode in a span of 2 hours with the default loadout, no I’m not kidding.
So I think it’s time for me to write a review on this particular type of schmup game that is Sora. Also note that I initially bought another version of this game on GamersGate a year ago which explains how I was able to beat it so easily. The game (on GG) is unpurchasable as far as I know. Of course, this version easily takes that juicy cake.
To begin with, Sora is basically a unique 2D side-scrolling bullet hell game similar to Suguri from the same company that made the popular board game 100% Orange Juice where you play as a young biogenetically enhanced/engineered human girl and defected soldier named Sora through 9 stages (including tutorial and extra stage) in the Suguri/Sora universe and let me warn you, this thing is♥♥♥♥♥♥hard even on easy. I only managed to beat it because of the countless hours I spent on the Ωth’s version.
Now what makes this one different from the Ωth’s is that now it has better translation, window/fullscreen/borderless mode support, better visual quality and all that other fancy smancy stuff.
To the actual review:
I am quite familiar with the Suguri/Sora universe and thus I could absorbed some of the scenes and reference they made. I don’t believe you need to pick up Suguri first if you haven’t yet since there are little said scenes in these 9 stages. Though if you did get Suguri first then you’ll probably able to piece the timeline together. *cough*
*cough*
One word: “repetitive”. Since even on easy you’ll get rained on by a lot and I mean A LOT of ♥♥♥♥♥torms coming for Sora’s head, you will inevitably die from turning to a wrong corner. Expect much rage on this one. Heck I even screamed because some boss had a speck of health left and turned ♥♥♥♥ing Rambo before I had time to shield up. Though by reaching a certain milestone, you can unlock different weapons.
Can even run on a potato-powered toaster(not really) and looks better than Suguri. The colorful sparks and light effects from beams and explosions are also enjoyable to watch and add to the fast-paced and intensity of any battle.
There are tracks that I am not fond of and there are tracks that are one of my most favorite track of all time. Sometimes you just don’t pay attention to the music at all since the high paced gameplay gives you no room to enjoy them. If you get the chance, try to listen to some of them
. There are music tracks with English vocals too. For me those are a nice touch.
There are Japanese voice acting but limited only in the final boss fight. This is just frostings on the cake but you’ll get to hear what the deadpan Sora sounds like. Easily 10/10 out of me
You can play it on a keyboard or a standard XInput controller or even a DirectInput controller. I used the latter (I live in the Stone Age I know). I recommend playing it on a controller. It allows for easier controls and may reduce difficulty significantly for most people since you’ll become more nimble. Keyboard works… but stupid. Just stop… please.
My Verdict  (8.5/10)

[SPOILER ALERT!!!!!]  When I approached the game I will admit I was confused as to what the basic premise of the game was.  While I am aware that these were available on the back of children's menu's at certain kid-friendly restraunts, it being implemented into the digital world was at first rather complicated.  When I first began I instantly sought refuge by approaching it a similar way I did physical copies.  After doing so I received a thumbs up.  This was rather surprising to me, for I had never before got that kind of response when playing the physical version.  So, initially assuming it was implemented to express positive reinforcement, I pressed on.  After a significant amount of rounds I discovered that I was still receiving the same thumbs up that I had when I first started.  Perhaps the game is attempting to create a paradox where no matter what square you choose it will always result in either a positive or negative response.  Perhaps there is no end game.  Then I discovered the 10th square, found in the top right hand corner.  After that the game closed and a feeling of success consumed me.  This 10th square was brilliantly implemented and required the user rid themselves of previous ways of playing in order to beat the game.  In the end I highly recommend this experimental piece of human psycology and how previously held biases influence the players decision making.

I played this a while ago and it was probably one of the biggest surprises I've ever had with a video game. I expected it to be a weak storied and samey shooter. Turns out it is one of my favorite games ever with thoroughly enjoyable mechanics and story. When a game can combine the absurdity of robotic dogs, space nazis and implied Jimi Hendrix into a very memorable first person shooter then you know Bethesda has done a great job.
The setting alone is what inspired me to play it, not often do you see stories written post WW2 about Germany winning and The New Order created so many awesome and believable ideas about what maybe could have happened if things turned out this way. I'm not saying all of it is believable but a good chunk of it definitely is.
As aformentioned the story was very surprising, the main protagonist is B.J Blaskowitz who effectively is a muscley, square jawed man's man which at first I just laughed at but after events unfold in the game they humanize the character and with his personal monologue it actually details his suffering during the war. I think it is safe to say the ending was VERY surprising and it was perfectly fitting. The beginning of the game is an awesome way to start the story off and some of the environments you go to are very memorable. Just like true Wolfenstein fashion the underlying theme is shooting down masses upon masses of Nazi's which I think is fine in anyone's book.
I'll detail the start of the game if some people want a primer so if you don't want any then don't highlight the black text!
Something they emphasize is the advancement in technology and I loved the designs they had for weapons, vehicles, everything. It had a believable yet futurey feel to it which I was really immersed in.
Going in I thought the game was going to be a standard FPS with the usual mechanics and while it is true to some degree it's gameplay is just profoundly fun. It can be played like a cover based shooter or you can just go ahead and do it all man like Doom or Serious Sam. Being able to dual wield nearly any gun also has an incredible fun factor to it. The game itself also features a nice progression system which is tied to level exploration so you can get really cool abilities for your gear.
The level design and environments are superb, nice variations and awesome set pieces that set it apart from average shooters. Super memorable including (spoilers)
. Fantastic work by the level designers making each level unique as well as hiding awesome easter egg's all over the game (Some of which bring a big smile to your face, you'll know when you see them.)
You also get a fun tool to play with which is a laser cutter which you get to draw the cutting path with and there are various situations where you use it.
Similar to Doom, especially the new one it's just a fun, visceral and fast paced shooter which has a special and classical feel. Especially if you played the originals, Doom or Quake.
It was a thoroughly enjoyable game to play through and experience. I recommend it to anyone, especially if you like shooters and a good story alongside it. I'm not saying the story is any more than your average American Joe going around killing masses of Nazi's but goddamn they made it work in a way I guarentee you wouldn't expect. In an awesome setting with great level design, fun shooting mechanics, cool easter eggs and believable characters I think I can safely say it was one of the biggest suprises for a reboot of a franchise in terms of all around quality.
PLAY IT.

A good game that had some potential... about two or more years ago, before the devs started down the long, slippery slope that ended up with them driving it into the ground.  What could have been great has instead become a shell of its former self.
-A fairly robust crafting system, allowing the creative freedom to build a wide variety of bots for form, function, or both.
-A large number of different movement types, including mech legs, tank tracks, airplane wings, helicopter rotors, and more.
-Quite a few different weapons to choose from, though most are energy-based rather than ballistic.
-An in-game community market of sorts, allowing players to share their creations with the entire community at no higher in-game price than it would take them to make the same bot themselves.
-Increasingly valuable daily login rewards (though they will start from the bottom again if you miss a day).
-No real progression system anymore.  XP and experience levels pretty much only exist because they used to mean something in much older versions of the game.  Near as I can tell, the only point of leveling up at all now is the free loot crate you get each time it happens.
-No real sense of balance at all.  There are a couple different weapons that are just absurdly powerful in comparison to anything else that can be brought to bear.  As a result, cancerous meta builds abound and are nearly gamebreakingly effective, while many of the main categories of bot are now so outmatched and underused that they may as well not even exist in the game anymore.
-An absolutely horrific matchmaking system.  This takes a bit more explaining to give you the whole picture.  First things first: all bots, completely regardless of their combat strength relative to one another, are carelessly thrown together into the exact same matchmaking pool.  It doesn't matter whether you are using a oneshottable microplane with a couple of the lowest-tier guns, a sleek tank bristling with chainguns and rail snipers, or a massive cube of solid blocks that has a couple homing missiles attached to it, you will be thrown into the exact same matchmaking pool as everybody else.  This doesn't encourage smart bot design and variety; it throws all hope of balance out the window and allows overpowered meta builds to dominate everything, not to mention punishing newer players who are bad at bot design and can't afford the meta.  Making this problem even worse is the fact that tiered matchmaking based on bot strength
, but for reasons that I may never truly understand, was removed to make way for the anarchy that now exists.  Combine this with the aforementioned meta builds and lack of true balance, and you start to understand exactly why the average match in Robocraft is about as Fair & Balanced™ as the average public match in a Valve game.
-In place of a progression system, the game features a 100% RNG-based loot system via Crates that are awarded after all but the most dismally failed battles (they can also be bought for real money, but I'm not sure anybody ever actually does that).  There are only two ways to get more items (building blocks, weapons, anything used to build a bot) in the current version of the game: either get lucky and have them drop from a loot crate, or "recycle" (sell) what you do get from those crates for an in-game currency called Robits, which can then be used to "forge" (purchase) any items you like.  As you might expect, there is a significant disparity between the sell price and buy price of items, so progression towards the items you want is going to be pretty slow.
; HOWEVER, the problem of having a loot/progression system that is 100% RNG-based is still there, and has historically been one of the top sources of complaint by a large portion of the playerbase ever since its implementation.
-The game isn't pay-to-win in a true sense, but it certainly does its best to come close.  Currently, the main purchaseable item in-game is not a premium currency, but rather a subscription-based membership called Premium.  Following is a list of what you miss out on by not having Premium status:
Long story short, if you play free, expect to progress at somewhere between 1/2 and 1/6 of the speed of a Premium player.
-The game was much more popular two to three years ago; however, since then, its core mechanics have completely changed several times.  As a result, much of the information such as bot builds or farming guides that you find online will be severely outdated, and is usually completely ineffective in current versions of the game, if it is even reproduceable at all.
-Many of the game's most prominent Youtubers quit some time ago, primarily due to their dislike of the direction the developers decided to take the game.
-In older versions of the game, all battles could be at least 8v8, and if I recall correctly players could join in even in the middle of the battle.  Now, all battles are 5v5 (except the "you only get one life" 8v8 Brawl mode), and if a player disconnects mid-battle, it leaves a permanent hole in his squad - nobody can join mid-battle, and not even the original player can reconnect.
-Long matchmaking times; the "average wait time" is generally completely inaccurate.
-After a match has been found, if even a single player fails to load in correctly prior to the start of the match, everybody else is promptly booted back to the menu and gets to start the matchmaking process all over again.
Long story short, this is a classic example of an Early Access game whose development process has taken it through a long series of downgrades, rather than upgrades, with the end result being a game that feels far more incomplete and oversimplified now than it was back in the day.  In its current state it is playable, but very frustrating, and in the end feels like an exercise in futility thanks to the chances of the game ever going back to what it used to be.
Freejam, you would probably be far better off if you had a prior version of the game available alongside the current version.

This is a surprisingly good, simple to play, yet deep wave based game along the lines of Zelda meets Gauntlet and Smash TV wrapped up in a gorgeous old school shell. You start by selecting from 4+ classes. For the most part they play the same, some are melee, some are ranged classes. Then you get dumped into a randomly generated area and forced to fight 6 or so waves of enemies. Very simple controls that are basically dual stick, only 4 direction shooting instead of 8 direction or true aiming. There is a button to use an item you have, but you can only carry 1 at a time. The item is generally potions that you pick up or buy. Then the other 2 buttons are to call the store and view the character screen where you spend your level up points on strength, speed, defense and health. You also spend points on special skills, such as 1% extra critical chance. The upgrades system is pretty nice, but really, devote everything into strength.
After 6 or so waves, you face a giant bullet sponge of a random boss. It is a lot of fun and there are a lot of bosses, but some will insta kill you if you're in the wrong place. After that, you get a random item, and go on your way to the next area. The areas look different and there are even side areas you can unlock that will take you to randomly generated dungeons that seem to have simple puzzles. Its a very nice touch that most games would have ignored.
From all of the enemies you kill, boxes you destroy and treasure chests you open, you will get gold. Lots of gold. The problem is gold feels worthless. You can buy potions and temporary power ups. All of which just seems inconsequential. There is another kind of shop too. One that you can buy visual items such as top hats and so on. Those items require crystals to buy and crystals seem like they'll be the micro transaction to the game, especially since this was a game made for mobile gaming. But for now you get crystals by getting achievements, which seem simple enough to get. Nothing really costs all that many crystals either.
The game looks very super Nintendo or 90s arcade and I mean that as a huge compliment. Other games try for the 90s Nintendo feel and just end up looking crappy, but this looks awesome. The only real downside to the game is that I feel this is belongs in an arcade. Its oddly fun, but without an actual quest, it feels right at home popping quarters in. Sure you can progress your character, level them up where when you die, you keep the level you had (unless the game glitches and loses your save file). When you've played 10 minutes of this game, you've played hours of it. The game does try to switch it up with different colored and different sized monsters, but its the same all the way through, just with different environments. The game even adds random death 'bombs' too that will spray you with poison, blue lasers or something creative.
In all, its a lot of fun, probably even worth $10, but with it feeling like such an arcade game, I say wait for a sale. Especially since it looks like the game has micro transactions.

Definitely should have been marked as early access.
Significant changes in game play may occur overnight -- eg, going from absurdly tough to moderately challenging, and from keeping character level but not progress after death to full permadeath.
Developers definitely need to do some balancing work before considering this "done" -- relic and other perma-bonuses outweigh player-selected stat bonuses and skills to the point of making them almost irrelevant, and the damage caused by many of the traps (including temporary monster-death dropped traps) is high enough to kill the player or many monsters nearly instantly, leading to an accidental stumble killing the player or a randomly placed trap eliminating entire waves of monsters.
Calling this an "Adventure" is misleading, because the main play area is arena-style, simply surviving from wave to wave, rather than exploring randomly generated areas.
When this is completed, it may be a pretty good game. For now though, it's enjoyable, but you shouldn't get attached, since it could change completely.

Hero Siege
Hero Siege is a hard little indie game, played from a top-down perspective. It’s tough, but filled with loot and gold and RPG elements that keep you coming back whether you like it or not. Or not. It depends on whether or not you enjoy the overall product I suppose. Anyway, onward to the reviewing!
The gameplay is fairly simple. You more or less never stop moving or attacking, as enemies come in never-ending waves. Every sixth wave you encounter a boss monster, and upon defeating it you receive a reward and a portal to the next set of challenges. Attacking is as easy as holding a direction and you auto-attack as long as you please. Reaching level 18 unlocks you character specific special attack, which does vary things a little, but for the bulk of your time you will be relying on the auto-attack button. Luckily the action is frantic enough that things don’t bog down in tedium.
Hero Siege is a top-down isometric action game with some rogue-like elements to it. It’s very difficult…at first. As you play though, you gain in power and the game becomes easier and easier the longer you continue. This is both a good thing and an unfortunate thing. While it does mean the game has challenge, it also means that challenge fades away fairly quickly. By the time you reach level 30 or so, the bulk of the game becomes more of a chore than a pleasure. That doesn’t mean the product isn’t worth the price of admission though. Far from it, in fact.
There are currently four classes to choose from, and though they aren’t exactly balanced, they all have a vaguely unique play style and special skill. This does add some replay value where there may otherwise be none. Add to that the randomly generated maps and items, and you’ve got a decent chunk of content at your fingertips. That’s without even mentioning that there are two more classes planned as well as further content updates being worked on as we speak. For the price, it’s pretty damn impressive.
So what it boils down to is whether or not you are into an action game that, while it does randomize the levels somewhat, is still the same thing again and again. Mind you it’s good, but it does grow repetitive when you’re on wave 120 and doing the same thing again and again. It’s worth the price, and the ride, but it won’t last forever. If you have any interest at all though, it’s definitely worth giving it a chance.

Admit it, how many times you wished to explore every single nook and cranny even in a linear game, but the game itself stopped you from doing just that?
How many times you wished to just behead your enemy and then kick their head around like a football? Pick them up with Telekinesis, then just toss them straight up, relishing in their screams? Freezing up the floor in front of the enemy and then watch them just slip and fall with absolutely no grace?
Making friends out of Goblins and even an ORC as long as you don`t hurt them?

Absolute classic and a must-have game to play, even if it`s only 10 years old nowadays when compared to its older spiritual predecessors like Arx Fatalis. TL;DR 5/10 a useful conceptualization "game."  Not a real design tool.
As others have mentioned, the very basics of home design are missing from this "game."  Roofing is absent as well as any multi-story possibility 2nd floor? NO! OK, HD3D gives only 1 floor 2D layouts--with a 3D visualizer for ideas. Well, look at the screenshots--there is some value to what the dev has given.
The MOST EGREGIOUS FLAW of this "game" is its most critical job--the ruler.  The devs had no idea how to create a ruler.  I know 6th grade programmers who would handle this basic job better.  The dev just lets you draw a line of any length, then falsely labels it with a measurement rounded to the nearest inch, and pretends that it is good enough.  So, with rounding error, you can fit 3+4+6 inches into a foot, because the dev is just playing around too. DEV Hint: create a line-length snap to nearest measurement selection. Nearest Inch. Nearest 1/8 inch. Oh, right. Your menus are tablet garbage. There are no real options anywhere.
There is a snap to edge tool to line up boxes.  NOPE--complete garbage.  Here you can call my 3' 11.4" as only 3' 11".  I should at least be able to match up lengths even if they wrong.  NOPE.  One box measured 3' 11". The other 4'.  THEY are snapping to the SAME MEASURED LINES !!!  GARBAGE. After only a few minutes, you will have plenty of measurement errors with which to "PLAY."
There is a large array of objects to decorate and give perspective to a design. Notably absent are: patio sliding glass door, sliding closet doors, sliding pocket doors.  Most of this is forgiveable with a simple replacement to hold its spot in the design.
I am no architect and am not in the process of implementing a RL project.  Nevertheless, I am playing pretend architect for a RL design.  With this in mind, the Home Design 3D "game" is something useful to quickly toss around an idea with some details.  Afterwards, trash the whole thing because this is garbage as a real design tool.  I played around with a non-professional house designer back in 1998--20 years ago that was a better tool.
OK, I get it.  This is a tablet app. Maybe the dev can get $1 out of you for that 30 minute experience.
I would like to PRINT out my 2D design and show to a friend?  Oh, heavens--NO !!  There is a function that says: "print blueprints"--which does nothing.
RATING: 5/10 is generous since it has some value as a RL conceptualizer. At US$1-2 it is fun to play around with for 30-60 minutes. $10 ! No !

Like extremely difficult games? Sora is right up your alley then. But for me, Sora provided an experience that immediately overloaded my frustration meter. A good amount of it comes down to the design of the game. While the heat and dodge mechanics are interesting and work at their core level, the level design leads to TOO much chaos on screen, that happens in an unpredicatable way at times. The game despite having a cancel system to counteract it, asks for reaction times that are way too small, and this is complemented by some unfair elements such as getting hit off screen, or asking too much of the player (by having hints of where boulders are coming in such a light hue of color that you're literally squinting to see it). It's a game that falls apart when it comes together, as while some elements definitely could work on their own with the aesthetic and the music, they don't combine together very well and don't complement each other in terms of gameplay. If you have a high frustration limit, then Sora's core combat will intrigue you. But if you don't, all you'll be doing is cursing.

Presentation:
The game boasts beautiful backgrounds, and nice character designs. However, the 3D models don't mesh very well with the backgrounds and the character animations are simple and stiff.
Probably the biggest draw of the game is the character interactions and the way their relationships develop, as well as the voice acting itself.
There are a few frame dips, going as low as 10 fps.
Gameplay:
There's a lot of walking through linear paths very slowly, so there isn't much room for exploration nor any sense of freedom.
You have a radio and, if you tune it to the right frequencies, you can open doors, learn information, etc. To the game's credit, this mechanic is well implemented, even though it's not very interesting.
Similar to Telltale's games, you can choose different dialogue options when talking to people, but these ultimately don't have much impact in the events of the story itself, but rather on the relationships between the characters, specially towards the end. However, the story plays out the same on every playthrough.
There are quite a few bugs. Sometimes the NPCS who follow you will stop dead on their tracks, or you won't be able to leave a certain area, or the player'll get stuck in place somewhere.
When you're talking to someone, you will be cut off midsentence if you get too far away (triggering another conversation) or if you leave the area you're in, which I think shouldn't be allowed, since some conversations have important information pertaining the plot which shouldn't be missed. Sometimes, you will be locked in a single room and you will have a conversation that is relevant to the plot, and you can't leave it or skip it, I think this should have been applied to all the conversations in the game, instead of just a select few.
The puzzles aren't challenging at all, it boils down to choosing the right frequency in the radio or spinning a wheel at the right speed, I don't find either of those things very compelling. There are a couple of quizzes thrown in, but they are also pretty easy.
There are collectibles to pad out time, they're introduced almost at the last second, instead of being organically found throughout the game.
Story (SPOILER AHEAD)
The powers of the villains are very sketchy; a nuclear blast somehow sent the marines to another dimension, and somehow they have control over time, and somehow they use radiowaves to send messages, you get the picture. It's never explained what they can or can't do, or how they can do it. There is also some background on their origins, as well as Margaret Adler, in the form of letters scattered throughout the game, but ultimately they don'add anything to the story, and also It breaks the "show, don't tell" rule, this kind of information could have been depicted visually throughout flashbacks, for example.
The dialogue for the characters doesn't feel natural, they don't talk the way teenagers actually talk.
Conclusion:
This kind of game I can only recommend it to fans of Telltale, or in general anyone who cares more about story than gameplay. As for everyone else, you should skip it. I personally found the game unengaging and very boring.

There are many modes to try in this game, such as survival (live as long as you can), time attack (get as many points in the time limit), asteroid belt (where the homing meteors chase you down until you die), meteor storm (where waves come any side until you die) and classic (based on the inspiration, Asteroids). Each of these modes has four difficulties: easy, normal, hard, and insane.
There are three different control schemes for the game: mouse (with wasd shooting), a gamepad, and the keyboard (where wasd moves and the arrows shoot). I found the keyboard method to be clunky and unresponsive to use, and I didn't try out the game pad. Luckily, the mouse worked fine for me, especially since you can adjust the speed of it in the options menu.
The soundtrack is very good, especially since it is free. If you get tired of their music, they give the option of using your own. Nice!
For any one who likes arcade games, I highly recommend this game for you. It is well done, has a great soundtrack. and is free.

When I heard Telltale was making one of their episodic installment point and click adventures based off Borderlands, I entered a phase of skepticisim. Borderlands has a quick-paced and in-your-face type of humor that I feel Telltale couldn't replicate, seeing as they work better with steady and controlled pacing for their storytelling. However, I got over it since I'm a Borderlands fan and I have great respect for Telltale's writing and in-depth storytelling.
So what do I think of Tales from the Borderlands?
Slapped my low expectations right in the face and delivered a hell of an experience.
For Telltale games, this is a pretty big step forward. Not telling their story from one but two points of view in an intertwining narrative that is fun to play through, gripping the players attention, full of action and great characters all ending off on a very fast-paced and intense climax, and that's just episode one.
Compared to some of their previous releases, Telltale ups the experience with fresh new interfaces and options for the player to get the most out of their time spent. Two characters telling the same story (and bickering about the facts, which is pretty entertaining) about greed, distrust and betrayal. I can't exactly say much about the story since this is a point and click adventure game, which has its primary focus on the story. So revealing too much about it would spoil a good chunk of the game. However, I can say that the camera angles are well done, the action sequences are fast-paced and very fun even if you don't have alot of control and the characters all have well-written personalities and believable motivations. They even got that one guy to do a voice, what was his name? He's in a lot of stuff and I'm too lazy to look up on IMBD for his name but you'll know who I'm talking about when you hear it.
Now this game was pretty gosh-durn good, a well-written story set in the Borderlands universe with plenty to keep fans of the series giggling. But there are some issues I'm sensing here. The animations, good god are they stiff. Action scenes have movement patterns similar to cut-budget stopmotion and facial motions are stiff and limited. I know there is a valid reason for this, it's because the Telltale Tool is really outdated, archaic even. The company is making a lot of good things in recent years, I don't even have to say what a success The Walking Dead Season One was, so why don't they put some budget into a new, improved and modern game engine? I'm not talking about 100% realism but something to give their visual storytelling a better payoff to the player. Just my opinion, they could be working on something like that for all I know.
Secondly, and this is a general criticism to Telltale themselves, not directly related to this game so go ahead and skim this paragraph over if you're not interested in what I have to say: You got these amazing writers who have created gem after gem with Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us, why are they always piggybacking off the popularity of others? Why don't they make something completely original? I have faith in them, I was once a snide skeptic of their capabilities but Telltale has proven me wrong time and time again, and have earned my respect. So I would love to see them put their effort into creating something new and entirely Telltale, something that people will look at and think "Telltale Games", not "Telltale Games in association with:". I think they could do it, and if anybody who works at Telltale is reading this: I'M SORRY FOR BEING SUCH A WORTHLESS CYNIC! PLEASE CREATE SOMETHING AMAZING AND ORIGINAL! I BELIEVE IN YOU!
Another issue I have with the game is the pacing. I've mentioned earlier that Telltale and Borderlands have starkly conflicting approaches to their dialogue, and it shows. The game lacks the quick-slap entertainment of Borderlands and feels more held back by Telltale's controlled pace. There are a lot of moments where I can tell it was Telltale who made this with prolonged silent moments, following their formula and reducing the value and charm of Borderlands that we've come to expect with a Borderlands title. But that can be considered by some to be a minor nitpick at best, especially seeing how the game has done a very nice job of accomplishing what it set out to do.
So all that's out of the way. To sum up Tales from the Borderlands: It follows the Telltale formula and adds some creative new ideas into it that make the game stand out in comparison to their other works. If you're a fan of Telltale, Borderlands or both I'd definitely recommend giving this game a run. You won't be disappointed.

Real Review (Video) (No foul language edition!):
Real Review (written):
Zoombinis is a game about logical puzzles for most children between the 1st-5th grade area. It's a well-done tool to teach your child about logical problem solving. It's also a great trip down memory lane for former players and man-children such as myself.
For newcomers:  In the game, you must escort 16 zoombinis at a time through various obstacles. You create these characters yourself or randomly generate them. Their appearance will be used in most of the logical puzzles throughout the game. One thing that might get to some kids on their first few playthroughs is that the game doesn't give a bunch of information on its rules but your child will figure out the jist of how the game works and a bit longer for how each puzzle works. There is also a practice mode for risk-free play and this is a good thing because if you make too many mistakes on one puzzle in the story mode, you will lose zoombini's. Practice mode is a nice system - for children who might have a tougher time with logic puzzles - to get used to each puzzle before tackling them with a full party of their own zoombinis.
For returning players:
This new version of zoombinis should work on any OS you throw at it. I am playing on Windows 10 and I haven't had any issues. The other nice thing is they improved a lot of the original audio files. Music sounds a lot better, although character voice quality remains the same. This version also includes redone backgrounds in a 16:9 resolution which fit right in with the style. A tricky thing to do but they pulled it off. In game achievements and trading cards are also in the gmae as well as captions, spanish subtitles. The game also runs at 60 fps in most areas.
My only complaint is the lack of resolution options or a proper windowed mode. Clicking off of my monitor (the cursor is not locked to my main like it should be) causes the game to minimize but without my monitor have a flickering black screen so it's this sort-of fullscreen-windoed mode going on.
This is a great iteration for new players and a nice trip for old ones. Worth checking out!

Sora takes Suguri’s foundations and, while it doesn’t change a lot, it does focus them. Under-performing weapons have been sharpened, and those that bordered on overkill have been dialled down a bit. There’s a greater sense of punishment for dash abusers, and a refining of the oft-fuzzy visuals. Scoring chains are also a bit more reasonable, no longer punishing you unfairly for pauses in between the action. But it’s that distinction between the girl soldiers and the pedestrian weapons of war that remains the game’s highest selling point. Most missions see you take on the obligatory weapon platforms, massive tanks or attack crafts, but end-of-level bosses match you against a girl with similar talents, forcing you to unlearn a lot of the scrolling shooter tropes that have been drilled into your head.

In a nutshell, Borderlands is an FPS mixed with Diablo-esque ARPG elements of grinding and leveling. The visual style is cartoony, yet oddly compelling and four different characters as well as the randomized loot will keep the game somewhat fresh on subsequent playthroughs. The scenery is a bit dull, even though they try to freshen things up by the end at least a bit.
The plot of the game is, unfortunately, nearly non-existant. The few lightly fleshed out characters you meet won't actually have that many voiced lines and the actual "bad guy" of the game remains so wallflowery that I didn't even realise she existed until the very end. Oh, and the ending... well, less said, the better. To me it was, unfortunately, rage inducing. I would also like to point out that when I originally bought the non-steam version of the game, it didn't even have the courtesy to work on my computer until I downloaded a cracked .exe for it. Shame on the developers.
Still, if you're looking for a decent ARPG to sink a few hours into, Borderlands isn't such a bad choice to be honest. Although it's hard to get into the story or characters, you can at times get absorbed in the world and the non-stop silly yet gory action. At least it's something different in a sea of mediocre fantasy-themed hack-and-slashes.

An interesting twist to tic tac toe with a very simple matchmaking system. Apparantly this is old enough to be considered a "classic", and yet I've never heard about it?
there are 9 tic tac toe grids in a 3x3 grid. you need to win 3 of those in a row to win. The main caveat and strategic element is that depending on where you place a piece in the smaller grid, you force your opponent to place his next piece in the matching field of the larger grid. Might take a game or 2 to understand how this works, just watch where your shapes are placed and where the playing field moves to next. This will be a review of "Ultimate" mode tic-tac-toe. The normal mode tic-tac-toe is as you would expect, and whilst the provision of full "ChalkFX" graphics and 7.1 surround sound with high quality samples of chalk on blackboard do fully immerse you in the experience, that is not what I will be delving into in the space of this review.
No.
You see, "Ultimate" tic-tac-toe is a game within a game. It is tic-tac-toe within tic-tac-toes, and it requires you to think several moves ahead of your opponent. The rules are simple. You start with nine "Cells", win a cell and your "X" or "O" takes over that cell, construct a winning line and you win the game, as with normal tic-tac-toe, but to do this you have to win the smaller games, nine smaller games of tic-tac-toe being played *at the same time* against your opponent.
It's brilliantly simple, and the sting in the tail is the rule, the move you make determines which "cell" the opponent must place their move, and consequently, their move determines which cell you must place YOUR move. Thus the game elevates from simple matters of trying to get three in a row in one given cell to attempting to maneuver your opponent into a position where they are forced to place a symbol in an empty space in such a way that gives you access to a cell that allows you a favorable position, or you might play defensively and play what seems like a nonsensical move, or even throw away a winning line, but in doing so prevent your opponent from gaining a decisive victory.
This isn't tic-tac-toe anymore. This is chess. It's chess at breakneck speed, it's a strategic knife fight that takes no prisoners, and ramps up in tension, two -good- players can quickly become entangled in multiple complicated dances with several cells on the cusp of victory or defeat and then a game of hopscotch ensues as each player tries to maneuver each other into a position where the opponent is forced into giving ground.
And it's free. Emphasis -
Find a friend, someone who likes mind-games, invite them for a game of "ultimate" tic tac toe, get a hot tasty beverage, and prepare to lose an evening as you engage in what will be the most tense evening of strategy that ranks up alongside the very best games of Chaos Reborn and X-COM.
... and it's Tic-Tac-Toe. What has this world come to.

Dungeonland...how am I Supposed to describe it? First off, it is hard, especially in singleplayer. This game is all about teamwork, because even the death of a single one of the trio (Mage, Warrior, Rouge, the classy combination) can cause the GROUP to lose! Whilst some might rant and yell about this being unfair, it is actually forcing you to keep wary of your actions, because every single mistake is punished by the game.
The classes, even the warrior, have LOW health and die very fast, which means this is not a run n' gun sort of arcade game. This is, especially in the higher difficulcies (with ADDITIONAL handicaps for pure torture that are optional), enforcing teamplay because the group has a shared 1-Up pool that is empty after 1 Wipe in general. On the other hand the Heroes can power up and kill enemies rapidly, unless a boss shows up for a tough time. This factor of random spawning is even more fun (and with "fun" I mean lethal) in the Dungeonmaster Mode. Here can a fourth player take the role of the guy behind the scenes by spawning monsters, traps, towers, use spells etc. This is fairly balanced though and the system is throught up throughly and in my opinion a good base for MANY eventful Hours in Co-Op with a DM.
Lastly, there is just one negative thing I need to bring up, the low amount of content, which again is different with every difficulcy and additional handicaps. A fifth map is slated as "Coming soon" and there is a HIGH chance of a lot of content getting added some time after launch (aka NOW). My recommendation is, that if you have friends (two or three of them) and if you are resistant against frustrating moments, then you should consider this game as an alternative for a fast-paced arcade Co-Op game, which also allows you to be the one for once who is in charge of all the goons of the place.
tl;dr A fast-paced arcade RPG Game for three to four friends that is ranging from hard to brutal in terms of difficulcy and allows to control the monsters yourself for once. Not a lot of content, more to come though and therefore I rate it with a 4/5 and a 8.5/10

I first played Dark Messiah way back when it first came out and it's a game I have constantly revisited over the years.
While I've sunk more hours total into any given Elder Scrolls game I've played, Dark Messiah by far holds my personal record of total completed playthroughs at too many to count but at least several dozen.
I keep coming back to it to try out new skill/weapon combos and novelty character builds and keep finding new little hidden stuff even after years of replaying and knowing the game essentially by heart at this point.
Therefore it's my personal nominee for the 2016 "Test of time" award.
By the way, this review is solely for the single player part of the game. The multiplayer part was a publisher-mandated hackjob that nobody wanted and I don't think anybody ever played or mentioned ever, period. Except maybe to highlight unneccesary publisher-mandated multiplayer mode hackjobs that nobody asked for.
On the technical side of things, Dark Messiah is an first-person action game in the fantasy setting of the turn based strategy games Heroes of Might and Magic, which I know bugger all about apart from this game.
Not that you need to anyway, if you've consumed any sort of fantasy media in your life, you are familiar enough with the the setting.
The game runs on Half Life 2's Source Engine and takes the same almost fetishistic joy in physics shenanigans and environment elements ready to be used to your advantage.
To my friends I often semi-ironically refer to it as the best game ever made based solely on the fact that it's an ego-perspective game where you play an actual character with a full body rather than a floating pair of hands attached to an invisible hitbox.
However this actually does hold some water. If you play other first-person games lacking full player character body after this, special mention going to Dishonored from the same studio (essentially an immensely watered down version of the stealth approach to gameplay in Dark Messiah, down to the same bugged up rope climbing controls), you'll see just how much immersion a full character model adds.
The game has RPG elements, allowing you to earn and invest skill points rather freely into classic Fighter/Mage/Rogue skills to finetune your playstyle. I find nearly every character build to be viable although some are definitely more broken than others.
There's several weapon classes (sword, daggers, combat staff, bow and arrow) with distinct combat differences, 10 spells (including Gravity Gun telekineses) many of which have additional or secondary functions (ice magic can freeze enemies as well as create slippery slopes on the floor if you feel like re-enacting Loony Toons routines with your enemies), stealth is almost always a possible option and then of course there's the environment kills and your almighty kick to the enemy's groin. You know what, I'm not even going to talk about those last two, just watch five minutes of a compilation on Youtube or something.
"Class mixing" is easily done and viable, but the real nice thing is that in any case one skill path doesn't neccessarily exclude you from anything else. Focusing on fighting also gives you access to decent daggers and staffs and the other way around, any build can use magic through collectable one-use-each scrolls, some weapons have magic extra effects, etc.
The levels are varied and decently sized with tons of hidden areas and bonus objectives, although the route of plot progression in itself is rather linear.
Speaking of plot, it's nothing special and about as unconventional and surprising as a harlequin romance novel.
The game is definitely not without problems. While the most glaring ones from the early days have since been patched out there's still numerous bugs concerning crashes, glitching through walls, (occassional) framerate problems, save data not being found, exiting the game resulting in a crash which basically means you might as well exit through the Task Manager to begin with, and more. The entire reason I own this game on Steam is that in the original version there were some issues that were easiest resolved by re-installing which I ended up doing so often my disk just gave out (however, this in turn is just another point towards the game's immensely addicting qualities).
The balancing can be wonky, weapon variety could be better and the sporadic platforming might turn some people off (being able to see your feet does help immensely though).
At 5 bucks and even less when on sale it's an absolute steal for an unjustly forgotten gem of a game.
Oh, one last thing:
Everybody always talks about bad console-to-PC ports of games but if you ever want to see the reverse look no further than the horrendously butchered console version of this game. Damn, feels good to be PC Master Race.

I immediately thought about this game as my "Test of time" award pick. I have bought it when it came out and loved it, then I played it a few years ago to "master" it and it was still amazing. Few months ago I had some free time so I decided to come back and play a bit - which ended in a full playthrough. What makes this game stand the test of time so well is its amazingly satisfying combat system - especially on higher difficulty setting. It's brutal, fast paced, it requires you to use the enviroment and look out for your stamina. And I have to mention again - it's extremely satisfying.
When you fight off a ghoul pack... dancing around like crazy, kicking, parrying, making the best out of opportunities to attack, trading off space around you for some time to regain stamina, trying not to get surrounded and looking for a good place to attack from... and then its over. Then you realise it was only a few seconds since the fight started and now you find yourself surrounded by corpes. The feeling is glorious. I will surely play this game again in some time.
*MILD SPOILER* My favorite fight is the one where you enter the city, you find Duncan and then you have to fight a necromancer and a bunch of ghouls. Trying to keep Duncan alive in this fight on the high difficulty is so madly difficult, ghouls kill him in one hit if he doesn't manage to block and there are few waves of them, coming at you from different angles. It's very frustrating but also very satisfying whenever you find a way to get a bit closer to keeping Duncan alive. I should probably say that you don't have to keep him alive and it has 0 influence on the story... It actually seems like the SHOULD die here (your character says a line when he dies), but if you are determined enough, he can be saved. I mean... we like challenges, right? :D

Then the Alpha 8.9 update. The Alpha 8.9 update added long awaited vehicles such as American Logies, Transports, Crow/Manned Turret HMMWVs and the Striker. Militia and Insurgents got Logistics, MG, Recoilless rocket and Transport Technicals. These new vehicles make for a new faster more dynamic gameplay and yet the game is still very balanced and FUN AS HELL!
Now for the cons. Now I understand that Squad is in Alpha and most problems will/have been fixed but here are some I am experiencing right now.
1. Server browser menu: Gliches out when reloaded, no favorites or history so its hard to find a server you've recently played on.
2.Destructable surroundings. This is a HUGE problem with the vehicles, this problem lets small trees and bushes stop a 30 ton vehicle instantly when realistically they should plow right through them.

Overall the game is very solid and has beautiful graphics. You MUST keep in mind that this game is in Alpha stage of development so it's only getting better. I would defenately reccommend buying the game but when it's on sale cuz regular price is expensive AF BOIIIIIIIIIIIII

Do not buy this as a substitute for bonafide home design software, which runs from 50 - 100 dollars, and probably (and hopefully) has about 5 to 10 times the amount of functionality this budget software has.
HD3d lacks a lot of simple stuff: ability to lock placed objects/walls/plots, ability to make multiple levels, ability to export plans, not to mention some inherant bugginess.
That being said, despite the mixed reviews, I figured 1.50 USD was worth it at least just to have a program I didn't have to open in a browser. I assume everything is to scale, so there is some basic merit to planning out your dream home - especially if you are nowhere near the stages of building it. While THE SIMS has the monopoly on furnishings and whatnot, you can get a basic idea of dimensions, measurements and by the time you're ready to splurge on actual design software, you should have a good handle on both your ideas and how to operate the program.
The program is simple, honestly too simple to use for my tastes, keeping menus and text to a minimum and having de/selection based around double clicking. Fine for 2D design, but when your software has a complex component like 3D building, your interface should keep up with the change in complications.
Bottom line - Not worth the 10 bucks it usually goes for. I'd say max I'd pay is 5 bucks, for a decent conduit for brainstorming what to build down the line.

♥♥♥♥in' LOVE this game. It's like a first-person only ArmA game except much easier in terms of controls, with easy accessibility and not very hard to understand, except for certain roles like Squad Leader that are 90% just communication with the team and guiding people, or the "Scout" class which requires a whole different style of play than the normal rifleman, favoring a stealth approach over a direct one.
All kits use a standard loadout, namely; A primary weapon, an offhand pistol, frag grenades, smoke grenades, medkit, and a shovel. Binoculars to marksmen, scouts and squad leaders, and squad leaders also don't have shovels.
Basically, this game is squad leaders telling people to shovel stuff like build fortifications etc, while squaddies just follow orders or request stuff like vehicles, things built or giving tips on approaches. There's usually one general in every game, and sometimes there's more than one and they start to argue and hate each other but that's fine, I still always manage to have a good time with my own squad.
This game is extremely social and, if your experience is anything like mine, you will most likely become absolute best friends for 2 hours+ with some completely random people online from other countries.
My best experience in this game is the first free weekend I ever played the game, creeping behind enemy lines (As a scout ofc) along with another stray member of the squad who just felt like the squad we were in were completely in the wrong place at the wrong time all the time so we took things into our own hands.
We watched enemies pour from the "Castle" outpost, I forget the map name but I believe it's the northernmost outpost on a forested, hilly map, as I looked through my binoculars and told him that I saw people spawning from the castle bunker. We were communicating in direct chat and got constant updates on our squad's movements and the general situation in their area so we knew if we had to fall back or relocate. We proceeded to the bunker and it was heavily fortified, as a FOB (Forward Operating Base, lets you build fortifications in a radius around it and spawn on it) had been placed inside it. We creeped up and there were 3 guys who hadnt seen us yet, I waited for my friend and then we coordinately gunned them down together. We shoveled up the barbed wire and went inside, then we came into a little shed with a strange radio (The FOB), and we both had no idea what to do, asking the squad and getting so-so communication from them so I layed ontop of the bunker trying to defend it, which I heroically did for a while, gunning people as they tried to leap across the field from us like I was a Soviet Officer gunning down deserters. After a while my american friend had figured out how to neutralize the FOB, which was by taking out the shovel and using right mouse button, and the camp was neutralized. I was shot in the head and screamed out in the microphone as I took my final breath. Then I told him it was ♥♥♥♥in awesome playing with you man, hopefully I'll see you on the other side of the map and we both took our farewells as I respawned. Our team rounded up the last enemies spawning from the Castle and the battle was won completely on that side of the map, neutralizing a key point and allowing the team to win. I saw my friend later on and we had a great time the next game and the game after that aswell.

so, as a person whose name is alex (though it is a very common name), the protagonist of this game resonates with me already. and as a person who has over 50 hours clocked on this game, has been in the community since before the game's release, owns a discord server with 430+ members dedicated to the game, helped build the fandom/wikia and gamepedia, is an admin/moderator on the subreddit, and was privileged with experiencing the arg associated with the game and building relationships with people as obsessed with the game as i am to the point where i was granted the alias "void mom" in the community, i am shocked and appalled that i have yet to write a review until now. so without further ado, here is every thought i can muster about this game. it will be split into headings for easy reading, so don't worry.
from the
:
as a
myself (joking, sort of), the opening few words have my interest. the description goes on to say that the game surrounds an "overnight island party gone horribly wrong." if you don't like angsty teen drama, then this is probably where some people jump ship, but bear with me here. on the steam
the game is tagged as
,
, and
. i typically look for these same tags when finding more cool indie games to play, so seeing all three of them applied to this one game was very convincing for me.
the gameplay largely consists of walking, and utilizing radio frequencies to interact with objects. a highly, highly common complaint that i will see about this game whilst browsing the steam discussions is that the game contains a
of walking. and for people who enjoy action-based games or simply want to complete the game quickly, i can see how this quality would cause some frustration. however, i would not say that all the walking is for no reason. OXENFREE strives to be very lifelike and realistic, and usually life consists of a lot of walking around. which gets really boring, i know. but many of these sequences of travel between map areas also consist of opportunities to talk to characters, which provide you with opportunities to potentially change the way a character might feel about alex or another character. these decisions ultimately sum up to certain endings. plus, it's more lore. however, not everyone will be interested in that.
that brings me to another gameplay functionality: the choice-based dialogue system. this is fairly straight-forward. a character speaks to you, and you select a dialogue option to respond with. at certain times, certain dialogue options will influence the way a character feels about alex or another character. you can tell when this happens by a small thought-bubble that appears above a character's head, containing an icon of another character. it is not indicated whether or not this change in opinion is positive or negative, and so it is up to the player to assume. also in regards to the dialogue system, there is a point where, if no dialogue choice is selected, the dialogue bubbles will disappear and characters will usually comment on alex's silence, which can, at times, affect character relationships. this is an obstacle for some, as the player might feel rushed to choose an option, or might not have enough time to read and select one. however, again playing off of the "realistic" quality of OXENFREE, real-life conversations are very fluid and instinctual, and there is no moment where you can "pause" to select what to say. you just kind of say it. though, thinking-and-saying comes more naturally to a person than reading-then-thinking-then-saying.
moving onto game length, an average first-time playthrough will take approximately 4-5 hours, since it will take time to figure out where/what all the areas are and how they connect since the map provided in-game is not 100% accurate to where the character stands and how the actual island is laid out. collecting all anomalies and adler letters may increase that time estimate. having memorized the island's layout and locations of collectibles, i've reduced this to about 45 minutes to an hour.
if anything about this game really impresses the people that play it, it is absolutely the story. as mentioned earlier, the game surrounds a seventeen year old girl named alex, who has brought her new step-brother jonas to an overnight island party gone wrong. this doesn't seem like that intense of an experience, until you uncover the "hidden chronicle" of edwards island. without getting too spoilery, there is a reason why this game is also sometimes categorized as "psychological horror." the game does not utilize outright jumpscare-y techniques to frighten the player (however, ng+ is a different story). rather, the game uses a more unnerving and unsettling approach, playing with sight and sound to creep the player out juuust enough.
besides the psychological horror aspect, the other thing this game does very well is the raw, visceral, believable characters and emotion. the voice-acting is very well-done, and each person in the game sounds almost
real and interact like real teenagers do. and going further beyond this, the game plays a lot with character backstories, particularly alex's (which, again without getting too spoilery, proved to be a very emotional experience for me and still is to this day).
in general, the writing is phenomenal and i would like to personally thank Adam Hines for writing the paranormal teen drama of my dreams. there's even tons of world war ii history (with some...
, we'll say) incorporated into it. this game is almost every interest of mine packaged into one indie game. another one of these interests would be puzzle-solving, which this game also does well without being too challenging.
i absolutely love the art in this game. it's not as polished or detailed as some games out there, but it has a charm that makes it just perfect for the story it's telling and the atmosphere it creates. Heather Gross did a fantastic job designing the characters with pleasing color schemes and diverse appearances and styles. also, the characters just look so dang cute and expressive in the polaroids. the environment also looks incredible and perfectly moody for what the game entails, and every tiny detail looks so lovingly crafted.
i'd have to say that behind the story, the soundtrack is likely the next thing to really make people fall in love with the game. Andrew Rohrmann, known by his artist alias scntfc, used both analog (
radio and reel-to-reel sound effects!) and digital sound to create a moody, atmospheric, and pleasant soundtrack. each and every track eventually becomes easily recognizeable and can elicit some extreme emotion sometimes (see: Days Past). some tracks also contain some oddities and secrets, such as morse code, or audio bits that can only be heard after some audio manipulation.
seeing as this review is lengthy as it is, i'll get to a final verdict.
i highly recommend OXENFREE to anyone with an interest in story-driven games, the paranormal, angsty teens, choice-based dialogue systems, world war ii history, and Stranger Things vibes.
and in closing, i would like to thank Night School Studio for making my favorite game ever, and just being a super cool developer team in general. you guys rock.

A wonderful milsim lite with meaningful updates and good developers. A game heavily focused on teamwork, communication and immersion. However, potential buyers beware, parts of the community are -extremely- unforgiving towards new players.

After you've played thirty seconds you've had the full experience. This game is extremely grindy, extremely repetative, and worst of all, extremely broken. Traps that kill you in a single hit, exp systems that are laughably unbalanced, and bugs galore. Stay away from this pile of garbage.

The combat is extremely fun, the enviroments are very well done and extremely pleasant to look at, and the gameplay itself is really a blast. Ultimately, this game is awesome. However, a major complaint I have is how often the game has to interupt you, throwing off the pacing, in order to retrieve children's toys at your resistence HQ, watch a virtually meaningless cutscenes, or engage in chit chat dialogue with the members of your team. The game really fails to make you care about the characters, yet goes on and on about them and their struggles. More often than not for the cutscenes I was left saying, "Who cares?" It's like the game knows you're really getting into the gameplay and combat and has to say "Hold up there, champ. Looks like you're having too much fun. Here's a cutscene followed by walking around your HQ to calm you down...."
Maybe that's something you care about, but I know personally I really care about a story that isn't fed to you and is left for you to discover through logs and the enviroment.
That, and performance issues are my only complaints. I needed a mod in order to get more than 60FPS, and when the mod was enabled a few areas throughout the game did not load correctly. This was an easy fix, restarting at the latest check point and hitting * on my numpad to turn it off but it was annoying the game did not natively have this feature.
Overall, the game is really a blast, the combat is very fun, the weapon mechanics work very well, the enviroments really are well set up. For the five dollars I got this game for on sale, it was exceptional.
If you like racing games and fun with friends, this is a awesome game, even if you play it alone too. :x
