Right ... since this program actually lists itself under the games section and the developers blatantly refuse to move it to the programs section despite repeated request, I'll rate this program as a game.
This has got to be one of the most boring games in existence. I've walked through the same rooms forever and there has not been one single enemy spawn yet. No monsters! No terrorists! No goblins that want to nibble at your toes. No hot alien vixens with rocket launchers. Not even a spider or rat to stomp on ...
The lack of enemies to fight is luckily not too bad, because it conveniently hides one of the other drawbacks of the game: the game balance is completely out of the window. I have not found any guns ... ever! What if a dinosaur with an AK47 where to appear all of a sudden? I would be dead in a second. The player is just way too underpowered and the difficulty level is completely over the top. Seriously, this game really needs a balancing pass.
The game does not even explain you anything. How the hell do I finish the first level? They could at least include a tutorial or a readme.txt file.
Also, the level design is pretty boring. No stairs, no elevators ... everything is placed on the same level. It feels like I'm thrown back 30 years in time and playing Catacombs-3D or one of the other early FPS.
As a matter of fact, the game requires you to design your own levels before you can even play. If I pay for a game I expect something that I can play out of the box. It's not even like Terraria where you get a basic level that serves as a sandbox, no, the game literally gives you emptiness and you have to start from scratch! How lazy can a game developer get?
Then there is the engine: while it at least runs fluidly, the engine is otherwise pretty poor. Graphics are only so-so and there are basically zero special effects. Volumetric lighting? Nope. Bump mapping? Nope. Any form of AA? Nope. AF? Nope. Blur? Nope. Bloom? Nope. HDR? Nope. Again, it feels like I'm playing something from the very early nineties. Even Doom had flashing lights, this game has nothing. Not even a nice parallax skybox.
Sound? Music? Forget about all that.
My conclusion is that this is an early tech-demo of an FPS in alpha status. At least the developer releases updates once in a while, so maybe it will one day be playable but in its current state it is NOT worth full price … or any price. Why is this not marked as an early access game????

HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥WAS I SURPISED.
This game doesn't have anything to do with Sonic (aside from including him and the cast as characters...among cooler characters), it's just a balls-to-the-wall  come-get-some cart racer.  I don't think I've ever played a cart racer that felt so damned... HARDCORE.  The characters are all varyed but fairly balanced, the maps get absolutely insane, ranging from peaceful mario-kartish maps to nightmares from hell and beyond worst than anything the Rainbow Road could dream up.  And you get to enjoy all of these things not just from a Driver's Seat, but from a Cockpit and from a Captain's chair as well!
The game is hard.  Even playing alone in world tour mode on "Easy" presents some challenge.  And it'll take you a good bit of practice to beat those same races on "Normal".  Step into multiplayer?  You better be prepared for a stomping, because those kids don't mess around.
I give this game a solid 8/10.  It would be a 10/10, but the marketing department loses 2 points for not letting me know I should have been playing this sooner.
BUY THIS GAME NOW.  Is it full price?  Then buy it.  Is it on sale?  Then buy a few extra copies for some friends of yours.  You won't regret it.

BL1 is a FPS enjoyable, fun to play, into a wild world where one can do whatever wants; weapons work fast, vehicles are easily mouse controlled; all is fast and responsive; it has a sadist touch at places; at I had no technical problem installing and using at a PC with single-playing. For me the best is the replay value, since it keeps the interest even when you already know it, playing as another character type, or as multiplayer, up to more 3 players. Youtube videos support any doubt about game-play and are a warranty no one gets stuck in the story line or at hard places. Believe me you get the most by playing the game as single player, up to discovering The Vault. Not all objectives need to be made as soon they are listed, some are intended you to come back. Sure one can get a help going multiplayer at hard places - setting your host name as “help” - but all are possible without others help, if you dare. This game is very valuable in hours, it can endure for months, and still be fun.
I had difficulties setting the Internet play working due to the need for router port forwarding settings, who were solved within the last updates - so Gearbox says. Sound and micro control is not very flexible, but work. Steam support has all the answers, an advantage of this being a game with some years.
Another top value for me is the instant rewarding system, a novelty for me at the time: every thing one makes right or achieve counts, literally, I mean, the count is visible in a perfect playable way. This itself can be interesting as a kind of wild economic system. The leveling system, the better weapons access, are truly effective for player motivation. And the story, nevertheless fable, is good enough to keep going for more, until The Vault.
I found after replaying BL1 more than a dozen times there were still new ways to explore it, finding some map paths, mods and even some community made maps, around a project named Oasis. The first wave of Borderlands I players, more than 3 years ago, were enthusiastic up to that point, yes. Unfortunately game updates made the access to those maps complicated and even technically not recommended as it can trash your saved games or crash the game. I just can hope one day that will be taken care by Gearbox, as a reward .
One of my greatest surprises were the extend of the maps outside the playable area, I mean, all those landscape are actual ground a player can walk into knowing some secret paths shown at youtube videos. I would love a BL1 revisited version could just open those access, mainly at the best DLC ever made: The Secret Armory of General Knoxx (level 50 recommended) . That and some modifications would make it re-interesting.
I saw too many players losing the value of the game by going too early multiplayer, where too high players make all the work for them, or getting some cheated modifications. My advice is first go at The Vault, alone. Then you will have another opportunity to play. Mods are another way to keep the interest. An advice: keep some saves from the lower levels. And please, never spoil a new player game by helping too much. The Steam 4 GOTY editions pack is a very good gift for your FPS friends. Nevertheless, again, do it alone the first time, It is worthy, if you dare! :-)

AI: Cassandra Classic, Rough with Permadeath on Crashlanded
This is the ongoing saga of:
Miu, a defector good with guns and medicine.
Zebo, a builder and green thumb.
Mac, a scientist who dabbles in the culinary arts.
After crash landing, our survivors take their belongings to a valley close by. Two large hills provide some natural protection, but the south flank is left completely exposed. Our survivors have a lot of work ahead of them if they want to make this valley a safe settlement.
Miu and Mac bring Zebo building materials and soon enough, Zebo has built a solid foundation for the colony. A roofed stockpile is kept just outside of individual rooms connected to a fair sized rec room built into the side of a hill. 3 Solar Panels charge 6 batteries connected to all the appliances in the rec room and a small freezer is built to house food supplies.
During the day, Zebo tends to his crops and small construction projects. Miu hunts and hauls. Mac stays glued to the research bench Zebo built in his room, only coming out to cook and eat meals. Raids are few and pose little threat.
As fall comes around, Jase, a barkeep, joins the colony. His skill in medicine outmatches Miu's and he's an even better cook than Mac. Our colonists welcome him and Jase quickly becomes a vital part of the community. Soon enough, both east and west flanks of the valley have been sealed by stone walls and doors while Zebo begins building defenses on the southern flank. Thanks to Mac's tireless efforts, the colony is able to build their first auto turret before winter and it easily fends off following raids. One summer day, Zebo proposes to Miu after only being together for 15 days or so, and she miraculously accepts. A marriage date is set in the near future. (So they can get to know each other better XD) Well before winter rolls around, the fridge has been expanded and is stocked with food. A geothermal generator powers a wall of turrets surrounded in sandbags to the south and a secondary wall of turrets powered by wind turbines lay to the north as a final line of defense. Daphne, our husky is pregnant with doggos and our colonists are confident and hopeful.
But not for long.
Raids quickly become more dangerous and the southern defenses require constant repair and rebuilding. Injuries are common, but luckily, no one sustains a fatal blow. As snow begins to fall, a massive volcanic eruption covers the planet in ash, killing all of Zebo's crops and lowering the temperature further. Luckily, our colonists are well prepared with warm clothing and food. Following an especially dangerous raid on the southern defenses, Zebo and Miu decide they cannot wait any longer and marry in the rec room amongst their fellow colonists. Everyone celebrates and as the marriage ceremony ends, thats when
A HERD OF 8 MANHUNTER MUFFALO appear on the horizon and head straight for the eastern entrance to the valley. On the way, they mercilessly slaughter a visiting group of tribals armed with nothing but clubs. They burst through the Eastern door and charge toward the colonists who scramble back into the rec room..only to be followed by Daphne, who reveals their location to two of the herd. The Muffalo start to beat down the wooden door that hides the colonists, but luckily turn away at the last moment. Zebo springs into action and repairs the door by repurposing the wooden stools in the area. Mac goes to his hi-tech research bench to bury himself in books and Jase calms his nerves at the tailoring bench. The colonists are safe for the moment.
After spending an inordinate amount of time arguing over where to stay (the zone mechanics are tricky to a newbie) the colonists agree to stay in the rec room and let Zebo deconstruct the walls that block off their individual rooms so that everyone can at least spend the night in their own beds. As Zebo finishes deconstructing the walls, Daphne beelines for a door in one of the rooms. Before the colonists can call her back, she's run outside and the nearest Muffalo sees Zebo. With a guttural roar, the Muffalo charges to the wooden door and beats on it ferociously as the colonists back away from the door. * SMASH*
The Muffalo is in! Screaming, the colonists flee to the last bastion of safety: the freezer.
They barely make it in as the Muffalo reaches the door, splintering the wood as it attempts to break through. Gun's at the ready, the colonists prepare for their end.. Yet somehow, the door holds! The Muffalo bores of banging its head and backs away to wander the rec room, leaving our colonists trapped in the freezer. Shivering in the cold, their only solace is the  the fact that they won't starve to death. Ironically, death by starvation seemed a far preferable choice over the stampeding Muffalo that now roamed the colony. Eventually, the colonists calm themselves down enough to sleep.
The next day, Zebo carefully tears a hole in the wall separating the fridge from the nearest room, and the colonists are able to take shifts sleeping in the bed there. They spend the day talking amongst themselves and dine on a stash of fine meals to keep their spirits high. As day three in the freezer comes around, the muffalo's rage subsides and they fall asleep just outside the rec room. Zebo quickly reseals the broken-down door and begins to fortify the area, while the colonists happily leave the freezer.. when suddenly the comms console makes a garbling noise and a transmission begins to play:
"MAYDAY MAYDAY! ANYONE OUT THERE PLEASE RESPOND!!! MY NAME IS CETI AND IM UNDER ATTACK BY MERCENARIES OF THE DEADLY SHANKERS!!" (the faction is actually called this)
Upon hearing the voice, Jase sprints to the console and issues a response:
"Mother?!! Is that really you!?!? It's me, Jase! Come to these coordinates and we'll provide you with shelter!"
The other colonists echo their support, forgetting the rampaging Muffalo just outside their doors for a brief moment.
"Thank you so much!! I'm heading to your coordinates now! *after a brief pause* It's good to hear from you son."
Too excited at the prospect of seeing his mother again, Jase cuts the comm link before remembering to warn Ceti about the Muffalo herd! Sensing more humans in the distance, the herd awakens and heads straight for Ceti..
She sees the clouds of dust from the stampeding Muffalo before she sees them. But by the time she realizes what's happening, there's no where for her to go and Ceti realizes she's trapped. That's when the mercenaries arrive behind her and true to their name, shiv her near to death. Leaving her to bleed out, the merc group from the Deadly Shankers proceeds to mow down the Muffalo herd and head for the southern defenses of the colony.
The colonists are able to fend off the brunt of the Deadly Shankers force, capturing one and killing two including their captain before the others flee. Seeing that his mother has yet to return, Jase sets off to rescue his mother while the others stay behind to assess the damage. Jase reaches his mother, the last of her life trickling away..
Ceti dies in Jase's arms..
Ceti's funeral is short. Jase says nothing other than revealing her profession as a botanist. She's buried by the flowers in Zebo's crops.
Following the Muffalo rampage and Ceti's death, there was much work to be done by the colonists. Jase could not keep up with the workload, and combined with the death of his mother, he succumbed to several mental breaks where he wandered the colony aimlessly, foregoing sleep and food. Each time, he was dragged to a hospital bed by Miu and tended to until he got better, but during one of his mental breaks, Jase caught malaria..
Miu did everything she could, but for all her efforts, Jase had always been twice the doctor she was, and he quickly succumbed to the disease, dying in a coma and extreme pain.
The colonists bury him next to his mother..

Strife pits two teams of players against each other, both teams are based at opposite corners of the map in their respective bases. Bases consist of one central structure, creep spawn points, three generators and a hero spawning pool. The goal of the game is to destroy the central structure of the opposite base, called the "Crux".
Players achieve this by selecting heroes with unique skills to combat the other team, both teams can select the same heroes. Each game, a player chooses one hero to be for the duration of the match. Every hero has four abilities that may be acquired and upgraded as the hero gains experience and levels up. Heroes abilities are often very similar to the ones of the characters of several other MOBA games.

This is one of the most absurd fighting games I've ever played, but in a good way. You literally can only use two buttons throughout the entire experience (even to browse menus and confirm selections). The gist of the game is this; you jump, you kick. Different characters will kick at different speed and angles. A power up meter is charged by kicking. Unleashing it (by pressing both buttons at once) will execute a character-specific special move. The simple-sounding system becomes very strategic as you try to anticipate and counter opponent's movements. The one-shot-kill nature of the combat adds unexpected levels of stress. The art is okay, but the animation is fantastic. This is a must-buy (when on sale) for some ridiculous fun.

Castle Crashers, the most simple beat 'em up that  will never bore you. With a large variety of characters ranging from a necromancer to a murder-crazed-bear with all unique abilities the game is as replayable as can be. Although an experienced player could complete the game in about 5-7 hours, you can really take all the time in the world, farming for pets, weapons and experiance, all of which there is alot of. Often with beat 'em ups there is a dull feeling after you have killed people for the millionth time, but due to the levelling and combo systems, the game is never dull and the way you fight can change depending on the weapons you use, the character you pick, what you upgrade and the pets you use. For example you could use your experiance to make you character a melee knight with alot of damage or defence. Alternatley some may prefer to use magic attacks or archery. This dynamic makes the game great for multiplayer, co-op or online, often i find myself using archery skills to defend my melee knight friends from a distance. Despite this it can definitley be fun to just sit back and play it by yourself as the game is very simple and in some instances you can play it thoughtlessly. With that said there is also an "Insane Mode" which is hard even for the most seasoned experienced player. But in insane mode there are 4 characters you can unlock by reaching far stages of the game, as well as this at the end of (almost) any playthrough of the game with every charcter, you unlock a new one, this encourages the player to replay and gives you more reasons to keep plaing the game. The pet system is also a complex thing that gives you another way to change the way you play, there are many pets and you unlock them through either finding them in a level, or buying them at a shop. These pets can give you abilities from shooting fireballs to jumping higher, there is a character for every playstyle and its fun to switch them up every once in a while.
As a final opinion, Castle Crashers is personally my favourite game of all time and I think it could easily be yours. 10/10.

This game was a huge part of my childhood. As I grew up, I began to forget about this game. Years went by, then I suddenly remembered, and wondered if I would ever get the chance to play it again. Enter TERC, who have released this remake of the original title, Logical Journey of the Zoombinis (1996).  Yes, this is a game for children, but I so happened to play this game for years as a kid. Due to that, I just had to purchase this title upon immediately seeing it had released.
From an adult perspective, the puzzles aren't too challenging, but you may not know what to do straight off the bat. From there, it won't take too long to figure out. If a child is playing this (depending on their age bracket), I'm sure they'll spend a decent amount of time on each puzzle, probably asking for assistance along the way - I know I did when I was younger. Hopefully they'll learn a thing or two along the way. And, if it gets too easy, there are various difficulty settings you can bump the game up to.
The developers of this remake have kept to the games roots in terms of the audio, with the dialogue, score, and sound effects remaining the same from the original game. It's definitely noticeable, however it's a nice throwback and it adds to the nostalgia. From the visual side of things, the game has received a nice graphical upgrade.
I probably won't play this for lengthy periods of time at once, but I will boot it up for when I want to remember those good times as a kid. I don't remember completing this game as a child, so it'll be nice to go back and achieve that.
This is a charming and well made remake. Kudos to TERC.

Perhaps the crowning achievement of Broderbund and the edutainment genre -- shortly before it collapsed into shovelware limbo -- Zoombinis is a pretty simple title designed to teach kids puzzle-based pattern recognition and analytical thinking. It's basic enough for an eight-year old but has enough foundation and staying power to still be a fun diversion to me two decades later. The difficulty scales up gradually the more Zoombinis you manage to get from start to finish, to the point where things get legitimately REALLY DIFFICULT to solve. Now if only we could get Alien Tales the modern treatment!
As far as port jobs go, this one seems pretty bang-up at first glance, but the threads start to show under closer scrutiny.
+ Everything's redrawn for HD support while staying pretty faithful to the original.
+ All the old voices and music clips are there in their 90's low-fi glory.
+ Seems reasonably well optimized and stable.
~ Newly redrawn scenery has bizarre choices of colour pallette, apparently in the name of making things seem less cheery and more adventurous. Some of them are pretty nice, at least.
- No manual or instructions for any of the games.
- Apart from the Zoombinis themselves, most of the other character sprites are clearly low-effort traces of the original animation cels.
- Loads of sound effects missing.
- Titanic Tattooed Toads, which was already the weakest point of the game, is now drawn out AND lacking almost any animation.
- Some pretty serious glitches, like difficulty never advancing, not being able to interact with the Zoombinis on Mirror Machine, and Bubblewonder Abyss generating unsolvable layouts.
- English is the only spoken language available, where the original was typically also available in French and German. This may not be of huge significance to those playing it for nostalgia, but the game was a great incentive as part of a second-language curriculum for children and now that aspect is gone.
That being said, the underlying framework holds up well and it's a nice nostalgia trip that I would recommend. I just hope it gets some much-needed patching.

2006, arguably the heyday of PC gaming. Few first-person games got the mechanics so right as Dark Messiah did.  Built on the Source Engine, it pulls everything Half Life 2 had going for it into itself.
- You have a body visible in first-person view! Look down! I have feet!
- Telekinesis allows for "gravity gun" fun! And other spells for messing with the locals!
- Duke Nukem's Mighty Boot, for punting Goblins off cliffs to your delight! Ahhh the screams!
- The Rope Bow! When most games were consigned to stairs and ladders, you could go anywhere!*
- Scripted events done right! With huge monsters and huge weapons!
- Combat any way you want! Stealth, magic, a massive sword! Did I mention the Mighty Boot??
-Mild RPG elements like upgrading your weapons/armour and spending skill points in skill trees (more like Bonsai trees, but still fun!)
- Be Good or Evil! Multiple endings based on your choices throughout the game!
- First-Person combat unmatched before or since! This is how the Elder Scrolls should have done it!!! Watch the vids, kids!
Pros:
LOTS! (It's five bucks as of this review too!)
Cons:
A matter of opinion. Find them all! Don't forget your jaded self is living 10 years into this game's existence. Everything seen here was first!*

Overall, my impression of the game is that it's fun.  There are a couple things that are unfun about it, which I would like to see changed in a future release.
1. Upon defeating the boss monster of an area, there's no clear indication of what the player is supposed to do next.  So I wandered around for a minute before discovering that a relic had dropped, and that I could enter a portal.
2.  Pressing "P" brings up a menu that allows you to purchase various items: stat increases, healing potions, etc.  However, doing so does not pause the game, and it prevents you from doing anything.  Which leads to death.  I'd like to see the Purchase menu pause the game while the player interacts with it.
3. When traps and enemies come into contact with the player, they damage the player at an alarmingly fast rate.  One thing that would be helpful is a brief period of invulnerability after being hit.  It doesn't have to be very long; half a second would do fine.  It would prevent "insta-death" from traps like the floating spiky ball.
4. Speaking of which, after you defeat the boss of an area, it would be nice if the traps would deactivate.  One time I wasn't even able to get my relic before getting killed by the floaty spiky ball.
Overall, like I said, I like the game; it just feels kind of unfinished at the moment.  Fixing the above issues would go a long way towards making it feel more polished.

SASRT  (=Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed) might be a Mario Kart clone, but that doesn't stop it from blowing the original out of the water.
Where Mario Kart games can really feel like they're mostly based on luck, SASRT is mostly  based on skill, even though you can still get a good item that would help you get the upperhand, but even then, you'll still have to use it wisely and have the skill to do so, or it will be completely useless.
Where Mario Kart games' races can feel pretty uninspired, SASRT's races are a pretty great demonstration of intelligent level-design. Every single inch of the races are calculated to reward you if you're doing good and punish you if you screw up.
Where Mario Kart games pace can feel  boring, SART's pace will barely allow you some time to blink.
Where Mario kart games single-player will gladly leave you the  first place in any race on any difficulty setting and make sure the closest opponent stays a mile away from you, SASRT's AI will rather hunt you down and take you out like there's a billion dollars bounty on your head
And don't get me wrong, I love Mario kart, especially Double Dash on gamecube. But Sega's SASRT is just so good it makes Mario Kart games looks like they're the SASRT clones.

A single player puzzle game wich is more clever than first anticipated. It starts out easy enough and will eventually get more complex and complicated to solve, but as far as I've experienced not in a too steep way. It is a specific way of thinking though, so being away from the game for a while and then coming back requires some time to get your head wrapped around it again.
This game is clever in several ways though. The puzzles require you to evolve your thinking, and then there's small notes left from other players. On top of that there's the "voice in the sky", the creator or whatever it now can be that somewhat guides you, and finally it's the enviroment and setting: seems digitally created, but where does it end and what's actually behind?
In short, the game gives you not only puzzles, but some kind of mindplay as well as to the setting of the game, questioning what the games reality really is.
What really makes this game priceworthy though is the contents. There's puzzles to solve to propel the story or what it should be called, but also small bonus objectives to be fullfilled. On top of that you have the chance to leave your own (predefined) comments to players coming after you.

This is the least intuitive, least flexible, most under tested program I've ever purchased. Shift+click does not let you select multiple walls. Shift+move does not allow you to adjust an entire room keeping its original proportions. Instead you move one corner of the room regardless of which command key you press while moving a corner, making it impossible to easily manipulate rooms. You cannot place a room inside of another room, meaning that you have to put up individual walls, which also is not easy. You put up one wall with the intended length, and then the wall next to it magnet clips onto the INSIDE edge, meaning you have to add half the width of your wall to the length of the wall you're currently placing. This occurs irrespective of your choice of magnet clipping in the settings option. It should connect to the outside edge of the wall so that your inside measurement stays the same (this is particularly important for odd widths of walls since you cannot make walls through half inch intervals). To make matters worse, once two walls have connected against your will, they still have two different drag points, so moving the corner does not move both walls, once again making it impossible to easily adjust corners. Additionally, measurements do not update as you're dragging the wall, so you have to guess where the right placement is. Never purchase this program. Zero thought went into its production. Right clicking does nothing, when it could have added additional functionality. They obviously wanted the program to be highly flexible, but then don't make easy alternatives to painstaking and difficult modifications. Shift, cntrl, right click, any of these could have been utilized to successfully create a program that is both flexible and easy. They had obviously never used Photoshop or GIMP, which both have incredibly intuitive interfaces, from which these programmers could have learned. This program is a prime example of why you need not just UI programmers, but UX experts who design the program for the UI programmers to realize. 0/10.

The combat is extremely fun, the enviroments are very well done and extremely pleasant to look at, and the gameplay itself is really a blast. Ultimately, this game is awesome. However, a major complaint I have is how often the game has to interupt you, throwing off the pacing, in order to retrieve children's toys at your resistence HQ, watch a virtually meaningless cutscenes, or engage in chit chat dialogue with the members of your team. The game really fails to make you care about the characters, yet goes on and on about them and their struggles. More often than not for the cutscenes I was left saying, "Who cares?" It's like the game knows you're really getting into the gameplay and combat and has to say "Hold up there, champ. Looks like you're having too much fun. Here's a cutscene followed by walking around your HQ to calm you down...."
Maybe that's something you care about, but I know personally I really care about a story that isn't fed to you and is left for you to discover through logs and the enviroment.
That, and performance issues are my only complaints. I needed a mod in order to get more than 60FPS, and when the mod was enabled a few areas throughout the game did not load correctly. This was an easy fix, restarting at the latest check point and hitting * on my numpad to turn it off but it was annoying the game did not natively have this feature.
Overall, the game is really a blast, the combat is very fun, the weapon mechanics work very well, the enviroments really are well set up. For the five dollars I got this game for on sale, it was exceptional.

I've never bothered reviewing a game before since there tends to be hundreds if not thousands of reviews already but this game deserves as many prasies as it can get. If you have a craving for any kind of realistic military type experience in an FPS this is the alpha and the omega. Nothing i have ever played has come close to this ARMA of course being in 2nd place.
First off the game rewards those who join squads by only making specialized kits available to those in a squad. Kits like Marksman, Medic or Heavy MG. This makes everyone want to be grouped up to play which completely makes this game unique IMO.
Once in a squad all squad mates can easily communicate with each other through a 3 button in game system which works beautifully. You can speak with everyone in your squad over a "radio" or everyone around you with 15 feet or so. If you're a Squad Leader you can speak with all other squad leaders individually or all at the same time. Communication is the most important part of this game hands down.
I play in a group which includes a number of service vets from recent conflicts and they have all mentioned the amount of detail work that Offworld has put into the sound in this game. I've never been in combat but for me just the way your gunshot echoes back to you off the hill half a kilometer away will send shivers down your spine and when you're in a massive fire fight... its literally deafening. You can't hear your squad mates 5 feet away from you. I can't count how many times i've had to ask the guy next to me to stop firing the damn 50 cal. so i can talk to the other squad leaders 10/10 for sound design!
The graphics are great by any standard though personally i'm for gameplay over graphics so if you're picky don't take my opinion too seriously. When everything is cranked up to 10 this game really shines for me... Though its not fully optimized yet so its hard to run everything at full tilt.
The maps though currently limited in number don't feel that way at all. There are different game modes and multiple ways to play each map in each mode so the gameplay always feels fresh. Plus being able to build up a Forward Operating Base (FOB) which includes weapon emplacements and defenses like sandbag walls and barbed wire literally anywhere you want, makes every play through different if you want it to be.
With the massive size of the maps and the ability to build anywhere there is truely next to no limit in how you want to play this game. You can always flank the enemy, there is so much space to do so. With recently added vehciles you can quickly sneak troops behind the enemy lines or you can line up all your squads and just push straight into the enemy front using combined arms. Rocket trucks, Armed APCs, Pickup Trucks with mounted 50 cal. machine guns, motorcycles. Eventually there will be helicopters and possibly even jets.
Jesus this review is never going to end so just do your self the favour. If you've been looking at this game thinking about buying it... Stop thinking. Get it... and JOIN US! You won't regret it.

Tl;dr:
What if Kairo met Q.U.B.E. but instead of puzzles you’re mostly dealing with actual platforming or exploration? That's how I see this game.
It’s interesting, I’ll give it that. It has some cool things. It has some trippy things. But it’s not going to stay with me and I don’t see myself telling anyone I know to try it out. When I saw the trailer at E3 it looked really cool but 4h after starting it here I am, a bit let-down that they didn’t explore some puzzle elements more.
--
Game looks ok and runs ok (~60fps with everything on disabled with almost all the recommended settings). Keep in mind the devs have said that if you have low fps, the physics will not react as expected (different jump distances, etc) but I only had issues with that at the very last section of the game, which lead me to fix the problem (on my end) that was causing 20fps when playing. Everything else was easily doable even with such atrocious conditions.
I liked the visual aesthetic of the place for most of the game. The music/ambience too. It reminded me of the scenarios in Q.U.B.E. but with grittier visuals more like Kairo. The music helps you
It ends up being linear for the vast majority of the time, although I’m very sure I skipped a part early on with some “advanced” platforming. I found everything to be intuitive enough to not need to look up anything online (and you shouldn’t unless you’re certain you’re stuck).
There’s no story. I was told Lucy was lost but other than that everything seemed too surreal and disconnected to be able to explain anything at all. This might be the reason people compare this game to Antichamber?
Walking pace is not sluggish enough that you want to sprint all the time, that is good. Sprinting has you manually breathing which didn’t really add much tbh. It distracted me from my hurting pinky when crossing long distances and it made some of the more complicated sections a bit more complicated. I have no strong feelings one way or another with it. I do find it odd that you can hyperventilate when running but not when walking.
If you like eerie or surreal landscapes, as well as puzzle platformers, you might want to check this out.

This is a competent title considering for a Free-to-Play twin stick shooter. This isn't my genre of choice, hence why there's very little play time for this one. But I had to give it a look and see if it was even worth installing. Generally, I find that twin-sticks are overly difficult for my tastes (and this one isn't any different) and I don't find getting the highest score possible all that compelling. You'll find six different game modes ranging from time attack, survival, 10-level campaign to classic asteroids play. Each adding some diversity.
PC options are pretty bare-boned. All you can change are audio levels and movement speed. (No resolution, fullscreen/windowed or other graphical options). You can play either the game's music or your own songs. You can also use either a controller, mouse or keyboard though the controller is the better way to go.
Music is decently up beat, graphics are nice and retro but big surprise there and combat has a decent amount of feedback. Though I feel like the only way you lose is by being overwhelmed. That just might be my awfulness with this genre. It's hard to argue with a good free game, even if it's advertising a game development kit. Solid action, decent variety and fun gameplay make it a recommend from me. If this is your genre of interest, it seems to be worth giving a look.

I love challenging games, but only the ones that are DESIGNED to be motivatingly difficult, not the ones that turn out to be frustratingly difficult because of DESIGN FLAWS. Unfortunately, "Not The Robots" belongs to the latter type, and it's tragic because I believe this could have been a superb game if only the developers had taken care of the details and weaknesses, of which there are so many that this turned out to be a very long review.
All things considered, this is a flawed game marred by many little design weaknesses and a core concept  that seems cool on the surface, but quickly turns out to be a flop. Don't be fooled, the game looks great when you see it, but play it for a while and you'll know exactly what I mean.
Back to the drawing board, "2DArray"! You never really thought this through, shame on you!
P.S.: I corrected some inexact descriptions and also want to add two things I forgot to mention:
1) The game has a very weird (anti-)progression system (allegedly "rogue-like") which I found counter-productive and demotivating: If you die, you always have to restart at Tower 1, but the game will still give you (and your enemies!) upgrades for your progress (at failing, LOL). In other words, the game somehow progresses with new opponents, new traps and new gadgets while you restart from the beginning over and over again (the towers are random-generated, but still have fixed rules like Tower 1 is always super-easy, Towers 3 and 5 never have sentries, Towers 5+ may have a tagging extra game, and so forth).
I noticed that you can exploit the procedural generation for your own advantage: Just survey the next level (from the CCTV camera) without entering yet. If you find it too hard or to your disliking, use the CTRL function (save game) to leave, then re-enter. Since the map's random seed is not saved, you will get a completely different map each time you enter. This can make a tremendous difference because some maps are 10 times easier than others despite being the same level nominally. For example, it's entirely possible to get a map where four out of five sentries are stuck in one room because furniture blocks the exit(s). But then again, you may get a map where you cannot even enter safely because enemies block your path and have their paths blocked as well.
2) The game also has a "story", told through voice actors, perhaps in a hopeless attempt to make it more interesting/endearing, but that failed as well; I quickly muted the voice acting because it's nerdy, out of place, distracting, annoying, and I didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ anyway. I mean, this is a super-abstract game about a robot eating furniture - END OF STORY!
Essentially, the base game was not thought through, tested and fine-tuned enough and all the ideas added to make it stand out from the crowd flopped - and tragically sank it below crowd level in the process.

Well this certainly took me back to my childhood! I remember playing this in class and loving it, foolish declaring to my teacher that I'd complete it before the term was up. She said I wouldn't and for once she was right. I never completed this game and probably never will. I even bought a copy to play at home after the term was up, had many cracks at it and gave up just as many times. Anyway it's nice to have a version that can be played on modern systems. The updated graphics are beautifully cartoonish, the movement of the Zoombinis is much more fluid. Thankfully the voiceovers of the narrator (Who always reminded me of Basil Fawlty), and the highly memorable characters like the pizza trolls are all the originals. The only change I'm not so fond of is not being able to create two of the same Zoombini anymore, meaning it's more difficult than the original (something I once thought would have been impossible). Still the number of Zoombins you have to rescue has been reduced so I guess it evens itself out a tad. Also, one tiny gripe is that you can no longer move a Zoombini once it's been committed to a move meaning you have to think a bit harder before putting them in place, which isn't a huge problem, I'm just lazy. Also the old and new audio seems to be slightly off balance in certain places but they have done a fantastic job re-doing and in some cases adding background music. Honestly I could waffle on for days about this game, it's actually given me a bit of a nostalgia buzz, but I'll end it with if you're a fan of logic and math puzzle games that can make your brain hurt (don't worry the game does make it up to you with it's charm), or if you've got kids that can manage to put down their smartphone for half an hour every now and then, get this!

This game is still enjoyable after all these many years. While the story may not be the most complicated affair out there, there are plenty of fun enemies, varied environments that make the best out of the Source engine from back in the day and a satisfying fluidity to one- or two-handed melee fights that a lot of other games (most modern games?) lack.
Once you got used to kicking your enemies down a ledge or into some spikes, you'll play other first person games and wonder why no other developer ever made use of your player character's legs in that way. Intuitive and fun!
I often find myself saving at certain parts in the game only to then try out all possible ways to kill all enemies using whatever traps / props / means the environment and spells/equipment one carries provide.
A few of the levels can be a bit hard to navigate and one gets lost here and there, but at least in some cases this adds to the immersion, for the most part though this is a strictly linear game; you won't be going back and forth a lot.
Very well worth a shot if you haven't played this yet! Just be nice to the poor goblins and orcs, I feel kinda sorry for 'em getting kicked around all day! x]

Sonic and All Stars Racing: Transformed, (or as I like to call it, SEGA All Stars Racing: Transformed) is a racing game featuring all of your favorite SEGA Characters race to the finish, as well as some random 3rd Party Characters. It features race tracks based off of worlds from Sonic games and most of SEGA's forgotten franchises and the racers vehicles transform from cars, to boats, to planes. So it's like Mario Kart 7, Diddy Kong Racing, that random Disney racing game and that Hot Wheels game that share the same idea of transforming race cars. I've never used a controller for the PC Version and I stuck to just using the keyboard, the nice thing about this is that you can adjust the controls for the keyboard to see which keys suit you more comfortably, and not just pressing random buttons all over the keyboard. The car and boat forms are cool, the boat forms are more fun as you can easily perform more tricks to get boosts. The plane form takes some time to getting used to when it comes to drifting while keeping your plane under control. The game features Career mode which is a series of different events, Grand Prix is a race to see who is the best, Time Trial is what you would expect, and Single Race is for racing on only one track, which I advise to try this feature out for practice if you just bought the game. The power ups can be useful at times, from the catchers mitt that catches the enemies weapon and being able to use it to your advantage, to chucking snowballs, ho ho ho. The All Star moves are back but are a bit disappointing. The first game featured the characters having their own specific All Star Moves with their own style and advantages, the sequel just transforms the player into the plane mode and fire's rockets at your opponents. There was also talk about special DLC that would feature more of SEGA's forgotten or internet favorite characters in the game, well it's been over a year and after that Yogscast guy was announced, I gave up on it since obviously SEGA only focuses on Sonic, they don't give a damn about their other franchises or even attempt to feature them in a new game again, and not just constantly porting their already made games onto every console. NaissanceE is a game that caters to people who enjoy games for the sense of exploration and the ability to see new and alien places. The main selling point of this game are its visuals and the way the game plays with its architecture and light is well worth seeing, as the visuals of this game are truly something else. It can be defined as a walking simulator, however it has plenty of platforming and puzzles that are peppered throughout to make things interesting and keep you invested. While many other walking simulator games have landscapes through which you only walk or run through, in NaissanceE you will spend almost as much time moving verically as you do horizontally, which makes traversing the megastructure littered environments of NaissanceE far more interesting.
The visuals are kept simple and the music and sound design are not overpowering except in few places where it feels intentional and designed as such. Because the visuals are so simple the architectural design of the world of NaissanceE becomes that much more evident and the landscapes which are inspired by both minimalist and brutalist architecture really stand out in this more subtle and controlled visual design. It is rare to be able to see landscapes which such rich amount of detail and being able to walk inside and outside these megastructures and seeing the vastness of it all is truly captivating.
The sound design is similarly "artsy" as are the visuals. I felt that the music fit each setpiece well, many of the tracks inside the game conveying a feelings of confusion, anciety and sometimes elation.They are not, however, tracks you would want to listen to out of context and they only really work within the game itself and the context within they are placed. You do not want to listen to these tracks over and over again, so it is good that he puzzles and timed challenges in the game are fairly easy to complete after one or two tries. I will however mention that the breathing noise the main character makes when you sprint is a little bit annoying after awhile and I was hoping I could have been able to disable it.
Gameplay wise the game doesn't offer an exceeding amount of things to do. You mostly move forward in the game, press some buttons, walk through some doorways and see what happens next. It is that last bit that makes the game exciting, seeing what happens next. It is not afraid to throw some real curve balls your way and you never really can anticipate what will happen next and seeing what happens next was always a joy. The game does occasionally almost intentionally seem to try to lead you astray and you may spend a few minutes in one place trying to figure out where to go, but those moments do not last for long. It is important to forget the conventions of traditional game design and just experiment if you are stuck.
I only wish the game was longer, I beat it is a bit over 3 hours, but those 3 hours I feel were very well spent. You will want to spend a few minutes in each area to just look at the environment as they are truly that gorgeous. The interplay of light and shadow is very prominent throughout the game and in many instances it is really inspirational and awe inspiring how the developers have been able to do so much with so little.
I wont talk about the story at all, since I think that is entirely up to personal taste and interpretation. At the end of the day, I feel that by now you will know if you like games of this genre, if you do, you will absolutely fall in love with NaissanceE.

First of let me say I am a big believer of realism in games. I think it has always played a significant part in games throughout the ages particularly tactical shooting games. I played games in my youth such as the original Delta Force games, and then later games like Operation Flashpoint, the original Rainbow Six and the original Ghost Recon Series. Realism an the brutalness of these games are what made them rewarding.
However Squad is not in the same league and falls short in many areas just like other games have done which claim to offer amazing team play experiences. The issues I found present in this game were :
1. There was no team play
2. Massive lack of visibility I'm running a pretty high end PC and I couldn't even see who was shooting at me half the time meaning I couldn't shoot back. Especially given point number 3.
3. Lack of decent weaponry, the multiplayer games I joined only had generic and uninteresting weapons often with no optics. There were a few guns with optics but they were all taken (surprise, surprise)
4. Communications didn't work, my mic works in every other game however pressing a variety of push to talk buttons meant it didn't work on this game for some weird reason.
5. Distance I had to run to try and fun some actual fighting. Which took about 10 minutes.
Overall I found this game rather frustrating and a perfect example of how not to introduce this level of realism into a game. On the games that I played every time it just resulted in two teams camping on top of two opposing hill tops trying to fire rockets at each other and randomly firing in the direction of the enemy. The lack of communication just made things worse.
What game developers like those that are developing this game need to realise is that realistic games like this have to strike a balance between realism and approachability. As new players (especially today where a lot of games make it too easy for players) its crucial now more than ever to try and attract new players to these kinds of game and demonstrate the reward and satisfaction that can be gained from working hard. Sadly this game completely fails to do this which means just like I have done others will also try it, not enjoy it and then refund it.
If I was to offer one key area to improve the game out of all the areas I have mentioned above, the key one is visibility everyone should have better optics, binoculars, guns should have options for magnified optics too. When you have people so far away and you have no way of seeing them, then it just destroys any enjoyment.

Borderlands is a case study in how to take core gameplay that's actually pretty good and still churn out a game so terrible that it's literally headache-inducing. A first-person shooter with Diablo style loot is a recipe for fun, although Gearbox didn't come up with the idea first. And it's on this level that Borderlands actually partially delivers, because it's a solid FPS with a ton of loot that should satisfy fans of dungeon crawlers and shooters alike. Unfortunately, everything else about this game is dull, repetitive, and annoying. The camera jerks up and down like Michael J. Fox when walking or running, placing a hamper on the action that takes some getting used to. Borderlands provides no variety in scenery, either. Every dungeon and overworld is just some vast, bland, lifeless desert thing, and what little life exists in the game is either trying to kill you or spouting off stupid humor. This is to say nothing of the game's ludicrous claim that it has thousands of guns when it actually has about five guns with varying stats. As much as I dislike Borderlands, I will say that I don't know of anything else that's quite like it, which is a shame. A competent developer with a little more creativity could have done wonders with the idea.

I'd seen this one go by on my steam now for a while, and I'm sure I must have looked at it at least 2-3 times, and every time I'm sure I must have taken one look at it and thought "RTS", or "tower defense" and clicked on to something else. Then last night I felt like I wanted to play a game but I couldn't decide what game to play, or even what genre, and so I went trauling through my Steam to see what it had for relatively cheap. Nothing really stood out to me but this one came up again and I noticed it had overwhelingly positive reviews, so I gave up and went to YouTube to see a let's play because I wanted to see what this was all about.
I wound up watching probably 3-4 hours of one by some guy doing a custom scenario where he started out with one person and nothing else because that felt like the kind of scenario that I'd like to play. I could've happily enjoyed that, but it was a recent let's play so that's all he'd played so far. That was enough to convince me to drop the cash on RimWorld, though, and something like 13-14 hours later I'm glad I did.
This is an amazing game, and I can't believe how much fun I'm having playing it. I could've gone my whole life with just those uninformed ideas about how since it's all just 2D graphics that it must not be much more than a tower defense or RTS type game, but I would've missed out on a pretty amazing experience. This game is just awesome. I had questioned how it could be what it looks like and be priced what it is, but no, you get your money's worth out of it.
Read some other reviews from people with hundreds of hours of game play if you want more of the nitty gritty about it, because there's a pretty good bit to it that I haven't begun to uncover yet at only 13 hours in, but let me just add in to that overwhelmingly positive review stuff with my hearty endorsement.
For me, I'm reminded of ARK: Survival Evolved in terms of building things, albeit in 2 dimensions instead of 3, and without dinosaurs, although there are some pretty big looking animals I've seen once or twice now. And I'm reminded a bit of This War Of Mine in terms of how emotionally invested I've become with my first few characters and their pets. I bought a pair of little dogs from a visiting trader passing through, and had only had them just barely long enough to train them up the first level, when a wolf wandered up near my camp, and, while a couple of pirates had come to raid my base right after a man eating Muffalo had come through and terrorized us for a few days and attacked it and knocked it out before I could get outside and rescue it, then proceeded to eat it at my front doorstep. Despite having just barely bought the dog, I was just absolutely heartbroken and furious at the wolf for coming up and trying to eat my dog. It made me a lot more protective of the dog my first character came with, even considering keeping him confined to my base from now on because I can't bear to lose another one.
Anyway, this game is a lot more than it probably looks like it is. I'm a convert for sure, and I'm gonna be coming back to this game a lot for quite a long time to come. <3

The reason behinde this was probably because of that cut he had gotten in a recent skirmish with the wildlife, beavers to be more presise. He was honored, and placed in a sarcaufugus. Hendrix made it himself, considering he was Thompsons closest friend. Some more days pass, and a ship crashs, and a non-vilonet man named Scizo or something is found in a crash. But, yet another pod crashed, and this one carrying the most useless person anyone could have ever met. A man by the name of Isov. Isov had a weird entitlement about him. he felt he didn't need to do ANY LABOR AT ALL. So occaitionaly he would help Watson with reasearch, and help train Raymond, the pet warg. But when it came down to it, Isov was the most useless human being in existance. Though, that didn't stop Hendrix from befriending him anyways. Hendrix was, by any means, a people person. He was a hunter too. And a fighter when the colony needed him to be. Now, a new day begins, and there is a woman on the comms channel, a criminal surgeon by the name of Toni. She needed some help getting away from a local tribe by the name of "The Orange Plain Nation". So Hendrix had her come, for he knew they were in desperate need of a medical practitioner. Her attackers, a male warrior, and a lesbian who absouloutly despised men. Hendrix, getting everyone into formation, repels the attackers. He bravly shoots down warrior, while the lesbian attacks the colony's solar pannel. She flees, when she realizes that her scum partner is dead. Hendrix leads the charge and scares her off for good. In the time after that, Hendrix found himself doing more for the colony, such as building a heater for Toni's room, and growing crops. But then, one day, a herd of angry boar enter the area. Hendrix knows what he must do. He gathers Watson and Lu, who are the only other two in the colony with guns, and they fight off the boar. When Hendrix realized that his, at this time, fiance'a(However you spell that) Lu was going to be killed by a boar, he bravely swooped in and meleed the boar to death, while 2 more boar fight him. In the days afterwards, a steel sarcophagus was made to honor Hendrix, and all his contributions to the colony. Without him, the colony may very well have died. Wolfenstein: The New Order is the best shooter I've played in a long while. It seems many shooters nowadays balance between delivering a good story or focusing on the gameplay and thus trip on their own legs trying to achieve both. Somehow Wolfenstein has managed to cram an acceptable story to the adrenaline-boosted gameplay iD Software games are most well know for.
While the story is in no way anything new or breathtaking, it still manages to be there and actually bring some context to the shooting itself. The world is quite fresh and imaginative and even though Nazis as baddies can often fall very flat, this new premise breaths some fresh air to the mix. Using Nazies as baddies, on the other hand, brings some texture to the enemies, instead of leaving them as some generic bad guys, killer robots or other meaningless crud. The Nazi aesthetics brought into the game is unusually uncompromising and the game has the guts to bring in all the swastikas, Sieg Heils and concentration camps (
) into view. My biggest fear about this game was that it would go the feel-good route of Iron Sky: trying to feel edgy by using Nazies as baddies, but watering them down to a degree that transforms them only to bad caricatures. Wolfenstein doesn't go there and does it with no bad taste at all. All in all the scifi-Nazi aesthetics is, in my opinion, ageless, also metal and black never go out of style.
Sometimes the pacing in the levels is a bit off, as well as the difficulty, but all in all the shooting feels nice even on harder difficulties (I played the game through on second-to-hardest). Enemies don't become bullet sponges so the challenge is fair. You have a plethora of cool weapons, all with their own situational value, and the perks associated with the weapons bring in some decent illusion of progress. Boss fights are ok, boss fights in general feel a bit outdated to me, especially in this genre, and the puzzle-ish gameplay feels frustrating until you figure them out.
. At least there wasn't too many of them.
As a whole Wolfenstein manages to combine some basic silliness characteristic to iD Software games and enough seriousness to make it beliveable. Even though the story is quite childish and the ending
I never felt a dull moment. Modernization of this genre can the done well and can be done bad, Wolfenstein definitely does it well.

It's good to quickly preview a plan and furniture layout.  A simple layout can be done in about thirty minutes.
Good features:
1) Quick to drag and drop furniture, walls, rooms, whatever.
2) All items are easily resized, including furniture, walls, beds, whatever.
3) The undo / redo is fantastic and allows you to try multiple options very quickly, such as for wall color, or wall paper.
4) Plenty of view options, including 2D and two 3D modes.
5) Plenty of models included, even things like people and a cat.
However, there are a couple of quirks.
1) When set to metric, the grid seems to remain in imperial measurement, So instead of ten squares being one meter, they are infact 3.12 meters, which is probably somewhere close to ten feet.
2) Object handles for walls cover the length label.  Labels really need to be placed away from the stretch/move handles.
3) Could not find a tub for the laundry ... it seems to have been omitted, or I couldn't find it.
Quite nice to use and test different layouts ... possibly saving money and time in the overall scheme of things.

Borderlands is a case study in how to take core gameplay that's actually pretty good and still churn out a game so terrible that it's literally headache-inducing. A first-person shooter with Diablo style loot is a recipe for fun, although Gearbox didn't come up with the idea first. And it's on this level that Borderlands actually partially delivers, because it's a solid FPS with a ton of loot that should satisfy fans of dungeon crawlers and shooters alike. Unfortunately, everything else about this game is dull, repetitive, and annoying. The camera jerks up and down like Michael J. Fox when walking or running, placing a hamper on the action that takes some getting used to. Borderlands provides no variety in scenery, either. Every dungeon and overworld is just some vast, bland, lifeless desert thing, and what little life exists in the game is either trying to kill you or spouting off stupid humor. This is to say nothing of the game's ludicrous claim that it has thousands of guns when it actually has about five guns with varying stats. As much as I dislike Borderlands, I will say that I don't know of anything else that's quite like it, which is a shame. A competent developer with a little more creativity could have done wonders with the idea.

This is probably the best educational game around, and while that isn't saying too much, it manages to be an extremely engaging and fun game, while also being very educational. As a child I sunk many, many hours into Zoombinis, and it taught me a lot about logic, problem solving and maths, and sparked lifelong interests in those areas - all while I enjoyed myself massively - it was easily one of my favourite games.
The game is a series of 12 puzzles, each having four difficulty levels that range from simple to teach you the basics up to hard enough to make anyone, child or adult, think a bit. These puzzles are interesting, varied and have really engaging theming, with characters that bring the world to life. There is an overarching plot where the player is helping all the Zoombinis travel across the map to a new home, giving a long-term goal.
The puzzles teach a variety of skills, all focusing on logic and problem solving, with a little mathematics thrown in. None of them fall into the usual educational game traps (quizzes, etc...), but rather teach by letting the player experiment, learn and apply their understanding in an iterative way - this is the best way to learn, and it is great fun. I never saw the game as 'an educational game' as a child, despite it teaching me a lot.
Most of the puzzles involve sorting the Zoombinis (who are composed from a set of features - hair, eyes, nose, 'feet'), into groups or applying them to situations. For example, the first puzzle gives the player two bridges, each will reject Zoombinis with certain traits (that the other accepts) - the player must work out which traits are allowed on each bridge in order to get all the Zoombinis across. This is a simple start, but as the game goes on, the puzzles become deeper and more complex, with interesting solutions. The game slowly increases the difficulty, teaching the child how to think to solve the puzzles before hitting them with the hard stuff.
The characters are incredbily entertaining, despite being a puzzle game with little real interaction, the game uses environment, animation and some dialogue to great effect to breathe life into it's characters - the Pizza Trolls are a favourite, and are timelessly entertaining. I still find myself saying 'MORE TOPPINGS' along with Arno.
This is quite possibly the best game you could buy for a child, and the age range it targets is surprisingly large - the difficulties vary enough to allow children of all ages and abilities to enjoy and learn from it. At it's more difficult settings, this would even make a great alternative to a 'brain training' style game for adults - the puzzles get hard and interesting, no matter the age. This is a great game to play with children, (or for siblings to play together), although it is important to let children try, fail and learn from those failures, rather than pointing out the solutions.
If you have played the game before, you may want to know how it compares. The update itself is mostly pretty negligable (which is mostly a good thing) - the most important part being that it runs happily on modern systems.
A few quality of life enhancements have been made - some of the slower animations seem to have been sped up a little to reduce the delay, but unfortunately a few places are still as slow as they were (particularly the mirror machine, which retains it's annoying need to flip the switch on and back for each Zoombini). A few of the animations also look a little odd (the toads jumping in and out, for example), but these are minor issues, and mostly a problem that won't affect the average player, only the veteran coming back where the puzzles can be solved quickly enough to make the delay seem longer, or notice the animation difference.
The graphics have been updated, but all remain the same at their core. Some places have been clarified a little (the placement spot for the Fleans has been made more obvious, the images in the mirror machine have been made clearer), but nothing changed in a substantial way. They look great, and retain all of the charm of the originals.
The game retains it's original sound, with the great music that is upbeat, with a hint of mystery, and the wonderful narrator, who adds humour and a sense of grand importance to what you do in the game. The audio quality is below that of a modern game, but I think TERC were right to leave it as is, the original recordings were spot-on, and a new version would have struggled to live up to the originals.
Just as fun as it used to be, a little prettier, and highly recommended. Easily worth the money.

There are three endings and you can choose for yourself how to proceed.
The puzzles themselves are easy at first as one would expect and continue to get more and more challenging. By the end of the game the puzzles are insanely hard and some can be quite time consuming.
All in all, the music and atmosphere make this one of the coolest puzzle games ever made.
As a side note: the Serious engine used to build this game is very impressive for what it does and runs efficiently. No crashes or memory issues. Wolfenstein: The New Order is the best shooter I've played in a long while. It seems many shooters nowadays balance between delivering a good story or focusing on the gameplay and thus trip on their own legs trying to achieve both. Somehow Wolfenstein has managed to cram an acceptable story to the adrenaline-boosted gameplay iD Software games are most well know for.
While the story is in no way anything new or breathtaking, it still manages to be there and actually bring some context to the shooting itself. The world is quite fresh and imaginative and even though Nazis as baddies can often fall very flat, this new premise breaths some fresh air to the mix. Using Nazies as baddies, on the other hand, brings some texture to the enemies, instead of leaving them as some generic bad guys, killer robots or other meaningless crud. The Nazi aesthetics brought into the game is unusually uncompromising and the game has the guts to bring in all the swastikas, Sieg Heils and concentration camps (
) into view. My biggest fear about this game was that it would go the feel-good route of Iron Sky: trying to feel edgy by using Nazies as baddies, but watering them down to a degree that transforms them only to bad caricatures. Wolfenstein doesn't go there and does it with no bad taste at all. All in all the scifi-Nazi aesthetics is, in my opinion, ageless, also metal and black never go out of style.
Sometimes the pacing in the levels is a bit off, as well as the difficulty, but all in all the shooting feels nice even on harder difficulties (I played the game through on second-to-hardest). Enemies don't become bullet sponges so the challenge is fair. You have a plethora of cool weapons, all with their own situational value, and the perks associated with the weapons bring in some decent illusion of progress. Boss fights are ok, boss fights in general feel a bit outdated to me, especially in this genre, and the puzzle-ish gameplay feels frustrating until you figure them out.
. At least there wasn't too many of them.
As a whole Wolfenstein manages to combine some basic silliness characteristic to iD Software games and enough seriousness to make it beliveable. Even though the story is quite childish and the ending
I never felt a dull moment. Modernization of this genre can the done well and can be done bad, Wolfenstein definitely does it well.

The Talos Principle is hands down one of the best puzzle games out there.
Everything from the detailed and beautiful environments and atmosphere, which is all eerie and just flat out mystical, to the reverberated sounds to the haunting and heavenly soundtrack. Everything is done with awesome polish.
Not to mention the puzzles are just satisfying as hell. The game eases you in as you expect then shortly begins to toss more and more compelling challenges at you. There are only one or two moments that I experienced where I felt like the game was being a bit of an jerk, but for the most part the later puzzles always have that sort of 'ah I see, I'm a frickin idiot' thing which, for some silly reason I actually don't hate.
The game also includes like LOTS of text passages and audio clips all in the form of email things. Reading them can give you some pretty decent reading material. The way the game has built this world is brilliant, the ocassional voice lines heard by the player through out the game also helps to create a very other worldly vibe that is really compelling.
Of course the game has its fair share of things that aren't the best. I often had the game just close for seemingly no reason or warning, nothing seemed to trigger the crashes, it just sort of happened at random moments, not sure if thats me or not though. The game often hides the secrets in really cheap ways, a lot of them are really clever and make you really have to think to get them. Other times though... Man, this game is a real joker.
I think the game has a lot to offer for anyone who is interested in first person puzzle games, like obviously. Its a must have. If you think you might like it but haven't played a game like this before, I highly suggest you give it a shot. The mood and atmosphere is reason enough to jump right in.

Zoombinis is a cute game where you use logic to help your crew traverse the land.
The game is a remake of an old educational game. It has prettier graphics and can run on modern machines.
When you start the game, you're tasked with creating your zoombini crew. They all have to be completely individual, and you create all of them from different parts.
After that is done, you're given your first real puzzle. There are 2 bridges that cross cliffs, and placed over gigantic stone faces. You casually place your little friends onto the bridges and watch them cross. Until suddenly, one of the rock faces sneezes and throws your Zoombini back to where they started. At this point you try and put that same Zoombini onto the second bridge, and see that it crosses fine. That's how the game's puzzles are done. They don't explain to you what you need to do, it lets you do it logically. After trial and error you'll eventually come to realise that one of the bridges sneezes when a zoombini that has pink shoes on crosses it, however, allows all others. It's a fun process.
The puzzles mostly focus on logic through eliminating what zoombini can cross where.
The art style looks really beautiful. The backgrounds are painted very nicely, and the Zoombinis themselves look friendly and colourful. The music is amazing. A real nice mix of instruments, and really gives you the feel of the world. I love the voice acting. It's over the top, but really light hearted and funny.
The game is very simple. It's aimed at younger kids, although anyone can really enjoy it. I'm 20 and had fun with this. Don't get this expecting a puzzle game that will keep you scratching your head for minutes. You'll figure out each puzzle in a decent amount of time. There are harder difficulties you can select, which again aren't insanely challenging, but still fun.
Overall, a very fun and simple game. Decently difficult and rewarding puzzles, with a beautiful world and music to accompany it!

Nice bit of fun for free.  It says free-to-play, which makes you think there might be in-app stuff to buy, but I didn't see anything like that.  It's just free.
It's similar to Asteroids, in that you are a single ship fighting agaist rock-shaped targets that break into 2 smaller versions of themselves when damaged enough.. then those break into smaller pieces, etc, until you end up with pieces small enough to destroy.
It's different from Asteroids because it doesn't have that intertia-based movement mechanic that made the classic game so difficult to master, which is a very good thing because this game is a lot more chaotic, and your movements need to be a lot more precise and quick.  There are also different kinds of space rocks, like ones that spawn in a big line on one side of the screen, then sweep across.. or ones that form a snake-like chain and chase you.
Controls are simple.. I played on a 360 pad, and one stick moves me around, while the other stick shoots in whatever direction I push it.  A or RT detonates a bomb that destroys a lot of the stuff on the screen.  There are pickups that restore your health, improve your weapons, etc.
There's a lot of movement on the screen, lots of color and everything gets pretty insane after a while.. there isn't a whole lot of excessive flashing lights and stuff, but just in case, if you have epilepsy, be careful about this one.. I just don't have a good enough understanding of that condition to know whether or not it'll trigger a seizure or something.
Anyway, It's not groundbreaking, or a super-original idea or anything.. but it's fun, the neon visual style is appealing, and it's free, so why not give it a try?

Nearly everyone has played a fighting game, be it Mortal Kombat, Street Fighter, Tekken, Dead or Alive, at least one of them. Some people play one and dedicate hours into learning movesets, combos, counters, specials; all kinds of complex, frustrating game mechanics. Others just pick a fighter and find a move that they can beat others with reliably. Still others try one and never play again, put down by the large list of things to learn in order to play.
With Divekick, all that complex crap is thrown out the window into moving traffic at rush hour. Divekick reduces the core of the fighting genre down to two measly buttons. I don't mean two attack buttons and a d-pad, I mean nothing but two buttons for EVERYTHING: menus, attacking, movement, everything (except pause, but that's besides the point).
'You must be joking, ' I hear you thinking, 'that sounds like a crappy mobile game, not a hardcore fighter!' Well, technically, it IS a joke, more of a parody really. Divekick is a jab at the fighting game genre, it's filled with in-jokes and references to prominent characters and people that mostly only hardcore fighter enthusiasts would understand. But even at it's core, it stays very true to it's roots.
The gameplay boils down to two actions: Dive, which acts as a jump ("Dive" into the air) and Kick, which launches your character at a downward angle to strike your opponent. Kick when performed on the ground causes your character to leap backwards, put these together and you have the basics of movement and attack. One hit causes a KO and the first to 5 wins is the victor of the match. Attacks that connect the head cause  the recipient to be dazed during the first few seconds of the next fight and each attack fills a special meter, which when both buttons are pressed, performs one of two special attacks depending on if you are grounded or in the air.
This all sounds very, very simple. Well, yeah, that's the point. While all of the 13 characters may seem similar, each has a different Dive and Kick motion which affects how you play them. Dive, one of the main characters, kicks down at a 45 degree angle, while Kung Pao  has a slower, more lateral kick that reaches further, but opens her up more to an attack. The Baz has a kick that spreads lightning behind him, which is what actually connects, not his foot. Furthermore, every character's specials are unique and provide either escape or approach and attack moves, even status effects in some cases.
The simplified controls therefore mask a very complex game that embodies the heart of fighting games, timing, quick reflexes, baiting and mind games, outthinking your opponent. This is magnified by the fact that many of the developers are avid fighter fans, who have spent a long time balancing and perfecting  the mechanics to create a game that's no less complex at it's core than say, Guilty Gear or Marvel vs Capcom. This is also shown by the many references to the competitive fighting game community that exist in the characters and one-liners.
Divekick also supports local and online multiplayer, with a ranking board. At the time of writing, I've found it hard to find other people to play with online, but I have found a few matches (haven't tried much yet).
At the end, this is a deceptively complex and refined fighter that attempts to remove all the endless movelists and combo strings that keep many gamers away from fighting games. In this gamer's opinion, it does it's job well. I highly suggest trying it out, especially if you like fighting games. Cheap too :D

It's a fun narrative-based game which requires you not only to make dialogue choices and make them quickly, but also allows you to stay silent and not say anything at all, which is definitely an interesting type of interaction.
