NaissanceE is a game of exploration, platforming, light puzzle solving, and an extreme feeling of eerie loneliness in these large abandoned structures. The world feels as if you are exploring what could be real buildings, but through the filter of a dream. Sometimes doors lead nowhere, sheer drops, or architecture that is beautiful but odd. All while being very very much alone, but with a nagging feeling in the back of your mind that something is following you or that you may not be alone. NaissanceE is very effective in feeling like you are on an adventure, and making you feel alone in a large civilization while a wave of eerie uneasiness washes over you.
While being a great game, it has a coule of flaws, one being trying to climb up and down ladders is ridiculous, and is what caused numerous deaths, but I don't blame the dev entirely as I feel the unreal engine is just that way with ladders. But, the real issue that I feel that people will have with the game is the last 1/4 of NaissanceE. This last part kicks up the difficulty a fair bit with lots of platforming and time sensitive puzzles. It all still looked really cool, but I had to redo several parts a few times, which kinda kills the momentum of the game. There are also several, very cool looking and trippy, but somewhat confusing puzzles parts in this last bit as well, and I at times had absolutely no idea what to do, but with enough wondering around I eventually found my way out. Aside from these couple of problems, NaissanceE is a absolutely great game. Anyone who enjoys the idea of a haunting exploration game should definitely check this game out!

The Talos Principle is a thoughtful first-person puzzler with an interesting story, environment, and philosophy.  The game guides you through the initial puzzles and sets expectations of what you should do with each item, including boxes, laser prisms, fans, and more.  The various levels are not overly intimidating and the majority of the solutions are intuitive (at least in retrospect).  There are essentially two levels of difficulty; completing the puzzles in a "normal" fashion and acquiring stars.  The stars are much more difficult to find and get.  My playthough took around 15 hours (base game, very few stars).  It's very reminiscent of Portal, but much morecontent.
The writing is well done and the world is intriguing, but be prepared to read.  While some of the story is provided via a voice in the sky, many of the details are fleshed out on in-game computer screens.  If you're intrigued by the philosophical choices throughout the game, you'll want to pay attention to the various writing pieces that are provided to you.  The game challenges your worldviews at nearly every turn.
The DLC, Road to Gehenna, is also a very worthy addition.  If you've been in the mood for something like Portal and haven't sated that since Portal 2, grab this game on sale for sure.

At first glance I thought, "Great, another sonic game to tear down the franchise," but Steam had it for $5 and I bought it for my kids to play.  Then I noticed quickly that this was a Mario Kart clone and I was excited.  The controls are good, the graphics are good, the level design is very imaginative, and the transformation niche does not get annoying.  And with some sort of leveling system, there is really a lot going on in this game.  It's made directly against Mario Kart, but it's different enough that you don't really think of it as a clone.  Downsides?  Yeah.  Mainly the drifting doesn't feel very tight, and it's mandatory to learn if you want to win.  Just like Mario Kart Wii.  While Easy is easy, Medium can quickly turn punishing.  Stick to Easy until you find the character you like, learn the levels, and get the drifting down.  But ignoring that, this makes a good party game.  I'm quite happy that they include split screen multiplayer.  Some games remove that when ported to PC.

Well, this game has both Nolan North and Troy Baker doing voices and their characters even have a conversation together. I sort of wonder how the universe didn't implode when that happened. Also, the most pleasant surprise was hearing Laura Bailey, one of my favorite VAs, as Fiona, the female lead.
VAs aside, Tales of the Borderlands has the storytelling and  the interesting and genuinely likeable characters of a typical Telltale game and the complete wacky insanity of the Borderlands series. Occasionally I had to pause the game to get over a laughing fit about something that happened and I really liked the flexibility in how you could mold the characters. Even better, unlike every other Telltale games, this one has multiple protagonist (a playable female protagonist after Clem!) and the way the story plays around with the idea of the unreliable narrator between the two characters and perspectives.
This game is actually a lot more active than most Telltale games, though, which was a bit of a surprise. I suppose I should have expected it, given Borderlands' frantic gun-'n-run mentality (or snipe and cackle, if you play like me) but there is more reliance on action/combat mechanics in this game. It plays more like The Wolf Among Us than The Walking Dead, for example, though I think there's actually more action in the first chapter of TotB than there is in a comparable TWAU chapter. Still, I'm definitely ready for the rest of the game (if I were more patient I'd totally just play it once it was all released since that's a more satisfying experience but...)

I'm gonna start with the cons bc I want to end this review on a positive note:
CONS:
- A huge♥♥♥♥♥epilepsy warning would have been nice in beginning of the game, bc I was feeling ill from all the flashes even though I don't even have epilepsy ._.
- FLOATY CONTROLS
I hate floating. At least when I'm not supposed to be floating. When I'm supposed to be floating that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ great but otherwise put me back on the GROUND.
- Breathing
an interesting mechanic, but when you're running from things and thru things and can't even hear you're own breath or sometimes even see the circle, starting whezing and dying out of nowhere gets tedious.
- BIGGEST CON: No real story??
I get this is supposed to be an atmospheric game, and to be fair for the most part the atmosphere is phenomenal, but if all you're going to give me is air I'd rather play something else. I did play it all the way through, and there were some excellent moments where the music really gets the feeling across, but if you're going to make the paths so open that sometimes it takes a bunch of backtracking to find out where to actually go it'd be nice to actually have something to find! Even if you don't want to have a legitimate story, which is fine for a game like this, it's be nice to have something to collect, little pages or blocks or whatever, just so there's a point to the exploring. By the end I found myself just trying to find the quickest route and not even bothering with anything else!
PROS:
- GREAT ATMOSPHERE
As I said in the cons, the music and the gameplay honestly flow together really well, and honestly I just wish there had been more of it!
- Breathing. Because breathing is generally a nice thing to do.
- SCENERY
While I had a bit of trouble finding my way around, especially in the second chapter, I didn't mind too much because there was usually something pretty awesome to look at! The graphics have aged a bit, but there are some parts of it that I don't think I'll forget! . . . Plus the tunnelers, or wall climbers, or whatever you call them, they made my day! Seeing them from a distance, I didn't think I'd even get to them, but then to actually interact with them?! It was great! Couple of annoying floaty puzzle bits, but it still was one of the highlights of the game imo
- A great experience
I don't think I'd recommend this game for it's gameplay, or the "story?" or the graphics. But overall, I'm really glad I played this finally. It truly is something that I think is better to experience than to watch someone play or just read a review about. It made my day, even though it also frustrated the hell out of me with some bits haha.
TLdr;
Overall a pretty awesome experience! There are some annoyances, fiddly bits and parts you'll probably die a lot, but if you're looking for something interesting to play that ♥♥♥♥s with your mind even without a story, this is the game for you!

First piece of advice, try to ignore the first trailer for this game, just dont watch it. a) because they give a poor representation fo the game experience, it's not all running in fear/being chased by a monster, and b) NaissanceE is something to be experienced first hand.
NaissancE is chiefly all about exploration, with some platforming and puzzles thrown in. There are some tricky platforming-centric sections, and some fairly derivative puzzle pieces, but the game it at it's best when the environment itself acts as a platforming/puzzle without being so obliquely designed to be a puzzle/platforming section.
But nevermind what NaissancE is or isn't, what this game represents is the best example I have ever come across of the experience of getting lost and meandering through supermassive blutalist environments that you've only ever experienced through film previously. This game evokes what it must be like to wander the expansiveness of Star Wars' Coruscant underworld, it matches Cloud City's monochrome/off-white locales, it has the impossible verticality of the city in sci-fi flick Brazil, and the imposing bleak of Blade Runner. It's a sight to behold, and, despite being "linear" in progression (this is not complete free-roam) you can explore large streaches of the city.
The city itself is dead but for the anthropomorhised entities (usually made of lights or blocks) you happen across. In a place that's designed for people, with areas that are clearly office blocks, causeways or plazas, etc. there are no people here. The experience is one of lone wandering on a magnificent scale. I can't think of any other game that has done an urban environment quite like this before.
This is not a game you have to finish, indeed there is little reward for doing so, but if you like exploring strange and unusual places to experience what NaissancE has to offer is a reward in of itself.

This is also what I imagined wandering around in the enormous engineered spaces of the Krell must be like -

I found a few of the sections had a "♥♥♥♥ you. ♥♥♥♥ you. ♥♥♥♥ you. ♥♥♥♥  you. Thank God. Oooh *look* at that!" structure, but I'm not especially accomplished at 3D platformers despite a love for Portal and HL.
In summary, it's an experience that will stick with me, and a world I'd pay to see a lot more of.
(And my personal belief is that it's a vast artificial word that is corporeal and not someone's fevered imagination. I don't care if the developers' lore aligns with that)

Lemme paint a little picture:
I was elected squad leader. It was my first time so i didn't want to disappoint. My squad spawns in on me and i see the majority of our team was heading up main street, fighting on the first contested point head-on.
The squad and i decide to swing wide the the west to a small house and set a rally point so we could have a safe hold out if the main firefight needs a point to fall back on. I'm dumb and have no idea how to commender a vehicle, so we go on foot.
Since we swung so far, we didn't see a single friend or foe, but heard the gunfire and explosions in the far distance. As we walk, we talk about interests, how we liked the game (it was a free weekend) and making semi-racist jokes about terrorists and poor countries.
One squadmate was bragging about how he had so many grenades for our team (the turban wearing team). Morale was high.
We get to the house, set up the rally and get bored instantly. We suit up once again and have the idea that we take the next town so when we do take the contested area, we will already control the next. But to do that, we would have to cross the gigantic field of what we assumed was wheat, out in the open. A good sniper could pick us off easily.
We circle up and brief my team. "Heads down, go fast, and if i saw drop, you drop." We start our sprint acoss the field, single file and looking for any sudden movements.
We make it to the back of the building we were aiming for. We circle up again and brief again, with a couple more jokes and such. Turns out, it was a small village, other side of this building was the main street that connected all the capture points together.
I heard a voice on the squad leader chat comms, there is an american humvee with a heavy machine gun on top in the point that the rest of the team was fighting, about 2 miles away. For a moment i thought the point he called out was our point, so i warned the squad.
After getting it clarified, and with a sigh of relief, we slowly start our way down the road toward the capture point.
I peek around the first corner down the road for about 30 seconds, making sure my squad has safe passage. Nothing. We again, single file, walked along the front of the building, being very cautious.
Once about three of us get on the front of the building, we start to hear some rumbling down the road in front of us.
"Oh S***! It's the humvee!! (squadmate i can't remember the name of) Get those grenades ready!! Fall back!"
We start sprinting as fast as we can to get behind the building again, as the humvee is just barreling down the road at high speed. Just before i get around the corner, the humvee opens fire and i get hit in the back.
I fall and it turns black. In th blackness, i hear my squad.
"Grenades going out!" accompanied by deafening gunfire where i could hear my squad screaming but couldn't make out the words.
I hear an explosion, and i could make out one squad mate say "I got you, but as soon as you get up, you gotta run back."
I get picked back up, i run my buns as fast as i can and follow the medic. I get behind the building once again, the two medics were there and a couple injured mates, among one of them, the guys bragging about the grenades. i ask him how he did.
"I threw all of my grenades and killed that humvee, but before that, a couple jumped out and held up across the street."
I peek around the corner along the side of the building to see two mates still firing across the road. Next to them in the ditch, a flaming humvee with black smoke billowing up that you could see from miles around. I was very proud.
I walked along the wall one more time to see the situation across the street, we had them surpressed well enough, i could see where they're hiding.
I tell them to stop firing and devise a plan, mixed with supressing fire and a smoke grenade, we flank around the side and about 3 minutes more of VERY cautious approach, we get all three of them. With heads held up high, we head to the capture point.
Our team takes the point behind us, we take the next point soon after that. And they run out of tickets and we win.
I congratulate my squad and tell them they were the best team a guy could ask for. I log out and never see them again...

I was concerned that I might not like BORDERLANDS, as I’ve played games with stylised graphics before and have found this type of design can reduce the immersive qualities that I love about gaming. I need not have worried. Borderlands is one of the best games I’ve played. The visuals are very impressive and suck you right in. This is open-world gaming at it’s best, with many large maps to explore as you complete the numerous missions. There are hundreds of weapons to collect and use, or sell along the way (gathering loot quickly becomes addictive). A wide variety of enemies will take you on as you progress up the levels. The combat is varied and the AI is good if not exceptional. Although there’s little story to speak of there’s enough humour to just about make up for this. It’s possible that some might find the missions a tad repetitive but I was so engrossed in the game that I didn’t tire of them and completed every one, including the 3 DLCs available. As for multi-player, well co-op is great fun but best played with people who you can rely on to share the loot.

First, a message to the developers of this game: Thank you so much. I was always a fan of the Arkanoid games and block-breaking games in general, and this is a great game that draws from those games in it's own unique way. Please, keep working on this game; it has so much potential to become even greater than it already is.
After typing, I realized that I got on and rambled. TL;DR I love this game, it has wonderful music, design, and is overall very replayable. 9/10, because I feel it could be so much more if the community asked it of the devs to add things to it.
Now, on to the actual review, which shouldn't be too long.
EM: Shader Attack is a wonderful game that draws from famous previous games such as Arkanoid to create a block breaking game that is quite enjoyable. If you ever enjoyed any games of that genre, you will enjoy this game, short as it may be.
This game has a beautiful art design, with all sorts of shapes that will appear in the background as you play, bounce the ball around, collect powerups... pretty much all of the actions and occurrences in this game will have some sort of effect on the background. It's so captivating that you will often lose yourself and lose a life if you're not careful. ;3 Along with this, you have the EM mode, which when activated changes the design of the background and the different parts of the game, making it even more intense and definitely meriting the seizure warning. The wonderful part of this is that there is a setting in the menu that you can use to reduce the imagery to a more basic form, which is still beautiful but is so much less likely to cause a seizure.
The actual gameplay is what you expect of this type of game: the simplistic moving from side to side and bouncing the ball off of different blocks, while trying to catch powerups. The paddle can be controlled using keyboard, mouse, or even gamepad controls if you feel like using them. Right now, there is only one gamemode, but there are many level designs that the game chooses from randomly for each ten level set that you play. While being simplistic, however, this does not imply it is an EASY game. Since the levels are generally easy and done in (at the most) 5 minutes, you would think that I've beaten the game multiple times in the 60 minutes shown. I have only succeeded once.So far, I have lost more than 20 times, and my beating the tenth level became hinged on one moment where I was blessed with a little bit of luck. For this reason, this game is so much fun and yet a great challenge; in only the short span of an hour, I became enthralled. Even better, this is the type of game that is perfect for when you need to wait on something, like a video or waiting for someone to arrive.
All in all, this game is great fun for the low price of $2, or whatever the price is in other currencies. In my opinion, the game is a 9/10, if only because I feel that more gamemodes could be added to increase the fun and challenge of the game. I have no doubt that the community (who voted this game up here) would have no problem with helping the devs create more maps for it.

Not The Robot wins my vote for most unique premise - a robot that eats furniture. We're talking a skinny robot that eats huge desks, and has the audacity to say it needs more.
In addition to furniture-eating, your robots needs to avoid traps, which may be lasers or other hazards, as well as moving enemies. There is no direct fighting in this game, so there is a large degree of stealth in balancing out which furniture pieces you want to eat now, and which you want to eat later. In addition, the game rewards your furniture gluttony with powerups that may shape the environment, or provide personal buffs. Acquiring buffs requires a sizable amount of furniture to be eaten already, so it goes back to stealth vs. food debate.
The game itself is fairly randomly-generated, and appears to be pretty unique across playthroughs. There's also a sliding difficulty which impacts the spawning of your levels. A level-up system will also impact your level's conditions. Your level is calculated across runs, based on performance, and increases as you do better. In layman's terms: the better you do, the harder it gets.
The game goes on sale quite a bit during major sales, and is definitely worth sale price.

This is a wonderful rogue-like procedurally-generated stealth-oriented game with brilliant mechanics, nice graphics and a good sense of humor going for it. The machines have taken over this office building and somehow you, an exclamation-mark-looking robot with a remarkable appetite for office furniture, are the only one able (and willing) to look into it and discover the truth waiting on the last floor.
In order to beat each stage and access the next one you'll be required to consume a certain amount of furniture, but here's the catch, the only way to avoid lasers and sentinels' line of sight is to duck behind those same piece of furniture. So yeah, it's not like you can run around consuming whatever you stumble upon. Luckily the game will try to ease up your time by providing rechargeable assets like stuns, teleportation, temporary invisibility and even means to modify the stage itself. In addition to the standard campaign you'll also find challanges (set number of floors with certain conditions/limitations) and operations (speedrunners-friendly stages exploiting a particular asset/trap)
NOTE: there is no character evolution, but you do earn XP which levels up the campaign itself, thus unlocking/upgrading traps and unlocking new assets. At the very beginning, with low levels campaigns, there will be little variety in enemy types, making early runs a little sentinel-heavy, but don't give up, get some more XP and the problem will solve itself right away!!

RimWorld is one of those games you could play every day for the rest of your life and have a completely different outcome each and every time. If you put into perspective the amount of random generation and events, then look further at the amount of details like relations between colonists, capturing enemies or even having your own colonists captured right down to their types of injuries.. you can tell a story.
It's a library of books, each game a brand new cover. Will you build a ship and escape or succumb to the dangers and mishaps around you? Will the favorite character who has fantastic shooting and a friendly face get mauled by a megasloth? Nobody knows. There is no script, only a story to be written after.
Aside from all of that, completely independent of it, this game supports mods. As we see from games like Garry's mod, mods can make a game immortal. Already, even before the game is done, there is a fantastic modding community adding things that we can only hope will be added by the developers.
TL;DR - Imagine prison architect 3000 years in the future except it's not a prison, it's the entire world. Oh and it has about twice the features and complexity. Plus mods.

So, at this point I don't consider myself all that great at writing reviews, but regardless, here we go.
This game, in my humble opinion, is a good deal of fun. It's something I occasionally turn on while in a skype call or listening to a podcast that is legitimately a fun and entertaining experience. And while this is good, at the same time, I can see why it may fall from recommended to unrecommended depending on the person.
I do not see this game as holding quite the candle to a good stealth game, nor is it too terribly amazing at the Rogue-like part. The randomly generated levels are surely a draw, but at the same time, it will occasionally craft explicitly unfair floors or challenge floors for you to play. Many times, during completing challenges, I would simply have to either get killed or restart because it would start with AI looking right at me, or with the items I would desperately need obnoxiously far away. And while that is not always such a drawback (as it is rather good when you beat a floor against all odds) it does make the challenges the game is packed with a bit more luck based than one might hope.
Other than that, the AI may occasionally seem a bit unfair, seeing you when you are behind things; having odd and sometimes broken paths around objects and rooms; and the rare but equally annoying points where the sentry bots always seem to miss unless you are low in health, where they hit with 100% accuracy.
I will say some of these things have frustrated me, but at the same time, I would still recommend this game. I found it to be a good distraction for the time I played it, and will continue to pick it up to resume my attempts at getting all the achievements and completing those pesky challeges.

Come for the kicking stay for the stealth.
Frankly this one of the most unintentionally funny games I've played and at times it's also genuinely fun to play. That said it's not without an abnormally large number of problems I'll be getting into. The game runs like butter in 4k maxed out (Source engine game from 06 after all) and the visuals have held up well overall thanks to some fancy lighting effects and general visual flair and well as a reliance on physics that would make Half-Life 2 blush. The lip sync is great and the animation is decent even though that's primarily because it's a Source engine game and you'll often recognize some canned animations reused over and over if you've played other titles on the engine. Faces are a mixed bag with some humans looking great and others obviously not being capable of and facial animation. All the monsters look great but the people aren't all well detailed and are sometimes more ghoulish than the beasts you encounter funnily enough.
One thing that could have made up for the wonky animations would have been good voice acting but unfortunatley that's another thing this game lacks to a frankly laughable degree. Things like he ability to see your feet and phyisically use your hands to pick objects up in the world (In addition to some slightly sickening head bobbing) make up for that quite a bit and can make it incredibly immersive at times even if you'll see your sword floating out of your hands or just walk past all the enemies like I did. The overly drawn out tutorial followed by a long drawn out linear opening are a few issues that keep you from getting into the meat and potatos of the game but during this time you'll have held every useless object in your hand (if your me) or destroyed everything with your awesome kick.
There is stealth, there's magic, swordplay (You can dual weilding daggers, using a sword and sheild, just a sword or a staff all of which can also be used to block with), archery and donkey kong which is my preffered playstyle. The most effective weapon is the♥♥♥♥♥♥lying on the floor. You'll find yourself mostly jumping on enemies as it ragdolls them even when they are already lying down, picking up a body to block attacks, kicking people and generally being merciless as enmies limp away only to get kicked. While kicking has limited stamina it's quite useful as ledges and spikes are everywhere. It kind of reminds me of Theid with the whole game feeling like a source engine version of that title for better or worse.
It's biggest problem is the lack of polish which only effects the 2 of the 3 most important things in the game those being the the gameplay and story. It's a wee bit janky and the occasional badly compressed FMV's are another thing that makes it a chore to sit through. In Half-life 2 if you got bored at least you could climb around the room and throw stuff. Funnily enough NPC's actually react twoards your bad behavior for the most part outside of cutscenes but then the game will reload a past checkpoint after you've been chastized even if all you did was throw a bottle or jump on someones head. I guess this is also because unlike Half-Life 2 you can ALSO kill pretty much anybody which could have lead to some awkward moments if you walked into a room and accidentally killed off an important charcter needed for progression.
I disliked everybody I met in the game which is why it's a bummer I can't just kill everybody all the way until the end of the game. Regardless the price is right and I advise anybody who hasn't already to pick it up as there is a lot of freedom in terms of what means you use to progress.
I don't know if it's really good or really bad but overall I reccomend it.
Oh and Ubisoft AND Arkane had a hand in it whcih probably explains a lot.

I really, really wish I could like this game. I love stealth, I love robots, and I love randomly generated stuff. The developer of the game is the guy behind The Company of Myself, one of my favorite games when I was a wee middle schooler on Kongregate. This game has a very inventive idea, a stealth game where you must destroy your own cover in order to progress. But this game shows that randomly generated rooms and stealth is NOT a good combination. It is frequently straight-up unfair or frustrating to play most levels. It had never really occured to me before, but a good stealth game requires a whole lot of meticulous level design in order to make the level work. When a level is quite literally just strewn together, all of that meticulous planning done to balance challenge and ingenuity is thrown out the window. Stealth and RNG simply do not mix, and I do not like this game; not for the fault of the author or the game itself, but the very premise of the game just doesn't work. It is very easy for a level to straight up ♥♥♥♥ you over, trap you in a tiny room with a sentry that you literally CANNOT avoid and you MUST get spotted in order to progress, and since there is no set route that the sentries follow, you can be literally stuck waiting a good five minutes for the sentry to look away long enough just to move to the other side of the room. Things like that, things that turn a good idea into a gimmick into a chore. It is not fun to play, as much as I wish it was. This is just an example of a good idea unfortunately making a poor game. Perhaps with better coding for the level generation or more forgiving sentry AI this game could be a lot better.

It's hard to judge NaissanceE. Really hard!
I think the main problem of this game is inconsistecy
On one side the game clearly pushes in creating evocative moments surrounded by mega-structures that make the player feel insignificant, and they work really really well. The only reason i kept playing was to see what i was gonna discover next.
On the other hand though, everything kinda leaves you with a lot of question marks, not only about what you see in the game, but also about what the hell the developers were thinking.
Examples (Mild spoilers): In one level you'll find an infinite staircase that takes you nowhere, and only one way to get out to where you were before...pointless...later you'll find another staircase that seems inifinite, although this one you actually have to climb for more than 2 minutes to get somewhere....2 MINUTES of straight running without any
Another example in one area you'll find some platforming puzzles to get at the top of 2 towers...once you make it to the top...the world will change color....and that's
Some area of the game are breath taking and beautiful, evocative and alien to the right point...something that could be out Blade Runner,  or some other amazing Sci-Fi movie. Other levels are a complete mess of geometries, and flickering lights to the point that i almost got sick, and totally annoyed.
Finding the right path is at times complicated, with small black staircases that are almost invisible in the dark.
The feeling is that this game wants to be "edgy" for the sake of it, but often failing at some basic concepts of game design and consistency. I shouldnt have to go and change the gamma in the options to be able to see where i'm going.
There shouldnt be a corridor that leads to the game closing itself on purpose, it's not "edgy", it's cheap crap that has nothing to do with game design in my opinion.
I found myself really struggling to finish this game, and the later levels felt more like a chore then a real game.
So, if you're in for an interesting journey, with a few very akward/annoying moments, and some really debatable game design choices, go ahead and try it yourself, i cant feel to recommend it though.

YIKES!
In a perfect world, either this game wouldn't exist, or all of its reviews would be just one word: YIKES!
Super Distro isn't just a badly-designed and completely-unfun game, it's also selfish. Selfish games are the absolute worst. They demand so much of your time and energy that you'll have difficulty going back to playing good games. Let's say you sit down and force yourself to finish this game. Even though the first level heaps mounds of crap at you, you just keep going. You gain a tolerance for the ridiculous design-decisions and poor controls. A sensible person would have given up on this game after a couple of minutes, but you soldier on. You've got the eye of the tiger, there's no easy way out, and you're the best around.
So what happens when you beat the game? Don't ask me because I haven't the slightest idea. Usually I finish games before I review them, even the terrible ones. But this review isn't about me, or the game, it's about you. You've beaten Super Distro, and now you're going to play another videogame. Let's pick a random game like uh...
? Alright. I've heard good things about that one.
The thing is, you've been playing Super Distro for so long, that you've lost your bearings. You'll try to play
, but you can't adjust. You'll be saying things like "The controls are too responsive!" and "These levels are hard but also fair. I can't handle it!" or even "Why am I playing a game that doesn't make me wish for the sweet embrace of death?!?!?" This is why I hate selfish games. They take everything away from you and give nothing in return.
Look. I'm only writing from experience. I spent a year playing Friday the 13th on the NES, because it was the only game I owned for the system. It took another year in order for me to re-adjust to playing games like Contra, Super Mario Bros, River City Ransom, and so on. Super Distro isn't the only game you own right? Don't consider it for a second.

What attracted me to this game initially is probably what brought it to everyone else's attention: it's visual style. The striking architectural designs and high contrast lighting make this a game that stands out from the crowd. This simplistic form extends into the gameplay, taking on the role as a basic first person platformer. The style is so consistent and immersive that it manages to make even basic geometric shapes send chills down your spine and it by doing so it accomplished what no other game I've played has managed...
I know NaissanceE doesn't necessarily advertise itself as a horror game, but it unnerved me to such a degree that most other self-proclaimed horror games have failed to reach that I feel compelled to refer to it as such. Here is why, in greater detail.
Much has been said about the game's atmosphere, from the limited color palette to the imposing structures and the stark lighting. What really made the game feel like a nightmare was the subtle nods to real world architecture and interior design. The whole game feels like an abstraction of reality,
like what you would get if you asked someone to draw something, but never allow them to look at what they were drawing. Many other games try to achieve the "nightmare" by having warped, celestial looking entities or having porcelain doll faces everywhere or lovecraftian horror creatures startle you. NaissanceE acheives the same feel using a minimalist appearance that resembles what you remember from a nightmare after waking up, rather than what the nightmare actually contained. Ironically, this grounds the visual style more into reality than other horror visuals that try a little too hard.
Sound is also used to great effect to compliment the imposing visuals. From echoing thunder to harsh stings to the loneliness of your own footsteps, all of it reminds you that this dreamlike world is vast and reaches farther than you can possibly comprehend. There is also a particularly noteworthy moment in the game (that I won't spoil) where the music and sound effects start to speed up as you progress and it does a brilliant job of creating tension and making you feel rushed even though you are in no actual danger.
It's a good thing that the atmosphere is phenomenal because without it the gameplay wouldn't be much to write home about. I have a few specific nit-picks that I will go over in more detail in a bit, but overall my impression of the gameplay was that it was very basic, but it served the atmosphere well.
What it boils down to is that NaissanceE isn't a game. It's an experience. The first person controls are simple enough that it allows you to indulge in the scenery without taking away from your focus on said scenery. They are fully generic though. The only really unique control the game offers is that you have to click every couple of seconds while you're running to avoid running out of breath. Thankfully, this doesn't distract from the game too much. Once you've figured out the timing, it's just as regular as everything else.
The game does occasionally try to throw in a some platforming sections or puzzles involving lights and shadows. These do help to break up some of the scenery but in a lot of ways I wish they weren't present. Some of the platforming adds to the dream-like feel I explained earlier, but mostly it is just frustrating, which I will elaborate on further. For some puzzles, it means navigating the same section of the environment several times to check if you got the solution to the puzzle correct and it really doesn't add to what makes the game stand out so much, which is the atmosphere, so now we're getting to what I mentioned earlier:
All of the nit-picks I've mentioned are miniscule at most and the atmosphere is so fascinating that it more than compensates for the other flaws in the game. NaissanceE is a truly unique and unnerving experience and if you're a fan of artistic games, horror, or you just want something a little different, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not playing it.

NaissanceE is an intensely atmospheric walking puzzle sim. It's a good experience albeit one that is still very incoherent in overall vision.
The walking simulator genre, or whatever you want to call it, has a lot of games under its belt. Not too many are like this one. The problem for me with its closest rival, Kairo, is that game just reeks of amateur game design whereas this one is slightly more polished and playable. That doesn't excuse some of the horrid checkpoints and mediocre mechanics for breathing. This one gets a recommendation only based on some of its superior art and music design.
Yea, Kairo has more colors and different puzzles, but none of it comes together to be even slightly believable, and nor did that game immerse me in its world. I mean I don't even know what the hell is going on in that game to the point it undermines the experience. While that happens here, I'd say the game does really well up until the ending parts, which kind of become too abstract and weird for their own good, undermining the art deco flourishes and other strangely alien stylings up until that point that promoted a more cohesive and grounded mood.
The major cons are the checkpoints for sure. I mean, just stop wasting our time please? I'm not gonna cast hell on this one like some others do, but it is noted that certain gameplay elements are confusing or cheap to play through. The breathing is a bit off to me, and in reality it's annoying to hear the character breathing all the time in such an unrealistic way. I'd rather tough platforming and better controls any day of the week.
Altogether that didn't ruin the fun for me, butI still felt that parts of the fan episodes and later areas were completely ridiculous and cumbersome for no reason. It doesn't harm the mysterious nature of the game, but nothing really approaches the coolness of the middle part for me. The ending is pure disappointment. I have no idea why you build up such an experience and then basically end it with a text. Something simple but much more creative could have been done after the boss fight. It kind of feels not worth the time in the end. But for nearly 3/4 of the game it does promote a really nice atmosphere that is worth experiencing.
Not much more needs to be said really. If you dig the artstyle plus light puzzle and platforming elements then fire this thing up in 4K with some SMAA and enjoy the ride. It's not going to blow your brains out or max every sensory nerve you have, but it's a solid addition to the walking puzzler genre, and most of the elements come off as fairly well presented throughout your journey.
It's a fun game. more like a Mario Kart ripoff, but still a lot of fun.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a partial reboot of the 1992 video game Wolfenstein 3D. It follows BJ Blazcovitch as he goes into war with a character from the 2009 game Wolfenstein (which recieved negative reviews, I believe. It wouldn't be partial if the 2009 game was consistent with previous games), but the raid goes bad, and he ends up paralyzed. Some doctors find him and he spends 14 years in an insane asylum, where the doctors try to improve his condition. Somehow, when he's needed most, he rises up from paralysis and saves the day! Somehow, through the power of plot, he falls in love with his old nurse, and they form a bond (which causes some out of place sex scenes, but only two.) He returns to his new girlfriend's home, and learns that the Nazis won world war 2, so he now sees it as his job to ♥♥♥♥ them up and liberate the planet.
The game also has a split timeline feature, but with only minor differences between the timelines. Different collectibles, paths, and characters, I guess.
I want to make it clear that one thing I do no like about this game is that it does not like AMD cards. For some reason, you need to rename the executable file from WolfWolfNewOrder_64.exe to WolfNewOrder_x32.exe and launch from a desktop shortcut, same with The Old Blood. Otherwise, your game will run slow as ♥♥♥♥, and look like Half-Life 2 on ultra low.
The game also has a perk system, where it requires you to do specific things to unlock more perks. It's pretty fun, but you might die a lot trying them. I know I did.
I also want to give the game a bonus plus for making the difficulty screen have the pictures from Wolfenstein 3D. It's pretty funny seeing Blaskovitch wear a bonnet.

Like a lot of other players, I want to reccommend this.
.  It's a game about stealth with a perma-death mechanic that gets really,
hard.
The first few buildings are a blast.  I can move around and practice stealth at my own pace, where I've got avenues to plan out how I'll avoid a laser or a sentry.  Power-ups aren't as mandatory, which can suck later on, but can be lifesavers.  The random generation of these floors was the reason I did a few runs, where I could consistantly get through them and enjoy my time.
There's a funny narrative that progresses with each playthrough (or attempt at it).  The only thing that holds it back are the later levels, which are likely to set you back to square one.
In terms of atmosphere, I love it.  There's an abode of unique effects prevalent in the way the game feels.  The music and asthetic match, almost as if I'm watching myself through a camera, and it really makes me feel like I
be stealthy about it.
*Sigh* and then there's the late game.
I'm talking floors 5-7.  I just sorta hit a wall.  Floor 4 has this perfect balance of cover to walls to sentries that makes it a challenge, but also still provides sufficient routes to try and tackle the floor.  Floor 5 on the other hand, feels like I'm robbing Trump's personal pornography stash.  The random generation aspect of the game's core feels OK here, but when sentries are introduced in such vast quantities as they are, it can take 2-3 minutes before they've cleared out of a room, and I can move again.  It becomes so painstakingly slow that I just can't progress.  I either pick off some cover, wait 7 minutes and move to the next room (where I may or may not get stuck), or I go completely bonkers and just leg it (which seldom works, but often happens).
The random aspect of the sentries makes it impossible for me to plan routes on these later floors, which is really dissapointing because I
planning a route is important in any game that considers itself a stealth-em-up (Stealth Barstard and Thief come to mind).  That being said, the sentries feel more like a broken mechanic.  At least in Deus Ex, Hitman and Wolfenstein I can squelch someone that detects me.  But without a reliable method of escaping, everything is very likely to come to a screeching halt.
That ties directly back to the perma-death aspect of the game.  Unlike Tower of Guns or Sword of the Stars, I don't
anything.  I don't get some unlock that might change the way I play the game.  I don't discover something that might help me get further.  Thus when I inevitably die on floor 5, I'm shoved right back into bureau buffet boot-camp, and will likely not get any further than I did before.  I'm really dissapointed with this, because I'm dying to find out what happens on upper floors.  I haven't experienced the true essence of what's there, because I can't get there.  The game is keeping me from enjoying the game.
It's a really interesting and unique take on a genre that has a lot of trouble doing things right.  The stealth can be a lot of fun, but it also can get extremely tedious to borderline boring.  I feel like someone on the dev team was drunk and just shouted "let's make it a rouge-like!" without realizing that the game would become impossible to a lot of the general audience.  Everything is there for a game, but there's so much I'd re-do.
- Make sentries like they were in Thief.  If you can't fight them, make sure you can avoid them.  This random-movement crap makes the game way too difficult to predict.
-  If the above can't be accomplished, provide a reliable escape mechanism.  Maybe make powerups into unlockables, with unlimited use.  I just sort of went through the game seeing them as "maybe get-out-of-jail-free" cards, that one was unlikely to find again.
-  It's made by a small team, and on a small budget, but for $10 I kind of expected to get a little more than 2 hours before the game hit a plateau and I essentially couldn't play it any more.  The other content just wasn't interesting, so I feel like I'm at fault for not enjoying the central experience, which I don't think is ever in a dev's mind.

Kind of wish I didn't have to give this game a thumbs down, since it's not a bad game. But just that there's not enough content to stay interesting for long. The novelty of the idea seems to wear off pretty fast and there's nothing much else to the game apart from it.
You play as a robot that travels from one office building to another with a single goal - to eat furniture. Not sure why exactly (we don't get a reason). However, there are dangers, ranging from unusually placed laser-beams which can only hurt you, but do not cut through anything else, some kind of floor heaters that switch on and off repeatedly, and sentries in a shape of floating robot heads that shoot at you. I kind of wish all these things had a reason to exist. Maybe they do, but it just is not apparent why in any way.
The levels are all randomly generated since it's a rogue-like. You also do not recover any health in between levels. So if you finished one level on low health, you'll continue on from the next one with the same health. Luckily you do occasionally find med boxes that can heal you, but again, it all depends on luck if one will spawn in the level or not.
You also get to find various gadgets which can help you, like letting you sprint, or place blocks to hide behind, or dig through a wall, or become invisible. These are all good, but you can only ever carry one at a time (unless you get lucky and find an upgrade that lets you have more), and if you want to pick another one up, you have to permanently drop your current one. One of my biggest gripes is that you can never see what the item inside the box is, so you've no idea if it's better than your current item or not. Again, you just have to get lucky.
Visuals are very nice in this game, but I am not a big fan of the music. It was a bit jarring. The sense of humour seems quite nice too. The game has a nice light-hearted feel to it.
As I said, it's not a bad game, but I don't feel it has enough content or excels much at what it does for me to recommend it. If you are into rogue-likes or stealth games, you might like it. Probably best to get it on sale, like I did.

Wow. A spectacular game.  I'm quite new to these reviews so I am going to separate it out in an orderly fashion.
Gameplay:
I have over a hundred hours in this game, most being in the past two months. I have improved and improved, however like most shooter games I do see the learning curve within the game- from finding the correct spot to place a healing station or simply knowing how to throw the frag grenade. Am I a professional? NO! That's the fun part. This game almost feels like it has no end, constantly improving your mercs and constantly improving as a player. Of course I see how some may argue that the in-game spending ruins the fun... People just pay to get the ideal merc etc. Yeah I guess that is true to a degree, but that doesn't make them advantaged. That's their own bad decision, the decision to cut short the experience of continuous improvement. I personally have never spent any money in the game, however at times I do feel tempted!
The mercs, unlinke what some people say, are incredibly balanced, each serving their own role. Of course Skyhammer may be better suited on defence on an EV map, but at the same time Proxy is better at a c4 map. Its very situational and its hard to say which is better. Believe it or not, I still only use Skyhammer and Aura, the two begginer mercs. To each their own is the best phrase here, we each have different gameplay, sniper (Vassili and Aimee), Engineer (Proxy and Fletcher among others), Assault (Skyhammer and Fragger among others) and Medics (Guardian and Aura among others)
I play on Singaporean servers and never feel the slight bit of lag. I play on the highest settings and have a decent computer. I can run the game at 100 frames with max settings... Pretty good! (Also, its not that the graphics are bad in the game, I also don't know how it isnt as graphic demanding as PUBG even though it has nicer graphics, maybe map size... I don't know :D)
I like playing competitive in this game, and am beyond thankful for ranked season four being back. Competitive is the best place to show off your skills but also have a fun time with friends, being a much more action-packed 5v5.
Is it pay-to-win?
NO. I have watched lots of YouTube reviews saying it is... They couldn't be more wrong. The only stuff you can purchase in-game with real life money are crates. Yes, by paying you may have more cobalts, but cobalts are simply just a difference in skin like in CSGO. If CSGO is not a pay to win, then nor is Dirty Bomb.
Improvements:
As I mentioned, I live in SEA and unlike the rest of the globe, I cannot play casual matchmaking with my friends. Most times we arent on the same team and consistently have to shuffle vote. Other times, we won't even get matched up together due to the lack of a lobby for casual.
Content seems to be coming out faster now, however I do see some areas in which it could roll out faster. Could the developers have a contest from which we vote on a character, like the fan base designs a character and there is a poll of some sort? This could ease the work for the developers and also speed up the outflow of contest, but obviously this is just an idea.
Apart from this, I really can't see any flaws within the game. For being a free to play game, I couldn't suggest it more. If it was a paid game I would even pay up to 50$ for it. It's an experience worth taking and living.

RimWorld is one of those games you could play every day for the rest of your life and have a completely different outcome each and every time. If you put into perspective the amount of random generation and events, then look further at the amount of details like relations between colonists, capturing enemies or even having your own colonists captured right down to their types of injuries.. you can tell a story.
It's a library of books, each game a brand new cover. Will you build a ship and escape or succumb to the dangers and mishaps around you? Will the favorite character who has fantastic shooting and a friendly face get mauled by a megasloth? Nobody knows. There is no script, only a story to be written after.
Aside from all of that, completely independent of it, this game supports mods. As we see from games like Garry's mod, mods can make a game immortal. Already, even before the game is done, there is a fantastic modding community adding things that we can only hope will be added by the developers.
TL;DR - Imagine prison architect 3000 years in the future except it's not a prison, it's the entire world. Oh and it has about twice the features and complexity. Plus mods.

I don't usually write reviews for games I have bought, but I feel I had to in this case, just to preserve your sanity!
During the game's intro, it declares that it will cause people to 'rage again'.  I thought it was a reference to difficult games, that are great, but can be frustrating at times, such as Super Meat Boy.  This was probably the dev's intention, however, this was not why I raged!
Simply put this a 2d platformer, and it seems there are a plethora of these going around at the moment.  The genre is going through something of a revival, and there are loads of really cheap, and excellent games of this type thanks to indie developers.
So why is this game so utterly bad?
First off, there does not seem to be any controller support.  In a game of this type, that is always going to be a major issue for me.  So then I went into the options menu to try and learn the keys.  Nope, there was no way to learn the basic controls, let alone change them!  At this point I could see many red flags, before the eventual red mist.
Next, the game starts.  Graphics were poor, really basic, and uninspired.  It made some genuine 8-bit games of old look pretty!  Music was repetitive and very grating.  Yet another factor to add to the overall miserable experience of this disastrous title.
Then the ultimate kick in the balls.  The gameplay...or sheer lack of it!  Platformers of all ilk, live and die (no pun intended) due to their gameplay.  A 'hard-as-nails' game, as this pupports to be, can be excused if it has fine gameplay, and the player knows that they died due to their mistake.  It's what creates a kind of zen moment in platform games, when you zip along, with only your reflexes and guile to keep you going.  Well, with atrocious level-design. clunky movement, and glitchy enemies, there is no gameplay whatsoever.
Listen I know this game is cheap.  That does not mean you should buy it.  In fact I think the dev should pay us all for the mental anguish that this steaming pile inflicts on the gamer!
Worst game I have played for as long as I can remember.  Avoid at all costs.  Trust me!

WARNING: Do not play this game until matchmaking has been fixed or you will get salty as the seas. This would otherwise a positive review as it is a good game. Also ignore the "Open Beta"
as this game has more than enough content to be a full game.
This is indeed a "Free to Play" game. The "grind" is just slow enough to make sure you don't purchase half the mercs within a week or two. Assuming your as if you complete the missions assigned to you, (you get new ones every three hours) play about two and a half hours per day, you can get a new merc in about four to five days without spending a dime. Sure, you can spend some money to get a loadout card with perks (or augments; they are small but not substanal improvements) or different weapons, so spending money only really gets you cosmetic changes although some of them do look quite nice, obsidian cards even more so. But as Shoe (one of DB's Devs) himself has said: "If you can't kill someone with a lead, you can't kill them with a cobalt"
A somewhat fast paced shooter, Dirty Bomb has many different mercenarys that all have their own unique take on your typical "class", so you can still fill the same role in your team even if you don't like the abilities or weapons they have. For example, if you don't like being tied to a single spot as a medic, you can change your merc so instead of having a heal station, you have throwable health packs, or as an engineer go from placing automated turrets to self detonating mines. This means that each merc is better or worse at some things than another merc of similar role is.
There are two game modes (objective and stopwatch), several objective types with fresh perspectives on classics, and multiple maps with different layouts, which won't get stale even after a few hundred hours, as each map has neat spots for deployables and parkour heavy routes to flank people to learn while avoiding hot lead. Combat is challenging and will reward those with fast relfexes and those who aim for the head with anything (except for melee) with twice the damage, but scoping in for a headshot may cost you yours as while you move fast enough to avoid quite a few rounds while firing from the hip, you move slow enought to be easily hit while aiming. Melee attacks will slow you down a bit and very short range, but can deal a decent to large chunk of health.
Matchmaking however, needs some real work as matches are quite often lopsided due to rather poor algorythms. As such you should expect to see ether a steamroll or a shutout about once every four to six matches, (especially so if you play a medic but your aim leaves something to be desired) so untill they "fix their sh!t", make sure your diet can take some salt, or your wallet can take a broken keyboard.
UPDATE: Matchmaking has gotten worse, as it's gotten so bad that nearly every game has ether shutouts or rolls. This is likely because the players from ranked have flooded into casual matches due to exessive ranked que times. As such, I don't recomend playing untill the devs actually decide to work on matchmaking rather than content.

At its heart, NaissanceE is intended not for those who want to experience a "game", but rather the ambient darkness a la Tsutomo Nihei's BLAME!, perhaps coupled with Piranesi's "Carceri". The experience you have is manifold, and compares well to Kairo (another game in a similar vein available on Steam). Where NaissanceE is pseudo-linear exploration and the accidental occlusion of puzzles - they sort of show up, rather than being presented to you as in Kairo - the atmosphere is much more pronounced here. NaissanceE reveals a measure of spectral light, causing movement to be rare and the interplay of light and shadow quite spectacular.
If you can deal with and enjoy a game that can be quite difficult in its platforming aspects (moreso than Kairo) but rewards you with the visual splendor that Pauline Oliveros' "Deep Listening" album evoked aurally - monolithic devices and structures rising from the gloom of nothingness, with a rather haunting ambient feel - definitely pick this up.
This is Danielewski's "House of Leaves" in visual form. Where does form define itself if not within the darkness of our own eyes?

A fantastic game that is worth buying. I could go on and on about this game for an hour, probably, but here's what I'll say.
The scenery and ambient music creates a very relaxing environment.
The puzzles vary in difficulty and allowing people to go back and solve harder puzzles later is a nice option this game offers.
The philosophical dialogues are thought provoking and can develop the ideas of many players.
The locations in the game are very open and leave a lot of room to explore.
Not only can you explore, but you get rewarded greatly for exploring, maybe you find a new star or you find one of the easter eggs hidden in the game.
The stars can sometimes be just the result of checking every single nook and cranny or the result of cleverly manipulating puzzles to work with each other, a bit of a con.
The movement controls were a bit frustrating with some things (like the jumping mechanic) but were overall okay.
The game was really long and you're only going to play through the whole thing and all of its endings if you really take the time to.
Overall, a game with good writing, music, and appearance. There's a lot to do, but the game doesn't pressure you to do everything at once, so that's good.
The Road to Gehenna DLC is also worth the purchase if you liked the game, even more beautiful scenery and challenging puzzeles.

The Talos Principle is a philosophical puzzle solving game. In most of the puzzles you are trying to find your way to the "sigil" which is behind walls and doors. Sigils are like Tetris blocks, and if you collect enough of them, you can open access to other worlds which contain more puzzles.
In the puzzles you use step-on buttons, laser-beam-controlled locks, fans, jammers, boxes, trays, and record-playback devices to open doors, jump over walls, or avoid moving mines or turrets. It is easy to learn who to use these items, but hard to master it. By solving the first puzzles, you learn techniques which will be useful in the later puzzles. Most of the puzzles are easy, but some are really hard. When you get stuck in a puzzle, the most likely cause is that you have not yet discovered a new way to use the items listed above. However, each puzzle can be solved with logical reasoning, and there is not too much repetition.
The philosophical part of the game consists of discussions with some mysterious person through consoles scattered throughout the worlds, and documents you can access with them, and recorded messages you bump into from time to time. There is also a voice from above that tells you to do or not to do things. You soon begin to wonder who are you, where are you, where do you come from, should you obey the voice from above, or the one you have discussed with through the consoles, and what is the great tower. I think it is possible to just play the game and skip over all the philosophical stuff, but by doing so, one misses a large part of the game, and the ending doesn't necessarily make sense. Actually, there are more than one ending you can choose.
The Talos Principle is a good game in its category. However, there are a few things that I didn't like too much. Most of the puzzles are bounded with walls, so that it is easy to see where the puzzles take place. While this can be a good thing, it kind of isolates the puzzle solving from the story. Also it is impossible to save the game within a puzzle. If there is a solution requiring multiple steps and then you make a mistake that makes it impossible to continue, the only option is to reset the puzzle and start all over again. Most of the time this doesn't matter, but with the really difficult puzzles that require precise actions, it is annoying to do the same puzzle 20 times, just because a laser-beam is two centimeters off or you forgot to bring a box to the other side of a door.
I would recommend this game to everyone who loves puzzle games.

Although it seems similar to other MOBA's, Strife is a beast all its own. They take some of the major concepts of other MOBA's and improve upon them, hence the term second generation MOBA. Here are some cons and pros.
Cons
-No Surrender. This is emphasized with the severe punishment of leavers.
-Limited Characters. A large roster but not as outlandish as other MOBAs.
-Single Map. You will get sick of the same map until they make more in the future.
-Grinding. Although you can get every resource available, it takes ample time.
-Levels. You wont find many players at low rank, resulting in a long grind upwards via bot matches.
Pros
-Couriers. Each player has their own, eliminating priority problems for item delivery.
-Ward totems. Instead of warding, you have strategic objectives to capture for vision of the jungle area.
-Custom Items. With enough resources, you can pick what pieces an item is made of plus a bonus enchant.
-Pets. The pets add two passives abilities and an active ability to a champion, changing how they play.
-Story. Though underdeveloped, a story campaign is available, adding more depth to the champions present.
-Humour. This title hasn't downgraded its content, resulting in smoking robots and egotists characters.
Comparable yet striving to be something more, Strife does fit the bill of being unique.

I've been playing Strife for like 80 hours more or less, and they're enough to make me write down few things.
First of all let me tell you that i'm not new to the MOBA world, i've played lots of matches in DOTA, LoL, Smite and Heroes of the Storm and the first impression i've had playing Strife was really awful.
If you like MOBAs because you like games that involve teamwork and ladders to climb to get a great ranking, let me tell you that Strife is NOT your game. Why? Well it's simple: the community. I've never ever seen such a toxic community as it's inside Strife. Whenever it seems that a match is about to be lost, say bye-bye to your teammates: there's a huge percentage of AFKs (even before the match starts), rage quits, negative attitude in chat during the game and (talking about the European Server) too much people playing from the East Europe (Russia and nearby countries) that TOTALLY REFUSE to communicate in English. I've encountered these problems both during normal and ranked matches.
I'm not saying "don't even try Strife" because i think it has the potential to be a nice MOBA, but with this community this game won't last much.

FunJam has here a potential gem of a game. Robocraft used to be a very interesting game that you could spend tens of hours with, just to play around with your robot. I suspect that the dubious updates are due to financial issues, but even that doesn't add up. What they are actually doing is literally getting rid of the "free players" and trying to get as many players as possible open up their wallets. however this will just lead to loss of many gamers and therefore also less people willing to pay for a unpopular game.
If you want to make a free-to-play you need as many "free players" as possible to get the paying clients, but if you want every player to contribute financially just ask for an early access fee. This game (if you put back in some of the old content like different cubes, research tree,...) is totally worth paying 20 or 30 bucks for. But with those game changes that obviously make Robocraft worse, you loose confidence in the capability of the developpers to finish the game.
Hence, I do suggest to everyone to give Robocraft a try but at the moment FunJam just doesn't prouve that they are a company worth investing your money in.

Quick Summary:
Rimworld is my favorite colony-builder. I regularly play others as they're released but this is the only one I keep coming back to even if it's been months since my last play. Does not feel like Early Access and absolutely worth a purchase in current state.
Detail:
An extremely detailed and addictive colony-building / simulation game. It may be listed as early access but it's been in development for years and feels fully featured and polished. The developer semi-regularly releases major updates that are often of the same quality as a medium ($10?) DLC pack for an 'AAA publisher' title and they're completely free. The recent Caravan update is a great example, adding the ability to travel around the entire world map assaulting enemy strongholds, setting up multiple bases, and trading of course.
There are also sometimes changes to existing features, but they're usually refinements and balancing or blowing out additional detail. Apparently there are bugs since I see fixes listed in the patch notes, but I've only ever experienced minor graphical glitches.
There's also a robust modding community which adds different object types and features to suit your interests. I'd recommend playing the base game for a while first and then deciding what you'd like to expand from there.
I feel like I should list some cons, but I really can't think of anything. I've been enjoying and playing this game on and off for a couple years now (not always on Steam).

Heres a TL;DR for those in a rush:
This game is much better than the console. If you've played this on the console and hated it, buy this version. Why? One simple reason: Unlike the console you are NOT restricted to choosing a class. The goods about this game are: Physics are utilized, despite being linear there are multiple ways to take on missions and groups of enemies, fun to explore, combat is fun, pretty much everything is fun in this game.
Whats bad about this game: Pretty old, sometimes easy to get stuck/lost.
Buy this game, its worth the money and has replayability.
Detailed review:
I remember getting this game for the console when I was younger and feeling like I missed out, due to you having to choose a class before the game start. Choosing your class determines what skills you can and cant take, and what weapons and armor you can and cant use and it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off that 1 of the 4 classes were locked off until you beat the game (or some♥♥♥♥♥♥like that). When I came across this game on steam, I almost passed it up beacuse of how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the console made this game seem. But at the time I was going to lose my internet in a few days so I decided to download it. Once I lost my internet (for maintenence reasons), I played this game. Holy hell was it fun. I could take what I want, when I wanted. Do you want to kick a dude into a nearby hazard (firepit, spike trap, off a ♥♥♥♥ing cliff/mountain), do it. You want to stab him? Yolo. You want to be a sneaky character that uses magic? Or how about a guy that is focused on combat that uses staves? You can do it.
Whats good about this game is that the combat is satisfying, and feels right. The fact that, despite being linear, you can still explore and sometimes even get lost. This game truly makes you feel like a protagonist, where you start off as an average joe but the more and more you level your skills, find (and even make) your own weapons, the more and more powerful you get. The level design is great. Not the best, not the worst, but good enough to have fun with. Be it using the environment to kill your enemies, sneak around, ambush, its just fun. The graphics are pretty poor and are nothing to write home about, but i feeel as if it fits the game. There is multi player, but I never checked it out. Something worth mentioning is you can really do what you want with this game, and as far as building your character for combat/utility, its almost as flexible as how Oblviion was in that reguard. Though it is discouraged through the rarity of certain items, it is possible. For example, I was able to build a mage that wore heavy armor. Was it hard to beat the game that way? Yes, very hard, but I found it fun. I might have always been running out of mana, but it wasnt impossibly hard, just hard enough to pose a challenge. While building something more forward like a warrior with a sword and sheild, or a sneaky character using daggers will do you justice, the game will still be challenging enough. The difficulty of the game is almost perfect. It punishes you for not using the environment to your advantage, punishes for poor skill, and punishes for blindly mashing the attack button. Also, the story is pretty good in my opinion. Dont ask me if the lore is friendly or whatever because outside of this game I have no clue about the lore of the might and magic universe.
However, with all the amazing things this game brings, there are of course some bad things. The graphics are pretty bad. They are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Bugs do happen. Not often, but often enough to note. No game breaking bugs thankfully. Despite this game being extremly fun, its pretty forgetable. Also, the end of the game feels... kind of disappointing. That might be me just being an♥♥♥♥♥ but thats just me.
I still reccomend this game though. Buy this game right now.
However if you come across the console version of this game, do everyone some good and burn that copy.

When I first learned to drive, I would sometimes drive around my hometown until I got lost, then try to find my way back to somewhere familiar.  Playing NaissanceE is a little like that.  The familiar made unfamiliar.
If you have an affection for vast spaces, inhuman scale, and the feeling of being lost, you might love this game.  I do.  It's one of those games that stuck with me.  Usually, I prefer rich stories, but there's none of that here, except for what your imagination brings to it.
I played the game imagining myself in those spaces, with no idea how I'd come to be there, no option but to keep moving.  The mixed sense of unease and wonder was really rewarding.
I've played the game through twice in the few years I've owned it, and I expect I will again.  I tried Kairo, which other reviewers recommend, and enjoyed it for a while, but found it too colorful, too busy, less focused.  I missed the stark, strange loneliness of NaissanceE.
This one isn't for everyone, but I think if you do like it, you'll love it.

The Talos Principle is a philosophical puzzle solving game. In most of the puzzles you are trying to find your way to the "sigil" which is behind walls and doors. Sigils are like Tetris blocks, and if you collect enough of them, you can open access to other worlds which contain more puzzles.
In the puzzles you use step-on buttons, laser-beam-controlled locks, fans, jammers, boxes, trays, and record-playback devices to open doors, jump over walls, or avoid moving mines or turrets. It is easy to learn who to use these items, but hard to master it. By solving the first puzzles, you learn techniques which will be useful in the later puzzles. Most of the puzzles are easy, but some are really hard. When you get stuck in a puzzle, the most likely cause is that you have not yet discovered a new way to use the items listed above. However, each puzzle can be solved with logical reasoning, and there is not too much repetition.
The philosophical part of the game consists of discussions with some mysterious person through consoles scattered throughout the worlds, and documents you can access with them, and recorded messages you bump into from time to time. There is also a voice from above that tells you to do or not to do things. You soon begin to wonder who are you, where are you, where do you come from, should you obey the voice from above, or the one you have discussed with through the consoles, and what is the great tower. I think it is possible to just play the game and skip over all the philosophical stuff, but by doing so, one misses a large part of the game, and the ending doesn't necessarily make sense. Actually, there are more than one ending you can choose.
The Talos Principle is a good game in its category. However, there are a few things that I didn't like too much. Most of the puzzles are bounded with walls, so that it is easy to see where the puzzles take place. While this can be a good thing, it kind of isolates the puzzle solving from the story. Also it is impossible to save the game within a puzzle. If there is a solution requiring multiple steps and then you make a mistake that makes it impossible to continue, the only option is to reset the puzzle and start all over again. Most of the time this doesn't matter, but with the really difficult puzzles that require precise actions, it is annoying to do the same puzzle 20 times, just because a laser-beam is two centimeters off or you forgot to bring a box to the other side of a door.
I would recommend this game to everyone who loves puzzle games.

The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle(yes, not a shooter), developed by Croateam, the same company which created ludicrously violent Serious Sam series. As far as I know, the design of puzzle in this game was originally created for the upcoming Serious Sam 4. But the developer decided to use this design to make a stand-alone atmospheric puzzle game, which is totally different from the previous games that they made. And they managed to create one of the best first-person games I've ever played. Yes, first-person games, including shooters.
The system is pretty simple as a puzzle game; you solve a puzzle, then solve more puzzles with more various elements and higher difficulty. You may start with a simple gadget to neutralize an obstacle or a threat, then you will need to use more complex mechanism, like recording your activity for a short period and use it together with your present action. The difficulty curve of puzzle is reasonable enough to go through from the start to the end. And thanks to the hub system, if you can't figure out how to solve one puzzle, you may solve the another puzzle to refresh your head, then revisit the previous one. There are three major hubs, which have their own architectural, environmental design, And each major hub is also consist of minor hubs that provides puzzle courses. What's reward of solving a puzzle? It's a piece of colored tetromino shape, which you'll need to collect every pieces with the same color to proceed the game.
Besides the tetromino shape, you'll also come acorss with golden stars, shattered around the minor hub area. Those are basically the secret elements in this game; you may try to find all of stars to unlock the secret ending, or just ignore them. Not only it's difficult to figure out how to get them, but it also requires the coordination with another puzzle room in the same minor hub. This makes the game more challenging, but don't be so obsessed with finding golden stars, of course. You can still see the ending without those stars, so don't be frustrated. :D
The design of atmoshpere in this game is just beautiful. The developer did a great job on creating the ruins of Pompeii and two other themes for each major hub with proper level design elements and undoubtedly impressive skybox. The soundtrack, which is another strong point of this game, is also great enough to boost your gameplay experience. The plot is pretty interesting, too. You will see computers around the area to figure out what was happened in this world, and to interact (or even debate) with the entity inside the archive. This game also provides lots of easter eggs around the level. But unfortunately, some easter eggs that I came across only disrupted my gameplay since I didn't get where it was come from. To me, easter eggs are mixed-bag in this game, to be honest.
In overall, The Talos Principle is a wonderful first-person puzzle game that I highly recommend to anyone, especially someone who enjoyed the Portal series. I can say that some parts are even better than Portal, like the design of puzzle, environments, soundtracks, and so on. It's definitely one of the best first-person games I've played. 9/10
