This game was just awful.  Sure I only played for twenty minutes, but I guarantee you it was twice as long as I wanted to play.  I absolutely wanted to give this game a chance because of its good reviews and cool aesthetic.  It reminded me a little of AntiChamber and Portal, but I kept getting vertigo from the awkward lighting and shading.  I get the intention was to be simplistic, but this game complicated the level designs too much and obscured many angles to require both light, patience, and a lot of guesswork.
Level design: I want to say that what I saw in my short time was fantastic, and I suppose to some degree, that would be correct.  But as a player, you're not eased into this world as you are in the aforementioned AntiChamber and Portal.  You start the game in an empty solid room.  Looks pretty good - I'm intrigued.  But the second you leave this room, you're met with the strangest blocky tower that you have to scale straight up following some ball of light.  And me being the adventurer, I tried exploring through these gross grey corridors, and guess what?  There are no secret areas or fun adventuring.  Instead, you must trudge through a terribly linear area that is rife with pitch black darkness and itss only challenge is to keep yourself from vomitting from the confusing landscape and constant lighting changes.
Gameplay: I love being taught how to play the game as I fumble through greyscale graphics and blinding light, only to be rewarded with a dead end, a place I've already been, or falling to my death because of how precise and narrow a lot of the ledges are while waiting for light to happen for a split second at a time.  The controls are just like any other keyboard and mouse game, but there's also this breathing mechanic for running, which is actually pretty cool and new and different and I'm into that.  And giving you about a mile's worth of empty runway to practice it on was a nice touch, but probably the only saving grace from a design aspect.  Oh, and everytime you die (most likely from a fall you can't see), the checkpoints are very unforgiving.  And not on a difficult scale (which something like 1001 Spikes does beautifully), it's more about how ANNOYING it is to drag yourself through all that damn WAITING for the light and constantly adjusting to the darkness.
Overall, it feels like there a ton of these kinds of games, the "walking simulator" variety.  But here they tried to shoehorn a bleak story, what feels like a last minute choice to make an otherwise boring protagonist a female, and jarring gameplay paired with vertigo-inducing graphics.  I get the impression that the developers were too busy jerking themselves off with how pretty the game looks and how mysterious it all is instead of focusing on something that could have been amazing.  Like I said, I wanted to like this game.  If they had a better tutorial level or 1st level, something to ease you into this new world and its rules, or even have more frequent checkpoints (given the nature that it's not neccessarily hard - just awful to experience repeatedly), or wasn't too dark and barfy, I would have given it another shot.

Do you remember the feeling you got when you saw the strange, grand architecture of Cloud City in The Empire Strikes Back? Or the impossibly huge geometry of V'ger in Star Trek: The Motion Picture? Or the cityscape in Blade Runner? Well, NaissanceE will bring back that feeling with incredible intensity.
No other game does grand environments like this, I promise you. It's mind-bogglingly huge and familiar and alien all at once, and when you start moving around it you realize that yes, you can get to that bright point on the horizon, it's not just scenery. It's a linear game but the city-type environments are surprisingly open, with optional paths to find here and there. The sound design does an amazing job of supporting the atmosphere, bouncing you between slack-jawed wonder and a creeping unease.
The catch is that's only about half the game.
The other half is split between claustrophobic halls and cubist nightmares. There are a lot of surreal, nonsensical rooms to run through that don't really mesh all that well with the cityscapes they break up. Chapters 5 and 6 (the game is broken into seamless Half-Life-style chapters) seem to double down on the weirdness, which was a little disappointing because of how much I enjoyed the city bits. The puzzles are also rather hit or miss, generally being rather easy and not very clever. I will say that there are some jumping puzzles in Chapter 4 that were pretty frustrating in how little sense they made, and an eye-searing puzzle in Chapter 5 that almost made me quit the game entirely.
The second-to-last chapter is pretty interesting and very wide open. It makes me think there's even more to find in the game, though there's no real payoff for exploration besides seeing what other weirdness the world contains. The last chapter is a little frustrating until you figure out what it wants you to do and the ending is pretty blah. I think there's something deep going on with the story but I haven't picked up on it. I just feel like there's something there. I honestly think the atmosphere is good enough to justify the purchase, but be aware there are more than a few flaws.

DiveKick is a joke, a joke meant for a very niche set of gamers, a set i would consider myself a part of, the Fighting Game Community.
Unfortunately its a joke that doesnt hold up, the premise is fantastic, remove the barrier for entry (complex button inputs and mechanic understanding) and make a fighting game entirely about the meta game, the understanding of your oponent, trying to predict their moves and then setting up traps for them to spring, this is encredibly satisfying or it would if about half the roster werent rather broken and somewhat unbalanced, there are certain match ups that are always going to benefit one character over the other, S=Kill (a parody of seth killian an ex capcom community manager) and the baz (a character joke from two best friends play i do believe) are really rather broken and somewhat overpowered
Divekick is at its best when being played purely with the characters Dive and Kick, this games Ryu and Ken except these guys are west philadelphia born and raised. The story and characters are great if you get the jokes, but theyre just jokes that after theyre initial chuckle value dont hold up much, and characters like Mr. N and Jefailey are really niche paradies of major people involved within the FGC not every person interested in fighting games are gonna understand those jokes, i chuckled at jebaileys head growing bigger with each win but i had to google the backstory to Mr. N just so i wouldnt feel like i was missing the joke,
not all the joke characters are broken wolvereine and Dr Shoals are pretty awesome and the idea of stripping a fighting game down to its purest form is interesting but this just about misses the mark unfortunately.
while i love that a game like this exists, the type of people who this game is really intended for probably already know enough about it to decide whether they intend to purchase it, and personally it isnt worth the full asking price, i got this on offer using money made from trading card sales but the idea of dropping cash on this, especially full price would have left me feeling very ripped off, the art work and animation quality are pretty poor as is the music, no great tunes here but obviously these arent as important as the gameplay, DiveKick is best played locally or with friends, who already play fighting games, and who stick to the unbroken characters, theres fun to be had here but theres a lot of problems too.
Ive had some collision detection issues with this, more than once ive sailed right through someone stomach and its not counted as a hit and looking online im not alone with this,
if you are interested in this game, just be prepared for a lot of faults and kinda amateur ish quality, even then dont pay full price for this, to be honest its got Humble Bundle written all over it so just be patient and im sure itll turn up for a fair price at somepoint, a great idea that i can only recommend to very few people and for this reason it doesnt get my recommendation however i will say the GGPO net code is freaking superb no lag problems for me so far.
all in all, buy with caution

Very entertaining action game. What really makes this game stand out is the melee combat. I really liked how the attacks felt weighty and how attacking different body parts will do different damage and different effects towards your enemy, seeing your enemy get injured and hobble away and show that he is at low health was also lots of fun because a lot of games don't show you enemy opponents get injured by your attacks. Environmental kills were also really fun as you can kick your enemy off of cliffs, into fires, into spikes and traps etc, you can get really creative with how you deal with enemy encounters and watching the physics of the enemy's corpse as they fall down a cliff or some stairs is fun too, which is because it runs on the Source engine. There is many ways to mix your character's build with a mix of ranged, melee and magic attacks which adds replayabilty.
The designs of the world and characters is very nice, the game has a great high fantasy atmosphere that feels like real lived in world. Despite being an older game it has aged nicely in this regard.
There are multiple endings which offers replay value and adds weight to the story as it feels you can choose to be the good guy or the bad guy, which was interesting while the story itself was a bit cliched. The level design is quite linear and at parts could get a bit annoying with backtracking but the way you can build your character adds replayability to the fun combat that you'll want to play again, as you try different strategies. Overall an underrated game in the Might and Magic universe that really stands out due to its fun combat system and kicking things.

So after finishing the first part in about 2 and halfish hours, I decided to write a review. This is yet another TellTale game that blew it out of the waters. I've seen both TWD and WAU and thought they were great, but this game, this game was awesome! A spin-off the Borderlands series was a brilliant idea by both companies for so many reasons. The game feels smooth, and this isn't just because I have a good computer (GTX 980, i7 processor, 16GB Ram.) The story intertwines so well between the TellTale side of the story, and the refrences and inclusion of the Borderlands series. I honestly feel as though anyone could play the game as long as they have beaten the 2nd game or have a base knowledge. The music is superb, and fits extremely well with the story/game. The gameplay hits true to TellTale's dodge-and-hit system, but feels so much better in an enviornment like Pandora. Beating up bandits in Pandora with this kind of combat makes me feel like I could do it myself (not really.) The 2 and half hours of gameplay I put into this game were well worth it. To anyone who is interested in purchasing this game, do yourself a favor, and get it A.S.A.P! Just these 2 and half hours of gameplay will entise you to getting pumped for the next episode!

I'm playing as Insurgents, leading a squad of 9. I've just been on the command-only radio with the other 4 squad leaders, and we've agreed I'll take my squad right to the back of the map and run interference to stop the enemy capturing the objectives closest to their spawn until our guys haev done the same at our end. This is an unusual tactic, considering the nature of this part of the map as deep enemy territory, but I feel capable enough to give it a shot. Ahead lies a small sandstone compound. 'Ok guys,' i say over the squad radio, 'pick a buddy and stay with him as we move in here.' This is something I always advise my squad to do; it minimises casualties from a blindsiding enemy, and allows a situation to be pacified if there is a sudden ambush in which one of my men is shot; there's always a gun to back him up. We move in slowly, knowing full-well that the enemy is on their way here. What they don't expect is for us to be here; we can't cap this point, so why bother?
Well, the longer it takes them to cap, the more time we buy for our guys about 3 miles away.
I instruct my men to take up positions inside the buildings on the point, advising them to keep away from windows but allow themselves a firing line into the streets and courtyard. Then, we wait less than thirty seconds before we hear the sound of an engine.
'Vehicle!' I hear my AT guy, stationed on a roof next to me cry out. 'Permission to engage?!'
'Granted,' I reply, and within moments I see the rocket flash past my vision, and a huge cloud of billowing fire erupt from the treeline. A confirmed kill. From around the burning logistics truck we just killed, we see a full squad of infantry. I instruct my men to stay inside as I open fire from the roof. After scoring two kills I quickly hunker down and hide, baiting the enemy. A simple AT team, they assume, no threat to them from close range.
They don't expect a full squad of 9 men.
For a few moments all I hear is the shuffling of boots. I remind my men that they are weapons free. A few moments pass.
The sound of 9 AK rifles rings out, and suddenly the compound is engulfed with the sound of gunfire. Less than a minute later, the gunfire stops.
All 9 of my men have survived thanks to the stellar work of our medics, who patched the two men who got hit within seconds. Every single hostile has been killed.
We hear another engine. 'Humvee!,' my AT shouts down to me from the roof, using local chat. 'Kill it,' I reply. Two rockets later, the unaware humvee is in pieces.
We successfully wiped a full squad of 9, a supply truck and a humvee without a single casualty, through a little planning an a lot of communication. And that is why I love squad. If everyone works as a unit, you'll have some of the best 'war stories' of your gaming life as a result of playing this game. As for the state of the Alpha, it may as well be a late Beta. It's really polished and apart from a couple of gnarly geometry bugs where I got a car stuck, and a few disconnects I haven't had any issues. The framerate is pretty lousy, but this is an early Alpha so for the time being I can forgive this. I run on a 970, 16gb ram and an i5, and it often dips as low as 30, temporarily. Usually, it holds at around 40. For once, however, this has not detracted from my experience to any great degree, because the simple aexperience of leading a squad into battle or being a part of someone else's squad is so exhilerating.
9/10, for any fan of milsim-lite (this isn't ARMA, it's somewhere between ARMA and insurgency), a sense of community, or just being terrified as bullets tear past your head and cut down your friends.

Classic FPS design done fairly well even if it overstays its welcome. The story is very long for an FPS. The collectibles are numerous and well hidden. The informative trinkets are insightful, the characters are actually fairly well done for a shooter, though they aren't really all that great or anything, and the graphics are unique. To round it out the weapons are well modeled and fun to shoot. I enjoyed the settings and stylization of this game a lot.
Using 1440p I get a very solid FPS without much stutter using Afterburner to limit to 60 and NCP Vsync. Otherwise I get stuttering with this engine. With that out of the way I also inject SMAA. The game is so much better than it was on the old consoles in the image quality department. With a 1070 plus you can finally experience this game at its fullest potential. I don't really have much else to say.
This is weird male fantasy stuff but it is quite immersive and involving, and at least the dev made effort to create and define the characters outside of the usual meathead nonsense. It has its poetical sensibilities much like Rambo or Predator do in the action film genre. It also probably drags on too long and the character might become a little tiring. As a full package this game is rarely matched in the FPS genre. There is also a lot of concept artwork and other unlockables. I like how you can go read about each character, weapon, and enemy much like an RPG would let you. Machine Games are a talented bunch.
Recommended.

It offers you the main campaign (Orcs on the March: Expansion for Armored Princess with additional content) and 2 other smaller campaigns (Champion of the Arena: Boss Battles in Gladiatorial Combat & Defender of the Crown: Battles in Unique Arenas). It took a very long time for me to get into Borderlands. Constant advertising and an unease with its relatively novel graphical style left me unwilling for some time, but eventually, at the urging of a friend, I finally took the plunge. The game has since become one of the more memorable titles in my gaming history.
By now, everyone knows Borderlands; it is often considered one of the best mergers of shooter and RPG, as it features fast-paced combat with an expansive list of firearms a first-person shooter should offer, and the pursuit of experience, new equipment, and missions that RPGs simply cannot go without. Weapons are procedurally generated from a list of parts, offering much variety in both statistics and feel, while enemies are numerous and diverse, all often incorporating uncommon "Badass" mini-bosses that add further challenge to ordinary skirmishes.
One thing that always stuck out about Borderlands in my mind was its charm. Gearbox found a pleasant mix of serious and comedic influences, allowing the player to simultaneously laugh and find a measure of immersion in the story around them. While, admittedly, the game is often quiet and features a number of dull, run-of-the-mill side missions, most with little or no voice acting to offer a sense of character, the setting and even balance of its tone continues to strike a chord with me even long after retiring from the game.
Unfortunately, what Gearbox didn't quite get right with Borderlands was balance. Weapons are quickly invalidated by level, balance between player classes is often questionable, and comparison between the different weapon element types can often find itself uneven.
In example, playing as a Soldier alongside a Siren often made me feel as though my weapons were borderline useless by comparison. Only by experience and familiarity with shooters was I able to make myself feel like a contributing asset rather than a health point hose.
In other cases, trying to use regular weapons to suit all occasions didn't feel like I was sacrificing a little to be ready for everything; it felt like I was sacrificing nearly everything to be ready for very isolated incidents. Even in situations where weapons of a specific element were intended to fall short - such as an incendiary weapon firing on a shielded enemy - it still gave the impression that using a normal weapon was an inferior choice.
Additionally, it feels hard to call Borderlands a title designed for the PC. Always-on voice chat, difficulties in getting the game to obey my settings, and one of the clunkiest menus I've used on a PC leave little to the imagination when considering how much effort was invested where.
Overall, Borderlands has earned its place in my library. While I have since worn the game thin and left it to collect the dust of nostalgia, it is a title that I will not think twice about revisiting should the opportunity arise.

is an exploration adventure game where you find yourself lost in a mysterious sprawl of dystopian superstrcutres trying to seek a way out, whereever "out" might be.
With an incredibly strong focus on atmosphere and ambience,
is visual showcase of delights for anyone who appreciates carefully thought out and well executed use of artistic and architectural technique. From careful use of light and shadow, to volume and negative space, the foreboding scale and perspective doesn't cease to impress.
There is a saying that the journey is the destination, and
takes this to heart. Rather than the setting being a medium to deliver conflict or puzzles to the player, the interiors, buildings, cityscapes and landscapes are the true star of the show. There are no NPCs to talk to, no notes left around to read to explain anything. There is no plot in the same sense that a nice Sunday drive ambling through the countryside is aimless. If the idea of doing nothing more than walking around and admiring the view doesn't interest you, you'll be bored to tears.
While I thoroughly enjoyed the game, it comes across as the kind of game that you'll either love or hate. It's brilliant for what it is, but what it is is something that only appeals to a small niche. If you enjoyed Thatgamecompany's
, or are a fan of Tsutomu Nihei's
, with its endless swathes of misanthropic edifices reaching to and past infinity, then
just might be the game for you.

One of the closest dreamlike experiences I've had in games comes from this title. It's a weird, atmosphere and often downright unnerving journey through realms of forgotten history, strange technology and expansive realms of unidentifiable peculiarity. It's abstract and strange, and there are layers of meaning when you look for them, but for the most part it's simply a fun puzzle platformer with one hell of a mood. It does a great job of creating a bizarre and changing world, but keeps connections to reality and understandable mechanics with just a hint of reality and logic so we can create a bridge between our character and the strangeness of the world.
There are some minor technical issues like screen tearing with lack of V-Sync, and some outright annoying and frustrating puzzle sections, but otherwise it's well made and doesn't feel cheap and the only other gameplay complaint is lack of mechanics, but it never feels samey or repetitive. NaissanceE is short, but probably fairly priced, though the majority of us should probably wait for a sale since it's a very love or hate kind of game.

Do not download this game. I could go on for hours about the laundry list of problems that this abomination has, but I'll try to summarize it.
-The heroes are not only boring and completely unoriginal, but some of the heroes are clearly just copies of heroes from Dota 2 or League of Legends
-The only way to really win the game is to kill the boss so that "Krytos" will help your team push; the game's only real mechanic is as follows: capture Krytos, win the game, as Krytos not only deals massive damage to towers, it disables them and prevents them from attacking.
-The game's crafting system makes no sense and ultimately does not effect the game at all; it's just a useless side feature.
-The game tries to implement different "pets" that give you bonuses, and while this sounds cool, there is only one pet in the game that is worth having, and it's the pet that the game gives you last.
-Any type of strategy is completely nonexistent, you just spam abilities and hope for the  best.
TL;DR: Strife is a game that tried to combine Dota and League, but ended up making some kind of disgusting hybrid of the two that can barely even be considered a MOBA. DO NOT download this game; you will regret it.

I have a bit of mixed feelings for Divekick. It's exactly what I predicted it would feel like gameplay-wise. Originally I bought this as a gift for a friend on the day it came out. I think the price was overkill. But it really depends on some factors:
- You like parodies made on Mortal Kombat.
- You're looking for comedy based on ethnocentrism or prejudice.
- You're not looking for cool combos. Just K.O's.
Overall I personally don't think the game is bad. Worth the daily deal of $2.50? Maybe. Depends on the factors I mentioned above. Otherwise you could do away without it.
In just under 1 hr you'll mostly see everything there is to know about this game. And from there on you can either keep playing it, or never play it again.
One thing I sometimes like to note about games is the credits. I counted about 50+ people that designed this game. This is too much for an Indie company imho. After all, the more complex Doom 3 was made by roughly the same amount of people before 2005. Divekick is the type of game that strikes me as a 5 man job. I'm fairly certain I've seen just as interesting web-based flash plugin fighter games.
The mechanics is sort of interesting. Each character seems to differ only by speed or boost to the dive (forwards/backwards) and the kick. I also feel that there is some weird collision system happening based on the dimensions of the characters. But overall it seems like you tend to get the most success of a K.O by allowing the enemy to attack first. There are special moves, however I ultimately still believe the many variations are caused by a change in speed.
For example, if you have a character that kicks at medium speed, you might notice that a character that drifts slowly may be more deadly as they tend to perform more of a flying kick rather than a divekick. But if you have a character that divekicks too fast, you may easily K.O someone that seems to be doing a slow-mo flying kick.
Although the music is sort of transparent to me. It's reminiscent to I guess classic games like Double Dragon and Streets of Rage.
As a tiny quarrel: Initially I thought the main menu wasn't very intuitive. After a minute I get it. But it still feels bad navigating thereafter. I quote from Albert Einstein, "Make everything as simple as possible, but not simpler." That certainly applies to the main menu in terms of user-friendliness.
It seems to be that a large portion of this game has a lot to do with online multiplayer. So I can't really say I'm getting the full potential out of this game. I wouldn't mind giving the ranked matches a shot. But so far on my Steam friends list, only sauce seems to own this game. So I guess I'm just going to have to divekick his butt one day from the other side of the world despite any lag :P

Oxenfree is a good game. Fun characters, creepy atmosphere, there are lots of things to find in the world, and the mechanics are a lot of fun. If you're okay with a walking simulator, you'll definetely enjoy this game. No spoilers, but sadly the game does have some inconsistencies and things that aren't really explained. I'm okay with certain things being up to interpretation, but there are glaring issues with the game's story. Most of these issues revolve around the ending and the New Game Plus mechanic, but I will not spoil them here. I'll just say that they bring up a lot of questions that either don't make sense, or contradict certain things that appear later or earlier in the game. This game is also very short, only taking me three~ hours to beat. It took me about two or so hours to complete the New Game Plus, so it averaged at about six hours of playtime total. I can't, in good consience, recommend this game for the price that it's at. Try to get it for ten dollars or less.
alright, i'm gonna talk about spoilers. look away if you haven't played.
The twist is really awesome. Really, REALLY awesome. Haunting, almost.
New Game Plus ruins the ending completely.
Alright, so, everything is in a loop. You have no idea how long this time loop has been going on, or why it's happening, and it's a super cool reveal that comes right out of the left field and pimp-slaps you across the face. Yet, in New Game Plus, the idea of multiple universes and multiple Alexs' is introduced. This is a direct contradiction to the ending of the game. In the ending, Alex is reminiscing, and then time is reversed. The exact same Alex is going back through time, and forgets everything. It couldn't possibly be another Alex because of that. The ending's "wow" factor also goes away because you now know that the first game is the original Alex timeline. The big punch of the twist is that you have no idea how long she's been looping, but it confirms that it hadn't looped before the first playthrough because of the differences in gameplay. If she had been looping before, the new content of the New Game Plus wouldn't be new. It'd be in the original gameplay, too.
Things aren't really explained very well, either. Why does Alex need to tune the machines to fix time? Shouldn't there be a machine to fix the overlapping time loop, too? Who made them? Why does Alex remember the time loops, but forgets about them in the overlapping time loop? If there's a multiverse of the game's scenarios, why did the New Game Plus happen in the first place? Shouldn't all the timelines be the same, in that case? It isn't as if the characters change, they're still the same people. How the hell does Mike come back from the dead? You may say that it's because the final major time travel scene can have Alex telling him to stay, thus changing time, but none of the other time loops changed anything until the machines were fixed. Why are there the machines in the small time loops, but not the big ones? Why does sacrificing Clarissa make her vanish from existence, isn't that the exact opposite of what the ghosts wanted? Why are the ghosts not uneffected by the time loops? Because they aren't effected by the time loops, wouldn't every timeline end up like the timeline from the New Game Plus? Again, the characters wouldn't act differently. They're still the same people. If there really are multiple universes, what happens to the Alex who makes it off the island? She wouldn't travel back in time, considering each time loop would create another universe. Does she just continue living her life? If so, why does the time loop twist at the end matter at all? Why would it matter if Alex were to stop herself from going on the island? Nobody dies. Friendships can be bonded over the experience. Hell, she can even bring her brother back from the dead. So why does it matter? Why does anything in this game matter?
New Game Plus is really cool, but it ruins the game story wise.

There are things I love and things I loath! Sadly, the things I loath are the most important.
The things I like.
I love the artwork and graphics style. I'm a big fan of how the characters appear to move in 3D space ever so subtly. I assume it's just a rotating avatar on 2D art, but the effect is sold very effectively. It looks lovely!
The music is different as well - for me, a plus.
The concept is cool too. The protagonist (Alex) has a radio and she can tune in to certain frequencies at different spots on the island and terrifying thinks begin happening and they're like "wow.. cool!" (lame) I'll get to all that in a minute.. Unfortunately I didn't play for long enough to tell you any more than that.. I know.. I'm a huge help.. The potential for adventure is totally there..
But let me tell you now what stopped me moving forward to find out...
It seems as though a lot of people like this game and that's great! I can totally see many merits! But I can't stand the characters. They SUCK! First of all they're always arguing in an annoyingly sly way. Backhanded insults in completely normal conversation, moody and so unnecessarily sarcastic at completely inapproriate times. (really winds me up.) haha. They whine and never seem to shut up. Even if you walk away.. far far away from them, they're still bickering and they're still talking to you and you can still talk to them.. There is no escaping them and it really bothers me, *they* bother me. I was up a massive flight of steps and this guy was waaay down on the beach.. he's all like "C'mon Alex, I'll give you a boost.. in your own time when ever you're ready.. Uhm, are you gunna go over or what?" Silence! I beg of thee! Hush.. your.. lips! I'm not even there.. but I'm coming... really slowly..
The best part was when I was on my own.. The silence was terrific! I could finally lap up some atmosphere. (which is a shame, because the game is full of it.. You just can't enjoy it because "blah blah blah blah blah!" It wouldn't be so bad if the dialogs were more realistic and had better pacing tbh..
I don't even know what they're banging on about.. Honestly I learnt nothing about the characters.. I even turned the subtitles on so I could read as they were talking.. Still had no idea what they were talking about.
You start off knowing nothing about Alex (you) and you're expected to talk to your friends(?), family(?) and answer for her.. Things about her family life and other.. stuff? Now you might be thinking "dude.. it's roleplay" - I love roleplay and this doesn't work.. It's frustrating and tedious. It's a constant battle of 'well how do I know?', 'what do I say here?' 'WHY am I saying these things?' - it's just not enjoyable, for me at least.
In one of the multiple choices, one of the things she could say was. "Sounds like a great idea!" I thought she'd be happy like "yeah, let's do it!" but she ended up being sarcastic for absolutely NO reason! "oh sure.. yeah.. let's DO that.. Idiot!" (she didn't say that.. but she may as well have done.) haha.. Damn, dude.. These characters, in my opinion, are so obnoxious! :') They've gone on a trip together and they just don't seem to like each other somehow. ..Also, when someone's talking, you go to perform an action like opening a door and their voice just cuts off.
AND.. Alex goes in to a cave after this.. dude.. She can't see him but he only JUST got in there.. she's like "ARE YOU OKAY? ARE YOU BLEEDING?! OMG!" (Bleeding? WHAT are you TALKING about?!) Man.. headache! Why not "Hey.. Where are you?"
It's a shame.. The game looks great! Like really bloomin' great! Perhaps I'll continue when I'm in a better mood?
Would I recommend it? Sure, if that person was already thinking of getting it, because it might just be me being me.. and it might get really good! There is indeed a lot of promise.

Despite all that, as I said before - I still recommend this. It looks stunning and is definitely worth a shot.. Someone else might play and not experience the aforementioned issue. :)

A game like this I wouldnt really expect to have much replayability, but to be honest, I will likely come back to this game like I do some of my favorite movies and TV shows.

This game is all about teamwork. With the right squad and Squad Leader, it's a ton of fun. The community seems mature and the squad leaders I've had know their stuff. I'd say 80% of the game is logistics and planning, and the other 20% is combat and/or sheer terror. You have to take into account geography, topography, logistics, cover, concealment, element of surprise, tactics, ammo conservation, and so much more to be a successful  member of your squad. 99% of the people I've played with are mature, they take orders from the squad leader well, and work well with the squadmates and other squads on your team.
The game is still in Alpha, but the developer has even larger maps, more vehicles, and better movement/physics on the way. The saying: "War is long periods of boredom punctuated by moments of sheer terror" holds true in Squad. When the fight comes to you, it's intense. The game sessions last long, and the replayability factor is excellent. I got bored of insurgency because I felt it was the same thing in some small CQB map every time. Squad is different, larger maps with diffrent tactics employed each game, which also vary from squad lead to squad lead.
If you are looking for a run and gun, COD or BF style of game, Squad is not for you. Squad is not something you can't even play casually IMO. It takes time to become decent at it and I think it's a perishable skill. I only have 23 hours on it, and I constantly learn more and more each time I play.

Please don't pay attention to the hours displayed here, I haven't played much on steam, because I use the version provided from the dev website, but I've played tons of hours of this already since it was in previous stages of development, and this game is the absolute best, and the one I play the most. It really has a lot of content and it's getting even more every new update!
You can compare this to Prison Architect and Dwarf Fortress, I've also played those games, I even used to play PA before RW, but when I discovered RW It was great change, then I was looking for something more deep (even though RW already was) and I tried DF and I was surprised by the amount of complexity that game has, but the lack of an actual GUI and graphics have been a letdown (mods just don't make it for me) so I still play RW a lot more than any other game to date, mostly because the developer has been paying really a lot of attention to his game and cares about the opinions from the players.
If you like strategy, management and simulation games, and you just want a game that has the most of everything, this is the very best for you. In this game, you just don't build a stable colony and deal with basic needs like hunger, resources, relationships and health in general, like a regular sims game. You also have to manage your pawns according to their skills to be more effective in what they do, And you also have to pay a lot of attention to external treats and deal with diplomacy, you need to think a lot and plan for the future of your conlony in almost all aspects which make this game a complete universe of possibilities.
Every new game you start is going to be totally different, starting from the place in the world you selected, you will have to make your own strategy, if it's a cold place most part of the year, you will need to think about getting heaters, warm clothes, food reserves and alternative ways of getting food, even eating your raiders or prisoners is a possibility! If it's a hot place you would need to turn your colony into a freezer to deal with heat waves and stuff. If it's a dry location, a way to deal with fires, and if it's a jungle, to watch out for the dangerous fauna (mainly to protect your pets and livestock) and diseases.
Like I said, don't think twice if you like this genre, the fact the game is still in alpha and it already has a world of features in it, makes me wonder what would it transform into in the near future, but it's a very promising game that has everything to offer and a lot of hours to never get bored of a single colony, or if you want to start again, it has a lot of replayability too.

Let's begin with the positive, there are two excellent elements in this game, music and atmosphere. Both of them are the main reason to recommend this game. Believe me, those two elements are top-notch
Unfortunately that means gameplay it is not one of its strong points. The sad truth is that NaissanceE can be a frustrating experience despite the short length of the game. The game should have provided more visual guidelines to help you find the way to go on, sometimes you find yourself trying to find your way through a series of jumps that lead to many deaths, as a result, the trial and error formula creates a sense of boredom and detachment from the game. It is a pity because as I mentioned before the game does a wonderful job sucking you in.
Another element which makes the game very tedious is the breathing mechanic, you have to press the left mouse button every two steps in order to keep running, if you fail to do so you will stop and will need a bit of time to recover from the effort. I understand the will to make this game a realistic experience but from a player's perspective this aspect of the game is a gimmick, it doesn't bring any fun to the table.
All in all, NaissanceE is an interesting experience which could have been more satisfying if the gameplay was better. Give it a try for cheap.

Funny Concept and great game.  The premise of the game is that you are a little robot moving from office building to office building trying to eat furniture without dying.  It has quite a few roguelike qualities.  Each level you play is randomly generated, so if you mess up you won't get another chance.  As you progress from building to building you get powerups and meet new enemies.  Each floor has an objective in order to move on.  At first it's as simple as eating a certain amount of furniture, then as you progress you'll have to touch certain spots on the floor in sequential order, eat laptops that have audiologs in them which reveals more of the story and why you're eating furniture in the first place.  The thing that gives it a lot of replay value is the fact that when you die, you get experience based on how many floors you cleared, how well you performed etc. and the experience will level up your game.  This is less of a character level, and more of unlocking new features in the games.  The leveling system takes turns with giving you an upgrade, and then giving you more obstacles to traverse through your next game.  This makes the game slightly more challenging and it makes you want to continue playing because it means you will most likely run into something new that you haven't seen before.  It does a pretty good job at balancing the difficulty for you and it does a very good job at setting up an effective learning curve.  Overall, It's a lot of fun and has good replay value.

Welcome to HELL!!!... The game is anything but mundane and is quite insane.  You start off doing minor navigation through a pleseant labyrinth of multiple choices of doors, stairways, and paths with a zen-like music feel.  Yes, this appears to be a relaxing game of adventure, right up until half way through and down the rabbit hole.   Hurry, Hurry, rush we go.  Time is a ticking or you get your licking.  Where little Alice, NO REALLY IT'S LUCY, goes nobody knows.  And the descent is simply maddening like a cross eyed Hatter.  Mind the gap, it's quite a trip. Seriously though, it took me about 10 hours to complete.  The first half of the game was relaxing, slow paced, with moments of stillness for trying to figure out where to go, and the last half is quite simply out of this world and like nothing I have seen in all my 20 years of gaming.  I believe it won somekind of Indie Choice Award.  And even though the last half was frustrating at times and had me helling at my computer screen (like it could hear me and could change the game because I said so) THIS GAME WAS WORTH THE EXPERIENCE!... And very glad I never tried a hit of acid.  LOL ;) ^5

I hate to give a bad review because so much about this game is good. The graphics function well, the controls are good, the music is fairly good (it always reminds me of Reckoner by Radiohead) but there's a killer: the sentry robots who oppose you on later levels appear to move randomly. This is death to any stealth strategy. You can hide behind something, but maybe they'll come around and see you, maybe they won't. You can slip past when you're not looking, but maybe they'll turn to see you just as you do, maybe they won't. This can definitely affect fun: maybe you'll be stuck waiting for several minutes while a sentry tracks back and forth along the same path, or maybe it'll leave the area right away. Given the rest of the game I'm surprised this happened because this is a fairly fundamental design error.

Awesome game!  What I most appreciate is the pace.  Frantic and action-packed enough that the tension is always on, yet slow enough that actual strategy and wit is needed to succeed.  This game has amazing boss fights and center-piece action sequences.  One of my favorites is when you're riding fawns through a long tunnel with an enormous monster hot on your heels.  In another you're in a river fighting a giant cat-shark while a battleship backs you up with cannon fire.  You have to ride far enough ahead to stay out of its clutches but close enough to forsee incoming obstacles.  It's that type of non-stop varied gameplay that makes this game so fresh and addictive.  I played it with my girlfriend co-op and it was a perfect fit.  On the couch or online its a blast.

This game is pretty much unlike anything i've ever played before.
At it's core, it's a (relatively) linear first person platformer, though with very little platforming. There are a few puzzles, but there's only one that requires any real thought. It's a mostly monochromatic game, lots of blacks and whites with one other color thrown in as a theme every so often.
The checkpoints are weirdly paced. Some sections are just badly designed. Others induce epilepsy even in non-epileptic people. The game is incredibly short and the ending is unsatisfying.
Despite all this, i can only recommend it.
The game exudes an atmosphere like no other, you need to experience it for yourself to believe it. The overall art design draws you in and the astonishing music keeps you firmly entrenched in this strange, vast world. The design is such that you are not questioning the developer on the strangeness of the levels, but the makers of the world itself - It really draws you in that much.
There is a sense of wonder to this game that i haven't seen before in 20 years of gaming. Antichamber comes close, but its experience is far more 'meta', where the game feels like a game rather than a world. In Naissancee, you want to know who built this place and what it's for. You want to see if you can get over there, you wonder what's in that room across the chasm, it edges you forward purely by making you want to see what this world will offer up next.
In the third quarter of the game, things get a little weird. The segue into this section doesn't really flow all that well, pulling you out of the experience for just a little bit. It does pick up again in a wonderful section where the game simply offers up gorgeous views for you to explore, untill you decide to continue.
The ending however is the only real letdown of the game. The rest is such an artistic accomplishment simply in its unpretentiousness (if that is a word) while still being grand and evocative, whereas the ending makes a 180 into a snooty pretentious cliffhanger.
Still, despite all its faults, Naissancee is a game you simply need to have played at least once. I think it's very much worth the price of admission, though it's understandable that this game feels very risky - At least get it when it's on sale. :)

Did you ever feel like walking/running through dimly lit hallways, with walls and floors that phase in and out of solid states? Welcome, you've found it!
I like puzzle games.  I like exploration games.  Sometimes I like them combined.  This is not one of those times.  If the puzzles are abstract and/or difficult, then navigation should not be.  If navigation is difficult, then the puzzles shouldn't be overly difficult, or at least not require excessive movements.  The movements and the ramifications for poor steps are obnoxious.  I want to enjoy my games, not be unnecessarily frustrated by them.   While the atmosphere of the game is good, the overall experience is hampered by the mechanics.  I just can't recommend this game.

After recently completing DOOM 2016 (also by id software) you can see the similarities in game play between the two. Although it's not as fast paced as DOOM you can defiantly see this game as the link between it and their older games like Quake 4.
The sound design is simply superb. The incidental music is very fitting and the effects are sublime. Probably the best sounding game I've played since Half-Life 2. If only more developers played as much attention to sound these days.
For a 2014 game the graphics are pretty good. While they can't compete with a more modern game like Rise of the Tomb Raider they do hold their own. Furthermore, unlike the aforementioned game by Crystal Dynamics, it runs extremely well on older hardware.
Just out of curiosity, I booted the game up on my now 8 and a half year old PC running an Intel core 2 quad Q9650 @ 4GHz and a GTX 970 with 8GB of 1066MHz DDR2 RAM. This mighty combo had no problems running the game at a locked 60FPS the entire game with all the settings at their highest levels at 1920x1080 resolution. Needless to say if you have a quad core CPU and something like a GTX 760 or better you should have no problems running this game at decent frame rates. Great Job id software!

A puzzle game with a side of existential crisis. This game has excellent puzzle design, and fairly good progression as well. I've completed all three of the major endings, and I am pleased to say that they are actually different. Props to the developers for creating a game that actually has different endings. The world building is performed through voice recordings , the master of the Process, and the fragments of articles, and emails. Overall, a great completionist game. It takes some time to get the final ending (to do it you have to solve all the puzzles, and find all the stars) but it gives a completely different ending which is awesome. The regular puzzles progress well, but the stars are sometimes insanely hard. Be prepared to really hunt around, and get familiar with the physics of the world.
The lore of the story is an unusual smashup of Apocrypha stuff (presented in a Judeo-Christian style, but super messed up), and mixtures of egyptian, greek, and eastern religions (primarily Buddism). The plot is somewhat forced, but there is enough there to keep the player thinking, and make it interesting.
Overall, this game is pretty short if you do the bare minimum, but if you completionist it, there is plenty of gameplay. Personally, I would rank this up there with the more challenging puzzle games I've played.

On the other hand, it's almost as if the developers did this because they were ashamed of how superior to all other surreal makeupyourownstory games (or even films) their creation is. Other than those misunderstandings with difficulty, it is beyond description and beyond good. Words can't do it justice. It's hard to believe there are people who can make something like this and remain completely unknown to pretty much everybody. All in all, there are great games like Portal 2 or Talos Principle, and there are masterpieces like this one. You may love it or you may hate it, - in any case, it's timeless.
EDIT: watching Youtube videos for the ending I realised that developers did try to reduce difficulty by adding considerable amount of new checkpoints. It DID NOT help. For the second day straight I can not get past last (or second to last) checkpoint although I think I nail a much better run at it than those on youtube (with an older version of the game). I simply have no idea why while having such a groundbreaking product devs decided to commit a near suicide by introducing those few extremely difficult stretches. Gamers are not you, people! This is a maxim no 1 of software development - "DON'T EVER JUDGE THE PRODUCT BASED ONLY ON YOUR PERSONAL IMPRESSIONS (unless you are developing a tool for yourself)". Sorry for shouting.

It's a formulaic ARPG. You pick up weapons, level up when killing monsters, fight bosses, and collect gold. It has an item fusion system where items can be fused together to create higher-level versions of the same item (if you've played Warframe, it's like that).
The voxel engine is refreshing - it beats the tired "pixel game" style currently in vogue. But there's no environmental destruction or creation. Or, really, *any* destruction that can't be found in a normal game. There's also practically no detail to the game, so it feels pointless to use a voxel render (if it even IS a voxel renderer) for this.
And worst, the game is just repetative. There's ten levels to the first dungeon. Every enemy requires 6-20 hits with your sword to beat, and magic is laughably crippled (mana regen is nearly nonexistant, and spells have very low DPS compared to regular attacks). The pacing is awkward and uneven, leading to difficulty cliffs before you find a specific item that allows you to get over them. There doesn't seem to be a death penalty, so more than once I found myself intentionally dying just to get full health. Running back down the dungeon took less time than running out, healing in town, and coming back.
The humor is nice, but the lack of gameplay options, uninteresting visuals, and generic gameplay just don't make me want to come back to it. Which is a shame, since it's clear that it's very polished (in the sense that it's smooth, has full-featured content, doesn't have glitches, and won't crash) and has a lot of work put into it.

It's really not a game for everyone, even those new to MOBA games. The current situation is that what little developing team that S2 has left for this game is shipping themselves to help with the Chinese client, so there's little care for the EU and NA scene. The game mechanics themselves are pretty standard, but teams compositions can be incredibly flexible and there's gold sharing. It does have a nice art style too, if you're into a semi-cartoony sort of thing. What my main gripe is, is the toxicity and the game client itself. You will often find ragers, people who ruin games and those who simply do not connect to the game, forcing unfair matches (4v5, 3v5, etc). ALSO the client and many of its features are bugged, including spectator mode. The client itself is in poor condition that certain features may fail to load for you, or that the client itself won't load properly. I have one little story about the game client crashing on me, then when I load to reconnect to the game and avoid leaver status, none of the windows or buttons will load and i'm stuck looking at the background splash of the client.
If you're looking for a nice and friendly MOBA, this might be your thing. But if you want consistency, stability, an active playerbase, a caring development team and all that other stuff, you need to run for the hills because Strife IS NOT the MOBA for you.

This game is amazing with a high potential to become an awesome game for a very low price. Yes it is early access and they are still working on it, there is no release date for a final version. The developer care so much and are always present in the forums and help if you mention problems or bugs and solve them in no time.
When I bought it, I had my first play through and after this I could start on a higher difficulty with the same character. I had my second play through and got the invitation to play the pre-release of the new version. Now, with the latest update, they over thought everything they made before, changed all dungeons and now on my third play through I have the feeling to play a brand new game!
You start with your character and your sword in a small village. You talk with some people and choose to become a hero, start with the tutorial and your first dungeon in which you have to solve puzzles, avoid mean traps and fight monster mops, mini bosses and the final boss at each level. Don’t forget to collect the loot, weapons, boots, gloves, shields, helmets, gold to prove you always have the best one attached. Combine the runes you find, put them into the sockets to make your weapons and armor much more powerful.  With the gold you purchase better weapons, potions and (if you like to) dresses and funny hats (you will do this later, when you have more gold as you need). Also you can buy pets, which are powerful helper in the dungeons. Some can do hard attacks, other spit fire, stun enemies or just take all the agro so you have a free hand to cast spells.
Spells? Of course you earn experience points with every kill you make and every new level you reach gives you one point to spent for spells and perks. If you spent enough points for one class  you can choose your subclass with even better abilities. Feel free to spent points for Warrior and Mage, this can be a good combination and depends on your style you’ll play.
You really should get this game if you like dungeons, puzzles, monster mobs and tough bosses. It’s really worth its money! Get it for your friend as well to play it in multiplayer!

For now, this review is just going to note some problems I've hadwith the game. I will be updating this review to talk about the game itself later.
I'm on Windows 10, 64 bit, and this is a pretty old game!
- Game often force closes when loading a new level. Quitting the game also makes it think it has force-closed. Enemies spawning also seems to cause crashes on occasion.
- The "rope bow" can create ropes that stick you into walls. Having two ropes next to each other can make it incredibly diffiucult to dismount the ropes and get on the ground. Save frequently (F6 is quicksave)!
- When trying to stay afloat among some rising water, the character makes some horrible drowning noises. Pretty grim! Minimise them by aiming upwards and holding jump.
- There are three difficulties: Normal, Hard, and Hardcore. I opted for Hard. The game starts off incredibly difficultly, but it quickly teaches you how to use footwork and the environment to dispatch your enemies. Unfortunately, you can be faced with a large room filled with multiple guards, and by far the easiest way to kill them is to use the environment (in this case, there was a chandelier which killed them in one hit). You get some more armour, weapons, and skills, and the game difficulty is bearable, and you're able to use your sword. However, there are some escort missions, and when you come across the orcs they can kill you (and your escortee) in one or two hits, if you're unlucky. You can change the diffiuclty mid-game by using the command line, e.g. to switch to Normal mode, type:
mm_game_easy_difficulty 1
mm_game_hard_difficulty 0
Or set the game to start with the parameters:
+mm_game_easy_difficulty 1 +mm_game_hard_difficulty 0

Small disclaimer first: At the time of writing this, I've never played a Borderland game for more than two hours in total. As such, I can't comment how well this fits into the style or the lore of the main games.
That being said, this is a great interactive story. Some of the many funny moments are pretty hilarious, but it still strikes a good balance between serious storytelling and humor.
The actual presentation is totally flawless. From start to finish of the first episode there is not a single moment where I got the feeling they reached the limits of their engine. It all fits like a very well directed and presented movie.
The game does contain gore, but it's about on the level of an average MadMax movie. Speaking of that, the story style so far in Ep1 reminds me a bit of a mix of MadMax and Indiana Jones. Not that they're directly borrowing story elements of those movies, but I definitely see some inspiration with the scenes and characters.
Not much to say about the hardware requirements. As long as you've got a seperate GPU it's gonna run at ridiculously high framerates, at max quality.

This is a good game, possibly a great one, with a few flaws that hold it back a little bit.
The puzzle design is generally very good and strikes the right balance between challenge and frustration.  I had to resort to online guides in a few cases though, usually when certain mechanics weren't made clear.  For reference, the following game mechanics might not be readily apparent:
* You can place boxes on top of the mobile spheres
* You can reach down to pick up objects from a lower level
* Jammers can be used on fans
The sigil puzzles (Tetris-like puzzles that require you to rotate and place different shapes to unlock doors) can be frustrating at times; especially the larger ones, as these often require brute-force trial-and-error to solve.
The story is interesting and it does enough to set itself apart from Portal (its most obvious direct influence).  The visual design is eclectic and interesting too.  The music is fine; it's not bad, but nor is it great - since it has to provide ambience without distracting the player when deep in thought, it can't make its presence too obvious.
I've definitely enjoyed playing it, aside from a few frustrations, so I'd recommend it, if you like puzzle games and some philosophy.

Tales From The Borderlands is the new collaboration between Telltale Games and Gearbox Software.
The game takes place after the events of Borderlands 2. You play as two characters: Rhys, a Hyperion worker who dreams to become just as big as Handsome Jack, and Fiona, a Pandorian
grifter. Their stories intertwine when they embark on a quest filled with greed, violence and humor.
I am gonna tell you this right off the bat: if you don't like Borderlands or the other games by Telltale, do not buy this game. You are going to hate. However, if you like both
of them like me, you are going to really enjoy this.
The first thing that I noticed from this first episode is its length: this game took me almost 2 and a half hour to complete. This is the longest episode yet of any Telltale episode,
or at least for a pilot. The writing was smart and hilarious as we have come to expect from Borderlands, and so far this is more well written than the Pre-Sequel.
The gameplay adds new elements to the Telltale formula: the character of Rhys has an Echo-Eye that makes it possible for him to further analyse objects and people in the environemnt,
while Fiona can use money to bribe people or buy items. Also, in one segment of the game, you can customize and use a Loader Bot to battle bandits. I would love for this to be
present in the future episode. The game does, however, lack puzzles and have multiple QTEs.
The graphics are nothing spectacular or worth mentioning, while there are your usual clipping problems when characters interact with other objects.
The soundtrack by Jared Emerson Johnson is not as memorable as the ones from Sam & Max or The Wolf Among Us, but it works when it's used.
Overall, Telltale and Borderlands fans should try this game out, especially for its writing and expanded lore. If you don't like neither of those, you should stay away from it.

Highly disappointing. A mediocre game at best in every regard. I would give this a neutral rating if Steam allowed that, but since it doesn't I have to leave a negative one.
Someone at Machine Games apparently decided that making 1/3 of the game fetch quests with no combat was somehow a good idea, even though the game is only 10 hours long at best. This isn't Star Trek: Elite Force. You're not walking around the USS Voyager for fan service during the non-combat segments. You're running around stupid♥♥♥♥♥sewers and the hole in the wall resistance base that NO ONE CARES ABOUT.
Enemy variety is pathetic. Officier dudes with pistols, armored dudes with rifles, dudes with shotguns who take forever to kill, giant dudes with gatling lasers that take EVEN LONGER to kill. Dogs that show up once every 5 levels, and flying robots that show up once every 7 levels. I guess there are also giant robots that you have to shoot in the back (the fancy firecrackers they call grenades in this game see their one and only use in stunning these guys), but I think they only appeared about 3 times.
Weapon variety is even more pathetic. Only 5 discounting the double barrel shotgun that you get like twice and the repeating laser rifle that you get for only the surprisingly lame moon mission. Later in the game you get an upgrade that makes it passively recharge. So instead of finding a wall to stare at you just shoot it a couple times every 5 minutes. Yaaaaay? This leaves you with essentially only the silenced pistol and the assault rifle.

A truly mind-expanding game, and one of my newfound favorite works of art.  This game is very... unique, and more mechanics-focused gamers might not take to it.  If, however, you're the sort of person who is receptive to experimental artistic experiences then this game will blow you away.  While it's not the most beautiful or the most emotionally moving game I've ever played (although it is very beautiful and moving), it without a doubt
the most jaw-droppingly awe-inspiring.  There were moments in the game which were so unbelievable that they left me shaking.  Physically shaking.
NaissanceE isn't going to give you all the answers, but that's for the better.  Using your imagination to piece together who and where you are is an integral part of the experience.  It's a game which lends itself easily to interpretation, and whether you choose to interpret things literally or metaphorically is up to you.  I chose to examine things from a literal point of view and the conclusions this led me to where equalled perhaps only by "2001: A Space Odyssey" in scope.  This is truly a hidden gem of a game, one I
recommend enough.

Not The Robots is a unique game, classified as a "Roguelike Stealth Furniture Eating Simulator". It certainly can justify that, as it is a lot different from any other game I've ever played.
Not The Robots places the player in control of a robot whose tasked with devouring office furniture. Yes, I know that sounds awesome, but there is a catch. The furniture must be devoured without being detected, in most cases. There are a few things that can "detect" the robot, such as sentries, or lasers (which are very difficult to avoid in open areas). There are a few rooms in which none of these are present, and you can eat furniture in peace, but for the most part, there'll be enemies to watch out for.
There are also numerous abilities that can be picked up from blue crates scattered throughout each room. These abilities can serve many purposes, my favorite being the pickaxe, which can be used to break through walls that are otherwise unbreakable. There are a lot of these to choose from, but I found it a bit annoying that I couldn't tell what was contained in each of these crates by default. This resulted in me disposing of other abilities (you can hold several abilities at once) just to see what was in another crate, usually disappointed by the result.
Not The Robots offers a variety of game modes to choose from. Aside from the campaign, there are operations and challenges. Both greatly extend on the length of the game (and even further, if you choose to perfect them) and serve as a break from the campaign of the game, which can become aggravating at times, especially when you die really far into it.
The game features mediocre graphics and sound, nothing too spectacular, but nothing to complain about. The colors used are rather dark, but that fits well with the "stealth" aspect of the game. There is also a story that's told in pieces collected throughout the game. They are rather difficult to find, I only found a few throughout my play session.
Overall, Not The Robots is a fresh experience, really unlike anything I've ever played. It has its merits, along with its flaws, but it packages itself well.

Forge Quest is an RPG-esque dungeon game.
Forge Quest is all around an exciting game, packed with eloquent and humorous dialogue. The classes are diverse and have their own interesting abilities to go along with them. The dungeon's designs are unique in their own ways and really bring out some of the core features of the game. The Boss's are difficult and have their own special attacks, aside from the fact most of them die to the chicken.
Pros:
- Interesting Storyline
- Interesting crafting system, could be more streamlined
- Classes are fun, have different aspects, have build up to more advanced classes suiting your playstyle
- Spells and abilities are unique to their classes and suit the builds of that character
- Weapon system is intuitive and easy to use
- Inventory system is well organized
- Differently sculpted items, some better fit classes, same with armors
- Cool pets
Cons
- Dungeons are extremely difficult to navigate, and can take upwards of an hour to complete if you take the wrong paths
- There are some spots where you can get trapped in by monsters and easily killed
- The crafting system is difficult to understand and use, could be more intuitive
- After a certain point, leveling and getting money becomes a grind, as it usually does in games like this
- Although the story progresses, a lot of it is similar to previous points in the game
- Pets can get stuck, lost
Overall Forge Quest is an extremely fun game to play, but the dungeons can get tedious as you complete floor after floor looking for the right door to take. The pets are fun to have around but can get in the way. Also having to activate the pets every time you want them to attack can get annoying.
Let me know if this review helps, but please, this is just my opinion.
Cheers

There have been plenty of negative remarks about this game, i didn't write a review on the main gameplay so i guess now would be best to share my experience of the game, especially with focus on some of the negative points which i noticed
1. 'Pay2win'-Some comments say this game is pay2win because you need to grind 40hrs plus before you can craft an item. The idea behind crafting items are to give regular players customised builds, if it were too easy to do then there wouldnt be any difference between a vet and an amatuer. IF you feel you dont have the edge against other players who already carry crafted items.....please play against bots, they really arent too bad and can often times kick♥♥♥♥♥♥against a human team. Once you get your goodies, be that elixirs or gems, go craft some:P
2. 'Long Games'-Some say the match itself is very long lasting somewhat of near an hour, in my play experience it depends on the team opposing you itself. If it were bots then the match lasts between 15-30mins, yes, it never exceeds 30 mins on an average. This brings me to what i feel is an inherent issue with match against humans.....Strife unlike other Mobas like Dota arent too harsh on death, meaning, if you have a team wipe chances of you coming back into the game and winning are high, in Mobas like Dota you are pretty much at a PERMA disadvantage after a couple of wipes, rarely could you as a team win, heck i have seen many people on other Mobas not even leave spawn because they know its only a matter of time before they are defeated and so no use playing....Strife tries to address this and hence why you can have long battles, especially against human teams....though a little annoying i find it good instead of being the best player with most kills in your team only to find your team mates died frequently so enemy has become OP.
3.'Turrents are OP'-Well, i guess this is right, turrents are OP even when you are maxed out and got full equips, but dont they have pets in Strife? some of those pets are actually there to buff against towers hitting you or can even buff & repair your damaged tower....another interesting game tactic imho, nothing to cry about if its not the same as most other Mobas.
4.'Lags'-This game had significant lag issues, i believe this was due to players selecting the DX 11 settings, if they used DX9 then it would be resolved. This issue itself has been addressed recently i guess because i can now play with dx 11 on my win 10 and experience almost no lags whatsoever during fights.
5.'Lackluster heroes'-This is a good point and i pretty much agree with the premise, the hero pool on this game are no where near what you would find on other Mobas, BUT over the years of my playing other Mobas i have found most everyone sticks to the select set of heroes who are considered to be 'Amazing/fun/Op' what ever you would call it, strife has its mix of those too and i feel it really needs more of them..on that point i have to say, recently they have started brining out new heroes more frequently than say..last year, so i'm hopeful:)
I know there are some more negative pointers out there but i felt these were in essence what formed most of the negative reviews out there.
Oh the positives...dont want to say much but
1. Gold--Gold sharing is kill area based, so if you are near a kill you share some, no need to time your last hit like other Mobas
2. Pets---adds a new dynamic, like summoner skills on Lol.
3. Couriers-Everyone gets them ...freee! so no need to spend gold to buy one.
4. Crafting-Everyone can craft the same weapon in many different ways, each weapon is customised and suits the players game play style.
5. Experience--I feel this game is fairly good for new comers to experience a playing a Moba. The only pointer here being play against bots to learn before you try human opponents. This could get you crafted equips before you have to face a human team with OP crafted weapons:P
Edit- i had originally given this a 8.5 out of 10, now i would revise this to 5.5/10, mainly because i absolutely hate the fact with a passion that in a ALL NPC game where you are the only human, you are forced to play with your dimwitted team and endure a slow and painfull defeat. This happens occassionally when your team decides to keep dying so many times that the opponents becomes too strong to kill. i say forced to play, because if you quit the match you will get a strike and atm i have 3...all because of quitting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥NPC only matches. If this continues i might even stop playing this game.

Not too bad, but it has its issues.
The gameplay is the usual driving around, driving around and picking powerups and completing missions.
It feels a little bit like Carmageddon, in terms of graphics and car behaviour, in both good and bad.
The car physics aren't exactly realistic but they are passable. Graphically the game is about 2003 level (game was released in 2009) so nothing really to write home about. Enemy AI is almosr braindead, with tendency to either follow the optimal driving line, or suddenly make a 90 degree turn on a straight piece of road and smash into the wall, and turn back the way it came. The player car seems to have about one gear which limites the car speed to a more manageable level (read: very slow.).
The opponent car performance is identical to yours so this makes chasing down enemies a challenge as the boost only gives you a small speed boost which is barely noticeable. The few zombies waddle about slowly about, In the open world section, there are some AI drone cars running around the tracks, you get pickups like boost fillups, damage amplifiers and repairs and collect artifacts (money). The mission location is indicated by a blip on a map and a tall pillar with particle effects. Missions give money and unlock more missions and car upgrades.
The missions are usual demolition pit races, protect an objective, solo checkpoint races or chasing down enemies trying to reach the beforementioned points, and of course, normal races around a track. Some of these are timed, but fortunately it is possible to retry them as much as you like. The races take place in main map so there is not too much variety to the gameplay.
But it is not a terrible game. Just a little barebones for €9.99.

Here's a basic review about this game:
Story: 7.5/10 - A bit lackluster, but it gets the job done.  Given that most of the game involves action there isn't as much need for an in-depth story, though it would have been appreciated.  Lots came in the form of snippets in books, which have copies throughout in case if you miss one.  Pretty decent overall, though not enough to really draw you in fully.
Gameplay: 10/10 - There's a reason why TotalBiscuit has sworn by this game.  The combat is amazing.  Makes me wish that more RPGs, such as Skyrim, could have just copied and pasted these mechanics into their games instead of try to make their own from scratch.  The use of rope arrows to help climb up surfaces was a nice touch, and the game is loaded with secrets...speccing in alertness early on will be a move you won't regret.
Dialogue: 6/10 - With story, this one was kind of lackluster, though thankfully it was enough to keep some of my attention.  The dialogue between the two potential 'love interests' in the game was absolutely ridiculous at times.
Art Style: 7.9/10 - You can definitely tell it is a Source engine game by simple nature of the fact that everything is nice and gritty.  Does remind one a bit too much like Half Life 2 in that regard, but it is forgivable; after all, this is the only actual RPG that uses the Source engine with any form of credibility.
Lighting: 4/10 - Probably more frustrating than some of the puzzles.  I had to fiddle with the effects because everything was too dark.  Giving the player the ability to use Darkvision from the get-go put me in a position where I thought the dark rooms were a mechanic rather than a flaw on the settings.  This, however, is mostly a Source engine problem and I couldn't expect them to provide me with a flashlight, so despite my griping it's a forgivable feature.
Overall experience: 9/10 - Definitely will be playing this game again, but more importantly this game has left me with some high expectations for any planned followups if/when they happen.  One thing is for sure though; this game has given me new appreciation for the Source Engine, and makes me wish that Dark Messiah wasn't the only RPG available on said engine.
-Kerian

Having a hard time rating this game, but in the end I have a harder time recommending it than not. Also, I have a hard time figuring how its pricetag is considered justifiable at $15. Seems like games of its ilk go for about $9.99. Value proposition is real I'm sad to say and, TO ME, this game is maybe worth $5-$8 to take a gamble on.
NaissanceE has a very interesting visual style - its landscape is striking and has enough unique pieces to keep locations feeling fresh. I also have to give the nod to sound design, where it largely feels amorphous and evokes a sense of unease & foreboding. Sounds feel like they belong and have a purpose, without sounding like a recognizable variation of things more based in our world (i.e. boring reality :-p). The visual and aural experience is a pretty a cool and well rounded one.
However, there are issues with the lighting sometimes proving to be too finicky. This basically happens during the more difficult platforming bits - almost always a bad idea in a 3D game - where you only have a couple of chances to succeed. After a handful of failures they dumb it down and pull out the equivalent to bowling-lane bumpers by decreasing gap sizes and such so that you can continue. I like that they have a way for you to move on, but this seems an inelegant way to do so. I have no problems if things like this occur when it feels like a failing of me or my abilities, but this feels like they recognize certain sections didn't work well and this was their concession - their patchwork solution.
Other times you'll just be stuck trying to get past a section. I prefer this over the lessening of difficulty, though certain sections are just overly difficult when you are worrying about finicky 3D platforming while wrestling with darkness. Perhaps a better crutch would be for light to slowly increase as players continue to fail, giving them a chance to use pure skill to continue. Seems like there are more than a few platforms (or whole areas even) somewhat unfairly hidden in shadow. Or times when a light source decides it's going to run away after you've activated it, which might as well be a fail state rather than letting you bump along in perpetual darkness.
Perhaps it is just me, perhaps I do just suck, but this is just how it seems in my (admittedly) short time with the game. The senses are certainly entertained with the games visual and aural flair, but the patience is tested a bit too much and feels like successes are further out of your control than they are within. I'll have a hard time coming back to this game.
