As a guy who enjoys kickass fighting games, Divekick is a pretty enjoyable kickass fighting game. The two button gameplay works well - it gives players only the bare minimum to move, attack, and defend, but that's all any player needs. As a result, the game gets to the meat of what fighting games are all about - reading your opponent and outplaying them. There's no elaborate combo system or pretzel motions to learn, so players can learn to play the game more quickly instead of just playing their character (though character matchups certainly have their importance). And because of the 1-hit KO system, anyone can be a threat - this isn't Marvel where a skilled player can steamroll a newbie with his eyes closed just because he knows touch of death combos by muscle memory. Every opponent demands caution and strategy, which keeps the game from getting dull (though it does get exhausting). The art is pretty bad, and the story mode isn't as ridiculous as it ought to be, but Divekick is about divekicking people in the face, and god damn does it succeed at doing that.
And don't be that guy who thinks only Street Fighter clones are allowed into the hallowed halls of the Fighting Game Genre. That guy sucks at fighters. Play Divekick.

Episode one:
I must say that I am very surprised with Tales from the Borderlands. Knowing fully well that Borderlands is all about jokes and killing with little backstory, I still expected Telltale Games to create a very touching, emotional game in which the player has a lot of sympathy for the protagonist(s) just like The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us.
This is not the case in Tales From the Borderlands though. This game, a ¡Telltale Game!, actually made me laugh, instead of cry(due to their emotional games like The Walking Dead).
The protagonists aren't as lovable as Lee/Clementine or Bigby, the story isn't as grasping as other Telltale masterpieces and the game doesn't play with your emotions while The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us did this all the time.
So, does this mean that this is a bad game? Does this mean that this game is not worth to be called a Telltale game?
I believe this game, though unusual when compared to recent Telltale games, should be seen as a masterpiece. Where this game lacks certain emotional and story traits, it completely makes up for it through humor and funny protagonists and characters.
Besides, a Borderlands game without the jokes and violence wouldn't really be a Borderlands game.
There were numerous events in the game in which I laughed out loud and especially protagonist Rhys is a blast!
I especially refer to the scene where Rhys blows the Vault Key seller's mind as one of the funniest scenes so far!
On a final note:
I do believe that The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us take first (TWD) and second place (TWAU), but Tales from the Borderlands should definitely be considered a great game. And who knows, maybe the game will prove me wrong. Second place may be up for grabs…

Full review with pictures and a tl;dr version here:
To say I was worried about Telltale’s take on the Borderlands universe would be a bit of an understatement. While I enjoyed Borderlands 2 quite a bit, I was never a huge fan of the Borderlands universe, as it just didn’t appeal to me. But they’re Telltale and they’ve yet to make a game that I considered bad. So I forged on, loading up the first episode of Tales From the Borderlands, hoping it would get me to like the universe a bit more.
I don’t think I ever expected that it would quite as much as it did. Telltale really took the series and made it their own, with new characters, new drama, and new locales, all while still using the same universe and basic characters like the psychos. Don’t get me wrong, it is unmistakably Borderlands. I just think that it’s a bit more likable of a take on Borderlands, is all.
So what’s it all about, then? It’s the story of a Hyperion employee, destined for a promotion, when all of the sudden his boss is thrown out of an airlock and his nemesis takes over, screwing him over and demoting him instead. After overhearing a deal his new boss has planned, your character, Rhys, decides that he’s going to screw his boss over and get to his deal first. It’s also about a woman, raised as a con artist, who’s trying to pull off the biggest con she’s ever pulled. Both of them, really, and how their stories get intertwined. And how they both get caught by bandits and are forced to tell their story to the bandit that caught them.
It is quite a story, too. True to Telltale’s previous works, the game draws you in from the beginning with an enticing story and then proceeds to play its strengths throughout the rest of the episode. In Tales From the Borderlands‘ case, this is primarily the humor. If you even slightly enjoy the humor of Borderlands, this game will have quite a few laugh out loud moments. It doesn’t miss a beat, or a chance to crack a joke, and I actually found it to be significantly better than the average Borderlands humor.
It is a Telltale game, though. One of the more modern ones, complete with quick-time events and all. You won’t be escaping them just because it’s based on a first-person shooter franchise. The game is a bit more complex than some other Telltale games, providing different points where you have to manage money or use Rhys’ cybernetic eye to scan different things but it mostly comes down to derivatives of the same core gameplay. They’re nice touches, don’t get me wrong – and they do make the game feel all its own in some ways – but, if you aren’t a fan of the core Telltale gameplay, you won’t become a fan of it by playing this.
Fans of Telltale’s games will probably find themselves right at home. That is to say, playing Borderlands does not seem to be a pre-requisite as of yet, the story being self-contained in a time period sometime Borderlands 2. While characters are referenced, primarily bad guys, and different iconic characters, like the Vault Hunters and psychos, may be unfamiliar to you, you aren’t particularly missing out on anything by jumping in right here. The game gives an ample enough introduction for new players and the only character that actually seems to be recurring so far introduces himself well enough just by being himself. That and people talk about him.
The game also has no shortage of difficult choices. While I only played through once, convinced that there isn’t much point in replaying with different choices until after more of the season is available, they made great efforts to tempt you at every turn. Money or loyalty? Honor or pride? I can only imagine that these choices will get harder as the game progresses, trying to tempt you ever further towards the selfish “dark side.” I hope, at least. Having not replayed because not enough of the series is available yet, it’s a bit hard to tell at this point how much these choices will affect the primary storyline.
It may be a bit hard for some to get used to the flow of the story, though. There are two characters that you play as. Rhys, the janitor that got screwed over, and Fiona, the con artist, are who you are given to play as. As most of the game is flashbacks, you will constantly be pulled back to present time, switch the character you’re playing as, rinse, and repeat. The game makes a point of making sure you’re aware of when this happens – and when it engages in hilarious indulging the story – but it can be a bit hard to keep up, especially when you start switching characters mid-flashback. I found myself wondering what happened to characters a few times, only to have them just sort of “show up” a while later, seemingly unscathed. Sure, I now know what happened to them. But it would have been nice to have seen that, rather than switch characters while they were in peril.
The cast is rather great, though. Voiced over by talent like Troy Baker, Laura Bailey, and Patrick Warburton, Telltale has made great efforts to make sure that each of the characters is convincing. They are also a diverse cast of characters that really show the difference between life on Helios versus life on Pandora. And they stick to their ways of life, regardless of what may come. Sure, you can make choices but they are all based on what that character would choose to do. Nothing as of yet seems all that far out of place.
I find that Telltale is really good at opening and closing seasons. Sometimes, the in-between can start to feel a bit like filler but we’ve yet to get to that point. As of right now, the game is a quality addition to Telltale’s lineup and I am quite surprised to have enjoyed the season’s pilot as much as I did. Not only that but, in clocking in at over two hours, the opening episode has made a name for itself as one of the longest single episodes of a Telltale game I’ve played in quite some time. I truly hope they continue with that.

"NaissanceE is a game, a philosophical trip and an artistic experience."
It's a simple game where you delve deeper and deeper into this beautiful grandious primitive structure and solve various puzzles to proceed.
The main idea behind the game is to make the player appreciate the loneliness, the feeling to be lost in a gigantic unknown universe and to be marvelled by the beauty of this world. A world which seems to be alive, leading the player, manipulating him and playing with him for any reason.  Walking in an undiscovered abstract structure brings questions about the nature of this world, about the meaning of this trip. Evocating and symbolic, the architecture and events will lead player’s imagination to find an answer, if it only matters.
A testament to games as an artistic medium. Definitely worth playing.

My favorite aspect of this title is how well it maintains a “spacious claustrophobia”. The game shifts among moderately sized rooms, tiny spaces, vast expanses, and extreme heights that can elicit an acrophobic response (fear of heights). I would love to play this game on Oculus Rift for sure. The size relation according to the player’s movement and perspective/value shift effectively convey the monstrous spaces and architecture. But what creates the dichotomy of “spacious claustrophobia” is that, despite the looming heights and open spaces, there’s a ceiling – the player can only guess what this ceiling is part of. Later on this contrast is intensified in the desert chapter.  The spaces and architecture create an enormous feeling contained within a very claustrophobic feeling.
On top of all that, there are all these buildings and objects and strange machines, but where are the inhabitants? The world is empty of any kind of sentient creature (except perhaps the host...perhaps). This compounds the odd feeling of "spacious claustrophobia” and lends to a constant sense of unease and creepiness.
Graphically the game is gorgeous. Fantastic value combos and muted color schemes add to the game’s atmosphere. There are too many opportunities for screenshots. Most of the textures in the game are smooth, but they blend perfectly with the other aspects.
There’s a lot of music in this game, but also plenty of silence. The selection of music is very appropriate, many eclectic tracks and many selections from Deep Listening by Pauline Oliveros, Stuart Dempster, and others. I actually picked up the Deep Listening CD as a result of the game, and also discovered some of Dempster’s other meditative work. The times of silence in the game are poignant and at times downright crushing. Play the game in a quiet place with no background noises and the silence in the game will definitely assault the ears.
Mechanics involve mostly running and jumping. There’s no “interaction button”, but walking into lights and cubes sometimes triggers environmental reactions. Running includes a breathing button-press mechanic, which must be timed properly to be able to run without trouble. This is important in later parts of the game where the player must continue to run without interruption or die. Speaking of dying and reloading, there's a lot of that at times, which occasionally becomes a mild irritation.
As to the meaning of the game…the developer states on the game’s website that it’s open-ended and intended to be looked at through different perspectives. For me, the game is about the cyclical nature of life: run, run, look where to go, look how to go, look when to go, run some more, get pushed and pulled by various forces, experience all the different values of emotions, run some more, and then rinse and repeat.

Wolfenstein: the New Order is a bit of a mixed bag. It looks good, plays smooth, its voice acting is also pretty neat and sometimes it gets to tug at one's heart (Max! Hass! Max! Hass!) despite being a game about constant murder and mayhem.
The game is set in two periods - first the final hours of the game's own WWII, where Nazis win the war and keep wearing leather; the latter part of the game is set in the 1960s, where concrete, black leather and German accent rule the planet and the Moon. However, this time there's a resistance movement in the game. Wolfenstein has never been a game about the "human" aspect of war, but the resistance characters genuinely instill something interesting into the game as you return to base between missions. Hell, there's a glaring reference to Jimmy Hendrix right in there, what's not to like about that?
Enemies are, well, cardboard cutout Nazis. Same size, same uniform, decent AI (mostly) so there's not much to go on there. The game's villains are a bit of a letdown but that's pickle there - we cannot obviously have a "cool" Nazi, so instead they cranked it up all the way to 11 with super weirdo Nazis. Deathshead is pretty much a given, of course. Mad and cruel scientist, with a James Bond villain vibe oozing from him. Even that name is weird - sounds like a Telletubby name for psychopaths. But it's fine, the game is satisfactory in what it offers. There's enough gore and mayhem to sate those hungry for bloodshed, challenging enough in combat (finished in Über difficulty - was decent) and there are even a few emotional exchanges for those who prize such occasions.

Underneath Clutch's snarly, indie, East Euro exterior beats the heart of a very average racer that gets repetitive quickly.  Sure, the races take place in a zombie-plagued future, but your tasks are essentially the same as in every other arcade racer out there, just with a "STALKER-ish" paint job.  There's fixed checkpoint races, (semi-) random checkpoint races, demolition derbies, "ram the other racer" races, and variations on these themes.  The fact that you're mowing down zombies between point A and point B is kind of exciting at first, but then you realize that there's far better arcade racers out there (say, the first GRID) and far better mow-the-peds-down racers out there (the old, but still vital, Carmageddon).  If you absolutely have to motor over zombies I'd recommend the top-down "Zombie Driver", which, while still an indie eyesore, gives you actual missions and guns.  Clutch: 2/5 stars.

It's entirely dialogue driven (edit: which I am fine with and enjoy other dialogue driven games) and yet the way conversations are put together means you are constantly cutting off the other characters if you ever choose to say anything. Not only does this mean that the patterns of speech are completely off, but you also rarely get to hear what someone was even trying to say before the prompt for you to respond is gone. If you are ever asked to do something the window before a character gives the video-gamey "We don't have all day" response is tiny, and then they keep repeating it without even taking the time to breathe. There are so many issues like this that I really can't stand listening to it. The art is nice and the voice acting was alright, I'm sure the game's story went to interesting places, but I don't understand how anyone can enjoy listening to the dialogue in what is, from what I could tell, a dialogue driven game.

The rampant translation errors and lack of any sort of tutorial led me to expect the worst, but this actually plays pretty well for the first hour or two. The handling is pretty smooth and there's a clever mechanic whereby hitting zombies gives you nitro, meaning that swerving into as many zombies as possible is often the fastest way to get around.
Unfortunately, once I unlocked a faster car and got to some of the larger races, I realized there's some incredibly blatant rubber-banding going on and it absolutely killed the game for me. It's frustrating as hell to get out in the lead in your zippy little sports car and gun the nitro only to have a hummer zip past you. This alone pretty much ended my interest in the game.
There are some other problems. There are a lot of side missions to do for cash to buy upgrades, but they're all variations on either hunting artifacts or smashing zombies and it gets old really quickly. There's very little feedback or information (not even a spedometer) and things are really rough around the edges. For example, the UI may or may not display your objective progress depending on how it's feeling at that moment.
Honestly, without the rubber banding this would have been a fun if slightly clunky semi-open world zombie-murderin' racer. As it is, it's just not worth investing the time in completing dull side missions and upgrading your car just to have the game decide that you should be in third place now.

If you've ever played the Ultimate Assassin series on Kong, and enjoyed it, you'll enjoy this too.
A stealth game with an interesting mechanic; you must eat your own cover (the furniture) to clear a level. Not all of it must go however, so planning ahead is key, and the patient are rewarded. Close calls are common, even at the early levels, and you will need to have both wit and reflexes in order to survive. Features some great abilities to choose from, such as invisibility, removing walls (which are otherwise inedible), placing immovable blocks, teleportation, sprinting, as well as some others. Using the abilities are risk however; in order to activate them again, you must recharge them by eating furniture, so you really want to use them when you need it most. The AI performs brilliantly, making me hate the sentry bots for their perceptibility, yet still feel fair, for they mess up occasionally.
The aesthetic is what really gets to me. It is obvious from the get-go that you have been dropped into some dystopian robot future. As I haven't completed the game yet, I don't know what our purpose is behind eating furniture, but throughout gameplay, the game drops subtle hints as to what might have happened, through the snippets of conversations (which are voice-acted quite well), logs, and advertisements of a dead civilization. It's subtle, it's dark, but most of all, it's creepy.
There were a few things that got on my nerves however. First off, the game has a leveling system, in which you gain experience each time you die, based on your performance in the previous playthrough. Every level grants you a permanent upgrade. Unfortunately, I can't seem to find a list of my upgrades anywhere, or else I am just missing it entirely.
The tutorial is extremely short, which always gets on my nerves, even more so then extremely long tutorials. Granted, it is a simple game, so you shouldn't have many problems picking up the pieces that the tutorial failed to.
Lastly, it would have been nice if they included some tooltips or any information on the differences between campaign, challenges, and operations. Tooltips for other functions would have been nice as well, however they are somewhat self explanatory.
All in all, a good game, well worth the price as it stands now at $6. At $10, however, it might not be everyones cup o' tea, althoguh I personally would buy it again at that price.

So Not The Robots is essentially a stealth roguelike, where, rather than lurking through dungeon tunnels or planning turns, you're evading sentry bots, avoiding lasers, and myriad other hazards as you progress through procedurally generated floors. Your uni-wheeled robot can roll fast to quickly break line of sight of armed sentries or keep up with a moving laser grid, as well as crouch to hide behind obstacles and avoid other dangers. To complete a floor, your robot must devour a set amount of furniture per level to unlock the exit and there in lies the strategy. Removing furniture means less places to hide, less barriers to block lasers, and makes getting to the exit that much more challenging. You have limited health and your only course of action when seen is to run and hide.
Besides your natural hiding skills, you can collect a limited use ability, from going invisible (but motionless) to placing a block down which you can hide behind. You can only equip one ability at a time and they can be used once before having to recharge (by eating furniture) so they must be used tactically and at the most opportune moment. Multipliers, logs that gradually piece together the story behind the game, health packs can also be found throughout each level
Besides the procedurally generated campaign, there are also 20 challenge levels to test your skills, so there's something for the speed-run fan as well. In both the campaign and challenges, you earn more points for not being seen, for collecting multipliers, and speed among other factors.
Controls are smooth and responsive. WASD to move, mouse to move the camera, other keys to crouch, use your selected ability. Gameplay is a mix of fast paced planning and maneuvering and evasive sneaking around obstacles to avoid enemies: procedurally stealth with a dash of puzzle elements (as planning what furniture to remove or not remove will help your escape, especially since sentry patrols will change once you open new paths).
---
After playing a bit more:
- There are upgrades found throughout the levels, providing things from an extra inventory slot (so you can two abilities rather than just one) and a scanner to see what abilities are contained in a box
- Found some cool new abilities. Dig lets you remove a wall and Sprint give you a few seconds of boosted speed. Dig is especially cool because it lets you alter the layout of a level, opening up new paths for you (and sentries) to use
- You also get extra points for eating all furniture and taking no damage. Upon death, you rank up and can unlock permanent upgrades
- The variety of hazards continue to impress. From moving energy walls with openings to pass through (giving the game almost a puzzle platformer vibe) to damaging floor pads, the challenge is very high

Dark Messiah of Might & Magic was a game I had played the demo for at roughly 10 years old. I passed so many hours kicking orcs off of high ledges in the sandbox area provided in the demo and finding it amazing how nice the game looked in comparison to Half Life 2. Recently, with some cash left over from the Winter Sale, I picked up a copy of it and spent two ~7 hour sessions playing through the entirety of the campaign and laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off.
Describing this game as an RPG feels somewhat disingenious, at least by my definition of an RPG. Those expecting a thorough, immersive high fantasy experience will (probably) be disappointed. If you're looking for some dumb, hack-and-slash, first person sword/magic combat, you'll get exactly what you want. Dark Messiah perfectly blends a mid-2000's E3 FPS tech demo and a hack-and-slash RPG. Kicking orcs, goblins, guards, and ghouls around is immensely satisfying. Hell, the sword-and-board combat itself feels nice and meaty. While I didn't focus on it too much, and only placed a few points into magic abilities, they do feel a bit lackluster, but Telekinesis is endless fun. Overall, the game makes up for its few faults by being immensely satisfying, fun, and rewarding
A word of warning, however. While now nearly ten years old, Dark Messiah is admittedly dated. Running on the 2004 version of the Source Engine, (I believe, at least, I know that it certainly isn't running on the Orange Box engine,) patch after patch has made the game a bit unstable. I experienced about 15 crashes between these two sessions, but considering the game's now low requirements, getting back into the game is just a minor inconvenience, this along with the rapid climb in difficulty will ensure you're saving quite frequently. There are a few things that don't quite play as well as they did in the unpatched, 2006 version of the game, one of my major gripes being the few boss fights speckled throughout the campaign. Some of them just are not particularly fun from a gameplay perspective, but luckily are few and far between.
Altogether, my run of Dark Messiah: Might and Magic came out to about 12 hours or so, playing on Hard. I imagine the game can range from about 5-20 hours depending on your difficulty and speed of play. Overall, if you enjoy physics combat gimmicks and kicking orcs off large cliffs, and generally just 'running up on fools,' and don't mind some early Source Engine jank, Dark Messiah is a game for you.

What is a good game? Generally, you can judge whether or not you like a game by how many times you've come back to play it. For how long will RimWorld treat you?
Are you a completionist? There are five difficulty levels, which you will get plenty of opportunities to get your progress wiped, even on the lower ones. Pick HC (no saves) mode, and you'll have to get creative. Set higher difficulty. Change start location to ice thundra, where the only things to eat, apart from snow (which is not very nutritious), are various body parts of your fellow colonist, who also happens to be your gay husband (Not that you weren't "eating" them already, when things were smoother). If you want new content, or more control over difficulty, you can look into mods, of which there are plenty.
Do you like stories? Developer doesn't position RimWorld as a "story generator" for no reason. Again, just don't use saves, and  you'll be facing quite some variety. The leg of that fella, who used to carry your concrete blocks around, got torn off by an angered wolf? No worries, there's an "euthanize" button, right in the "medical operations" menu. But who's gonna carry concrete blocks now? Guess, it's gonna be that granny who can only read books and occasionally draws sceneries Bob Ross style. Oh wait, she won't, cause she's too old and incapable. Guess the winter might get pretty cold.
There are things in RimWorld not to like (although I've played alpha16 for few hours and encountered a few very nice improvements): some dare questions, some are just straight up silly (ones I don't like): the game is not perfect. But I did play RimWorld for 80 hours (during like a month of having it) in alpha15, and I'm probably gonna play it for a comparable  amount of time in alpha16 (potentially alot more); and I can't see myself not also checking the game whenever the next big patch is released.
So what am I saying here? For my money, RimWorld is one of handful of games that are actually worth buying on Steam going into 2k17. There's many things to like, so for the game to misfire on you completely, you probably would have to be a happy possessor of severe ADHD (note how long-winded I've made this sentence, so the actual ADHD people won't get through it and get offended). Buy it, then treat it as an IQ test: don't start judging it before it confirms that you are smart enough.

NaissanceE is a game that doesn't know what it wants to be -- as many have noted, it begins as an exploration game, with truly amazing use of light, sound, and architectural design to give the sense of an vast, chill, abandoned underground landscape. In the early parts of the game, you find yourself wanting to hide from nothing more than light and shadows moving about in an indescribably sinister way. In the midgame, there's an astonishing underground city, which brings to mind Blade Runner, Brazil, with a bit of 2001 thrown in.
And then it suddenly turns into a frustrating "hurry up before you die" platformer, where there's no exploration, and you have to struggle even to reach the next checkpoint. If you get past that section of the game, it wanders even further afield, losing all sense of the atmosphere and enjoyment with which it started. I have a decent amount of time in this game (over 300hrs) and as someone who thought Dota was too slow when I first picked it up and thought LoL wasn't just too toxic but also too punishing to new players who had never picked up a Moba before; Strife is without a doubt the BEST MOBA for players who are trying to pick up the genre for the first time.
The first MONTH of Strife I got my butt kicked almost every time. I had a win % under 40% and I thought this game was insanely brutal to new players (which it was but not on purpose) BUT there was just something about the game that made me keep playing and learning the items that work for not only the hero I've chosen but for my playstyle as well, was one of the things that kept me going.
Strife is probably the third best MOBA overall but it can be the BEST imo and it's not anything about the characters because the characters are fairly balanced tbh. It's about getting people to stick with this game and choosing it over Dota or LoL which it is way more fast paced and easier to pick up and play but it isn't some MOBA that is targeting casuals like Heroes of the Storm. This isn't some uber casual friendly game (although more casual friendly than Dota).
Because there aren't MILLIONS of ppl playing this game the flaw is the Matchmaking system and I use the term "flaw" loosely because it's really doing the best that it can with what's available. Fact is getting out of Slate is tough because there are only a few thousand ppl that play this game worldwide consistently and so you will go through and get in games with higher rated ppl and even just 1 2.2k rated person in a game with a majority of Slate players, that 2.2k is going to completely destroy everyone as they should.
The remedy is obvious, there needs to be more players across all ranks and when that happens (if that happens) we will really get to see how great this game is and honest to god I don't even want to touch Dota or LoL despite ppl constantly harping on me to play it with them.
Strife has the Skill factor, it has customization, it has literally everything needed to make it a powerhouse but it just doesn't have the players. People who are willing to respond to a challenge and climb up through the ranks.
It took me nearly 2 months to climb out of "Slate" to "Bronze" and I've gotten close to silver recently but it's probably going to take another month to get to that as well. I am in games with people (consistently) that are gold/diamond and although I have learned a lot once again, the gap between a bronze (nearly silver) player vs a Gold/Diamond player is like putting me in with Slate players. The way I can dominate Slate games (when I do randomly get into a slate heavy game) is the way the higher ranked players dominate me and it's motivation for sure but for some ppl they aren't going to want to work that hard to try and improve especially if they are / were high ranked in a different game.
Oh that's the other thing, ppl coming from LoL who play and they don't bother figuring out how the game is different and they just try and do things like how they do in LoL and then get mad when that stuff doesn't work. Strife maybe a MOBA and it for sure has been influenced by Dota and LoL but it isn't Dota or LoL and ppl need to realize it. I am constantly seeing folks try and push uber hard at low levels and they play insanely aggressive at low hp and then conservative at high hp (which may not be a LoL thing but a lot of ppl coming from LoL do it) and then wonder why they keep dying.
I think this game is atm pretty great and if you pick up the game, give it a real shot and not just something you play for a few days and throw away. It's a very very good game with a lot of skill and strategy going on and if you give it a real try I think you'll come to enjoy it as much or maybe even more than a LoL or a Dota.
I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a change from LoL and Dota

An exciting, well-balanced shooter/sneak game with some puzzles, a touch of horror, and a great story. Let me explain.
The first-person shooting in this game is simple and straightforward. No clunky controls or a needlessly complex loadout in which half the weapons are completely useless. Assault rifle with a grenade launcher, shotgun, semi-automatic pistol with an attachable silencer, a scoped rifle, grenades, knives, and an awesome futuristic plasma gun. All you need to kill some nazis (oh, you can also pick up mounted machine guns when you have the oppurtunity).
Sneaking is more of an option than a real necessity. While there are some maps where you have nothing but a knife, it's not absolutely required that you sneak kill every single nazi guard, but BOY is it much more satisfying. Heck, even when you have guns, getting a silent kill on a nazi commander is still fun as heck. You also have throwing knives and a silenced pistol to get the job done quietly. I think what I like most however is that the game doesn't FORCE you to sneak around. It's an option of the player, not a requirement of the gameplay (except in a few maps). Wanna go full terminator and massacare everything in your path with duel assault rifles? Or would you rather be a ninja as you silently throw knives into nazi crotches and jam them into nazi necks? Huh? What's that? You wanna do both? Well, I've got good news for you gamer! "Wolfenstein: The New Order" is here to satisfy all your bloodthirsty fantasies!
Are there really puzzles in this game? Sort of, but they definitely play a smaller role. Much like HL2, this game is much more focused on the action than the puzzles, but there are a few they throw in every now and then. You can also go on scavenger hunts for extra items in each match, but once again, they're not required. However, it is a nice way to take a break from all the ruthless nazi killing.
The "horror" in this game really amounts to nothing more than a few short pop-up-chase scenes that involve a pretty terrifying monster. They made me jump and got my blood flowing, which is all they were meant to do. I don't usually play horror games because the constant adranaline rushes wear off pretty fast, but in this game, the jump-scenes are placed appropriately and far apart.
The storyline is the icing on the cake. I won't go into full detail since I want to keep this review spoiler free, but I will say a few things. The characters are unique and interesting. The dialogue is rich, clever, and offers some comedic relief when it's needed. The story isn't anything really unique (just imagine HL2 but remove aliens and replace combines with nazis), but that's completely fine. It's told fairly well, and while none of the story beats seem at all believable, it's told in a way where I never felt that I was taken out of the experience.
I had two issues with this game. The first one was the final boss fight. It was generic and 100% predictable, which I would usually be fine with, but I expected more from this game after playing it all the way through. The second problem I had was the "two storlyines" illusion it gave if you wanted to replay the game. Really, it's the same game twice with only a few  minor aspects changed. Still, the replayability on this game is very high, so I'll probably be playing it twice anyway.
All in all, this game was a refreshing, fun, and enjoyable experience. 8.5/10

An excellent puzzle game that stands out above the crowd in all respects.
The puzzle design is great, taking straightforward mechanics in creative and mind-bending directions and interacting very well with the environments (especially the secret stars, which often require bending the rules and interacting with level features outside the puzzle boundary or in adjacent puzzles).
The story asks tough philosophical questions, demands you try to answer them, and then actually feels like it's holding you to those answers, which is pretty impressive. It does fall into the "collect the left-behind logbooks" cliche and the "two competing guides" cliche, but it also adds some unique and thoughtful elements.
Visuals are great and atmosphere is great. Secrets are numerous, and hidden at the right difficulty so you'll find some but not all without extensive work. There's good quality of life features like fast-forward and loading previous autosaves. And it accomplishes the rare feat for a puzzle game of actually feeling LONG: I logged 18 hours to finish the main story and a third of the challenge stars, so I still have side content left to go.
Overall I'd highly recomend this game to anyone who likes puzzle games.

I have no nostalgia for the Metal Slug series, but can't imagine that could really save this game.
Gameplay consists of sending units from your base (you take a set of 8 different types) to destroy the base on the right, and that's it. Most units have a special attack that charges up over time and can be triggered.
This isn't a bad core concept, but it's also nothing special and it's easy to find free flash games that have a similar, if not better, execution.
On top of that there is an energy system, premium currency for booster items, regular currency for upgrading units and base attributes and DLC packages with characters that can't be acquired any other way.
With so many ways in which the game restricts you from having everything it should offer something amazing, and it simply does not.
There is little to no strategy involved in winning levels, requiring little more than grinding enough money from earlier levels to upgrade your units to be strong enough (or pay some premium currency for helpful/cheaty items).
The only thing that felt at least somewhat novel was the POW system (short for Prisoner Of War), in the levels you can free prisoners. Freeing all prisoners in an entire chapter gives you a passive boost to an aspect of gameplay separate of the base upgrades or unlocks new units. The problem is that even this system is weirdly designed and trying to get money out of you. Prisoners are 'hidden' across the levels in random locations that need to be hit with charged up special attacks. You can use a booster item (for every single level) to get at least one prisoner for completing the level, but even with that it could easily take 3-6 playthroughs of every level just to get all of them.
This game is free, so you should not expect much.
But I'd feel we should expect more than this.
Mobile games can be properly ported to Steam, but not like this.

Take on the role of an Automaton as you awaken to hear the omnipotent voice of Elohim, your guide come would be creator in this clever puzzler.
You start with not much apart from instruction from Elohim to solve a series of puzzles to collect 'Sigils', Tetris shaped keys that enable you to move further and further into this varied and beautiful puzzle world. Along the way you access computer files via terminals located throughout the levels that both tease interesting insights as to an underlinging reasons for this worlds existance, combined with extracts of philosophy and stories from the classical world that will interest players that enjoy these topics.
As you progress you have the opportunity to use a range of tools that you unlock via the Sigils that help to make the puzzles more engaging and thought provoking as the game progresses. With a forbidden tower that Elohim restricts you from on pain of death, the game allows you to take on puzzles that Elohim has designed for the self betterment of your kind, according to Elohim that is, as well as puzzles that are off Elohim's radar and seem important to the ongoing narrative of your journey towards self enlightenment and understanding the world that you occupy.
The puzzles themselves range from easy tests that take but a few minutes to much harder thought provokers that may leave you stumped for much longer. Logical and lateral thinkers will enjoy the challenge and the games design enables you enoy equally thirty minutes play solving a couple of puzzles to more dedicated sessions where you can make serious progress towards the game's climax.
Highly recommended for players that enjoy exercising the brain and for those looking to pass the time with a different and intriguing puzzler.

I usually try my hardest to stay away from puzzle games because I personally get annoyed at them but at one condition, if the story is interesting like Portal for example I'll focus on that instead of the puzzles itself.
I can tell you after playing almost 40 hours of the game including the Road To Gehenna DLC & all the grey Sigils from all the stars you collect (there's so many secrets to find it's overwhelming) will frustrate you if your not paying attention to your surroundings. (Most of the puzzles are very clever even if I may struggle at them & I absolutely loved solving the Sigil Puzzles from every gate in the game)
No matter what your views on the world are whether religious, political or scientific this game from the makers of the Serious Sam series will explore all sorts of arguments about humanity that for me honestly left me thinking for hours about my own beliefs as a human being even though these questions are for our unknown robot protagonist following an unknown God's orders.
I usually would explain the story of a game but The Talos Principle is one of the few games that I urge you to play it blind (including the Gehenna DLC) & make your own interpretation of the story because in my honest opinion this game needs to be showcased in schools everywhere because the beauty of this game to me is the diverse opinions people would make out of this game's questions (when they finished the game) via the terminals you read + the debates with the Milton Library Assistant (including the world of Gehenna's terminals from the DLC) & the time capsules you listen to.
Performance wise the game runs fine on 60 FPS & you have a lot of options to tinker with so that's always a plus for any game to me.
The only flaws which are few that I will point out are the bonus content DLC which honestly besides the Making Of video (very interesting watch) everything else didn't appeal to me, the prototype DLC is only for players that want to know how the game's puzzles were formed in the final build of the game & some of the Star locations were frustrating to find like for example
star or any stars that involve ridiculous amounts of jumping (sometimes inhuman amounts of precision) even though the movement is very strict on where to jump.

Overall this a huge achievement for Croteam outside of their norm of making FPS games & I hope in the future they make more philosophical games because the talent of outside sources like Tom Jubert of Faster Than Light & The Swapper fame keep players like me interested in the story.
The entire soundtrack for the main game & the DLC are delightful too from beginning to end so I highly recommend buying the soundtrack too.
EDIT: I gave this game the “Suspension of Disbelief” Award

For the vast majority of the experience that is NaissanceE, I felt like a little kid in a closed mall with the power out. A vaguely threatening ambiance cloaks the situation, but there doesn't seem to be any direct or immediate danger present. And still, I count my steps.
NaissanceE is not a horror game, but why the hell not? I believe it might have to do with the game's emphasis on the exploration in place of the peril. The tension accentuates the experience, instead of directing it. A good portion of the unease stems from the horrifically inadequate lighting provided in many parts of the game, shrouding corridors, stairwells, alleys, catwalks, bridges, entire landscapes in a suffocating darkness. In these portions, players would have to tentatively traverse ahead by the seat of their own senses, or wait for stray lights to draw near (enough) to cast looming shadows of pillars and banisters onto surfaces to indicate where the ground ends and the void, or more appropriately, "Everything Else" starts. I refuse to call it "nothing" because although the spaces in the game have the capacity to be quite vast, every square inch accommodates the game's expert sense of mood. In some parts, they underlie curiosity; in others, perhaps wonder, or that persistent unease we were talking about. One wrong step, you won't just take a tumble into inky nothingness– you'll whoosh past stories and stories of additional architecture you wouldn't even have been aware of.
In NaissanceE, you are alone. And there will not be a moment that goes by without that reality trailing your awareness. This is easily the main factor that contributes to the unnerving tone of the game. Rolling cityscapes with intermittently lit windows, dark underground cubist caverns, miles of interior deserts– walk on, walk on. With such detailed environments, it's a bit diminishing to realize that you are following a linear path. Not to say there aren't manymanymany Many detours one would have to take to find the right one. These pathways seem so organic and natural to the world they're based in that it isn't just beneficial to the game's open-world illusion– often times, it's preferred. I wanted to wander and meander and occupy every space I could discover.
NaissanceE nails the exploration part of the game so well, the other parts of the game simply seem duller in comparison. There are several puzzle aspects throughout, which only ever halted the process of immersion and got me wishing I was someplace else doing something else. It's also heavy on platforming, which seemed to work its way into the "gameplay" without much fuss. Naturally, the platforming segments were the ones that posed the greatest challenge to get through, especially whenever the game started taking inspiration from the fever dreams of Brutalist architects and schizophrenic minimalists. It also doesn't quite find the right way to end. For all of its sound and fury, the final sequence of the game doesn't provide any form of endgame closure to the experience. While it would have been blasphemous to the game's values, or even outright impossible to give a concrete ending to all that had come before it, the game doesn't seem to end so much as stop. Perhaps just as well, as the game isn't about its ending but about its experience; an ending might've ironically allocated more attention into what the game is ultimately building towards, instead of letting the journey justify itself. All the while, backed by an understated but essential soundtrack. Just listen. The music almost seems to inhabit the space you explore. That's good company.
8/10
((Side Note: Though the game's themes and tone hearken back to 2001: A Space Odyssey on a number of occasions, there is only one direct reference found in the game. Can you find it?))

Was a US medic in a squad assaulting a school held by the militia. Three squads went into the area and intense firefights occured. I started to patch people up as they got shot, but it occured the attack was faltering. A retreat order was issued by the Squad Leader... But few marines were still trapped in the school and couldn't fall back. I disobeyed my SL's orders and ran into the school whilst under heavy small arms fire. After taking out some Tangos, it became clear there was only one other guy left, named Ronald. Ronny was a rifleman but his squad didn't make it. It was jsut the two of us
We quickly ran up to the second floor - where the metal stairs and a doorway were the only way to get up there.
It was eerie. The battle had shifted to anoter part of the town, gunfire was far awaybut there were still footsteps around us. They knew we were still here. They were coming for us.
In squad chat, I cried out for help - the response was to hold out for as long as we could as they were under fire elsewhere. Ronald was scared out of his mind. I told him I was a medic and 'we would make it home'. Even i didbn't believe my words.
The footsteps came closer. Ronald st up his firing line to watch over a window in the main courtyard while I watched the doorway that led into the hallway. Then we started to hear the clank of feet on metal stairs --- I aimed my weapon at the doorway....
The first three charge the doorway and fall to the ground. The next two try to run across the hallway and fall flat on thier face.
They start shooting at our windows and force us to lie on our belly. One more tango enters the doorway and manages to make it into a room opposite Ronald's position. The milita man didn't like Ronald's grenade.
Running low on ammo, Ronald and I switch positions constantly to cover our reloads.
To ruse the enemy and buy time, I tell Ronald to chuck a smoke at the door. (If you ever played CS:GO, you'd know NEVER to run through smoke). We buy time and throw our last smokes and maximse their usage. The militia start getting fed up by us that one of them decide to charge through the smoke. He gets a bullet off on me- just a flesh wound.
Once we ran out of smokes, the situation outside the school had changed. The US forces had pushed back the militia and started a counter attack. They were getting close back to the school.
Tragedy soon struck - a milita sharpshooter snuck onto a neighbouring rooftop and shot Ronald straight in the back. Ronald cried out and I quickly switched to my M4 and shot at the sniper with my last mag.
Disregarding my own safety and right in the middle of the hallway, i started to heal Ronald just hoping the enemy wouldn't go through the door. Just barely hanging on, I told him one more time: "We are going to make it home, Ronald!"
We fell back further into the hallway in a back room. Once again they started to charge the doorway.
11....12......13.....14......
Multiple hostiles down!
The doorway was littered with bodies.
One more came through the doorway - but with a grenade in his hand. He manages to toss it before we take him down. Ron manages to get out of the room - I'm no so lucky.
The frag explodes infron of me and I see a balck screen with my heart beating. I'm about to hit "give up" but then I hear Ronald continuing to fight and telling me to hold on. In muffled squad radio a friendly marksman mentions he can see dead "militia in a doorway being mowed down" through his binoculars.
The map lights up with blue arrows appraoching from the west. Help was coming! We were going to make it! A medic comes and revives me back to life.
Eventually, US forces managed to take back the school and win the game. About ten players ask Ronald and I what happened, to which we respond "We just wanted to go home."
Basically, two marines managed to hold off for 14 minutes and took out 17 militia.

I picked up this game in a Humble Bundle after seeing the potential in its atmosphere from some of the screenshots a few months prior. For a few bucks its okay... but kind of lacking in too many departments to be enjoyable on many of its aspects.
The game's core elements are platforming + puzzles, and atmosphere. There is no story at all, despite the fact that an opening cutscene depicts the player running from some black blocky streaming through the air and then telling the player that '(name) is lost'. I actually forget the protagonists name, because it and the black thing were never relevant in the game once. The black creature showed up exactly once in a fantasia-esq musical scene 15 minutes before the end of the game with a white stream-creature and they both flew off into the sky. There are no other characters in the game, no writings, or lore in any discernable form. So you have to judge the game on its other two aspects.
The puzzles and platforming make up the only 'game' element. Unfortunately, this also is lacking in a lot of ways. The pacing and nature of the game's puzzles don't really seem to build on each other at all. In some ways that's not necessarily wrong, but it really makes the game feel strange. The opening of the game has a few simple puzzles, followed by a lot of walking and platforming and platforming and more platforming and even more platforming, and then you do a few small to medium puzzles back to back before its back to platforming for a while chapter, and then no platforming at all until the very end of the game where it is only platforming. The platforming is more or less solid as long as things arent moving, and when platforms are moving its fairly solid still but occasionally you will be unable to perceive where a moving platforming should be properly traversed, leading to some annoying deaths. The end chapter is more or less a platforming boss, which will require a lot of grinding to beat as you will have very little idea of what to run or jump to in order to continue in a several phases. Perception seems to be an issue here, even if not an often occurring one. Puzzles are more or less easy, only two require you to stop for more than a few moments to solve, usually because you have to see if your inputs created the right outputs. The game seems to have some optional areas one can enter, but unfortunately two of them were more or less trap rooms with no exit until the player tries some random thing in order for a door to open. These were pretty unfun as there was no point to go into them in the first place; the exit is where the player entered. Another specific puzzle gave the player a choice of a stark black or white room, flashing shadows or lights for a fraction of a second to show an otherwise hidden path. This was disgustingly eye-straining and whomever had the idea for this shouldve been put in check for it, and in no way should this have made it into the game in the form it is.
Atmosphere is... mixed. The scale of the residential areas is genuinely impressive, but leads to vertigo as the downward climb chapter has the player scaling down a huge vertical shaft along cliffsides where these residences are. The game gives a feeling of unease in some of the more 'residential' type environments simply because of the emptiness of the locale and the intentionally unsettling music, but there isn't anything to fear though as there are no other entities in the world to interact with. Lighting is well done and gives some places a good ambience, probably the most impressive thing I can say for it. However, at one middle chapter drops all the atmosphere in favor of crawling through tubes and platforming across fan shafts. Its a strange abrupt shift and feels out of place.
The game performed fine and usually ran at 30 or 60 fps depending on how much had to be rendered, but only had to hesitate to lag during major loading zones. There are a good amount of graphic options and keys are rebindable, but strangely there is no volume slider. The music isn't too loud but it still could be a problem for some. All saving is checkpoint based. The game controls well and has good KBM + Mouse implementation, but it would probably be playable with a controller if you felt like you had to. The game is short at 4-5 hours with not much replayability except to poke around for things you haven't seen before. I can't really recommend this game unless you like the visuals as that's all there is to appreciate here I think.

If there's one thing this game does well it's to provoke your imagination to create an awe inspiring and "epic" game experience. You'll find yourself alone in an impressive futuristic structure of some sort, uncertain if it is of human or alien origin, or consists of something more abstract than matter entirely.
I think the most illustrative example of what you're getting into with this game is this: I'm still not sure whether or not I managed to make it outside of the game's normally playable bounds. I took every opportunity I saw to attempt reaching areas that I didn't think I should be able to reach. And, every time I did make it to a new area, I found myself questioning whether or not I had succeeded. Was I skipping part of the level? Was the part of the structure I was currently exploring meant to be for visuals only, or had the game developers intended to allow the player to wander freely in this area?
The difficulty of puzzles and the frequency of checkpoints felt perfect, and the few challenging action-y/platformer-y parts of the game didn't frustrate me in the slightest. Some other reviews I have seen found the game frustrating. Perhaps avoid this game if you are bad at creative problem solving and lack the imagination required to fully immerse yourself in the experience.

Silly, accessible, and somehow enjoyable.
Divekick might seem like a joke at first, and while there are certainly many of those to be had for long time fighting game fans, it is actually a surprisingly refreshing take on an aging genre.
I'll be blunt, with the exception of Smash Bros. and the Soul Calibur series on a good day, the vs. fighting genre for me is all but dead. It had its hayday, and I've never cared much for the competitive level of it, which seems to be about all the legs it has left under it anymore. My enjoyment of it lies in the more accessible entries these days if I can glean any at all, and the failure to innovate on the genre as a whole has by and large left me moving on to other things.
Along came this odd duck though, Divekick. While it still falls to some of the same trappings of any other vs. fighter, the incredibly simple yet deceptively strategic gameplay breathes some much needed new life and individuality into this game.
It is truly that simplicity that makes this something more than just another vs. fighter. You have two buttons, one for "dive" which makes your character jump, and another for "kick" which makes them do their diving kick attack. If you use the kick button while not in the air, depending on the character, you may have another mobility option at your disposal, but it still only ever requires two buttons.
That's it. There are no d-pad/joystick movements. There are no strings of perfectly timed combos and reversals. There are no complex 360° movement requirements while in the air at the precise timing where your foot reaches your standing opponent's armpit. There is only dive, and kick. Sounds boring right? Surprisingly not!
I found myself playing this more often than I expected to, given my apathy towards the genre in general, and the fact that it managed to keep me playing it beyond the first 10 minutes is testament enough. You see, as simple as this concept sounds, there really is a game to enjoy here. Each characters movesets vary slightly, and with every attack being a one hit-KO, it's all about the mental aspect, faking your opponents out, knowing your character's strong opponents and weak opponents, and really just some plain ol' good luck/timing.

Ahh such a classic game. I remember playing this on the xbox and spending countless hours finding different ways to kill enemies! Without further a due lets jump in shall we? Ill split this review into the following categories: gameplay, graphics, audio, and story.
Probably the most entertaining aspect of this game is the gameplay. It's first person with a very fluid feel to it. You play the game by picking from the skill trees (or putting points into multiple trees effectiely becoming a hybrid) and using weapons that correlate to that tree. Warriors use shields and sword, mages use staff, rogues use bows and daggers, etc. I played through the game as a rogue/warrior hybrid and gotta say it was fun as hell. The physics engine is hilarious, theres nothing like spartan kicking a ghoul over the castle walls. The game is not all that long which is fine because for what the game is trying to achieve the length was perfect. I could go on forever explaining the combos, power attacks, etc you can use but ill just use a bulleted list to give the highlights.
Honestly not a whole lot to say here. The audio isnt anything special. Sound effects sound appropriate and the background tracks/combat music aren't especially exciting or annoying. For this part i'd just say "meh".
Decent graphics, some models and enemies looked a little neglected to some of the other characters but I suppose thats to be expected when you don't spend much time looking at them as you do punting them into a wall of spikes.
If you want to know what I mean look at the cyclops and goblins in the game. Compared to orcs and humans they look lackluster but again im not going to sit here and rag on it like its a big deal this game is FUN.
Ok so this part, in my opinion, was very well thoughtout. I won't spoil the main plot of the game as that would ruin some of the fun but do know you can essentially choose to be good or evil. Because of this "choice" system (there arent that many choices as say, dragon age) there are multiple endings which may add some replay value on top of the desire to want to play through again as a different class. It starts out simple and adds enough throughout the game to keep you interested. Its not AMAZING but it was cool and had a nice twist to it, albeit one that probably a lot of people will see coming. All in all, pretty good.
-I did encounter some minor bugs here and there but nothing game breaking. Of particular annoyance was a sound bug in which the sound effect of flys near dead bodies would "follow" you around regardless of how far you got away from the body. A simple reload will solve this.
-I played through two times to get the endings and i recommend your first time through just to play without much worry about secret areas and hidden items, then on your second playthough take the time to looks for the secret areas so you get cooler weapons/armor and more skill points.
-SECRET AREAS ARE "NOT" required. You can easily beat this game with the weapons that drop from enemies/you find in your path way and youll have plenty of skill points to make your character into a decent hybrid or a focused badass.
Id rate this game a 8.5/10. Plenty of fun and defintely worth the money if on sale!

I'm going to break this down based on MOBA (Massive Online Battle Arena) players vs non-MOBA players.
(Apologies for being last non-MOBA players but this part is still helpful for you):
If you're a fan of LOL (League of Legends) you will enjoy Strife and hopefully, like me, prefer the ability to customize gear over time. LOL players you will probably miss the character sheets and abilities earned for leveling up your player profile.
DotA (Defense of the Ancients) players, honestly it depends on which side of the fence you fall on DotA. The hardcore DotA players will probably dislike Strife with the exception of the overall build variety per character and the ability to use your powers against towers. The softcore players that mostly play because their MOBA friends do will probably prefer Strife as the penalties when having a bad game are not as severe and the versatility of pets and items make the game fun.
HotS (Heroes of the Storm) players, in my opinion this game would be the next step up as far as MOBAs go. HotS is a rather basic MOBA with little over all customization, no resource requirements (Gold), and no items. This would be a great transition if you were still trying to learn the MOBA format but didn't feel you were up to LoL or DotA just yet. In time this could compete with the big two but not just yet. Only cons I foresee for HotS players is lack of familiarity with the characters (seeing heroes you know from other games is awesome) and the lack of Blizzard's chat server. Here you do get Steam chat but that does interfere with MOBA play.
My breakdown for MOBA players is
with the potential to get to 10 in time. Most veteran MOBA players should enjoy the differences my personal sadness is that to truly jungle it takes a lot of time to create the right custom items and so far I've only successfully done it with Hale.

The customization is fairly easy to pick up on, there is a story mode that helps you learn the basics and the vs AI (Artificial Intelligence/Bots) mode is solid, the bots can be challenging but are not so overpowering that new players are guaranteed to fail.
In short for those of you out there looking to try your first MOBA, join in this will be a great learning tool and if we find enough people to support the game perhaps you'll be on the ground floor of the next big MOBA to hit the market.

Age of Empires II HD, falls within the real-time strategy (RTS) game genre which I have recently had the opportunity to delve into. The family-friendly teen rating while maintaining a competitive and strategic atmosphere draws my attention like warm apple pie. This unbiased review will assess and primarily focus on the third and most recent upgrade, ‘The Rise of the Rajas’, which was released December 19, 2016.  I purchased the upgrade on Steam and appreciate that this content is available through such a user friendly website. ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ DLC captures and embodies new features added to the original game with Southeast Asian civilizations, inventive maps, fresh campaigns, and it also has improved some playability glitches.
Even after three upgrades, SkyBox Labs and Forgotten Empires have again continued to show faith in their work with exciting and intriguing, unique material.  To describe the expansion’s gaming concept would be that it attempts to retain playability within a beautiful history of Asia, unfolding in an all time favorite game with new elements that the original lacked such as diversity, strategy, and aesthetics.  I am sure this game would seem a little clunky compared to modern RTS PC games.  Limitations include retention of the original version lower resolution and continued similar basic unit control. Yet, the cinematics and gameplay of this expansion are instantly familiar to any user who is accustomed with the initial adventure because of similar civilization pattern developments. A fast-paced dynamic continues with a similar speed of progress through empire advancements. However, expectations of an upgrade can be broad, not knowing what will be released and I can see how a gaming community familiar to certain cinematics would be looking for a unique or contemporary approach to this issue.  Nonetheless, Age of Empire II HD still retains a solid and loyal community.
Four new civilizations bring an underrepresented international populace to the multi-national gaming community and I applaud the inclusiveness of Southeast Asia.  These civilizations include the Burmese, Malays, Khmer, and Vietnamese, all of which have their own unique upgrades and each civilization feels well planned and special. Research into these civilizations to get accurate army and naval nomenclature must have been enjoyable, as I appreciated exploring each one. First, the Burmese civilization is a monk and elephant civilization based upon the Pagan and Toungoo Empires with a unique unit, the Arambai. The best aspect about playing the Burmese is that the relics are visible on the map. This is such a nice surprise because I love collecting all the relics. Second, the Malay civilization is an infantry and naval civilization based mainly upon the Srivijaya and Majapahit kingdoms with a unique unit, the Karambit Warrior.  The Malays advance quickly, have exceptional harbor technology, and their Karambit Warriors can hoard and mass in huge numbers, as they each count as ½ a unit.  However, their weak armor is easily defeated when the army is spread out and need to be micro-managed to stay together and function as one entity.  Although frail, they are quick and work best against other specialty units due to their vast numbers. Third, the Khmer civilization is a siege and elephant civilization with their unique unit, the Ballista Elephant. Khmer buildings are beautiful. The developers designed a phenomenal castle emulating the actual Angkor Wat Temple. This structure is found in Cambodia and was constructed by the Khmers. I think the developers made a great match. Lastly, the Vietnamese is an archer civilization based upon previous dynasties with a unique unit, the Rattan Archer. These foot archers are this civilization’s saving grace.  This was my least favorite civilization in the expansion, but the Rattan Archer has incredible speed, good range, and tougher armor after their upgrade.  Upon playing all these civilizations, I noticed some of their architecture is similar to the original and some had innovation throughout and effort put into them. I understand that there are so many empires within earth’s history and that not all the buildings can be historically accurate. However, more variety of the architecture and building structure would have been great with exception to the Burmese civilization.  This civilization was my favorite because their architecture had beautiful shapes, even with patterns of faces built into the fronts and borders. Historical inaccuracies frequently have to be sacrificed for playability and it is common in games with some historical contextual elements to do this. From there you would see the creativity expand for playing purposes to enhance the realistic approach, such as having the same buildings for similar civilizations. Although I would have preferred each civilization in the entire Age of Empire II HD line to have their own unique line of architecture for every building.
Five new random maps and five new special maps include 13 multifarious terrains with broad biospheric variety. These choices open up methodology for scenario development and strategic advantages. There also is a new scenario editor with a spotlight on the amphibious topography which creates options including both land and naval warfare in innovative platforms.  My experience with the original maps has been positive but I was blown away by the improved variety.  The ‘special maps’ also elicit advancement in scenarios and strategy.  Some examples include plunging canyons, relics stashed in odd places, moss covered jungles, unit paths in shapes like a snake or an eye, and arduous terrain. Various water levels also gives the option of only building a navy and forgoing a land militia altogether. There is also a wider variety of animals which adds artistic value.
The upgraded campaigns provide innovative challenges which require player ingenuity and organization.  Unlike the original campaigns, the missions are more creative. They also add aesthetic topographical content, specially designed music, and interesting storylines that are fun and engaging.  Particularly, the turtle theme in the Vietnamese campaign was threaded throughout and I thought that was a pretty and attractive touch.  One playability feature that I am really excited about is that my progress is remembered through my profile in the campaign. Previously, I had to remember where I was at or else I would forget and end up replaying a campaign.
Many of the prior problems with Age of Empires II have been resolved.  Namely, there is an improved AI which makes a more challenging foe. Instead of mindlessly attacking, the new AI seems to use some reservation and decision making skills, such as attacking along paths and taking more notice of where my units are on the map.  Multiplayer seems to also run smoother and has improved game function.  Furthermore, before the upgrade I noticed unit animation stutter when my units would occasionally freeze and float, ghosting across the terrain.  They would also glitch out and appear to be moving forward while facing and walking backwards, a funny illustration of classic moonwalking. These glitches seem to have walked off the moon with this fantastic expansion. In a final assessment, ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ proves to be captivating as well as progressive.  It extends the Age of Empires community with diversity, as well as bolstering playability, especially in multiplayer. These innovative civilizations, curiosity tapping maps, winning campaigns, along with enhanced upgrades and motivational narratives, ensures that the ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ is and will continue to be, an amazing addition in the Age of Empires II HD franchise.

Every now and then a game comes along about once or twice in a generation that really grabs me and doesn't let go. It happened with Shadow of the Colossus, Myst, Hotline Miami, and others throughout my years of gaming. To make a long review short, The Talos Principle belongs among that group of games that truly and genuinely made me feel the true joy of video games.
To say it's art would be trite but I do think this game tells a story that is both unique to the medium and uses the best of the medium to its advantages.
You are an android that awakens in a world full of puzzles and danger, guided by a faceless voice that beckons you to solve the mysteries of the world to attain sigils and use those sigils to complete your task, which is unknown to you at the onset.
Through first-person puzzle gameplay you move through each world attaining sigils, all while finding logs, emails, and recordings of a world long since forgotten. Occasionally you even get into an argument with an AI that makes you question your task and whether you are indeed worthy of being equal to humans.
As stated earlier, the gameplay is done mostly through Portal like segments with the occassional fit-the-tetromino puzzle. It's nothing super novel but it is a calming experience that really makes you get into the contemplative state that I think the developers would want you in.
While the puzzles in themselves are fun, it's the piecing together of the narrative through those logs and conversations where the game really grabs me. Not only was I questioning what was happening in the game but also in the (real) world around me because of the Phillip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥(PKD because Steam blanked out the last name) like writing of the passages. It's been a long long time since I've experienced a story as rich and fulfilling as the one in The Talos Principle.
The story and writing only gets better in the DLC
. Taking place parallel to the main story, the DLC tells the story of those who came before the main character and the community that they formed together. I'm not one to overly cry during games but there were passages between the characters that were so utterly human that it brought tears to my eyes, and the characters aren't even human! The DLC truly felt like an expansion of the old days where it was different enough from the main story that it didn't feel like witheld content for the extra buck.
Aesthetically the game is also gorgeous with its bright pallete and beautifully crafted worlds. The reds and blues of the lasers contrast against the landscapes to create amazing wallpaper material. Got a little motion sick from the game at first but thanks to the FOV slider it was fixed right away.
The music really adds to the zen-like feeling that the game is trying to push with a soft-ambient soundtrack that doesn't distract you from the puzzles and passages. Like the rest of the game, it's hard to believe that the composer also worked on the Serious Sam series because it is such a stark contrast to those games.
To sum it all up. If given the resources and time, this is the game I would want to make. Perfection is always in the eye of the beholder but to me this game is perfect.

In all honesty, I actually quite like the core game of Metal Slug Defense. It's an interesting take on tower defense that repurposes old sprites into a different genre. It's a nostalgia trip and a delightfully funny action romp that could eat your time away.
If only this PC version wasn't so fixated on destroying your wallet, I'd recommend it to everyone. As it stands, one cannot progress past a certain part of the campaign without either getting lucky, spending an exorbitant amount of time in the multiplayer or paying for better units.
While the campaign is a no thrills trek through every arena, what I truly enjoy is the Mission Mode. That allows you to play with all the units from the game in quick, challenge based objectives. It can be a bit unfair at times (which falls in line with the Pay-To-Win mentality of the game), but it is quite fun.
What isn't fun is making progress through the map and hitting a brick wall. The game cleverly masks this by claiming certain levels are "Hard", but that is a bunch of malarkey. What SNK Playmore has done is just boosted the players ego until they eventually hit one of the "Hell" levels.
In these scenarios, the enemy already has units out at the start and charges forth with units you cannot possibly obtain yet. It makes for frustrating, soul crushing defeats that leave you wondering what you're doing with your life. A game shouldn't make me question my own mortality.
I could maybe get on board if there were a buy all pack for $10, but SNK saw it fit to sell you 12 characters for $30. That isn't even every piece of DLC available, either. Couple that with the way you're trickle fed medals, which act as currency for power-ups, and you might as well not bother.
Nothing about the pricing structure in Metal Slug Defense is redeemable. To make matters worse, the multiplayer doesn't even work well. If you wanted to grind out medals online, you might be waiting upwards of 20 minutes to find a match. I've got much better things to do than stare at an alien twirling a ray gun.

For those of you who played Carmageddon, back in the late 90's, this game is the spiritual successor.
Created by a Russian based development house, the game is all the more charming for it.
Gone is the cliched smart♥♥♥♥♥♥teenage driver, who is trying to find / avenge his family / girlfriend / teddy bear , instead you play as a Hunter who will take on various missions, thus earning upgrades, etc.
The missions are of the standard type Kill / Capture mostly, with Escort and Timed runs thrown in.
The controls are simple and easy to pick up, so the learning curve is minimal, letting you get straight to the fun.
And this is where other racing games have seemingly lost their way, because they focus more on a teeth grinding level of challenge, invoking frustration.
It involves a time commitment to play those games - is it a game or a relationship ?
With this game, I can pick it up, play it, and leave happy, because it gave me a fun experience.
And that is exactly what I paid for.
