A War Story That I Will Always Remember.
There my squad was,
me as the medic, running from cover to cover popping smoke and reviving my fallen squad members.
Our quiet, but powerful Centurion who always managed to get the job done when a BTR showed up,
SirSheniqualaquisha who was the jokester of the squad but was a true marksman, with the highest recorded kills of the squad
Painapple, our other medic that I could always count on to get the guys I couldn't and even pick me up.
All led by our loud-mouthed, crazy leader peterm, that we would die in battle for.
We had secured a village on the road and had dug ourselves in, having built an FOB and had taken positions in the shrubs and building along a river crossing where we presumed the enemy were coming. We were the only squad up north, all the other squads were in a stalemate with the russians over an objective. Some of us wanted to go break the stalemate but we knew if we lost our objective we would crumble.

So we held and waited.
There was a few spread out gunfire, nothing SirLaquisha couldn't handle. We decided to push up, our squad leader warning us if anything happens fallback to the fallback line. We agreed and made our way to a poppy field. Suddenly gunfire was all around us, the enemy was coming for our objective Pain went down, as did Centurion, then Sir went down in a flurry of shots. It was just me and peterm. We threw all our smokes and made the long crawl back. peterm saw them first. There was at least three squads that got to the river crossing so we sprinted back and at this time the other guys had spawned at the FOB and had taken position. Gunfire started going off in the village while me and peterm sprinted back.
We made it to the edge of the village when peterm gets shot. There was a soft thud and he went down in front of me, he yelled  "♥♥♥♥ing run!" and I ducked into the closest hovel as he went down on the road. I peeked a small window and saw a enemy squad on the other side of the road on top of the hill. They didn't notice me, thinking peterm was the only survivor. But I realized that I was surrounded. The only door was the one facing them so I sat on the inside of the doorway, gun at the ready. I told my squad with a shaky voice, guys I'm surrounded, but they don't know I'm here. I think I'm a goner. There was a moment of silence until my squad leader yelled out "alright boys let's go save our ♥♥♥♥ing medic!" there was a silent agreement and then the most intense firefight I've been in.
We held the objective from 3 squads and a BTR and it was glorious. The rescue mission failed
but by god was it close.
So what are you waiting for soldier? Get out there and ♥♥♥♥ing squad up!

Age of Empires II HD, falls within the real-time strategy (RTS) game genre which I have recently had the opportunity to delve into. The family-friendly teen rating while maintaining a competitive and strategic atmosphere draws my attention like warm apple pie. This unbiased review will assess and primarily focus on the third and most recent upgrade, ‘The Rise of the Rajas’, which was released December 19, 2016.  I purchased the upgrade on Steam and appreciate that this content is available through such a user friendly website. ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ DLC captures and embodies new features added to the original game with Southeast Asian civilizations, inventive maps, fresh campaigns, and it also has improved some playability glitches.
Even after three upgrades, SkyBox Labs and Forgotten Empires have again continued to show faith in their work with exciting and intriguing, unique material.  To describe the expansion’s gaming concept would be that it attempts to retain playability within a beautiful history of Asia, unfolding in an all time favorite game with new elements that the original lacked such as diversity, strategy, and aesthetics.  I am sure this game would seem a little clunky compared to modern RTS PC games.  Limitations include retention of the original version lower resolution and continued similar basic unit control. Yet, the cinematics and gameplay of this expansion are instantly familiar to any user who is accustomed with the initial adventure because of similar civilization pattern developments. A fast-paced dynamic continues with a similar speed of progress through empire advancements. However, expectations of an upgrade can be broad, not knowing what will be released and I can see how a gaming community familiar to certain cinematics would be looking for a unique or contemporary approach to this issue.  Nonetheless, Age of Empire II HD still retains a solid and loyal community.
Four new civilizations bring an underrepresented international populace to the multi-national gaming community and I applaud the inclusiveness of Southeast Asia.  These civilizations include the Burmese, Malays, Khmer, and Vietnamese, all of which have their own unique upgrades and each civilization feels well planned and special. Research into these civilizations to get accurate army and naval nomenclature must have been enjoyable, as I appreciated exploring each one. First, the Burmese civilization is a monk and elephant civilization based upon the Pagan and Toungoo Empires with a unique unit, the Arambai. The best aspect about playing the Burmese is that the relics are visible on the map. This is such a nice surprise because I love collecting all the relics. Second, the Malay civilization is an infantry and naval civilization based mainly upon the Srivijaya and Majapahit kingdoms with a unique unit, the Karambit Warrior.  The Malays advance quickly, have exceptional harbor technology, and their Karambit Warriors can hoard and mass in huge numbers, as they each count as ½ a unit.  However, their weak armor is easily defeated when the army is spread out and need to be micro-managed to stay together and function as one entity.  Although frail, they are quick and work best against other specialty units due to their vast numbers. Third, the Khmer civilization is a siege and elephant civilization with their unique unit, the Ballista Elephant. Khmer buildings are beautiful. The developers designed a phenomenal castle emulating the actual Angkor Wat Temple. This structure is found in Cambodia and was constructed by the Khmers. I think the developers made a great match. Lastly, the Vietnamese is an archer civilization based upon previous dynasties with a unique unit, the Rattan Archer. These foot archers are this civilization’s saving grace.  This was my least favorite civilization in the expansion, but the Rattan Archer has incredible speed, good range, and tougher armor after their upgrade.  Upon playing all these civilizations, I noticed some of their architecture is similar to the original and some had innovation throughout and effort put into them. I understand that there are so many empires within earth’s history and that not all the buildings can be historically accurate. However, more variety of the architecture and building structure would have been great with exception to the Burmese civilization.  This civilization was my favorite because their architecture had beautiful shapes, even with patterns of faces built into the fronts and borders. Historical inaccuracies frequently have to be sacrificed for playability and it is common in games with some historical contextual elements to do this. From there you would see the creativity expand for playing purposes to enhance the realistic approach, such as having the same buildings for similar civilizations. Although I would have preferred each civilization in the entire Age of Empire II HD line to have their own unique line of architecture for every building.
Five new random maps and five new special maps include 13 multifarious terrains with broad biospheric variety. These choices open up methodology for scenario development and strategic advantages. There also is a new scenario editor with a spotlight on the amphibious topography which creates options including both land and naval warfare in innovative platforms.  My experience with the original maps has been positive but I was blown away by the improved variety.  The ‘special maps’ also elicit advancement in scenarios and strategy.  Some examples include plunging canyons, relics stashed in odd places, moss covered jungles, unit paths in shapes like a snake or an eye, and arduous terrain. Various water levels also gives the option of only building a navy and forgoing a land militia altogether. There is also a wider variety of animals which adds artistic value.
The upgraded campaigns provide innovative challenges which require player ingenuity and organization.  Unlike the original campaigns, the missions are more creative. They also add aesthetic topographical content, specially designed music, and interesting storylines that are fun and engaging.  Particularly, the turtle theme in the Vietnamese campaign was threaded throughout and I thought that was a pretty and attractive touch.  One playability feature that I am really excited about is that my progress is remembered through my profile in the campaign. Previously, I had to remember where I was at or else I would forget and end up replaying a campaign.
Many of the prior problems with Age of Empires II have been resolved.  Namely, there is an improved AI which makes a more challenging foe. Instead of mindlessly attacking, the new AI seems to use some reservation and decision making skills, such as attacking along paths and taking more notice of where my units are on the map.  Multiplayer seems to also run smoother and has improved game function.  Furthermore, before the upgrade I noticed unit animation stutter when my units would occasionally freeze and float, ghosting across the terrain.  They would also glitch out and appear to be moving forward while facing and walking backwards, a funny illustration of classic moonwalking. These glitches seem to have walked off the moon with this fantastic expansion. In a final assessment, ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ proves to be captivating as well as progressive.  It extends the Age of Empires community with diversity, as well as bolstering playability, especially in multiplayer. These innovative civilizations, curiosity tapping maps, winning campaigns, along with enhanced upgrades and motivational narratives, ensures that the ‘The Rise of the Rajas’ is and will continue to be, an amazing addition in the Age of Empires II HD franchise.

Brilliant!  The game really is brilliant as it ties together so much of what you'd expect from a game.  The game will challenge your definitions of life -- though the designers more than moderately presupose that their definition is the most appropriate one -- and it does so in the most intriguing of ways, seemlessly threaded into an appropriate puzzle environment lead by a story that fits perfectly.  Each puzzle feels like it has a purpose while the story itself adeptly questions the notion that anything has a purpose.  My only critique, were I forced to provide one, would be that the historical philosophical bits grow slightly tiresome as they don't seem as well juxtoposed with the story as the puzzles and various "chactacters" are, but this is probably a matter of personal preference.
Game play is simple.  Puzzles are just challenging enough and they do a good job of walking you through the mechanics as the complixity ramps up.  It sprinkles some more and some less challenging puzzles as you progress leaving the hardest as optional, though optional in a way that makes you really want to see what happens if you complete them.
Overall, 10/10.  Buy the DLC.

This game is a ton of fun. It's made by Splash Damage, who made Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, and Brink. I loved ET, but was dissapointed by brink. In some ways, Dirty Bomb feels like the game that Brink could have been. I like the weapon mechanics better, and while it's not as parcour heavy as brink was, it's very fast paced and includes wall jumping mechanics that allow for some rewarding uses of the map.
The game is not as balanced as it could be in some ways, but the maps are great, the heroes are great and each have their own flavour if not entirely unique designs. This game allows you to swap heroes mid fight similar to other games, but limits you to a squad of three you choose before starting a match. (Or in a small window during a pre-match lobby). This mechanic works well for a number of reasons, but I think the limited size is noteworthy because it means that players who have paid to unlock more characters aren't at an advantage over others, as there are two characters available to all, plus a weekly rotation with an additional three.
Characters are pretty easy to unlock via in game currency earned from matches. Some are more expensive than others, but even the expensive ones are not a real grind. Cards are also pretty easy to earn, either paying a premium to pick one you want, or trying your luck with RNG loot boxes. There are missions to complete to help earn extra currency, with new missions every 3 hours. These missions are pretty great as well as you can play for a short time to clear a few, or play a lot and complete more throughout the day.
I've bought a character pack, and will likely buy another character or two once I've had more of a chance to try them all out. I can't see myself buying loot boxes, but I understand they're in the game because that's part of a free to play model. As far as I can tell, the rarer stuff is cosmetic, at least after the bronze tier, so 'pay-to-win' doesn't seem to be a problem.

Dive kick is quite simply one of the most fun and interesting games I have played this year and while for the most part I would love to leave it there I just cannot do so. Dive kick is one of those games that appears once every so often out of the blue and is possibly one of the fun and simplest games I have ever ha the joy of playing in my lifetime. The games developers Iron Galaxy studios are well known for their ports of popular gaming franchises to consoles and PC's including the soon to be port of Borderlands 2 for the PS Vita and developing the lacklustre game 'Wreckateer' for the Xbox 360s arcade.
Dive kick is a fighting game to its core with the simple premise of knocking out an opponent with a twist-- you must jump into the air and hurl yourself towards the opponent to DIVEKICK them to win the match using just two buttons for jumping into the air and dive kicking your opponent. Rounds end quite quickly with a typical match lasting between 2-5 minutes long and for the most part it becomes a frantic battle to try and stay as high in the air compared to your opponent in hopes of getting them off their guard, that is not to say however that Dive Kick has no skill involved. I found myself trying to outsmart my opponent by various different tactics such as; standing still and waiting the psyche out my opponent, however in the air, going for make and break by instantly jumping and diving for a quick kill and more.
Before you start a match you are introduced to a variety of characters each with their own stories and unique abilities which allow for higher jumps, faster kicks and in some cases even slight hovers. After the characters and skins have been chosen you are then given a new option to choose a gem which act as the games help for your character... most of the time. There are some gems that are there purely for either fun or a means to show off! I am talking of course about the YOLO gem, a gem which gives the opposite player a 4 round lead only needing to dive kick the opponent once to win. I found myself most of the time choosing YOLO gem to challenge myself, to see if it was possible to actually win but I could never succeed.
My first impressions of DiveKick were quite literally this: What? I can play a fighting game without learning ridiculously hard to pull of combos, anyone can jump into it and know exactly what they need to do to win and it's fun to play? Where do i sign up!? Because that is what it really is, a game which anyone can play without having any prior knowledge of what the game is about or what they need to do. It is a game that brings people together for a forgotten sense of whimsical enjoyment and fun that seems lost in many fighting games lately and is a game which relies on playing tactically and biding your time and not knowing more than the other person and being able to pull off a move without your opponent screaming 'how did you do that?! that's a clear advantage!'
Sadly however the game is not as much fun by yourself and should be primarily played with other people either locally or online. That is, if you can connect to someone to play with in the first place. I found myself waiting for long periods of time to finally find a person to play against during the launch week of the game and ended up just turning the game off all together, unplugging my console and going over to a friend's house to play it with them instead.
It must be stated however that Dive Kick is fun, there is no question about it. It's a game that brings together the enjoyment of playing together with friends and is a simple idea done right. Dive kick should be a title picked up by everyone and anyone who has a PC or PS3/Vita. Dive kick gets my sphere score of a 8/10 for its sheer replay-ability, hilarious characters and great system. Kudos Iron Galaxy Studios and the team behind Dive kick! I am here hoping for DLC/Dive Kick 2!

Let's have a moment of silence for how deep the gamedev has sunk.
Exhale slowly. (Hopefully you are still alive.) Now take a deep breath. (Hey?)
What is a good game? Generally, you can judge whether or not you like a game by how many times you've come back to play it. For how long will RimWorld treat you?
Are you a completionist? There are five difficulty levels, which you will get plenty of opportunities to get your progress wiped, even on the lower ones. Pick HC (no saves) mode, and you'll have to get creative. Set higher difficulty. Change start location to ice thundra, where the only things to eat, apart from snow (which is not very nutritious), are various body parts of your fellow colonist, who also happens to be your gay husband (Not that you weren't "eating" them already, when things were smoother). If you want new content, or more control over difficulty, you can look into mods, of which there are plenty.
Do you like stories? Developer doesn't position RimWorld as a "story generator" for no reason. Again, just don't use saves, and  you'll be facing quite some variety. The leg of that fella, who used to carry your concrete blocks around, got torn off by an angered wolf? No worries, there's an "euthanize" button, right in the "medical operations" menu. But who's gonna carry concrete blocks now? Guess, it's gonna be that granny who can only read books and occasionally draws sceneries Bob Ross style. Oh wait, she won't, cause she's too old and incapable. Guess the winter might get pretty cold.
There are things in RimWorld not to like (although I've played alpha16 for few hours and encountered a few very nice improvements): some dare questions, some are just straight up silly (ones I don't like): the game is not perfect. But I did play RimWorld for 80 hours (during like a month of having it) in alpha15, and I'm probably gonna play it for a comparable  amount of time in alpha16 (potentially alot more); and I can't see myself not also checking the game whenever the next big patch is released.
So what am I saying here? For my money, RimWorld is one of handful of games that are actually worth buying on Steam going into 2k17. There's many things to like, so for the game to misfire on you completely, you probably would have to be a happy possessor of severe ADHD (note how long-winded I've made this sentence, so the actual ADHD people won't get through it and get offended). Buy it, then treat it as an IQ test: don't start judging it before it confirms that you are smart enough.

Guns, more guns, and yet more guns... if you have an insatiable need to shoot things and sift through hundreds upon hundreds of dropped items, in the hopes of finding that one rare gun that's marginally better than the one you already have, then this is most definitely the game for you. Oh, and it's pretty dang fun too.
Borderlands is a sci-fi loot-fest shooter set on an alien planet. You play as one of 4 "Vault Hunters", on a quest to find and open a mythical vault that may or may not hold untold riches. Each of the characters has one unique special skill, plus a set of strengths and weaknesses (better in one weapon type versus another, etc). Unfortunately you can only pick one character at the start of the game, so if you want to try different characters out, you'll have to start multiple games. That kind of sucks, but it's not too big of a deal ultimately, and adds incentive for multiple playthroughs (if you are into making that kind of time investment). The shooting mechanics are pretty good and it's cool how many different types of weapons there are. It allows for tons of experimentation and variety. Gameplay basically consists of discovering a new area, collecting a bunch of quests that need to be fulfilled (though many are optional), completing said quests, getting more loot, leveling up, and proceeding to the next area. Rinse and repeat. Even though that might sound slightly boring on the surface, I assure you it is not. The game mostly stays fresh throughout and the writing is pretty good, bordering on laugh-out-loud funny at times (the game doesn't take itself too seriously). And oh yeah, there's a cute little robot named Claptrap... 'nuff said.
There are a number of DLC campaign add-ons available as well. I believe all of them come with the GOTY edition, but if you don't have that version, I'd say it's worth picking them up after completing the main story (except maybe the Underdome DLC, which I haven't played), assuming you enjoyed the base game.
In summary, if you like games with a cool sense of humor that involve first-person shooting things and/or lots of loot drops and weaponry, pick this up. It has a great style, good mechanics, and enough content to keep you occupied for many, many hours. A-

Brilliant!  The game really is brilliant as it ties together so much of what you'd expect from a game.  The game will challenge your definitions of life -- though the designers more than moderately presupose that their definition is the most appropriate one -- and it does so in the most intriguing of ways, seemlessly threaded into an appropriate puzzle environment lead by a story that fits perfectly.  Each puzzle feels like it has a purpose while the story itself adeptly questions the notion that anything has a purpose.  My only critique, were I forced to provide one, would be that the historical philosophical bits grow slightly tiresome as they don't seem as well juxtoposed with the story as the puzzles and various "chactacters" are, but this is probably a matter of personal preference.
Game play is simple.  Puzzles are just challenging enough and they do a good job of walking you through the mechanics as the complixity ramps up.  It sprinkles some more and some less challenging puzzles as you progress leaving the hardest as optional, though optional in a way that makes you really want to see what happens if you complete them.
Overall, 10/10.  Buy the DLC.

I was massively impressed by this game.
The puzzles were intelligent, challenging, and often forced me to completely reexamine the spaces in the game and explore different possible perspectives. There were lots of Ah-ha! moments, but also lots of experimentation, lots of interesting discoveries, and several surprises. You get to choose your own pace, solving the puzzles you can as you move around, maybe getting clues or ideas to help you go back and work out earlier problems.
The well-designed, well-executed puzzles are the real sell for this game, but the story is good, and the game's overall atmosphere gives you a lot to think about. As often happens, the ending of the game is a bit of a dissapointment in comparison to the broad concepts the game tries to tackle, but if you look at the whole experience as a place to start thinking about some of the questions it raises, and not a way to answer any of them, I think it can be useful.
The DLC is just as good if not bettter. Taken as a whole, the Talos experience is one of compelling environments, difficult and rewarding puzzles, and quite a lot of food for thought, all aided by magnigicent voice actor performances, good writing, and a well designed, satisfying game world.

is a simple arcade game. You play one of three witches flying through the levels trying to reach the exit. While doing so you can collect coins, stars and shoot enemies. The different levels can be accessed through the world map. In total there are 8 worlds each with 9 normal levels, 3 bonus levels and one boss battle. So there is a lot of content.
I admit I was and am still a little bit on the fence for
. The "wow, interesting, fun" aspect which is the reason for most of my reviews is somehow different here. But I just can't find any reason why I should NOT recommand the game. From a pure objective perspective the game is really good. While the overall gameplay between the witches is the same and the changes are rather small, they are important and noticeable. For example is the range, style and strength of the broom attack different for each of them which can make a change on how hard a level is to complete. Also while there are 8 worlds they all feel different enough to be justified. Every 4 level a new gimmick is introduced which keeps the game fresh and interesting (bouncing walls, giant enemies, different fluids to swim trough, reduced gravity, ....). The world and level design is really strong and show the creativity of the developer. Mixed to this are some puzzles (mostly needed for getting the three stars in each level) which do challenge your head. Additionally there are a lot of secrets and shortcuts. And the game still has a lot of content.
So what is that keeps bugging me? I think most of my concerns come from being an achievement hunter. In order to unlock all achievements you need to play through the game at least two times and play each level multiple times. You need to collect all stars, need to win the time challenge (which also shows the creativity since the shortcuts are important now) and replay the whole game in New Game+ (IMPORTANT NOTE: You need to beat the game with each witch having completed the same amount of levels to unlock NG+) with three new characters. So all in all I probably replayed some levels far too often for them to be still enjoyable. Added with the high skill level needed to beat some of them, there is a lot of frustration potential and I probably cursed more then recommanded for my health. Also most achievements are connected to the boss challenges where you have harder versions of the normal bosses. Like really hard.
On the other hand again the developer was (during the time I played the game) very active in the forum, helped with a lot of questions, gave away tips and secrets and even changed minor parts of the game to make it more accessible. This deserves some praise in my eyes and is one of the reasons why I recommand the game now. So if you are looking for a creative game which can give a lot of challenge - if you are searching for it - and can take away a lot of your time I don't think you can do much wrong with
.
PS: If you have any questions just comment on the review and I'll try to come back to them as soon as possible.

Miracle Fly is a fun little indie platformer that avoids many of the pitfalls that indie platformers tend to have.
To me, its biggest strength is you never feel like you're getting locked out of content. Most platformers are level based, and more levels are unlocked as you complete currently available ones. Though no matter how skilled I am, there's a good chance at some point there will be a level I simply will not be able to beat, and as a result, I miss out on experiencing anything from a few levels to an entire chunk of a game. Miracle Fly avoids that by having multiple paths on level selection screen, so odds are you will usually have more than one level to choose from in order to unlock more levels. Additionally, stars can act as a cushion for when you get into a difficult situation. These stars are collected by getting all the gems in a level, collecting a certain coin in a level, or defeating a world's boss. For a certain amount of stars, you can revive yourself at the location of your death in a level and receive a few seconds of invincibility. There will always be a limited amount of stars available and within a level the cost of revival doubles with each use, so it isn't feasible to abuse the feature to make the game a cakewalk.
The game is also flexible in its requirements to complete a level. Reaching the exit portal with time to spare is the only task required. You’re welcome to collect all the gems, get every coin, or defeat every enemy, but ultimately such objectives are optional. However there is incentive complete them, given that the aforementioned revive mechanic is tied to gem collection and the occasional coin. This allows for an overall flexible approach that can be rewarding without feeling punishing.
The levels have a gradual increase in difficulty as the game goes on, but never feels insurmountable like I’ve encountered in other games. Levels become longer and more complex, puzzles are more demanding, enemies increase in quantity and get harder to kill, gems become tougher to collect, bosses increase in difficulty, and health powerups become basically nonexistent. I only take issue with the last change; if anything, health powerups should’ve become more common as the game went on, when the player is more likely to actually need them. In the game's defense however, two of the three playable characters are able to regain health under circumstances, but depending on the level at hand, they might not have the abilities best suited for success.
Another strength of Miracle Fly is that it never gets stale. Many platformers are mechanically sparse, and end up becoming repetitive or poorly ramping up the difficultly to make up for the lack of mechanics. Miracle Fly is always introducing new blocks, buttons, and enemies. Additionally, the three characters you can choose from differ in their abilities, strengths, and weaknesses, so even if you prefer one, you’ll likely use all of them at some point in the game. Some gameplay aspects introduced are more obtuse to figure out than others, but I never felt like Miracle Fly was getting old as I played it.
Besides the previously mentioned issues of limited health powerups and occasionally hard to understand mechanics, I’d say another problem is it’s easy to become dependent on the revive feature to complete a level. Odds are, you’ll have a surplus of stars to blow by the time you start reaching levels you need to revive in, and may become careless as to how often you use them. Then, as stars become more difficult to amass as the game goes on, you might find yourself suddenly stuck on a boss level with 0 stars, meaning you’re expected to traverse the level and beat the boss while taking no more than few hits, sometimes that’s doable, sometimes it isn’t. When it isn’t, then you’ll retreat across the level selection screen to find any levels where you didn’t get all the gems or maybe missed the coin so you can scrounge up enough stars to at least get a 2nd chance. While I don’t think the revive mechanic needed to be drastically different, maybe limiting revivals to 1 per level would’ve satisfactorily given the player a safety cushion while encouraging them to get better at the game and not waste their stars.
I purchased the game for $1.99, and with over 20 hours in it so far, it was most certainly worth the money. Even at $7.99, considering the girth of content you get, and it being a relatively pain-free experience, I would say it’s worth it. Between the gameplay, level design, and art, you can tell a lot of effort was put into this game, and a fun experience awaits you if you give it a try.

I pledged to this game sometime in early 2014, I was expecting nothing more than a nice little management game with a sci-fi setting.  What I wasn't expecting was a game that has expanded into probably the deepest and most engrossing simulation I've ever had the pleasure of playing.   The game plays as a sci-fi, firefly inspired 'dwarf fortress' style management/simulation game with heavy storytelling elements.  You initially play as a small group of survivors from the space ship equivilant of a cruise ship you were all aboard that has gone down, you crash land in escape pods on a rimwolrd and are tasked with building a colony to survive.  You don't control the colonists directly bu task them jobs and 'occupations' and they will go about their way.
Each update brings an incredible amount to the game, There's always a new interesting mechanic that forces new tactics and new storytelling elements. I've never seen a developer as involved with the community, He's constantly active on public media and often responds to feedback.  I remember once someone made a request on the subreddit for the idea of rescuing allies and giving them medical treatment without a negative penalty, Tynan agreed and released a patch the day or so after.
If your looking for a deep management/simulation or want to try Dwarf Fortress but are intimidated by the interface, this is the game for you.  Up there with Kerbal Space Program as the best early access games ever.

This is a strange game, a unique game.

You're introduced with a relatively clear experience, an oppressive tone (yes, that's a plus, it opens with such captivating mystery), and challenging platforming. The game could've used more direct writing to make its meaning more clear beyond a general feeling of fear and stress.

I can't quite but my finger on it, but NaissanceE is an extremely abstract exploration focused platforming game. Between the unsual enviornments, the almost foreboding atmosphere, and the strange soundtrack, this game is liable to confuse anyone who plays it. Having just finished the game myself, I can't help but feel like this game wasn't meant to be understood. Maybe with some pondering, and a chance to sleep on it, I might be able to discern some solid meaning from this game.
For those questioning whether they should buy this game or not, I can't really say for sure. Overall, I enjoyed playing NaissanceE, the enviornments were uniquie, the puzzles were inspiring, and the music and ambiance really set this game apart from any other abstract indie game.
My problems with the game, however, are that in many cases, I felt absolutely lost (apart from the times where you should feel lost). The game avoids handholding like an akward prom date, and I often spent unneccesary time wandering around aimlessly through the same areas, tryign to figure out how to progress. My other problem is the game's relative length in comparison to it's regular price (currently $20 as of writing this). I realize that creating large areas to explore takes precious time and money to produce, as well as the almost ludicrous cost of the Unreal Dev Kit Liscense, but I managed to complete the game in (as Steam has recorded for me) 3.2 hours. Take it as you will, but it felt just a bit short for $20.
If you're into abstract indie games, absolutely pick this up now, but if you're not quite sure about it, wait for it to go on sale, and pick it up.
TL;DR ~ It's super trippy, has nice visuals, atmosphere, sound design, music, and all around game design. Lacks solid direction, but is sometimes done intentionally. Buy it on sale if you're not sure about it, otherwise get it now! This game is a gem! :D

The illegitimate, obscure, and hidden son of Limbo and Kairo, both excellent games that I somehow can't find myself comparing to Limbo but that I love more than Kairo (and I do love Kairo). This game doesn't have the recognition it deserves and is somewhat of a ghost or hidden treasure on steam.
Those two short comparisons and analogies, one of them humorous, do not do this game its proper justice, or prompt you to play the game. This game is a 3D platformer/puzzle game. It is absolutely surreal, and absolutely beautiful. The architecture and detail in this game are amazing and the environment's sprawling expansiveness is sometimes overwhelming.
This game is exploration based, please take your time playing it. It's non-linear but there are set paths to take. There are also a lot of false-paths that can take you nowhere, because the point is not creating a path to follow but an environment to explore. You will get lost. A lot. And you might like it.
You might not like it. The game is isolation. These expansive enviroments, detailed. Cities. Houses, apartments, bars, sewers, offices, temples, completely abandoned. The isolation and loneliness is incredibly creepy. You will start to wonder where everyone is. What's going on? What happened? Don't think about it too much, or do. It doesn't actually matter, until certain things occur and you *really* wonder what's going on. It's not a horror game, it's not a "Creepy AI killed everyone in the lab" or "Creepy AI killed everyone on the ship and wants to be God" game, it's just a genuinely creepy game and experience.
You'll encounter a lot of strange things in the world of NaissanceE, and you'll get lost in the world numerous times. You'll die a few (dozen) times if you're not great, but thankfully the game has a forgiving learning curve: A checkpoint system.
The puzzles range from linear, simple platform/adventure game style puzzles to abstract and lateral-thinking puzzles. There's also, again, a lot of exploration involved, remembering where you've gone, which areas lead where, and a lot of hidden paths to the next location. It's not Physics/Math based like Portal or Antichamber, and not nearly as lateral thought-demanding as Antichamber, but again, It's different from both games. It's closer to Kairo or Limbo. Puzzles where you'll have to look around, explore the area, look at the big picture, look at the little pictures, and figure out what you've got to do. It could be as simple as moving several blocks around, to having to trigger several switches to get blocks where you want them to go, to more complex puzzles (usually involving disappearing and black matter blocks :D)
The soundtrack is great. I don't know what Yoga you do, or if you even do Yoga, but it's everything from wonderful sounding new-age ambient music that fits the exploration atmosphere (Stuff I'll usually hear only in Yoga Classes), or creepy tones and whispers that fit the isolation atmosphere. And then for the fast paced platforming actions, there's furious and wild beats that get your mind racing and your adrenaline pumping.
The price is fair for the game. It can be a long trek, or a shorter one depending on if you get lost a lot (whether literally getting lost, or just admiring the expansiveness and beauty of the environments.) There is some replay value to it just because of the environment and ambience, but if you've got the puzzles down it can lose its appeal fast, like other puzzle games.
If you're looking for a creepy, ambient game I would recommend this game. If you're looking for a great platformer, I recommend this game. If you're an artsy gamer who likes architecture, quality, or exploration, then I strongly recommend this game.

I've been a big fan of the Wolfenstein series since childhood, having played
many years ago.
breathes new life into the RtCW storyline, and it excels in many aspects of gaming.
The game offers nothing short of a challenge on higher difficulties, requiring the player to use both stealth and the creativity of their mind in order to dodge and weave around Nazi sightlines. On lower difficulties, the game becomes a satisfying shoot 'em up, with responsive gunplay and creative map design. The game gives the player a wide arsenal of simple and complicated weapony in order to get the job done. From knives to laser cannons, you are almost never left without a bloodshedder in your arms.
Despite a rough continuation in the RtCW storyline (independent from the Wolfenstein 3D, as W3D et al. are not canon), following

manages to encapsulate the story to players both familiar and foreign to the series. To sum it up: "We are at war with the Nazis, and, with the inventions of General Deathshead, they are winning." The story in TNO is both entertaining and engaging, allowing the player to modify their story through choice made through the game. The games characters are unique in personality, and are entertaining in their own right. Even the nameless Nazis you rampage through hold their own little bit of personality, as they communicate and interact with each other.
The game has some pretty sweet visuals, and has aged fairly well, even in the span of only a couple of years. The only real complaint with graphics is that many textures, particularly those on desks and tables, are flat, and may take away from immersion.
Overall, W:TNO is definitely a great game, and holds very minor flaws. If you are a fan of shooters, stealthies, WWII, or just want to spill some Nazi guts,
is the game for you.

Guns, more guns, and yet more guns... if you have an insatiable need to shoot things and sift through hundreds upon hundreds of dropped items, in the hopes of finding that one rare gun that's marginally better than the one you already have, then this is most definitely the game for you. Oh, and it's pretty dang fun too.
Borderlands is a sci-fi loot-fest shooter set on an alien planet. You play as one of 4 "Vault Hunters", on a quest to find and open a mythical vault that may or may not hold untold riches. Each of the characters has one unique special skill, plus a set of strengths and weaknesses (better in one weapon type versus another, etc). Unfortunately you can only pick one character at the start of the game, so if you want to try different characters out, you'll have to start multiple games. That kind of sucks, but it's not too big of a deal ultimately, and adds incentive for multiple playthroughs (if you are into making that kind of time investment). The shooting mechanics are pretty good and it's cool how many different types of weapons there are. It allows for tons of experimentation and variety. Gameplay basically consists of discovering a new area, collecting a bunch of quests that need to be fulfilled (though many are optional), completing said quests, getting more loot, leveling up, and proceeding to the next area. Rinse and repeat. Even though that might sound slightly boring on the surface, I assure you it is not. The game mostly stays fresh throughout and the writing is pretty good, bordering on laugh-out-loud funny at times (the game doesn't take itself too seriously). And oh yeah, there's a cute little robot named Claptrap... 'nuff said.
There are a number of DLC campaign add-ons available as well. I believe all of them come with the GOTY edition, but if you don't have that version, I'd say it's worth picking them up after completing the main story (except maybe the Underdome DLC, which I haven't played), assuming you enjoyed the base game.
In summary, if you like games with a cool sense of humor that involve first-person shooting things and/or lots of loot drops and weaponry, pick this up. It has a great style, good mechanics, and enough content to keep you occupied for many, many hours. A-

Not often i use my brain in complicated things, and i've been suprised by the puzzles i have gone through so far, it's been very interesting to learn and find ways around and avoid going on the steam community guides section... hehehe. This beats the hell out of Portal, thats for sure!
I completed it and its been a positive journey, i recognise the voice of Elohim from SWTOR as one of various characters, most notably Darth Arkous on the Shadow of Revan expansion. Also learning about the meaning of life, death and what is laying inbetween, lots of philosophy and discussion about things. Some of this about Life i already knew because having sat on the fence and watched humanity from that point of view i learned a bit as much as i learned from within myself for years on my own, strengths, weaknesses and other points. So in that way the reason it's interesting is how it furthers that very point and see it from another point of view which has helped in understanding another level to this whole philosophical idea that i honestly didn't think of.
The Graphics are almost completely natural and thats a hard thing to do for a lot of the game makers i have seen, in section A you walk through a greek/roman building, it's longish corridor makes you wonder what it was like from the view of an ancient greek, macedonian and a roman to walk through buildings like that and be at awe about the complexity of the pillars, the surrounding balconies and ceiling, the polished floor. In Section B you are in an ancient egyptian room with statues of various animals on display and inside Section C is a replica of a 15th century church from the looks of it, minus the bibical stuff you find in a church. Then there is the sky.
For all the good however i have one problem with the game i don't like much, the missing ability to tune out the bird noises specifically in the background, after enough of the section A puzzles, im' getting headaches listening to that buzzing noise constantly. i mean generally you can block it out with the effects on zero, but that takes away the sounds of other things including those the otherside of a wall that could give you an insight into something you can't see directly but you know is there. I was just glad to make it to Section B where there are none of those bird noises.
So yeah, i very much recommend the game and if it were not for those bird noises i would of given it the full thumbs up.

Metal Slug Defense is a pretty good game if you like the genre.  If you've played games like Warfare 1917 then you might know what the gameplay is like.  It's a defense game where you need to combine offense and defense to push back the enemies and destroy the enemy base(or a boss in this game).  It's a type of gameplay that's easy to learn but can be difficult to master.  The game is great as a single player strategy game that you can play if you've got a little bit of time but I haven't played the vs mode yet.
This game doesn't play anything like the old Metal Slug games so if you're a fan of them then there's no guarantee that you'll like this.  The DLC is quite expensive and should be able to be earned in-game(my opinion) but you should be more than powerful enough to overpower the enemy if you grind a little.  There are reports of a bug that makes your SV-001 tank disappear if you remove it from your hand so I suggest checking the forums to see if it still exists before you think of removing it from your hand.
All in all it's still a fun game even with its flaws.  I suggest checking it out since it's F2P and you don't need to buy the DLC to enjoy it.  Probably would have been better as a $10 title that comes with all of the DLC.

One of the things video games struggle with is human dialog, especially when they introduce player choices. It's often stilted and flows poorly, if it's written well at all. Many games can get serious kudos if they manage to get dialog and conversations right. Oxenfree is a game that gets it very right and it might be enough to cover its flaws.
In Oxenfree, you control Alex, a high schooler who's gone to a beach party on a small island with her friends. However, the island has a dark history and Alex and her friends have to uncover it to find a way to save themselves when the night takes a turn for the worst.
The thing that Oxenfree does best is its conversations between characters. Your four friends are fairly chatty. The dialog is natural and well-written, but what Oxenfree brings to it is that you're given up to three dialog choices, and when you makes those choices, you can interrupt your friends. Mass Effect did this, but your friends in Oxenfree actually react to it. It's such a minor thing, but it goes a long way toward immersing you in what is going on.
Night School Studio is comprised of some former Telltale Games developers, so it should be no surprise that your dialog choices affect the story and how other characters think of you. However, instead of an outright "character B will remember this" type statement, you don't really get a lot of feedback on when you're changing hearts and minds. The only feedback you get is a little thought bubble over someone's head with someone else's face in it. It gives some indication that they're thinking about that person, but not explicitly why. I like this a lot because it made my own choices feel more natural and less like I'm trying to push a friendship slider in one direction or another.
What might turn some people off is that there isn't a lot more going on here than walking around this island and talking to your friends about the weird stuff that's happening. There's some very light puzzle solving, and you can choose to do a lot of backtracking to find collectible items that flesh out more of the mysterious island, but don't expect to manage an inventory, or jump on a platform, or shoot anything. I'm not sure there was any point in time I could've "failed", just dozens of opportunities to alter the story in negative ways.
While the gameplay is very light, I could not stop playing Oxenfree. I played it all over the course of a single day with the game lasting about 5 hours. The intrigue-filled story and the immersive dialog kept me around. If I was going to put it down at any time, it would've been during some of the item finding I did, where there wasn't a lot of dialog but still got some payoff by finding another piece of the mystery. It nails a foreboding and dark story without being totally grim or colorless. It's the perfect way to spend a winter weekend.

Interestingly enough, the only thing that tells us that this is supposed to be a season finale is that the scope of the events escalate rather quickly towards the end; otherwise, it is one of the most generic TellTale point ‘n’ click episodes. A good one, but not as great as Episode 4 was.
Sam & Max return from the edge of space and time, only to discover that their neighbourhood has gone to hell. Literally; Hell has opened its gates and most anyone who we met during this season ends up in a predicament or two, including a few who are suffering some kind of torture in the bowels of the netherworld. So, it is up to Sam & Max to save them, whether they want it or not.
Gameplay follows a similar setup as the last episode, with several separate small stories next to each other. Since this is a TellTale game, these are all required to complete some central task, or in this case, two: first we wreak havoc in Hell, then we try to deal with its new management.
The problem is with the latter, the second half of the episode. It lacks proper weight, something that would show us that it ends and entire season of adventures. Instead, it feels like just completing one of the random tasks in any other episode, only this time there is nothing after it. It hurts the general quality, even if the writing is still funny as hell.
But, in the end, it is still a solid Sam and Max story, and I have to admit, probably a little better ending for the season than the one from Season 1.

Divekick is a recent addition to the fighting game genre developed by Iron Galaxy Studios and released in late August.  Everyone loves fighting games, right?
No.  Not everyone.  But why?
The fact of the matter is that for most fighting games the barrier to entry is complexity.  Players must learn about each of the characters, how to perform special techniques, and master precision combinations on a six-button layout just to be able to compete.
Divekick throws all the rules out the door and introduces simple yet absurd gameplay.  The madness begins with a simple premise: there are no movement controls, and there are only two buttons: Dive and Kick.  Pressing Dive makes the player dive into the air, and pressing Kick while in the air causes the player to kick downward towards the opponent.  Pressing the Kick button while on the ground causes the player to jump backward away from the opponent.  These are the only ways to move around the arena.  All divekicks are one hit kills.  The first to five kills wins.
Not exactly what you would expect, huh?
What if I told you that it’s one of the most engrossing fighting games released in the past five years?

In a time when fighting games regularly introduce complexity, it’s refreshing to see a game that breaks fighting games down to the bare essentials; strategy.  None of the 13 characters, each of whom dive and kick differently, are severely overpowered.  There are  no long combos to memorize, no comeback super techniques.  With no complexity, all that’s left is mind games; the ability to fake out your opponent, the rush of emotion when a plan is executed and comes together flawlessly.
While Divekick is generally understood to be a parody of the fighting game genre, it also unearths concepts that have been buried under layers of complexity for too long and brings the genre back around full circle.  Divekick cannot be recommended enough for any fighting game enthusiast willing to try something nice and silly..

NaissanceE is not an easy game to review. It is one of these exploration games that a cynic might call walking simulators, but NaissanceE actually has enough gameplay to call it a game. Still, a term that might be even more fitting is tech demo for the UE3.
So NaissanceE is sort of a one-man-project from Limasse Five a.k.a. Mavros Sedeño. It seems like Limasse Five wanted to make a 3D game and was able to do the environment and level design, some animation and a bit of programming. But he had absolutely no clue about 3D modeling, texturing and creative writing, so he nearly completely avoided these jobs.
Take a look at the screenshots to see what the game looks like. It does have its style and surely it is nice to look at. But while the lighting job was probably quite difficult, the modeling and texturing (or nearly complete lack thereof) still make it seem like not a lot of effort was put into it. However, this may be forgiven if you consider that the game was a one-man-project. The graphics completely rely on the advanced lighting technologies of the UE3, that's why I suggested to call NaisssanceE a tech demo earlier.
In terms of gameplay, NaissanceE is a bit like a 3D platformer. Actual puzzles are rare, you just have to keep going. The challenge lies in the fact that you have no objectives and no idea where you are supposed to be going, so you have to explore the area a bit and figure it out.
Regarding the context and the storyline, the short answer is that there is none. You may interpret the game however you like it, but NaissanceE does not try to push you in any particular direction.
The game lacks some attention to the technical details. When I opened the UE console with the TAB key, it covered two thirds of the screen and would not close. When I called up the Steam overlay, the game crashed. It also does not install silently like most games on Steam do. And a lot of default strings were not replaced, which is just lazy.
Also, the distribution of checkpoints is often quite weird. Sometimes it felt like I was systematically not reset to the last checkpoint, but the one before that. This also adds a lot of unnecessary commute to the game if you die often.
NaissanceE is not a long game. Even if you take the time to explore, the first runthrough should take about 4-6 hours. A replay could be accomplished in an hour or two, speedruns take about 45 minutes.
For a one-man-project, NaissanceE is indeed quite impressive and a nice experience. But if you consider the lack of features most games have and the corresponding lack of effort, 15€ does seem quite a bit pricey. Definitely wait for a sale or reconsider that this a one-man-project.

In short, if you like Blame! - the manga by Tsutomu Nihei - you will find a world filled with similar visuals. It is definately a beautiful game, enhanced by some very awesome ambient music. All of these are taken from existing compositions by three different composers and are used to enhance certain scenes and images. Although they don't form a coherent listening experience, they do enhance the overall mood in a wonderful way.
Sadly, the one thing that is lacking is narrative. Not a story in the normal sense, but a form of narrative. Why is Lucy lost? Where is Lucy? And who is she? Who is she running from? The game starts - innocently enough - with three words - Lucy is lost, but sadly it doesn't go anywhere from there. This short sentence is the starting point for aesthetically awesome adventure, that sadly left me a bit cold at the end.
The puzzles itself were totally fine with me, even the platforming bits were fine, except for the tunnel level - that one got a bit too annoying in parts.
Would I recommed this game? Hell yes! It looks beautiful and has some of the coolest architecture and designs I have seen in a long while!

This incredibly cheap game represents many hours of good entertainment. This excellent 1st person shooting game (not even close to open world RPG as TES) is presenting an advanced combat system full of opportunities, like using the main characters superpowers (that means his right leg) to kick your enemies of heights, maybe the best feature of the game. You may also throw anything you find on the ground at your enemies in combat, like a dead body, a small clay pot or a barrel. I would reccomend the barrel as that may actually destroy wooden floors. The combat in this game requires more of the player than many other games, especially in the start. You have to see the possibilities around you in order to defeat enemies of equal strength to you (Equal strength in the start, before you get to the fancy stuff). You have to search for heights, throwable items or spikes to kick them on that is there for the only purpose of helping you kill your enemies. In some locations there is even secret traps you might trigger to help you against your enemies.
Just to settle the way your character advances through the game for all who might wonder. There is no direct class and leveling system. In the start of the game you will always begin with the same character, and he will be step by step customized by your choices. As you complete objectives you will gain skill points, and you may use those skill points to become a better fighter, learn new spells, become a better archer, better sneaker or even gain more hitpoints.Then you may make a balanced character or maybe a character that only knows how to fight with his sword. I myself has played much with the sword/archer combo character, and I found that quite entertaining and would reccomand that if you don't have any preferences yourself.
There are in total two weapons you may craft yourself in the game with a very complicated and overdone crafting system, yet maybe more realistic than most games. Both of these are swords. There are many secret locations with magic equipment, traps that can kill you or other fun stuff.
The story of Dark Messiah is a standalone story, but it is recognizable with the story of the strategy game Heroes of Might and Magic V, set to the world ashan. Many people think the plot weak, but if you have played the Heroes V vanilla campaign you will recognize characters and elements, and the plot will seem quite strong. I might say that the main character in Dark Messiah is the son of two characters that you meet in Heroes V. There is a love story in this game as well, where you have to chose between two women eventually, but it hardly affects the game's outcome at all.
Many people are dissapointed because the online servers to the multiplayer version are shut down. That does not mean that there is no hope. I think there are still hosted servers if you do some web research, or check out the steam community, but the official servers are shut down. I have heard about a few guides to find servers to the multiplayer game, but I haven't felt any urge myself to try it.
There are a few bugs with this game. The most major one in my case was that the program Dark Messiah of Might and Magic.exe stopped working every time I tried to quit the game, but that is not a major problem, and it will not affect your saves if that worries you.
The animations and graphics of the game are staring to get a little poor, but the game is 9 years old, so that is to be expected. I would compare the graphics to TES IV: Oblivion. There is still an incredible amount of detail in the game despite the old outdated textures.
Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is a very enjoyable game, and I ensure you that you will experience a most powerful right leg. If you want to buy it I would suggest you check out Heroes of Might and Magic V as well (not VI and VII). I bought Dark Messiah with the Heroes V pack, and I reccomend that game as well (but it is not as good as this).

Despite not really being interested in Arma after watching people play it (it seemed slow and without teamwork), I picked up Squad after watching several people stream it and I'm glad I did.  It's early access but what I've seen so far is enjoyable to play and the mechanics, whilst still not complete, are reliable and consistant.  Some early access games have very problematic gunplay (e.g. H1Z1: KotK) but not with Squad.  It's already robust enough to already have a popular competitive scene.
The community is very helpful and there isn't much trolling on the community servers I've played on due to a very high admin presence  (I play on Rusty in Places servers mainly).  I was also surprised that 95% of people play the game seriously and don't "lone wolf" or not communicate with their team mates.
Updates for the game seem quite regular (several times a year), which isn't bad considering the devs are making the game in their spare time, it's not their 9-5 day job.  They also have a very good relationship with the community which is essential for early access.
Even if you've not played a military simulator before, I'd recommend watching some game play on Twitch, you might become as hooked on the game as I have.

I completed it and its been a positive journey, i recognise the voice of Elohim from SWTOR as one of various characters, most notably Darth Arkous on the Shadow of Revan expansion. Also learning about the meaning of life, death and what is laying inbetween, lots of philosophy and discussion about things. Some of this about Life i already knew because having sat on the fence and watched humanity from that point of view i learned a bit as much as i learned from within myself for years on my own, strengths, weaknesses and other points. In Section B you are in an ancient egyptian room with statues of various animals on display and inside Section C is a replica of a 15th century church from the looks of it, minus the bibical stuff you find in a church. Then there is the sky.
For all the good however i have one problem with the game i don't like much, the missing ability to tune out the bird noises specifically in the background, after enough of the section A puzzles, im' getting headaches listening to that buzzing noise constantly. i mean generally you can block it out with the effects on zero, but that takes away the sounds of other things including those the otherside of a wall that could give you an insight into something you can't see directly but you know is there. I was just glad to make it to Section B where there are none of those bird noises.
So yeah, i very much recommend the game and if it were not for those bird noises i would of given it the full thumbs up.

It is currently the free weekend for this game, and all it took, was a single, short race, in order for me to purchase it! I love this game. I've been hooked on it, all day. My brother and I have had several matches, I've been on single-player a fair bit, and I've played with some random people, online. All in all, my experience, so far, has been a great deal of fun, and wowing at the surprisingly tasty visuals, given the style of graphics.
The game runs beautifully for myself, with an ASUS 760 OC, and my brother, with an XFX HD-5750. You might well have already gathered, but this game is simply not that graphically taxing. My brother and I both have an FX-4100 - mine is overclocked to 4.2GHz, whereas my brother's CPU is at stock, and for him, the game runs at 60fps, at a 900p resolution, with everything maxed, except he has motion blur disabled. I have even gone a step futher, and forced 8x Supersampling, and 16xQ CSAA - the game still runs butter-smooth. So, to summerize, this game should run beautifully, provided you're not running a computer with a Pentium CPU, 32MB SD-RAM, an ATI Rage 4MB GPU, and Windows 95, like my first Windows computer!
One of the things I love about any game, are things that I can unlock and earn. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed has more under the hood, than you might initially think. You'll see on Steam, that there are in-fact - as of this review's post date - 50 Steam achievements to earn. To my knowledge, there are 144 career stars to earn, ranging from various game-modes, with 3 difficulties: easy, medium, and hard. There is a GP mode (Grand Prix) allowing for 10 Grand Prix Wins. Time Attack mode sports 40 tracks on which to race, 20 being entirely different. There are 160 Staff Ghosts to beat, and each one is a different difficulty of time made on each track, from Easy to Expert. The game has 28 vehicles/characters to choose from, each with Mods, totaling 168 unlockable Mods, and if that wasn't enough, they can each be leveled up 6 times, using a simple experience system. While playing the game, you will do some impressive, and not-so-impressive things, earning you stickers - there are 100 stickers to collect, 3 of which can be shown-off on your license.
As of the post date, there 2 bits of DLC available to you, currently £4.98 in total. I must admit, the DLC doesn't interest me, as I simply don't feel it justified to pay for minor content I feel might as well have just been in the game, at launch. To each their own, as they say.
I do find the graphics to be very pleasant. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed uses only DirectX 9, so don't expect flashy DirectX 11 features; this is a Sonic racing game, pure and simple.
The music gives me a sense of nostalgia, with that unmistakable, Sega sound, however, after a while, the constant "Sega sound" blaring in your ears, may start to drive you crazy, so consider turning down that music, or disabling it!
The controls are tight, simple, and easy enough to learn, provided you don't struggle with the TV remote, or putting on slippers. The wired XBOX 360 controller, works like a dream with this Sonic game, so don't hesitate to plug it and press that Start button. In-fact, it's so nice and comfy with the controller, that I've never tried it with the K&M!
You might be wondering whether the multiplayer modes are any good - well, from where I'm sitting, they are great, with all the typical game modes found in single-player, and the ability to choose the very same characters/vehicles you've been leveling up and modding, all of which adds to a brilliant experience with your family, mates, or indeed strangers.
All in all, I've had a lot of fun on this little gem, and I would certainly, strongly recommend it to any Sonic fan, or a fan of relatively old-school, kart-style racing.

This is among the top 10 games I've ever played!  It is about as close to being perfect as any adventure/puzzle game I've encountered, and I'm a huge adventure game enthusiast.  I'd describe it as a first person non-shooter adventure/puzzle game.  Where to start?
First, the story is extraordinarily well done.  I've read science fiction novels with worse stories.
You start out as a robot awakening and a voice that seems to come from all around you instructs you to get all of the "sigils" and go to its "temple".  You wander through what appear to be ancient Roman ruins finding "sigils" that are each tetrominos of some color (typically green, yellow, or red).  But... all is not as it appears.   For one thing, there are these computer terminals everywhere and somebody keeps texting you and telling you not to believe the voice (who do you trust?).  As the game unfolds, you start getting more and more clues about what's really going on.  It keeps you guessing and there are several jaw-dropping moments when you realize that something in the game isn't the way it's presented.  At the same time that it's mysterious, the story avoids "X Files syndrome".  That is, the writers actually know what's going on and everything's weird for a reason.  There are three different endings and one of them really does explain everything.  I recommend doing all three.
The puzzles are all very well done.  They always require the mind.  Sometimes, they require manual dexterity, as well.  There are "bad guys" that can get you, but this only resets to your last checkpoint.  The game is non-violent in the sense that sentient, living creatures do not get harmed at all.  Some parts are adrenaline-pumping and being reset to the last checkpoint by the aforementioned baddies can be really frustrating, but they don't actually kill you and they themselves are just dumb machines (not even intelligent robots like you).  People who are opposed to violence on moral grounds should be fine with this game.  Also, although you can freeze the baddies, and, although there are occasionally conditions under which you can even arrange to destroy some, you never actually stop them in simple ways like shooting them.
The majority of the puzzles, though, involve no baddies at all.  Much of the time, it's just you solving problems.  Even when it involves baddies, if you're trying to muscle or dex your way through, you're doing it wrong.  In every puzzle, without exception, the primary tool you use is your brain.  When manual dexterity is involved, that itself should be a synch for pros of first person shooters.  It's problem solving that counts.  While some of the puzzles are hard, the game slowly introduces you to concepts so that puzzles that seemed hard early on are child's play later.   Some of the puzzles seemed almost impossible to me, but there were solutions and, if I thought enough about the problem, I would solve them.  Although I was challenged, I never once had to go to online walkthroughs for the first two endings (though there were a few things I just didn't get for the third one).
What I particularly love about the problem solving is that, beyond thinking outside of the box, the game designers go to great lengths to create a box in your mind for you to think outside of.  Sign posts point the way to each of the sigils you have to find.  Each sigil is found within its own, enclosed area, however, who said you have to do what you're told?  (Very mild potential spoiler) things get interesting when you try doing stuff you're not "supposed" to.  There really aren't any rules, but they really make you feel like there are.  At some points, I was even uncannily scared to break them, but, then, part of the fun is not knowing whether or not you should break the rules.
Another thing I particularly like is that they don't limit you artificially as to where you can go in a lot of areas.  In fact, some areas have lots of extra scenery they didn't even need to put in, but it's just fun wandering around looking at the beautiful world (and we all want to find Easter eggs, right?  Maybe exploring will find some?  But, then again, maybe all you'll get is a nice view).  If there's some place you don't think you can go and you work really hard to go there, convinced there's an Easter egg, there might be one, but there also might not be.  What I love about this approach is that you can't make guesses about problems to solve based just on the fact that it's difficult to go somewhere or do something.  They keep you guessing.
Another thing I thought was really well done is that other robots have left QR codes on the walls.  If you point your mouse at them, your robot can read them.  The QR codes are real.  For the exception of a few Easter eggs, all of them say exactly what the game says they say if you point something like the QR reader on your phone at them.
The themes of the game are highly philosophical and existential.  If you like philosophy and intellectualism, I think you'll really like it.
I have just a few criticisms that lower this to a mere A from the A+ it could have been:
1. For one of the endings, there's some stuff you need to find that, in my opinion, were just dumb and involved such non-mental activity as looking in random places rather than actually problem solving.
2. I personally like games that do not have action or dexterity based puzzles in them at all.  This game is so unique and cool that it really could have stood on its own without any.  It bugged me that it had any at all.  If you're like me in this regard, be warned that there are some sections where, although primarily mental, you have to use your manual dexterity for maneuvering and timing, which I found annoying.  They were all doable, but some of them were frustrating (and not fun for me, since it's not what I like).  I'd go so far as to say very frustrating in a few places, though, overall, my experience with the game was great.  If I wanted dexterity based gaming, I'd play an actual first-person shooter.  This game is too special to have that kind of stuff in it.
3. On Mac OS, I had to play it in windowed mode rather than full screen.  It would get stuck on full screen, but played just fine in windowed mode.
A few tips and tricks that you'll definitely want to make use of, if you play:
1.  Go into the keyboard options and configure a few things: (a) specify a key to change to dashing mode (otherwise you have to hold down Shift to run and you need to run for the dexterity based solutions -- also be warned that major changes of location resets this), (b) learn the key to toggle between first person and third person perspectives (the game starts out in first person, but I found it easier to play in third person, because I could see what I was doing better), (c) learn the keys for using items 1 and using items 2 (I believe the default is that Q is the first use item key and E is the second).  The difference only comes up with connectors.  Q allows you to pick up and put down connectors while maintaining their connections while E often (but not always) terminates the connection.  The left mouse button is the same as E.  There was at least one puzzle that REQUIRED me to connect a connector to a bunch of different points and then move it with everything still connected and that would have been impossible with the left mouse button (and the instructions don't tell you there are two different use item keys that have different effects).
3. You can set keys for turning and looking up and down (I used the arrow keys for this).  If you do this, you can use the game mouselessly.  This was great for me, because I overuse the mouse at work and don't really like mousing.
4. The game uses autosave, which is really nice.  The thing to know is that you can go back to any of your saves (they're by date and time).  You don't just have to start from the latest save, though this is not immediately obvious (at least it wasn't for me).

Let's have a moment of silence for how deep the gamedev has sunk.
Exhale slowly. (Hopefully you are still alive.) Now take a deep breath. (Hey?)
What is a good game? Generally, you can judge whether or not you like a game by how many times you've come back to play it. For how long will RimWorld treat you?
Are you a completionist? There are five difficulty levels, which you will get plenty of opportunities to get your progress wiped, even on the lower ones. Pick HC (no saves) mode, and you'll have to get creative. Set higher difficulty. Change start location to ice thundra, where the only things to eat, apart from snow (which is not very nutritious), are various body parts of your fellow colonist, who also happens to be your gay husband (Not that you weren't "eating" them already, when things were smoother). If you want new content, or more control over difficulty, you can look into mods, of which there are plenty.
Do you like stories? Developer doesn't position RimWorld as a "story generator" for no reason. Again, just don't use saves, and  you'll be facing quite some variety. The leg of that fella, who used to carry your concrete blocks around, got torn off by an angered wolf? No worries, there's an "euthanize" button, right in the "medical operations" menu. But who's gonna carry concrete blocks now? Guess, it's gonna be that granny who can only read books and occasionally draws sceneries Bob Ross style. Oh wait, she won't, cause she's too old and incapable. Guess the winter might get pretty cold.
There are things in RimWorld not to like (although I've played alpha16 for few hours and encountered a few very nice improvements): some dare questions, some are just straight up silly (ones I don't like): the game is not perfect. But I did play RimWorld for 80 hours (during like a month of having it) in alpha15, and I'm probably gonna play it for a comparable  amount of time in alpha16 (potentially alot more); and I can't see myself not also checking the game whenever the next big patch is released.
So what am I saying here? For my money, RimWorld is one of handful of games that are actually worth buying on Steam going into 2k17. There's many things to like, so for the game to misfire on you completely, you probably would have to be a happy possessor of severe ADHD (note how long-winded I've made this sentence, so the actual ADHD people won't get through it and get offended). Buy it, then treat it as an IQ test: don't start judging it before it confirms that you are smart enough.
