Tales from the borderlands is quite possibly one of the best written games i've ever played.
I'm new to telltale games. A year or two ago, i decided to watch a playthrough of the three newer sam & max game, however, so i knew their basic writing style. I consider this even funnier than those games. Just about every character so far, save for yvette (one of your main character's friends) has had some line that made me laugh, from Vasquez's comparison of spaceships and male genetalia to Loader bot's...Loader bot. Easily one of my favorite mechanics in the game is Rhys's echo eye, which allows you to scan most gameworld objects, and often has either references to the main series borderlands games, funny descriptions, or a mixture of both.
The gameplay is...well, a point-and-click adventure game. you know what you're getting into. however, there are QTE segments in some of the more action-oriented scenes, which-surprisingly-don't suck, and manage to give you the feel of  an action game like the original borderlands(es).
I only have three complaints with the first episode-number one would be Vasquez. His voice actor is Patrick Warburton, who i know best as Brock Samson from poker night at the inventory. While i like him as a voice actor, he only has one voice, and sometimes it's a bit hard for me to remember that i'm not listening to Brock Sampson, I'm listening to Hugo Vasquez. However, after I heard his voice a few times, it became easier for my brain to diferentiate the characters. Number two is a small moment in the world of curiosities (minor spoilers, you may want to look on a paragraph down). As you go through the first time, you see some characters from Borderlands 2 and 1, seemingly mounted and stuffed on pikes. One of these is Shade. you cross the hall, hopefully listening to the commentary and scanning the characters for more good dialogue, until you come to a locked door. You're sent back through the hall, seeing that the case previously holding shade is empty. A few steps later, you get jumpscared. Now, I'll admit hear and now tat I'm a wuss, and I shouldn't have gotten asscared as i did, but it was a moment that dampened my enjoyment of the game.
My final complaint is a somewhat big one: the choice timer. At most points where you choose your action, there's a small bar ticking down.  This bar can go quite fast sometimes, and you're required to pick your option before it empties in the middle. This can be troublesome if you want to decide what to say, or in some cases do. It puts unnessecary pressure on the player, even if it can be alleviated by the dialogue following being amusing. There also tend to be dialogue while the bar is ticking down of the character you're talking too waiting for your response, so if you want to hear all the dialogue-and trust me, you do-you have to wait until the last second, which runs the risk of missing your chance to pick. a simple button to pause time so you have a chance t decide on some of the more fast moving decisions might be nice, but it's not necessary.
Overall, Tales From The Borderlands is a wonderful game, and i wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone-be they a fan of telltale, borderlands, or even neither, as the story is so far rather accessible to anyone. if i would have to rate it on an out of 10 scale...well, i wouldnt, i would rate it 10/-10, because it's just that good.

A surprisingly great game. The core gameplay mechanic is just okay, nothing too spectacular, but the variety in the levels is incredible - approximately every group of four levels has a new theme and introduces new mechanics, and even in mid-level-group, often a new monster or special block of some kind is introduced. I've played about 90% of the game at this point (excluding going back and doing "time attack", and excluding the extra boss battles that are unlocked by that), and it hasn't felt repetitive at all. Even redoing levels to get missed gems, and for time attack, is mostly not repetitive, though there are occasional gems that require precision timing to get and require restarting the level if you miss the timing, which can get tiresome.
Aside from those rare issues, the level design is wonderful too - lots of variety, and *usually* some kind of visual clues when there's a hidden passage or some kind of surprise is lurking.
On the negative side, it has some performance issues for me on the levels with lighting effects (on a Lenovo Y50, which is powerful enough to play Arkham Asylum, so getting sluggish in a 2D game is a little disappointing). I noticed it hesitates more in full screen mode than in a window, so it might be that it struggles with a 4k resolution screen.

Usually when I have a lot to write about a game or whatever I’m reviewing, it’s because some aspect of it either blew my mind or disappointed me. People are interested in what I have to say after I played Oxenfree, but it’s hard because Oxenfree is a very solid, respectable game. I recommend it to people looking for a small, good story, but that’s about all I've got.
I loved the characters. I love their interactions. I loved the effects of the dialogue on events. Oxenfree was a linear story with relationships that changed. All of the characters were frustrating teenage brats. It was wonderful.
I feel a little strange writing a review of a game without having a pedestal and a pointing stick to outline every little thing in it that blew my mind, or I hated. Oxenfree effectively used established expectations in games to create something good. It’s a solid story that used its mechanics in an interesting way. It’s a good way to show simply how these things can all be harnessed and used well.
However, it didn’t do anything that I believed was revolutionary. And while that may sound like an insult, I don’t mean it as one. Not every single game needs to revolutionize anything. I will play and enjoy every single Telltale Game, regardless of whether or not it gives me something new. Oxenfree is a good game, and that’s just fine. Give me more of this sort of ghost story. Give me more light interaction games. Give me more.
Play Oxenfree for a good ghost story with meaty characters. Enjoy it for that. And please, Night School, give me more.
4/5, highly recommended to people who like things that are good.

A simple yet decent title, Miracle Fly comes to Steam with nothing to make it stand out amongst the flurry of indie games but somehow still entertains. It looks and plays as if it should be a mobile app due to its basic level design and lack of a riveting story plot. However, the most appealing aspect about this title is that it’s easy to become good at, even for inexperienced players with the genre, and offers a good escape from all the mainstream games that are saturating the market.
Players will be happy with the selection between three magical girls, not having any kind of complex design but remaining . Each have staffs that fire in different patterns including shooting stars, a single laser beam, or three consecutive fireballs, respectively. Choosing between these three gives you slightly different play styles, but ultimately they are all similar as you propel yourself in a certain direction with each shot.
Gameplay in Miracle Fly is simplistic, requiring only a mouse to play yet still needing some time to get used to. To be able to maneuver through trap mechanisms and sluggish enemies that cling to walls and ceilings provides quite a challenge sometimes as levels get harder. This difficulty accumulates until you reach the boss levels, which are more tedious than normal areas. For those players out there that are addicted to collecting, there are also blue gems to collect within each level, equating to around 82. Fans of Steam achievements will need to hunt all of these down in order to complete the game, adding onto the replay value for some.
The graphics throughout Miracle Fly were bright, cute and basic. It really made the player feel as though this was meant to be a relaxing game to take your mind off of everything else. Not only that, but it brings a nostalgic feel to players who have played Super Mario World in the past. This is coupled with the slightly annoying music that’s reminiscent of tunes from The Sims 3, which can start to get on the player’s nerves after awhile.
Overall, Miracle Fly delivers a nice little getaway from the heavy stuff like the first-person shooter or hack n slash genres. It’s entertaining yet can still get frustrating at times as it’s easy to die when not giving full attention and can also become repetitive rather quickly.

Warning: The game is extremly difficult, the cute graphics are deceptive, if you are looking for an easy game this is not it.
Miracle fly is a puzzle platformer with the gimmick that you move your character by shooting behind you. At first the controls feel really weird, but after you get used to it they are great. If you are playing with a gamepad you have to rebind the keys because the default setup is not functional.
You can choose one of 3 witches to beat the levels, on the way through a level you want to collect gems that allow you to unlock bonus levels. Bonus levels are generally more difficult than normal levels and often require you to find a hidden secret or solve a tricky puzzle to collect all the gems.
There are a ton of levels at least 80 and the game also does a very good job of introducing cool new mechanics at a regular pace, the game never got boring for me. As i mentioned earlier, the game is extremly difficult, especially if you are trying to collect all the gems, but it is designed in a way that just completing a level is usually not a problem. If you ignore gems and a level is still too difficult for you, there is a limited option to revive.
The bossfights are difficult, all the bosses have multiple stages and the later bosses require some pattern memorization to beat them, but even if you know what to do the execution is still difficult.
Conclusion: If you like difficult platformers like super meat boy or dustforce and aren't afraid of the gimmicky movement you should give this game a try.

Some people still have the misperception that DiveKick is an extravagant joke, simple, and not an actual game. This could not be farther from the truth. DiveKick is a full fledged legitimate competitive game. It defines the concept of "easy to learn; difficult to master". There are a lot of characters and while each essentially just dives and kicks, they play so differently that you are forced to strategize.
If you love fighting games, you'll love this. If you don't love fighting games, but kind of wish you did, you will probably still love this. Also, on top of the multiplayer, it has a really amusing single player "campaign" that familiarizes you with each character.
Buy a couple of copies. Share one. Make it your go-to "I have 20 minutes to have fun" title.

Despite not really being interested in Arma after watching people play it (it seemed slow and without teamwork), I picked up Squad after watching several people stream it and I'm glad I did.  It's early access but what I've seen so far is enjoyable to play and the mechanics, whilst still not complete, are reliable and consistant.  Some early access games have very problematic gunplay (e.g. H1Z1: KotK) but not with Squad.  It's already robust enough to already have a popular competitive scene.
The community is very helpful and there isn't much trolling on the community servers I've played on due to a very high admin presence  (I play on Rusty in Places servers mainly).  I was also surprised that 95% of people play the game seriously and don't "lone wolf" or not communicate with their team mates.
Updates for the game seem quite regular (several times a year), which isn't bad considering the devs are making the game in their spare time, it's not their 9-5 day job.  They also have a very good relationship with the community which is essential for early access.
Even if you've not played a military simulator before, I'd recommend watching some game play on Twitch, you might become as hooked on the game as I have.
Explain like I'm 5: It's like CS:GO on a bigger map with multiple squads on each side, vehicles and the games last about twice as long.
So far I'd definitely recommend Squad.

Dirty Bomb is like Counter Strike meets Overwatch. Its gun play is like CS, you kill enemy within 5 shots and engagement is super fast. Mechanic wise it's like Overwatch or Team Fortress 2, each class have special abilities and weaponries to make that class's play style unique.
Upside:
It's definitely faster paced than Overwatch, which I like a lot. Unlike in Overwatch, where a super tanky front line like Reinhardt or D.va with a healer Mercy is very hard to kill. Tanky heroes in Dirty Bomb can absorb  at most 5 shots more than a normal hero. Healing is usually done between engagements, not during fights. You can't expect to tank enemy fire while healing and survive. This is the key difference Dirty Bomb has from Overwatch and TF2, which makes the game fast and fun. This mechanism also requires less effort on the player part to cooperate with one another. You can simply drop your healing station/packs or ammo station/packs somewhere and forget about it. Your teammates can still benefit from your ability.
Another great design is that support heroes are not weak on their own, they can be just as deadly as a normal attack hero, if they have good aim. This, again, lowered the requirement of teamwork which is a luxury when you play pub games. This also make people more willing to play medics, knowing that they can score just as many kills as playing other hero types.
F2P aspects in Dirty Bomb is very fair. There's nothing you can't buy with rewards from matches that you can buy with cash. Match rewards are generous. It doesn't cost much to buy heroes and load-out cards, and there's daily tasks to get even more gold.
Downside:
Some heroes are imbalanced and don't have obvious counters , like Phantom who moves fast, is invisible and quite tanky and can kill people in 2 hit with his sword.
Matchmaking is broken. It often results in stomping games. Maybe because of the lack of concurrent players.
Sniping is not as satisfying as in other games.
Hero designs are repetitive, more than half the heroes are medics. Some heroes are quite similar, like Kira and Skyhammer, Vassili and Aimee.
There could have been more heroes. 20 is not enough for a dynamic meta.
Characters lacks sophistication and are not as vivid as those in Overwatch.

Pros:
-Weapons feel very nice and ahve a good sound to them.
-The radio system used is a very nice touch since not very many games have communications between squads that is actually efficient.

-Main complaint I have is how the character moves, the movement doesn't feel very fluid and has, to me, a noticable delay for most actions. While I know this is to simulate realism, personal expereince in similar situations (I.E. Paintball and airsoft) makes it an annoyance when my character is killed because he couldn't dive for cover.
- Some of the guns have odd behaviors, where the damage of a round between burst fire and semi is different when it should be the same, the weapon doesn't  magically change its calibur of round.
-There is a very noticable lack of varity to weapon attachments, when chosing your loadout, you have a choice between a rifle with no sight attached or one with a simple red dot sight on it. For me this is annoying as I have always preferred a sight with a small amount of magnification like an ACOG or something similar.
Overall this game is a fun one but doesn't really cater to my tastes specifically. If you ahve the money I'd recommend picking it up as the communication within your squad is better than any other I've seen in a long time.

Dark Messiah is a fantasy action game dressed up like an RPG.  As the nameless one you will explore castles, crypts, caves, orc villages and more on your quest to...I am not sure what the quest is but there is plenty to do/kill along the way.  However you better love the combat (melee, archery, magic) and scenery because the RPG aspects are bland and minimal.  There is character building but it is simple and never really changes how you play the game, just makes you stronger in your particular discipline or allows you to equip special weapons.  Also the skill points to “level up” are only available by completing quests, and there is a set amount so it takes forever to build your character and you are very limited in how strong you can get.  There is inventory management, but no stores to buy and sell, and what you find is also very limited.  Want to interact with NPC characters, there is none of that either except as scripted cut scenes.  As an RPG Dark Messiah is a failure, but as an action game it’s decent but very repetitive.  I made it over half way through hoping the game would get deeper or the story more interesting, but this really is just an action game at heart, and a fairly generic shallow one at that.  If that’s what you are looking for Dark Messiah is not a bad game, however if you are looking for an RPG as I was look elsewhere.

Free or not this game is the biggest waste of time you'll ever encounter and no it's not P2W either... Here's why:
This game is great if you play it casually... meaning, you don't care about obtaining 100% of the P.O.W's or getting S ranks on every stage. This is basically the epitome of the meta in this game... Just perfect every stage and replay them to rescue prisoners (meaning, wasting your stamina)
Here's the catch, you need items in order to earn S ranks on stages... and items cost currency. So you're basically in this endless loop of replaying stages (without using items) in order to earn currency so you can buy all 4 items and then attempt to earn the S rank on the stage.
Build enough money to buy all the items, then replay the same level with all the items activated.
You proceed accordingly: You toss out a couple lower level units real fast, send in the Metal Slug characters you've unlocked and then finally throw out the tank style characters to finish the job. Guaranteed S rank.
That's all you do.
If you throw money at this game for "special units" you're a dolt... The "P2W" aspect is a myth because it's strictly a cosmetic thing. You literally can't S rank a stage without using those special items, and those special items don't cost real life money... just in game currency (which can be edited FYI)
Even if you manage to S rank a stage, some how, by not using items, it was merely luck because the game is built for you to just continue to waste your time grinding currency to basically cheat on each stage with over powered items... fairly lame game design.
I got bored after basically S ranking the first 20 stages by simply using items to win... what a joke.
If the design wasn't so lazy and involved some actual strategy intead of trying to beat a time limit by using every cheat (a.k.a. item) at your disposal... it would of been a better game... But what do you expect from some mobile junk app?
I'm actually quite upset with the developers because the Metal Slug series was always about skill, not about buying items to beat stages easily. This is just a shameless cash grab targeted at the plebs with addictive personalities...
It's just a sad state the world is becoming that people are so easily duped and idiotic to fall for this crap without seeing through it before it becomes too late. Thankfully, I've been kind enough to do the work for you...
I'm not saying to not play the game (as terrible as it is), just don't support the stupitidy of it by throwing money at it like a complete imbecile as it won't help you in the long run... I've explained the game mechanics quite clearly, the items determine a perfect win, not the paid for units.

This is one of the most compelling games I have played.  It is a mash-up of choose-your-own adventure and a little bit of the classical adventure game genre.  You play as a teenage girl introducing her new step-brother to her friends at a beach party on an abandoned island.  Things take a sudden spooky, sci-fi twist, and you must not only navigate the mystery of what is happening, but constantly interact with your NPC step-brother, your friends, and mysterious things in both meaningful, consequential ways using dialogue, as well as having chances to engage in playful, pouty, or fearful interactions during mundane events, like, like navigating the gamefield between plot events.
The voice acting is superb.  The story is outstanding, and has multiple paths and endings.  The atmosphere is a mixture of spooky, but never very scary, science fiction.  The narrative keeps the player on her toes, never quite sure what is happening, and offers some surprise challenges on an initial play-through.  This is a well-built sci-fi/horror type story that has some cool game events that test memory, logic, spatial skills, and a good understanding of some sci-fi trophes and just basic human interaction.
However, I had some issues.  The game seems to have been designed for a controller.  Mouse and keyboard function, but you'll want a controller in your hands; I played using WASD and a mouse and was disappointed.  Once I attached a controller, however, the game play became smoother, faster, and much more compelling.  While you are not obligated to use a controller, you'll be much happier for doing so.
There are some quality of life issues as well: while the game and map are small, you'll often climb hills or scale walls that take a few boring moments.  Given the mysterious nature of the game, you might find yourself reclimbing and rescaling these walls a few times looking for hints or clues, only to have found nothing and rolling your eyes as you reclimb and rescale the walls.  I never spent more than a few minutes exploring, but it gets tiresome watching a snail win a race.
Furthermore, I have encountered two irritating bugs that caused me to exit the game and repeat short sections.  Both of these involved my NPC step-brother unable to path-follow my character correctly.  The step-brother NPC, in my case, got stuck while scaling walls and there was some apparent trigger, wherein he needed to be next to the player character in order to move into a new zone.  All in all, I lost a few minutes while quitting and repeating a short section, costing me no more than five or so minutes, but it was nonetheless bothersome and detracted from the otherwise incredible mood and mystery of the game.  For me, it was like an interruption in an intense part of a movie - sure, you can rewind a few minutes, but you roll your eyes and the tension has been lost.

My favorite genre is fighting games, no series is alike, each with their own mechanics, gimmicks and unique cast of characters. Divekick takes a unique turn on the genre by being a 'gag fighting game' in a sense. Divekick take the traditional fighting game mechanics and strips it down to the basics: Mind-games, pressure, and positioning.
Divekick as all fighting games has it own gimmick which is that it is a simple, basic, striped down fighting game. Divekick is a 2 button fighter composed of 'best of 9' matches, each round is sudden death (One hit KO) and last 20 seconds.
Divekick is a gag fighter but it is also a really good fighting game, its simplist style is a great way for newcomers to learn the genre and to learn about basic mechanic in fighters such as mind-games, pressuring, positioning, and match-ups but it as simple as this game is, it also offer a great degree of high level play. Experts of the genre can still have a great time with this game and still have feeling of high leveled, competitive gameplay.
Whether you're a newcomer to the genre or a veteran, this is a great to pick up. It's is not meant to be taken as a serious game but even then there is still that bit of high leveled play that veterans like and newcomers can come to like.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #38 - Dark Messiah of Might & Magic
I played a number of the very early Might & Magic Games.  In particular I remember playing a ton of Might & Magic VI.  I remember it as a role playing game before the Heroes of Might and Magic series overshadowed it with a completely different type of gameplay and focus on strategy.
Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is a different beast altogether.  It's not a turn based strategy game like Heroes is.  But it's also not an RPG like the original games either.  This is more of an action RPG, with an emphasis on the action.    You do have some RPG aspects, for example the game provides 3 skills trees, one for melee, one for magic, and a third for other skills.  The early skills are cheap, so it's easy to dabble in each of the skill trees.  I found this to be good because I was primarily focusing on melee, but early on I found it extremely helpful to train a heal spell.  I noticed I wasn't really healing on my own, but I would slowly get mana back, so being able to trade mana for health made things a lot easier.
Even with the skill tress and RPG elements, I still consider this game pretty RPG-lite.  If you are looking for an open-world type game, this isn't for you.  The story is linear and really the game feels more like an adventure game with an emphasis on combat than a typical RPG.  This may sound like a turnoff, but the combat is actually a lot of fun.  I really liked the feel of combat.  It isn't just smashing buttons or turning on auto-attack.
Another nice aspect to this game is the interactivity with the environment.  The game encourages you to kick the crap out of your enemies, either into a fire, or into a convieniently placed spike rack, or over the edge of a railing.  In fact arguably your foot is the best weapon in the game, at least from what I saw.
Probably the most fun I had in my hour of play involved a chandelier.  I cut a rope which caused this chandelier to start swinging around.  Meanwhile I had about 4 guards chasing me.  I'd run past the chandelier while it was on it's upswing, and the guards would stupidly follow me without paying attention and get smacked as the chandelier came back down.  It was kind of ridiculous as I'd watch the guards body ragdoll it's way across the room as if it was hit by a wrecking ball.  After about 3 laps around the room, I had killed all of the guards by chandelier.
My only complaint about the game was it was rather crash prone.  It crashed 3 times on me in the hour I played.  Once it crashed on startup, once it crashed as I was quitting the game, and once it crashed in the middle of the game.   Perhaps this is from me running Windows 10 (the game came out for Windows XP).  Looking at other reviews, this doesn't seem to be a common issue, so it may just be something specific with my setup.
Overall, the combat alone is enough to make this game fun, and to earn my recommendation.  I did not check out the multiplayer version of this, so my entire review is only based on the single player game.

Overview
By far, the most fun MOBA I've tried. I only have about 30 hrs on the game as of this review, so this is more first/second impressions than anything in depth. Regardless of it's flaws, it's a heck of a fun little game.
Pros
- Last hit gold gain is shared among your team. No more fighting your own teammates.
- Harsh penalties for leavers, afkers, and anyone with toxic behavior. As a result, what little I've interacted with the community, it seems helpful and nice.
- All heroes/champions unlocked at the start.
- The soft pay walls are solely cosmetic.
Neutral
- You will need to spend some time playing to start to build gear (customize recipes to fit your playstyle) or acquire "pets" (couriers). It doesn't feel restrictive to me. For example, I've played maybe a half-dozen matches tonight learning how to use a new hero--I don't feel like I need specialized recipes at this stage. I'd like to tweak things to fit the hero and how I'm playing him, but it will be a while before I feel like I've learned the hero well. I should have enough materials to tweak recipes then. In other words, the pacing seems right: by the time you feel confident with a hero, you'll have enough materials to kit him out for the most part.
Cons
- It's in beta, or feels like it still is. There are some bugs, frame drops, and sometimes uncooperative servers (which drop you). Thankfully, I haven't been dropped in a week or two, but frame drops still happen.
- Low population playerbase. It will take quite a bit of time to match if you want to play people and not bots. Also, because of the low population, the likelihood of getting skewed matches is higher. From what I understand, they've tweaked the matchmaking to make it the best they can--the lack of people is really the problem.
- Leavers. I'd say maybe half my games have ended 5v5. The most frustrating is when someone DCs before the match can even get underway.

By the way, even if this was made by the guys that made Serious Sam, this game is the opposite of a non-brainer. There's also philosophy and reading, lots of it, though its not necessary to solve the puzzles or advance.

-Hilarious take on choice based adventure games
-Good use of the Borderlands setting and characters
-Great voice acting
Cons: -No Clap Trap

If Pandora is such a terrible place, why would anyone want to live there? As Sasha tells Rhys near the end of the first episode, "It doesn't mean I like it!" Indeed, Pandora, a backwater planet full of bandits and mutants, savage wildlife, and lost alien civilizations, would rank low on the list of 'best places to raise a family', but to visit? It is never boring.
It would be a mistake to think that just because Tales from the Borderlands has stripped away your guns that the game is now tame or lacks the trademark insanity that made the shoot and loot RPGs smash hits. Playing as both Hyperion company man Rhys and Pandoran native con woman Fiona, players get to set out on an adventure for fortune mostly free of the bleak doldrums that have typified TellTale games since the company's popular Walking Dead series. Rhys runs like crazy from bandits that want to kill him just for breathing air, given Hyperion's reputation on Pandora. Fiona has to haggle unsavory types in backroom bar deals without blowing her cover. They are not nice people, but that doesn't mean they're not one note characters. Depending on how you play them, Rhys may either be a ruthless business man willing to sacrifice his friends or show surprising loyalty that hopefully won't come back to bite him later. Ditto for Fiona, who as a Pandoran native is used to taking what she needs to survive Borderlands' nasties. If the situation requires her to play the part of a psycho, she'll happily say, "YOU ARE MY MEAT BICYCLE!" without a second's pause.
They are brought to life by the amazing duo of Troy Baker and Laura Bailey. Troy Baker, better known as the Joker in Batman: Arkham Origins and Booker DeWitt in Bioshock: Infinite, makes Rhys both slimy and funny, a guy you love to see win when the chips are down and laugh at when things don't go his way. Laura Bailey is no stranger to puckish rogues, being one of the voices for player characters in Saints Row the Third and Saints Row IV, and imbues Fiona with the right amount of swagger you'd expect from somebody who has to live on Pandora. Rounding out the company of characters include Rhys's best friend and accountant, Vaughn, and Fiona's gun loving sister Sasha. While not as well rounded as Rhys and Fiona, they do serve a useful role in seeing what makes the protagonists tick. Special kudos to Patrick Warburton as Rhys's evil boss Vasquez, a guy you hope gets to eat a bullet before the end.
In a story that features cameos from other Borderlands noteworthies (including one particular vault hunter if you caught the episode title), the laughs come fast and furious. Well written throughout, the best stuff happens after Rhys and Fiona meet up and start contradicting each other's story to say what really happened. So not only do you get choice based adventure gameplay, you're dealing with two unreliable narrators who are both lying to make themselves look better.
The game isn't without its weak points. The humor takes time to get going and occasionally falls flat on its face, but most of the time it does hit. Unlike some people, I missed Clap Trap, Borderlands' robot mascot, and hope he makes an appearance in later episodes. If you play for the puzzles, expect none except for the choices you make. An inventory based puzzle game this is not. The cursor is frustratingly hard to see when it's not hovering over a hot spot, making quick dialogue choices a chore until you get somewhat used to it. Just as in Walking Dead, the game relies on quick time events to handle the action, which will either be fun or frustrating depending on how you feel about them. Finally, the game teases unlocks for Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel but has not shipped with them, yet.
Even if you've never had an interest in Borderlands in your life, Tales from the Borderlands is a wild send up of TellTale's previous choice based adventure gameplay. Light on puzzles and long on laughs and decision making, it's worth going back to Pandora. Again.

This game deserves a 10/10.

For fans of the Mario Kart series, you will not be disappointed.
Most clones of Mario Kart tend to be pretty terrible. Nearly unplayable, with ugly graphics, horribly designed stages, uninteresting characters, and just... not very fun to play in the slightest. They tend to be just quick cash ins on the Mario Kart crowd. Sega's latest crossover extraveganza doesn't fail to please. While, at the core, it may look like just your typical Mario Kart clone, it is so much more. Not only do you race by car, but mid-race, you could find your car transforming into a boat or plane.
There's a single player campaign mode that allows you to play through a ton of challenges. Drifting, tank fights, flying through rings, and standard races. There's plenty to see and do in All-Stars Racing Transformed. There's a huge variety of weapons at your disposal to take out the competition and while not as interesting as those found in the Mario Kart series, they are fun to use and do the job. With 20 tracks (21 if you count the DLC track) and a currently still ever growing roster of characters, the fun is endless.
Did I mention the online is fantastic, as well? Because it is. It's your standard online with 5 different game modes, but there is absolutely no lag, which is always a plus.
So, if you're a fan of Mario Kart and also love SEGA and their IPs, you'll love this game.

I echo the views of those who say this is a game of two halves - one consists of pure exploration, and the other consists of time-sensitive first-person platforming.
The first game is magnificent. The sense of scale NaissanceE provides, the sheer immensity of its environments with seemingly endless verticality is unrivalled by any other game I've ever experienced. The world is utterly alien, and so completely sterile and lifeless, I actually began to hope I'd make human contact. The unique mechanic of manually forcing the player character to breathe during periods of strenuous activity, and the yelps and periods of recuperation required after a long fall, act to remind the player that they are controlling a human body, and that there is nothing else in the world which bears this sense of organic fragility. I began to make up my own story as to what I was doing in this world - I, who had been born, traversing a world without birth or death. Who made this world? How did I get so out of place as to arrive here? The game provides no story, no explanation, no end and no beginning, beyond that which you want to assign it. I thought it was superb.
Unfortunately, the second game comprises tedium and frustration as you jump from moving platform to moving platform, punctuated by regular trips, falls and checkpoint-reincarnation. Additionally you will regulaly fumble about in pitch black, only knowing when you've hit a wall because the game has stopped the head-bob animation, and watch in dismay as the aforementioned sense of scale is transformed into stifling claustrophobia.
Fortunately the first game is much, much longer than the second, which makes NaissanceE easy to recommend, but I never actually finished the second game - I had to watch the last minute of gameplay via YouTube as I simply could not pull off the ridiculous jumps required. Quite why they thought it would be a good idea to send off this otherwise pensive, almost zen-like game of exploration with a swift series of firecracker bangs is beyond me. It leaves a sour taste in the mouth after an otherwise sumptuous meal.

NaissanceE and Kairo share many stylistic and gameplay similarities.  Both prominently feature first-person exploration of vast, compelling brutalist architecture, monochromatic visuals (frequently, but not always greyscale), a profound sense of isolation, a deliberately ambiguous plot and practically-undefined protagonist, as well as an overarching dreamlike quality to the entire experience.
Where Kairo is primarily exploration and puzzle-solving with some occasional light platforming, NaissanceE is primarily exploration and platforming with some occasional light puzzle-solving.
Some of the setpieces in NaissanceE are truly impressive and encourage stopping to just look around and take in the sights.  While you're occasionally dropped into somewhat vast and seemingly open-ended locations, it's a fairly linear experience with defined periodic auto-saves.  (One minor annoyance - you'll re-trigger the auto-save right after you re-load a checkpoint which caused a second or two of hitching on my system.)

Strife, let me tell you about this game. It is a great, free, and easy moba for people to the genre (ofc im not new). League of Legends and Dota 2 are the casual mobas that have heavy emphasis on farming and balance in the lanes from early game to late game and both have bosses whose death has plenty reward. Strife however, seems to lack the farming potential from dota and lol because well, no offense, but the items are not too important. Most damage items only give you around 50 damage(from when im playing) when you already have a hundred damage in very early parts of this game. Ganking isnt too easy unlike Heroes of the Storm because keep your distance from a person and your regen will heal you back in no time. Stuns and slows dont arent effective either compared to these other games because the stuns are too short to buy enough time for follow up damage and to ensure a kill, and some slows are too weak or do not last long. And one more thing, the hp points players receive very early are too much compared to the damage of the spells most heroes have. It will take around 2 people to ensure a kill on a regular person, but that shouldnt happen. Most of the time gankers should have an easy time solo killing but in this game  that is just not the case. Forgive me for my complaints, but s2 games, if you put these things into account, this will be a great moba. WorldCreator is an okay tool. It has some issues which make it very difficult to use. The biggest problem is it's quite crash-prone. For seemingly no reason, the program will crash, and your work is lost.
The image overlay also cannot be made transparent. You can't see your isolines through the overlay image. There is no shortcut for toggling overlay image visibility; you are forced to move your mouse to the menus and select "hide" or "show."
WorldCreator is quite clunky. It's often difficult to tell if the render is even working. When you click generate, the progress bar may remain blank and it will appear as though nothing is happening for varying periods of time dependent upon the map size, isolines, post-processing operations, etc.
Generally speaking, I don't recommend WorldCreator. There is a better alternative - WorldMachine. It is not on Steam, but it is a superior product overall. I have never had it crash, even when working with a lot of different operators and a large resolution heightmap.

I will say this off the bat: This game is more of an interactive movie than it is a game. Although it's geared to both Borderlands and Telltale fans, most Borderlands fans will be disappointed. There's hardly any segments where you can shoot people, and when there is, it's a bit clunky. After all, it is a point and click game. However, Telltale fans may be disappointed, because there's less interaction than say in The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us. I'm both a Borderlands and Telltale fan and I enjoyed it immensely.
In case you don't know, this is an episodic based game. From what I can tell, each episode is about 2 - 2 and a half our long, and there are going to be 5 of them. Using math, that means each episode costs $5 (not counting the Steam sales), which means you're practically watching a full-length movie for only $5. Telltale usually takes around 6 weeks to release each episode, but usually there's a huge gap in between the first and second episode, so watch out for that. You might want to wait until all episodes are out and the game is 90% off.
The story of this game is great. As I've hinted at previously, this does feel like a movie, and has the storyline of one. You play as Rhys, a company man who works for Hyperion, the big bad company if you will. You're a weakling, so if you try to be a badass it usually doesn't work, and the results are funny. You also play as Fiona, who's a bandit (and more of a badass than Rhys). However, both of the characters don't like to use guns, so don't expect first person shooter action. What I liked a lot in this is that killing people is more realistic than in the Borderlands games, so even a single bullet is lethal to everyone in your group.
Now, the gameplay: there isn't much of it. Again, it is a point and click game, so most of the gameplay consists of walking around and clicking on things. However, there are a bunch of action segments (DO NOT use an Xbox controller to play this unless you want a really hard time trying to "click" things in life-or-death situations. The buttons are colorful, though.) This game does contain some looting. You can pick up money and other items which can help you later in the game, like buying different items. There are a couple of segments where you actually can walk around and loot cash and other things, which are interesting. It's a linear game, so you have a set amount of items you can take and use on a set amount of things. If you're a Borderlands fan, you probably won't enjoy this, because there's hardly any Borderlands gameplay here.
Overall I loved this game, being a big fan of both Telltale's games and Borderlands. The story is great, the gameplay is interesting, and this time around a Telltale game actually felt like the 2 and a half hours were worth the 5 dollars. If you're a Borderlands fan, I wouldn't recommend it unless you're not looking for shooter action. If you're a Telltale fan, I strongly recommend this since it's Telltale's best piece of work so far, but there are less story-influencing interactions. Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5 out fo 10.

As a beginner to landscape art, I am going to share a few thoughts on World Creator after having used it for some time now. Hopefully this will be useful for beginner/enthusiasts as well as some more professional developers looking into whether this is worth buying or not.
At first glance, this software appears quite daunting compared to the other node-based alternative (Which I have spent 100s of hours in - if not 1000s). But it isn't quite as complex as it first appears. Personally, I started with the presets and after using them I cannot emphasize enough the value of the preset library. The competitor does not supply anywhere near such a vast amount of preset landscapes or previews of what the different filters do. I found myself scrolling through the vast library of presents to find something similar to my landscape, then loaded it and looked into the filters/settings and built my own based on it. I imagine most beginner/enthusists will only need the presets to make fantastic terrain.
Another aspect of this software which really stands out is the erosion. After using the node-based alternative for all my projects, I found that the erosion was "realistic" but too predictable. World Creator's erosion is HIGHLY advanced in comparison. In contrast to a couple erosion methods, World Creator has over a dozen (and probably 2 or 3 dozen) erosion methods with not only material loss but material gain (deposition). The results are phenominal! Just check out the demo and prepared to be impressed.
Although I could go into many other great filters and selectors, the other part of this software that I found invaluble is the isolines. The alternative has a custom drawing environment, but this is far easier to work with. If you have a general landscape design, all you need to do is draw it. It's so simple and yet you get exactly what you want. This really makes designing any landscape you want (or your employer wants) as easy as drawing a few lines.
Now of course there are some drawbacks...
Unfortunately, World Creator does not have an overview view and the ability to shift the fractal plain. Unlike the alternative, it appears that the landscape is generated in one shot. You can't see what the fractal would create outside your area of interest. This was something I really liked about the alternative software. I can literally pan around the "world" looking for the perfect mountain. Unfortunately, not so in World Creator.
The other serious drawback I find is the single core processing. This is huge... I have a machine that has 8 cores and I can only use one of them. It makes processing times much longer. Its definitely not a deal-breaker but I really hope the devs change that. I don't believe any other 3D modeling/design software is single core. ;)
Overall, World Creator is excellent at what it does. It is a fantastic tool for realistic terrains. While the Steam version's 4096x4096 max resolution restriction is a bit coarse, it is definitely good enough for background terrains and can be used cleaverly for foreground. You also can't beat the price!

It is passing strange to realize that this came from the same studio that gave us Serious Sam, which I loved, but is so different in tone from The Talos Principle.
Serious Sam was a throwback to the times of the first Doom and the original Duke Nukem, when FPS were run and gun fests, and fun was measured in number of enemies slagged per minute. It had a story, it had lore, but it was all about explosions and the shooting. And then came The Talos Principle.
The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game. You play a robot, making your way through what seems to be a simulation, solving fiending puzzles and unlocking sigils for some mysterious purpose. That's the set-up, and very little more is communicated about the backstory.
The tone is difficult to define. The game does not attempt to drill any lessons into your head, just raise questions about sentience and sapience, about free will vs predestination, about faith and religion. Throughout the game, there are terminals (which you don't have to read, but you should) that rarely have anything to do with progression in the game, but have various excerpts from books, e-mails, diaries and papers, but none of which try to convince you what is true and what isn't. It's very well done. There are audio diaries as well, very melancholy, but so well acted and written that even though you've already realized what's going to happen when they wind down, it's still heartbreaking.
Something else that the terminals allow is for your character to have a "voice", as it communicates with an entity in the terminals, allowing you to voice your own opinion about what's going on. And there are also paint buckets allowing you to leave your own messages on the walls of the world (albiet canned responses from a number of very appropriate-sounding lines).
The graphics are good, though the "glitches" that appear to show that this is a simulation grates a bit. I know why it's there, but it's annoying. Some parts are better than others, particularly near the ending. Sound design is also good, though I must confess that I preferred the music near the end more than in the main game. It's very soothing and soft, but I liked the tone of the music near the end a lot more.
The gameplay itself is pretty good. As I said, the puzzles are fiendish, and you can definitely feel a progression as you head towards the Red and Gray levels. I personally hate the ones that depend on dodging mines, but I guess YMMV.
It's a good and clever game, which could have very easily been a Portal clone but instead did its own thing which is for the best. The tone elevates the game enough that I did not think of it as being analogous to Portal until the very end.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a new beginning for Wolfenstein. It's an attempt to make the story work, the gameplay modern and breath new life into the grandfather of FPS games.
I couldn't tell you a thing about the story. I don't remember anything other than something about Nazis, buildings and a guy called Deathshead? Basically the Nazi's win WWII and you're living in a world where they Nazi regime has total dominance of the world. You're a part of the resistance movement. The story is pretty forgettable but they do a decent job making the characters in it likable. There's a homebase you return to where you can talk to the resistance members and they all have personality and flair to them. There's a few moments in the story where you get a chance to make some choices and it does affect the storyline in some ways; characters can die, settings can change. The main character, BJ, has some good writing for him but overall, the story feels like it's here to drive the gameplay.
There are some great setpieces - there's a level on a giant bridge which really stood out to me in particular - but the story doesn't really connect all these missions well enough. It feels a bit disjointed at times but it does create moments where the gameplay can take over.
And the gameplay is what kept me here. The shooting feels great; it's violent, it's over the top and it feels really solid. Nearly every weapon feels like it has weight, like it has killing power and you've got a large arsenal to choose from. You'll get things like pistols and shotguns, to stranger things like laser rifles and welders. You can upgrade your guns through combat, encouraging you to mix up playstyles and try different weapon combinations. Dual wielding increases firepower but decreases accuracy; you'll want to think of what your fighting against and how best to counter it.
The artstyle/art direction is really great- the 60's sleek design meshing with the Nazi stone architecture creates a lot of great clashing moments of style. A lot of this game still looks gorgeous, violently so at times; you'll see death camps, giant robots, ruined cities and it all looks believable and never feels like a huge shift in tone.
I ended up really enjoying The New Order - more than I thought I would. If it's on sale, I'd say to pick it up. It's really fun and mindless and honestly, sometimes that's just what you need. The gameplay is solid and the story is engaging enough to keep you interested for the length of the campaign. It's not something that I think you'd be revisiting but for the 10-12 hours you might get out of it, I think it's worth it.

Is Talos Principle the best puzzle game ever made? In other words, is it better than Portal? That is probably the question that is on your collective minds.
Yes and no. It is a lot more cerebral than Portal. Portal was much more based on fast-paced action and timings, in Talos you can take your time. There is a very nice difficulty curve to this game. At times it feels like you've done many similar puzzles in a row and it gets a bit stale and then the game immediately throws something hard and different your way. Some of the puzzles are ridiculously hard, some require (literal) out of the box thinking, some are trying to misdirect you from the real solution.
There is a heavy story element to the game which I personally didn't care about. It is a nice addition and probably many people liked it. I only cared about the puzzles and sharpening my own logical thinking skills.
Technically this game was refreshingly good. The graphics are nice for a puzzle game, the voice acting and writing is top notch, I didn't remember seeing any glitches and I had zero crashes. Very rare in todays world, indeed.

Naissance is a first person exploration/platforming game that really tests your dexterity, patience and above all else, it tests your mind.
As a game, naissance will throw a myriad of light shows and spectacular vistas at the player, the scenery here
is some of the most atmospheric you're likely to come across in any game to date. These vistas are seriously grand in scale, traveling through massive industrial emptiness to an abstract and claustraphobic dome that seems to defy the very laws of physics, the game will test your perception and direction as light flickers through shapes and obtuse angles resulting in, at times a very disorientating and uncomfortable experience. Atmosphere is the strongest element in Naissance, it reminds me of the cold confines of H.R.Gigers biomechanical art, it also reminds me of Blade runners dystopian cityscape and Halo's towering architecure. I can certainly see the influence on Naissance.
Platforming and exploring, plus a few puzzles here and there is really all this game is about. Its the world you inhabit that, to me personally, is one of the most interesting and original ive had the pleasure of witnessing. The gameplay revolves around moving through what can only be described as some sort of machine, from pont A to B there will be some tricky platfoming and the odd mind bendingly strange puzzles to contend with, this is the pattern each chapter takes, you are clueless as to why you inhabit this world and the story never explains itself beyond what you interpret yourself. The first half of the game is a lot more open than the second half, which places you in smaller confines with considerably harder platforming sections. These section will frustrate the player and the checkpoint system is far too spread apart resulting in some annoying repetition. All in all though, Naissance is certainly unique and definitely warrants a journey into its hautingly vast abyss.
+ Amazing and atmospheric world
+ Simple and responsive gameplay
+ Interesting platforming and puzzles
- Checkpoint system is poor
- Non existent story
- Navigating world can be frustrating.
Overall:
8/10

A very nice animated racing game for those who always liked the genre, great tracks, great music, and a nice crew of characters to pick from.
The gamplay is easy to pick up for its simplicity, but as you go on playing, you discover there are some tricks to improve the general driving, like doing pirouettes on the air to boost up, finding shortcuts on the tracks, and mastering the items to attack other characters, and for those who seek a challenge, the time trials against developers' "ghosts" are really hard to complete. There's also an online mode where you can play with strangers or with friends, unfortunately, time has rendered online lobbies kinda lonely, and you'll find yourself waiting more than what you are willing to for a race that lasts barely a couple minutes, there's also local mode if you have several controllers.
For those long time fans of SEGA, there are many references to previus titles, like Jet Set Radio, Space Channel 5, Wreck-it Ralph (oddly enough) and more; so it doesn't feel like just a re branding of a generic racing game, but as a part of the world this company has created over the years.
The music is nice, upbeat and suits the levels, there's an anouncer with a very loud and over the top acting who will inform of the events during the races, it can be turned off for those who find it annoying, and each character has an unique song for their All Stars power, which makes it more enjoyable when you get to do it, and very frightening when you hear another player getting it.
Overall, this is a very nice game to play either with friends or alone, it offers casual fun and big challenge as you progress, a perfect gift for a young kid and a completely non-shaming acquisition for a hardcore gamer fan of the genre

This game was released September 30, 1999, and over 13 years later they re-released it on steam with a new expansion. They are STILL releasing expansions for this soon-to-be 18 year old game. If that alone doesn't tell you how fun this game is, then nothing will.
But if for some reason you do need more information, I'll try and help with that too. If you played this game earlier in life and loved it, then get it; it's got everything the original game has plus new civilizations, maps, units, etc, etc. If you haven't played this game before, then I still highly recommend it. It's got a ton of great game modes for different play styles, a great selection of world civilizations to choose from, multiplayer (<-which I have yet to have a problem with), steam workshop, and a bunch of great ways to just kill your enemies (use a couple onagers and a wall to slaughter a contingent of infantry, use trebuchets to carve a path through the trees to kill your brother while he struggles to fend off a horde of untinking AI, destroy your brothers docks in an island match so he can't sail his war elephants over to kill you, get pushed into a tiny corner of the map with access only to trees and still somehow come back to kill everyone).
The game also teaches great micromanaging skills. It teaches inflation, start the game paying 14 gold for a hundred stone, and end the game paying 700+ gold for one hundred stone. It teaches the importance of manipulating your enemies' religious beliefs to get them to do what you want, and it teaches the uses of exploiting religious relics fro monetary benefit.
This game also taught me to respect the Eastern Roman Empire. The double walls of Constantinople will rise again!

Overall this is a very good game, but if you are not into puzzles it's not for you.
The biggest flaw of the game is that the puzzles feel like a chore after a while, but the theme of the game makes up for it. It is a challenge to test your faith, and you're supposed to feel dread over the many many challenges. I recommend taking a break of a few weeks in between playing it so it feels fresh.
Flaw number 2 is the story of the game. Most of it is delivered via texts you find on computers. There is at least one in every world and 2-3 texts every time. After a hvile i gave up on reading them because it took too long and didn't make sense if you couldn't remember the ones you read weeks ago. The other part is delivered via the persons (or are they persons???) in the game. None of them makes much sense and I for one have no idea what is really going on yet. I plan on one day sitting down and reading all those texts through, but man... I must be really bored on that day.
The 3rd flaw is the messengers who can help you if you can't figure out a puzzle. You have a limited amout of time that you can use them. When you use one, you can't be sure that they actually tell you what you want and you have so few of them that you feel cheated when you don't get the information you need. They also take a lot of time to get, which is just annoying.
The 4th and final flaw of the game is tetris puzzles. Everytime you complete a puzzle, you get a tetris block. You need to arrange them in a certain pattern to proceed. Kind of like a mini-game. But it feels out of place and uneccesary.
Now to the positive stuff :)
-  The puzzles are hard (which is good) and sometimes they feel impossiple. If that happens, stop playing and come back the next day and you will see it in a new light. It works for me.
-  One of the people who talk to you is a girl who drops some very interesting monologues about life (she the one who talks in the trailers)
-  Elohims voice is what you expect from a god
-  Letting the snake into your heart
-  The gliches in your field of view to remind you that there is something wrong with everything
-  The QR-codes from other people that have come before you. Some of them are very unsettling
-  The existential dread you feel from time to time
-  I am scared of Elohim and what he will do to me if I let the snake into my heart
The gameplay is what makes this game good. The puzzles are well-crafted and I haven't seen anything like them before. Plus, you could probably write a looong article about the texts and dialogue and what they mean. The creators have definetely put a lot of work into this.

I pledged to this game sometime in early 2014, I was expecting nothing more than a nice little management game with a sci-fi setting.  What I wasn't expecting was a game that has expanded into probably the deepest and most engrossing simulation I've ever had the pleasure of playing.   The game plays as a sci-fi, firefly inspired 'dwarf fortress' style management/simulation game with heavy storytelling elements.  You initially play as a small group of survivors from the space ship equivilant of a cruise ship you were all aboard that has gone down, you crash land in escape pods on a rimwolrd and are tasked with building a colony to survive.  You don't control the colonists directly bu task them jobs and 'occupations' and they will go about their way.
Each update brings an incredible amount to the game, There's always a new interesting mechanic that forces new tactics and new storytelling elements. I've never seen a developer as involved with the community, He's constantly active on public media and often responds to feedback.  I remember once someone made a request on the subreddit for the idea of rescuing allies and giving them medical treatment without a negative penalty, Tynan agreed and released a patch the day or so after.
If your looking for a deep management/simulation or want to try Dwarf Fortress but are intimidated by the interface, this is the game for you.  Up there with Kerbal Space Program as the best early access games ever.

Originally I was quite reluctant to buy the game as it comes with a hefty price tag for an alpha/early access game and the original reviews weren't that great (I think I added Oort Online to my wishlist a few days after it was announced on Steam). Well, over the Christmas period I felt like treating my curiousity and I have to say I did not regret it. I must admit I was originally sceptical about the performance (i.e. the portal system) and of course, knowing other sandbox minecraft-like games, about sharing a world and having half finished builds and destroyed landscapes (I always hated people that filled up holes they dug with random blocks they could find and eventually some parts of the land looked like a waste dump). Needless to say, Boundless does not have that. The plot-system works perfectly and I have to say the amount of levels and available plots is already well balanced. If you build outside your plots then within a few hours (was it 8 or 12?) the world will be regenerated. It's genius! And different players' plots close together are automatically considered a settlement/town and the one with the biggest build gets to be the mayer. Really cool idea!
Performance so far is very good, despite being in an Alpha state, I rarely have connection issues (shortly after Winter sale started, I did not get one stable connection, happens to the biggest companies, nothing I worried about). Anything else is fluent and without issues.
I particularly like the design and the graphics. It's cute but not too cute. Some of the animals and hostile units are well designed, though I have to admit currently I have only seen 4 different ones (each strength of that mob has a new design, similar to other games, so technically that makes it 20?)
Only being in Alpha status (can't repeat that enough) but some people seem to be able to build amazing statues, houses, palaces, mansions, plazas and and and... the game offers to help with anyone's ideas and fantasies. I wonder how much more is to come at release. Also a great idea was introducing comets.
A few things that I would like to see introduced:
- currently there is no "liquid" system. Lava and water are fix blocks, can't be transferred, can't be used in any way. Some people built amazing places, but it looks like they basically built them below the water level in order to be able to have fountains and waterfalls in their builds. A system similar to Minecraft would be quite a bonus.
- more entities, the 4 animals plus the road runner do get a bit boring after some time and they are basically everywhere
- I also hope that entities will eventually learn that they should not walk into water or lava otherwise they die. Currently they just graze like everywhere else, can't breath and drop dead.
What I don't like:
- Some resources seem impossible to find. I have even followed guides in the forum where to find certain high profile resources like gems or titanium and gold. But in the past few weeks since I started playing (196 hours according to Steam), I have basically found 5 resources of Titanium, no gems whatsoever (other than the ones the high leven mobs drop or are in comets since the last update).
- In combination with my first dislke, some items are just horribly expensive to build. As an example, I have not found any gems yet, however it needs 2 refined gems blocks for a tool or weapon. These two refind blocks consist of 1 compact gem block each. Again each compact gem block consists of 10 raw gems. So 20 raw gems for 1 weapon or tool (there are alone 4 tools if I recall properly, and there should be 2 weapons at least). And again, in 196h I have not found one gem by mining. Apart from the fact that I don't understand why I first have to compact a gem (makes no sense, by the way) and then refine it. One step would be more than enough.
- Too many different sorts of coal (what for?): soft coal, medium coal, hard coal. I think that's a bit over the top. One single type of coal would suffice, in my opinion.
- I'd also say the skill tree and points need revising, but then again, it's not finished yet, so during Alpha I can live with that. Some skills are a bit difficult to understand and the description doesn't really tell what the skill does. I.e. it took me over a week to find out that glass is a skill to learn but not in the skill tree where I was looking. It's confusing.
One thing I find particularly strange are the people playing. Whilst I had some really stupid questions in the forums and great support and helpful and well meaning people. It's a complete different story when logging in. People don't talk much to each other, even saying hello, often I would get a hello back but then people just ignore others again. For a MMO a bit weird.
Also, and I think that's the most annoying part: I do understand everyone is quite eager to have a pretty build and as it is with other games: not having it messed up by others. But to be quite honest, some players take it to a whole new level. I walked through settlements with signs "don't mine here", "don't take this here", "don't build here", "ask before you build". I don't get this. If you don't like playing with other people, why bother buying a MMO? Makes no sense to me. It's a community game, so if you don't like being around others, you probably shouldn't buy this game but stick to single-player games.
I can't wait what's up next and what the next update will bring.

Updating my review of this game, now that I've sunk a ton of hours into it.
First off, I'll have to get this out there right away: the game is pay-to-fun. Not necessarily pay-to-win, as you can win quite a bit as a free player. The biggest problem in the game that I currently see is the fact that free players don't get nearly enough robits from crates. It is possible to build a decent bot as a free player, but it'll take you several hours worth of grinding, and you won't be able to access superpowered modules easily.
In short, the game requires that you buy premium to enjoy it, which really sucks. Freejam needs to remove the stupid 33% recycle rate for new players, it's bad enough that they only get up to 4 components in crates.
-
So, let's say that you really like the game and buy premium. I would have advised against it, but... hey, what's done is done. At least the game is enjoyable now, right?
Well... no, not really, and here's why. Freejam likes to update their game every now and again, and almost every update brings new balance changes. This ends up doing three things to the game: killing the current meta, establishing a new meta, and breaking a lot of peoples' bots.There is no consistent experience -- what worked yesterday might not work today, and what was garbage yesterday is now overpowered and appears in every match by the dozen.
As if that wasn't bad enough, Freejam seems to also be discouraging creativity. The Community Robot Factory, a place that allows players to purchase designs from other players, seems to be challenging building from scratch as the primary way to obtain a robot. Thusly, with every meta shift comes a slew of identical clones, with seemingly everybody attempting to jump on the meta bandwagon before it shifts again. And whoever rejects the established meta gets damned to Robocraft hell, along with electroplates, aerofoils, and missile launchers.
-
So in conclusion of this review, the way Freejam promotes their product is not as their motto, "Build. Drive. Fight." would suggest. Rather, the motto should be "Pay. Copy. Repeat."
Pay. In order to enjoy the game and access the full experience (without spending 6 months grinding), you absolutely must buy premium. Freejam isn't even trying to be subtle anymore, their game is pay-to-fun and they know it.
Copy. Creativity is for noobs, and homemade bots are all terrible. Instead, you must follow after the established meta like a good little sheep, no matter how lackluster and uninspired the designs are.
Repeat. Once a new update hits, which will undoubtedly break all the robots that you've worked so hard to buy, you will need to repeat the entire cycle again. Pay for more months of premium, wait until the builders come up with a new meta, and then follow it some more.
The entire cycle repeats itself endlessly, leaving at best a dull experience that is only comparable to watching a grandfather clock tick back and forth, slowly losing momentum until it eventually dies.
What I've stated are just the big issues that I see in Robocraft currently. There's loads of other problems right now as well; insect legs don't work, plasma deals too much DPS, the current league MMR system is trash, camera controls negate piloting skill ceilings, players are dissatisfied with the Megabots' return; the list of grievances goes on and on.
So what does this mean for new players?
Well... to be blunt, don't waste your money or time. I don't even play Robocraft for fun anymore, I feel obligated to play it since I've purchased lifetime premium. If you're into interesting action games that are free to play, you should definitely turn away from this one.
You have been warned.

This may actually be my first review on Steam - in the 8 years I've been active here. I'm an old-timer... from the late 70s, and I have a pretty long and diverse Steam catalog - in addition to owning a ton of games across console platforms. My kids were the ones who got me interested in games like Minecraft. So this is where I begin my Boundless review.
Being completely bored of Minecraft, and hoping for something "more", I branched out. Boundless was something I randomly found on Steam - and decided to go for it. And I'm SO glad I did. The level of immersion, the gameplay, the graphics and attention to audio detail & fidelity... all AMAZING, and done professionally. Boundless has sucked me in BIG TIME. Way, way more than Minecraft or something like Creativerse could ever offer.
I'm still relatively new to the game, having logged in 6-7 hours so far. But those hours have been so entertaining and rewarding. There is always an Objective to meet, a Level up allowing new skills, etc. So gratifying and with great pacing. Understood that this game is still in Early Access, but the amount of things that you can do right now is SO completely worth it.
I began not having a clue what I was doing... slowly learning as I went. Currently, my character is holed up in a cavern that I created, overlooking a bog at the side of a huge mountain. There is flora and fauna aplenty... Awesome eye-candy at 4K resolution. For me, the best part of this game is its ability to easily suck you into the entire experience. it's all about immersion. The attention to detail and visual/audio fidelity is what really makes the game shine through.
Best moments so far... Mining deep into a mountain, I occassionally heared what I thought was thunder, followed by an occassion explosion. After a couple of times, I decided to check it out. Running back to the entrance of the mine and looking up to the sky, as I heard another roaring sound. To my amazement. there it was. A meteorite.. streaming down to the plant's surface. Getting louder and louder. I watched it crash not far from my "claimed" bog house (was very nervous for a few moments). So cool. And just like that, it was time to put the mining hammer away and explore the new meteor site! While I won't tell you what happened next, I will say that the subsequent moments were completely unexpected, nail-biting and just completely cool.
Again, it's all about the experience, the story that you're creating as you go. The immersion. To me, that's what a great game is all about.
Boundless is an awesome experience. I already love this game. I am really hoping to see this continually expand over time. It's a terrific game right now, but the promise of even better things is really there. I hope we're in for the long-haul with Boundless.
So hat's off to you, Wonderstruck devs and designers. Boundless is TOP NOTCH in my book.
Highly recommended.

I'm about 80 hours in, and still really enjoying Boundless.  As a voxel-based building game, it is largely similar to Minecraft, with significantly nicer graphics and better tools to build complex shapes with finer detail.
The portals in particular look really amazing, and can be built by pretty much anyone.  They appear as a seamless doorway to another world. Players have built networks of portals to connect the current 12 worlds' and their major settlements.  Each planet feels like a distinct place, and most have some very beautiful scenery (Andooweem is my favorite recently).
The cities are particularly interesting as there you can see different creations built up next to each other to build large creative spaces.  Some have themes of ancient ruins, or a steampunk city, while others are more whimsical, like Pixelgate, which features a lot of excellent pixel art.
As an early access title, the game is not 100% complete, but new content is constantly being added.  Recently patches have been adding content about once per month, most recently adding meteor strike events where meteors crash into the planets and spawn monsters.  Beating the event awards some valuable resources, including the portal needed for portals.  The Devs actively engage with the community on the game's forums, including arranging events for players to build elaborate sculptures, and dropping large meteors on the heads of large hunting parties.
So far the end game is focused on building and crafting.  Some players compete to build the best shops, which I highly reccommend new players should take advantage of, as there are some materials that are a bottleneck early (such as glue), but readily available from player shops.
I've really been enjoying the game.  It is fun and relaxing to play, and offers a lot of appealing sights in both the procedurally generated landscape and in player creations.

Borderlands was a new project by Gearbox Software back in 2009. The game had a lot of unique features and settings. A first-person shooter set on a sci-fi planet - Pandora, with a lot of focus on RPG elements. The game was very well reviewed and recieved a various amount awards, including several Game of the Year's. Visually the game is beautiful and covered in cel shading, giving it a very comic book / hand-drawn look. The game took cel shading so far, that people often associate the game with that specific art-style. Thanks to the cel shading, the game could hide behind pretty simple textures without appearing low-res, as the game does not have to look realistic.
Pandora is a very hostile planet, as you quickly get to experience with the regular human bad-guys and also a selection of aliens and mutations. You get to choose between 4 characters to play, each with it's unique ability and weapons. There is a leveling system where you gain experience and level up specific perks for your character and set-up. When you level up, so does your enemies, and occasionally you encounter a 'Badass' (stronger and more dangerous than the regular), as well as a bunch of unique variants and bosses.
This game rewards you with more loot than your grannies wrinkles. You will drown in a sea of a billion different weapons, with different ammo types, reload speeds, firing speeds, scope zooms, damage etc. IT NEVER ENDS! There are 4 types of bonus damage; fire, explosion, shock and corrosion, all with an advantage and disadvantage to specific enemies. Luckily, you don't wear or find any armor in the game, only a shield and health augmentation, that has about as many billion combinations as the weapons.
A lot of people compare Borderlands with Fallout 3. They are in reality very different from one another. Borderlands is very humoristic and bright, while still being twisted and deteriorated. This game is not set in a post-apocalyptic world that has been beautiful. Pandora itself never was a peaceful place, and the name should hint it's secrets within. Borderlands never really focus on a good story either, it's just about the loot, man, the LOOT!
This game shows it qualities when played in Co-op, where 4 people can do all this nonsense together. It really starts feeling like an MMO RPG when fighting the harder bosses in co-op, grinding everywhere - and then then rewarded with loot. There even is PVP arenas for fighting over the loot too. If co-op is not an option you can still enjoy it in Single-Player.
