Probably the greatest atmosphere i've seen in a game ever. Great graphics, Great sound assets. Great Soundtrack. Ewokes haunting feelings of awe, loneliness, madness, anxiety, absolution, existensialism, confusion, disorientation, mystery and joy. It's a beautiful abstract piece that says so much and so little at the same time. It really shows how to merge art with gaming.
Now some of you might worry that this is just another linear walking simulator, in my opinion it is not. There's a lot of walking and exploring, granted. But there are puzzles, platforming and failure states too. Which makes NaissanceE qualify as a game.
These puzzle-platforming segments are seamlessly blended into the narrative, so seamless in fact it is sort of hard to notice when the game transitions from puzzle to exploration. Although the game never tells you where to go or what to do, i never found myself lost, As i imagined what i would do if i was in the protagonists shoes, and acted accordingly. I "role-played" if you will.
Over all NaissanceE is probably the most immersive game i've played in a good while. And i especially recommend it if you like the atmosphere of Cube, Eden log, Brazil, Enter the Void, Pi or The Matrix. Those are movies, i know, but that is not to imply NaissanceE is more of a movie than a game, it's very much the opposite as it doesn't even have any cutscenes at all. It just has a similar atmosphere to said movies.

The positives: I love the atmospherics - it starts as a corridor type exploration game but then the player is rewarded by vast mechanized vistas which are simply beautiful in their art deco, machine-minimalist style.  The expansive area you are exploring  is evocative of the vast complex hinted at in the film Forbidden Planet - mechanized perfection but no people - perhaps a society which had been destroyed by its own quest for whatever the complex was designed for.   There were times I simply stood and admired the vistas which were presented to me starting at Level 8 (Big Well).  The sense of scale and my own insignificance in this world were amazing - excellent use of lighting, perspective and industrial haziness - a fantastic technical achievement and a terrific use of the procedurally rendered immersive world concept.
The negatives: be prepared for frustrations - there is a lot of precision/timed jumping skill required - the fascination with this began to seriously wear off in several levels where it required repeating the level dozens of times to get the timing down, and finally wore off completely on Level 28 (Magnetic Pain) where you have to walk along a spinning turbine shaft to gain access to a tunnel.  I know intellectually that I would be able to eventually master the level through repetition to get the timing down but I started to simply wonder why I was spending my time in this way and lost interest at this point.  I much preferred the puzzles in the game which required logic to proceed versus the obstacles requiring dexterity and timing.  I couldn't help thinking that
.  In the case of Level 28, for instance, it would be nice to provide me the choice of either walking along the spinning turbine shaft or solving a puzzle that would stop the spin - this would make for a more satisfying experience and widen the potential audience.  Fortunately I am blessed with enough dexterity to play this game but I couldn't help thinking of those who might not - I submit that this game should be more about exploration and solving puzzles rather than being nimble and quick enough to jump here or there at precisely the right time.  If I ever find myself confined for a long period of time with nothing else to do, I'll return to the game.
Overall - I recommend this game just for the ability to view some of the vistas rendered in the game, but realize you will likely need to repeat levels many times in order to advance.  You may even decide to give up on it as I did but don't stop before Level 8 - Big Well.  This is a world worth visiting just to see it - a Cubist Grand Canyon if you will - well worth the cost of the game.  Note however that I cannot speak to whether there is a satisfying conclusion to the game.

NaissanceE!
In a nutshell: a great minimalistic experience, set in a mysterious greyish-white monumental dream-like maze, some features of which resemble the real world, some rather like strange monolithic constructs.
Making most of the limited color scheme and basic geometric shapes, the game pulls of a pleasantly mysterious atmosphere, epecially in the many open parts which are free for the player to be explored. It is intriguing, sometimes scary, sometimes awe-inspring. Even though there is literally no story, the vague, allegoric mood present makes its own sort of narrative, with blocky ghosts flying around your head while a giant musical instrument submerged in sand plays some music for you or platform chases by giant floating worms.
Gameplay here is certainly secondary to the atmosphere, but nevertheless it was pleasant enough UDK-platformer-faire, with some puzzles and a sprint-breathing mechanic built in. However, I didn't like some middle parts where you are disoriented by pitch-black darkness constantly and have to randomly find some glowing cubes for reference. Pretty frustrating. Still, it was decent enough.
Music was as expected, minimalistic, but very well used for atmospheric effect, be it during exploration or during chase scenes. No complaints here.
In short, if you like experimental minimalist games with great atmosphere get it. Just don't expect any clearly explained story or AAA-class gameplay and you will be greatly pleased.
Have fun!

Stupidly simple yet brilliantly balanced and with a lot of depth, Divekick is a game that's equally fun to play whether you're a hardcore fighting game player or you never even saw any of the games in the genre.
Each character has different speed and angles of dives, along with two special moves that you can use to get a tactical advantage. The fights are incredibly fast! This is an instant-kill game, meaning that you win a round with only one hit. Sounds tough? It is! You need to constantly try to outsmart your opponent, baiting him and setting traps.
Divekick proves that fighting games don't need to be intimidating, nor sport hundreds of moves and combos. It's lighthearted with lots of gaming and pop culture references and fighting game in-jokes. It might not look like a work of art, but it doesn't need to, as long as it provides some good laughs and easy-to-learn-hard-to-master mechanics. Which is exactly what it does great and why I wholeheartedly recommend it!

It really is an exploration game - because its environment is so unusual. Mostly monochrome, with subtle shades and mostly abstract, cubic architecture, the game surely stands out. The shapes are ranging from entirely abstract to vaguely familiar, the spaces are ranging from uncomfortably tight to uncomfortably vast - and the result is a unique environment that's not tailored to you rather than outright hostile. The impression is enhanced by the eerily atmospheric soundscape.
Gameplay-wise, it's a mix of exploration, puzzles and first-person platforming. Who doesn't like first-person platforming? :) But it's well-done, properly checkpointed, and frequently intermitted with exploration and puzzles. There's an interesting gameplay mechanic: you need to regularly press the button to breathe when you're running - otherwise you run out of breath.
The puzzles never become a routine. You might get stuck on some of them - but I never had to watch a walkthrough. As usual, you just go back to the game the next day.
All in all, it's a very good exploration game. I can easily recommend it, especially if you liked Kairo. Can be played with a controller - only the menu doesn't support it.

When I've seen this game for sale, I must confess that the first thing that came to my thoughts was that this was just a 'Elder Scrolls' generic or something likely. Dark Messiah of Might & Magic is amazing. The story isn't great and is kind of cheesy, the RPG system is pretty basic. Obviously, you can choose from various melee weapons, bows (that have interesting arrow types like rope arrows) and magic so nothing new here. I haven't played any other Might and Magic game (although the ones that have complain about the story) so no nostalgia points here either. So what does it make it so special?
The combat mechanics.
Oh my goodness does it feel good to corner an enemy and kick him into spikes, through a railing, off a cliff, off the stairs, into a fire or just make him trip and fall on his face (with really awesome ragdoll physics coupled with some enjoyable sound design) if he happens to trip over the stairs as your foot connects to his stomach. If that's not your flavor, how about throwing anything that can be picked up at your enemies, watching it connect with his face and then the orc/soldier/whatever falling as his partner attempts to charge at you? Oh, you don't enjoy picking a fight, well, just loosen an arrow into that suspiciously shaky wooden column and watch how your enemies start panicking and get crushed by the barrage of barrels and crates. There's plenty of environmental hazards to exploit (even unique ones in every level), just don't get yourself killed. If you want to use a sword as well, go for it - decapitating angry guards is just as fun.
To illustrate, I'll got through a section (no story spoilers) that I've replayed a dozen times just because it was so enjoyable (BTW, I rarely replay any game/section of a game so you have to really impress me): I'm on some sort of mountains/cliffs as I sneak up on an orc and kick his♥♥♥♥♥off the cliff only to hear him scream as he falls to his death. I then dash towards the next one, give him a few slashes with my sword and shield bash him into a wall of spikes to which he sticks like glue. As his friends start to head towards me from the other side of a cliff, I block the path by standing on a plank connecting the 2 cliffs from which I kick my enemies off only to hear the gulp and scream as I see them disappear in the water bellow. I continue as I encounter 2 orcs one of which looses balance after my well placed heavy sword thrust, slams into the wooden railing, only to see it shatter as the orc goes off the cliff and I manage to execute the other (after a few well placed light and heavy swings) by sticking a sword in his stomach and then in slow motion (which really makes you feel the power of your action) kicking him off the blade. I proceed forward, kicking, slashing and bashing through orcs as I make my way to the top where a cliff is separated by a small scaffolding bridge. I see my enemies running towards me and as I turn slightly, I notice the supports of the bridge. One slash later, I see the bridge collapsing and my enemies plunging to their doom. I then find a way around it by going through a narrow path, shooting a rope arrow on one of the nearby trees, climbing it and continuing on my way.
At first I thought this would get boring, but it never did. The great level design kept presenting me more challenges and ways to overcome them. I used magic to freeze my enemies into popsicles, burn them, make them fight against each other. I used melee weapons and even managed to actually smelt one (optional) not by going into the menu, but by positioning the stone container over the fire, melting the metal, pouring it into the mold, etc. The stealth is pretty solid,: it is harder for enemies to notice you the darker it is, the sound of your footsteps matters , they investigate if they suspect they saw something.
To sum up, if you enjoy kicking guards and watching them fall to the wooden floor, only for it to collapse and the guard die because he just kissed the ground of the lower floor, then slashing, stabbing, impaling, freezing, burning, turning against his friends, kicking, shield bashing, throwing stuff at, killing with environmental hazards like rocks and barrels anyone that stands in your way, then this is your game.

Episode 4 of Tales from the Borderlands was brilliant. Easily one of the funniest episodes yet with choices that impacted the entire series, which is crazy. I'm really curious how this series is going to end but goddamn, I commend Telltale and Gearbox for this masterpiece.
EPISODE THREE REVIEW
Goddamn it, this series just gets better and better as it progresses. Episode 3's release kinda shocked me as I wasn't aware it was coming out until the game updated on Steam but it was definitely worth the wait. Even halfway through the series, they're still adding new characters that are lovable in the same way that the main characters already are. Gortys is a surprisingly amazing character, probably one of my favorite from most of the recent episodic games I've played in a while, the episode didn't fall short of making me laugh hard at some scenes, such as Fiona saying "Touchgoal" in victory of defeating some enemies and Gortys talking about Rhys' tie.
This series (as I claimed in my review for the previous episode) is well on it's way to being my favorite Telltale Games series period, and this episode just furthers that claim.
Only negative things I can say are the that I encountered a few glitches, one which crashed my game and wouldn't play to the point that I had to completely re-install the game again, which wasn't a pleasant experience, but that didn't take much away from the brilliant experience I had with this episode.
Play this right now if you have any interest in the Borderlands series whatsoever.
EPISODE TWO REVIEW
I just finished Tales From The Borderlands Episode 2 and holy ♥♥♥♥, this is my favorite Telltale series ever. It's so funny, entertaining, fun to play and I love almost all of the characters. There was some twists that I didn't see coming and the Loader Bot character is hilarious. I'm honestly so happy that the second episode finally came out and I can't wait for episode 3.
EPISODE ONE REVIEW
I just finished episode one of Tales From The Borderlands, Zer0 Sum with my sister (She was Fiona, I was Rhys) and that was perfect. Incredible story, hilarious moments (I was crying from laughter at points) surprisingly amazing action sequences, easily-likeable characters and it's everything and more that I expected from the game.
It's also a surprisingly long Telltale episode, clocking in at around 2 and a half hours if you take time to explore and interact with the characters.
I rarely give these out because I don't think there's much that's perfect, but that was a 10 out of 10. Definitely pick it up and play it. If you love the lore of Borderlands, love Telltale Games, or both, you will love this first episode. (I rarely give out score-based reviews as I don't want to be entirely bias and give a critical review on the media, but honestly, I had no faults with this starting episode.)

Oh, sorry, forgot that I actually had to write more than one sentence to review something.
Well, this game OOZES with nothing but love and adoration for Borderlands - from the recurring or mentioned characters, to the numbers, the colors, the loot, even the culture. Veterans will, most likely, feel utterly immersed in this as soon as they step foot on the planet Pandora - possibly even earlier - and get to experience a new perspective on the setting.
Borderlands has always dipped into dark humor, or even swung from the wacky to the bleak, and as the series has gone on the 'mature' moments have grown number. Backstabbing, death of characters, descent into insanity or tragic consequences. Well, from Episode 1, it certainly looks like Tales from the Borderlands will probably continue this tradition - at least dependant on your choices. Tales looks to be darker than one may expect, though you'll find the reasonably varied humor still intact. If you want your Borderlands experience to avoid any serious tone, you may not like the atmosphere of the game.
In addition, in comparison to other TellTale games, I feel like this game suffers most in the combat - especially compared to their last release, The Wolf Among Us. There are less distinct branching paths in combat, and many interactions involve rather less choices than I would have liked. So those of you who adored the TellTale action scenes may feel slightly put off here unless the theme carries it enough for you.
But does it pull off the Borderlands theme, if a little dark, and taking away any 'real' FPS elements? Absolutely. Great characters, great individual mechanics between the two playable ones that I look forward to seeing develop in later episodes, and an interesting cocktail of motivations, possible futures and a healthy dose of unreliable narration
, a writing technique I never get tired of seeing. If you've played so much as any Borderlands game for more than a few hours, and at least one TellTale game, you'll find the near-flawless mix here.
Really, beyond the combat - and even then, the action scenes in the earliest episodes are often a bit restrained in TellTale games of late - it's extremely hard to find any fault as long as you like the TellTale formula.
Besides, if you've never tried a game from the studio before, but are a Borderlands fan - maybe now is the time to try it out for yourself. Just be warned that, from a single episode, you're paying a premium for 2.5 hours worth of playtime at most, without replaying and finding different (moderately) branching stories.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a new beginning for Wolfenstein. It's an attempt to make the story work, the gameplay modern and breath new life into the grandfather of FPS games.
I couldn't tell you a thing about the story. I don't remember anything other than something about Nazis, buildings and a guy called Deathshead? Basically the Nazi's win WWII and you're living in a world where they Nazi regime has total dominance of the world. You're a part of the resistance movement. The story is pretty forgettable but they do a decent job making the characters in it likable. There's a homebase you return to where you can talk to the resistance members and they all have personality and flair to them. There's a few moments in the story where you get a chance to make some choices and it does affect the storyline in some ways; characters can die, settings can change. The main character, BJ, has some good writing for him but overall, the story feels like it's here to drive the gameplay.
There are some great setpieces - there's a level on a giant bridge which really stood out to me in particular - but the story doesn't really connect all these missions well enough. It feels a bit disjointed at times but it does create moments where the gameplay can take over.
And the gameplay is what kept me here. The shooting feels great; it's violent, it's over the top and it feels really solid. Nearly every weapon feels like it has weight, like it has killing power and you've got a large arsenal to choose from. You'll get things like pistols and shotguns, to stranger things like laser rifles and welders. You can upgrade your guns through combat, encouraging you to mix up playstyles and try different weapon combinations. Dual wielding increases firepower but decreases accuracy; you'll want to think of what your fighting against and how best to counter it.
The artstyle/art direction is really great- the 60's sleek design meshing with the Nazi stone architecture creates a lot of great clashing moments of style. A lot of this game still looks gorgeous, violently so at times; you'll see death camps, giant robots, ruined cities and it all looks believable and never feels like a huge shift in tone.
I ended up really enjoying The New Order - more than I thought I would. If it's on sale, I'd say to pick it up. It's really fun and mindless and honestly, sometimes that's just what you need. The gameplay is solid and the story is engaging enough to keep you interested for the length of the campaign. It's not something that I think you'd be revisiting but for the 10-12 hours you might get out of it, I think it's worth it.

I really wanted to like this game... I had done my research looking at screenshots and videos (I really wanted to go see Aquatopia on Solum) and gave Boundless a try despite my initial misgivings. I was hesitant about how it's been in early access for so many years, with still so few people playing it. I usually love sandbox builders, but THIS game... I couldn't stomach looking at it for much longer, and I immediately refunded. I have literally seen Minecraft texture packs which made that older game almost look better in some regards, and one of Boundless' strong points was *supposed* to be its graphics as many reviews here even state. Even with every setting on Extreme (the highest possible, ran fine, there were no glitches and my PC is perfectly capable), I wasn't impressed and felt so much of the texturing was too simple.
To start with. Character customization is very limited. There are two body types (a second smaller one, but still not very feminine), with a very paltry selection of outfits on certain skintones/head ornaments, and you cannot mix and match any of those. Whichever one comes with the body type or head that you like, well, that's what you get for your outfit. And back to the underwhelming graphics... The textures on these were blurry, and the feline nose looks like a kid drew some Lion King fan art with a fuzzy Photoshop brush. On top of that, it's just one button you hit over and over to cycle through all of these preset combinations. One button, that's what the 'character creation' is.
The portals are a neat gimmick, but as a new player you only experience the starting one and then not for a while. Seeing the planets up in the sky is also neat. But that's about it. Much like WanderFish YT's review, "Sorry guys but if you expected what was in the trailer you won't get it." Of course, I know being a newbie you're introduced slowly to mechanics, I'm not expecting everything on a silver platter. But there's something to be said for hooking people early on with a good first impression, a starting experience to give you a taste of the game before tossing you into the resource grind.
The landscape... is not that beautiful or immersive at all. The only pretty thing in the game that I'll give credit to is their water, with reflections on it looks gorgeous. But take that away... and the block textures of the ground and the tree leaves are often eyesores, flat plains where you can see the seams and not enough grass to make you feel like there are organic-shaped flowing hills of wavy grass. I'll admit there was one tree trunk texture that was decent, successfully giving the illusion of roundness and tricking me into thinking it's cylindrical, was impressed by whatever artist did that one... but the ground textures were so offputting. It reminded me of one of those bad cartoony Minecraft texture packs where you can see each individual block and how little actual texture work has gone into it if you get up close to it (which you do early on, mining.) Particular offenders to me where simple ones like Sedimentary/Igneous Rock, Metamorphic, Sand, things like that. Did not like, and you know in a game like this that's what you're going to be looking at a large portion of the time.
To be fair, the UI and aesthetic they've got going is pretty sleek, as well as their design style for the (limited amount of) critters. That helps a lot in their marketing media on the Store Page, I'm sure, it certainly made me believe the game is a lot prettier and more polished than it actually is. A minor nitpick, but even things like certain audio/sounds are off. Hammering Sedimentary Rock makes a hollow sound like hammering wood, it sounds fake and breaks immersion.
I realize that, yes, it's still in Early Access. But there comes a point when you can't keep using that as an excuse. This game was listed on Steam back in Nov 2014. For that many years, and being part of a genre already pioneered and duplicated by so many, I'd have expected a lot more progress.
Like Space Invader's review says, the price is too steep for what it offers, and I share that "complete lack of desire to see what else this game has to offer." If Boundless were cheaper, I might consider it negligible enough to let it slide, I could wait, watch, and hope they improve it... and they'd get to keep some of my money. But at $35, I'm going to play it safe and refund. Especially when there are many other alternatives (even voxel games like Stellar Overload doing -40% during the Winter Sale, which Boundless refused to take part in) clearly illustrating I could get more bang for my buck elsewhere.
I did not see anything that truly impressed me, I had to ask myself numerous times "Am I actually having fun?" when I usually enjoy the genre, and saw enough that actually repelled me as far as quality and polish. I'll admit I didn't put in enough time to see if there's depth or enough content... the visual surface of the game was enough that I didn't want to dig deeper and go beyond the 2hr mark. It's a statement in itself that I was irritated enough to quit out even before then at 1.3hrs and call it early.

Been playing this one for months now.  Very realistic but difficult was my first impression.  You will NOT easily spot the enemy unless that person is foolish enough to wander at you in the open.  This is the first such sim I've seen which forces you to actually LISTEN to people and employ coordination.  It gets talked about a lot in other games, but in this one this patttern of behavior is the only way to win consistantly.  People that cannot respond to instructions and use cover will chafe and suffer here.  Those that can follow the directions of a squad leader over voip will be richly rewarded and immersed.  Once you realize that the key to winning is the acquisition and holding of territory, you will really begin to get good and have a real sense of acheivement.  Killing the enemy is helpful, but body counts are secondary to everything else.  Actually spotting and killing the enemy soldier on your own is hard and actually fairly rare, just as it is in real life.  Most of the time, the only enemy you see is a dead one you may walk past.  If you're fortunate enough to actually spot an enemy, it's highly likely he's already aware of you.  The most frequent condition under which you are aware of the presence of an enemy is suffering a bulet wound.  If you are good enough to see the fellow first, you are probably beginning to function properly as a matter of habit.   For people that desire realism as close to the truth as it gets, this is your game.

It's free-to-play and not necessarily pay-to-win on the original, better mobile version. You can also purchase units with medals in that version. No pressure, no harm done. You get medals over time (if you're willing to part with that) and so spending money is merely an express method to getting what you want faster.
It remains free-to-play in this version, but you cannot under any circumstances purchase units with medals. Instead, you have to fork out upwards of 30+ dollars (Canadian) for not individual units, but for entire packs of units. This monumentally insulting flaw paints this as an indisputable cash-grab, and nothing more. The original, mobile version was a decent way to kill time and didn't force you to spend money at all; this version is mostly unchanged but FORCES you to spend hard-earned money on units you might not even like, and in groups, too, rather than units that you actually want.
What if I don't want all of the Ptolemaic Army units but just want the Metal Rear? Well the joke is on me, then, because I'd have to fork out $16.99 regular price for that ONE pack (there are two for the Ptolemaic army, but that's just one group). The joke is not just on me, but on all of us.
So what of the way it plays? Well, unfortunately much of the interface remains unchanged. Sure, you can change the window resolution in the title screen, but that's the only thing that makes this resemble a PC title. On top of that, which buries the hatchet further, is the garbage control system. A fighting game based on the Fighting Game Community, at first glance Divekick may seem like some rinky dink Newgrounds flash game, but once you get your hands on it you'll see that it's actually a legit fighting game based around one single move.  When most people think fighting games, they think long 10 minute combos and mashing 15 buttons on an arcade stick.  Divekick is almost the antithesis of that since it only uses 2 buttons and each round is a 1-hit kill.  Because of this, beginners and experienced players will be on a similar playing field and can both enjoy themselves (that is not to say, however that pros will be dominated by noobs).  The depth comes from the meta game of using your fundamentals, gimmicks, spacing, and mind games. I'd say it's well worth your money since the game lets you have some silly fun but also allows you to really dive into the meta game of fighting games.
tl;dr: Play Divekick. It's a good game.

NaissanceE isn't really just a game.  It's an experience.  And an amazing one at that.  To start, as shown in the trailer, you are taken and thrown into a room.  You have no idea where, you have no idea by what, and you have no idea why.  Heck, you don't even know who you are.  But thats not the point of this game.  What you DO know, is that you need to LEAVE.  As you progress, you get the feeling that something is wrong.  Theres nothing out there hunting you specifically, no horror-game spooks.  But you start feeling that something about this huge-scale world is... off.  Like you just don't belong.  The largeness of this world, the ambiance, how the entire UNIVERSE that you're in seems to play with you and mock you, is unsettling to say the least.  As you spend time with this game you're no longer a person playing a game, you are the person inside NaissanceE.  Every cliff you look over will make your heart race.  When you are in complete darkness you will feel it.
There's no real storyline, per say.  But after a few hours of play you almost understand the "storyline" anyways.  The only real thing directing you on what to do is the checkpoints.  Sometimes they read "going down" or something of the sort.  But that's it.  The ambiguity of this game is amazing.
Now for gameplay.  Its first person, where you can walk, run, jump, and crouch.  Theres certain mechanics you have to do throughout the game that require all of these functions.  Some of the play is fast-paced, where you know you need to get somewhere RIGHT NOW and really feel a sense of urgency, while others is more laidback. The obstacles are fun, and the puzzles are puzzling.  People have alot of problems about the checkpoints, but it's not that bad.  There were some annoying times, but the way i see it, if im not annoyed at least once then the games not hard enough.
Overall, I highly recommend this game.  Even without the gameplay, puzzle part (which is awesome), just the sheer number of times you just look at this world and think "wow.... I have to climb through all THAT?!" is worth it.  The world itself is very playful, and this is undoubtedly one of the most beautifully made games ive played.  Bravo.

I got hyped about this game reading reviews. After playing for more than half of the game, I honestly regret buying it, even in 75% discount price. This game might have been great in 2006, but it's annoying in 2015 and not really fun. I could overlook the technical aspects due to game's age (except for the forced motion sickness mode), but even the gameplay mechanics are poor compared to newer games (or even, say, Half Life 1).
Enemy variety is tragic. There are like 4 different enemy types, everyone looks the same, and an area is usually populated by a single type or two. You fight them over and over again.
The fact that you can use environment to kill is cool, but in this game you are forced to do so, and you're almost forbidden to use standard means (like, a sword!). Because the enemies are extremely hard when fighting the standard style (they can parry as fast as you can strike and they never miss a parry), but they are extremely vulnerable when anything hits them. Throwing a jar at them can yield a better result than hitting them with a sword from behind to a neck (really, because a jar or a barrel knocks them down and you can then kill them instantly, but hitting them from behind to a head doesn't... makes real sense, and definitely not a gimmick!). So using environment is not a great addition to your fighting style here, it's shoved down your throat and you need to use it all the time.
The game is full of bugs that either make you fail instantly or prevent completion of the area. I had to load a past save several times to work around those. Make sure you save (and don't rely just on a quicksave).
You'll get stuck on anything and everything. Using ladders, ropes, jumping through a window, all of that is incredible pain and you'll often die because the engine is dumb.
The lighting is so bad that half of the game is well lit and the other half is pitch black (like house interior during a day). Enabling HDR makes it even worse. You can't see a damn thing and you need to use night vision a lot just to work around poor lighting. Adjusting gamma doesn't help too much, you'll still see sh** and the rest will be blinding bright.
The hitboxes and targeting, oh damn. Very often you hit something completely else, like a wall *behind* a person. Performing an execution is a random chance whether the game considers you in the right place or not.
The UI for switching weapons is far from usable. You can switch from sword+shield to a bow, but you can't switch back. You can either switch bow->sword (and only then add a shield), or switch bow->shield+random weapon (usually not the one you want). Very clever.
Forced motion sickness. Oh yes, you human weaklings, the developers will let you suffer, you deserve it. You can disable head bobbing, but that's the least of the problem. The image tilts every time you strafe. Every time you move sideways, your view moves unnaturally, right side up left side down, or vice versa, like boat swaying on a see. I found a way to disable it, otherwise I'd have refunded this immediately. You can see my solution on
.
I ended in chapter 6 in crypts, fighting zombies. I didn't see sh**, everything was pitch black so I had to constantly toggle night vision, and it was near impossible to execute a zombie, because of targeting glitches, so the fights took eternity. There was no fun in that.
How long can you enjoy throwing barrels at people and kicking them from ramps, when you're forced to do that a thousand times over and there's no other way? 9 hours seems to be my experience. (In hindsight, I was really persistent.)

Once upon a time, on a cold desolate planet where the highest tempature ever recorded was 30 degrees fahrenheit, a colonist ship droped 6 humanoids onto the surface to make a community for its empire. They were not human, but instead a xeno race of cat-people called the Orassan, used to frozen planets and extremely cold tempature. They all got to work making their homes against the mountainside with a perfect defensible area to put up walls and two corridor-like entrences to their new home. They only relied on their survival meals and the hunted meat of the local fauna, which often times died within the traps set up. They had no need for heaters, for they were comfortable in tempatures that would kill a human without heavy elemental protection, thus saving them electric power used to generate the hyroponic basins to grow what other food they could muster. Several humans they resuced joined up and assisted the Orassan colonists in their daily lives, but the power had to be diverted more towards keeping the fragile humans warm while the kitty colonists constantly enjoyed the weather, especially the Orassan; Bee, who ran naked with her tail swaying happily outside in the snow while her human allies sought the warmth of the common room. But more and more humans came to the colony until the 6 xeno cats were outnumbered, but strengthened their bonds to the humans, the only issues in the colony weren't the frequent raids swept away from the Orassan firepower, but rather the food supply, or lack thereof. Soon two other humans joined that contributed nothing productive to the colony except for extra firepower, they were downed during a raid with pirate sappers in which the Orassan doctor had to euthenize them to end their suffering. Many were happy in the colony that the super ugly human was dead, but the real danger showed itself in the form of helpful supplies in the wrong places. On the last days of the colony, ship pieces fell onto several houses, killing 3 colonists while a random drop-pod supply killed another in bed... but the worst was yet to come. Another raid happened, this time tribespeople came into the killzone corridors to the colony, but one kitty colonist wasn't smart and stood right in the middle of it all, only to be accidently gunned down by her lover. Bee lost her beauitful tail and was later killed by a manhunter pack while sad she lost her tail. The last two colonists starved because they didn't know how to cook and refused to eat a raw potato. Thus ended the tale of the Orassan colony, Nachtigall of the Norden Sturm faction.

Built a tribe of primitive people's after their homes were destroyed by massive machines of death. We built houses for ourselves and set upon mining great amounts of steel. We then constructed an enormous round hut and named our village Steelhut after it. We set upon building more buildings than we could use, incase any nearby tribes people decide to join. After 2 new recruits, and a couple small raids of 2-3 tribesmen, we decided we needed to enclose our farms and houses with steel walls and steel buildings. With this completed we fortified the only entrance to our village.
The head shaman had been working on new magics in the great hall of the steelhut. After discovering advanced clothing like dusters and cowboy hats, as well as how to forge steel weapons and great bows. We set upon making these weapons and equipped our best hunters with great bows. But we were after a new magic: electricity. Our tribe had seen electricity before, in lightning storms and the machines, but out shaman believed we could harness it for ourselves. Though she predicted it would take many months to finalize.
Several months went by quietly, and winter was nearly upon us. Food crops had been plentiful and our hunters had bountiful hunts. Pemmican was stocked up, but electricity was still being researched. With only about a month left of research we hear an outsider call our tribe. A machine collector named Braun was being chased by a violent gang of people. My people did not want this outsider among us, but the shaman believed that perhaps Braun's knowledge of machines would help our people uncover the secrets of electricity. So we offered Braun residence, and prepared our warriors to defend our homes.
As Braun's arrived at the village the raiders after him had begun closing in. Braun went to grab a steel mace, as the pacifist shaman cleaned the great hall. As the Raiders closed in my people quickly realized they were outmatched as the Raiders carried rifles and guns. Our best warrior was shot dead almost instantly. A second warrior shared a similar fate right afterwards. Another warrior was downed so the shaman set upon rescuing her, but was shot by the raiders doing so requiring her to rest and heal after setting her friend down in the hospital bed. Next almost instantly two more of the warriors we're incapacitated, so the remaining warrior and Braun back up. The raiders advance killing Braun almost instantly before my warrior kills the raider attacking them. After seeing three of their own drop and so many of mine drop the raiders decided it was time to pick up their losses and grab our injured survivors and haul them off as prisoners.
Down to three villagers all injured we had to make do with doctoring. The least injured was the shaman who was first to recover and then began tending to the others. However warrior who survived his last stand began to come down with an infection. He died shortly thereafter. Soon due to all the death and destruction that occured our pacifist shaman went outside and then berserk. She began attacking all the local wildlife without remorse until a lowly squirrel tore her throat out... The person the shaman rescued recovered after these events and woke to find everyone around her dead, blood splashed on the walls and floors. So she did the only logical thing...she kept researching electricity. Being an excellent researcher she managed to discover the secrets to electricity in only a few days time, and armed with that knowledge swept out across the land abandoning the decaying husk of the fort she once called home.
10/10 would save someone to have my village overrun by mass gun wielding murderers again.

I'm not going to fawn all over this piece like the other positive reviews.  I hate puzzle games, and I hate indie games.  I only got about 75% of the way through this one.  But I like the Talos Principle.  The game has a few problems, but I still recommend it at 20 dollars or below if you're a puzzle fan.
The graphics have an eerie beauty, along with pretty good sound design.  Optimization is pretty iffy.  I destroy this game's recommended specs, but I could NOT get a good framerate without certain graphical options looking pretty bad.
The backstory of the game is nonsense, biologically speaking, but it more than serves its purpose here.  Meanwhile, at the forefront, you awaken as a robot in what quickly reveals itself to be a simulation of some kind designed to develop your programming.  Your only companions are a big booming Judeo-Christian god voice from everywhere, recordings of the simulation designers, and a sarcastic, unfunny computer AI that likes to ask you philosophical questions.  Story fragments exist on terminals in the form of western or middle-eastern ideological pieces, and emails between the humans who designed the system.  Personally, I find it hard to believe that a bunch of genius computer scientists would have designed such a simple simulation to train a true A.I.
The puzzles exist in a half dozen chambers for each world, with seven worlds for each temple, in a total of three temples, for the most part.  There are some tertiary puzzles to solve of the same types if you want one of the game's different endings.  As you acquire more Tetris pieces, you unlock more components to solve puzzles with.  These are usually things like pylons to redirect energy beams, boxes to stand on, and so forth.  By far the coolest one is a recording device that records yourself and everything you interact with, and after you play it back you can then interact with your other fictional self to complete otherwise impossible tasks.  However, every one of these tools, with the exception of that one, are "abilities" that should have been unlocked at the beginning of the game, not major features of it.
Most puzzles resolve themselves pretty quickly, but by the second temple the "samey-ness" some people describe feeling has fully taken root, and the game becomes fully repetitive and tedious.  Some of this has to do with the plodding pace at which the story is delivered, but for myself, I couldn't get past a singular realization: there is only ONE puzzle in this game.  This theme is, to use the technical industry phrase, "Not enough stuff."
Every single puzzle in the game would resolve itself in under a minute if you had one, maybe two more of something.  One more box.  One more jammer.  One more pylon.  You can literally go into any puzzle area and ask "Okay, what did they not give me enough of?"  and you will thematically already be at the puzzle's solution.  Yes, there are many puzzles, and definitely yes, there are an astounding number of variations, but only within this ONE THEME.  A bit through the third temple it felt like the game was simply gating the end of the story in an attempt to extend its lifespan.
Some object interactions by the player and collision detections are highly restricted to limit the mechanics and solutions during puzzle-solving to a few of the same iterative solutions.  I did not appreciate this.  Yes, there are sometimes multiple solutions to a puzzle, but only a few pre-designated by the devs.  There are ways of preventing players from breaking your game without unnatural restrictions.
So, why do I still recommend this game after ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over it?   Because my complaints, though accurate, are mostly personal preference.  That makes them even arguable as to whether or not they're important to the fundamental design of the game.  I would have liked to have seen a greater variety of mechanics in the puzzles, with more solutions.  More philosophical diversity was badly needed for an older gamer like myself who has seen all of this material before.  The sometimes absurd degrees of restriction in movement and interaction with the environment limit further solutions from being possible, making the game on-rails more than I'd like.
But at the end of the day, most players will not - and would not - care about those complaints, and so Talos Principle stands as an achievement for both indie and puzzle games, and mostly deserves all of its success.

RimWorld is a top-down God/Colony simulator. Artistically similar to games like Prison Architect, RimWorld expands on the "do as I have commanded" gameplay of similar top-down titles, and throws in a healthy dose of colonial revolt, complicated romances, creepy breathing and calamity, just to make things exciting.
In this story, a colony of 5 that had crash-landed on a an arid, tree-less plain. It was cold, food was scarce and shelter was nowhere to be seen. A few seasons later, the colony was flourishing. Food and medicine a-plenty, other space-faring travellers found salvation when they joined the crew. They had healthy trade relations with other nearby colonies and tribes. A few disagreeances and minor arguments broke out between certain opinionated individuals, but for the most part everything was OK.
Then a pet boomalope exploded right in the middle of the trade plaza due to malnourishment. It exploded on one of their trade partners. They didn't like that.
A battle broke out, they escaped. They thought they were safe, but it turns out this outlander colony was allied with certain powerful people. Several more seasons passed.
I can still hear the mortar shells exploding around me... the cries of my colonists in pain... the crackle of the fire burning my colony to the ground...

I loved this game so so much that I replayed it 3 times to get all the achievements and then immediately bought and played the DLC (also very good). While the story was mostly in the form of written text, the combination of Portal-esque 3D puzzles plus the intriguing problem of robots with no humans kept me going. I also liked the way the story was revealed -- first with broad brush strokes and adding in finer and finer detail about the problem as you progressed, rather than only filling in a part of the painting at a time. I also desperately want a continuation game that takes place where the first game (ascension ending) leaves off. If you don't like text-based stories or 3D puzzles, then this game is not for you, but if you do like them then it's THE BEST.

In summary, this game incorporates all of my wishes for "Minecraft 2". It's Minecraft with much improved graphics. It's an MMORPG with a singular universe, and features the most amazing, seamless portal system I have ever seen in a game. It's literally a window to another location that you can look into in real time! And if you want to check out what you see, simply step through the portal. It features mining, caving, and building, pretty similar to Minecraft. You can be a merchant, a miner, a warrior, etc. There is a pretty deep RPG skill tree and crafting systems. You can also get trade stands and request bins, set prices on your items you want to sell, and build a shop that others in the world may stumble into. Like I said, it's Minecraft MMORPG with amazing portals, better graphics, and an actual player driven economy. Even in it's current state of early access, the game runs great. I can't put it down.

Oxenfree is a game I had low expectations for. I, sadly, had a majority of the game spoiled for me, as I watched it on Youtube, but I let myself experience the last hour blindly. The game blew me away, frankly. The characters have well written personality, each being made significant throughout the game. It's a game that really makes you think, 'If I do this, will it effect _____?' The ending, no matter what, is purposely unsatisfying, but it makes it work, and that's a thing that's hard to do. It's a game that you won't understand most of the plot until you reach the very end.
Oxenfree not only breaks the 4th wall countless times, but has it's own unique style of doing it. It perfectly explains the 'New Game' feature to a game, but that's only if you play until the end. The characters have their quirks that mess with the story, and that's okay. I found myself frustrated when an issue I thought had been resolved ended up escalating.
It has great mechanics and graphics. Oxenfree manages to turn a 2D Adventure and Choice-Based game into Horror, which is hard to do. Not only that, but it has an amazing soundtrack. The story itself is great and all, but the soundtrack adds to the experience.
The AI inwhich the characters talk through journey's, especially long ones, keeps the entertainment fresh. The game is short, and that's due to the small setting we're given, but that can be made up for with the multiple endings, and the constant chase for getting every achievement, which is impossible to do in one playthrough. The game left me with many theories, and I hope to find an answer the more endings I get.
What really made the game so entertaining is the witty humour, constant thrills, and all in all outcome of my choices. Oxenfree has become one of my favourite games, and I think it is a great start for Night School Studios. ( Excluding the mobile game they made. ) I hope to see more from this game. Not exactly a sequel, but maybe some form of DLC.

Been playing this one for months now.  Very realistic but difficult was my first impression.  You will NOT easily spot the enemy unless that person is foolish enough to wander at you in the open.  This is the first such sim I've seen which forces you to actually LISTEN to people and employ coordination.  It gets talked about a lot in other games, but in this one this patttern of behavior is the only way to win consistantly.  People that cannot respond to instructions and use cover will chafe and suffer here.  Those that can follow the directions of a squad leader over voip will be richly rewarded and immersed.  Once you realize that the key to winning is the acquisition and holding of territory, you will really begin to get good and have a real sense of acheivement.  Killing the enemy is helpful, but body counts are secondary to everything else.  Actually spotting and killing the enemy soldier on your own is hard and actually fairly rare, just as it is in real life.  Most of the time, the only enemy you see is a dead one you may walk past.  If you're fortunate enough to actually spot an enemy, it's highly likely he's already aware of you.  The most frequent condition under which you are aware of the presence of an enemy is suffering a bulet wound.  If you are good enough to see the fellow first, you are probably beginning to function properly as a matter of habit.   For people that desire realism as close to the truth as it gets, this is your game.

This is a fascinating game; an adventure with Telltale style aspects, but in a 2.5D environment. You, Alex, are exploring an island with your new step-brother, your best friend, and a couple others.  Then things get weird; spooky weird. The primary interactions relate to choosing comments to make, and using a radio to turn into frequencies. It's a fascinating story, told well with full dialog and a beautiful island to explore.  It's also legitimately disquieting at many points - there are these time jumps that intrude throughout the story and can be really creepy. But ultimately it's really a story about the relationships between these characters, and they're all believably deep. I finished in 6 hours (going really slow), and I'm tempted to play again to change dialog choices and see how much things change. The art style is very nice, and the music is strong too.  I can't really put into words why I liked this game so much, but I definitely recommend it to anyone who wants a spooky (not scary, spooky) game that really explores people's interactions with each other. Strong story, strong characters, beautiful world, unique interactions, and strong music add up to a different, and very worthwhile experience.

Boundless is one of those Minecraft-like games where you explore, harvest resources, build shelters, and craft items.
Visually appealing, this is really the strongest thing Boundless offers.
After travelling through 4 or 5 different biomes, one thing is consistent - this is a world of tall mountains and hills with very little flat surface. You must constantly press the spacebar to hop up to the next block, making travelling a slow and frustrating process. Other games like this solved this issue by allowing the player to automatically hop up a single block without having to use the spacebar.
The caverns are typically a deep vertical drop. I rarely came across any that opened up horizontally, or had a gradual descent. Instead of being a fun exploration, it was a “chore” of navigating down to the lower level without dying. I ended up avoiding them altogether because it wasn’t worth the time or effort this early in the game.
Building & crafting are pretty standard affair for a game similar to Minecraft. A grindy task of gathering the right materials to craft the item you want to make. Nothing new stood out in terms of how crafting worked. This isn’t a negative or positive - that’s just how these games play out.
Wildlife - strangely in the 4 or 5 biomes I explored, there appears to be 2 creatures that populated the world, Wildstock and Spitters. I would assume others exist, maybe hidden deep within the caves, but I didn’t see any. A lot more variety in the creatures that inhabit this world would go a long ways in giving the illusion that that this was a fully fleshed-out world.
I never ran across any players, but I did find a handful of their homes - typically build on a hillside or mountain due to the lack of a flat surface. To the game's credit, player homes and items are protected from theft or destruction by other players.
Throughout this experience, I was frequently getting pop-up messages telling me that I was about to be teleported back to the starting location in 30 seconds. This suggests that the game has serious stability issues.
To sum it up, this is a game that tries at competing with Minecraft and other clones like it. Visually appealing and offers protection from theft, but it falls flat in everything else. Exploration is a frustrating experience and there is little variety of wildlife. Crafting and building isn’t remarkable. And to top it off, you get annoying pop-up messages about getting pulled out of the game.
This game sells on Steam for $34.99 US - that’s a steep price for any game of this genre. Especially for a EA game that rightfully needs to be priced around $10 to $15 with what it actually delivers on.
So with just barely over 3 hours of gameplay, and a complete lack of desire to see what else this game has to offer, I am giving Boundless a thumbs down.
If the developer wants to comment, please do - for a game that has been on Steam for 3 years, I would most like to know what is the long-term plan for Boundless and when is this game going to be fully released.

Wow... Just wow. I really didn't know what I was getting myself into when I bought this game. I thought it looked cute, and a little spooky. I thought it'd be a fun ride but it was so much more. I haven't felt this moved and emotional since I played Undertale. So, where to start?
Well if you look at the basic stuff  that you tend to look for in a game, it's all pretty decent. The art style was odd at first but seemed to grow lovelier the longer I played. It felt so innocent like a cartoon I might have seen on Disney in the 90's or perhaps from an episode of Kim Possible. But it was a clever deception on the part of the developers that lulled me into a sense of safety before anything bad happens. The music is also well done, if a little repetitive at times, but it changes on you just enough that I wasn't too bothered by it. Not only that, but the music suited the mood and whims of the game so well, that there were moments where i was seriously concerned for the characters just because of the change in music.  This, combined with astounding voice acting that sucks you in, really made the difference.
All of that aside though... what really hit me with this game was the story. When the game starts I'm thrown into a conversation with the characters without a life vest and have to feel my way out. But it was just what I needed. It forced me to focus on the other characters. Learn about every body's personalities and history, and the more I learned, the more I forgot they weren't real. I grew to love all of them. Even Clarissa, who it turns out has a softer sweeter side I didn't expect. I genuinely wanted to help them and when I failed on a puzzle or watched as someone pluged to their death: I was terrified!
You know... I was curious about the meaning behind the name Oxenfree. So I looked it up on wikipedia and it said something to the effect of "a catchphrase to indicate that players who are hiding can come out into the open without losing the game". That is what this game is about. More than ghosts, or time warps, or all the other terrifying and wonderful things that this game has in store. For me this game was about real people exploring who they really are, how they feel, and finally coming out and saying it. Being honest without losing "the game". And hot damn, it was worth every minute. I cried, and I laughed. And when the game had ended, all I wanted was to go and play again.
Forgive me if I don't go into much more detail than that. I really don't want to spoil this game for anybody. It is something that needs to be experienced first-hand for yourself. It's not a long game, but it's memory will be sitting with me for a long time to come. If you love games that catch your heart and leave you thinking, then I know you will love this game beyond a doubt.

This game was released September 30, 1999, and over 13 years later they re-released it on steam with a new expansion. They are STILL releasing expansions for this soon-to-be 18 year old game. If that alone doesn't tell you how fun this game is, then nothing will.
But if for some reason you do need more information, I'll try and help with that too. If you played this game earlier in life and loved it, then get it; it's got everything the original game has plus new civilizations, maps, units, etc, etc. If you haven't played this game before, then I still highly recommend it. It's got a ton of great game modes for different play styles, a great selection of world civilizations to choose from, multiplayer (<-which I have yet to have a problem with), steam workshop, and a bunch of great ways to just kill your enemies (use a couple onagers and a wall to slaughter a contingent of infantry, use trebuchets to carve a path through the trees to kill your brother while he struggles to fend off a horde of untinking AI, destroy your brothers docks in an island match so he can't sail his war elephants over to kill you, get pushed into a tiny corner of the map with access only to trees and still somehow come back to kill everyone).
The game also teaches great micromanaging skills. It teaches inflation, start the game paying 14 gold for a hundred stone, and end the game paying 700+ gold for one hundred stone. It teaches the importance of manipulating your enemies' religious beliefs to get them to do what you want, and it teaches the uses of exploiting religious relics fro monetary benefit.
This game also taught me to respect the Eastern Roman Empire. The double walls of Constantinople will rise again!

NaissanceE is the nicest walking simulator I've played. The challenges are thought provoking, but simple. The first person platforming can be irritating. The breathing mechanic feels oddly out of place in a game where nothing chases you.
However, I wouldn't have it any other way. The puzzles aren't why I'm here. I'm here to immerse myself in the atmosphere, the environment. Experiencing in first-person the megastructures of the first few levels makes you feel small, insignificant. And I love it. The claustrophobic tunnels of the stages afterwards aren't as aesthetically enjoyable, but the level design is just as intriguing.

Age of Empires II HD is a high-definition edition of the classic real-time strategy game adds little more than bugs.
- Includes the great Age of Empires II and its expansion
- Solid Steam Workshop support
- Multiplayer is a buggy, broken mess
Overall, I give this game a 6.5/10 because it has enormous potential. After all, the base game is still enjoyable and visually attractive (excepting the units that were never beautiful), and you can smoothly download content from the Steam Workshop. However, the HD edition fails to improve on the original's gameplay in any way, and numerous bugs mar what should be an excellent multiplayer experience. Hopefully, Hidden Path will eventually fix the problems so that epic eight-player matches with hundreds of units on each side can entertain strategy fans until our civilization, like ancient Rome, falls and fades into the annals of history.

For this review, I'll briefly focus on the good, meh and bad of the original mobile version before talking about the Steam version.
Good:
- Without too many issues, you can complete the game without spending a single dime if you're patient enough.
- A lot of stages, units etc.
- Good presentation.
Meh:
- Play this game in short bursts, because the gameplay can get repetitive and shallow. Though, there are rare occasions where there are stage hazards (invincible enemies underneath the playing field shooting upwards etc.) to mix things up.
- More grinding sessions than a dollar strip joint, but there is Autoplay for already completed levels and the occasional Raid option to cash in directly.
Bad:
- Medal prices are a TOTAL scam, given the huge amount of expensive units and items. Standard price is 30 Medals for a buck, while the sale price (100 for a buck) makes much more sense and should be standard instead. This is THE major flaw of the game.
- YMMV, but if you meet cheaters online, they WILL anger you for at least a minute.
===================
Now, moving on to the Steam version:
It has no improvements over the mobile version, it's a direct port. In fact, it's worse. It's in fact a bigger scam because you can't even buy units with Medals, you can only use real money. Not only that, you HAVE to buy them in packs, you can't pick the ones that you want.
Verdict: I don't know what's worse; this or King of Fighters 12.

Talos Principle is a portal-esque first-person puzzler set in a world where you are an AI that is trying to understand the world you are in, while solving puzzles to progress to new areas.  The game slowly introduces you to new items and combines them to make the difficultly progress throughout the game, but rarely ever feel over-burdening.
There was the odd puzzle that really stumped me (such as Eagle's Nest), but the more difficult challenges are left for unlocking gold stars, which you can skip if you want and still experience the core storyline to the game, but I enjoyed the game enough that I worked through till I eventually unlocked everything.
The game designers have done a good job of making you find new ways of using the items you are given to complete the puzzles, which helps the game stay fresh as you go along. The voice acting is well done, and although the graphics are fairly plain compared to modern (2017) standards, this didn't detract from the enjoyment.
A definite recommendation if you like this genre, and I would recommend the Gehenna DLC too.

So now we're at the third game of the series and after the events of the second game, Marine is now left without her very very useful fairy companion and only has five out of thirteen warriors and not much time left along with not many places left to explore.
The third game picks up where the 2nd left off.  Also, this time you get to keep the characters you recruited in the second game for the whole adventure.  You'll also be able to pick up Hirado for part of the game and Karine until the ending.
One thing that is different in this game is a good chunk of the dungeons are more side scrolling and you jump from place to place.  There are still dungeons that are the more traditional top down view as well.
Overall, this game has a much more solid story and more interesting characters than the second game had and one of the better endings.  This is a lot more solidly recommended than the second game was and overall the 3rd and 5th games are probably the best in the whole series, with the 4th being close behind.  This is definitely where the series starts to shine.
Overall pros:
+The side scrolling perspective is pretty neat and changing things up makes things more interesting
+Definitely a lot more customization is possible here and there are multiple solid parties to have.
+The lack of Jeanne for the game actually does make it more challenging and you have to change up your tactics.
+A very good plot for this game to add to the overarching one.
Neutral points: (Stuff that may be good to some and not so good to others)
&The banter between Jack and James.  It can be considered funny to some, but may be grating to others.
&For a large chunk of this game it seems like Marine is being distracted from her quest to help Jack and Salome and it's repeatng the same issues as the second game had.  It actually ended up being to her benefit, but we won't find out why until the beginning of the fourth game.
Overall cons:
-If you are importing, the cap to imported characters is even more annoying in this game.  The biggest annoyance was having to spend a good amount of time to get Abu back his Cure KO ability.  That does give this game a slower start than the second had.
-If you are a completionist, this game has some very annoying missables.
-There's a really annoying bug that randomly unequips the Eternity Trident from Salome late in the game and it can happen at very frustrating points.  Make sure to check after every battle to ensure she's still got it equipped because if she goes back to human form, you have to rest to get her back to mermaid form.
Also a note on this game's official guide as well.  The guide for this game is the worst of the series.  It's worth getting on sale because it does have some useful tips and the maps are great to have.  However, expect to also have to look elsewhere for quests and secret rooms since those aren't all detailed in the guide.  Also, the guide posted on Steam is a great supplement to help with 100%ing the game.
So overall, very solid entry and after playing this one I can see why the series is so well regarded and very much recommended.

Millennium 3 is the 3rd installment of the 5 part Millennium series.  Yes, that means you should probably start with the first one.  That being said, each part is different.  The main character remains the star but the story stays fresh with a blend of characters from the first two along with some new recruits.  You can import your save game from 1 to 2 to 3 etc. and you get to keep your gear so that makes the series more rewarding.
The plot in M3 is quite enjoyable.  The level design is nice and includes some big dungeons.  So far, I found the characters in 3 the most interesting.  There is also a lot of humor in the game with funny dialogue between characters.  The main difference between 3 and the first 2 is that M3 uses a lot more side scrolling maps.  At first, I found it a bit strange but you get used to it and it adds some visual variety and some fun jumping adventures for Marine.  Otherwise, the plot is building up to the tourney at the end.
The game has a lot of achievements that are fun to get.  If you are an achievement hunter, play the series on hard mode.  It's not too bad (I typically do not play games on hard mode) and you'll get a lot of extra achievements for it.
If you're on the fence about this game, keep in mind that on Adorlea's official site you can play a demo of the full game that lets you play the actual game for 1 hour.   I would recommend that you start with Millennium 1 however.  You can play each game as a stand-alone, but it will be harder and the plot / characters won't be as meaningful.
Overall, Millennium 3 is a very fun third part of a great rpg series.  Aldorlea's RPGs remind me of SNES rpgs, which I consider the golden age of RPGs. (Chrono Trigger, Final Fantasy III, Earthbound, etc.)   If you enjoy character driven rpgs with some humor, you can't go wrong with the Millennium series.

Divekick is a fighting game you won't need to spend hours in a training mode practicing combos that'll never land anyway in order to get better. You may not immediately click with its unique parody of fighting games and general poking fun at the fighting game community, but at the very least, you'll probably be pretty good at Divekick by the end of your first match due to its elegance in simplicity.
1 Dive Button.
1 Kick button.
1 hit and you're dead.
5 rounds won and you're godlike.
1 hell of a good time.
That's all you really need to know to get started playing Divekick. Jumping and kicking moves you forward and pressing the kick button while on the ground hops you backward, which can  you can also attack during. You couldn't ask for something more approachable.
Divekick's depth comes from managing the space between you and your opponent and trying to outwit one another to land that crucial winning blow. All thirteen characters have unique kick angles and characteristics that are suited for beginners (Dive and Kick) all the way up to characters that require a lot of skill and patience (S-Kill and Stream).  All special moves in the game are activated by pressing both buttons at once on the ground or in the air. It's just up to you to figure out how to best utilize them.
Multiplayer is what makes Divekick truly shine. While the AI can be good for getting to know your character a bit, the game's honestly a much better affair when paired with other players either online or locally. The implementation of GGPO keeps matches online mostly silky smooth, though the lack of a proper 4-8 player lobbies is a bit of a bummer.
Even if Divekick is targeted at folks who love their fighting games, its simplistic approach, low skill barrier for entry, and lighthearted nature make it easily recommendable and enjoyable for anyone simply looking to have a good time.

In a nutshell, I would put this game somewhere in the space between the later part of the Myst series (or perhaps even Obsidian, if you are more traversed in the puzzle-adventure genre), Antichamber and Half Life (1).

The atmosphere, scale and foreboding sci-fi loneliness is fantastic. No doubt, the designers made a smart move by holding back on fancy textures in order to concentrate on what makes the particular graphics of this game so spectacular. The soundtrack is to die for, think Blade runner meets Prometheus with a hint of Akira. In four words - synthesizer sci-fi film noir.

The story is minimalistic, at best. But for me, this was in no way a bad thing. Simply put: you are lost, deal with it. The game play in itself is quite straight forward, first person platforming with occasional environmental puzzles. Although when you happen upon a an “actual” puzzle you will know it, the traversal of the world itself can in many cases present like a form of puzzle solving. Some of these specific platforming puzzles can be straining (read: frustrating) due to the inherent problems with the “first person platforming” medium, but these moments are (according to me) few and far between.
If you like the sense of scale and loneliness from Myst, the type of first person platforming made famous by Half Life, and mind f-ing absurdity in the stylings of Antichamber, then this game is for you.
