A cult classic from the creators of Dishonored, Dark Messiah is an interesting game.  It's listed as an RPG but that's misleading; it's like calling Dishonored an RPG.  Both have skill trees, both have a very small amount of decision making which results in low chaos vs high chaos in Dishonored.  Without spoiling anything, Dark Messiah is similar in that regard.  It's not truly an RPG, you don't have control over your character's physical and personality attributes and there are no dialogue choices or anything like that.  There are simply three major plot decisions.
One particularly interesting aspect in this game is that you don't necessarily play as the good guy.  I'll just leave it at that without spoiling much.
This game is known primarily for its gameplay mechanics, combat in particular.  It's a first person action game that has separate skill trees for melee combat, magic, archery, as well as some miscellaneous skill trees.  Furthermore, there are different types of melee weapons to choose from: twin daggers, swords, and staves.  Each has different properties, pros, cons, and combat animations.
One of the best features of this game's melee combat is that you have different swings/strokes depending on your movement.  Holding W and releasing a power attack for example delivers a different attack than holding A + power strike.  This is something I've demanded for years, and this is one of few games that offers it.
Most spells are offensive and elemental based but there are some exceptions.  The player is expected to go down every weapon skill tree apparently, since archery is too useful in boss fights.
This being a source game, it's almost entirely physics based.  Arkane Studios took advantage of this and emphasized using the environment to kill your opponents.  Knock down a bunch of heavy debris on them, kick them off of a cliff, impale them on spikes, you name it.  Combined with the ability to chain spell effects and other things together (e.g., spill oil on an area and light it on fire with a fire spell or arrow, or shoot a lightning spell into water to electrify it), Dark Messiah seems to provide more ways to kill opponents than any other game, and you can see from my library that I've played a lot.  Even more ways to kill people than Dishonored, which lacks the environmental emphasis.
People often say that The Elder Scrolls games should have this game's combat.  They are absolutely right.  Conceptually, this game has the best combat mechanics of any action game.  However, despite everything I just said, the gameplay/combat is riddled with flaws/oversights, the game lacks an engaging story/plot (RotFodder's pizza analogy is spot on), and it may be a bit too long for its own good.
The combat is fantastic on paper but has flawed execution.  First of all, the game is quite rough around the edges and clipping issues are fairly common which is extremely annoying.  There are some stupid delays when blocking attacks and counter attacking, or using daggers, and other situational things like that.  Also, unlike most first person action games, you actually have to be very precise with your swings.  It seems like the player's hitbox with melee weapons is actually the weapon itself; this makes sense, however it's not good in practice.  This type of thing only works in a game with very precise swinging and more fluidity, like Shadow Warrior and Dark Souls games.  Reach/range is really wonky in this game.  Goblins seem to have the same reach as humans and orcs.
At the end of the day this game comes across as quite clunky by modern standards, but by 2006 standards it must have been a gift from God (I didn't play it in 2006 but I've played plenty of 2006 games in 2006, Red Steel was the best action game I had played at the time).  Because of it's clunkiness I find it less enjoyable than Dishonored as an action game.  Dishonored's mix of advanced action mechanics and unbelievable, flawless fluidity is only matched by Shadow Warrior and Shadow Warrior 2 as far as first person action games go.  But then Dark Messiah has so many advantages like the environmental uses, spell/effect combos, and more varied melee attacks than Dishonored.  As usual, we'll never get it all.
Dark Messiah is known to be challenging, but it has that old school unbalanced challenge where if you raise the difficulty, enemies just deal far more damage than you even when using the same attack.  It will take around ten flame arrow spells to kill a regular human opponent for example, but they can kill you in four (and that's with upgraded max health).  If you like unbalanced no holds barred difficulty then perhaps you'll like this, otherwise I recommend sticking to Normal mode which is more balanced.  I favor balanced difficulty with smart AI.  This game's AI is functional enough although hilariously bad at times.
Dishonored is known for its stealth, and that's one area where this game lacks.  It's far more linear than Dishonored, the climbing system is awfully clunky and barely works (clunkier than Thief Gold's even), and you're generally unable to one hit kill enemies from behind even with backstab.  This game is clearly meant to be an action game first, stealth game secondary. Dishonored and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided are the only games I've played that are equally proficient at both.
In terms of atmosphere, this game bears an uncanny resemblence to Thief at times.  Some sections even tricked me into pressing Thief's key bindings!  The resemblence is so strong at times, particularly in crypts.  This game also has a Rope Bow for shooting rope arrows into wooden surfaces... sound familiar?  Although Thief's rope arrows are less restricted and work more often.
It's no secret that this game relies entirely on its combat.  The plot and all of the dialogue are pure cheese.  It's cliche after cliche.  Character development is mostly non existent.  This is all intentional though, the game is not meant to have an enthralling story or serve as a drama of any sort.  It's just meant to provide a challenging but very fun killing experience.  It mostly does that, although its clunkiness and lack of polish makes it frustrating at times.  Plenty of times this game would get tiresome and repetitive, but then I'd unlock a new ability and all of a sudden it's fun again until I use that ability many times.
TL:DR - This game is all about killing things and it has very good killing mechanics overall, the best on paper as far as action games go but the fact that it's somewhat clunky and very unpolished can make it annoying.  It's meant to be fun and challenging, and it mostly succeeds but with a number of hitches.  It drags on a bit and gets tiresome toward the end.  Decent game, I'd love a sequel on Source 2.

This is a great kart racing title, especially for PC: the port is pretty solid, and performed well for a mid-range laptop (AMD Radeon 6650M with 1.9 GHz Dual Core AMD A4 3300M). Mods basically transform you favorite racer into the best racer suited to your needs, as it modifies stats in such a way that you can basically have the same stats as other racers by default. Each racer has around 5 mods each and also the default mod.
WORD OF ADVICE BEFORE PURCHASE: This game requires you to play the Single Player World Tour Mode in order to unlock most characters. Most characters CANNOT be unlocked in any way, shape or form via alternative means. The World Tour Mode also has a ridiculous difficulty spike for some Normal Missions, and both Hard and Expert modes. It is required to play through missions in harder difficulties to earn enough "Stars" to unlock content and to unlock more missions to then unlock more content. If you want to play this with friends as a pick up and play, you might be dissapointed. Try finding a save file somewhere on the internet, if that is even possible?

So I got AoE 2 a couple of days ago and haven't played too much, so this review is written from the perspective of a completely new player to the game.
Overall, Age of Empires is very enjoyable and brings a retro feel, which is kind of nice every once in a while.  Also, as you might expect from an old game, even a toaster could run Age of Empires, which is obsviously a positive.  I've not yet experienced any performance issues due to the game itself, only due to my terrible ping.
The gameplay itself is very enjoyable as well.  There are many strategies I have seen employed over my three online games already, and undoubtedly more that I haven't seen yet.  The way you play the game is entirely flexible and the game typically doesn't steer you in a particular direction (minus the tutorial, of course).  The many civilizations that you can play as further add to the game's flexibility; just find the one that suits your playstyle.  I'm very excited to see what strategies and tactics I can come up with using the various civilizations in future games.
Regarding the online community, there are many cool people online to play with.  Unfortunately, there are also a number of, let's say hostile players online, especially if you are the reason for a team loss.  If you jump into online play too early like I did, expect to be called an idiot several times per game...
TL;DR
AoE2 is thouroughly enjoyable, though it does have a steep learning curve.  Find your playstyle and you'll have a load of fun!

I am genuinely gobsmacked with this game. I have held off for a good while due to it being:
1. early access.
2. what looks like an expensive minecraft clone.
But, The trailers look so damn good and combined with the 20% sale on steam and a bout of insomnia I took the plunge and got it. I was ready to mash that refund button at 1hr 59mins if needed with my early access hating thumb....First of all you choose from a small selection of placeholder characters to start the game. No customisation options are in at the moment.(see comments for some info on future plans) Then the adventure begins. Initially it was pretty much as I expected. After the astonishing first look in game at the portals (genuinely amazing) from the staging area it progressed into Minecrafty like gameplay consisting of mining, exploring, crafting and building with great looking scenery and a much ignored feature in a lot of modern games, decent ambient sounds which really crank up the immersion. After 15 hours or so of enjoyable gameplay, I felt fairly self sufficient. So after setting up my little home by a lovely lake set into the side of a hill I decided it was time to go exploring.
What I found is what I believe sets this game apart and took it to another level. I found an entryway into its incredible interworld spanning portal system.  I saw the potential of it once I found a portal in someones home leading to what they called the "capital" (I think its called Moebius Manor on the starter world I am on). There I found an enormous interconnected hub of cities, shops, landmarks, statues and a never ending range of strange creations. I can only imagine the 1000s of hours it must have taken to create this. It was like living D&D Planescape for those that have read/played it. I had found sigil! Running thro a portal into a shop, then passing on into someones garden on a different planet, then finding myself in a medieval castle on yet another world. Amazing.
Now these portals, you can craft them, place them, link them across worlds (yes the game is not on a single world but across many). One shot use portals or fueled portals which remain active as long as you keep them fueled with shards. You could set up a shop in a cavern under a mountain, link the doorway to a portal, and open the other end to a door on a road in a settlement, giving you access to other players and also living your secret life as a hobbit away from civilisation.
Some of the highlights for me so far - A great (but currently awkward to use in some ways when underground) land claiming system, lovely visual storage methods, a great looking character upgrade system (skill points) which by the looks of it will promote specialisation when leveling the character, grappling, the amazing portal system, its runs pretty damn well.
20 years of just online pc gaming, and countless years spent on anything game related before that means I very rarely am surprised by games now and more usually I am disappointed but I have to say this one genuinely left me gobsmacked. Its potential is enormous. Its price could cause it some issues tho depending how it is priced at release. It needs a healthy community to thrive. If it gets it, that will be something to see.
Edit - Final thoughts: A lot of changes are happening with the game and some features are not fleshed out fully but from what I have seen so far I think it would be worth buying at release if it continues on its current course. Be aware that presently, concurrent player count is very low so expect to experience a lot of solo time.
I cant recommend early access to anyone. But I certainly would say stick it on your wishlist and keep an eye on this one.
I will update the review if anything changes my mind, or it gets released.

I remember seeing a review someone wrote about Insurgency, something to the effect that kids play CoD, adults play BF, and veterans play Insurgency.  Screw that, Vets play Squad.  Even in its early access stage the game runs smooth, and is fully playable.  It does have its frustrating things, like not being able to mantle over low walls and other objects like you can in BF and CoD, however it is still tons of fun.  It can be frustrating getting a squad leader that has no clue what they are doing, or just simply doesn't care.  And vice versa, it can seem to be a daunting task to fill the squad leader role, but it becomes second nature after doing it only a few times.  Just like in reality, as a squad leader you need to take the feedback of your soldiers and incorporate it into your plan.  Your soldiers will see things that you do not, so you should welcome feedback, it helps you learn the ropes of taking command and having that responsibility.
Communication is key, the entire enemy team could be filled with pro players, but noobs can stomp them into the dirt simply by communicating better.  It can be a pain to communicate on 2 different channels at once as the squad leader, on one side you have your squad, on the other you have the other squad leaders, but after doing it a few times its easy.
Don't micromanage your team, they have played the game, they can be a rifleman well enough, or a medic, give them the freedom to take some initiative and be a living, breathing, thinking tool for warfare.
I have only had the game for a few days, but im already in love with it.  If you want a shooter that is realistic, and based purely on communication and squad level tactics this is the one.  This game may not kill arma and put it to bed, but it will give it some serious competition once the full vision of the Devs becomes reality.
Its great, its a game, have fun playing it, and don't be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nazi dictator just because you are the squad leader, but don't be a douchegbag squad member that doesn't listen to♥♥♥♥♥♥ this game is based purely on teamwork at a 9 man squad level.  Don't be afraid as a SL to let your squad steer your actions, some of them probably have alot more time on the game than you do, and don't be afraid to give you SL suggestions either.  A good SL is stuck with their nose in the map and constantly on the radio, its easy to overlook the small things, keep your SL apprised of the little details from time to time so they don't forget about the squad level while trying to maneuver on the platoon level.  That may seem a little "out there" for some people, but the command structure of this game is seriously very accurate to real life rank structures.  The only thing missing is a breakdown of a squad into two 4 man fireteams, with team leaders per team taking orders from the SL and maneuvering as 2 seperate elements.
So keeping it short, if you are a vet, and you want to play a game that actually caters to veterans with combat experience and small unit tactics this is the only game you want to play, screw arma, screw BF, screw Insurgency, this is the closest you will probably ever get to reliving your glory days as an infantry team leader or squad leader in a virtual world.

The occasional boss creatures are also pretty cool. Levels are long and very well made, with plenty of secrets to find,

I cannot say anything about the multiplayer as I haven't played it, but I find the game to be worth getting regardless.

Despite only having played this game for 2 hours, writing a review of it that is less than 10 pages will be difficult. I usually dont like to do this, but there are so many thing going right and wrong for this game, Ive got to break it all up.
Graphics/Art Direction: The game looks fine, its graphics options are solid, and its use of light is phenominal. I understand and appreciate why it lacks color, and Ive got no problems with the game in terms of how it looks.
Level Design: This is where the problems begin. While the game does a great job of letting you scamper around HUGE structures, there are plenty of places in the game where what you have to do to advance is either unclear, poorly placed, or nonsensical. Also, while I appreciate the desolate look they're going for, the entire game could use a little more to make the environment look just the tiniest bit lived in. For people who say that would ♥♥♥♥ with the designer's vision; there are several rooms that are fully furnished and clearly designed to be lived in. Why cant we get a tiny bit more of that? Worse yet, the envionrment alternates between structures CLEARLY designed for human usage and traversal, and structures that are clearly not, with paths leading though both, with no real common sense defining the layout of the "city" (which appears to be what we're looking at). It goes several steps beyond abstract architecture. Also, for any who were wondering, there is no "story" or "plot" or background. Nothing is ever explained as far as I can tell, which is fine, but its just another thing to note. There are also multiple instances where they pull the old "all these rooms look alike and are chained together" gag, which gets old really fast, as well as some really poorly implemented non-euclidean elements that honestly come out of nowhere. This extends to easter eggs, many of which will force you to restart from your last save. I once got caught in a looping staircase that I couldnt get out of by going either direction, it took me a solid 10 minutes to realize that this was both not the way I was supposed to be going (there ARE several repetitive staircases in this game) and that I couldnt escape. WHY WOULD YOU HAVE SOMETHING LIKE THAT IN A GAME LIKE THIS?
Long story short; the level design is nausiating at times, but pretty to look at, and you will need to look up a walkthrough at least once.
Sound: This is probably the biggest failure of the game. Its sound design is like bad prog-rock; it almost seems designed to offend the sensibilities of those playing it. While sometimes it harmonizes with the game's atmosphere with long synth-horn sounds, a'la Bladerunner, most of the time its composed of random little background trills, clicks, whines, and other mechanical noise, which is a bit unnerving, but for the most part its just distracting.
Gameplay: NaissanceE is a first person platformer, so it has all the problems that come with that, especially since you cant see your feet. If you've played this kind of game before you know what Im talking about. On top of that, the distance you can fall and how much damage you take seems to change with the weather, with some 5ft drops putting you near death, and some 10ft drops getting landed with no problems at all. There is a sprint and sprint-jump mechanic which requires you to breathe with the bumpers (I played with a controller, sue me), but it doesnt really add anything to the game. For the most part you just look for new places to jump to, then move on. There are some fairly solid puzzles (I think I found 3 over the course of 2 hours), but they're not really anything to write home about. The game's biggest problem is that there appear to be rules that its not telling the player. For instance, there are a series of wind-tunnel areas in the game where you have to walk along the shaft of what seems to be some kind of windpower generator or something. Fine. At random, the game will just decide "♥♥♥♥ you" and push you back and kill you with a gust of wind. There is no text explaining WHY this happens, and no way of knowing WHEN it will happen, but it happens none the less. I suspect it has something to do with taking too long, but I cant be sure. Overall, unremarkable in the gameplay department.
Ive got so much more Id love to say about this game, because I sorta enjoy it, but I still feel the price is a ripoff. To boil everything down; its got nice environments that are sometimes intentionally annoying to navigate, the occasional puzzle, and horrible sound design, but for the most part its an unremarkable walking/jumping simulator. Just go play Mirror's Edge with your monitor's color settings turned down or something. I wouldnt recommend this game in a million years, or unless its price drops below $10.

On a very bored Friday where I failed to attend my college course, I decided that the zany scrapes of Sonic, and his new friends including Team Fortress, Shogun and Football Manager was for me. I installed the game during its free weekend and had no issues installing, the download was fast and despite the relatively small file size, the game had amazing graphics, or at least, as amazing as you can get with hedgehogs and Team Fortress characters.
My initial issues with the game included controls, the game is clearly designed for the use of controllers and more customised peripherals, like steering wheels with pedals. You cannot configure the controls or the graphic settings out of game which makes it quite annoying, especially if you're attempting to change your resolution or find out what runs best with your computer set up.
When I finally got into the game and began to drive around (as expected, I was Sonic), the game was relatively straight forward, and perhaps I wasn't looking clearly enough but the presence of a tutorial is extremely lacking, and I found myself looking at the control lists to understand what I was doing.
The multiple vehicle system was something very unexpected, but not entirely unwelcomed once I had adjusted. The boating system is a little awkward at first, but I eventually found myself enjoying the neat tricks you can perform once you're up in the water. Planes are extremely fun and as expected, driving is an absolute pleasure in this game. It's almost like driving along the higher hills of Scotland or Wales in the late summer.
The game is particularly easier than most other driving games, due to the fact you have weapons, and aiming is extremely simple, you can disarm your opponents using balls of ice, fireworks (don't try that at home) or even pufferfish. It makes the game truly dynamic and forces you adapt at every turn, using every skill in your arensal to evade the traps your opponents have set out for you.
The levelling system for your characters is extremely benefical, and allows you to customise your loadout depending on the map, this allows us to separate out the good drivers from the great ones, who will adjust their abilities according to their map. For people new to the game, the system helps ease them into customisation of their vehicles, but allows pro-players to efficiently edit their load-outs.
If you've got nothing to do this weekend, I highly reccomend this game. It's a fun little timewaster, and even if you don't enjoy racing games, you will find yourself lost in it.

NaissanceE is a first person perspective exploration/puzzle game.  The environments seem oddly made for human beings to navigate through them (stairs, doorways, tables, platforms) but yet are forebodingly pristine and devoid of any sign of human or animal activity.  It feels like being in the equivalent of a hamster trail made for human beings by an unseen superintelligent entity.  In that vein, it strikes me as eerily similar to the alternate universe at the end of 2001: A Space Odyssey.  This game is a work of art.  But it may not be everyone's cup of tea.  If you liked Portal, Antichamber, or Proteus, you will probably appreciate this game.

In short Wolfenstein: The New Order is story-driven FPS with sneaking and explosive action. The game is set mostly in 1960's Nazi-Europe. I played the game once through, took about 16h on über difficulty. Completed missing achievements in 3h. I have played both Wolfenstein 3D and Return the Castle Wolfenstein, but didn't know about 2009 version of Wolfenstein until after playing this one.
If Doom(2016) is a near-perfect upgrad to 90's shooters, Wolfenstein: The New Order brings the shooters from 99-04 to modern times. If you remember games like
, this is something very similar. Healthpacks and armor from the 90's era are still here, but so are the varying levels, scifi/fantasy settings and somewhat serious tone from the later era. Skill tree is there to remind us that this isn't just a graphics update but a part of an an evolution of a genre.
What W: TNO does right is the core mechanic. In First person shooters the shooting should be fun or atleast enjoyable. That hasn't been the case in quite many games in recent years. Most CoD4 look-a-likes have failed to understand that there should be something of a feedback from shooting people in games. I'm not talking about XP or pop-ups but a feeling that I'm doing something violent to another (virtual)person. So after I had charged through the trenches of the first level with dual wielded assault rifles, I took a long look behind me and saw a bloody mess. Although the gun sounds are somewhat lacking in this game, the effects on enemies made me feel like I was shooting guns, not playing laser tag.
Another thing W:TNO does right is it's skill mechanic. Although the skill mechanic is mostly boosting your existing abilities, it works like a charm and it rewards you for playing in a certain way. Unlike many other games with similar mechanics, you get certain skills for doing certain things. If you sneak, you unlock sneaking perks, and if you use explosive you unlock explosive perks. Progress towards skills is not lost on death, so it is relatively easy to obtain all skills during one playthrough.
The games atmosphere gets also an honorary mention. Although the plot revolves around the goofy idea of Nazi Germany winning world war 2 using robotic dogs, the plot stays dark from start to finish. The story sounds absurd but the game stays true to the idea. The world and it's characters act like it's the most natural thing and there exists only handful of moments where the game implies that this might be ridiculous. So the game isn't making fun of itself but let's the player decide if he takes it seriously or not.
The story relies heavily on characters and they are very well built. Most of the characters remain memorable even after just a short introduction. Enemies instill fear with their actions and your friend have their own reasons to keep on the fight. The soundtrack adds to the atmosphere though it isn't exactly true to the timeframe.
There are also some features to critique. The game is easy.  I usually pick the medium difficulty with games but in this case I changed to the hardest after 1 hour of playing and found that equal to medium in many other games. I barely had to replay any parts because there was plenty of armor and health around even on the hardest difficulty. The intelligence and the amount of enemies is also lacking so the game is easy almost to the finish line. Then again I like the fact that the difficulty only ramps up enemies damage, they mostly die quite easily on harder difficulties too atleast if you aim for the head.
The graphics are decent. The game worked just fine for me and looked good enough, but the inconsistency of graphics affected the experience some what. Forced depth of field, no simple AA-setting and some blurry textures made the game occasionally look unnecessarily ugly. Most levels where colorful and the level design was good enough for most of the time. There has been reported serious performance issues with AMD GPU's and the game has  frame-caps so do some research before buying if you think these might affect you.
So it's a fun shooter with a decent storyline. Sure it's not the game of the decade, but well worth the 7 euros it costs these days. If you're not into FPS games, this hasn't got anything radically new in it for you to try it. If you happen to like single player FPS-games, this is a must buy.

I have forever steered clear of Early Access titles. I'm a skeptic, maybe even occasionally a cynic... and this game, ever since becoming an early supporter over two years ago, has been an incredible surprise.
For me - this game is the first exception to investing in Early Access.
I've been playing online games since the days of MUDs (MMOs without pictures, for the kids out there). I played a lot of Meridian 59... and had my entire life devoured during the first week of the release of one of the early MMOs with actual graphics - EverQuest.
This game is one of the first games in a long line of attempts that has brought me the same sense of adventure, wonder, and 'stop what I'm doing and look at the scenery and environment' moments as some of the games that I regard as classics. Everything from the subtle ambient sounds, to the huge open world, leaves me feeling like I'm exploring an untouched new world.
I'm a climber and backpacker, and I spend a lot of time exploring places that often feel as if they've never been seen by another person... and this game brings me hints of that same sensation.
Aside from the sense of wonder and adventure, the Devs are highly active, respond to feedback and suggestions, and have been hands on with this game on a day to day basis since I first backed it years ago. I have never felt like my investment has been abandoned. I've put a lot of hope into this game, and the Devs have responded with a very obvious passion and love for this game... and they continue to do so.
The skill tree continues to grow throw development, and those of you who enjoy crafting, building, exploring, and investing in a character, a home, and a world will absolutely love this game.
In short, there are few games, if any, that I would every as highly recommend as this one... and I rarely leave reviews. I'd rather be playing... which is what I'm off to do now.

Awesome puzzle game. It has all I like in a puzzle game: good puzzles (of course) and an interesting story that gives me a reason to solve them (no matter how good they are, if the game is just a dry collection of puzzles, I just can't be arsed to solve them).
The game has you collecting "sigils", tetris-like pieces, that you use to unlock new levels and progress in the game. In order to get to those sigils, you need to use several tools to navigate closed levels by unlocking doors and disabling traps. You start with levels that are solved using only one tool and as the game progresses, new tools are added to your collection, keeping the challenge fresh.
You appear from nothingness in this strange world with a robot body, and a God-like voice tells you to collect the sigils to gain the divine favor and enter some sort of Heaven. You don't really know where you are or what's going on really, but as you progress, you find terminals where short pieces of text give you some background that allows you to sort of figure out what's all about. A misterious entity in the terminals will also make you think about what it means to be human, and question the intentions of the voice. Quite interesting stuff.
The writing is done by Tom Jubert (FTL, The Swapper), and indeed this game has left me with the same sort of positive vibes as The Swapper did.
Totally recommended.

Probably time to write a review...
If you're interested in teamwork, communication, coordination, and tactical gameplay mixed with good visuals (easily has the best explosion effects of any FPS), excellent sounds, smooth animations, and a swathe of game features and content from building a Forward Operating Base in whichever way you like (any combination of sandbags, HESCO barriers, razorwire, HMG bunkers, resupply points, etc... and many more to come in the future) to experiencing realistic equipment in the hands of real life factions like the US Army or an Eastern European militia.
However, the real incentive should be knowing that the game is in pre-alpha, and that there's much, much more to come. There's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of new features and content, on the drawing board and in development, that will eventually make an appearance in Squad. Everything from tanks and helicopters to the ability to drag the bodies of incapacitated teammates is planned (see the following link for a full list of confirmed features).
My advice to the prospective buyer who's on edge about cashing in $40: monthly development recaps are posted at the end of each month on Squad's website
. Read through a few previous recaps, and if you're feeling patient wait until the end of this month for the January recap, and get an idea of what's in development and what to expect in the near future. Right now, that's the Stryker APC for the US Army, a British faction, mortars for FOBs, and more.
My only gripe right now is performance. The devs are well aware of it, and the last major update (V8) drastically increased performance. Focus on optimization and more performance updates in the future are to be expected. I have a mediocre/decent gaming laptop (GTX 960M, i7-4720, 16 GBs RAM), and run with basically everything maxed for 25-30 FPS. Conveniently enough, I am both a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ and have low standards for framerates from many years of potato PCs, so while this may horrify you (I really don't understand the people whining that they have to have 60 FPS), it doesn't bother me in the slightest, and the game looks fantastic. I could lower my settings for 50-60 FPS and still have the game look great, but I'm a bit of a purist that way. So while performance is no no way whatsoever a gamebreaker, it could be (and will be) better. If you have an AMD, I would be especially careful about buying Squad if performance is a real worry, as AMDs don't do as well on Unreal engine (not a Squad issue, but an engine issue, and Unreal is looking into this).
Anyway, that's my piece.

After spending 7 hours in this game for one playthrough of it, I stare at my screen absolutely dumbfounded, attempting to find words to describe.
Oxenfree starts off as a a typical 70's, 80's, 90's-type "high schoolers go to a party & weird♥♥♥♥♥♥happens" kinda plot line. Even boiled down to getting drunk & maybe high on a secluded island. & Then you go exploring & that's when the weird♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. Simply put: the island is haunted. As cliched as it sounds, it's the characters that drive the story; that get you attached to; that you fall in love with.
You've got Clarissa: the person who hates you for hates you for seemingly no reason. But, there's a reason. & You may or may not agree.
You've got Ren: your best friend, a goofball, but a bit of a slacker.
You've got Nona: Ren's love interest & Clarissa's friend. She's...nice. Not much more to her, honestly.
You've got Jonas: your new step-brother, serious, but knows how to relax.
You've got Michael: your biological brother who is possibly the reason for your parents' divorce; I'll let you figure that one out.
& Then you've got Alex: That's you. That's who drives the story. That's who makes the decisions.
Gameplay-wise, it's a lot of getting from Point A to Point B. What's unique about it is that you're given a radio to use along the way. It's pertinent to the story & gameplay. Finding secrets, progressing the plot, fixing problems, even just listening to some random music on it (which is a nice little polish), etc. The radio is everything.
CHOICES MATTER. What you say matters. As I said, the story is the major driving point of the game. It's a "choose your own adventure" game; one that works, because there's a lot of games that way that have feature but, in the end, they don't REALLY matter. This game has many endings, & many lines of dialogue that affect further dialogue.  You can even choose not to say anything & just let the dialogue choices fade out (that is an achievement).
The dialogue actually feels natural. The way the characters interact with each other all feels real. I must commend the voice actors for managing such a feat. They are truly talented.
The sound & ambience fits the atmosphere. Early on, it's cheery & peppy, but gets more eery & dark the further down the rabbit hole you go.
Being as it's a bit of a side-scroller, the character models are very simplistic & not much to look at. The background, however is gorgeously painted; it looks hand-painted in all honesty. You also collect pictures as time progresses, & they're somewhat simple, but charming in sort of contrast to the rest of the game that somehow still matches.
Conrols...just hit left, right, up, down, do an action, look at map, mess with the radio. Very simple. Not much to it. It's fluid & it works.
The ending though...or, at least the one I got...it'll ♥♥♥♥ you up. I'm one of the few people who doesn't give 2 ♥♥♥♥♥ about spoilers, & I don't want to spoil it. Because it had that much of an impact. I have not been left speechless by a game's ending like that in a LONG time. It had me on the verge of tears, & I'm not a cryer
I want to say that this game has replayability because there are multiple endings & secrets to get but...it's definitely a game you can't play a first time again. You can go back into it with a different midnset as far as what you're going to do & what you choose, but you CANNOT play it a first time again.
I wish Steam had a better rating system other than recommended or not. Because, it's honestly worth more than $20; I'd pay about $35, & I bought it on sale. Definitely buy this game. Definitely play it. You will NOT regret it.
If you're reading this, I can only assume you read my full review. This is my first seriously thought out review & I hope I did well. Thank you for your time.

At first I was a little put off by Divekick. I'm sure most of you know what I mean. A game that was originally a joke, has only two buttons, and technically doesn't offer the full fighting game experience. HOWEVER, and yes it must be caps, Divekick is a wonderful fighting game! The gameplay is fast and tactical. Fights are very match-up based, but don't count out skill. Yes there is strategy, and yes skill does matter. Reaction time, knowing the character you're up against, and personal play-style are all very important factors. At a glance, this looks like a game you could pass on. I was worried I'd play it for five minutes and be done with it. Yet I find myself smiling and laughing all the time while playing. Online is well implemented and exciting. Characters are so different from one another that there is a lot of space for you to expirement and develop your own unique style of playing. Seriously, I don't know how many ways to say "This game looks simple, but don't judge a game by it's jokeyness." Divekick is a silly, yet serious fighting game just as Borderlands is a serious, yet silly FPS/RPG. I'm not saying it's GOTY material, but I'm saying it is well worth the $10 price-tag. I'd recommend this to all fighting game fans, whether or not you're into 2D fighters. If I went back in time to fix mistakes from my past, I would make sure to buy Divekick again! It's really good, and very fun! Isn't that what gaming is all about?

Single best modern day shooter out there at the moment.
Does everything that the description promises, a tactical squad based shooter where the focus is not in the individual but in the group as a whole.
I've always loved and hated Battlefield series, and this game is the step up from the chaotic and frantic battles that series had. While it may be boring to watch, I promise you. The game has your heart beating fast every second you're even near a firefight.
This is due to following reasons:
AUDIO
-The game audio is absolutely fantastic. Gunshots echoing in the distance sound imho better than anything in battlefield where it is filled with surplus noise. The simple near miss of a bullet whirring and snapping past your head is enough to send shivers down one's spine. You hear the snap long before the gunshot itself and this alone leads to a horrifying tension that any second somebody could've already killed you without you even knowing it. This speed of sound delay and fairly closely authentic sound design is a masterpiece in sending the proper ambiance to the battlefield.
Especially when you've hit the deck after that near miss and you're crawling under fire hoping to your dear life you won't get shot.
VISUALS
-While not comparable to Battlefield series, it is still a fantastic game to look at and delivers a great set of battlefields. The effects themselves are beautiful and to me, they look quite realistic which only add to the overall feel of the game.
Once again I draw comparison to Battlefield game series where everything from maps to explosions looks like a hollywood blockbuster film. This game looks visually less cluttered and real, and you know that everything you see can be fatal, from shrapnel from explosions to bullet tracers. Again, this brings a lot of tension to the table. Seeing that puff of dust kicked by an explosion? Probably a teammate got himself blown to the afterlife.
GAMEPLAY
-Single most important piece of this game is the successful feel of killing the heroes. What has made me hate Battlefield series is the overabundance of vehicles, everybody jumping off moving airplanes to rpg others mid air to hijack another plane. It's pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and anybody who even attempts to drive a Humvee like it was BF is gonna get themselves shot in an instant, and this punishes the team since it means that's one less humvee for a good 20 minutes time, everybody hates those wannabe heroes for wasting assets and tickets. It's honestly beautiful. Everything in this game revolves around teamplay. Vehicle assets act great at supporting infantry elements and vice versa. Squads working together, one defending a fallback point from enemies trying to disrupt backlines to two squads attacking a hostile point while one flanks behind. If people cooperate as squads, it is the single most satisfying feeling I've ever had in a video game.
Weapons recoil properly leading to single shots being by far the most common firemode. It is great that not everybody is spraying and praying like no tomorrow.
This game is not Arma either, but it is the perfect middle ground for tactical military shooters. What makes it feel arcadey are the spawn points, but that's just a minor complaint.
To address some concerns you might have:
"The game looks boring, just walking for 15 minutes and dying without ever even having a chance to fire back! No thanks"
Yes, the game can look boring from the outside, but when you're controlling the character itself, it is intense as hell. Kills are not handed to you on a platter like they are in most other video games. Even if you begin taking fire, a good smoke screen can, and will save your life letting you retaliate and think about your options.
"The game is in early alpha"
Indeed it is, but the devs are implementing new features at a steady pace, and the performance has seen a great big boost over the last few months. Trust me, this project is worth supporting for.
An absolute must buy if you're into modern shooters where teamwork is paramount to survival and success.

I LOVE OXENFREE.
Now that I have that out of my system, here's some more text, to fill up some space. Oxenfree is a "teens being teens and there's ghosts" story. But it's so far from that stereotype it only barely fits. The narraration is excellent, the story is simple in premise but gets deeper the more you explore, and the radio is a really rad mechanic that somehow doesn't feel overused or frustrating despite being, well, the main mechanic.
Also it's GORGEOUS. I wasn't sure if I liked the style at first (tiny characters on a big background) but as I played it really suited the overall feeling and setting of the game. You're small, facing something huge, it works out. The soundtrack is also good at setting the mood and I'm very glad I bought it. Invoking a tense mood without a ton of jump scares or QTEs is a big feat.
With all that being said, I did have some glitches. My main issue was that one of the people following you in the game became stuck on climbing walls. I emailed the Night School team and received a response pretty quickly explaining it is a known issue and giving me a lot of options to fix it, which worked. I was pretty impressed by their team for responding to my email quickly and helpfully instead of getting an automated message so I'm kind of a fangirl now, oops.
So anyways - a good game that sets a really cool mood. It's the video game version of the stories your friends told with a flashlight under their chin, in a good way.

A free game, but not recommended if you're a free player. The free PREMIUM didn't quite work for me since I played the game a few years ago (before legs) so I played as a peasant player. It almost feels made to be frustrating if you aren't PREMIUM.
For example:
-When you get loot crates (playing games, logging in, purchasing, etc; the primary source of parts) there are two rows: PREMIUM row and peasant (not real name) row. The PREMIUM row, from my experience, is the only one to actually have a chance of Epic or Legendary loot, but if you aren't PREMIUM, you don't get the stuff that pops out of that row, as you may imagine. In my game time, I didn't end up getting a single Epic/Legendary, but they popped up often enough in the PREMIUM loot area.
-Recycling is another way of eventually getting parts, but the rate is like getting paid in pennies to save up for a car if you don't get the triple recycle rate & more/better items each game from PREMIUM. Ended up with ~4k "Forge" after ~4 hours, where the good parts are above 100k. Better get used to Uncommon and Rare weapons if you don't drop 50 big ones for the Beta.
There are also a few other issues, such as long wait times (in less active gamemodes) from low playerbase, stuttering, and hacking (didn't even see a report option; they seem to trust their Easy Anticheat. (EDIT: you can report people on the dev's website)) Some dude just hovered above the enemy spawn in suspended animation, insta-blowing up enemies around him every few seconds. They couldn't damage him.
Waaaay too much of a cash grab, especially for a Beta IMO. Doubly so for one that's been in Beta as long as this one. Acts like a phone app as much as they shove PREMIUM down your throat, reminds me of in-app purchases. I could consider $30, but $50 is way too much. I consider the asking price of $50 to be the price of the full game experience. You can also pay 10 bucks a month, but that stops being economoical very very quickly
I don't remember a great deal about the game from way back when, but I did notice a change that you CAN indeed form parties even if you are not PREMIUM. So that was a nice change. It's not a bad game if you drop 50 smackaroos and play with friends; mechs are always cool. Just doesn't feel worth $50, especially if you dealt with all the frustrations of not being PREMIUM. Maybe when it leaves beta. Props for not abandoning the game despite being in Beta for so long.
Should probably be noted that a friend I was playing with found it quite fun for the 3 days of his PREMIUM, but when we went over the stuff he was getting that I wasn't (and the price) he highly doubted he'd be playing when it ran out.
P.S., fixed some misobserved info.

Just finished ths game, and so far it is the best example of games as art that I have ever come across. So refreshing to not really have to have characters, or a story, or powerups, or a series of objectives... Just an intriguing world to explore; It's features stark, abstract, and sometimes beautiful, it's purpose unknown, and perhaps unknowable. The music is fantastic when it appears and is always tied in perfectly with the aesthetics of your immediate environment.
There are genuine challenges to be found here and there, mostly in the form of abstract logic puzzles, but what the game really strives to create for the 'player' (perhaps 'participant' is a better word in this case) is a series of utterly unique experiences, eliciting awe, wonder, confusion, anxiety and, in smaller measure, but no less memorably, joy. The sheer scale of some of the environments will blow your mind, while others will constantly challenge your perceptions and deny you a clear, point-A-to-point-B objective. It is one of the few games I have played with the maturity to realise the important role that can be played by minimalism. It has its frantic moments, but they are made all the richer by the quiet, meditative chapters that can be found in between.
You could potentially finish the game in 6 or 7 hours, so based on that alone it might be a bit expensive. But in terms of the amount of original ideas packed into one game, it really is excellent value. I can't recommend it highly enough to enyone who wants to experience something unique in their gaming life.

Once upon a time, on a cold desolate planet where the highest tempature ever recorded was 30 degrees fahrenheit, a colonist ship droped 6 humanoids onto the surface to make a community for its empire. They were not human, but instead a xeno race of cat-people called the Orassan, used to frozen planets and extremely cold tempature. They all got to work making their homes against the mountainside with a perfect defensible area to put up walls and two corridor-like entrences to their new home. They only relied on their survival meals and the hunted meat of the local fauna, which often times died within the traps set up. They had no need for heaters, for they were comfortable in tempatures that would kill a human without heavy elemental protection, thus saving them electric power used to generate the hyroponic basins to grow what other food they could muster. Several humans they resuced joined up and assisted the Orassan colonists in their daily lives, but the power had to be diverted more towards keeping the fragile humans warm while the kitty colonists constantly enjoyed the weather, especially the Orassan; Bee, who ran naked with her tail swaying happily outside in the snow while her human allies sought the warmth of the common room. But more and more humans came to the colony until the 6 xeno cats were outnumbered, but strengthened their bonds to the humans, the only issues in the colony weren't the frequent raids swept away from the Orassan firepower, but rather the food supply, or lack thereof. Soon two other humans joined that contributed nothing productive to the colony except for extra firepower, they were downed during a raid with pirate sappers in which the Orassan doctor had to euthenize them to end their suffering. Many were happy in the colony that the super ugly human was dead, but the real danger showed itself in the form of helpful supplies in the wrong places. On the last days of the colony, ship pieces fell onto several houses, killing 3 colonists while a random drop-pod supply killed another in bed... but the worst was yet to come. Another raid happened, this time tribespeople came into the killzone corridors to the colony, but one kitty colonist wasn't smart and stood right in the middle of it all, only to be accidently gunned down by her lover. Bee lost her beauitful tail and was later killed by a manhunter pack while sad she lost her tail. The last two colonists starved because they didn't know how to cook and refused to eat a raw potato. Thus ended the tale of the Orassan colony, Nachtigall of the Norden Sturm faction.

The game itself is good, really nice to spend some free time, and while it can get grindy at times its not so bad for a free to play, the reason for the negative vote? They totally screwed up the steam port, Here goes the full explanation.
The steam version is totally Pay to Win! :In the android/iOS versions of the game you can purchase new units with Medals, a type of currency that you can earn through wifi matches and completing maps, but in the steam port you can only use medals to buy items (fairly useless) and MSP (the other not so valuable currency), the units are only available as DLC on steam which means no real money = no new units, not to mention that they rendered medals now useless.
The port screams LAZY: There is no real difference between playing this on an android emulator than on steam, the graphics didnt get any rework so they look pixelated even in the lowest resolution, they didn't bother changing most of the text so you can still find instructions telling you to "tap the screen", and there are no new functions or shortcuts added to make use of your keyboard, click=tap and thats it, thats the port.
Inferior version than mobiles: The game was released in an earlier version of it compared to mobiles in every aspect except one, the units, the current steam version lacks some content and the event that is going on right now on mobiles for the game's first anniversary, while that is not much of a reason to complain as SNK will surely update it soon its clear what SNK's priority is, money. I didnt want to make an extra point for this but i must mention that you also cannot transfer the data from your mobile to steam so you have to start from scratch, without a chance to get shop units for free.
Thats it for my rant, as i said in the beggining the gameplay is really good, they gave the series a new aproach while keeping the whole Metal Slug feeling on it, and the process of gaining new units in mobiles gives the game a true feeling of progression, it just feels right, but as the game is right now on steam i cannot recommend it, if you really must give the game a try do yourself a favor and use an android emulator or play only the campaign and stay away from multiplayer in steam and hopefully SNK will soon realize their mistake and make the steam version as good and F2P as the others.
TL:DR: Lazy port, P2W, Mobile versions are much better. I swear i dont try to make text walls they just come up naturally.

After 2 new recruits, and a couple small raids of 2-3 tribesmen, we decided we needed to enclose our farms and houses with steel walls and steel buildings. With this completed we fortified the only entrance to our village.
The head shaman had been working on new magics in the great hall of the steelhut. After discovering advanced clothing like dusters and cowboy hats, as well as how to forge steel weapons and great bows. We set upon making these weapons and equipped our best hunters with great bows. But we were after a new magic: electricity. Our tribe had seen electricity before, in lightning storms and the machines, but out shaman believed we could harness it for ourselves. Though she predicted it would take many months to finalize.
Several months went by quietly, and winter was nearly upon us. Food crops had been plentiful and our hunters had bountiful hunts. Pemmican was stocked up, but electricity was still being researched. With only about a month left of research we hear an outsider call our tribe. A machine collector named Braun was being chased by a violent gang of people. My people did not want this outsider among us, but the shaman believed that perhaps Braun's knowledge of machines would help our people uncover the secrets of electricity. So we offered Braun residence, and prepared our warriors to defend our homes.
As Braun's arrived at the village the raiders after him had begun closing in. Braun went to grab a steel mace, as the pacifist shaman cleaned the great hall. As the Raiders closed in my people quickly realized they were outmatched as the Raiders carried rifles and guns. Our best warrior was shot dead almost instantly. A second warrior shared a similar fate right afterwards. Another warrior was downed so the shaman set upon rescuing her, but was shot by the raiders doing so requiring her to rest and heal after setting her friend down in the hospital bed. Next almost instantly two more of the warriors we're incapacitated, so the remaining warrior and Braun back up. The raiders advance killing Braun almost instantly before my warrior kills the raider attacking them. After seeing three of their own drop and so many of mine drop the raiders decided it was time to pick up their losses and grab our injured survivors and haul them off as prisoners.
Down to three villagers all injured we had to make do with doctoring. The least injured was the shaman who was first to recover and then began tending to the others. However warrior who survived his last stand began to come down with an infection. He died shortly thereafter. Soon due to all the death and destruction that occured our pacifist shaman went outside and then berserk. She began attacking all the local wildlife without remorse until a lowly squirrel tore her throat out... The person the shaman rescued recovered after these events and woke to find everyone around her dead, blood splashed on the walls and floors. So she did the only logical thing...she kept researching electricity. Being an excellent researcher she managed to discover the secrets to electricity in only a few days time, and armed with that knowledge swept out across the land abandoning the decaying husk of the fort she once called home.
10/10 would save someone to have my village overrun by mass gun wielding murderers again.

I'm a fairly deeply involved player of the Android version of this game, and despite my aversion to the F2P / pay-to-win game style that mobile game devs love, have spent a decent amount money over the months to get certain units for my "deck." I'm also a long-time fan of SNK, and Metal Slug in particular. But, for Playmore to re-release this mobile game on PC with no way to carry over your progress from the mobile versions, and then to give us (even more) exorbitant prices for non-basic units, leaves me disgusted.
I used to recommend the mobile version to my friends as an example of a F2P game done right -- nice pixel art, fairly balanced gameplay, from a developer I (used to) respect -- but the idea of grinding through the levels again only to have to pay in order to get units I've already spent months acquiring on the Android version an insult. Hopefully Playmore can do something to make it right, but the way it's looking right now, this is the last straw. I'm not spending any more time or money on the Android version, much less the Steam version. They added cloud save upload to the Android version a few revisions back; I doubt it'd be anything but a financial decision to not allow players from mobile to use their saves an the Steam version.

Everything was great, sun was shining, colonists were smiling. Then the Pirate Band attacked...
RimWorld is a top-down God/Colony simulator. Artistically similar to games like Prison Architect, RimWorld expands on the "do as I have commanded" gameplay of similar top-down titles, and throws in a healthy dose of colonial revolt, complicated romances, creepy breathing and calamity, just to make things exciting.
In this story, a colony of 5 that had crash-landed on a an arid, tree-less plain. It was cold, food was scarce and shelter was nowhere to be seen. A few seasons later, the colony was flourishing. Food and medicine a-plenty, other space-faring travellers found salvation when they joined the crew. They had healthy trade relations with other nearby colonies and tribes. A few disagreeances and minor arguments broke out between certain opinionated individuals, but for the most part everything was OK.
Then a pet boomalope exploded right in the middle of the trade plaza due to malnourishment. It exploded on one of their trade partners. They didn't like that.
A battle broke out, they escaped. They thought they were safe, but it turns out this outlander colony was allied with certain powerful people. Several more seasons passed.
I can still hear the mortar shells exploding around me... the cries of my colonists in pain... the crackle of the fire burning my colony to the ground...

Long story short, this game is gonna be more than just a game. It's going to be a social network in it's own right. It's simply amazing, and also in a very good state considering it's still an Alpha.
Now, for the longer version of this review, I'm gonna start with the negative bits first because there aren't many at all and not really "negative" but more consequences of an alpha version of a game that hasn't been marketed at all.
1) The game feels dead. This is because of it's early stage, so not really a downside, but for those like me who expect to see cities teeming with players (like in the trailer), you might want to put those expectations aside. There are still some select groups of players that are still active, mostly builders. The only con of inactive players is you can get bored pretty quickly if you're not too much into mining and building (on your own). Not a lot of social activities to do, although the forums are pretty active so if you try to bring people together, you will likely succeed.
2) Leveling up requires work. Don't expect to do some little tasks and grow in level. You need to put serious work down, such as mining and hunting. The good thing is almost everything you do in game earns you experience, so if you're active you can still level up quicker.
3) Complex skill system. I say complex because a beginner won't know where to start. Every time you level up, you get skill points, which you can use to learn all kinds of things such as crafting tools & equipment, crafting machines as well as abilities to enhance your character's speed, jump, tool usage, etc. There are literally a lot of skills, so before you start using your skill points randomly (like I did), have a look around all the skill trees and see what you can learn and use. You also get cleanse points with every level, meaning you can revert a skill back, but these CPs are limited, so you still have to be considerate when choosing your skills.
Now that I've narrowed down the negative bits, I'll be talking about why this game is awesome and why it's gonna be huge.
I see Boundless like the love child of Minecraft and World of Warcraft, with features drawn from a whole lot of other games as well.
1) The game allows you to choose your activity. You can be whatever you want. You can be a builder, building things for the community to admire and use. You can be a business owner, having a shop that makes you a lot of money. You can be a hunter. You can be an explorer. You can be a begger on the streets of Therka Market or in the slums of Krakendown.
2) Everything in-game is player made. All those huge cities and towns are built by players. Which is just amazing. Some of them are nicer than the others, but just the fact that a lot of people come together in one place to build settlements is just amazing.
3) Great trading system. You can buy and sell everything using shop stands or request baskets (think auction house). No need to stay online and chase people to do manual trading. Although you can do that too, which is awesome because it simply allows you to trade anything for everything. Wanna trade some wood for some iron? You can do it. Wanna trade that iron for some coins? Nothing can stop you.
4) Love the way using stuff works. You don't need to be special in order to use that high-tier item. If you got the dough, you can buy it. No need to gain skill points and materials in order to craft it. Although, if you're broke, yeah, you need to go down those caverns and get materials. Provided you don't jump in a lava pool by accident.
5) Going back to building, it just works. A lot of flexibility in building structures. Not a lot of content in terms of furniture, but there are a lot of block types and variations and you also get those chisels which are used to shape blocks to add that extra detail.
6) Again, related to building. Every player earns land plots with every level gained. To place a land plot, you need a beacon. Those beacons are using fuel in order to stay active. As long as a beacon is active, all land plots connected to it are indestructible by others. This means all your builds are safe, as long as you keep that beacon fueled up. This also ensures the land doesn't stay occupied if the owner is not active anymore and it also gives people incentive to play the game and keep everything up.
7) Portals. The main means of transportation in Boundless is portals. Just like the ones found in Valve's Portal. They're just awesome. Imagine having your house on a planet, and the bedroom is on a different one. It's that easy. Just walk into the portal and go out on the other side.
8) Planets. Everyone loves the idea of planets. Different places to go, with different flora and fauna (although there's not much diversity at this stage yet). But all those planets have a purpose, not just for the sake of it. There are 3 planets per region. Every planet has a level of difficulty which affects the level of mobs, the speed at which you mine and also the richness of resources. There are a total of 12 planets as of now, 3 for each region: Europe, Australia, US East and US West. What's crazier is each planet acts like a server. If you're from Europe, you can still visit planets from the US or Australia, but expect these to be a bit laggier than your planets.
There are a lot more awesome, tinier features, but these are the things that stood out to me. Again, the game is in it's early stages, so not a lot of players around which makes the game a bit boring at some point. But you can still meet people and have fun. Also because of the fact there aren't many people around, those who are are usually very nice and polite. Everyone's keen to help new players and build a family that will carry on through the main release.
I'd recommend buying this game. Even if you get bored of playing it, make sure you keep an eye on it's development because it's gonna be some big and eventually, you'll buy it anyway.

Probably time to write a review...
If you're interested in teamwork, communication, coordination, and tactical gameplay mixed with good visuals (easily has the best explosion effects of any FPS), excellent sounds, smooth animations, and a swathe of game features and content from building a Forward Operating Base in whichever way you like (any combination of sandbags, HESCO barriers, razorwire, HMG bunkers, resupply points, etc... and many more to come in the future) to experiencing realistic equipment in the hands of real life factions like the US Army or an Eastern European militia.
However, the real incentive should be knowing that the game is in pre-alpha, and that there's much, much more to come. There's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of new features and content, on the drawing board and in development, that will eventually make an appearance in Squad. Everything from tanks and helicopters to the ability to drag the bodies of incapacitated teammates is planned (see the following link for a full list of confirmed features).
My advice to the prospective buyer who's on edge about cashing in $40: monthly development recaps are posted at the end of each month on Squad's website
. Read through a few previous recaps, and if you're feeling patient wait until the end of this month for the January recap, and get an idea of what's in development and what to expect in the near future. Right now, that's the Stryker APC for the US Army, a British faction, mortars for FOBs, and more.
My only gripe right now is performance. The devs are well aware of it, and the last major update (V8) drastically increased performance. Focus on optimization and more performance updates in the future are to be expected. I have a mediocre/decent gaming laptop (GTX 960M, i7-4720, 16 GBs RAM), and run with basically everything maxed for 25-30 FPS. Conveniently enough, I am both a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥ and have low standards for framerates from many years of potato PCs, so while this may horrify you (I really don't understand the people whining that they have to have 60 FPS), it doesn't bother me in the slightest, and the game looks fantastic. I could lower my settings for 50-60 FPS and still have the game look great, but I'm a bit of a purist that way. So while performance is no no way whatsoever a gamebreaker, it could be (and will be) better. If you have an AMD, I would be especially careful about buying Squad if performance is a real worry, as AMDs don't do as well on Unreal engine (not a Squad issue, but an engine issue, and Unreal is looking into this).
Anyway, that's my piece.

Single best modern day shooter out there at the moment.
Does everything that the description promises, a tactical squad based shooter where the focus is not in the individual but in the group as a whole.
I've always loved and hated Battlefield series, and this game is the step up from the chaotic and frantic battles that series had. While it may be boring to watch, I promise you. The game has your heart beating fast every second you're even near a firefight.
This is due to following reasons:
AUDIO
-The game audio is absolutely fantastic. Gunshots echoing in the distance sound imho better than anything in battlefield where it is filled with surplus noise. The simple near miss of a bullet whirring and snapping past your head is enough to send shivers down one's spine. You hear the snap long before the gunshot itself and this alone leads to a horrifying tension that any second somebody could've already killed you without you even knowing it. This speed of sound delay and fairly closely authentic sound design is a masterpiece in sending the proper ambiance to the battlefield.
Especially when you've hit the deck after that near miss and you're crawling under fire hoping to your dear life you won't get shot.
VISUALS
-While not comparable to Battlefield series, it is still a fantastic game to look at and delivers a great set of battlefields. The effects themselves are beautiful and to me, they look quite realistic which only add to the overall feel of the game.
Once again I draw comparison to Battlefield game series where everything from maps to explosions looks like a hollywood blockbuster film. This game looks visually less cluttered and real, and you know that everything you see can be fatal, from shrapnel from explosions to bullet tracers. Again, this brings a lot of tension to the table. Seeing that puff of dust kicked by an explosion? Probably a teammate got himself blown to the afterlife.
GAMEPLAY
-Single most important piece of this game is the successful feel of killing the heroes. What has made me hate Battlefield series is the overabundance of vehicles, everybody jumping off moving airplanes to rpg others mid air to hijack another plane. It's pure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and anybody who even attempts to drive a Humvee like it was BF is gonna get themselves shot in an instant, and this punishes the team since it means that's one less humvee for a good 20 minutes time, everybody hates those wannabe heroes for wasting assets and tickets. It's honestly beautiful. Everything in this game revolves around teamplay. Vehicle assets act great at supporting infantry elements and vice versa. Squads working together, one defending a fallback point from enemies trying to disrupt backlines to two squads attacking a hostile point while one flanks behind. If people cooperate as squads, it is the single most satisfying feeling I've ever had in a video game.
Weapons recoil properly leading to single shots being by far the most common firemode. It is great that not everybody is spraying and praying like no tomorrow.
This game is not Arma either, but it is the perfect middle ground for tactical military shooters. What makes it feel arcadey are the spawn points, but that's just a minor complaint.
To address some concerns you might have:
"The game looks boring, just walking for 15 minutes and dying without ever even having a chance to fire back! No thanks"
Yes, the game can look boring from the outside, but when you're controlling the character itself, it is intense as hell. Kills are not handed to you on a platter like they are in most other video games. Even if you begin taking fire, a good smoke screen can, and will save your life letting you retaliate and think about your options.
"The game is in early alpha"
Indeed it is, but the devs are implementing new features at a steady pace, and the performance has seen a great big boost over the last few months. Trust me, this project is worth supporting for.
An absolute must buy if you're into modern shooters where teamwork is paramount to survival and success.

Oxenfree is a simple, yet cohesive experience. You travel to an island to hang out with friends, but end up exploring it to slowly unravel a mystery.
The controls are simple, as you're pretty much just walking around or choosing a dialogue response. The dialogue system is the main attraction to the game, with every response being fully voiced. Most of the time it works well, but often the dialogue can get interrupted, causing you to miss a lot of flavor text. Sometimes I found the responses to have the wrong tone for what I expected, as I thought my character would be lighthearted, but the actual response would end up aggressive. Often the pacing of some flavor text would be off. While walking to a new destination, there's nothing to do along the way, but the dialogue goes on for much longer than the actual distance you have to travel... so you get to your destination and just sort of stand there waiting for it to finish... if you keep traveling, the whole dialogue gets cut off abruptly with no chance to repeat it. Sometimes your objective is far away, and the characters don't interact with each other at all! It's a very odd pacing issue that causes the game to feel unnatural.
The majority of the time the character interactions are great, and I found myself wanting to listen to everything. Some of the character's personality traits are not obvious at the start. I wish there was more buildup and development there before the story actually begins, to get a better feel of how people will respond to you.
My biggest gripe comes with the navigating, really. The paths around the island are often narrow, and your character walks everywhere, with no option to run or fast travel. Sometimes I get stuck on little corners and end up going the wrong direction or not able to smoothly change paths. The paths themselves are very convoluted, and the overworld map is vague as♥♥♥♥♥♥ There are road signs everywhere, but they're never exactly at the intersections of two paths. Combined with how slowly your character moves, you can find yourself backtracking a lot which just ends up being frustrating.
There are some collectables in the game, but they are not necessarily super obvious or necessarily all obtainable until much later in the game. Again, backtracking all the way through the world a second time to collect everything seems like a real chore. They do clear up a bit of details to the story, however.
The music and atmosphere were superb, and I was specifically impressed by the supernatural story and gameplay elements, as they really felt grounded and realistic to the world. I thought there was even more potential for them to get crazier with those aspects of the game, but it's a fairly short and direct experience. By the end, I felt like my time was well spent and I'm glad I got to experience the game. I think there's some replayability in the game due to some of the choices, achievements, and collectables, but it's by no means necessary to get a full experience. I spent 5 hours playing through it without trying to see and do everything.

For those who are beginners or experts, Precision XOC is and perhaps will remain the best software for overclocking NVIDIA GPUs. I've used EVGA Precision X since I got my NVIDIA GTX 690 back in 2012. This software is meant for overclocking experimentation on NVIDIA GPUs. As everyone knows with the risks of overclocking, wanting see how far you can push your GPU before you start seeing clipping issues or artifacts is one of those things that many pc enthusiasts like to find out. However, keep in mind that EVGA supplies this software for an "At your own risk" basis. They're not telling you that you have to overclock your GPU to have great performance, but this tool is availiable should you want to make advanced modifications. Although overclocking is encouraged among the PC community, have common sense here. If you don't know what you're doing with GPU clock or memory clock speeds, don't mess with them. You don't want to be the person that breaks their brand new $1000 GPU card, because of making the mistake of performing changes without realizing what happens to your GPU under those conditions.
