Original review below.
_______________________________________
Boundless is an open world building game with an emphasis on cooperation and community.
Setting
The world is lush and visually appealing. Split into different areas based on location (EU, US-W, US-E, AUS), each area has 3 planets of different difficulty levels. Each area can be travelled too regardless of where you choose to begin your journey, so you can explore every planet. Currently, the major differences are gem types, weather types, water/lava lakes and colours of items within the worlds. I'm sure as the game develops through Early Access more variety will become apparent, making journeys to each world more rewarding. Player character appearance can be changed through a menu setting and there is only one race with no discernable benefits, again this may be subject to change if character creation options are added.
Music
Worth a mention in its own right, it's actually a pleasent experience to wander the different planets listening to the gorgeous soundscapes that have been created for the game.
Graphics
Again, very visually appealing - think World of Warcraft mixed with Sphax BDCraft.
Gameplay
If you like open-world, sandbox games where you gather resources in order to build structures or create items, then this will appeal.
Skills are gained through experience and you can tailor your character down several different profession types - Builder, Explorer, Gatherer, Hunter, Merchant. There are objectives for each profession as well as overall daily/weekly objectives. These are a nice addition that reward XP and coins as well as giving you mini-goals to accomplish.
The overall aim is that you do not master every skill, this is where the co-operation and community angle comes in. Instead you can focus on a specific path and then team up with other players who have specialised in other areas so you can support each other.
As it is Early Access this area is not fully fleshed out and the most rewarding areas are gathering and building, however development is continuing in this area and thankfully, these two are developed well enough to make a current purchase a rewarding experience.
Community
Very supportive, although it was a little while before I met other players, when I did I was shown a lot that the world had to offer. Since then, I've met many more and each has been a friendly sort. There isn't much opportunity for griefing, and the developers have a beacon system that locks your building plot so it can't be trashed.
Developers
Fully engaged. They are receptive and welcoming of any raised issues and, from my experience, personally respond to each raised item on their forums. This is definitely a case of Early Access being done right.
Cons
It's Early Access, not everything is implemented yet, and some things are a bit unbalanced - e.g. some tools you can make don't seem to offer much improvement and the tiers of tools are a bit tough. The crafting system is intuitive in some ways but a bit baffling in others, e.g. it isn't obvious to know which skill set unlocks which crafting trees (however, there is a great site called
which provides a comprehensive break down of skills). Aside from unlocking landmarks, there isn't much more to exploring other than the wonder of finding interesting building projects of other players, however dungeons and rares are in the pipeline. To be honest, most of the cons I can think of are due to things not being fully developed yet - but that's Early Access for you. If that bothers you, you might be best off waiting until a later, more complete edition is created, however its current state is playable and entertaining.
Worth it?
In my opinion, very much so. I've whiled away many hours gathering and exploring the worlds. From a cost to play-time point of view, I've had my money's worth so everything on top of this now is bonus - and it looks like a bonus that will increase as the game develops further.

This is the first Might and Magic Game I've played. So my review will be based on that.
First of all, THIS GAME IS SHORT. You can probably beat in < 10 hours meaning one day of zoning out on the computer and bam, the final boss is down. The game is divided into 10 chapters with each chapter representing an area. Secondly, this game is as linear as it gets - there is an order for every place and you can't go back - just like FFXIII.
The leveling system is also a bit weird - everything is done in skill points which are obtained by going through the storyline. There are a few optional skill points as well - for finding secret areas or completing optional quests but those are few and far.  You determine your characters "class" by spending skill points.
Another thing to note - THERE IS NO TRADING. You can keep items in your inventory, use them, or drop them. That's it. The only healing you get is either through magic or healing items and mana restoration is only available via mana items which can only be found. So be very careful on how you use what you have.

This game is actually more fun than it seems at first. Yes, it's repetitive and focused on co-op, but you can still enjoy playing it solo provided you like FPSs and loot systems.
One of things I like most about this game is that it rewards your exploration. It's something I wasn't expecting that the designers of the game seemed to have predicted, and I'm really happy for that.
Now one of the things I DON'T enjoy in this game is the weird difficulty. The enemies levels don't scale, so for someone like me who likes to complete all the quests in the game and explore it's easy to be overleveled and make the game a cakewalk. In some parts, however, the difficult has odd sparks that seem more arbitrary than natural, and sometimes almost unfair, with some enemies taking huge amounts of health from you.
Despite the repetitiveness nature of the game, it's samey environments and not-so-interesting quests, I still enjoyed this one more than I thought I would. If you like shooting things in the head and allow yourself to get hooked on the loot mechanics, you might enjoy it too!

Borderlands, a loot based adventure? More like Hoarderlands
Borderlands is a loot based RPG-FPS with Co-Op Elements, What makes borderlands so special is the playable classes, unique humor, and the millions of guns that exist. You start on a bus with the choice of 4 different characters. Each one has a unique skill tree that can be manipulated for different play styles.
You have Roland, An assault class with his special skill being a deployable turret.
Mordecai, A sniper class who has his pet bloodwing as his skill, deploying it makes it fly and attack enemies over a distance.
Lilith, A Siren who has the special ability to Phasewalk (Become invisible for a period of time, releashing a shock wave when ending).
Brick, A berserker (Tank), Who has the beserk skill that allows him to pound and punch enemies to death easily with increased survivability.
All four characters are better suited to certain weapons that can be enhanced with their skill tree, Their special abilities can also be upgraded to do more damage and have more unique aspects. The class system makes for wonderful Co-Op.
The plot is unremarkable and cliche, You play as 1 of 4 vault hunters who seek a vault that is said to contain amazing wonders and loot. There is nothing really special about the story at all, But borderlands shines when it comes to colorful characters and unique even humorous quests. The game is open world and has huge spawling levels but for the most part this coupled with hordes of enemys can make travel boring over time, Prepare for a ton of walking. Borderlands also has vehicular combat, the controls are wonky and wierd but manage somehow to get the job done despite working against players.
There is tons of guns, So many you will get rich off selling them. Borderlands prides itself on its gun system, creating guns using a system that allows for millions of different combinations. Although this sounds awesome you will probably see guns that look similar. Borderlands top tier loot is powerful, unique and legendary weapons haave unique properties and will keep you playing.
The Graphics and sound hold up, Although some textures could be better but there is really no problems wiith it comes to this catagory. The Art style is unique and fits the humor of the game well and the soundtrack is immersive and fits the different locations.
Overall Borderlands is a unique Loot based FPS-RPG, Despite having a few problems and a lackluster plot, Borderlands makes up in its Humor, Loot, and Unique Characters/Art Style/Skill Tree system. I would recommend Borderlands greatly, especially if you are looking for some of the best co-op on PC.

I probably would have enjoyed this game had I not played DOOM 2016 just before it. since this game was a stepping stone to DOOM in many ways. The gunplay is great, the world is interesting and has a great style. The cover system was a bit strange, and even after completing the game, I was not fully used to it. I also found dual weilding to be useless in almost every situation, especially because doing so means that you cannot sprint.
My biggest problem with the game is the stealth system. There are several points in the game where you are clearly supposed to be stealthy. This is fine, if the stealth system is decent. I had extremely inconsistent results with the guards. Sometimes, I was spotted around corners, from across the map, from behind the guard. And once you've been detected, you're not going to be able to hide and re-stealth, you have to play like Rambo for the rest of the level. And even if the game works properly on this front, you are only able to one-shot back stab about half of the guard population, especially later in the game, when many more guards are wearing heavy armor or piloting mechs. There is also supposed to be a silencer for the handgun, I picked it up on 2 seperate occasions, but it never equipped, so every time I tried to execute a guard silently, the rest of them heard me.
While I did just complain a lot about the game, it is fun, you get to fight Nazis on the Moon, what else do you want? I think anyone who is used to the traditional modern day FPS should play this, it is much more inspired than something like Call of Duty or Battlefield. After you finish with this, then play the new DOOM.

An excellent kart racing game that would normally be negatively seen as "Just another Mario Kart Clone" but is actually superior to that franchise on a few elements, and all around less frustrating to play. If you like Mario Kart and Sega games this could be nice surprise.
Now what exactly is so good about it? First off, the controls are excellent, especially the drifting which feels natural and more interesting that the Mario equivalent.
Also the items, while not extremely innovative, take care of the biggest problem in Mario Kart: Blue Shells. In this game, the Blue Shells are replaced with something called the Swarm, which adds obstacles in the region of the race that the first players are in. This slows them down but it can still be dodged if you are skilled, making it far less frustrating and more fair.
The fact that the races change during the course of multiple turns is also very nice, and the maps themselves are very fun and differents. Even the way to unlock new maps and players, the Carreer mode, is very fun and gives a nice sense of progress.
And the game can be both challenging and more casual based on how you want to play, but it still feels more fair than how Mario Kart ususally ramps up the difficulty.
All in all, a nice game I greatly recommend!

This game annoys me. It covers only four real transporters, and the rest are "nanobots" (so they can transport chemicals in both directions). And these two-way transporters work ONLY from higher to lower concentrations, rather than evening the concentrations in an only statistical sense, like in real cells. In that sense, I'd consider it "educational" only in the barest sense, and it's not super-fun as a game either -- but it could be. The only reason I'm voting "yes" is that with so few reviews a negative one would be devastating, and I'd like to see this improved upon. One of the most atmospheric games ever. It's like playing through an Escher piece writ large, only way, way creepier.
This game makes me *feel* things I don't in other games at all - isolated, agoraphobic, claustrophobic, disoriented. It's way more horrifying in a lot of ways than any survival horror piece, yet it's also beautiful and awe-striking.  There's a whole bunch of dichotomies going on in this game actually - Its aesthetic is both austere and clinical, yet also baroque and dramatic; and the music is often simultaneously beautiful and immensely creepy.
The only real downsides to the game were a very surreal middle-section that feels as though it clashes too much with the tone of the rest of the game, and an ending that was terribly abrupt. The main setpieces, however, were absolutely stunning and worth the price of admission alone. The game does a very good job of making you feel tiny, and feels more like a real, cohesive world than almost any other game I've played, since STALKER.
Overall, damn worth the money.  HIGHLY recommended.

This game is exactly what the synopsis says. The artwork, the environment, the soundtrack, the atmosphere, the sense of loneliness and exploration. It's all really well done and makes this one of the most immersive games I've played. One thing alone however, stops me from giving this an amazing recommendation and a 10/10.
That is, as probably most other people have said...Checkpoints! It really, really needs more of them. Because you will die a lot, from mistimed/misclicked jumps, to falling off a ledge, to taking the wrong route (as it's really not obvious sometimes where you need to go). In one area I had to complete the same puzzle 6 times in a row, to then keep dying afterwards because of a confusing gameplay mechanic
. I came close to turning the game off out of sheer frustration, and that is something I never thought I'd do with a game this beautiful, as the world is so compelling and drives you onward to discover more.
So I will recommend this game, because while some parts of the game you will have to redo several times, in the end it usually pays off and is worth the hassle of retrying to see more of the world. But be prepared to test your patience to the limit on certain areas.
So at the moment, as this game stands, I'm giving it a 7/10. But with better spaced out checkpoints I could easily give this a 10/10

I bought this game during the winter sale after reading the reviews here on Steam. I am a fan of Arma, but I wanted a more accessible game without losing the sense of realism or teamwork. Squad, to me, is the perfect match. I've only played a handfull of hours so far, but the first impression is solid.
Squad is somewhat similar to the battlefield games in that you have set objectives to capture, but at the same time very different due to its slow pace and tactical gameplay. I especially love the fact that Squad has an easily accessible and built in voice-communication system that is not only functional, but is also used by the vast majority of players. This enables a high degree of teamwork both internally in the squads, but also between different squads. This is, in my opinion, one of Squads biggest strengths as it motivates most players to communicate actively and work as a team.
One of my gripes with Arma is that it's a bit clunky - especially when trying to navigate buildings, etc. This is not the case with Squad. Squad has the realism and tactical gameplay of Arma, but it feels a lot less clunky and a lot easier to navigate.
At the same time, Squad is still an Early-access game and an Alpha-version at that, meaning that some bugs and issues are to be expected. Personally I have only ever experienced one issue with this game and that is the "Server closed connection" issue. This disconnects me from the game-server at random times. I haven't been able to find a cause for this and while it's extremely annoying I don't find it to be game-breaking.
All in all, this is an exceptional FPS, and if you, like me, are a fan of slower-paced tactical teamwork games, this game comes highly reccomended.

What I really enjoyed about Wolfenstein: The New Order is that the gameplay supports numerous different playstyles. Sure, there are times when you have no choice but to go in guns-a-blazing, but most of the game provides the option of stealth/assassin gameplay as well. In particular, I  greatly enjoyed using knives; the challenge-based upgrade paths encourage you to try new things and get better at the playstyles you prefer, and they give genuinely helpful upgrades--for example, the ability to hold a second knife in your inventory, allowing you to kill two nazis with thrown knives before you  have to pick them up or find new ones.
The story, of course, is ALSO amazing. Machine Games has created a detailed, inctricately-portrayed alternate history, where you can see the horrors of a victorious Third Reich, but ALSO the small joys and lives that individuals have carved out for themselves. It's really a meaningful experience to see the little home/base that the resistance created under the very nose of the nazi beast.

Due to its simple (yet not outdated) graphics you can easily keep track of the thousands of things you have to think about while surviving on Rimworld. Not only that but it will most likely run well even if your machine is not meant for gaming (like mine). However it is not for the faint-hearted since its realism is brutal. If you're looking for a sims ripoff then stay away from this game.
If you want to attempt to build a colony and survive in a harsh world then this game is for you. Your colonists will bleed, get infections, get sick, have their limbs ripped off by bears or raiders' weapons, go berzerk because they haven't eaten in days and start killing everyone around them, mourn their deceased fellow colonists, bond with their pets, get jealous of each other, fall in love or get rejected, and soon you'll find yourself immersed completely. At points you will feel sad or happy because of what happened. Raiders broke in the place where you keep your sick and killed a colonist who was unable to move due to her injuries. Or you had no food and when your vegetables were ready for harvest, the temperature changed to a "cold snap" and they died off so now you have to go to extremes to survive...
You will soon find yourself having to make important and ethics-challenging decisions. A colonist has had brain damage and won't be able to move or do anything ever again, but is alive. He can only be fed. You have little food. Do you euthanize him? Or do you keep him alive? A person is 81 years old and is being chased by pirates and wants to join your colony for shelter. If you ignore him he will die, or be enslaved, or worse, but if you accept him he will offer less than what he will consume and he will have a myriad of health problems because of his old age. He may be the sweetest old fellow or an antisocial pyromaniac - you don't know. Do you accept him or ignore him? See the challenges in this game are not only low food, or being overrun by raiders or wild animals.
So then you completed the game at the easy difficulty. Then you can either move to a higher difficulty (which is completely gameplay-changing) or start browsing the workshop and play the mods.

Back at about the year 2015, Me and my Dad were searching for something new to play, as my Dad searched through the list of games available he found Boundless. I have never heard of this game before and i was interested into seeing what the game was capable of and what features were to be added in the future.
Me and my Dad both got the game, checked it out and liked quite well. I lasted to play on and build a house on Solum, one of the US East servers, it was quite enjoyable and very challenging but quite rewarding. This is nothing like Minecraft even though you can try to relate certain things between the two, here are the Pros and Cons for Boundless:
"NOTE: These are my thoughts on Pros and Cons and are not intended to predict anyones thoughts or enjoyment, I am just sharing my thoughts about the game so that you may know what you might enjoy, and what you don't before you purchase the game.
These thoughts are also most relevant to Early Access as it stands at the date of this review, there is a lot more in store for this game and things will change as the game grows."
Pros:
+ You get to travel across planets to other servers (It is an MMO after all)
+ The Community is super friendly and very helpful
+ The Worlds regenerate it's resources so that a planet never runs dry
+ You can level up and earn plots to claim chunks of the map, which also cancels out World Regeneration
+ You take on important professions based on what you spend your skill points on, Example: Builder, Miner, Fighter, Crafter, Trader and/or a balanced mix of professions
+ The skill tree is easy to grasp and offers the user great abilities
+ Upon release you can make/rent your own Planets (Servers) and mod them to your liking
+ World Builder allows you to create your own biomes and worlds
+ Player Based Economy
+ Great Art style and Graphics
+ Combat is nice, fluid and challenging, lots of spawns and fun, crazy battles
+ Creature Combat is very intense when a large mob forms, you have Spitters shooting single projectiles to shooting bombs at you, Hoppers who will explode on near contact, Wildstock who will try to ram you multiple times and Cuttletrunks that fly through the air shooting homing projectiles at you, sometimes with an explosive twist
+ Meteors fall from the sky and provide valuable loot used to fuel portals and craft high end gear
+ Chisels which allow you to decorate with finer details such as Bevels, Slopes and Square chunks which can form stairs and other neat and wonderful ways to create your projects
Cons:
- This game is Early Access after all, so expect there to be bugs that need to be flattened, you can help by posting on the Boundless Forums if you decide to own the game
- Death is painful, especially when your holding some expensive tools in your backpack, even though you don't drop anything on death. On death all tools in your backpack take 25% damage, this can be reduced with some skill points, but this is only as you get higher level and takes a good portion of skill points to obtain it to the point of 0% damage on death. Unless you like risks, it's best to leave a vast majority of expensive tools behind in storage before you head out.
I'm sure there is a lot more i could mention here, but overall it's a very great and well thought out game, it is Early Access, and things are coming together and things are constantly being added to make it even better, I hope this review will give you some ideas about the game and the content it has today!

I bought this game during the winter sale after reading the reviews here on Steam. I am a fan of Arma, but I wanted a more accessible game without losing the sense of realism or teamwork. Squad, to me, is the perfect match. I've only played a handfull of hours so far, but the first impression is solid.
Squad is somewhat similar to the battlefield games in that you have set objectives to capture, but at the same time very different due to its slow pace and tactical gameplay. I especially love the fact that Squad has an easily accessible and built in voice-communication system that is not only functional, but is also used by the vast majority of players. This enables a high degree of teamwork both internally in the squads, but also between different squads. This is, in my opinion, one of Squads biggest strengths as it motivates most players to communicate actively and work as a team.
One of my gripes with Arma is that it's a bit clunky - especially when trying to navigate buildings, etc. This is not the case with Squad. Squad has the realism and tactical gameplay of Arma, but it feels a lot less clunky and a lot easier to navigate.
At the same time, Squad is still an Early-access game and an Alpha-version at that, meaning that some bugs and issues are to be expected. Personally I have only ever experienced one issue with this game and that is the "Server closed connection" issue. This disconnects me from the game-server at random times. I haven't been able to find a cause for this and while it's extremely annoying I don't find it to be game-breaking.
All in all, this is an exceptional FPS, and if you, like me, are a fan of slower-paced tactical teamwork games, this game comes highly reccomended.

Episode One Review
Coming to this first episode as a fan of both the Borderlands series and the recent Telltale games projects, I admit to being a little skeptical. The strengths of the Borderlands franchise was also more in its loot & shoot gameplay rather than its stories or its characters, which doesn't seem to suit it well for an adventure game. At the same time, while I am a big fan of Telltale's recent Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us episodic endeavors, earlier attempts at properties that were a bit more action oriented and less walking and talking like Jurassic Park and Back to the  Future were less than impressive.
I was pleasantly surprised, then, when I came away from the first episode of this series with a grin on my face and a sense of excitement and anticipation for the remainder.
The game plays like the recent Telltale adventure games mentioned above, like The Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us. Unlike the early telltale adventure games, Tales from the Borderlands plays out less like a traditional adventure game and more like an interactive episode of a borderlands TV show. This may sound like a bad thing to some people, but I would assure them that it isn't. At least in episode one, this isn't a game about picking up inventory items and combining them to solve puzzles using some sort of Elpis Logic. In fact, there really aren't any puzzles at all. Instead, imagine a well animated and entertaining Borderlands miniseries, except you get to make all the major decisions and live with their outcomes, from how you treat a guy you are asking for directions to whether or not you betray an acquaintance. Most of the gameplay involves this kind of dialogue choosing or decision making, almost all of it on a timer. The rest takes place in rather well done quick time events that take place during the action scenes.
A quick note on QTEs: I'm normally not a big fan of these, and playing with a mouse and keyboard I still don't like the whole "mash the q button" one. But, overall, they felt smooth and unobtrusive. For the most part, it consists of pressing a directional button or clicking a moving target on the screen. They make up a decent portion of the game, especially the climax, but I never felt particularly annoyed at them, and they almost never took me out of the game or its story.
A game like that may not sound that much fun, and it might not be if the story and writing weren't so well done. I won't go into much detail on the story or the characters, but I found them to be quite entertaining.  The main story is told as the main characters are recounting it to a third party, giving them the opportunity to bicker about how things really happened, a trick that I enjoyed. The story itself begins as a heist which is always a lot of fun, and the writers know how exactly how to hit the beats of the genre to keep the story moving and for comedic effect.
In terms of comedy, while there were some jokes that didn't land, most of the game is pretty funny. I had a couple of laugh out loud moments, and there are a lot of little touches that made me laugh or smile outside of real jokes. I think the key is that, with a couple exceptions, the games humor either comes organically from the characters (often as a result of a dialogue choice you made), or from the nature of the world of Borderlands itself. It doesn't really feel forced.
I particularly enjoyed the cast of characters that they have already drawn so far. While the they are a little cliché, this actually works to the games advantage, as it allows you to choose, through dialogue, whether you want to play them against type or to the hilt. This makes them feel surprisingly well developed for a game series that usually paints its characters with nothing more than some joke filled catchphrases. In the end, I actually want to see where the story is going, not because of the plot, but because I want to spend more time with the characters and see how much (or how little) of themselves and their relationship changes over the course of the story.
And that is the feeling that I was left with at the end of the game- anticipation. I had a great time playing, and If I could have moved onto the next episode right away, I totally would have. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Borderlands, or who wouldn't mind a more light hearted telltale adventure game than the Walking Dead.
TLDR: Surprisingly entertaining and well written. Recommended.
A last note for those of you who don't know the Borderlands Universe: Given that I know it pretty well, I'm not the best person to talk to, but I think the game is pretty approachable to the initiated. As I recall, none of the major plot or comedic notes hinges on an inside joke or knowledge of the games, so you should be fine. Most of the issue will be not knowing what the planet is like and the kind of people who inhabit it, but given that one of the protagonists comes in as a relative outsider that might actually be fitting. If you wanted to do some research, maybe look up a short plot summary of Borderlands 2.

The Good:
- Fantastic atmosphere, both from the visuals and the audio.
- Some levels are mind-bogglingly huge. The level of detail, even in out-of-the-way or inaccessible areas, is very impressive.
- Actual gameplay, including both platform and logic puzzles. Contrary to what you might think from the game description, this isn't just a walking simulator.
- Neat breathing mechanic. It would be cool to see this used in an Amnesia-type game.
- No story, no dialogue, and no explanations keep pretentiousness to a minimum.
The Bad:
- Doesn't stick with any gameplay mechanic for very long. The moving lights, sliding puzzles, rotating fans, etc. only make appearances in their own individual chapters and are never mixed together.
-  A few areas are almost too dark or disorienting to navigate.
- Directional cues vary from subtle to non-existent. Sometimes this adds to the game's atmosphere, but it can also become incredibly frustrating.
- Only 3-5 hours long. Not much replay value either, unless you really want to explore.
If you think this sounds like your type of thing, go ahead and buy it. It's definitely not for everyone, though, so if you're on the fence, wait for a sale.
It's also worth mentioning that the game takes a lot of inspiration from Tsutomu Nihei's manga “BLAME!” If you're a fan, this game is definitely worth a look.

NaissanceE is a game of light and shadows, or at least that's what it
you to think it is. In reality it's a little harder to describe; an experience constantly evolving, that at it's core doesn't quite fit into any one genre. It's a game about exploration; about discovery and self interpretation that requires you to find your own way and make sense of your surroundings without the funneling and hand-holding we have become accustomed to. It's an incredibly ambitious project for such a small development team, one with numerous jaw dropping moments and incredible artistic direction, but it's abundance of anomalous design decisions and a handful of seemingly minor but highly frustrating problems leaves it hanging somewhere in the middle of "fully recommended" and "proceed with caution."
NaissanceE is in essence an art project with scraps of gameplay taped to it at odd angles. Making your way through the alien structure you find yourself in is largely a hands-off journey, but for what it lacks in interactivity is made up for by the sheer amount of visual and audio stimulation. The architecture is incredible in scope, from massive chasms to the many mind-bending hallways that mess with your head before rearranging their framework to form a new path forward. NaissanceE is at its strongest during the moments that bewilder and amaze without an accompaniment of confusion, moments which begin to occur more and more rapidly and on a grander scale the deeper into the world you get.
Interspersed between the wandering and sightseeing are occasional platforming and puzzle elements. Neither encroachs upon or disrupts your progression for more than a moment, but serves as a nice supplement to the experience and fleshes out the gameplay to be something more engaging and further immersion (an unusual mechanic involves you needing to time your breathing to keep sprinting for long periods of time, which while odd at I actually came to appreciate for making me feel like I was playing a person and not a camera on wheels). While many self described "exploration adventure games" consist of nothing but walking from point a-b, NaissanceE actually has quite a bit of "traditional" gameplay that, while basic and secondary to the overall focus on exploration and player defined narrative, makes it hard to dispute that it is indeed a "game" and not just an "experience".
Having played NaissanceE to completion, I have no doubt of the very clear and focused vision the developer obviously had when creating this game. It's unlike anything else I've played and at many times simply a wonder to behold. But along with this vision came an abundance of technical and design missteps, the most prominent and unacceptable of which is the checkpoint/save system. The only way to save are at checkpoints purposely placed at points in the game, but the problem is that these checkpoints are much too far apart from one another.
Death is an annoyingly common occurrence do to how easy it is to slip off a ledge as well as the general trial-and-error method of solving many of the puzzles, and because of this you are largely required to replay large sections of the game because of how sporadic the checkpoints are. I spent at least 1-2 hours going through the motions trying to get past a handful of troublesome sections, a tiresome affair that at times made me want to stop playing and never look at the game again. I can't say it strongly enough how much frustration would have been avoided had there been a way to manually save, and I can only hope that the developer reads this and the complaints on the forums and adds it in. In its current state it's almost bad enough for me to not recommend the game at all, as those less determined than I may find themselves giving up early on and not at all unfairly. A handful of other less prevalent technical problems also cropped up (a bothersome fan being the most aggravating), but updates seem to be on the way so they hopefully won't be a problem much longer.
NaissanceE's other problems are mainly a fault of its inherent design of having the player figure nearly everything out for themselves, with no guide or clearly marked route through levels to guide them. Many areas are almost too big for their own good, leading to a lot of dead ends (some intentionally misleading by design) and wasted time running in circles because I didn't see the staircase on the side of a wall or mistook a doorway for a meaningless gap. This becomes less of an issue the longer you play, as certain patterns begin to reveal themselves and you get better at spotting the fakes passages for the real ones, but early on it's definitely a problem and one that will discourage a lot of players from continuing as they are literally left walking in the dark.
Ultimately, no matter how exasperated I got at the save system or the time spent entirely lost in the maze like structure, I kept returning to NaissanceE because regardless of these issues the world it creates is so remarkably compelling. When everything clicks it's an experience unlike anything else, captivating and creative in ways I have rarely seen in any game. It asks a lot of the player, more so than it has a right too (namely to stick with it past the awkward first few hours and its abomination of a save system), but if you can accept those issues it becomes something that you need to see and play for yourself...after a few patches.

with it's atmosphere. The fascinating ruined
environments, and the lone island feel to the worlds

TL;DR:

a great philosophy surrounding it. And although the
game may be simplistic, it is still very challenging and great fun.

As a big fan of Minecraft, my first draw to this game was the Minecraft-esque feel this game was advertising. Survival voxel open world where you can build stuff and explore deep dark caves. After having played it for an admittedly few hours, I find myself enjoying it quite a bit. It's much more refined than the typical Minecraft experience but it has a lot of areas to improve on.
For starters, the objectives system is great. The one thing I and many others desire in Minecraft is direction. Sure we can build to our hearts content, but the objectives give us something to aim for, almost like a quest system. It's great but after just a few hours you really start to hit a hard roadblock in terms of advancing. You have to gain access to deep recipe tiers that require many levels, but the experience grind seems far too slow for opening up recipe tiers. You too quickly lose that desire to go further because the goal seems too hard to reach. Overall, though, I really like the system and imagine the balance curve will get ironed out before full launch.
The second thing I love is the character advancement. It is truly deep - like MMOG deep. It's almost dauntingly deep, in fact. I feel like the experience gain rate needs to be dramatically increased if you even hope to get halfway through the advancement tiers, let alone "max out" your character. Granted, the devs may be intending people to band together and specialize in certain advancement, but, let's be honest, so many people play online games like a single player game this concept doesn't always succeed - instead it leads to people getting frustrated and unable to advance at an acceptable rate and quit the game. Regardless, I love the system. With a little increase to experience gains I think it will be a game changer in the voxel, open world game scene.
On top of it all, the game has a great art direction and is quite pretty at times. It runs a smooth 60 FPS on my system except when I enter the flashy player-made cities (the fact that we have player made cities is awesome in and of itself!).
Overall, my only complaint is the rate of experience gained - it's seems just a bit too slow. Or maybe I just haven't found the big experience gains out there yet. Either way, this game shows a lot of promise and hopefully starts to pick up a big audience - because Boundless feels a bit empty right now.

Dark Messiah has one of the better combat mechanics in a game to date. In many ways this game is absolutely fantastic despite its problems. It still looks stellar even though the graphics  won't compare well with today's standards. It is really funny, I mean the ragdolls and physics in this game is just hilarious at times (perhaps not intented though).
But it is also frustrating, and with a forgetable story full of shameful clichés. Despite high production value in cut-scenes and music, the voice acting makes you shudder of embarrassment, and you wonder who this story was written by, and targeted to. I can only come up with 8 year boys who know nothing about the other sex. This game could easily be used as an example of shameful tropes and predictable storylines in videogames. Feminist or not, most people would find the story quite horrid.
Perhaps one of the biggest annoyances is that even though the game looks and feels great, and runs with no problems on today's machines, the engine just feels a little clunky. You miss a lot with your sword and your character feels a clumbsy. It doesn't feel like the source engine is the greatest choice for this type of game. At the same time the physics and ragdolls are just the whole point of this game. The game constantly encourage you to use objects,in your surroundings, and kick things around. There are many way to get rid of your foes that does not involve your fighting skills. Kicking foes off from cliffs just never gets old.
The game gives many options of fighting, but in my mind going full sword combat is the only real way to enjoy the game because it is easier that way, and probably the most fun - It just becomes bonkers. The worst style is to do a little of everything because there is not enough skill points for just one style. This is too bad because you probably want to try the all the fighting options the first play-through, but it is better to play through several times, specializing.
You might find the game too hard the first time, but I promise it will get easier as you understand how it works. What can cause a lot of frustration is the reach of both you and the foes. This will result in you getting hit a lot because you will strike too late, thinking the foes are not close enough.
What is really great is that it is a game you really learn to master, you don't just level up. In fact "levelling up" happens at fixed points and is not based on how you play. A great way to replay the game is to try something completely different which really changes gameplay and provides many other creative ways to get rid of your foes. I did find the stealth/thief option the least interesting even though I love stealth games.
Speaking of thief, this games will feel very familiar if you like the earlier thief games, for example there is a rope-arrow which really makes this game much more enjoyable. Another similar game is dishonored, but Dark Messiah is better in that you won't get punished for being creative. Dishonored is ultimately a much better game though, but not as ridicoulous. This ridiculousness is one of Dark Messia's strong sides and a strong reason to play through.
Dark Messiah is an old game but the graphics are still enjoyable and you visit many great locations. The source engine gives lots of life and depth ot the game. The fighting mechanics are really good even though the hitboxes are rather confusing at times. When you master the mechanics well it feels quite awesome.
I do reckomend it. It runs really well, has great ideas and fun mechanics that will make you laugh. It is often dirt cheap as well. Just don't care too much about the story. This game is about mechanincs, not about story (Even though story is important, it is not necessary for a good game. A good story and horrible mechanics is a bigger problem in my mind - like BioShock infite for exaple). But is not hard and serious as dark souls.

Episode One Review
Coming to this first episode as a fan of both the Borderlands series and the recent Telltale games projects, I admit to being a little skeptical. The strengths of the Borderlands franchise was also more in its loot & shoot gameplay rather than its stories or its characters, which doesn't seem to suit it well for an adventure game. At the same time, while I am a big fan of Telltale's recent Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us episodic endeavors, earlier attempts at properties that were a bit more action oriented and less walking and talking like Jurassic Park and Back to the  Future were less than impressive.
I was pleasantly surprised, then, when I came away from the first episode of this series with a grin on my face and a sense of excitement and anticipation for the remainder.
The game plays like the recent Telltale adventure games mentioned above, like The Walking Dead or Wolf Among Us. Unlike the early telltale adventure games, Tales from the Borderlands plays out less like a traditional adventure game and more like an interactive episode of a borderlands TV show. This may sound like a bad thing to some people, but I would assure them that it isn't. At least in episode one, this isn't a game about picking up inventory items and combining them to solve puzzles using some sort of Elpis Logic. In fact, there really aren't any puzzles at all. Instead, imagine a well animated and entertaining Borderlands miniseries, except you get to make all the major decisions and live with their outcomes, from how you treat a guy you are asking for directions to whether or not you betray an acquaintance. Most of the gameplay involves this kind of dialogue choosing or decision making, almost all of it on a timer. The rest takes place in rather well done quick time events that take place during the action scenes.
A quick note on QTEs: I'm normally not a big fan of these, and playing with a mouse and keyboard I still don't like the whole "mash the q button" one. But, overall, they felt smooth and unobtrusive. For the most part, it consists of pressing a directional button or clicking a moving target on the screen. They make up a decent portion of the game, especially the climax, but I never felt particularly annoyed at them, and they almost never took me out of the game or its story.
A game like that may not sound that much fun, and it might not be if the story and writing weren't so well done. I won't go into much detail on the story or the characters, but I found them to be quite entertaining.  The main story is told as the main characters are recounting it to a third party, giving them the opportunity to bicker about how things really happened, a trick that I enjoyed. The story itself begins as a heist which is always a lot of fun, and the writers know how exactly how to hit the beats of the genre to keep the story moving and for comedic effect.
In terms of comedy, while there were some jokes that didn't land, most of the game is pretty funny. I had a couple of laugh out loud moments, and there are a lot of little touches that made me laugh or smile outside of real jokes. I think the key is that, with a couple exceptions, the games humor either comes organically from the characters (often as a result of a dialogue choice you made), or from the nature of the world of Borderlands itself. It doesn't really feel forced.
I particularly enjoyed the cast of characters that they have already drawn so far. While the they are a little cliché, this actually works to the games advantage, as it allows you to choose, through dialogue, whether you want to play them against type or to the hilt. This makes them feel surprisingly well developed for a game series that usually paints its characters with nothing more than some joke filled catchphrases. In the end, I actually want to see where the story is going, not because of the plot, but because I want to spend more time with the characters and see how much (or how little) of themselves and their relationship changes over the course of the story.
And that is the feeling that I was left with at the end of the game- anticipation. I had a great time playing, and If I could have moved onto the next episode right away, I totally would have. I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Borderlands, or who wouldn't mind a more light hearted telltale adventure game than the Walking Dead.
TLDR: Surprisingly entertaining and well written. Recommended.
A last note for those of you who don't know the Borderlands Universe: Given that I know it pretty well, I'm not the best person to talk to, but I think the game is pretty approachable to the initiated. As I recall, none of the major plot or comedic notes hinges on an inside joke or knowledge of the games, so you should be fine. Most of the issue will be not knowing what the planet is like and the kind of people who inhabit it, but given that one of the protagonists comes in as a relative outsider that might actually be fitting. If you wanted to do some research, maybe look up a short plot summary of Borderlands 2.

The game is progressing, though it is taking it's time. The devs are onto something very ambitious, but as of now the game lacks intuitivity and is not very enjoyable for the type of game it is. A game that is about crafting, building, exploration and survival has to above all things, be intuitive. Just navigating through the menus for crafting and other aspects in the game is just killing the flow of gameplay and it's a shame.. I hope they are onto fixing that.
The User Interface is very well done, it's one of the most visually pleasing interfaces I have ever seen in a game.
Though the item tool selecting is a bit obtrusive and again, unintuitive. They are trying to innovate on too many fronts and it leaves for some things to be rather lacking instead of adding to the game experience. Animations are not yet fluid, I hope they are onto that as well. I haven't found a proper roadmap for the game, but simple things like a fluid resource gathering animation are lacking. Every single block I hit with a tool just makes me feel like I am wasting time because there's a pause between every hit, it's unimersive and it puts me out of the moment of the gameplay.
The creative directing is done well, I can tell that that is becoming better as well. You're not a boring human, you are an Oortian, and there is lots of diversity between character models.
The FOV slider seems to not do a whole lot because even at 110 the items I'm holding are just in my face like I am studying them with a magnifying glass.
This game is one of those cases of ambitious = takes time. I can't really say it's very playable at the moment with all the faults I have encountered in the simple gameplay, navigating and intuitivity. On top of that the graphics seem smudged and weird, the world is too amplified and it just makes looking for a place to make a house a pain.
Hopefully in the future I can leave a more positive review, because I do like where the game is going, it's just not anywhere yet, though I am hopeful.

Hi Luke, I've been trying out the game a bit these past days and I must say that the progression tree and the skill points system is really nice. I at first looked at this game as a simple survival game which is not the base concept. Though now that I understand that it is about players working together to fill in for eachother and build a civilisation, I encountered other problems.
It is really unclear for new players to understand what they have to do to actually visit a new world or how to actually find a settlement.
With the concept of the game being about becoming unique and picking a trade so you can build a economy. I find that for players that like to progress more by themselves the game is a little unfriendly. Just building a simple starter home in the wilderness required me to unlock various skills that just don't fit the playstyle of my character. I feel that there has to be a balance between self-sustainability and co-operative interaction.
In order to find a new world I learned that you can visit new worlds by crafting something for your token, but to get those items needed to craft a simple workbench you would first kind of have to become a miner, because gathering the fragments needed simply asks a player to mine a lot. Which kind of defeats the purpose of uniqueness per character, everyone is a miner because to do very basic things you need to mine deep and long. I will change aspects of the review soon since I figured out that the leveling mechanic is actually quite fun.
Another thing is that because the game is so player-driven, it's also very easy for settlements to be absolute eyesores, defeating the aesthetic aspect of the game, that's why I think some basic skills should be included for every character, because right now people don't even hire builders and there's buildings without doors and simple square abominations of buildings because franklyt, people don't have access to decorative items that match the detailed look of the items in the game that could improve the look of cities.

I want to recommend this game. Aesthetically, it's perfect. A dark, forbidding, brutalist world to explore. I've lost count of the times I've just been stunned by the game's architecture, and stopped to look around.
Unfortunately, here are some other things I've lost count of:
The amount of times I've died and thought 'Really? There hasn't been a checkpoint for THIS LONG?'
The amount of times, a few seconds after I respawn or load in, the game has frozen for a second (this happens every time).
The amount of times I've been able to see through walls while moving quickly - and come on, this shouldn't happen in a game with textures this simple, should it?
The amount of times I've been killed because of how poorly the character movement controls and how short a drop can kill you in this game.
The amount of times I've foolishly tried to use the Steam overlay, which crashes the game for me every single time.
Aside from actual glitches which I hope will be ironed out in an update, the gameplay itself simply doesn't help. The proportion of the game spent trying to complete absurd platforming challenges instead of being allowed to explore this fascinating environment is unbearable. As for the puzzles, they're essentially fine, but as previously mentioned, falling off a ledge halfway through them is pretty un-fun. And then there's the weird breathing mechanic, which frankly adds nothing to the game.
What ultimately stopped me from wanting to continue with the game at all was a section where the player is expected to walk along a lengthy pipe, parts of which are  rotating, others of which move up and down - in what appears to be a wind tunnel. In the particular part of the pipe I was up to, you first have to walk along a series of moving, floating cubes to reach the next section. Then you have to run past some rotating obstacles. Then you have to run along another section with a series of cubes being thrown at you which instantly kill you if you are hit. Then you have to run along some beams that move up and down. Then you die, because a gust of wind has at some point during the aforementioned series of challenges, picked you up and blown you away. Why does this happen? Not sure. How is the player expected to know when the wind is going to become dangerous to them? Don't know. What is the player supposed to do to survive this? No idea. Sometimes the wind simply blows you into a wall, which doesn't hurt, but the wind seemingly never stops once it begins, so you're forced to re-load a save anyway.
If I'm missing something blindingly obvious here I apologise, but at the moment I have to treat this game as simply being broken.
I can't emphasise enough how much I love the way this game looks and sounds. It really makes you feel small, and the abstract electronic music complements that feeling perfectly. It's just a shame that a game so seemingly great should be so keen with its gameplay to stop me from playing it ever again. NaissanceE is a beautiful art game trapped inside an alpha-release standard puzzle-platformer.
So with this review climbing up the store page a bit, felt it was worth updating. I've played a bit more of the game since my initial review, having FINALLY managed to progress beyond that awful platform section. Apparently, the fan automatically blows you away after a certain amount of time, not just at random. I don't know how you're supposed to know this, but there it is. The other reasons are that 1: the developer has announced plans to fix bugs and include more checkpoints in the next patch, which would be a great improvement, and 2: the developer has made clear that the platforming sections were 'old-school' and difficult by choice, not accidentally. So it's a reserved recommendation - if you're a fan of atmospheric exploration games, pick this up but be aware that there'll be some real challenges (hopefully more reasonably checkpointed in future) to struggle through unless you're a master platformer. And if you're looking for a hardcore platformer, maybe pick this up but be aware there's a lot of wandering around lost in-between.

Admittedly, I was really worried when I heard Tell Tale was making a Borderlands game. Borderlands is sacred territory for me, one of my all-time favorite series, so I was really worried they would miss what makes it special. I was wrong.
In fact, they've captured it perfectly, and perhaps even given the world more life and character than a co-op shooter could ever muster on its own. I went in expecting a slow TWD style game (and to be fair, there are points like that, there has to be) but when the action ramps up it takes it to 11.
Many don't enjoy QTEs, and if that's the case then this is your warning, after all it's a Tell Tale game so you should expect them. However, no other Dev has done them right, and they never feel like a burden, at least to me.
The story is shaping up to be fantastic, and there are even some legitimately surprising twists that fit well. It also appears that your actions do have a significant effect on the story as well, perhaps even more so than in previous games like TWD.
My only complaint is a sign in issue with Tell Tale Accounts, the GUI seems to freeze and it doesn’t appear to be any way to get away from it other than forcing the program to close, but I'd wager this will be fixed in the coming days.
All in all Episode 1 has me dying for more, and if the next 4 episodes are anything like the 1st, it's going to be a bloody blast.

Like "The Swapper", NaissanceE is a sci-fi game touching on themes of isolation and the definition of life. While scaling down towering apartment complexes, feeling your way through pitch black corridors, and clutching against the wall from a burst of wind as you cross paths miles above the ground you encounter you'll discover remnants of a human life now either erased or abandoned. From strip clubs to a child's room with the television still running, you'll get a feel for life in this steel monolith.
Though advertising itself as a puzzle game, NaissanceE fits more in the realms of a first person platformer. You'll spend more time falling from missed jumps than stuck on puzzles. Many of these moments are built to hammer in the player's mind the sense of vulnerability and insignificance to the towering structures around them.
During one segment, the player must traverse over a thin walkway overlooking huge steel structures hundreds of feet below. The wind at this height is lethal, and the player must sprint to sections cut off from the wind or be thrown into certain death. These segments evoke a real sense of panic and fear that the game's breathing mechanic is built around.
Breathing serves both as a way to contrast the main character as something familiarly organic against the metallic world around them. Player's must manage their breath as they run, keeping it under control. Should the player panic and lose its rhythm, they will find themselves partially blinded and slowed considerably.
Though I am currently unfinished and only two hours in, NaissanceE is a strong contender for my game of the year, without a doubt. If you're someone who enjoys games like the brooding sci-fi atmosphere of games like The Swapper or enjoy the rarely seen FP Platformer, I strongly suggest you pick up NaissanceE.

Alright, so I'm gonna start by saying I had seen this game before and it sat on my wishlist, and I bought it when it was super on sale over Christmas, so I didn't pay full price.
However! I totally would have paid full price for it ( the sale included the soundtrack/OST bundled with the game ) because this game is amazing. I'm not a huge fan of supernatural/horror games because they actually freak me out, but this game doesn't actually have really any of the typical horror elements. There aren't jumpscares, there's not an insanity system, there's no timers or creepy voices or a lot of the things you would find in other horror games like Outlast or Amnesia. The antagonist in Oxenfree is mostly unseen and is present just enough to be slightly creepy keep the player engaged in the game.
My favorite part about this game is the characters. There are only five of them, and you don't see all of them for an equal amount of time, but the dynamic dialogue system and the fact that how you speak to the different characters really impacts how they react to you and even how the antagonist reacts to the other characters and you. It's definitely a game where your choices matter, even if most of the choices you're making are what to say to whichever character is speaking to you. It might not feel like every single choice matters, but it really does.
I really love the radio mechanic in the game, too. It's unique and something I haven't seen before as a mechanic. It makes the most of a puzzle mechanic in a game to weave together horror and puzzle genres rather beautifully. It also adds a degree of difficulty, especially in later stages of the game ( I remember having to look up the solution to one of the puzzles at one point because I just had no idea what I was looking for ).
It was just a very well done game, and even if one run of the game doesn't take all that long ( it's like Firewatch, you can totally run through the whole game in one sitting if you have the time and dedication, it draws you in almost as well ), there's an interesting and yet another unique bit where whatever you did in the first playthrough has an effect on a second playthrough if you choose to play it again.

Recently my weekly game night with buddies was occupied by the cartoony craziness that is
. It's a solid, fully featured indie side scroll cooperative hack 'n slash, beat 'em up arcade brawler. I think that covers all the genre bases, but what I liked most here was the nostalgia over those great web games from Tom Fulp and Newgrounds!
This is by
, who also created
. I haven't had the pleasure of playing that yet. Like the best of those little Newgrounds flash games,
has fantastic creative vision in both art and design. I wouldn't be surprised if the art were the strongest selling point for most folks. Animations, effects, enemies, environment, the whole package looks awesome.
Gameplay is nothing earth shatteringly new but it is good fun. The main campaign mode is the best part; the arena mode and little mini games are fine, but didn't hold my interest long. There's a decent variety of playable characters, each with differing special properties and magic attacks.
I didn't dig too deep into combat mechanics, but it's neat to use new combos, learn enemy tactics and weaknesses. You can brainlessly button mash through basic enemies. However, Insane mode is another matter entirely, presenting all the challenge a hardcore player could want from this type of game.
Some replayability is present if you care about unlocking all characters and exploring the more interesting weapons, properties & magic. Let's not forget the pets you find and unlock; these critters provide buffs or attacks of some sort. Newly acquired weapons might hit harder, swing faster, reach farther or add an effect. Special items like the shovel offer utility (e.g. digging for treasure).
I love what happens in a cooperative match after you save a princess following a boss fight. Such a great idea to punctuate normal play with those funny moments. I like also how you have to individually loot health and gold. It keeps everyone on their toes and a bit competitive.
I didn't mess with any DLCs, most of which appear to be new characters.
I did use the Steam Controller to play this. It is strongly recommended to use a controller for this game. The improvement in my performance over mouse and keyboard was surprising, and it just feels way more natural.
Thumbs up! Recommended to anyone looking for their next casual co-op with a group of friends.

A superb dialog-rich, story-centric adventure game, with excellent script, characterization, graphics, animation, music, and sound.
Sounds perfect, right? Well, it won't be everyone's cup of tea: gameplay is very linear, walking around is slow, and you'll be listening to a lot of dialog. It's more a choose-your-own-adventure game than a point-and-click quest. The most free-form adventuring you'll do is if you go for the collectibles to get an achievement (and learn more about the background story in the process).
My complaints are petty. There's not quite enough time to make dialog choices, and the dialog bubbles sometimes might appear off-screen if you're standing near an edge, so a few times I didn't manage to click in time. Also, I wish it was longer: I realize a lot of effort went into creating content for various choices the player makes, but since I don't plan to replay, I would have preferred fewer choices and more upfront game length. Finally, though the script is a delight, I found the dialog to be a bit too precious at times. Everyone in the game sounds like an English major.
Whatever. I thoroughly enjoyed it and hope for more games from this great team.
I would also like to thank the developer for supporting Linux. Much appreciated!

Dark Messiah of Might & Magic puts players in a first-person perspective, allowing them to immerse themselves in the legendary Might and Magic universe as never before.
It is also the world's first fantasy action game to feature a complete first-person combat system. It takes full advantage of the Source Engine's exceptional technological enhancements in areas such as character animation, advanced AI, real-world physics and shader-based rendering.
I have played this game during my early childhood and I must admit that once I started playing this game I felt stuck to it and completed it over and over again multiple times.
A game that despite being released in 2006, it’s yet fully capable of taking down some modern games within the same genres.
A fine example of what a good adventure and a first-person action game should be, Dark Messiah of Might & Magic is a remarkable example at its finest.

The adventure that this game is capable of, is reasonable with the addition of secret places that contributes to a careful exploration of each area players find themselves in. Despite being strictly locked only to its main quest and some other minor side quests, it also contains a short amount of role-playing and key decisions throughout the game.
The storyline isn’t the best, it lacks a strong backbone or a base to begin from, and it is based mostly in surprise elements and new elements that will always shape players way of thinking and seeing things as they progress further in the game.

The graphics Dark Messiah is capable of projecting with its Source Engine, despite not being the best for its time, are still pretty good and well-balanced with the game play mechanics and user interface.
About the game mechanics, it is focused not only to give players a very pleasant first person melee/ranged combat experience with many different styles and opponents, but also a strong presence of the use of the surrounding game atmosphere and items during all sorts of conflict.

Despite the rich game combat moves the game allows players to execute, you might feel that most conflicts you face will be ultimately resolved by the use of front kicks combined with the use of the game surroundings and objects around to terminate your enemies.
This can be easily a 'Pro' for most players since it is quite enjoyable to watch enemies being kicked off to spikes or to be kicked off against fragile wooden crates, but maybe a 'Con' for some.

The user interface in this game is simple, clean and again, it does match well with everything else giving players a very good gaming experience.
There is only one way to access your character info, skill points, and quick toolbar which is located at the right top side of your inventory that offers a very simple and easy way to access everything you want.

Despite this game containing more sounds related to the atmosphere of each part of the game than music itself, both are pretty much reasonable in the end I would say.
The voice acting is decent I believe, but sometimes it just feels that it doesn’t fit whenever there is music being played during a cut scene and voice simultaneously.

The game difficulty is very well balanced to meet the tastes of those who wish a enjoyable adventure without struggling that much, to those who want it hardcore with difficult opponents.

The game price that has also been the same for the last few years is incredibly worth it, with or without sales, the content and adventure this game has to offer is totally worth its base price.
I would rate this game 79 out of 100 or 3.9 out of 5.0 stars. An enjoyable adventure with a fair amount of content and a vast adventure with decent graphics and game play for a very good price.

I've been keeping an eye on this one since it was Oort.
Great concept, and the plans for what's ahead are even more exciting, especially if they are implemented as planned.  From what I've seen, I love the art and the concept behind the whole design.  I do wish there were more blocks/items/character designs, (even more than what I've seen planned).  Not because there isn't enough planned, but because this game has so much potential in its art direction, and concept, that it could easily be three times what's currently on the drawing board (that being said it's a very large drawing board as it is).
A relativley small but extremely active community, (active in game, on forums, on the crafting wiki, etc.).  It has consistently surprised me how a small number of people are able to keep a forum going as if there were 10 times as many, and how things continue to noticeably grow in game and out.  I can't wait to see what this game becomes if instead of crying "the game is dead!", people begin to stick around and turn it into a larger community.
That being said I can't stress the word "community" enough.  This isn't a bunch of minecraft players who happen to play on the same server, or a bunch of scattered dirt houses in the middle of nowhere.   This is a community of people communicating and working together to make huge builds, systems of cities, and so much more.  Everyone I've seen in the forums, I've also seen in game, working to make this game as good as it can be.
The game isn't finished yet.  There's a lot to be desired, but a lot in the works.  If you want a great game, you should wait.  If you want to contribute to what could very well be a great game, I would suggest you buy in now.
It's got a ways to go, but it's come a long way.
Edit - December 2017
I'm liking the progress, but I must say, the trailer is quite stretched. There's a few things that don't work the same way, such as only being able see through a few active portals at a time, and grappling hooks not working like that anymore, that EXTREMELY hinder the "expansive" and "exploratory" feel that the trailer gives this game.
These features were changed for good reason, and may be changed back in the future, but as of right now the trailer is a tad dishonest for the game in its current state, and would be better taken as an image of what they want it to be, not what it is.

Here's a little story about how a single colonist completely demolished the colony.
One day my colonists had come across a rocket launcher. I decided to give it to my favorite, most skilled colonist. A few days later a squirrel had gone mad and I sent that same colonist to go kill it. He had decided to walk right up to the squirrel and shoot it at point-blank range... with a rocket launcher... You can guess how badly that went. The explosion caused a massive ring of flames that my other colonists had tried (and failed) to extinguish. The colonist that shot the rocket had been caught aflame and began to run around crazily as he had realized his mistake (and also because he was on fire). Luckilly, he had escaped but was gravely injured. All my colonists were too busy extinguishing the very quickly growing fire to treat him and his injuries were quickly infected. The fire had quickly engulfed the entire map as my colonist died of infection.
The morale of the story?
Don't use a rocket launcher for killing mad animals...
especially at point-blank range...

Overall, 8/10. It just needed a little more to do per area wise.

NaissanceE hits the ground running – or rather, its protagonist does. The opening moments serve as a compressed summary of all that the player is about to experience. Disoriented, panting, lungs pumping air like every moment could be their last. Rows and rows of identical hallways swoosh past. Are the walls really shrinking in on us or is it just a trick of the camera? A glimpse of the assailant giving chase causes the pace to quicken, accentuated by a sickening electronic noise trill. Before long, we come face to face with the creature just moments before falling into a pit that carries us to safety. Safety being relative. As the world we’re introduced to is anything but friendly and familiar.
In a way it’s the older brother of
, one who transitioned from
to
while attending college. Second cousin twice removed to Antichamber, losing almost all of its puzzle genes while retaining the mind-twisting level design. NaissanceE stands proudly next to other modern takes on the puzzle adventure. Progression, while linear, always fits within the massive scope of any particular area. You’ll get lost in the larger maps, poking around in the corners feebly in hopes of finding direction or a sign of life. What plot there is to be told is presented entirely through the environmental clues left behind by whoever came before you. There’s no dialog to be heard, no monologuing audio diaries or scraps of paper to pick up. The only text ever seen is the chapter titles and the main menu options. Everything remains a mystery.
Most of the time is spent simply navigating the large maps with occasional platforming segments to break things up. A breathing mechanic comes into play while sprinting for a short time. Every few seconds while sprinting, a circle will appear on screen. Hitting the right button (defaults to Mouse 1) while the circle is there will make your character take a breath and they will continue running a little longer. Fail to do so and they become winded and slow down drastically. Not something you want happening in the large maps or while jumping from cube to cube. On the note of platforming, I found some of the sequences to be irksome. Some involving awkwardly shaped landing areas and altered physics took me out of the moment if only briefly. I feel like the game could have been better off without those or with a little more care taken with them. You’ll also get to play with some cubes that are sensitive to light sources for a few puzzles, but none of them are particularly difficult.
NaissanceE expertly grasps the concepts behind what makes lonesome wandering compelling. The lights are on but nobody’s home. An expansive view of an area could show thousands of lit windows though you never get the sense that anyone is ever sitting behind them. A few poorly spaced checkpoints and unintuitive platforming segments annoy but don’t detract from the overall experience. As challenging of a play as it is a listen, your hand is never held in the labyrinth. The atmosphere is stifling, mysterious, beautiful. I felt compelled to explore as much as I could even if I knew there was a dead end ahead. In the 5 hours it took me to reach the incredible last moments I remained entranced.
Though, I don’t really know what it all means.
