Listen up, kiddos!
It's time for another good ol' round of first person, shoot 'em up, run and gun, non-stop action! ... Oh, what's that? We're not just rehashing the same game again?
Yeah, that's right, and if you're familiar with Telltale Games, and you played the hell out of "The Walking Dead," "The Wolf Among Us," or any of their other similar titles, odds are, you are going to love "Tales from the Borderlands," just as I did. Esspecially if you happen to already be steeped in the Borderlands story.
Now make no mistake. If you're not familiar with Telltale Games, but you are familiar with the Borderlands IP, this may not be what you're expecting. Telltale Games are story driven, heavy dialogue, narratives that feel much more like a movie than a game. That's not to say there isn't action. Hell, this is Pandora we're talking about, and it's just as violent and bloody as you remember it! But this is not an FPS, so don't be expecting one.
As per the norm with Borderlands games, the writing is witty, hilarious, and, more often than not, brutally heavy on the dark humor.
Also important to remember, TtG release things episodically, so although you'll be starting out with only about a 1 and a half to 2 hour game, that will be extended as the new seasons are released periodically (at no extra charge, of course). It really turns in to about the same thing as waiting for the new season of that show you like... but usually much faster.
Bottom line, if you love games from Telltale, or you happen to really love the story in Borderlands, this one is for you.
So go buy it, OR I'LL... EAT... YO'... BABIES!!!

Thirty minutes in:
So I'm about thirty minutes into NaissanceE and it's as atmospheric and otherworldly as you might have hoped. The environments are expansive, monolithic, not in terms of being open to exploration but in terms of sheer scale. You feel small, lost and utterly alone in this world. It's a world that feels alien and weird, not in the twisty Escher-esque sense that Antichamber had, but like you just don't belong in this place. Even though it isn't a horror game, there's a distinct feeling of tension and apprehension of the unknown, and the unsettling sound effects add to this. It's been a linear journey so far, but I don't mind that. It's a world I want to venture further into and discover more about.
--
Two hours in:
2 hours into the game and it continues to impress. There have been a few challenging platforming sections interspersed between the traversal and light puzzle solving, but for the most part, it's all about the experience. Some might say it's boring, too much walking, but if there's one thing the game has excelled at since the start, it's making you feel small, insignificant within the massive alien spaces. That has been the highlight for me, just traveling through this mysterious complex. You exit from a narrow corridor into a gargantuan space that makes you tense just looking over the edge, and then you realize you have to find a way down. The game doesn't hold your hand, doesn't direct you where to go, besides the visual environmental cues. The game is certainly linear, don't expect a sprawling world, but you do have to find your way and it's easy to get disoriented, lost, turned around. The game has a fantastic atmosphere: mysterious, engaging, ominous, otherworldly.
As for negatives, there's one mechanic that at the moment feels more extraneous than integral to the overall experience. It complicates a simple action, and while it kind of feels almost Receiver-esque in the sense that you have to focus on an action that is usually automatic, I don't think it has really added anything to the gameplay yet. One platforming section was quite frustrating and I ended up just turning up the gamma to complete it. Also I found some checkpoints can be bit too spread out, but that's only been an issue two or three times.
--
Three hours in:
The developer said that the game's four to five hours long, but I'm thinking that's only if you know exactly where to go, how to go there, not die (repeatedly). I'm still on the second chapter. Probably should shave about twenty minutes of my overall play time, because I got stuck on a puzzle with a solution that was annoyingly obvious once I figured out what I was overlooking
My gripe about the checkpoints still stand. Some of them are just too spread out. You'll do some difficult platforming, get a safe area, start another difficult section, die, and then the checkpoint is back at the start of that first section. While you're just traveling and exploring, it's not an issue, but once you're dealing with sections where you can die because of a missed jump after making some progress, it can be frustrating.
But despite this issue (or at least I consider it an issue), the game has not lost any of its luster or mystery. I think the world in this game is by far one of the most alien and atmospheric I've experienced. It's not alien in the way that Avatar's world was, but alien in the unsettling sense that this is truly not a place made for or by humans.
New mechanics are introduced, mainly to offer interesting platforming and puzzle scenarios. It's great when you just have to stop and admire some cool sight, and NaissanceE has had moment after moment like that so far. The sound effects are as well great, really adding a sense of place and tone.
---
Seven hours in:
Yeah, 7 hours and I finally reached Breath Compression. I guess me, first person platforming, and keyboard/mouse controls don't mix well.
But I'm still absolutely loving this game. It does something very well, that I've usually only experienced in sprawling open world games and it's the feeling of seeing something interesting in the distance and then after 10, 15, 20 minutes of traveling, turning the corner and seeing that landmark before you. NaissanceE accomplishes that so well, enticing the player with weird and intriguing architecture and structures far away and then later, you exit a corridor and you're there.
It's a great feeling, that makes the game seem less like a linear adventure and more a journey where you're discovering the path. You never feel pushed or pulled in a direction, the game never takes control of your camera to direct you or tell you to head that way or in this direction. It's masterful in that aspect, subtly driving the player forward not through objective markers or compass arrows but with cues in the environment and the reward of exploration and discovery.
Now while the game is linear, it's certainly not tight corridors. Many areas have surprised me with how open they are, and all have been interesting to explore and just be in. Beside the exploration aspect, the gameplay seems to favor more platforming over puzzles, with a few light based puzzles and several challenging platforming areas.

What can I say about this game?
Not enough, and far too much at the same time. This kind of thing gets old in really short order.
I saw the Jimpressions episode on it months ago, and thought he'd been rather scathing towards it.
I, Lord Crocosquirrel, hereby admit to being wrong. If anything, he was being overly nice to it.
Downright polite, if what I've seen of it is any indication. Not that I made it any farther than he did.
Here's the why:
First, it's a "horror" game on Steam that was made by an indie dev. I've seen a few good ones, but the overwhelming majority are a pile of flaming squirrel dung.
Options Menu: Slider for voice control when there's no voice acting. That's a minor thing, admittedly, but it foreshadows the rest of the experience.
Shoddy controls:  It has controller support, but the only thing that works is the left analog stick. Not a single button works. The keyboard controls work, but are so laggy as to be nearly useless. Might as well just stand there. It's not like littel Timmy is going to turn in place anyway.
Graphics Quality: The less said about this the better. The environments have been hacked together from Unity assets, and the model of the boy in his spiffy hat looks like it was done by a pack of drunken gerbils. Hell's armies are Nazi stormtroopers, and we don't talk about the mummy you have to kill right off the bat.
Gameplay: In the description of the stream I did on this game and a trio of other, less s**t games, I said the game was Digital Homicide levels of Bad. I stand by that statement. You can't turn in place, so kiting an enemy is pretty much out, the flamethrower won't follow you, but keeps emitting the way you were facing. Firing at an angle is difficult at best.
To put a big red bow on the entire mess that's supposed to be combat, not only have we no way to heal, not only does the enemy not even have to be facing your direction to kill you dead, but you have to line up with your target pixel-perfectly and hold it there, or you're not going to do ANY damage. No real audiovisual feedback, so you don't know if you're going to kill it soon or it's going to beat you to death with a stick from three hundred kilometers away.
The little pink bow comes when you die, and you inevitably will. You have to quite to desktop before you can restart, and the cutscenes aren't skippable. You can't even click through the text.
The *music* is just fine-- taken from Incompetech, of course, but I'm guilty of that myself. No foul there, and in fact that was probably the ONLY intelligent thing the developer did.
Needless to say, I'm not giving this a recommendation. Avoid as if your very soul depended on you NOT playing this game. There are better games out there that cost much, much less. Go play those. Seriously.

Fantastic game.
Taking you back to 90's shooters with a modern edge to it, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a fantastic joyride of violence. The gameplay is top notch, mixing fun stealth elements with incredibly satisfying gunfights.
The weapons, such as dual wielded shotguns that take up the majority of the screen, have fantastic audio and visual feedback, that let's you feel the power behind them.
The soundtrack (Composed by Mick Gordon whom also did the soundtracks for Killer Instinct and Doom) is fantastic, jumping between heavy metal and subtle guitar pieces. It creates the perfect moods.
The story is actually quite good, with a lot of care given for the Details and your character, BJ, is someone you actually care about, something rare in FPS games.
The downside, however,  is the game seems to be terribly optimised, especially for AMD graphics cards. I am running a RX480 and the game would have the strangest stutters regardless of the graphics settings. Hoops had to be jumped to get the game to run "Mostly" smoothly, such as manually setting up a texture cache folder, renaming the executable and having to run the program in admin mode. The Vsync is absolute garbage and I reccomend using your Graphics cards built in V-sync instead. This is an unfortunate mark against an otherwise fantastic game.
If your willing to fiddle with settings, absolutely get this game, it is fantastic. Just don't expect to get a perfect 60FPS all the time.

For those of you who dont know what this software is (y are u here) this is EVGAs graphics card overclocking and monitoring tool for EVGA NVIDIA graphics cards I use it mainly to monitor my GTX 980ti Classified, sometimes I will mess around with the overclocking features.
This program has a amazing OSD (On Screen Display) that shows up in games and allows you to monitor your GPU (graphics card) on the fly as you are playing games.
My GPU came out of the box with a extremly conservative fan curve (fan speed) on it, I used this software to change the fan curve to the "aggressive" curve and my GPU temps went down (as I was expecting) and my FPS went up (not by alot but a little is better than anything).
If you are a owner of a EVGA GPU and want to do more with your GPU get this program.
The only downside of this program is it only works on EVGA and NVIDIA GPUs so it will not work on AMD GPUs.
PS: For AMD users there is a program that MSI makes called MSI Afterburner that works for AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.
Overall I give this software a PaulsTwoCents Seal Of Approval

Three strangers touched down on a frigid alien rock at the edge of known space.
As streams of burning debris rain down around them, the frightened survivors, still nauseous from the sudden awakening from hyper sleep, struggle to get their bearings amongst the jagged rocks and pine trees.
They hastily assemble a shelter near steam geyser, hoping to syphon off enough warmth to avoid hypothermia in this world of endless winter while their cat frolics happily in the snow.
The three marooned travellers barely scratch out an existence on their snowy hillside, eventually moving in to a rocky cavern in the hopes escaping to a better life underground. For days the team had been digging out steel and components from the remains of some ancient buried machine, to construct a wind turbine, providing power and much needed heat for their new subterranean town.
After weeks of scraping by on small game and rodents, the harsh winter has driven off the last remaining animals. The survivors are left starving in their glorified hole.
For former Actor, Cob, the hunger is too much to bear. In a last act of theatrical drama, he takes off his clothes and wanders around, eyes glazed, setting fire to everything in sight before shuffling off in to the icy darkness to die of hypothermia.
The two remaining travellers manage to extinguish the blaze but not before the heater is destroyed and the walls are breached exposing them to the -21° air outside.
Starving and shivering, the two remaining shipmates are slowly brought down as they attempt to gather the necessary wood to make repairs.
They collapse in the snow as their frostbitten limbs splinter and break off. Freshly cut logs clutched permanently in their frozen hands.
Their faithful Cat hearing their cries of despair rushes over and begins to eat them.
10/10

Do you remember why you play games?
Maybe it's so you can carry out dangerous missions you couldn't do in real life, like operate a cement mixer, join two pieces of wire together, fetch tools, pass notes to people across the other side of a small room or search for mouldy concrete.
Maybe you actually do want to do something original, like pilot a submercible or go for a spacewalk on the moon - but only for about a minute or so.
Maybe you want to play a stealth game where the enemies line up with their backs to you along a convenient linear path. Or maybe a first-person-shooter where the guns get worse throughout the game to the point where you only manage three shots before you need a recharge like a cheap mobile phone. Maybe you prefer exploration in dull, predictable areas until a blue cursor bothers to appear on a door handle - the only one you can open.
Maybe you like sitting through cut scenes every five minutes and listening to the inner musings of a man with a voice so gruff only whales can distinguish his words.
Maybe you think modern graphics are overrated and long for the days of average textures and poor environment detail. Maybe you like seeing the graphics constantly drawn and re-drawn while you play. Maybe you never saw the point of anti-aliasing and wished they'd just stop supporting it. Maybe you wondered what the fuss with physics engines was all about. Maybe, in spite of all this, you still have a large hard drive and want to fill it with 45GB of data.
Maybe you'd like to see every cliche and kitchen sink from every shooter in the last fifteen years slapped together like a clay model of desperation and dung. Maybe you'd like a nice twee song at the end to make you feel better.
Maybe you'd like another boring Wolfenstein spin-off, one which can't even pay homage to the original without ruining that too.
Well congratulations, your day has truly come.

For the first 10 minutes of my journey, Boundless was a pretty good upgrade to Minecraft. Then, as I was learning about plots and fantasizing about one day owning enough to encompass an entire planet, someone approached me. That alone broke any remaining ties to other sandbox games that thrive on you being alone with your thoughts and feeding off your creativity to do things you could do in any other game. *someone approached me* and asked how I was doing? What a crazy concept, that people just walk around and ask how you are in this game. He must be bored :/. The fellow mentions that he owns a nearby shop, and that if I needed anything, which I probably would, that I should spend my arbitrary currency there, and invited me to follow him to see it.
That's all it took. Seeing a shop run by a player, and seeing that player journey out into the world to find clientele in a fairly philanthropic manner told me everything I needed to know about how in depth this game would be. The first week was full of exciting discoveries: massive player-built cities, incredibly diverse terrain and cave systems with mining that actually rewarded you appropriately. The second week was full of ambitious ventures that didn't QUITE work out, but still fueled my desire to achieve more. The weeks since have been an endless journey of learning and scientifically testing theories and ultimately creating a multi-planet trading company based in a huge market with mining base camps spread throughout the stars.
There is simply no limit to what you can achieve in Boundless. This game offers something for every kind of player, and every kind of player who doesn't think they fall in to any category for "kinds of players". The community is full of rich characters and supportive groups of people that want nothing more than to help you on your journey. The developers are just as friendly, and always patient. The content is endless, the gameplay is always fun, and
well basically, there is no reason not to buy this game. It is hands down the best sandbox game on the market, and if you want something to crush your jaded cynicism about early access games, developer forums, and sandbox communities, this is the one. Hope to meet you in-game, fellow Oortlings :)

Paradise Lost Meets Osiris' Trial Simulator.
But in all seriousness...
I've seen very few games where the story and the gameplay don't directly interact at all, yet, because they stay out of each other's way, each shines brightly to create a grand experience.
There are a lot of interesting passages to read and audio logs to listen to in this game.  There are also a ton of puzzles which will not only test your patience, but prove how incredibly stupid and incompetent you are.  If you've played Sigils of Elohim (the side game that is FREE) to any extent, well, you might handle the sigil puzzles but the main ones will likely frustrate you after a time.
Don't expect some grand drama or any combat or action (outside of you evading mines) or anything like that in the first couple of hours.  While some puzzles can have heart-pounding moments, the overall game is slow-paced and contemplative.  Spend as much time as you need slowly reading the various snippets and graffiti on the walls, or gradually planning out your strategy as the voice in the sky mocks you for how slow you are in the most passive-aggressive of ways.  (But heed him, though, as reacting to it brings
.)
I've played other puzzle games, but few have thoughtful pieces of writing that I can read through and enjoy.  Now sure, the philosophical concepts might not seem as impressive to people who have contemplated the nature of Artificial Intelligence and Personhood, but hey it's still a great thing to come across these days!
I dare say that, no matter how frustrating these puzzles are, you'd might regret not picking this up!

Date: 2/25/16
Review Number: 27
Game: You Don't Know JACK (group review, classics)
From (Creator Publisher): Jackbox Games
Played On: Steambox (controller/keyboard)
Steam Price as of Review: $2.99 per game, $20.00 for all the classics
Total Time played: So much time
Review:
Having at least eight different versions of You Don't Know Jack in my steam list, I had a feeling that these were going to come up sooner or later, and so rather than bore you with the possibility of multiple reviews of what is essentially the same game done over and over, I'll just compress this down to one review, though it's the Television version that gets the lucky posting.
Now I have been a huge fan of trivia games for some time.  Nearly every time I have deigned to grace others with my magical presence in a social situation has nearly always been in a bar that has trivia, and indeed my wife has an even greater breadth of trivia knowledge than I do.  However, for the most part, I have found many trivia games, games that by their nature should be a social event, to be somewhat lacking on the PC and mobile devices.  However, there is one specific series that has kept my attention for a large chunk of my portion as a breathing meatsack on this planet, and that is the You don't Know Jack series by the now named Jackbox Games.  Now for the most part, trivia games have a very simple formula, you get asked questions, you answer them, and the fastest/most correct/best at distracting other players ends up winning.  But what sets games apart in this genre is the social experience.  are the questions amusing enough to keep a group entertained?  Is the gameplay smooth enough to be somewhat transparent and intuitive?  Are the questions easy enough to be generally answerable without insulting most player’s intelligence?  If you can positively answer at least two of these questions you usually have a sellable game, however YDKJ has generally gotten all of them right.  The questions are actual solid trivia type questions on par with even the more taxing game shows, yet they are framed in a almost slapstick environment that keeps players totally entertained.  The multiplayer is seamless (particularly in the newer games from the party packs) and has been the source of many a shouting and cheering match at family gatherings.  Even the voice acting is golden (though I prefer the newer announcer Cookie over Schmitty anyday), adding humor without drowning out the actual game itself.
All in all, YDKJ is the type of game that you buy and play and play and play until the questions start repeating themselves, and if you are able to get to that point while having four players running the game every time, you probably know enough people to run for public office, so be sure to be graceful in victory.  Or pay your opponents, whatever works in your political arena.
Game’s Fate: Removed the old ones from the steambox, but I keep the new ones.  Party games don't get any better than this.
Buy/No Buy: Specifically on the classics?  They’re awesome, but unless you are a trivia nut, save your money for the newer ones in the party packs.  Now the new ones.  Those are a buy

It's not exactly Walking Dead, and it's not exactly Borderlands. But if you enjoy one or both of those, you should love this game. It still keeps in a lot of Borderlands elements (inventory, loot, humor, etc.), while still playing like the familiar Telltale point-and-click adventure.
The first episode offers a lot (about 2 1/2 hours if you look around), and you're immediately latched to the characters. You know about everyone's motives about the second they show up, and know if you like them or not. The writing is still Borderlands-style, so you may get more for your mileage if you're familiar with the series, but it's very well done. It's not full of boner jokes (yet), but there's still the silly stuff in there. The game relies a bit more on the inventory like Sam & Max than Walking Dead (still no combining items again, though) ie. Fiona's character uses cash that can directly influence conversation, whereas Rhys's lets him scan things to let you learn more about the world, and sometimes find items. Which works well from being based on a game centered on loot.
All-in-all -- it's humorous, well-writ, suspenseful, and most of all - good. If you're hesitant in any way, you could pick up on a sale, but as a fan of Telltale and Borderlands it was worth every dollar. And I'm sure even non-fans would enjoy the ride this game gives you.

Great moba on the road to finding a happy medium between casual and competitive.
Right now, the developers seem to be searching for the footing of their original vision - gameplay geared towards a less toxic community experience & room for creative player gameplay. Sadly, the game is fumbling in this area.
Overall the meta game is easy to understand and fun to play. Unfortunately the game falls into the same pitfalls of most mobas - Its community. There is a range from extremely nice people to very toxic players, to leavers and griefers. The toxicity is enough to ruin anyone's day though it seems ( and I stress the word seems ) that the developers want to solve this problem.
Another major impetus for me here was the ability to build any character anyway you'd like; Diverging from set character roles. This is another major failing. When the game's beta started, there were a few heroes and the idea worked though needed some further refinement. Now that the roster has grown to about thirty characters, roles are definitely set. When playing against others, characters are contantly built identically and the same usual items are used again and again. This detracts from the creative spirit and is reminiscent of Dota 2.
Positively, ranked mode was recently added along with interesting characters coming regularly. In the way of player agency, each are afforded a pet (from a selection of twelve) and allowed to craft items with different attributes. These seeds were planted since the alpha stage and go a long way in winning any match.
Beyond the player interaction, this game is amazingly fun with friends and if you can find a couple ~ definitely give this game a try. Not to mention, the art style is beautiful. If the developers can really own their vision of a better community ( Which sister moba, Heroes of The Storm has a greater handle on ) and more creative ways to build characters - This will be one of the premier mobas out there.

It's time to give this a short review.
Hands down this is the best photogrammetry software available. The results are astonishing and extremely detailed. At the same time it's BLAZING FAST in comparision with other software such as Photoscan (even 1.3). But it's not only fast, it's extremely precise. Photoscan (which I must have used easily over 1000 hours) does get the job done, but it looks like it is still aimed more towards topography using drones. While Reality Capture really likes to capture real life scenes with tiny detail and even thin objects. The superior generation of depth maps is key here. It does detect much more detail and the production of meshes is unmatched. I have some saved meshes at roughly 150million polygons. This number alone is insane, but RC can go much further than that. And these meshes are still manageable because they come in smaller sub-parts AND can be simplified through RC itself.
The texturing usually takes the longest time, however the results are simply perfect. As perfect as your photos allow of course.
You don't have to be afraid to throw thousands of photos at RC (2500 photos are allowed in this license I think). It will align them and it will run stable and fast doing so. If you are familiar with other Photogrammetry software, you will be shocked how fast and perfect Reality Capture does align the cameras.  There is a ton of options to tweak the process and results.
It takes a while to really understand Reality Capture but for beginners there is a "Start" button which really everybody can use and get some great results out of it. Of course the results vary depending on the quality, number and type of photos.
There was a problem with the license server (@Steam?) for roughly 24?hours, so all users couldn't use RC. I hope this doesn't happen anymore, because other than this minor issue the software is really good.

This game has such a great first half. Seriously exemplary and I am recommending it specifically for that purpose.
The story is so compelling and interesting. The gameplay, level design, the story itself, and basically everything about the game is wonderful.
However, I almost don't recommend the game. It suffers from a lot of just trashy design right at the end. Everything goes from being logically challenging and entertaining to being blatantly annoying and just extremely rushed.
I don't want to give too many spoilers, but at about the half way mark you take a vehicle that is rather large for what it is, but then it just feels like you hit a brick wall as far as the entertainment value is concerned. Every level after feels like it's just more of that level for no reason at all. The boss fights stopped being fun and started just being really boring. The only thing challenging about the final boss is the pure♥♥♥♥♥♥that is the level design, hands down one of the most dissapointing turns of the game. Had I known the game was only going to be annoying for the final half, I would have simply stopped half way because I absolutely hated the way this game ended.
There was nothing fun about half of the game. The story was completely rushed to find a conclusion and the conclusion itself wasn't satisfying in any way. The main bad guy is someone you see twice in the game.
I'm so emotionally invested.
/sarcasm
Another dumb part of this game is the fact that absolutely none of it was over the top scifi like how I wanted. I wanted glowing nazi's, I wanted crazy weapons that do ridiculous things, I wanted silly magic, I wanted a story that doesn't wrap up about as clean and efficiently as a 30 car pileup caused by a downed cargo plane full of deer♥♥♥♥♥♥ All of a sudden everything just goes to crap in the story, no real build up to it, no real reason explained as to why it happened, but whatever.
The core game is really fun, you'll probably have a lot of fun playing it, but you will get really annoyed by a lot of the things the game does wrong. And I mean really ♥♥♥♥ing annoyed.
I also hate how short this game is. It suffers from what a lot of games suffer from. It doesn't feel like a whole game. It feels like a tech demo almost. How do they compensate for the lack of a longer story? They throw in audio logs, which is fine because that part ended up being really cool. What else did they do?
They made it to where half of the game is just replaying the game with a slightly different aspect. That is hands down the worst thing this game could have done. I really don't think I'll ever play this game again, I have no reason to.
The decision at the start determines one thing: Armor or Health upgrades. That's it. Realistically, someone who spends a little less time fooling around would finish the story in under 8 hours. Double that. That's the whole game.
All in all, it's visually stunning, plays really well with very few bugs (knife throwing is done horribly, as well as the grenades, and switching weapons, and the weapons themselves are all a major let down by the end).
I have a whole bunch of other reasons why I didn't really have fun with this game, but overall, I think most people will have a lot of fun with it and it's really not even that bad of a game. Bethesda just did what it does with literally everything, a full on nuke to the foot at a certain point and it just never recovers for me after that.

I wouldn't say it's the best FPS out there at the moment, it's up for debate whether it's even the best free-to-play FPS, but it's certainly far-and-away the best free-to-play FPS of its kind. It's got a fair few problems - most of them very small, granted - but none of them are enough to prevent the game from being an enjoyable FPS experience.
It is one of those free-to-play games where it's hard to avoid spending at least some money on it if you're going to be putting a lot of hours into it, especially if you're going to be taking it more seriously – unlocking mercs without spending real money happens at a snail's pace – but that's hardly a huge deal.
The combat mechanics are very solid. Guns are a little hit-or-miss but mostly feel good, the walljumping mechanics are finicky and extremely situational but satisfying to use when the opportunity comes up, it's very accessible but still has enough depth to stay interesting. If you're a picky nerd like myself who likes to tweak settings, the game is very customizable if you have the patience to faff around with UE3 configs (if you're used to Source config editing, it's the same kinda thing except about five times as awkward) which is a huge plus in this day and age where you're lucky to get decent FOV options, let alone proper configs or, god forbid, a developer console.
The non-combat aspects of the gameplay are where it starts to fall a little more flat. Many of the maps are convoluted and unintuitively laid out. Some maps seem to have about 539 different flank routes judging by how many different angles people find a way to show up from. Objectives (while, granted, quite diverse which makes for a lot of variety) are often vague and seem to be fighting against the game's combat rather than blending with it to create a coherent gameflow. It's difficult to really tell sometimes how much impact your actions are having (if any at all). Individual mercs, with only a few exceptions, all have the same kind of sillhouette and colourscheme and are honestly pretty close to indistinguishable from each-other at a distance when playing, which can make it tough to know what exactly you're fighting. Take all this with a pinch of salt if you're looking at taking the game more seriously and playing ranked/PUGs/etc. because as you would expect it seems a lot better, but for me personally this game is my "can't be bothered to play Quake" option so that's no great comfort.
If you've played any significant number of hours of Team Fortress 2, you should be used to enjoyable but very rough-around-the-edges FPS games, and this game is one of those through-and-through. It's flawed in areas, but it's well worth playing regardless. Whether it's worth investing a lot of time and money into is another matter, but the beauty of free-to-play games is that you can figure that out for yourself at no cost except time and disk space. It's fun, give it a shot.

I don't really know where to begin and if I don't control myself I probably won't know where to end, but I'll do my best:
When you see a game trailer buzz words things like open world, sand box, dynamic quests, proceedurally generated whatnots with exploration, crafting, multiplayer, pve/pvp and multiplayer building limited only by your imagination, you get intrigued.
Or at least I used to. Before every game used them whether they delivered on them or not.
This game is being developed in a market so saturated with the stuff, I stumbled upon it randomly only after sifting through 4 or 5 'Discovery Queues' cuz I was bored.
The development team is constantly updating and testing new things (a lot suggested by players in the forums) on their test server while the 'live server' where you usually play is always filled with helpful and friendly people.
I was luckier than some out there. I started out in a location that wasn't far from some other people. A couple beaconed off plots were ignored but then there were many others that were either beautiful gigantic castles or cozy homes starting out from scratch. I log in a day or 2 later and see even more people and the buildings even more developed. Real neighbors.
I ventured over into the forums and found many other planets with settlements, towns and cities already made by different communities from all over the world. Many invited me, all were friendly and welcoming.
Portals. You gotta love them portals. Seamless travel from one planet (server) to the next. Many have made portal networks between cities, linking you to whatever community you want to be a part of.
Community. The devs made an amazing system, great art style and graphics and all based on intriguing lore, but you know what really gets to me? The community. It's half the damn game. One player invited me to his build off on another planet. Gave me a tour. A shining castle of beauty it was. All around it? Countryside, some floating islands and rocks, forest.
It's been about a month now. Along with new and old players being invited to his place, there is now the beginnings of a city, homes, public baths, monuments, aquaducts directing water all over the city to peoples builds. All this built from nothing but a community discussing ideas.
Dungeon crawler? Yeah, they made a huge tear in the city terrain delving deep into the abyss below, filled it with lava and traps/portal and jumping puzzles and now we have a diabolical obstacle course of doom that the community is having loads of fun trying to complete.
A true player driven economy. It's not all worked out yet, but there are already cities developed to be markets. Players made these. They make their store fronts, sell their stuff for what price they feel is competitive. I travel to specific planets and cities just to buy from specific stores and window shop others.
Early Access right? Bugs and things not working right? Sure sometimes. If you expect to find everything working like minecraft and instantly get bored the minute you see something doesn't, then I invite you to try meeting some of the community in game. I've met people from all around the EU, NA and Oceanic servers and every one of them showed me something new I could do, places to explore and builds to collaborate on.
Crafting. I'm not grinding to craft all the tiers of tools and machinery. Personally, I barely have Iron tools and a few machines. I've been too busy having fun and doing stuff with the community. 133 hrs under my belt already. So yes, there's a lot you can do.
It's pre alpha, yeah. It's also something that lives up to all the buzzwords mentioned above and reminds you of how you felt when you first heard them and imagined the possibilies.

Similarities to Minecraft
1) I found myself building a castle on top of a mountain similar to what I would build in Minecraft, but with out some of the features like corner stairs.
2) It is an open world sand box games with voxel graphics. Granted, this is a genre of its own now, but Minecraft is likely the most successful of the genre and is inherently a reference point for other games to be compared to.
3) (Conditional) I did not encounter any other players in my ten hours playing; however, I did see quite a few abandoned beacons. While I'm sure the longer I played the more likely I would encounter other players, the ten hours I spent playing felt single player. I say this is conditional because, from what I gather, the initial spawn location is randomized. This means I really just pulled a short straw, but a big appeal to this game is the multiplayer aspect.
In short, I found myself doing the same activities as minecraft, the game is of a similar genre, and it felt single player.
Differences to Minecraft
1) The portal aspect of this game looks very interesting and I'll likely come back to explore that in more depth.
2) The grapple was fun - especially when dual wielding. Although, it would be nice to have a "pull yourself up" function. I spent a lot of time dangling wondering how to fix my situation.
3) The crafting was different. Not a big fan of arbitrary wait timers. While those timers do add a since of supply and demand and/or the necessity to expand one's facilities, they also slow the pacing. Which makes a game spent grind materials for crafting even slower. Although, we live in a fast paced world so that might just be my over stimulated bias.
Hope this is helpful. Definitely the most time I've spent reviewing a game.
Regardless, I'm going to switch my review to a thumbs up. Having an active developement crew is a HUGE plus and worth supporting.

Tales from the Borderlands. Another great installment from the developer we know and love Telltale Games. But don't let the title fool you. This is not your regular Borderlands game; It just have the title, humor, and the backstory of the franchise. It's a brand new game with a completely different genre and story taking place in a completely different universe story-wise. A game by Telltale Games is a point-and-click adventure game designed to be enjoyed with a enthralling single player story and character development. A dialogue driven story where your choices have enormous consequences. One thing I can assure you is that Gearbox has no influence over Telltale Games and make games in such different ways that it's not even humanly possible to try to compare the two. In my personal opinion, I suspect that Telltale Games will do something brilliant with the title that Gearbox has not yet succeeded and thus far with Zer0 Sum the odds are really good. They can take any title and story and turn it into a game with extremely satisfying results.
I didn't buy this game because it is titled Borderlands - I got it because it is labeled Telltale Games. So should you buy Tales from the Borderlands? Borderlands fan or not I guarantee you it will be worth every penny. My favourite racer of all time. Even better than Mario Kart.
It is increadibly fun, and the vehicle trasformations bring a unique aspect of gameplay that I have not really seen in a racing game. Driving one second, and flying the next. The trasforrmation animations are pretty cool too.
This also brings another aspect to the forefront: the maps and level designs - they are amazing. What is really great is how dynamic they are. On one lap you are driving around like a regular cart racer, then on the next lap, the world is ripped appart as the vehicles trasform, while trying to dodge debris and take a completely different route from the previous lap. The worlds are really beautiful too, and there are some cool models scatered throughout - like that cool dragon.
Graphics are really great. Diffenitly the prettiest kart racer out there. They really colpliment the art style, and the vehicle models are really detailed, especially while watching them change. Music is perfect and well-suited to the games style. Controls are also great. Really responsive - and not just accelerate, with left and right turn. When flying, you have control over the pitch. You also have to control the awesome weapons. Then there is the flipping which helps you get boost, and lastly there is the drift button which is key to winning or lossing.
The only draw-back is some of the characters. Sega does not have the licences like Nintendo, and some of the ones they do have are a bit riddiculous: like a couple of those wierd dance characters. You do get Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Shadow and Dr Eggman who are the cool Sonic characters. But you also get crappy ones like Amy, and a few of his "Friends" littered throughout the tracks. There are also many characters that I have no clue who they are, since many are old console characters which never made it to PC. You do get many cool ones like Team Fortress, Crazy Taxi and the like. But, you do get some which may become dated as time goes on like some real-life race driver lady, and Wreck it Ralph. With all this in mind, however, all the characters are pretty well balanced. You don't get and overpowered or too weak characters in the game - they all have their pro's and cons.
With all this, the awesome amounts of unlocks and achievements, this game is stuffed-full of content, and even more fun with friends. You have to get this game.

This is amazing software - I prefer it much more than its competitors at the moment, mainly for it's processing power.  With the competition, even if they allow for over 50 camera shots (for entry-level purchases), throwing 2k pictures at a scene takes an impossibly long time to generate results with the competition - with RC you can have some decent output in half the time or less.
It's so good in fact that collecting scenes has widened from 'a good deal of planning onto collect the right pictures to re-assemble a scene' to include scenes that I can do ad-hoc in 20 minutes or less handheld.  I can blow through a few of those a day with RC, and simply don't have enough time to try these 'fun' scenes out with other software.
Like all photogrammetry software, however, there is a steep learning curve that requires a lot of research and knowledge in a lot of different areas - if you're willing to ride that learning curve out, it will reward you with magical results.

From an industrial engineering point of view this software is not ready yet. I played around with demo, before purchasing one month sub to conclude my anlyses. I compared it to Agisoft Photoscan side by side with same photosets. Agisoft stays as my choice, while I will keep an eye on this for further improvements.
Overall is very good if you are interested in doing objects which you have access to from all sides or on a turn table. If you are reconstructing installed items in tight spaces with access only from 1 out of 6 sides you will find it losing details as well as forcing watertight mesh. Usage of DSLR is advised as it does not work properly with mobile phone cameras.
Pros:
Amazingly incredible Processing Times
Better quality dense clouds
Understands depth and overall dimensions of objects better than Photoscan
Vertex coloring scale settings
Does not run out of memory on highest settings (32gb)
Supports 3D scanners, but not all kind.
Reconstructs better meshes of small, round and curved objects
Cons:
Alignment algorythm is worse than Photoscan, had to manually create control points several times.
Alighnment in draft mode results in single merged component, while higher settings alignment splits the model into different components.
Loses details which are beyond primary object but are clearly seen, even with background detection off. While they are reconstructed just fine in Photoscan.
Dense clouds are sparser than Photoscans.
Difficult to navigate UI
Forced Watertight meshes
Enormous file size of exported meshes
No .wrl or .stl export option
Settings are poorly explained
Works bad with mobile phone cameras, usage of DSLR is advised
Currently aimed at hobbyists and 3D Artists.
Overall the main selling point is SUPER FAST PROCESSING TIME. Another point i ticked for myself is more precise (even though sparser) dense clouds and meshes.

After using the promo license at both a world renound 3d VFX studio and at home for 8 months I feel like I can safely write a review people can trust.
Reality Capture Has been a massive part of my daily work, producing solid 3d models for a big VFX pipeline, The interface will take a fair bit of time to use as the way it works is fairly unique, however once a basic understanding is aquired you can really speed up your Photogrammetery.
One thing I feel needs to be highlighted higher up is that you NEED an nvidia graphics card, as CUDA processing is the backbone of this software.
When Comparing RealityCapture to Its main competetors, you tend to find yourself looking at just how quick it is, And its amazingly simple workflow which can be delved into to change each individual setting related to almost everything.
This is great for people like me, who try to configure the software to produce the best results for each different scan type. Sometimes spending more time configuring than processing!
One thing I must say to newcomers to this software is READ THE HELP PAGE INSIDE REALITYCAPTURE. enable tutorial mode, it will walk you through all the settings and how they work.
For people who are unable to remove images. Change the workflow of a 'pane' to 1ds mode and then select the images you want to remove from calculation, then in the 'component view' below the 1ds pane, click the dropdown box where it says 'enable in alignment'.
Pros:
The software is Fast and can handle massive datasets
Control point addition tools are incredible
Fast turnarounds for exports
Mesh outputs are very detailed
Simple mesh decimation/reduction tools
Quick UV/Texturing
Processes a simple shoot in seconds, 12 frames of a facial capture at 2k will produce roughly 1.2m polygons
Cons:
Lack of 3rd party documentation
Requires nVidia GPU
8bit texture exports
Expensive if wanting to use it as a command line based program.
Conclusion:
While the software may be confusing at first, I really suggest reading the help documentation. It is incredibly in depth!
I also highly reccomend joining the 3d Scanning Users Group on facebook for help, we are really into this stuff and are more than happy to support newcomers!

Boundless is one of the many voxel based crafting/exploration games. The games it has most in common with (that I'm aware of) are Creativerse and Minecraft.
What's good about the game:
- Very very pretty
- Great music/atmosphere
- Amazing community
- Active devs
- Chisel system, this allows you to customize the shape of blocks to some extend, allowing for more elaborate creations.
- Smart stacks, great way of managing your inventory
- Seamless transition between different worlds. While this is cool and amazing, the individual planets (that I've visited) are not super varied. While in Minecraft you can run for a long time in one direction and find lots of different biomes, here you'll find a couple, and to find more, you'll have to travel to other planets. I like this better, as it also changes the skybox etc.
Cons:
- Mechanics not very well explained. The tutorial is very basic due to the nature of early access. However, if you want some pointers, either asking on the forums/discord, or checking videos by Jiivita (or one by me) will help.
- Quite grindy. Mining is very slow, and some things you need are really really hard to find. However, one thing to take into account is that this is an MMO. Stuff is slow, but if you make friends and interact with people, you can get stuff done more quickly and in a more fun way. So this can be a pro/neutral/con depending on what you like.
- Not a whole lot of 'gameplay' content. There's lots of blocks, and hours upon hours of fun to be had. However, if you're looking for a game with things like farming, loot, pets etc., look elsewhere...at least for now! This is in early access, and there are lots of plans for development. But if you're expecting a game where you can automate everything or build a big working farm, this stuff is not in (yet).
- The price. This held me off for a long time. However, now I feel like it was money well spent, but it was a barrier to entry. This leads me to another point. If you spend some extra money for the adventurer tier...you get access to the world builder. This lets you design biomes, worlds and assets using a (initially confusing) very nice flow-chart system. I'm absolutely in love with this, and think I will play with this more than I'll be playing the actual game!
Overall, this is a wonderful game that's going to give me many hours of creative fun! There's not a whole lot of 'game' here yet, next to the mining and building, but reading about the dev's ideas makes me very excited indeed!

It was a long time in coming, but I'm finally ready to give this game a positive review.
Like plenty of folks out there, I've had some bad experiences with Early Access. I know the sorrows of owning abandonware, and maybe a game or two that should've been abandoned. And Boundless came out a looong time ago, in fairly rough shape, and for quite some time I held my breath and prayed that it wouldn't die a cruel death. I'd say the initial release was a bit premature, and you can still see the effects of it in some of the older reviews, but the devs have been on the right track for a long time and things are only looking better.
The game is still in Early Access, with all of the bugs and resets that that entails. Ultimately, with an Early Access game, you have to judge two things:
1) The devs' vision for their game
2) The devs' ability to actually execute that vision
For a long time, I was in love with #1 but feared the worst for #2. But this game has continued forward at a steady pace and has picked up momentum as it goes. The devs have been responsive to player input throughout the process, but not so sensitive as to lose direction. And they started out slowly with building lots of the basics behind the scenes, but the tangible results of their efforts are more and more obvious every day.
In a nutshell, what you're getting is a beautiful game that lets you build beautiful things, in a way that's easy and fun to share with your neighbors. The current community is still small but incredibly friendly by Interweb standards, and your ability to interact and collaborate can lead to some mighty fancy team projects. Right now, even exploring the natural beauty of the worlds is rewarding in and of itself; once they add in more PvE objectives, there should be even more out there for the adventurous types. The visuals, the interface, the crafting--everything is good now but continues to improve on a steady basis.
It took almost 2 years of fear and paranoia and nail-biting, but I'm finally happy with my purchase and confident that the devs are reaching their goal of creating an incredible game. If you'd like to be a part of the process, now's a pretty good time to get on board.

A towering achievment of small game design. Oxenfree could be called a walking (and talking) simulator - the gameplay, such as it is, is largely based around the dialogue choices you make throughout the story when interacting with the non-player characters that accompany you on your journey. The controls are simple, and while a certain mechanic (controlling your characters small radio) can be a bit finicky at times, never so much as to detract from the immersion.
So what's so special about this title? The execute level on this thing is in a rare class. The art and music are perfectly on point. The writing swings for the quiet fences - the attempt to write naturalistic conversations and to convey character through them, could have gone very wrong. It didn't. It could have got terribly tripped up on its supernatural/sci-fi aspects, but it didn't. The pacing pulls you along and then wraps itself up before you have a chance to get tired of the company of the characters. Then, it gives you a reason to want to jump right back in. This thing is expertly strung.
In sum, the rare case of an appealing vision, executed flawlessly. If "thoughtful character piece with supernatural/sci-fi complications told as walking-talking simulator" does not sound like your cup of tea, then by all means pack another blend. But if that sounds like something you might enjoy, have no reservations because Oxenfree is astoundingly good.

Three strangers touched down on a frigid alien rock at the edge of known space.
As streams of burning debris rain down around them, the frightened survivors, still nauseous from the sudden awakening from hyper sleep, struggle to get their bearings amongst the jagged rocks and pine trees.
They hastily assemble a shelter near steam geyser, hoping to syphon off enough warmth to avoid hypothermia in this world of endless winter while their cat frolics happily in the snow.
The three marooned travellers barely scratch out an existence on their snowy hillside, eventually moving in to a rocky cavern in the hopes escaping to a better life underground. For days the team had been digging out steel and components from the remains of some ancient buried machine, to construct a wind turbine, providing power and much needed heat for their new subterranean town.
After weeks of scraping by on small game and rodents, the harsh winter has driven off the last remaining animals. The survivors are left starving in their glorified hole.
For former Actor, Cob, the hunger is too much to bear. In a last act of theatrical drama, he takes off his clothes and wanders around, eyes glazed, setting fire to everything in sight before shuffling off in to the icy darkness to die of hypothermia.
The two remaining travellers manage to extinguish the blaze but not before the heater is destroyed and the walls are breached exposing them to the -21° air outside.
Starving and shivering, the two remaining shipmates are slowly brought down as they attempt to gather the necessary wood to make repairs.
They collapse in the snow as their frostbitten limbs splinter and break off. Freshly cut logs clutched permanently in their frozen hands.
Their faithful Cat hearing their cries of despair rushes over and begins to eat them.
10/10

The best way to describe Squad is a blend between the arcade-y feel of Battlefield and the uncomprimising realism of ArmA, though it is a simplification. Squad puts heavy emphasis on communication both within and between individual squads, which can be a flaw as much as the strength of the game. The inability to find a standard level of communication between servers and squads can be frustrating, even making the game unplayable at times. Servers have attempted to inplement rules banning for squad leads for lack of communication, however this seem poorly enforced. That being said, in a good squad and a good team, Squad provides one of the most rewarding experiences gaming I've had. Though it currently lacks the features and the polish of both ArmA and battlefield, as it is still in Alpha afterall, it still feels like a complete game and I would highly reccomend the game if you're willing to deal with all the issues prone to games in Alpha.

Further Update, because one of the developers has come on here and accused me of "trolling":
"CapturingReality", the company behind "RealityCapture", released this program as a free-to-use-as-long-as-you-let-them-collect-information-on-you beta in December 2015. I've been working with photogrammetry for the past 5-6 years, using primarily Agisoft Photoscan. Naturally, I jumped at the chance to test out a new software that claimed to be faster and more accurate. At first, all was great, despite the weird user interface and random crashes and sometimes inaccurate-looking models. There's no doubt that it's a very fast software: it can do in 30 minutes what it takes photoscan a couple hours to process. However, and it's a big however, I'm not convinced of the "accuracy" of this software's results, and the developers have shown themselves to be very arrogant, time and again.
So, in short, I've been using this software for almost a year: I have experience with it. In some respects it's great, but overall, between their pricing strategy and general attitude, I just get a bad vibe from it.  If you're a professional who makes more than 80k per year from laser- and photo-scanning, it might be a good investment, but for the STEAM community, which is mostly made up of hobbyists and independent developers, I can't in good conscience recommend this software over any number of open-source or cheaper, non-rentware programs.

(I was mad but this is still my opinion) This game runs horribly, I know it's only in Alpha but it is garbage. I have a GTX 970 and an i7 processor and the game runs at 45 FPS, there are few good servers for me to play on, there are a lot of empty ones. I joined one server that was 150 ping instead and nobody would talk to me in chat or voice coms ( yes I was in squad chat), and I had to run for 10 minutes to get immediatly shot and had to do it over again. I am extremely dissapointed and now I own a 50$ tech demo that steam won't let me refund. I sincerely hope this gets better in the future because this is one big lie. Everyone says it's amazing, every review, every friend who has it, but it really isn't. "you just don't understand the game" I know, but it's supposed to be a simpler version of tactical shooters for beginners and newbies, yet it seems more like a poorly optimized running simulator.
UPDATE (THIS IS WHERE THE GOOD PART IS): I thouroughly enjoy this game in the right circumstances, when I am in a good populated servers with a friend. The intensity of it is great. I was playing medic with a friend and we were in a desert village. We were clearing houses with our squad leader and a rifleman when we start taking fire. Squad lead goes down and the rifleman starts returning fire as my friend and I (the medics) start getting our leader back up. Then the shooting stops and it goes dead silent. Something moves out of the corner of my eye and I hear a clinking at my feet. "is that a grenade?" "OH SH*T" We bolt out of the room and everyone gets killed and I'm bleeding out in the next room. I try to start healing the other medic and I hear some footsteps down the road. The entire enemy squad walks in and takes me out.
Super fun and intense, even if you're not winning. Though this doesn't happen all the time, it's worth it. To sum it up, the game is fun but horribly optimized. Although I do reccomend it because it is bound to get better, I mean, it's alpha.

Posted elsewhere in 2010, since I revisited this game recently, I feel the need to post this here.
Dark Messiah could have been an excellent (though still extremely linear) game. For one, the game's combat is probably one of the best uses of melee combat in a FPS, with excellent hit detection (but still not perfect) and combat that puts lots of importance in good use of the environment. It works for a bit, but then after a while something simply feels off and it does get boring if this isn't the first game you have ever played.
The game gives the illusion of having varied way of playing through it. The warrior, mage, and assassin archetypes are all present with the addition of archery. Now these "classes" aren't static in anyway as you don't pick who you want to be at the start of the game. Instead you are awarded character points for completing objectives with which you are able to allocate to three different character traits: combat, magic, and "other" (which consists of stealth skills, stamina and mana boosts, etc). Because there are a finite number of character points available, you will need to place these points in each category with care, as being a generalist in this game will simply make it much harder. However, the care needed to put points in some categories is further increased due to the simple fact that many of the skills and the ways of approaching this game are simply a waste of time (in that they are useless) or are completely un-entertaining.
An excellent example is in the "stealth" route of character creation. For one, the game is far too linear for implementing any real semblance of "stealth" game-play, and the only real use for stealth is for scoring one-hit kills on unsuspecting enemies (which are great, because after playing "through" this game many times, sometimes it is nice to be able to avoid a drawn out confrontation). The problem is, there are very few hiding places and opportunities to use stealth, because even if there are shadows to hide in the place usually is very narrow hallway. If you have some space to maneuver, the places are usually very well lit and makes it hard to sneak anyway. In all, putting any points in this skill is an utter waste simply due to map design.
Archery, like stealth, is also unsatisfying and character points are best spent elsewhere. Unless when used in conjunction with stealth, arrows do very little damage, and you will only be able to get in two, maybe three, shots in before the opponent is in your face before you need to switch to a weapon with the ability to block with. Sounds easy, but switching weapons requires a lengthy withdraw from sheath animation and by the time you pull your weapon out you already lost lots of health in the mean time. Granted, this danger could be avoided if you pull out your weapon earlier, but that would sacrifice the ability to fire more than once… so in the end, really, there is no need for archery in this game unless certain things were tweaked.
The tweaks about to be mentioned would also benefit melee combat as well, as using a sword/staff/daggers (why are daggers in fantasy games always in pairs?!) because combat in this manner also suffers from issues.
Weapon damage in this game is too flawed. Quick strikes simply do no damage at all, now it does make sense they are weaker than power strikes, but hacking an enemy in the face should at least some effect. As a result, there is no reason to quick strikes, and you'll mainly rely on strong strikes and kicks, neither of which do any real damage either. This simply makes the game an especially grating experience on harder difficulties as you receive far more damage from attacks but still inflict very little unless you use power strikes, but being extremely slow, you'll get hit many times before you can strike yourself. This could have been easily remedied with a sidestep or back dash system of inputting a direction twice and quickly hopping in the direction at the cost of a fair portion of your stamina. You know, spice up the combat, something this game needs. This is where more flaws come in, the power attacks only come in two or so animations in a game with pretty precise hit detection this is an awful combination.
The weapon swings in a set path, and with it the camera jolts with the swing, the result: you have very strange attack animations, with limited functionality in battle as the swing arc is a such a strange plane it will often miss your intended target. It is really hard to accurately portray this, but if you were to pick up a staff (the "crowd control weapon") and use it's power attack, you'll see first hand by what is meant by attacks being unresponsive. What could have remedied this would be a simple directional input plus attack button scheme which would result in a different kind of attack. Step to the side for a sweeping attack, forward for a power overhead strike, back for a stab attack; you know to spice up combat and do it in a logical and intuitive manner.
Blocking is yet another sterile facet of combat. It is always the same animation, and it is uninteresting to perform (though in dispensable). What could have been done to make it far better is incorporate better animations, maybe more depth to it (like needing to block directional attacks) and adding the ability to actually parry attacks. How that would work would be simple (and intuitive) like the directional attack idea: direction plus block button when timed versus an attack would bat away an enemy attack allowing for you counter attack with your weapon or kick. I believe this feature and the directional attacks had they been included in this game, Dark Messiah's combat would have been epic, but alas, innovation isn't attempted nearly often enough.
Kicks are a great tool and are probably one of the highlights of the game. They allow you to clear paths, kick enemies off ledges or into spikes and fires, and break through an opponent's guard. But since swinging your weapon is either too weak or too slow, so the last example is, for the most part, pointless. In fact, the combat outside of kicking, combat is so ineffective and stale, you are better off playing through just blocking with your weapon and kicking your enemy to their death. Once again, here is another transition that leads to yet another flaw of the game.
The combat is so boring, and the developer seemed to notice this as well, that the game is over reliant on using environments to kill the opponents. So much so you will find spiky wall thingies everywhere for some strange reason. It gets ridiculous. Luckily, many of these spiky wall thingies happen to be in some of the more interesting maps (albeit linear) in a FPS to date. The Orc fortress and cliff side houses being the high point (stupid pun intended), and offer a great many ways and places to kick enemies off of ledges.
The last way to play the game is with magic, and compared to all the other ways you can play this game, it is the most effective. But no all is well as not all spells are made equal and the only ones worth using is the basic fire bolt, lightning bolt, heal (if you don't have enough food rations or health potions), and maybe charm (though never really necessary unless you are being mobbed by many ghouls or during that duel sequence with a Orc clan leader). The trap spells (and most of the others), are kinda useful, but they're nothing but a fancy way to waste mana and character points.

Lets answser the basics shall we?
What is boundless and is it worth you investing your time into it?
The TLDR; Its worth your time.
First Lets talk about multiplayer.
This is an MMO, Each world is a shard like each system in EvE Online. All these worlds are connected. These servers are spread out across real-world locations meaning you will always have good ping but still have the ability to travel to worlds hosted on diffrent timezones (most of which do not suffer with much latency either). When you connect, you join a world for your region along with everyone else, everyone is connected to the same system of planets.
Claims and your bases.
The first thing you do is claim land which is immune from others tampering with it unless you add them to your claim. As you progress you increase the amount of land you claim, claims are similar to chunks in minecraft but are also limited to hight (so people can claim above and below your claims if they wanted to) this is because the terrain varies drastically and you could have multiple bases stacked ontop of each other in a mountain or underground as an example. You can add friends to your claim via your beacon and they too can extend your claim with their plots. Players working together can claim much larger areas as a result.
Progression.
As of writing this review, you progress via leveling up some basic professions (such as mining, trading etc) and eventually start netting you rewards, an example would be hitting mining level 20 giving you 1000 coins and 10 land plots. Aparently the currently level cap is 50, meaning that each player is capable to earning a finite amount of currency this way, players can then buy and sell items via the market mechanics to gain or spend said currency.
Economy and Construction.
These are the two main areas fleshed out in boundless currently. Progressing though the various tools and machines you will eventually want to buy and sell items depending on what you need and have overstocked. Harvesting takes time, crafting takes time and you cannot repair tools so having someone specialized in making and selling tools in your village ro nearest market hub means you can just buy tools and continue to focus on other things. Good shops tend to spring up portals and other shops around them and before long you end up with a thriving little market trade hub for your area, world or even the entire system of worlds.
PvP.
There is none, I wish there was some because it would open up other elements like territory control, defenses, alliances and wars but its not aparently on the cards.
PvE.
Guardians and Titans oh my! So there will be these flying city-like bosses floating around called titans that will require whole guilds to raid... as of yet, not seen anything of them or their elite mobs called "Guardians". They are however planned and sound awsome. For now, each planet has a range of diffrent mobs ranging from rank 1 - 5 of each type, more hostile planets have harder mobs and more types so on and so on. So far the game is not very challenging on the whole survival front, similar to Minecraft in that regard except no ender dragon or wither.
Gear.
Recently updated tools look awsome, currently no diffrence between the various types with the exception of the chisel which is used to slope blocks when crafting your stuctures. Think carpenters blocks mod for minecraft here. Currently an iron shovel mines just as fast as a hammer and/or axe, the tooltips claim they are suited to diffrent roles but that is not implemented yet. There are no armors of any kind in the game thus far but the lack of any pvp or serious pve threats make  this a mute point until such features emerge.
Price.
Is too darn high! the only redeeming factor in this is that unlike your average crafting survival sandbox this is a true MMO with officially hosted servers, so the B2P model makes more sence than if it was a singleplayer minecraft or trove clone. So long as the developers deliver it will be worth the investment. However note this game has been around 2 years already (recently renamed to Boundless from Ort Online), EA is always a risk but this developer seems very professional from what I've seen in the dev blogs and youtube interviews.
My Inputs.
I fear that the developers might be missing the potential scope of this game. The shard system implemented means you can truely have a diverse multitudes of gameplay scattered across multiple worlds, while I wouldn't reccomend themepark worlds It would be nice to see peaceful space for building and trade, hostile space for war and conflict, unknown space for hazzardous exploration. I really hope they expand on its potential beyond just a nice relaxing enviroment of people to build a town and trade with people, you can do sooo much more. Doing so would attract people from other target markets people who only want to fight other people would need people to supply them weapons for example, then the economy would truely be driven by a need... but I'm starting to ramble xD
Should you invest?
Yes, its one of the more finished games in EA, its development continues at an exceptable pace and the community is very welcoming and friendly... even if their forms are confusing and the documentation of what is and is not yet in the game is alittle lacking.

I discovered Boundless through my (rather short and fussy) wishlist. Whilst browsing the store a few years ago, I was very impressed and intruiged with the concept and design of the game. Years later (bringing us to now), I was confused as to where Boundless had come from - until I discovered it had replaced Oort Online (with a much better, snappier name!).
Although I haven't played this game for too long, let me tell you that calling this game a "Minecraft clone" is a foolish misconception. In many ways, this game is already far better than Minecraft, including the graphics, which I would find it a joke to be compared to Minecraft, as it is easily better than the vast majority of games out there. From the first minute I jumped into this fascinating world, I was perplexed by the astounding beauty that the brilliant developers have poured into this game, however, there are some things which could do with tweaking, adding and even removing altogether.

To begin with, progression is somewhat slow, and at certain points in the game, I felt like giving up. This could be due to how long it takes for a crafting table to make tools and produce the amount of blocks before that needed to make a stone hammer. I would politely suggest experimenting with maybe half, or even 25% of the waiting times you have to experience at the moment, as it will make the game a lot more enjoyable.
Now, I know you awesome developers out there are probably working tirelessly to get this feature out there as soon as possible, but with no tutorial, it makes progress even slower. You have missions in the top right corner as a rough guideline, but they aren't really ideal.
Another suggestion I have which could make trading more relevant in the game is by adding tool upgrades so that players can personalise their tool, make it faster, more durable etc. etc. now, I do apologise for my ignorance if this is a feature already in the game, but I thought I would put that out there as a little idea.
There are a few other problems I could dwell on, but I do understand that as this is on Alpha, most of the content has already been thought out, and will simply be implemented with time. Overall, I love the concept of this game, and it has insane potential. The way the game is going, it will be no time before everyone will know about this brilliant game. All of the friendly staff and Devs, keep doing what you are doing! It's great!
If you are on the fence on buying this game, at the moment, I would suggest you not to buy it, or at least wait until they release a tutorial as the game is quite complex, and in my personal opinion, I think this game can't do without a tutorial, but as I said before, the developers are well aware of this, and who knows? It could be here by next week!

Boundless is currently in Early Access, even though it absolutely doesn’t appear as so.
That means you will face bugs, glitches, sometimes stuttering and temporarily incomplete
features. If you cannot handle with these things, them come back later at 1.0.
There’s absolutely no problem in that. However, if you think you can handle it just fine, them welcome aboard. You won’t regret it.
Boundless has an incredible potential and the developers are always listening to the
community feedback. You can be sure that, if you have a problem and post about it on the game
forums, they will see it and do their best to help you.
But it’s so much more! The graphics are outstanding, with textures that blend together
within each other, gigantic LOD and modern post-processing effects.
There are beacons that protect your creations from griefing and, to maintain the world,
every part of it that isn’t inside of a beacon regenerates at every 8h (sometimes it takes more,
sometimes less).
The ambient music is unbelievable, and one of the greatest I have ever heard in a game.
If you are outside, you can hear the birds, the animals around you and the wind. When you enter
in a cave, you can hear the eco of the wind passing through. (And more. I don’t want to spoil it
for you).
The crafting is distributed between three... Four...FIVE (?!) machines: The Workbench,
the Extractor, the Compactor, the Refinery and Mixer. There’s also the Furnace…The Power
Core and… I think you understood what I mean: it’s huge!
So, yeah, this is it. There’s a lot more them what I was able to write in this review. You
truly have to see for yourself. Even though the game is in Early Access and has some bugs and
uncompleted stuff, it is, still, a lot of fun. I surely recommend it.
P.S: This is my first review and English isn’t my main language, so sorry for any
mistake you may encounter during your reading
