Three strangers touched down on a frigid alien rock at the edge of known space.
As streams of burning debris rain down around them, the frightened survivors, still nauseous from the sudden awakening from hyper sleep, struggle to get their bearings amongst the jagged rocks and pine trees.
They hastily assemble a shelter near steam geyser, hoping to syphon off enough warmth to avoid hypothermia in this world of endless winter while their cat frolics happily in the snow.
The three marooned travellers barely scratch out an existence on their snowy hillside, eventually moving in to a rocky cavern in the hopes escaping to a better life underground. For days the team had been digging out steel and components from the remains of some ancient buried machine, to construct a wind turbine, providing power and much needed heat for their new subterranean town.
After weeks of scraping by on small game and rodents, the harsh winter has driven off the last remaining animals. The survivors are left starving in their glorified hole.
For former Actor, Cob, the hunger is too much to bear. In a last act of theatrical drama, he takes off his clothes and wanders around, eyes glazed, setting fire to everything in sight before shuffling off in to the icy darkness to die of hypothermia.
The two remaining travellers manage to extinguish the blaze but not before the heater is destroyed and the walls are breached exposing them to the -21° air outside.
Starving and shivering, the two remaining shipmates are slowly brought down as they attempt to gather the necessary wood to make repairs.
They collapse in the snow as their frostbitten limbs splinter and break off. Freshly cut logs clutched permanently in their frozen hands.

Borderlands easily deserved its Game of the Year nomination (and win on the Xbox) as an FPS with some RPG mechanics.  There are only a few failings to find in the hours of bloody entertainment you'll get from this very well-made game.
Borderlands is, first and foremost, a first-person-shooter, which gives potential players an idea of what to expect from encounters.  Shoot bad guys, run away from bigger badder guys, come back with better weapons, shoot the bigger badder guys, rinse and repeat.
Once we include the elements of an RPG like looting the bodies of your victims to find better weapons, shields, and modifiers, the game slows down considerably as you do a lot of looking at numbers to see if any of the five guns that just dropped are better than the one in your hands.  Thankfully vendors where you can sell junk loot for cash are common.
Another RPG signature is an epic plot.  And Borderlands does have a decent storyline... but it falls flat on the delivery, using simple text-boxes and very short audio files to advance the story.  While this certainly appeals to the "I just wanna blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up" crowd, anybody looking to be entertained by the story will find themselves disappointed that what is actually a fine yarn of a space-western was so neglected to be brought to its true potential.  (In fairness, the DLC does a MUCH better job at entertaining you in their respective stories, although the stories are delivered in the same fashion.)  On the flip side, the bad parts about RPG-style quests are also present, namely that Borderlands is essentially nothing but a series of fetch quests.  At least a fast-travel system exists to get you right back to your turn-in point whenever you're done, but that doesn't turn on until about halfway through the game.
However, you're hardly worried about how a tale is present when you have a guy wielding an axe chasing you looking to turn you into his "meat poppet" while another hulking specimen is shooting electric rockets at you and you're still on the cooldown of your action skill and there's an entire private military company deciding to hunt you personally down while honestly all you're trying to do is get an old guy some beer, and did I mention the axe-murderer is on fire?
Borderlands is grand fun, chock-full of intense action sequences, memorably hilarious (if one-dimensional) characters, and just plain fun.  Get a friend to play it with you and go shoot some lightning.

The best way to describe Squad is a blend between the arcade-y feel of Battlefield and the uncomprimising realism of ArmA, though it is a simplification. Squad puts heavy emphasis on communication both within and between individual squads, which can be a flaw as much as the strength of the game. The inability to find a standard level of communication between servers and squads can be frustrating, even making the game unplayable at times. Servers have attempted to inplement rules banning for squad leads for lack of communication, however this seem poorly enforced. That being said, in a good squad and a good team, Squad provides one of the most rewarding experiences gaming I've had. Though it currently lacks the features and the polish of both ArmA and battlefield, as it is still in Alpha afterall, it still feels like a complete game and I would highly reccomend the game if you're willing to deal with all the issues prone to games in Alpha.

I have been following Boundless since I first saw the trailer at Paris Games week back in 2015. When I saw the updated trailer at PSX in December 2016, it became somewhat of an obsession. I purchased the game in early January 2017 and it has since become my favorite game to spend time with. DO NOT dismiss this game as "just another Minecraft clone" Boundless deserves much more than that. There's no denying that Minecraft as well as other Voxel games are an inspiration here, but Boundless aims to be much more than just a prettier version of those games.
You should know that before you jump in and Wonderstruck has been very upfront about letting potential customers know. You should be prepared for occasional bugs, glitches and even server wipes. That being said, Boundless is incredibly polished for an EA title.
What drew me to the game was the freedom, but also the structure. Let me explain... I generally don't like sandbox games too much. I like the IDEA of them but with most I have fun running around for a while and then get bored and quit. I like a bit of structure and direction in my games, it's just the way I am. Boundless has the perfect mix of both. The absolute freedom to play how you want is certainly there, but it's joined with a solid objective and leveling system to keep me engaged and progressing. At over 50 hours and counting I have not hit the wall of stagnation that normally do in sandbox titles. There's always something to do or work on in Boundless and the systems are masterfully interwoven to keep a task in front of you at all times. Another aspect that drew me to the game is it's aim to be a fully functioning MMORPG. These systems are NOT fully implemented yet, but I can honestly say that if the game is already this fun without them, they will only add to the overall experience. An important note here is that the game plays equally well as a solo experience or as a group. I generally have 1-2 hours max for a play session and I have no problems getting on and making a bit of progress before logging off. Long play sessions are not mandatory and the save system is very well implemented.
Wonderstruck has been amazing at communicating with players and facilitating a genuine conversation about making the game a better experience for all. If you have ever wanted to shape a game by sharing your ideas, Wonderstruck is fostering that community here. The forums are extremely lively and you can expect the devs to be responsive and active. In my 3 months with the game I have seen player suggestions not only listen to, but actually taken and implemented into plans for updates. The devs communicate weekly on progress made and we have been seeing almost weekly update to the live version of the game.
A side note: I have seen some comments on hesitation due to the length of development with this game. Normally this would be cause for concern, but after you play and realize how massive and ambitious this title is, it is actually comforting that they are taking the time needed to get it right.
The best gaming community I have ever been a part of, hands down.  Everyone has been fantastic since day one. Being a fairly obscure early access title, info and gameplay guides are pretty much non existent. This would be a huge problem as Boundless is a game of very complex intertwining systems, but the community is filled with players both new and old that are more than willing to help and guide fresh players. The forums are fantastic and there is a player Discord as well.  I have already made legitimate friends here and I expect I will make many more in the future.
If you are looking for a game that offers creativity, community, challenge and endless possibilities, Boundless is a game you should consider. If you purchase in Early Access, you need to be prepared for an incomplete experience, but you will also have the access and ability to shape the final retail product. The retail release version 1.0 is scheduled for some time in 2017. Join now or wait for release, but give Boundless a chance. I believe you will be glad you did.

I have been watching the game for a while now, it used to be called Oort and looked very interesting. So after a few years I noticed this on my wish list again and it appeared to be still alive and being actively worked on, I was looking for a building game to relax with and took the chance to buy it and check it out for myself rather than watch gameplay vids.
I must say that it is visually one of the best looking voxel games I have ever seen with a nice art style. The sound and music is very well done and fits the world perfectly so you get some nice moments while exploring when the sound and music just fits perfectly with the vistas around you.
It's a gather/craft game that has so many recipies and machine build chains that its a bit daunting at first, the lack of information available can be annoying but this is early access and stuff changes anyway. The lore is good, and the theme is more about ancient technology discovery and using that to progress rathger than magic/classic fantasy style, I am finding some aspects of progression hard though, like finding certain extremley rare crafting materials that never seem  to spawn , hours of searching and Im still looking, so it's not an easy game that just hands everything to you, which I quite like.
If you are interested in voxel style build and survive games with a unique twist I'd recommend this game, although it seems to be much more aimed towards community coop playstyles than the solo player due to the time it takes to get things made and constructed, I like the fact you can't just repair tools, once they are gone they are gone, some people may not like this type of grind, but it's not as bad as you think, especially in lower tiers.
Right now it's awaiting some large updates due to an impending release, so jumping in now to learn the game and get a feel for it should be on your mind as I suspect server wipes are coming. I am really hoping that my friends get into this later as it would be perfect with a good active community. Right now it seems a bit quiet on the European server I play on but I suspect most of the vets are holding off any serious play until the updates come.
Over all I enjoy playing and look forward to more!

If you, like me, are intrigued by a Puzzle game with an Artificial Intelligence theme, you will thoroughly enjoy "The Talos Principle".
The game mechanics themselves are simple enough to pick up, and as you would expect the puzzles become more and more difficult the further you progress. The game does not really aid you in solving these puzzles, so you do feel rewarded for your logic and problem solving when you complete a level.
The main feature of this game for me was the extremely philosophical storyline, which had me questioning myself, and my beliefs. If the deep philosophical nature of the game is a bit much, you can play it minimalist and just play through the puzzles. However if like me you are interested in the philospohical, there are lots of computer terminals throughout the game which are optional and will beef the story out a bit, as well as make you further question yourself.
Overall the game is a strong 8.5/10 for me, mostly from the story, but aided by the fact that the game works perfectly and fluidly without me having encountered any glitches or bugs during my playthrough.

As rather the opposite of a Sonic fan, I figured I'd try this game's predecessor, "Sonic and SEGA All-Stars Racing", and to my surprise it was a lot of fun.  It had a lot of similarities to the Mario Kart franchise, but it tweaked the things that didn't work and made it its own game, and I loved it.
This game improves upon its previous iteration tremendously.  The execution of the vehicle transitions doesn't seem forced at all, and that along with the tracks actually changing and evolving during the course of each race makes each match an adventure that lasts just a few minutes.
The weapons have changed greatly and no longer feel overly similar to standard Mario Kart fare.  Nearly everything is fresh and interesting, and the only guaranteed screw-yous have to be intentionally set up rather than simply fired.
The controls are great, the online multiplayer works very well, and the characters are different enough to be easily recognizable at a glance.  Even the heads-up display is great.
The only complaints that I have are that it's very graphically intensive, meaning that you'll likely have to drop your resolution a lot if you're running a fairly old video card; the announcer's trackside chatter is now practically gone; and new characters can only be unlocked in World Tour mode, rather than by simply playing the game and spending the resulting points.
So yeah, while I do still rather dislike Sonic, I highly recommend this game for everyone who likes mascot racers.  It's a good deal at regular price, but if it ever goes on sale, JUMP ON THIS.  You won't regret it.

Let's be clear on this, it's an endless runner made up of a bunch of assets. While it's not technially an asset flip (i.e. I can't find an asset demo that is this game) the assets are pretty stock and the game is boring.
You swim, collect bubbles, avoid the deadly (?) plants, and then get eaten by sharks.
What interested me was the video intro, thinking it might be a survival game or something (think Raft, Stranded Deep, etc.) but no. You don't have a raft, you'll never see the rendering quality of the swimmer like in the video, and you'll play it for about 10 minutes then forget about it.
The description is deceptive. Maybe there was some point in time where you could see "Atlantis" but I thought, from the description and video, this was some kind of exploration game. If going in a straight line seeing bubbles, various sea life, and some plants is your idea of exploring, maybe the developer will want to hire you.
Oh and there are achievements. Well, you get an achievement for almost every meter you make it in this game. No creativity whatsoever in these so they're just there for you to pad your achievement collection, if that's what people do.
I get it's "early access" and some people will say "there will be more" but I don't see it. The three modes the game offers are the same thing but with a different coloured ocean. Early Access is a cheap out for this developer and game. This thing isn't going anywhere and in 6 months to a year, it'll be the same maybe with a whale or somehing added.
Finally this was a VR game, as much as the developer might say it wasn't, it's clear. The menus are VR, the screens just activate when you hover over them, and 9 times out of 10 you'll accidently activate the menu system when swimming or browsing the menus. So a VR game that isn't VR.
At least it was less than a $1.

I've played a handful of matches. As a LoL/HotS/Dota player, I know this is definitely not enough to appropriately judge any MOBA game, but these are my thoughts as a new player: If you want to play this game, you have to want to support the a game that is still iterating and that hasn't quite reached its full enjoyment potential yet.
In my matches against players and AI, none of my games have ever ended in a full 5v5 yet. One person in a game will leave, then this will be followed by the rest of the team. This makes it unenjoyable from the get go, since the team that has the greater amount of AFKs are made to play an uphill battle, and on top of that suffer rating losses for it (yes, you lose PVP rating when your team AFKs and the game ends in a defeat, even if you are the only person on your team who is still in the game. Your opponents will also gain rating for the victory even though you had no team except yourself.)
Bugs are also apparent, even in my few games played. The client has issues responding after accessing the Steam overlay in game; your game will occasionally not accept any commands except movement, and sometimes it will accept no commands at all, forcing you to hard restart the client; graphical issues exist, such as the Minerva skin from the CE package displaying an amorphous black-and-yellow blob for its Black dye texture in game despite the textures appearing appropriately on the customization screen.
For what it's worth, I genuinely like the hero design of the game's characters, but the issues with matchmaking, leavers, and game-altering bugs is severely hampering what would otherwise be a highly enjoyable game experience. For now, I am not recommending this game, as I cannot see myself continuing to play Strife if my experiences continue as they have been so far.

I really didn't want to give this game a negative review because in most cases, they're never viewed as reasonable no matter how reasonable you attempt to be.  Edit: And of course, no one actually gives a flying ♥♥♥♥ about actual technical♥♥♥♥♥♥
So here's a heads up: There ARE technical issues to the game that play a role in this review outside of subjective preferences.
Here we go.
First off, the technical issues keep me from enjoying this game whatsoever.   I've been looking for a new co-op game with a friend for the longest time and it seemed like Castle Crashers, a seemingly esteemed title, would be a flawless experience to try.  Unfortunately, multiplayer online gameplay has serious input lag for whatever reason.  There are *massive* stutters that occur whenever someone does something.  They may be only 50-200 milliseconds long, but it's significant enough that it absolutely ruins the feel of the game.
While I wasn't expecting to encounter any technical hiccups for a game so well received, I'm also not the type of person to not seek for a solution.  Suggestions that I've found were stated to render the game at a lower resolution.  We knocked it down to the smallest resolution the game supported and the game was still stuttering.  Less so than before, but still to an unacceptable degree to play the game.  On top of the fact that the resolution was now 640X480.  I couldn't even read the controls.
There were literally no other suggestions other than dealing with in game settings.  I can online imagine this is because of the engine itself and not the game.
That, is the primary reason I cannot recommend this game.  The online support for it is just too shoddy and unstable for me to even recommend.  IF someone has another attempted solution (it is NOT the result of a bad connection), I would be glad to hear it.  However, my patience has really been tested because now I move onto the subjective part of the review.
The controls and combat don't feel satisfying and instead are exercises of frustration and cramping in my thumbs, and there's an even bigger problem.  Maybe it's the stutter.  Maybe it's the lag.  But the characters have too little width of the attack on the X axis of the game.  You literally have to line up your paper thin characters to the paper thin enemies.  The worst part?  You have 0 mobility when attacking on the ground.  Meaning you cannot correct for the utter lack of horizontal range (up and down, which is the "side to side" of your character.  Again, the X axis of the game).  This is mitigated by jump attacks but you still suffer from the "thinness" problem.
It's simply unfun to me and feels unsatisfying to play.  I could barely make it through an hour or two before my thumbs started to cramp from thumbing the Xbox controller.
That's not to say the other parts of the game aren't good.  The humor is there, the artwork is there, and I'm sure it's stupid fun with more people.  But the controls just suck for me.  And the technical issues with multiplayer make it even worse.  I cannot recommend this, and I'm actually pretty disappointed and sad to do so.
The technical problems may vary from person to person, configuration to configuration (and it should be said, my computer far surpasses the technical requirements), but the buyer should be at least weary of these issues.
Maybe the other reviews are nostalgia tinted, maybe they didn't have the technical issues I had.  But I don't like the gameplay, and the technical problems don't make it any better.

Literally a perfect game.  Oxenfree defines itself with it's incredible story-telling, it's natural dialouge, and it's many twists and turns on a path that will eventually leave you sobbing at your computer desk.  The game is expertly created, and everything from the music and sounds, to the little things like the size and shape of the different walking paths all add up to make this into an incredible experience.
I keep running through it over and over in my head, trying to figure out if there's a single part of the game that distracted from the experience or made the game worse, but I can't find a single instance.  If you can wrap yourself into the story of the game (something not very hard to do)  You'll find yourself not wanting to stop until it's over.
In fact, the game isn't that long of a play.  My playthrough was almost 4 hours, which in a lot of games does not feel like a long time.  This honestly works in the games favor, as a full an detailed story can take place without any part of it feeling like it was just for the sake of lengthening the "runtime" so to speak.  Ever second of the game is involved and important, and the time it takes to play the games lends itself to replayability, and accessibilty to people who think story games take to long already.  Honestly I was worried the game would be too long for me to play it in one sitting, but I was very happy to find that was not the case.
The dialouge of the game was incredible.  Not only did it feel realistic, and easy to follow along with, but it prompted all of the right emotions from the player.  At the beginning the dialouge is between friends, with jokes, and small arguments,  and the player is often allowed a chance to speak up and take part, but also has the right to say nothing.  Each of the options you have as a player feel unique, and they do have an effect on the game, but at the same time the game doesn't let you purposefully break it by choosing an answer just for that reason.  There was never a time I felt I was unable to select a dialouge option that didn't fit me (even if I had felt that way, I could choose not to say anything at all.)
The music and visuals were great.  The soundtrack is phenominal, and is perfectly in tune with the games story and feeling (mind the pun.)  Not once throughout the game did the soundtrack distract from the experience and constantly throughout it provided essential emotional context to the scene.  Perhaps the best thing about the soundtrack was that it wasn't ridiculously loud like many games tend to be nowadays.  However no game is complete without perfect visuals too.  Oxenfrees visuals felt perfect, as they were able to portray beautiful scenery, as well as be just vague enough to allow for exploration.  It felt like throughout the game I was moving throughout a portrait, with so many incredibly beautiful landscapes, as well as plenty of fine detail along the paths.
I could go on and on about how incredible this game is, but it is worth noting that no game is defined only by each individual part examined alone.  I mention all of these things - the dialouge, the visuals, and the soundtrack - because these are what pull the player in and make you never want to stop.  In truth, the game is much more than the sinple sum of it's parts.  It is so much more than can ever be explained through it's pieces, because it is an experience.
This is one of the greatest games I have ever had the fortune of playing.

A solid addition to the FPS genre.
You are William J Blazkowicz, a Nazi killing machine. In this alternative time line, in which the 3rd Reich wins World War II, Blazkowicz lays dormant in a mental hospital. 14 years pass, and he is awakened and once again called about to battle the forces of evil.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a worthy continuation of the Wolfenstein series. A classic first person shooter with all the usual tropes: big guns, tons of ammo, nigh-impervious hero, and thumping music. Tear through rooms of enemies soliders filling em with hot lead, or, when given the opportunity, skulk around unseen and have your knife silence your foes. The game is gritty while embracing the absurd (though, I won't spoil more than that). But there is more to wolfenstein than a pile of bodies. The story is deeper than the old school FPS and present the player with 2 times lines which provide different characters, some bonuses (one contains armor upgrades, the other health) and occasionally different ways to play through levels. Though I felt they could have done a lot more with this concept in regards to game play, it was a surprising element that simply left me wanting more.
The game does a decent job of variety while not over staying it's welcome. Weapons have alternative fire, alternative versions and dual wielding, so the player has a variety of load outs at their disposal. Aside from larger than necessary gun models and explaining how to dual-alt fire (perhaps I missed the message in game) I don't have any complaints. There are automatic save checkpoints which are fairly distributed, however there are times they occur in poor conjunction with cut-scenes. Sometimes you are forced to play a cut-scene over and over (the skip function is hit or miss as the game is loading during some of these scenes) which can be annoying. Other times, the save occur after a scripted interaction, and upon reloading, that interaction disappears (costing you items) or the save happens after a battle but before you stock up on items. So upon death, you get to stock up again and again... and again.
Enemies are relatively fair - they have terrible peripheral vision to enable a lot of leeway in stealth, though the ability to see through smoke which can leave the player at a massive disadvantage. The stealth portions aren't mandatory but it's noticeable when the game expects you to play to that style. The perks system provide the player with additional bonuses upon being unlocked, but play style is dictated by the situation more so than player preference. Uber can be a challenge (particularly if you haven't unlocked all the perks) but if that's still not enough, the enigma codes provide players with alternative modes of play, if you find all the codes and figure out how to unlock them.
Wolfenstein is an excellent game with a few surprises to go along with its solid genre defining elements. I hope future iterations expand about the alternative time line and maybe clean up some of the problems I had with auto-saving but it was predominantly positive and fun gaming experience.

I've played this game with a couple of friends a bunch over the last couple of days, and have played a ton of it on a different console, and I can simply say that this might be the best Kart Racer ever made. It takes everything good about Mario Kart, gives you more ways to increase your speed based on your skill, and has many different ways to play any character allowing you to play with anyone you like and have your optimal stats.
The course design, give or take a level or two, is always on the point. There's nothing more satisfying than learning a course and being able to flip and drift constantly. The ways the courses are laid out and change really allows you to visually tell how much better you're getting at playing, and it's always a nice feeling.
The graphics of the game also manage to shine quite well. With a well optimized engine allowing for nearly anyone to play, it's almost a surprise how good this game manages to look. The small details in everything from the Casino Park level to the Jet Set Radio level pop out quite nicely, and manage to look good even at top speeds.
The gameplay of the game is fun, simply put. I really can't think of another way to put it. The items are fun to launch at your friends or enemies, and they can all be avoided with other items or skill. If you dislike Mario Kart simply because of the blue shell, this might be your game. All three of the vehicle types are also perfectly balanced, and feel great to play with. It's just fun watching your car swiftly turn into a plane and then continue flying against your opponents.
If you're looking for a game to sit around and play with a bunch of friends online, I would highly recommend this one. It just never gets old.

If you're reading reviews then you've probably seen the similarities to "a prettier Minecraft with more block choices" mentioned, if you are a builder, sculptor or artist then this game outweights Minecraft in most aspects, different planets give different coloured resources giving a huge amount of choice, you can build extremely complex scupltures with the chisel tool ( 30nstillgaming is recreating a life size Mount Rushmore with character faces from the game on Twitch). Unlike Minecraft there is no eqivalent of red stone and there's no creative mode (at least not yet, I say this as the devs created their own engine so techinically anythings possible for them with time, funding and manpower), for now you will have to build live, and gather, trade or buy your resources as in any MMO.
This game isn't just offering "be a builder", although building your city to compete to be displayed on the map & be crowned "Capital" of your planet is going to be a part of the game to bring in the independant traders, it's not going to be the only mechanic.  This game is going to be a sandbox MMO where players design the cities and infrastucture, multiple planets with 120 different biomes to explore, these will span across Playstation and PC (some of the planets will be rented servers connected to the main game allowing their renters some control over what happens there). Already announced soon there will be guilds with multiple chapters, boss raids on Titans, RPG elements in the form of skill trees so you can specialise in one skill tree or generalise to be a jack of all trades (Perfect for the Alt-o-holics among us), Farming & capturing animals (Yes I want my intergalactic zoo!).  These are not live in the current version game yet though.
Currently we have 12 planets, Land claming, adding friends to your beacons so they can build with you, an extensive crafting system, a huge array of building materials - both mined and crafted blocks, warp conduits for your quick 1 way trips, buying/selling plinths so you can make money, permanent portals between planets that require fuel to stay open, a large array of mobs getting more difficult as you explore the outer ring planets, smart stacking where all types of a similiar resource only take up 1 slot in your bag, grappling hooks for exploring, player created towns and communities on most of the hospitable planets. The content is being released fairly fast - I am reading through old reviews and can't even fathom if they are talking about the same game, so I'd advise reading only reviews dated from Jan 2017 onwards if you want a current review of progress.
If you're worried about Early Access games never being released (especially with the time taken with this coming from a browser based game and then having to be completely re-written code wise to evolve properly), this one has the backing of Sony and it was one of the games Sony just showcased at PAX East allowing Playstation players and PC players to explore the Dev world together.
Other concerns you might have;
There's no griefing, as long as you build within your beacons + plots no-one can touch your stuff, but if you choose to make huge public roads outside of beacons then world regeneration will kick in if no players have visited and the area will revert back to it's natural state. Plots are unlimited and earned by leveling up.  There will also be beacon fuel required to make sure inactive newbie huts are not littering the living, evolving MMO world but this is extremely simple to craft.
The devs are extremely interactive on the
forums and consider all your suggestions, respond to bug reports, they can also be seen in game on an almost daily basis checking out reports and testing things. Dev updates are weekly and game updates are coming on average every 10 days.  The Steam forums look dead becasue all the action happens on the main forums.
Currently the population is not huge, max I've seen online at one time is around 50 people across the servers so far, but most players are still active in the forums and community Discord awaiting updates even if they are not playing.  It's actually pretty good for getting to grips with the game, (this game currently only holds your hand so far) and having your choice of nice real estate to build on and grab some prime market stall spots near portals - I can't imagine it will stay this way once guilds are implemented so I'm taking advantage of it.
Cost wise it may seem more than other similar games, but it's still pre Alpha in the progress of crowfunding - so you are actually buying into a support tier and not just buying the game.
So the bottom line then - if you enjoy exploring or building, especially creating your own player made towns and large sculptures then feel free to jump in right now, you will get your moneys worth.  However, If you are looking for an MMO with guilds and titan raids or farming and animals I would honestly wait a bit for more updates.
I shoudn't need to repeat that this game is in very, very early access right now and is lacking in core MMO content - the message is all over this page before you click purchase.

The perfect mix of casual and serious, RimWorld offers an amusing and enriching experience from 30 minute episodes to several hour slogs...
You sit back, plan for nearly everything from frontal assault to weird infestation...  and succumb instead to sadness, ennui, and hunger.
You return emboldened, ready to fight not just enemies but the forces of nature, and build a giant wooden fortress with pool tables, freezers, barricades, and turrets...  and watch it burst into flash-fire-fueled destruction.
You live, you learn.  Mostly, you DIE, you learn.  Each trial offering another glimpse of a horrible outcome to avoid.  There is enough randomness to keep it interesting and keep you challenged, but never so much that you aren't rewarded for solid planning and careful manipulation and management.  Growth and survival require both constant whack-a-mole style problem solving and a dedication to slowly-but-consistently evolving your technology through research, upgrading your equipment (smithing/gunmaking) and skillset (training), resource acquisition through hunting/farming and mining, and architectural wizardry to ensure you can grow your small utopia without exposing a Death Star style vulnerability.
Is it perfect?  No, because it doesn't strive to be.  It strives to be immersive, fun, and a combination of dramatic and silly that makes even a dismal failure a reason to smile.  And when the moment arrives that you feel you've begun to crest the wave and cement your hold on the wilderness, you can bask in that pride or partake in the numerous community-driven mods (Dystopian horror?  yes, please!) or preloaded scenarios to mix it up.
This isn't necessarily an "only" game.  It's one to mix with virtually any other genre, for when you want a change of pace.  Every session offers a slightly different challenge and a new mixture of elements that demand new strategies and offer lasting lessons.  It's one of my 7 "Steam favorite games" that I find myself coming back to every few days.

The Talos Principle is, at it's essence, a very good first person puzzler. It starts out easy with very few mechanics and gets gradually harder over time, but never too hard. Throughout the game you also follow a very philosophical story that is neatly integrated into the game and never overbearing, but present enough that you have it in the back of your mind while playing.
The game also contains lots of hidden content, easter eggs, optional (very hard) puzzles and tons of stuff to do for you completionists out there. The game itself is great and certainly a good addition to every puzzle fans collection!
Pros:
-Challenging puzzles of varying difficulty
-Servicable graphics that range from "okay" to "beautiful", good aesthetics too
-Different puzzle areas all have a theme to them, from Greece to Egypt
-Many different puzzle elements that are self explanatory but have some depth to them
-Good game length for a puzzler (20-30 hours for completionists)
-Good story
-Very beautiful soundtrack
-Good voice acting
-Multiple Endings
Mehs:
-Some of the games puzzles require a lot of thinking outside the box, which can get somewhat frustrating
-At some point the game gets repetitive - the story keeps you going, but by the 20 hour mark you look forward to the end
Cons:
-The DLC isn't all that good - it is essentially more of the same with some new voice lines, but I was expecting a bit more (not necessarily a con if you really enjoyed the base game)
-The DLC also has some REALLY hard puzzles that I couldn't figure out if my life depended on it and require way too much "Outside the box" thinking to be really enjoyable
As you see, the cons are only DLC-related - and yet, the DLC is still fun if you liked the base game, at least for a while. Definitely recommended!
Personal Score:
The Talos Principle: 8/10
Road to Gehenna DLC: 6/10

I will update this review as I gain more experience with the game.
This is a MOBA, or if you prefer a Dota style game, that is said to be more for the casual player. Despite that, I think this game has some really deep strategy and some intense action. It's not that it's casual, it's that it's super easy to get into and some of the mechanics are designed to remove toxicity between players.
Pros
-Easier to learn than MOBA's like LoL and Dota 2
-Gold earned through last hits is split between players. This and other mechanics help reduce toxicity in game between teamates.
-Really polished for Beta
-Art style, and story world have a pixar feel, with a little darkness.
-New twists with neturals on the map like Baldr and Cindara and the white ape.
-Pets, that's right! You can have pets that further allow you to customize the way you play. It adds abilities and attributes to your hero.
Cons (Keep in mind, it's still in beta as of the time I'm writing this review 6/8/2015)
-Limited number of heroes
-Heroes could differentiate themselves better with their abilites. Some heroes feel the same as far as gameplay is concerned.
-"Ultimate" abilities could use a little more Ultimate-feeling to them.
Overall a great game that everyone interested in a MOBA should try. And why not when it's free to play! And not pay to win.

Castle Crashers is a very good game.
It may seem I haven't played it much, due to the small amount of time (12 hours) I have recorded on my Steam account, but I played it for several years on the consoles. Maxing out around two characters at around 2010.
The story is about a hero, yourself, who goes on a quest after his king's castle is raided and robbed of a magic crystal.
There are multiple bosses, each with an interesting new tactic with which you need to adapt to.
The game IS hard, you will need to attempt certain levels multiple times to be victorious. After completing the main story, depending on which character you were when you defeated the game, you are given a new character and unlock "insane mode".
There are four characters to pick from at the very start, which all have their own special weapon and magic. In total there are 31 characters (including the two DLC ones (Pink Knight and Purple Knight (Blacksmith)), and one special one. More on him in a moment) which you can choose from.
There is one character (two on the Xbox version) which you require to perchase a seperate game for. Hatty Hattington, which you require to own Battleblocks Theatre and Castle Crashers on the same Steam/Xbox account; or on Xbox, you can only get the alien character by getting an achivement on Alien Homind HD.
I would only recomend playing this game with a friend or group of friends, as it is much more fun that way. I played through it first with two of my brothers, then alone, and quite recently with a friend. I definitly found it more entertaining with a friend, but I still liked it without.

Squad. I tried this game out on free-weekend. Coming from a run and gun kinda background (Doom, Quake, CS, DoD, etc) it was a little hard to get into. I didn't know how to play so there was a lot of running around. Lucky for me Squad has an amazing community, and veterans quickly took noobs under their wing.
Out of all the games I've played over the years, this has had some of the most intense combat moments. My second game we were all ambushed on a road with our 2 humvees. 1 humvee made it up the road into the village. The men in the second humvee were all bleeding out. We quickly re-organized and by using the second humvee as cover, we slowly backed it down the road to get those guys up. It was just an amazing experience.
Pros:
-Great map building (There always seems to be a great fire fight going on)
-Great sound effects (Gun battles are intense)
-Huge amount of room for people to work as a team
-Community. (If you're a solo player you won't regret trying to meet people in this game)
-Gameplay is fun an fairly easy to learn
-Solid dev team
-Active server admins (Most servers have admins on all the time so TKer's/griefers get booted quick)
Cons:
-Some bugs are still present but I haven't found one that is game-breaking or makes me want to insta-quit.
I figure I should put more cons but I just can't really think of anything else that really bothers me. Everytime I log in I enjoy my experience. I guess thats the bottom line. After almost 80 hours recorded, I still haven't logged out without having a good time.

You need the tactics, the communication, the coordination, the reaction time/reflex and the aim to succeed in a match.

As it says in their FAQ: ''Squad seeks to bridge the rather large gap between arcade shooter and military sim''
This game is for those out there with a competetive mindset and want a game that require skill and teamwork to win.
If you want to take a step further into the more professional side of Squad, join a clan/team and you will get to play scrims, tournaments and other events against other teams. It makes this game a whole lot more entertaining.

The under-appreciated older brother of Borderlands 2. The game is less polished than 2, but still gives the fun loot-'n-shoot experience. The game is well optimized, and the guns are innumerable. The quests are varied, and once you finish the storyline, you have the option to play the story over again at your current level and continue your leveling and face harder enemies with weapons and quests scaled to your level, allowing tons of gameplay hours. The DLC expands the game even further, raising the level cap and adding interesting new quests, enemies, and equipment. It's also where Gearbox started their wonky sense of humor, with more personality and oddities in the characters than the base game. If you liked Borderlands 2, then you should have fun playing through the original.

The game is expertly created, and everything from the music and sounds, to the little things like the size and shape of the different walking paths all add up to make this into an incredible experience.
I keep running through it over and over in my head, trying to figure out if there's a single part of the game that distracted from the experience or made the game worse, but I can't find a single instance.  If you can wrap yourself into the story of the game (something not very hard to do)  You'll find yourself not wanting to stop until it's over.
In fact, the game isn't that long of a play.  My playthrough was almost 4 hours, which in a lot of games does not feel like a long time.  This honestly works in the games favor, as a full an detailed story can take place without any part of it feeling like it was just for the sake of lengthening the "runtime" so to speak.  Ever second of the game is involved and important, and the time it takes to play the games lends itself to replayability, and accessibilty to people who think story games take to long already.  Honestly I was worried the game would be too long for me to play it in one sitting, but I was very happy to find that was not the case.
The dialouge of the game was incredible.  Not only did it feel realistic, and easy to follow along with, but it prompted all of the right emotions from the player.  At the beginning the dialouge is between friends, with jokes, and small arguments,  and the player is often allowed a chance to speak up and take part, but also has the right to say nothing.  Each of the options you have as a player feel unique, and they do have an effect on the game, but at the same time the game doesn't let you purposefully break it by choosing an answer just for that reason.  There was never a time I felt I was unable to select a dialouge option that didn't fit me (even if I had felt that way, I could choose not to say anything at all.)
The music and visuals were great.  The soundtrack is phenominal, and is perfectly in tune with the games story and feeling (mind the pun.)  Not once throughout the game did the soundtrack distract from the experience and constantly throughout it provided essential emotional context to the scene.  Perhaps the best thing about the soundtrack was that it wasn't ridiculously loud like many games tend to be nowadays.  However no game is complete without perfect visuals too.  Oxenfrees visuals felt perfect, as they were able to portray beautiful scenery, as well as be just vague enough to allow for exploration.  It felt like throughout the game I was moving throughout a portrait, with so many incredibly beautiful landscapes, as well as plenty of fine detail along the paths.
I could go on and on about how incredible this game is, but it is worth noting that no game is defined only by each individual part examined alone.  I mention all of these things - the dialouge, the visuals, and the soundtrack - because these are what pull the player in and make you never want to stop.  In truth, the game is much more than the sinple sum of it's parts.  It is so much more than can ever be explained through it's pieces, because it is an experience.

I've had my eye on this game for nearly two years, back when it was Oort Online.  Finally took the plung a few months back as I noticed updates started rolling out weekly.  No regrets!  This game is awesome!  It's a similar to Creativerse and Minecraft, but much more fun IMO.  It's a voxel game, but not just a flat area to play within.  There are unique and varied planets that are essentially regional servers.  Players can travel to any of the 12 worlds, each of which has it's own 'flavor' or style, along with different resources and creatures to be found, passive and hostile.  Not only that, common resources like stone and sand will have different tints depending on what world they were harvested from.  So basically, you can craft a grey stone hammer from grey stone, and go to another world and get red stone of the same type and craft a red stone hammer.  Now there is no differece between the red or grey aside from color, but that concept allows for crafting of tons of different tools, machines and building blocks.  If you like block games at all, you MUST give this game a try.  Even if you haven't played any block building type games before but have a creative streak, this game will give you hours and hours of fun.  If you're not so much into building, there's hours worth of exploration, discovery and a great community to be part of!  It runs very smoothly on my rig, i7 CPU and GTX 970.  Impressive for an EA game.

This game will blow you away.
This game goes beyond the limits of a choose your own adventure style story and immerses you in a world that's filled with mystery, decisions, stories, fear, life, death, easter eggs, and more. Oxenfree is a story where you get to infulence what happens next. Every single choice you may will change your fate and the fate of others.
The Good Part:
*This game is beautiful. The textures, models, artwork, it's all beautiful! The voice acting in this story/game is top notch and just plain perfect.
*The quality of the audio is insanely high, each voice has character, and it just doesn't sound like an act. It really feels like you're there with the characters. The actual game mechanics themselves are very clever and very simple. 4 Buttons to move, 1 button for actions, and one button for a pocket radio. It's that simple.
*Another thing worth mentioning is how the game is played, which is a super start idea and is executed well in this game. The game itself puts you in a 3d world, but in a 2d perspective. Besically, you can walk in every direction, but youy see everything from one angle only (I recommend looking at gameplay screenshots to see what I'm saying here). While you're in this 3D-2D enviroment, the dialogue options will appear as speech bubbles coming from your character, and while other characters speak you can see little bubbles over them.
*The story itself is super rich, filled with action, never gets boring, and always has you on the edge of your seat.
The Bad Part:
*It's a one time only thing. The first time you finally finish the story, you'll be sitting there feeling super accomplished, but once this beautiful story reaches the last dialogue line, that's it. Sure, maybe you can play it a few more times to see the different story paths you can take, but you can only do so much. It's like reading a book: after reading it once or twice, it's time to move on.
*If you have to stop the game and decide to come back on later, the game will not tell you what you were doing and it wont rewind a bit in the story just to give you a refresher. I'll use the book example again...it's just like a book: If you come back to the book later, you may not fully remember what was happening. Unlike a book however, you can't go back and read the previous two pages. If you forgot why you were walking around the forest, good luck!
In Conclusion:
It was actually a struggle to find things I slightly disliked about this game because it's just perfect in every way imaginable. This is definately a 10/10 game and you bet I would play again. You need to try out this game sooner or later, because you will have the best 3-4 hours of your life...

At first I figured this would just be a bleh Mario Kart Clone, but after playing it for the last few days with friends, I've honestly come to the decision that it is arguably better than Mario Kart.
Mario Kart loves to give the lower-placed players better items to 'equalize', including that oft-despised Blue Shell.  In this, the "Blue Shell" analogue is a swarm of bees.  The bees however do NOT guaranteed knock up the first place person.  They can dodge it if they pay attention/slow down, making it be less of a guaranteed "HAHA GO TO SECOND PLACE"  This single change on its own is a great improvement over Mario Kart.
The stages are just about at the right length to be fun, not long enough to drag on (I've yet to run into any Rainbow Road race that takes 20+ minutes and is just soul-crushingly bland once the prettiness factor wears off).  Changing vehicles definitely makes it fun as they all handle differently.  For folks who don't care about weapon powerups, there is Boost Mode, where all powerups are just boosts.  No shooting other players, just rely on your own skill.
The racers seem to be decently different, but there are ways to modify them after playing as them long enough to shift their stats a bit, so if someone takes your precious Sonic, you can take another character and mod their vehicle up to have equivalent stats to Sonic's, given enough time with that char.
Overall, if you grew up with a Sega and love arcade-style racing games, give this a try.

Most will have played Skyrim by now, so I'll compare to that to save time.
This game is very similar to Skyrim, but it has a few significant differences.  It is not open world, you have to follow a linear story; there's still plenty to discover throughout the game.  Character builds still touch on warrior, mage, and thief aspects, but it's almost all combat-focused.  The REAL difference in this game is the physical interaction.  Smithing, for example.  You can't smith-and-sell like in skyrim with all the complexity of a miniature free market, but you can go through each step of smithing.  You see your hands and all the objects move as they should; everything is suitably realistic.
This realistic physical detail applies to EVERYTHING in the game.  The way your arms and body (this game has full body awareness, just look down and see your body) move during combat, running, kicking, everything.  The only thing not covered is grabbing and pulling levers with your hands.  This PHYSICAL DETAIL in absolutely everything you do is intoxicating to me.  Even the environments and enemies are full of physics and interactivity.  Throw boxes and barrels, the way you climb ropes, the viewpoint as you look around actually follows your head, and even when you die the camera follows where your eyes would be on your physical body as you fall down.(Yes, it can feel a bit mirror's edge-y when you run, but the only free-running is vaulting onto things)
This combined with the fantastic combat (better than skyrim's combat imo), plenty of character customization, and beautiful artistic design make the whole journey enjoyable.  I suggest playing on the hardest difficulty to make your character build choices feel like they really affect what you're doing.  (If it gets frustrating repeating areas, just play on Normal at first)
tl;dr - YOUR ARMS AND LEGS ♥♥♥♥ING MOVE LIKE REAL ONES AND YOU CAN INTERACT WITH EVERYTHING PHYSICALLY HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥YES! 11/10

was quite a treat to the eyes.  It's a murder mystery story combined with a point-and-click adventure title, a hidden object game, AND with minigames along the way.  Though the story may be quite cliche, the visuals and programming are quite well done!
Join Alicia Griffith, an ace detective who hoped to get a little relaxation after already solving a murder mystery.  Strangely, her idea of relaxing from a murder mystery...is by solving another murder mystery (that's commitment!!!).  In this game, you'll basically have a tutorial and 4 acts:  The murder scene, a quiet town, a creepy mansion+graveyard, and some ancient ruins.  After completing one act, you'll be unable to go back to a location in a previous act.
The visuals of
are quite well-done and are wonderful to look at.  Though there are CG animations with the characters that feel strange or out of place.  Of course, if you're a perv, then it's good for you to know that you'll see Alicia Griffith and her cleavage quite often during the events of this game.  Overall, though...it's a quality that took some talent to accomplish.
The minigames/puzzles ranged from simple (which most of the puzzles tended to be) to difficult.  I saw myself only skipping 3 puzzles throughout my playthrough.  The Quetzlcoatl puzzle, the key puzzle, and the sun/moon puzzle.  If you're stuck on those puzzles, don't feel bad...I couldn't solve them either.  Most of the other puzzles, though are very simple and I haven't had a reason to really click the hint button often.
There is one strange issue I had on my 2nd playthrough where clickable areas/backgrounds were replaced by plain white boxes.  This may be due to me alt-tabbing mid-game.  It was resolved when I shut the game down and rebooted it.  Aside from that, the only real complaint I had was that the voice-acting would occasionally mistake the pronunciation on a word or a typo would catch my attention.
So...to recap:
PROS:
+ Hot protagonist
+ Great artwork/visuals
+ Good voice-acting
+ Mostly simple puzzles
+ A helpful hint / puzzle-skip button (if you're stuck)
CONS:
- Some puzzles I have no idea how to properly solve
- Occasional typos
- Occasional misspoken words

EDIT: This review was posted on relase day and so only considers the initial build. Typically when reviewing a game so early on in it's lifecycle I'd return to the game after updates so I could update the review to account for any issues that had been resolved. HOWEVER, as the developer is dismissing any issues brought up on the game forum as "design choices" I'm unwilling to dedicate any more time to this particular title.
Deep Fear is a procedurally generated endless "runner" that was originally Greenlit as a VR title. The store page for the current release however has no mention of either VR support or plans for it's addition in the future.
As soon as you start the game however it's immeaditley obvious that the game is still designed around VR implementation. The main menu is managable but the in-game HUD is placed off-screen above the character and requires you to pan your view upwards to t which is far from ideal as this also moves you in that direction.
Comments on the forum indicate the game is an asset flip with the developer responding that some assets are store-bought and some are original content. I personally have nothing against "asset flips" but it will obviously impact others decisions whether or not to buy the game.
The achievements which were my primary reason for buying the game are another aspect that others will have issue with and whilst it does have more than the typical game it's closer to Zup! than Sisters in Hotel as it does require some effort to unlock them rather than just idling the game.
The visuals are clearly an example of "sex sells" and it's obvious this is why the game is in third person. The third person camera makes for poor controls though and the crosshair - when it can be seen - seems to be too far ahead of you, meaning you often go everywhere but where you expect to go.
There are three game modes which are identical except for the colour palette. During each run you collect shells/coins that you can then spend on extra health, increased speed or additional characters. The health purchases however are consumable and not a persistent upgrade.
Whilst there are a number of questionable design decisions you can't really argue with what you get for the price, whether discounted or not. However at this point I'd recommend holding out to see what state it's in after a few updates.

Before I get started, there is something I should mention: DO NOT PLAY THIS ON A MAC.  For some reason, the Steam controller doesn't work properly with the Mac version.  I ended up using a PS3 controller instead with a 3rd party driver (though I don't remember where I got said driver) and even then, it only worked when physically plugged in and crashed the game when it was in Wireless Node.
That weird Mac version quirk aside, this is a wonderful game, but only if you have a working controller.  Repeat: you NEED a controller for this.  Your nerves will thank me.  Escape Goat is a basic get-to-the-exit platformer and the main game isn't too bad with a mild-moderate level of difficulty and is short enough that you could conceivably beat it in around a couple hours, but doing so unlocks the All Intensive Purposes dungeon.  This is where you get stages on par with "Super Meat Boy" and "I Wanna Be the Guy" with a greater emphasis on the latter.  Overall, it's not so much cheap as it is very unforgiving with certain sections demanding pixel-perfect jumps.  A few stages in particular literally took me several hours and I've beaten all the regular and Dark World stages in "Super Meat Boy." Honestly, I'm not even sure a Steam controller could handle this due to its lack of a good D-pad.
If you're looking for a fun challenge, then the main game will satiate you.  However, if you're looking for a serious platformer ordeal and/or you have masochistic tendencies, All Intensive Purposes is for you.

I remember playing Worms at a friend's place when it had just came out, and I had a lot of fun playing versus friends locally on just one PC.
Playing Worms Revolution brought back some of those memories, however I ended up playing Worms Revolution mainly as a single player game. Some people say that Worms is a multiplayer game, and you're supposed to play it with other players, but I see nothing wrong with playing Worms solely for the single player campaign. If you do, just think of Worms as a sort of puzzle game, and you will probably get a lot of enjoyment out of it. Some of the missions were frustatingly difficult thanks to the incredibly accurate AI, but that just made completing them feel that much more rewarding.
I played this game at the same time as I was playing Worms Clan Wars, and in my opinion Worms Revolution is by far the superior game. You can read my review of Worms Clan Wars
. I gave that game a negative review, not because I think it is a very bad game, but because this one is, in my opinion,
much better - and quite a bit cheaper as well.
Here's a few of the pros of Worms Revolution:
- The narrator (which is actually
in this game, unlike that annoying woman in Worms Clan Wars)
- Plenty of challenging missions
- Interesting weapons (the only weapon that I missed was the Teleportation Gun from Clan Wars)
- Water physics
I can't really think of any big cons. The new worm-classes (Soldier, Scientist, Scout, Heavy) were a nice addition, although not really necessary in my opinion. It can also be a bit hard to find people online, especially if you want to play  a ranked match.
Still, I definitely recommend this game.

It's an okay beat em up. I'm sure I would have enjoyed it more if I would have played it when it came out and more people played it via multiplayer. But because I did not I wasn't able to indulge much in that. The game itself has it's moments of cleverness but there are some unnecessary difficulties with the game. Specifically the way the game handles lives and checkpoints forcing you to play the game in a very boring fashion (which for a beat em up is not fun) or ensuring you grind levels to then advance on more difficult stages. I only encountered this problem once or twice but when frustration has less to do with your ability and more to do with the game being unforgiving it's tough for me to look at it positively. Especially when most parts are so simple, so you don't expect random gross increases in difficulty.
The big saving grace is the artwork, humor, design, music and enemies. It's worth playing at least once.

An excellent free to play shooter from the makers of the old Enemy Territory. If you liked ET, then there's a very good chance you'll enjoy this too.
Shooting and gun handling feels smooth, while lower damage numbers keep players alive longer than games like Call of Duty, giving players more chance to move about and avoid death with good positioning, and movement.
And oh boy, the movent is good. The ability to long, and wall jumps on maps designed for it, allows for great positional play. (Assuming you can keep your team organised, of course.)
The game also boasts an excellent range of characters that are very well balanced (with the usual tweaking and on-going balancing these games are known for).
Those positives aside, however, Dirty Bomb doesn't boast a competitive pricing model for current and future character releases. Other games with character rosters such as Paladins offer much cheaper alternatives. It also sadly uses 'must login everyday or counter resets' login reward system, coupled with at least one required match to be played before recieving it. So if the servers are down, or you're busy, you'll potentially find your daily rewards reset which may frustrate some.
Sp while perhaps their better known game, Brink, might have failed to get this formula working, (and not for the right reasons) Dirty Bomb excels. So far the game boasts a small, but dedicated community of players (ast least here in Australia), a testimant to how solid the game is.
And as an aside - the game scores bonus points for Cricket Bat melee weapons, snarky british character dialogue and one extremely sarcastic announcer.

A solid addition to the FPS genre.
You are William J Blazkowicz, a Nazi killing machine. In this alternative time line, in which the 3rd Reich wins World War II, Blazkowicz lays dormant in a mental hospital. 14 years pass, and he is awakened and once again called about to battle the forces of evil.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a worthy continuation of the Wolfenstein series. A classic first person shooter with all the usual tropes: big guns, tons of ammo, nigh-impervious hero, and thumping music. Tear through rooms of enemies soliders filling em with hot lead, or, when given the opportunity, skulk around unseen and have your knife silence your foes. The game is gritty while embracing the absurd (though, I won't spoil more than that). But there is more to wolfenstein than a pile of bodies. The story is deeper than the old school FPS and present the player with 2 times lines which provide different characters, some bonuses (one contains armor upgrades, the other health) and occasionally different ways to play through levels. Though I felt they could have done a lot more with this concept in regards to game play, it was a surprising element that simply left me wanting more.
The game does a decent job of variety while not over staying it's welcome. Weapons have alternative fire, alternative versions and dual wielding, so the player has a variety of load outs at their disposal. Aside from larger than necessary gun models and explaining how to dual-alt fire (perhaps I missed the message in game) I don't have any complaints. There are automatic save checkpoints which are fairly distributed, however there are times they occur in poor conjunction with cut-scenes. Sometimes you are forced to play a cut-scene over and over (the skip function is hit or miss as the game is loading during some of these scenes) which can be annoying. Other times, the save occur after a scripted interaction, and upon reloading, that interaction disappears (costing you items) or the save happens after a battle but before you stock up on items. So upon death, you get to stock up again and again... and again.
Enemies are relatively fair - they have terrible peripheral vision to enable a lot of leeway in stealth, though the ability to see through smoke which can leave the player at a massive disadvantage. The stealth portions aren't mandatory but it's noticeable when the game expects you to play to that style. The perks system provide the player with additional bonuses upon being unlocked, but play style is dictated by the situation more so than player preference. Uber can be a challenge (particularly if you haven't unlocked all the perks) but if that's still not enough, the enigma codes provide players with alternative modes of play, if you find all the codes and figure out how to unlock them.
Wolfenstein is an excellent game with a few surprises to go along with its solid genre defining elements. I hope future iterations expand about the alternative time line and maybe clean up some of the problems I had with auto-saving but it was predominantly positive and fun gaming experience.

All around an awesome singleplayer shooter game with only one negative aspect which is The game does not seem to run at a stable framerate even on modern amd gpu's. My framerate is all over the place and i'm running i5 3570k with amd 280x and most of my graphic settings are on low.
Nevertheless I have managed to enjoy this game because it has an interesting theme of alternative history where nazis won the war and have crushed almost every last bit of rebellion. The story is well thought out and the characters you meet have very different personalities and they have some interesting dialogue, but the main character is just a bit too much of a meatbag so there is not much of any meaningful character interaction with him. Luckily The setpieces are what makes this game enjoyable. They vary greatly from big fortressess, to prisons and labour camps and underground sewer systems.
Gameplay is mostly linear with some bigger shooting gallery areas and some of the scripted events and puzzles are well thought out but those are not that challenging. You have a basic selection of weapons too with one energy type laser weapon that also can be used as a tool to cut things, which most of the puzzles boils down to. But most of all you can dual wield shotguns and assault rifles! Pacing of the campaign is well done and does not wear you down with long cutscenes or endless enemy spawners. Some missions missions you can sneak too, but you won't fail if you get detected, so you can just blast your way through. There could be more variety in enemy types, since it's mostly energy weapons for these guys and normal weapons for the other. So the gameplay is quite straightforward and does not present you with that much of a challenge. At least the enemy ai is decent and you do have to be aware of your surroundings and change from cover to cover at times. One gripe I have about the shooting mechanics is that in a game like this I don't care for having lean from cover and aim down sights, but it gives you an option to play slow or go all out with dual wielding and try to find all The health packs so you can over charge your health meter and make some evil nazis very unhappy.

A little history, this is, in essence, the predecessor to dishonored. Yes they are completely different game worlds but it is made by arkane stuidos, the company who also made dishonored and arx fatalis. They don't make many games and there is one thing in common with all of them, the environment is great <--- this is coming from a guy who will rarely even notice, nevermind applaud environment.
If you havent played any of these games then let me give you a quick breakdown.
You play sareth, midevil apprentice to old wizard man who goes on a wonderful adventure filled with swords and spiders and undead creatures playing tag. The story is predicatable and cliché but not badly told.
You being the standard multi-talented rpg character can choose to become the most powerful (headless) warrior/mage/assasin of your time.
So why is the environment so good? Why would I reccomend this at least as much as the much smoother and more polished dishorored? Because you have one of the first games to try realistic physics and while it failed magnificently in some ways, it is still one of the best attempts going. Sure you kick someone within ten yards of a cliff/spikes and they go flying over it after tumbling forever and ever. But alot of objects can be played on both by you and the enemy, even combining in interesting ways with certain spells.
One of the nicest things that is so rare in games is that you REALLY feel different depending on what skills you choose. Stealth is ridiculously OP to the point of breaking the game at stealth 3, while magic only playthroughs are as challenging sub 10 deaths in super meat boy 106%.
The game is completely linear (which I like), even when you make a choice it barely affects any outcomes. Save this guy or not, heres a potion, or a sword, or a chance to kill the annoying one. The most significat differences are the 4 different endings and even there the actual difference is nothing at all, not even really worth exploring.
The enemies are one of the nicer parts, every enemy plays differently. Bigger, smaller, stronger, weaker, come in groups, come alone, have certain elemental weaknesses or can only be hurt in one spot. On the counter side the AI is stupidly exploitable, (this can be fun), but the hardcore player might be very dissapointed.
