RimWorld is a game of survival and management where you are stranded on a foreign planet post-shipwreck, with limited supplies and only a few survivors to work with. You don't control your colonists directly (except during combat), but rather provide jobs for them to do and you set up what jobs each colonist is allowed to do in the "Work" tab. You will need to build shelter, find food, defend yourself against hostile tribes, and keep your colonists from going insane. The amount of crazy mishaps that can happen in this RW are what truly keeps things interesting. Similar to Dwarf Fortress your colonists can go insane after being put under extreme loads of emotional stress, causing them to snap.
RW was initially released in 2013, outside of steam, and has been steadily improving ever since. The game feels very complete and is already packed with enough content to keep you entertained for weeks. There's already a decent modding community too, which is one of RW's strongest selling points at the moment. I've put over 140 hours into this game at the time of writing this review, and I've still not seen and done everything.
You begin the game with all of your colonists standing around in a pile of resources. The first steps to survival are building houses for your colonists to live in and growing crops or hunting for food. After covering the basics, you must decide what you'll do next. Will you create some storehouses, maybe a freezer to keep your food from rotting? Will you set up some defensive walls or traps to keep your crew safe from invasions? Or maybe you'll decide that crafting a masterwork-quality chess table made entirely out of marble is more important than anything else at the moment.
After awhile, you will begin to experience raids from outsiders. This can be anything from a few guys with clubs and bows, to a heavily-armed force of armored, gun-wielding pirates. Characters in this game benefit from cover around corners of buildings or behind objects like sandbags, rocks or trees. During combat, you will usually "draft" each individual person and control them directly, otherwise your colonists will generally carry out their normal tasks rather than actually go out and fight the raiders.
You can just move a character behind some cover and let them fire away, or control their every action and micromanage them like you would in a real-time strategy. If you're not a big fan of intense micromanagement, you also have the option to throw down turrets and watch the raiders get torn to ribbons while you kick back and relax. It all depends on how difficult you made your starting scenario, really, since primitive tribesmen don't really have access to automated gun turrets. The raids will continue to grow in size as your colony's wealth increases, making the game steadily more challenging as you play.
Your colonists don't just lose HP when they're hurt either, individual parts of their body are wounded. For instance if a colonist is shot with a gun, it might wound their torso or permanently shoot off one of their fingers. Your men can lose eyes, hands, legs, and even organs. Don't worry, after installing a few peg-legs, hook-hands, and golden eyeballs your colonists will be as good as new. Diseases have immunity rates, characters can develop permanent psychological conditions like dementia, and they can even start off with old battle-scars or health conditions like asthma or clogged arteries. This level of depth can be seen in virtually every aspect of RimWorld, and is one of the main draws to the game.
Currently the game's primary objective is to build a spaceship to escape the planet for good. You actually get to build the ship piece by piece, too. However, leaving the planet is ultimately up to you to decide. In RimWorld, you make your own objectives, you decide what it means to "win". Maybe your goal is to survive endlessly and build a huge, impressive, impenetrable fortress that will last for decades. RimWorld is moreso a sandbox game than one with a strict, singular goal. As gameplay updates comes out and modders get more creative, I imagine there will be more goals as well.
RimWorld takes a lot of inspirations from DF, but it is by no means the same game. First of all RW does not have strata (Z-Layer), everything occurs on a single elevation, which means you cannot dig underground or climb on top of mountains. DF is an incredibly complex experience with virtually-bottomless gameplay depth, while RW is a lot more basic by comparison.
RW has plenty of depth and content to keep you entertained for potentially hundreds of hours, but comparing RW to DF is like comparing an Olympic swimming pool to the Atlantic ocean. Both are fun, both have depth, one is just on an entirely new scale. I don't think it's a fair comparison, because RW is not trying to be DF, it just took inspirations from it. It is also worth noting that RW is fairly easy to get into compared to DF. People often find DF daunting due to it's cryptic interface and vague visual style. However even without watching tutorials or reading guides, an absolute beginner will understand the basics of survival in RW.
Unlike DF where huge droves of migrants regularly come in from out of the blue, RW expects you to use it's prisoner system to obtain more colonists. Sure there are a few random events that give you a new colonist here and there, but if you really want a big crew you'll have to take prisoners. Opponents who fall in battle can be captured and taken to a prison cell that you build. From there, they will need medical treatment and food. Once healed up, one of your colonists will act as a 'Warden' who can chat with the inmate and attempt to recruit them.
Recruiting can take a long time, and is harder for some than others, during this time your prisoner will use up valuable time and resources. You may also choose to release them, execute them, or just ignore them and sell them off to traders as a slave later on. This system is very cool, as it allows you to sort of pick who you recruit rather than just getting handed a completely random colonist you may not even want.
When I originally checked out RW on steam and saw the artstyle, I was immediately disgusted. Everyone looks like hideous blobs of flesh, everything and everyone is ugly. It's like Prison Architect but worse in every imaginable way. Even as someone who doesn't really care about graphics, I legitimately find the artstyle to be both disturbing and distracting. I understand that it was designed to be simple, but there's a fine line between low-quality graphics and zero-effort visual garbage. The developer has said the artstyle is final, sadly, so don't expect the game to get prettier overnight just because it's in early access. Thankfully the game is very mod-friendly, and there are already mods to alter the visuals.
The audio on the other hand, is great. RW has one of the most beautiful and cozy videogame soundtracks I've ever heard. I absolutely love RW's music. It's got a really good cowboys-in-space feel to it with some nice tribal beats to fit the uncharted-planet-survival theme, and a few of the tracks remind me of Earthbound or Faster Than Light. The music is dynamic too: relaxing and calm while you're building and managing your colony, then switches to a more upbeat track during combat sequences. The sound effects are decent as well, nothing stands out too strong aside from the occasional alert sound of a colonist dying from an extreme infection from an improperly treated gunshot wound, or the sound of a party ending -- which both use the same exact alert sound, because apparently the developer has a twisted sense of humor.

This is Freejam's game, they have every right to do what they want to the game, and the majority of complaints revolve around the progression system being too slow, which I personally disagree with.
However, I have to unfortunately suggest that new players curious about the game hold off on indulging until the developers figure out exactly what direction they want to go. They continue to remove features that make the game enjoyable and replace them with features that are mere shadows of what they used to be: the shift from an 8v8 building-destroying game to a 5v5 "king of the hill" game being the prime example.
The game is free, and I fault nobody for trying it out, you may even like the game in its current state. More power to you. I can't continue to support the game, and while I don't want to add to the cacophony of "BRING BAK OLD RBOCRAFT LOL" I will be quietly keeping track of updates to see if they ever make a change that's actually good for the game. If that involves rolling back the game to when it was still enjoyable, or reinventing the wheel yet again and trying something completely new, I'll be happy to return and change my review as long as it's a positive change.

An excellent free to play shooter from the makers of the old Enemy Territory. If you liked ET, then there's a very good chance you'll enjoy this too.
Shooting and gun handling feels smooth, while lower damage numbers keep players alive longer than games like Call of Duty, giving players more chance to move about and avoid death with good positioning, and movement.
And oh boy, the movent is good. The ability to long, and wall jumps on maps designed for it, allows for great positional play. (Assuming you can keep your team organised, of course.)
The game also boasts an excellent range of characters that are very well balanced (with the usual tweaking and on-going balancing these games are known for).
Those positives aside, however, Dirty Bomb doesn't boast a competitive pricing model for current and future character releases. Other games with character rosters such as Paladins offer much cheaper alternatives. It also sadly uses 'must login everyday or counter resets' login reward system, coupled with at least one required match to be played before recieving it. So if the servers are down, or you're busy, you'll potentially find your daily rewards reset which may frustrate some.
Sp while perhaps their better known game, Brink, might have failed to get this formula working, (and not for the right reasons) Dirty Bomb excels. So far the game boasts a small, but dedicated community of players (ast least here in Australia), a testimant to how solid the game is.
And as an aside - the game scores bonus points for Cricket Bat melee weapons, snarky british character dialogue and one extremely sarcastic announcer.

Borderlands is a co-op shooter with rpg elements that sets you in the far future on a planet that is ridden with bandits and monsters were your goal is to find a hidden alien vault with full of treasure.
The game starts off very slow and begins to be even slower later on despite the beginning sequence really pumping you up for more that doesnt really come in that way. Most of the time the gameplay is that you get quests and run from point A to point B and either destroy , activate or collect a thing. The only difference is sometimes the setup and humor like that you have to shoot♥♥♥♥♥♥that stuck on fans that powers something. There arent really any choices to make or any variety except the bossfights who end up to be bullet sponges that you dont really need any tactic for. You dont really mind this because weapons usually feel very good to shoot and there are lots of diffferent types of enemies that have different types of weaknesses, atleast if you get a good weapon drop that actually justifies the bonus against a type of weakness over the dps the other gun you currently have is.
The balancing of the game is terrible aswell. Most of the weapons you find are♥♥♥♥♥♥ some weapon types are obviously totally inferior to others and enemies end up later to be bullet sponges that you sometimes can only beat by abusing the bad ai or find better weapons. The game also gives you a couple of characters you can play with different abillies but Brick is obviously the best choice because his ultimate gives him tons of damage per second and makes him almost unkillable because of his fast health regeneration.
The artstyle is okay, its nothing really impressive but doesnt look bad whatsoever. Only thing i disliked was the fact that the whole time it was just mostly either yellow desert sand or grey and black indoor settings.
The game also suffers from a lot of bugs, not only sometimes questlines can be broken or you can end up stuck, the GOTY version sometimes doesnt recognize that you own all the dlc´s. Also the driving physics are terrible.
The dlc´s are almost all of them bad or okay at best, but i just list them up for convenience and dont add this in the final scoring.
-Zombie Island:
Pretty idiotic unbalanced, would be fun but there arent many quests and the map is very liniar. You can beat it at directly at the beginning of the game when you unlocked the transport system. Only difficulty was the fact that there were so many zombies but rarely any ammo drops. Okay tough if you start it at the beginning of the game and the artstyle is nice. Finally something different than desert.

Terrible and everyone knows it because it just adds some wave like game where the only reward is just a skill point or two. There arent any loot boxes to get and the difficulty is so high that the reward isnt worth it when you are able to beat it. Up to this day i didnt even bother finishing more than one level.

Basically the high level version of the Zombie Island with claptraps instead of zombies . Except it doesnt share the awesome artstyle. Isnt that unbalanced tough and humor is great, still not really good but not bad either.
-Armory of Knoxx:
Terrible map design would be okay or good dlc but the game sends you driving from one part of the map to the other just to buy time. The whole map is just a huge highway with enemies that annoy you and destroy your car. The end loot is good tough but that was the only reason i played it.

In all seriousness, it's a great shooter; the gunplay isn't as meticulous as that of DOOM's, but the game's not nearly as repetitive. It skirts the line between serious and ridiculous and it's kind of amazing how a 2yr old (at the time of reviewing this) game about robot dogs and Nazi mechas did war drama better than 'realistic' Infinite Warfare (or, arguable, any CoD game since 4).
It's not as good as Half-Life 2, but it's probably the best shooter since Half-Life 2.

Have been looking for a realistic, tactical FPS other than Arma as I deep inside mever wanted to purchase Arma (thank god I found this before I did), and Squad is exactly what I was looking forward to. Before you buy however, make sure you understand what you are buying. The game is hyper-realistic, you can not go lone wolf and run and gun. You have to work together with your squad, taking orders from your dquad leader and working together to benefit your team and win (even if that includes sitting on a FOB to ensure it doesn't get taken over and never actually getting in a firefight). Some games you will not get a kill. Some games you will get kills but never know how as the enemy you killed was barely visible. The gameplay and realism is amazing, and the community one of the better I've been a part of and is definitely a refresher after playing games like Counter Strike. The only complaints pertain to things that will be fixed as the game becomes more complete or things that the engine can not handle but do not need to be in the game (breakable walls, AI, etc.).
Final Words: Amazing game, but do not buy if hyper-realism, teamwork, and sometimes boring situations are not for you. Highly recommend.

Amazing game. The story was engaging, the characters were interesting, and every choice actually indeed mattered to the ending you receive. It balances horror themes and comedy relief perfectly, where you feel surrounded by what makes horror scary, but not suffocated by it. Many games go for the "scare you until you want to cry" approach, being a one-dimensional horror game that only cares about giving you the jitters. This game transitions horror into the plot perfectly in a way that makes it feel scary naturally, without anything being forced or obvious scare-bait. It's horror in the good old traditional way of horror, like old Japanese horror flicks, rather than what the industry has morphed horror into. No jumpscares, no "BIG SCARY MAN CHASING YOU", no hiding in closets from a monster you can see. It is atmospheric horror at its best; or what would be its best if the game didn't give you companions that you positively endear and care about the fate of. It's not a horror game, it's a game that implements horror into its setting (FANTASTICALLY). Don't go into this game expecting just another scary horror game that Youtube channels would love to react to; expect a wonderful story that is paced just right to keep you in constant anticipation and suspense without any forced scares.
Amazing game that I highly recommend. My only gripe is the dialogue system, which sometimes gives you long choices you have to skim through due to being on a timer, thus sometimes causing you to choose the response you didn't actually want. That is a minor thing, though. If you're looking for a good game, you should buy this one. It's overall wonderful and extremely worth the money.
After 225 hours, I think I can definitively say - just go buy it. Tales of heroism and despair await you.

Once upon a time, I reviewed Boundless shortly after its name had changed from Oort Online.  I gave it a thumbs down, with the side note that I bought in because I believed in it, and it had serious potential.  It's been about a year, now.  New games have come and gone.  Boundless has been under development by its dev team.  So, how does it hold up?
Before I get to my usual "What Works?", "What Doesn't Work?" and the "TL;DR", first, Boundless is a MMO-Block-Buildy game.  It's sort of like Minecraft, only on one centralized server, presumably with
of people running around also doing stuff.  Put differently, Boundless is a very pretty, more authoritative Minecraft clone where you are a giant teddy bear using naturalistic technology possibly stolen from the Na'vi.  No, I'm not making that up, either.
First, I noticed some RPG mechanics for mining, building, fighting monsters, and some other stuff.  This is a good thing to add, because it makes the first couple of hours of gameplay more interesting (and, this game's first few hours need more interesting gameplay, but we'll get to that.)  They weren't there two years ago, and I feel like you can 'skill up' quickly enough for it to be fun, even if the results just aren't that awesome (usually you do a thing faster.)
Next, the menu-driven crafting system is much improved from where it was in 2015, and I like the direction it's headed.  As you construct things in the game world, certain combinations let you interact to begin crafting.  Instead of needing to arrange certain items in a grid, you just choose what you want from a menu.  Simplicity itself, I really like this.  I feel like, as someone who's put the game down and taken an extended break, that certain items like the fire pit/furnace combination could be spelled out a little more explicitly for players, but ultimately, the crafting system is good.
The game is also very well-optimized in this early state of its development.  I'm running the game on a HP 500-217c with factory hardware (in other words, an aging system), and its defaults hold a consistent framerate well.  It's always a good sign when a game is reasonably well-optimized.
First, and most frustrating, the controls.  For some reason when I turn my character with my mouse, if I turn too quickly, my character snaps back to where the game thinks I should be pointing; turning with arrow keys turns the character at a slower rate, but requires me to take my hand off of the mouse.  It is possible to turn normally if you look upwards or downwards far enough, which is clunky and error prone, and frankly just plain wrong.
, and this alone would be a big enough issue for me to thumbs down the game, except that there are other problems.
Your game should not be fighting me when I want to do something,
.  I recommend that the developers revisit the basic controls and fix them.
Second, game pacing.  This game starts off lethargically slow, to the point of boring me halfway to sleep.  Finding wood, whacking wood with a totem (heh), and crafting a basic workbench is OK, and comparable to other works in the block-buildy genre.  Figuring out where to place the workbench relative to a base beacon is exceptoinally irritating; some nearby blocks work, others don't.  There's no indication - have fun guessing!  ...That's an unrelated problem however.  It's something else worth fixing.
When you
figure out where to place a workbench, and start getting stone, you get ground to a halt by the crafting process itself - it takes about 2:30 to make a single stone tool, at Crafting Lv.1.
In MineCraft, if I have sticks and stones, I have a stone tool.  To cook meat to restore your HP?  2:30.  While I get that the developers may want to control the pacing for technical or game design reasons, your early game cannot afford to have such horrible pacing.  For what its worth, because the game is more interesting I lasted more than the two hours I lasted back in 2015, but I was experiencing serious anti-fun while doing it.
It was at this point that I really stopped this particular play session.  There's been a lot more added to the game, but when the game is fighting you at every opportunity - not a figure of speech - there comes a point where continuing is more painful than stopping.  Because this review is intended to help the developers build a better product, I'm considering recording a YouTube video of my experiences to help with getting this game up to snuff.
This game has awesome ideas, beautiful visuals,
While I give this game a downvote, I want to re-iterate something I said at the coda of my previous review: this is a game where, problems aside, one can easily see that the developers are putting blood, sweat, and tears into this work.  The craftsmanship of the bits that aren't messed up is exquisite.  I can't justify telling anyone to drop $34.99 USD on this game, but I don't regret my purchase, as this game is much closer to being an awesome experience than it was two years ago.
I encourage anyone who owns this game to reinstall, and give the dev team notes on what you're seeing.  It seems like the developers took my previous review, really read it, and tried to make the game better.  They didn't argue - they really want this game to be enjoyable.  Tell them what's wrong with it, they need to know, so that you can justify your purchase.

Escape Goat is a puzzle platformer in which you must double jump your way out of a fiendish dungeon with only your wits and your magical mouse pal to help you. It's a short game (4-ish hours), but will probably feel even shorter if you blaze through it the way I did. Escape Goat is not a particularly innovative game, but it's tremendously successful at pulling off it's core concept. The platforming controls are incredibly tight and satisfying. This is one of those games where it's fun simply to move around within the levels.
Each zone of the prison has a unique theme and iterates on one or two key puzzle mechanics. The levels themselves manage to pull an impressive amount of variety from single screens. The music is pleasant, and a little bit moody. The graphics, oddly enough, are one of my favorite parts of the game. The color palette reminds me of the early Castlevania titles, with weird blues and purples standing out against dark and gloomy backgrounds. The whole package is surprisingly atmospheric for a game that is otherwise a pretty stripped-down platforming experience. If you enjoy puzzle platformers even a little bit, I strongly recommend picking up Escape Goat.

In a nutshell: a very good (and different than the mainstream) game, with some flaws. Highly recommended, and the price is very low; give it some initial love, and you will be rewarded by several hours of enjoyable gameplay.
Want details? Read below.
When I first heard about this game, I thought "Come on, melee fighting in... first-person view only? Ridiculous." It turns out it is way better than I thought. The game actually manages to be very enjoyable, despite the fact it has its flaws. Yes, the first-person view is a major flaw because you can't see much, as a big part of the screen is covered by your shield, your daggers, or even your own hands when using some spells. However, in practice it is not as bad as it sounds, and in some ways first-person view makes things more interesting, provided you get used to the hitboxes of your weapons.
The learning curve is rather steep in the beginning, but it gets better soon. The game is not an RPG really, but has some RPG elements. There is no experience or stats; you earn skill points as you complete your objectives, and you can use those skill points to learn some abilities or spells; neat and simple. There are no classes; instead, there are three skill trees, somehow representing the typical fighter, rogue/archer, and mage classes. However, the player is free to distibute skill points as he/she pleases, so it is quite possible to be a warrior with some magical or stealth abilities, and such combinations actually work very well in practice. I personally found the sword fighter + archer combo quite enjoyable, and probably the easiest way to play this game. A "thief" build is also interesting, and it is actually quite possible to go stealth for the most part of the game.
Melee fighting is probably the most interesting aspect of Dark Messiah. You have some fighting moves, and using them you can make your opponent walking lame, or you can decapitate him. Fighting is far from being the usual, boring click fest. It needs player's skills instead.
As usual in similar PC games, the controls are clunky, and some players will probably quit playing early because of this. For example, hold left mouse button "for a second" to activate power attack; hold direction keys while holding down the left mouse key to activate alternative power attacks; additionally, hold space bar for a jump attack. All that when you have a bunch of enemies in front of you. Seriously, if that's not clunky controls, I don't know what "clunky controls" means. Things would be way better if you could use a controller instead of mouse and keyboard. Nevertheless, once you get used of the controls, melee fighting is really enjoyable. It has not the nice controls of Dark Souls, but it is still quite enjoyable. Most players will probably pick a warrior combo because of this, despite the controls.
As in Half-Life 2, you can use the environment to get rid of your enemies. Shoot a loose supporting beam so that the barrels above fall on a bunch of bad guys; cut a rope so that a rock pendulum hits a mighty cyclops that blocks your way; kick your enemy so that he falls off a cliff, etc. Physics reminds Half-Life 2, and that's not a coincidence, as Dark Messiah uses the same game engine. Using the environment is just another nice aspect of the game.
The plot is nothing innovative, but it is certainly interesting. You are a guy, trying to get an ancient artifact from the bad guys. Nothing new so far; however, there are two hot girls hitting on you. Leanna is the "good girl" who will fight on your side in many cases, and eventually falls in love with you, although she is too shy to admit it openly. Xana is some kind of a succubus, a demonic creature that lives inside you, gives you useful information depending on the situation and, most importantly, comments on what's going on. Xana's commentary is actually the funniest part of this game: she is jealous about Leanna, and always has some ironic and quite funny comments about her.
A spice of humor is spread all over the game. It's not only Xana's comments mentioned above, but also NPCs talk to eachother, quite often in a funny way: enemy soldiers talking about their boss ironically, goblins discussing if they should eat the orc they just killed, and several other things that will make you smile.
There are some nice cutscenes, but luckily the developers didn't overuse them. I am really tired of today's ridiculous "AAA" games with a cutscene every few seconds and zero gameplay. Dark Messiah is definitely not one of them, and I am quite happy with that.
Eventually, you will have to take decisions, which leads to a few different endings of the game. However, the game is basically linear; personally, I prefer that instead of the chaotic gameplay of Elder Scrolls, for example - although a lttle more non-linearity in Dark Messiah would be nice. Not to mention fighting in Dark Messiah is actually way better than the simplistic fighting in Elder Scrolls. Hard to remember a similar, but non-linear game, that managed to keep me playing till its end.
Graphics are typical for the Source engine used. Although not that realistic as in modern games, graphics certainly serve their purpose very well. I also liked the music of the game, and in general sound does its job: no complaints, no awards. Voice actors also do their job, with Moon Dailly performing very well as Xana.
There is also a multiplayer mode for Dark Messiah. I imagine this would be quite fun, but sadly it is non-existant in practice. Official server is down, probably because this game was first released 9 years ago. Unless you have friends interested to play, forget about multiplayer.
I read some people had techinical issues with this game. This was not the case for me; no issues in a mediocre laptop running Windows 7 64 bit. No FPS drops, no tearing, with maximum quality settings on - very good performance, typical for the Source engine used in the game. I had a few game crashes, especially when running other programs in the background, but nothing really serious, and probably caused by the laptop's low RAM.
The game is rather easy in "normal" mode - provided you pass the steep initial learning curve. There are some annoyingly hard enemies, but in general you won't have serious problems beating the game, including bosses. Expect a 20-30 hours of gameplay in your first playthrough, if you want to explore everything and find all secret places in the game. Replayability is rather low: once I beated the game, I started over using a stealth build and tried a different ending but, other than that, there is no more replayability to talk of.
Final verdict: I don't give a positive review easily, but Dark Messiah definitely desrves it, despite the flaws mentioned.  Taking into account its price, I'd say it's a bargain, and highly recommended.

Escape goat is quite the pleasant experience, having an array of few but interesting mechanics you can opperate your characters with, which side by side with the incredibly solid level design makes for a really smooth experience. The level design even if kind of complex at times, never gets to be actually frustrating, even if 2 or 3 levels can take you a not so low number of attempts.
The graphics do fit perfectly what would be outright retro rather than just pixelart alone (something plenty of people should learn the proper definition of both), not breaking sprite sizes or their self impossed colour limitations, which never interfere and only help how you read the maps (which is something I see multiple sidescroller games screwing up). And let's not forget the kickass soundtrack.
The only problem I have with the game is the free expansion it comes with. It isn't bad, but the level design clearly follows a different philosphy, and one that is a lot more trial and error, which for a 1 room type of level system is fine on itself, being able to see the entire of the map from the start, but unfortunately it has a lot of areas that require really precise timing on top of the puzzles themselves, which in the end do end up feeling frustrating.

It is important to keep in mind that this game is pre-alpha. This game is constantly changing for the better, it seems as though there is a new update every week.
While I agree that in its current state it is very much grindy for a solo player, the devs are still working on tweaking crafting and player progression. From their posts on the forums they plan on incorporating skill trees, guilds, and loads of other features.
I don't understand why there are mixed reviews on this game though. They state in the game description that it is only for players who want to be actively involved in the games development. Speaking of development, I started playing this game before the C++ update they were working on. I stopped playing until last week while waiting for that update. The update has since launched and they have been constantly adding new features to the game.
If you're looking for a finished title this game isn't ready yet. It does look amazing and the exploration I've been able to take part of has been a blast, but it isn't complete yet. That being said in its current state it is a lot of fun (at least in my opinion).
Regarding the pictures and video in the game description.
Titans currently do not exist in the game (that's the big block looking thing they grapple onto towards the end of the video).
Large portals to other servers are not currently in the game (they were in the game before, but I think after they did the C++ update they decided to tweak them so they would be more stable).
Capitals (the large city you see) aren't currently in the game. I feel these will be incorporated again when the game is closer to 1.0.
Once again, this game is still pre-alpha and they are making great progress.

I come back to this game every few months to see whats new. This weekend I logged in and found a game that finally feels like a game that has potential to keep my attention for a decent amount of time. Here are the things I like about the current game play.
You get plots of land that become yours and people cannot destroy your creations: I love this because it encourages creativity in a multiplayer game. If you're playing with friends you can give them rights to work and manage your land. When this game goes live and there are massive player made cities it'll be pretty sweet.
The more you play the game the more plots of land you unlock: This is probably the greatest thing they've added recently. As someone who likes to build things I found that previous versions were really limited because you had a set number of plots. Once you filled them up there wasn't much left to do. Over just one weekend in the current game mode I've earned more plots then I can keep up with for building things! I love it.
There are multiple planets: The game has an exploration element to it where you can teleport to other planets. These planets orbit each other and you can see them in the sky.
This game is a Minecraft type game so yeah, you have to spend time farming blocks if you want to do stuff. If that's not your thing then you probably won't like this game. I like it better then Minecraft because it's prettier. I don't have to setup my own server and manage mods for multiplayer. It has builtin creation protection without needing a mod for it.
Overall it's a good game and it's not even finished yet.

An over-saturated genre that we all know, mobas.I'm sure most of us that do try something different from LoL and Dota 2 are having a hard time picking something to rise to their expectations but, guess what, this game just might be it.
Now without actually playing it's easy to just say it's a Dota  and LoL copy, in reality it's not.You will find yourself impressed by what you're about to play so I'll give this game an open beta review as it stands right now and hopefuly by the time you're done reading it, I might have convinced you to try it out at least.
Graphics: Definitely something to enjoy about the game, it's cartoonish a little and the atmosphere does feel a little like World of Warcraft.It has a lot of details and the champions look great.
Sound: Well might I say not only are the sound effects realistic but the music is also awesome enough to make you buy the soundtrack.It makes you get into the atmosphere of the game and makes you curious to find out more.
Gameplay: There's a lot to talk about here since it's quite complex, but what's particulary attractive about this game is that fights are really short simply because each hero's health doesn't ever get as high as you see them in Dota  2 to take 5 people to kill one person.The health and damage balance makes things go faster and smoother.
Towers take agro towards an enemy hero if he targets another hero while under it but what's also interesting is that here you can actually damage towers with your skills, that's right developers found it unusual to not be able to do that.
There's this out of combat regeneration which basicaly doubles your hp/mana regen while you're out of combat, furthermore it's even faster if you're sitting next to a tower, lets you stay on the lane for longer.
At lvl 4 you will unlock the crafting system which basicaly lets you change the components of an item to something of your desire (no not everything, but something of the same tier).It will add slight bonuses to that item also as enchantments if you choose to, but it requires more gold to build the item in return.
Pets support you on the lane with different abilities:1 active and 2 passives, each pet having their own unique abilities.
In conclusion I will write the pros and cons this game has:
Pros:
-Teamfights are short and smooth due to lower health compared to other mobas
-All heroes can carry in the game no matter what their main roles are.They got the abilities to carry and potential through regular items
-Towers can be hit be skills.Any skill works on it and really speeds up things especially for skill damage heroes (no it's not op)
-Out of combat boosted regeneration when you don't attack or get attacked back for 5 seconds.Laning was never this fun and it solves the issue when running out of mana.
-All heroes are free to be used.That's right, all heroes are unlocked for you, you don't have to buy them.
-Pets are really unique and can be used to support your hero in ways your lane partner may not.
-You can queue for a match with a pre-selected hero already.Now people can stop nagging you never picked the support!
-Warding at this moment is done by walking near some pillars and activating them for your team.It provides vision until it expires or until the enemy claims it.No need to buy wards, just walk next to them like a boss.
-Cindara is the primary objective boss that if killed lets you summon a big ape that shuts down any tower it's fighting and lets you take it out while it's shut down.Unique once again.
-Generators, the last towers to defend your base, have a shield that has to be taken down before any health can drop from it which in most cases makes it hard for creeps alone to take it down.It requires actual players to have to take it down.No backdooring from creeps.
-Even if the match is against you, it's easy to get a comeback because even if the enemies are fed items themselves don't provide as big of a boost as other mobas, but the boost is still there
-Good ban system for leavers and afkers
-You can unlock a costume/skin for a hero by renting it for some time and the price drops for each time you rent it until it reaches 0 when at that moment it's yours.Means all skins can be bought easily through time.
-They're intending to go for esports already and they constantly organise tournaments and streams.
-Replays,spectate,streams,top 10 videos, all within the game menu.
-Awesome pinging system, just like in LoL
Cons:
-You can queue with as many friends as you want online, besides if you're 4.That can be bothersome for some people but I expect it to change.
-Towers hit quite hard, it can be stressful for newbies.
-Too much gold is being received when destroying a generator
-Pre-selecting your hero before queue means it will try to find you 4 players that didn't pick the same hero as you.It can limit the queue results.
-Cindara is hard as hell to defeat requiring 4 players to defeat her the entire game.
-Queues are not always so fast due to the game needing a bigger playerbase, but in most cases it lasts between 2-5 minutes.Things are fine for Europe but for US it needs a stronger playerbase.
-After 5 min when a person left or is afk, the match is safe to leave but a notification doesn't always pop up to tell you it's safe to leave.You have to check by pressing tab.It may result in you getting a penalty for not knowing wether it was safe to leave or not.
Edit: Ever since this review had been written S2 ( the company developing this game) has abandoned support for this game just like they did previously with others games made by them. Do not invest any money in this game whatsoever until this game is sold to another company.

I first played this game back in 2015 when it came out, played it for a while them promptly quit to play other things. It had unfortunate timing, with the overwatch beta opening that same year, and with a larger audience to cater to with their class-based shooter, it helped DirtyBomb go overlooked by many people. Tie that in with a♥♥♥♥♥♥review from a few popular reviewers (AngryJoe & others) It had what many people would call a rough start.
However the development team has shown that they want to do something positive with the game, and i can respect that. Some genuine passion has been put into this game, and to what could be considered a small playerbase, they are doing their best. They have released two mercenaries recently, as well as relatively quick balance changes appropriately, they have improved matchmaking (although I'd still like to see it improved moreso). There are genuinely good games, with a good chalange and teamwork, however it is very common to have one team significantly stacked in comparison to another. This problem has been adressed on the reddit page for dirtybomb.
Enough of the drama though, time for the positive. Excellent gunplay, interesting and fluent movement, and fantastic optomisation, I can't recall having ever had a crash, or even a significant frame drop since the most recent patch (Granted it has been a significant amount of time since I last played, it could have been improved long ago). The classes are all very interesting and unique, granted, they don't have robots or an ape but let's give them some time. Most every merc has their own unique ability, not just new twists on the same old idea, and for the most part, well balanced. Keep in mind a lot can be learned from game knowledge and gamesense, but there are still a few outliers but the devs seem to want to make it known they are trying.
Overall, a great game that is heading in a positive direction. I am eager to see where this goes.

There arent really any choices to make or any variety except the bossfights who end up to be bullet sponges that you dont really need any tactic for. Only one table, and I didn't like the table.
Most of the ramps are narrow and placed far enough to the side that they're hard to shoot if you catch the ball and let it roll down the flipper. There are some classic pinballs where shooting ramps always requires momentum, but they usually have steeply sloped flippers so you're not screwed if you're playing from a standing start. This table tries to have the gently sloped flippers of a slower table and the ramps of a fast table and it feels poorly tuned as a result.
The goal structure differs from your typical '90s Williams solid state in that it's unusually long and serial. There are lots of time periods to reach and each requires charging the time machine with several T2-esque ramp-to-ramp shots and then locking 3 balls for a multiball mode. Time periods are gated by collectible crystals so that you have to do them in order. Seeing all the content would require a really long play session. So I guess if you're so good that your ramp-to-ramp flow never falters and you get sick of running out of goals on other tables, this is for you.
(BTW, the video mode is excellent)

Note: I received a key from the developer to share my thoughts on this title. This means my review has not added to the percentage rating on the store page.
We play Eliosi, a diminuitive bounty hunter who needs to prove that he can be just as tough and fierce as the big guns. You move from map to map (5 total) hunting a target (boss) and collecting optional power upgrades.
The controls are basic but easy to pick up and intuitive both with keyboard and mouse, or a controller. Twin stick shooter style, hold down a button to shoot and then you move, jump and dash. You have a main gun and can collect different weapons and useables, but unfortunately they have very limited uses and then they disappear. They are often very situational for the surroundings. If a rocket launcher appears on the map, you have a clue to look out for a breakable wall, for example. If you collect a jetpack, expect some complicated jumps up ahead. I would have preferred being able to permanently add these to my collection and having a proper loadout, but perhaps that would have been too unbalanced.
It's primarily a top down action shooter; but has quite a few platforming elements. The problem is the controls aren't quite tight enough for a real platformer, making it hard to move whilst in the air and not as precise as it should be. I felt the shooting was on point though and would have preferred it simply as a shooter.
The graphics are great! Very beautiful, with each level having a distinct environment. I loved the bright colours and the intricate detail. The art aesthetic feels really special and I would have really enjoyed this in a more relaxing setting. Both the visuals of the gun shooting and the sound effects have impact and feel satisfying. The music works very well with the fast paced sci-fi setting and the cutscenes are interesting and detailed - although there is no dialogue. They manage to give you a feel for the game from animation alone, without needing words. Visually this game presents a very attractive package.
You gain health from exploding health objects in the surroundings but at some points you can easily get one shot by the enemy. When you load from a checkpoint, you always load at one health, not full. You really have to pay close attention and are constantly dodging and shooting. Sometimes monsters can ambush you from the terrain and they always have the advantage in numbers. Movement feels pretty solid and if I died during combat, it was usually my fault for not responding quick enough. It felt very challenging for my geriatric hands and I did end up quite frustrated early on, having to repeat entire sections multiple times. I did get better with time, but I'd personally describe this on the higher end of the difficulty scale and for those who like a challenge and don't mind repeating sections when they die.
There is an interesting ability of being able to use a checkpoint to save - or destroy it to get a move speed bonus. You may need those move speed bonuses to complete the game in the allotted time, but with the amount I died, I couldn't sacrifice many checkpoints.
A major flaw in my opinion is the static camera angle. It's top down and there is a lot of environmental interaction - such as triggering doors, activating things, shooting health, jumping from platform to platform and you can't change the camera angle at all. No rotation. As such, sometimes the environment simply gets in the way and you are blind. At one point I was jumping from leaf to leaf and there was simply no way to see where I was going other than to guess - this is poor level design at work, and leads to a death that is absolutely not my fault. I can't say I was a big fan; maybe it's because I was expecting a corridor shooter instead of a narrative FPS.
The game is approximately half nazi-killing action and half insipid story activities (i.e., fetching stuff, interacting with characters, and watching cutscenes). The FPS mechanics aren't very solid and felt kind of sluggish to me--the direct opposite of Doom 4 where dying means that you're the only person to blame for messing up. The weapons are bland and weak--except for the rifle, they've all got poor range, which is irritating in situations where enemies are peppering you from a distance. Quite a few of the enemies are total bullet sponges, something that gets annoying very quickly. The "puzzles," all involving this annoying and fairly worthless laser gun that's forced upon your over and over again, are all of the same style and get tedious in the first couple levels. About half way through, I wanted to quit, but finished it for the sake of finishing it.
However, the writing, story, and atmosphere are all quite good.

So here I find myself writing up another Friday review for some faithful, interested gamer out there and I wouldn't have it any other way. With that said welcome to another Friday video game review here on In The Mind Of My Mind with your friendly neighborhood gamer Zalgo_Cometh. I been waiting and wanting to get myself a copy of this game from I heard they were making a part two after all the success the first game received. We reviewed Sonic & Sega All Star Racing two years ago and now its back for round two.Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is a racing video game developed by Sumo Digital and published by Sega. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is the sequel to Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing, the fourth installment in the Sega Superstars series, and the eighth racing game in the Sonic the Hedgehog series. Do you think the sequel lives up to its predecessor  Let's find out on today's exciting episode of Dragonball Z..........wait wrong show; I mean on today's blog review.

Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is a mascot-based racing game in which players race against each other using characters from various Sega franchises, although it features many new mechanics and improvements from the last game. The most obvious is that, at certain points in a race, vehicles can alternate between car, boat and plane modes. The car mode handles similarly to the previous game, in which players can earn boost by drifting around corners or performing tricks whilst in the air. Boat mode features true boating physics, requiring players to consider their vehicle's turbulence. They may also be affected by waves made in the water, some of which can be used to leap into the air and perform stunts. Plane mode, the fastest of the three forms, gives players the freedom to move both vertically and horizontally. Like the other modes, players can 'air-drift' around corners to earn boost and can also perform rolls to quickly adjust their position, earning boost for narrowly dodging obstacles. Players alternate between these modes by driving through blue transformation gates. Certain tracks in the game terraform as players proceed through them, offering different play-styles between each lap.
What’s Good:
Game-play: I must say Sega really listened to the fans and went all out to improve this series and I certainly see it as a worthy competitor to the Mario Kart franchise. With a wide variety of tweaks and subtle game-play enhancements this game certainly has quite the competitive edge to offer. When playing this game it certainly feels like a true race that is determined mostly by skill and not just sheer luck. From the changing track layout to the varying modes of transportation to the subtle handling differences in the varying modes of transport; Sega has offered up a selection of any and everything imaginable to affect a racing game of this wacky and nostalgic nature. Add into that the wide character roster of old and new faces alike and you simply cannot go wrong.
Replay Value:
With such a wide cast of characters to explore how could you not have replay value? Add to that a variety of race modes and tracks for both single player and multi-player enjoyment and you will be begging for a break. Sega went even further and gave us a leveling system for each character and different car mods to unlock and explore for each of your favorite characters. This is what you call some serious replay value.
What’s Bad:
Story-line: WHERE IS THE STORY LINE? WHY DO I NOT KNOW HOW THESE CHARACTERS ALL GOT TO THIS DIMENSION? WHAT ARE THEY EVEN RACING FOR? Hell the most important question of them all is why Sonic is even driving a car when he is obviously the fastest participant of this whole racing game? Trolling aside it would have been nice to have a dedicated story-line to help add value to the game and develop more interest in the varying characters.
What Should Have Been Added:
Pretty much like I said that only main thing I would have wanted to see was a properly fleshed out story to help solidify this game.
Final Thoughts:
I am definitely glad to see the success this game is receiving and hope that Sega and Sumo Digital continue to make this a worthy addition to the kart racing game genre. especially since its the only kart racing game I know of that has a version for PC which is way easier to get people to play on locally than with a handheld or a console. I hope to see continued variety of character inclusion from the illustrious Sega collection of characters they have at their disposal.

Fly in the House is a poorly optimised game that can be kinda fun.
Going round smashing stuff is pretty enjoyable, especially when you just forget about trying to kill the fly entirely.
However the fly is almost impossible to kill on purpose, and likely to be killed by accident while trying to achieve something else, by Sod's Law.
This makes the several challenges on each level that require quick, or accurate, killing of the fly, near impossible and extremely frustrating.
Which would be forgivable, if you could just ignore them.
However the worst part of the game is the way you progress.
To progress to the next area, you need to:
Kill the fly in story mode.
Beat the target score.
Complete Everyone one of those impossible challenges (kill the fly in a Super Fast time, kill multiple flies in X time, hit the fly without breaking Anything else in the level)
Find Most of the objects in the level.
Find most of the achievements in the level.
I might have even missed some of the tasks.
Even just making it so you have to kill the fly, and get the (actually ridiculously high) target score would make progression actually, you know, fun. But no, you have to achieve the impossible.
I've managed to unlock the second level, somehow, but unlocking the third looks to be beyond me.
So no, this is not a good game.  Shoddy implementation. Super difficult Luck based challenges. And  a dire game progression system.
The first I could forgive. The second I could forgive. But the third one ends up making the game just no fun at all.

TL;DR Once upon a time this was my favorite game, now it is just a shell of it's former greatness...
Having put over 2k hours into this game, I feel that I can write an honest review. Like most of the commenters before, I agree that there has been sharp decline in quality over the past 4 to 5 months. I started playing this game soon after it's launch (just after hoverblades were introduced as a movement type). Orginally there was a clear progression path giving a definite purpose to playing. You win some matches, you get some RP, you buy some parts to upgrade your bot, you play some more matches, you win some more RP, etc. Now that there is a crate system, the purpose of the game is lost. Crates are great if you happen to get a Legendary weapon or module, but not when that item is unavailabe because you don't have Premium on your account. Pay to win is a term thrown around with a lot of free to play games, and Robocraft has started leaning in that direction with this crate system. Previously, premium would help level faster which would increase the amount of parts you could have on your bot, so "pay to win" was not quite right. Now that they are relying on RNG to determine what you get from winning/losing a match, and you are limiting what players earn by 1/2 (without premium), this becomes pay to win. Pay to win more garbage parts, but pay to win none the less...
With that out of the way, we can begin to discuss the gameplay updates. Weapons will be added that would hopefully balance the game, but the devs do not balance current items before adding new ones. Removing features that have become second nature to players like myself in order to try to retain new players, has become the norm for updates. I understand that the player base for this game has dropped drastically, but randomly changing key functions of the game is only alienating your core audience and people will continue to uninstall. There was once a time where FreeJam would send out a poll and ask the players what they would like in the next update. This was fantastic. There would be list of 10-15 update ideas, and the community would vote on their favorite 3-4, which FreeJam would then impliment in the next update...
Without getting specific, I would point at the last three updates as the worst yet. Adding garbage, removing key functions, and just bowing down to the casual gamers who play 3-4 hours and then uninstall... Why do you think they are uninstalling? I would venture to guess they saw "build, drive, fight" and thought it might be fun! But then login and see enormous bots with massive guns just tearing them apart, or physics defying drones sniping from a distance with no hope of taking them out of the sky. For a player like myself, you adapt to the game and bots and do what you can. For a new player with no idea of what is going on, this is just brutal.
I once spent all day and all night playing this game. Now I log in and play one match and quit. Player quality, game quality, community quality have all seen a sharp decline as of late, and it just makes me sad... Review done...

Summary:
If you prefer a forgiving, flashy kind of pinball, PFX 2 might be more to your liking, but if you (like me) like your pinball a bit more realistic and / or already know Timeshock from the 90s, don't hesitate to shell out the money and get your fix!
Highly recommended!
The Long One:
I was very happy to see Pro Pinball return to the PC- I loved the series back in the day and Timeshock is the shiny crown jewel of the four PP tables. Hells, I still have the original CDs in a box somewhere :D
If you're more familiar with recent videogame pinball, prepare for a surprise. Timeshock is a pretty accurate simulation, with very accurate physics and a steep learning curve. This is a game where you can pull off tricks like dead stops, airballs, soft and hard nudges and a couple other trickery that work on an actual physical table. And you wil lneed a certain bit of finesse because Timeshock is not an easy table to beat. Some shots require carefull juggling of the silver ball, and the layout is complex enough to require a bit of adjustment.
But there's a lot waiting for you.
Like most pinball tables, the "story" is less than stellar. Some scientist tinkered with something really experimental and accidentally scattered the whole universe, which is BAD. So she jumped into her time-machine and got bcak into her past which is your present and now you must save the universe. For some reason, this involves a lot of pinball.
The Timeshock table is a highly stylized beast of a pinball. Center stage is a glowy green crystal, surrounded by figurines representing several time zones. Timeshock mines its time-travel theme for all it's worth: The goal of the game is to collect fuel and crystals in four eras, time-warp between said eras and not only rack a lot of points, but also save the universe by reaching the wizard mode and create an anti-timeshock.
The amount of modes and little surprises the game crams into one table is astonishing. There is a clear structure: Enter time zone, find fuel, power up the warp engine, lock balls into time machine, then leave the era and snatch a crystal fragment on the way... but there's so much more, from unique missions to ramp frenzies and the elusive midnight mode. Even after months wort of playing time (pre-Steam) I am sure I haven't seen everything Timeshock has in store.
The "Ultra" already signifies that this is not the original, which IS a bit dated. Ultra Timeshock looks much better than the pre-rendered table of old, with crisp dynamic lighting, beautiful reflextions and colourful flashy lights. It stays true to its roots though: This is not an over-the-top "videogame", it's a honest-to-god simulation. The table is presented without scrolling, there are no animated characters suddenly assaulting your balls, and the stylized look creates a somewhat sparse background for the silver ball. This may make you frown, but the stellar soundtrack and the hilariously hammy voice-acting will turn that frown upside down.
A fun little extra is the "glassless" mode: At any time you can remove the table glass and move the balls around with your mouse, and this is actually a valid way to get to know the table and figure out how to beat missions. It's a gimmick but it does have its use.
All in all, Timeshock is a table for pinball enthusiasts longing for a hard, honest simulation. It takes time to rack up decent scores, and mastering the whole table may well take a few weeks, but it's great glorious fun.

Hunkered in a small mud-walled compound, my squad waits with rifles pointed west. We've been getting our asses handed to us the entire game. We fall back, form new defensive positions, and eventually get routed to fall back again. We can't get help from the other squads, who are all off in the woods somewhere building tree forts or measuring rifles or whatever it is they do when they're not fighting on the objective.
Even though we're constantly retreating, I'm playing squad leader to a group full of good players. They're working together and following my directions. The Americans are marching us across the map, but we're making them pay for every inch of ground. A shout goes up. Smoke grenades are popping in the poppy fields to the west. They're coming at us again.
By the end of the game, my boys are calling me "Boss" and answering commands with "yes, sir." We lose the match badly, but my squad earns the highest unit score by a long mile. I log off, feeling ten feet tall.
Squad is fantastic. It's a game that presents itself as any other military shooter, but in playing it, it is something so much more.

Massive tips to anyone considering purchasing Boundless or has purchased Boundless:
1. Check out the Boundless forums at
- Sign up is free, you do not need to purchase the game to interact on the forums. The forums contain a lot of information on current state of the game, updates and aims/goals.
2. Pre-purchase from the Boundless website - The site contains about 10 different packages each with their own perks, there is something for everybody there.
3. Don't treat it as purchasing an Early Access game, treat it as if it were a pre-purchase - As with all early access games it is a gamble on whether or not you immediately will receive your moneys worth, I can guarantee you that you won't. Boundless has come a long way and still has a ways to go, it is definitely getting done and many features are operational however are not yet implemented into the game. What makes New Order a great entry in the Wolfenstein series is that it takes place in 1960.  Blazkowicz is in a coma following a battle in 1946 and wakes up only 14 years later in an asylum and - to his surprise - notices that WW 2 ended with German victory. He sets out to find the remaining members of the resistance (people he may know from the '40s) and to unite them against an even more dangerous villain.
This setting is great; also, the prologue telling the events of 1946 is also pretty long. This time the occultism-obsessed Reich is replaced with soldiers having a lot of armor and many mechanised units such as the Panzerhund or the Stomper which is the Wolfenstein version of the AT and T from Star Wars.
Graphics-wise the game is pretty as usual thanks to the 5th iteration of the id tech engine which debuted back in 2011 in Rage. This means relatively high system requirements and 50 gigs empty space is a must. Gameplay-wise we are back to a linear shooter where you shoot first and ask questions later. Combat is fast-paced and the option to dual-wield weapons is pretty great!
Stealth gameplay is implemented, too. Sections often have a patrolling commanding officer; you know this as the game puts their signal (i.e. distance) in the upper-right corner of the screen. Here a silent approach is recommended otherwise reinforcements will keep arriving until you deal with the commander.
Regardless of which gameplay method you prefer the game gives you perks. Using all weapons and all methods you can get these that either mean you can carry more ammunition or you have better health regeneration. Beside the story-related achievements most are connected to these. As for achievements: it wouldn't be a Wolfenstein game without secrets. You collect golden items (medallions, chalices, swords etc.), health or armor upgrades, letters and enigma codes that you can open from the main menu.
Characters Blazkowich meet are great companions. In fact, at the beginning of the game you make a decision as to who to save from two of your comrades. A 2nd playthrough is a must if you'd like to see the timeline with the other comrade; interestingly, depending on who you save you complete a different minigame for opening locks (you either hotwire panels or carry out lockpicking). You often return to the hideout between missions to converse with the others and throughout the game you can find several newspaper cuttings elaborating on the events of 1946-1960.
New Order is a great shooter with a relatively long (10+ hours) campaign, great characters and an amazing story. Machine Games did a great job by picking up a classic and giving it a new, interesting story. The many cutscenes and the great characters were the items I primarily missed from Rage; Wolfenstein, however, delivers in all areas.

A great first-person RPG that demonstrates you don't need complicated skill trees or a plethora of side quests to have fun.  This game gets the basics right and is rewarding for the player no matter what upgrade path is chosen.
When the original MM series ended with The 3DO Company, Ubisoft bought the rights to the franchise and began to reboot it.  Dark Messiah was one of the first games rolled out and while it shares the name, it does not share any lore with the games prior to Ubisoft's acquisition of the franchise.  Players take the role of Sareth, apprentice to the wizard Phenrig.  The story starts with Sareth as a young adult, sent to collect a special crystal as his final test from Phenrig.  After doing so, Phenrig sends Sareth on a journey to the city of Stonehelm to deliver the crystal to Menelag, a friend of Phenrig.  However, Phenrig does not send Sareth on this journey alone.  Before leaving, Phenrig uses his powers  to summon a companion for Sareth to travel with known as Xana.  Xana melds herself into Sareth's body and becomes his source of advice, much like Link and Navi (only sexier).  When the two finally reach Menelag, they learn he is searching for a special artifact called The Skull of Shadows.  Unfortunately, Menelag's journey to the island where the Skull is hidden has been delayed due to necromancer attacks on Stonehelm.  Sareth's arrival in Stonehelm proves advantageous though and after a few setbacks, Sareth makes it to Skull Island.  But terrible visions begin to plague him and Xana begins to speak cryptically.  To make matters worse, the leader of the necromancers is pursuing Sareth and seeks to use the Skull for his own reasons.  Can Sareth recover the skull in time before this prophecy everyone is talking about comes true?  It is entirely up to the player how this story ends.
Dark Messiah is played from a first-person viewpoint.  This has lead some to compare it to Skrim or other high-fantasy  first-person games.  While most of the game is combat and exploration, it is important to note that Dark Messiah is a linear experience.  It is closer to Half-Life 2 in terms of its level structure and closer to Chivalry in terms of its combat.  Level design is very good nonetheless and once you get the rope bow, things really get interesting.  Sareth's body is fully rendered, meaning you can look down and see your feet and what you are currently wearing.  You can also look around without reorienting Sareth's body, scale ledges if you can jump to them, climb ropes/chains, and even swim underwater.
In Dark Messiah, skill points are your upgrade means.  You gain skill points through the completion of objectives and the killing certain "boss" creatures.  Killing average enemies does not net you skill points, meaning you need to spend them wisely.  Sareth has three skill trees to dump points into: Combat, Magic, and Miscellaneous.  Combat allows you to use special attacks, aim better with bows, and use weapons with skill requirements.  Magic is all about offensive, defensive, and status effect spells.  Miscellaneous deals with stealth, health improvement, increased mana, and poison resistance.
No matter your skill point build, enemies are very hard to kill in this game, even the spiders.  Awareness is your strongest tool in combat.  Enemy standing by a ledge?  Kick him off.  Barrels just lying around.  Pick one up and throw it at an enemy.  Oil pots?  Throw one at an enemy and light him on fire. Got the freeze ability?  Shoot a patch of ice on the floor, laugh as a guard slips on it, then impale him as he writhes on the floor.  Sam Fisher?  Pick up the corspe of your back-stabbed enemy and hide it in the shadows.  Many rooms have physics booby traps and cutting ropes/kicking supports often leads to some hilarious kills.  The combat can be infuriating at times and a Mage build really does'nt work as well as you might think.  You'll have the most fun with a Melee build or Stealth build.  Every build has unique weapons and clothing to find though so pay attention for secret areas.  Also, food is health so if you're injured just eat three cured hams, two strands of raw garlic, a mashed banana, and five pies.
Each of my three playthroughs took me around 10 hours.  There multiple endings to the game and while I have not seen them all, I can say some are very similar.  I have not tried the multiplayer component of the game but its is 8 years old so I would not expect a thriving community.
A testament to the versatility of the Source Engine, Dark Messiah should not be ignored for its age.  One area the game is lacking in terms of presentation is facial animation for its human characters.  The Pre-rendered cut scenes are OK but, anything in game feels a little awkward.  But you won't be spending a lot of time staring at faces thankfully.  Exploring abandoned temples and underground catacombs is quite enjoyable thanks to great lighting, sound, and visual effects.  Sareths's spells give off light and each sound unique, wood splinters and groans, water drips deep underground, and wind blows in high up places.  Music is just right and not overbearing.  Voice acting is great for the most part with every actor playing their part well.  Weapons, shields, and armor each look very different from one another.  Every melee weapon type has its own animations.  Sareth even holds his arms and hands in different ways depending on what spell you are about to cast.  Objects have weight as you would expect from the Source Engine and as I alluded to above, ice and fire behave as you would expect them to in a high fantasy world.  Being a Source Engine game, I was able to run Dark Messiah at high settings without any problems for the most part.
One problem I encountered with the game was the frost and poison daggers.  For some reason, when I equipped these weapons, I had a massive FPS drop.  Fooling with AA seemed to resolve the issue but it would never stay solved.  Another problem I encountered was every time I quit the game, it crashed and I was forced to close the program.  This did not have any effect on the game at all but to anyone reading this I recommend saving
you quit the game rather than saving
you quit the game.
A fun first-person RPG with challenging combat, good level design, and a unique story that is not Skyrim?  Dark Messiah's your game.  Nab it on sale if the short campaign discourages.  Once you play it through, I think you'll agree that it has elements you wish would show up in games more often.  What you see is what you get, and there's nothing wrong with that at all.

You win some matches, you get some RP, you buy some parts to upgrade your bot, you play some more matches, you win some more RP, etc. Now that there is a crate system, the purpose of the game is lost. Crates are great if you happen to get a Legendary weapon or module, but not when that item is unavailabe because you don't have Premium on your account. Pay to win is a term thrown around with a lot of free to play games, and Robocraft has started leaning in that direction with this crate system. Previously, premium would help level faster which would increase the amount of parts you could have on your bot, so "pay to win" was not quite right. Now that they are relying on RNG to determine what you get from winning/losing a match, and you are limiting what players earn by 1/2 (without premium), this becomes pay to win. Pay to win more garbage parts, but pay to win none the less...
With that out of the way, we can begin to discuss the gameplay updates. Weapons will be added that would hopefully balance the game, but the devs do not balance current items before adding new ones. Removing features that have become second nature to players like myself in order to try to retain new players, has become the norm for updates. I understand that the player base for this game has dropped drastically, but randomly changing key functions of the game is only alienating your core audience and people will continue to uninstall. There was once a time where FreeJam would send out a poll and ask the players what they would like in the next update. This was fantastic. There would be list of 10-15 update ideas, and the community would vote on their favorite 3-4, which FreeJam would then impliment in the next update...
Without getting specific, I would point at the last three updates as the worst yet. Adding garbage, removing key functions, and just bowing down to the casual gamers who play 3-4 hours and then uninstall... Why do you think they are uninstalling? I would venture to guess they saw "build, drive, fight" and thought it might be fun! But then login and see enormous bots with massive guns just tearing them apart, or physics defying drones sniping from a distance with no hope of taking them out of the sky. For a player like myself, you adapt to the game and bots and do what you can. For a new player with no idea of what is going on, this is just brutal.
I once spent all day and all night playing this game. Now I log in and play one match and quit. Player quality, game quality, community quality have all seen a sharp decline as of late, and it just makes me sad... Review done...
