Developer: Mykhail Konokh
Publisher: Kiss Ltd
Steam: Fly in the House
Just one thing to note. I as a reviewer. Have never been a fan of calling something utter crap. If you watch my YouTube channel you already know this about me. I think everyone has a dream or vision. Whatever you want to call it. Who am I to say that it is utter crap. I don't know how to program a game nor go about any means of marketing it. My stand point comes completely from that of a consumer. Nonetheless though I can see where something works and something doesn't. So I will be fair but try to keep a positive attitude. You can expect me to point out problems or what I believe to be mistakes. With that in mind.
Fly in the House is what I like to call a chaos game. The basic idea is that there is a fly, wait for it, in the house. You must smash it by any and all means necessary. How? By apparently taking it out on IKEA furniture. You will fling chairs, TV's, tables, you name it. You throw it. Along with the basic gameplay there is some other game modes thrown into the mix. From using only a flashlight to find your prey. To Fast destruction mode.
Sounds fun enough right? For the most part. Sure. Given its price tag of $9.99 though I have some issues. I can accept the games simple nature. However Fly in the house is a one trick pony. After you seen the trick, you either laugh or don't. That's it. The end of show. Throwing furniture around a house at a glowing ball of fly can only be spun so many ways before the concept becomes repetitive. This is mostly due to the way the game progresses. Which is through repeating the levels over and over again. Every level has a set of goals or things that must be done to get to the next level. Some of them are easy and some of them can get slightly annoying. What this ends up becoming is repeating content. This isn't how you keep me excited about a game. The same environments no matter how loaded with little secrets becomes dull.
So why not skip the level? You can't. You have to play that level until the next one is unlocked. To be quite honest, I never even made it past the first level. There is so many silly requirements. I got tired of seeing the same level over and over. Speaking of the level. The graphics are actually not that bad.
It looks pleasant enough to the eye. Also just about everything is smash-able. Which is entertaining. The first time. Plates shatter, statues crunch, and even the roof can come in. Which the fly can escape through much to my chagrin. Everything feels like it has the weight of the object. Followed by the usual crashing noise of that object being thrown out a window or bursting into flames. As far other details go like story, soundtrack. They aren't really a prominent aspect in the game. Its all about that stupid fly.
Controlling the game is weird subject. At one point the cursor would move through objects you could pick up. Making it impossible to tell where that cursor was. This was patched out thank god and made the game a little bit more friendly to picking things up. However strange things like objects flying out of your hands cause you turn the camera too fast. Do and will occur still. I don't know if this was done on purpose or a design flaw.
Another issue with the game was the lack of options. Now I am not a graphics Nazi or anything like that. Some options would've been nice though. You got mouse sensitivity and anisotropic filtering. No rebindable keys, no resolution control. It is what it is. Then again, should I have been really expecting that much? Probably not.
To its credit. I think Fly in the House is a family friendly game. Just about anybody can pick up and play this game and get a basic idea of what to do. If all the levels were unlocked from go. I think I would've had a much more pleasant time completing all the hidden goals, exploring, and smashing all the levels Sadly this isn't the case.
Also they dropped the ball on something that could've added a really neat element to this type of game. Mutliplayer. Split screen local co-op could've added a layer of complexity and fun to the simple nature of the game. Smashing things alone is fun. Smashing things with friends? Way more fun. Adding a strange death match mode where one has to protect their fly and kill their enemies. Could add some much needed fresh ideas and change of pace. While still using everything in the game. Also give this game some replayability that isn't demanded and shoved down your throat.
I know my criticism sounds a bit harsh. I did enjoy the idea of the game. I think with a little bit more tinkering and way more content. This could've been a great game. In its current state though. It simply is lacking.
To wrap up the point in fly paper and move along. I would only recommend this game if you really, really know what your buying. Aside from reading this review. Go watch a video of someone playing it. If you think you will enjoy that first level. Replaying it for atleast a good hour. Now after all that and you're still sure you want the game. Wait for a sale. Now go ahead and buy the game. Why? Simply because there is already some amazing games in the $5 to $10 range. That probably will give you a bit more then Fly in the House does.

There's not much to this game besides walking and talking, but I quickly found myself really engrossed in the story and invested in the relationships between the characters. It starts as a bit of a mystery and unravels into paranoia and intrigue, all while testing the limits of your already somewhat tenuous friendships. There are no jump scares here, just a growing sense of foreboding eating away at your brain the longer you spend on the island. I love the dialogue mechanic, where you must decide quickly what to say -- sometimes interrupting others -- or else say nothing at all, affecting how the other characters perceive you. Great dialogue (and spot-on voice acting) keeps this game together when the walking gets too slow. Sometimes you have to travel quite far to get from one place to another, and having to backtrack because of the super low-fidelity map can make that particularly frustrating. But it's worth going slow the first time, to find all the little extra content, and to really get wrapped up in the mythos of the island our heroes are exploring.
It was cool to see how the game starts to affects subsequent playthroughs, as well. I could see myself playing multiple more times and discovering different endings, although having to endure some of those long walks again means I will definitely want to wait some time before having another go.

If you're looking to go to war and get PTSD but not get sand in your♥♥♥♥♥♥this is the game for you.
Squad is as immersive as it is tactical and it requires you to think as well as you can shoot. You will die a lot. You will experience the true chaos of battle, reliving all those Hollywood scenes of shellshock. The maps are huge, like an actual combat area and you don't just 'spawn'. You have  one main spawn and you're trying to take objectives on the map for tickets like in other FPS conquest modes. If you want a spawn closer your squad leader has to put down a rally point or one of the squads has to lay down Forward Operating Bases. The way the maps are laid out this makes tactical placement in relation to the objective paramount. You can literally put them anywhere on the map as long as there's not enemies within 50m. Gotta get it close, but not too close because if the enemy finds a fob and digs it up you lose tickets. Oh, also there is a base building system that will have you attacking and defending heavily barracaded murder fortresses.
You absolutely have to join a squad in each match. Just like in combat when you start taking shots you're not gonna know where from, you're going to rely on your squadmates giving you headings and the leaders marking the map. Running around as a lone wolf in Squad will only get you killed, you won't have an objective without a squad leader, you'll pizza when you're supposed to french fry and you're gonna have a bad time.
But that's also the best part! The community is absolutely fantastic, totally welcoming to newbies, and I'd bet the cost of the game that no matter what server or squad you hop into they will show you the ropes if you just say your new. Half of them are vets in real life which makes it that much more immersive when you get into "the♥♥♥♥♥♥"
But bear in mind this is a game for those hardcore or realism enthusiasts. It's like if Red Orchestra/ROII, ARMA, and hardcore battlefield had a baby,  then at the same time minecraft, Americas Army and Insurgency had a baby, and by some miracle those two babies met and got it on. That's this game, man.
The fob and squad system make it to where unlike other FPS's you will never fight the same battle on the same map twice.
And it just gets better with every update.
One more thing: a mic is absolutely necessary, everyone actually uses them and will expect you to!

First and foremost with Oxenfree, you have to jive with the controls. It's simple WSAD/arrow-key movement, but exploration is mostly constrained to very thin paths. So long as this doesn't grate against your nerves, you'll probably enjoy what the game has to offer. There are no key rebinding options in-game, I haven't checked whether you can alter them via an .ini file (as you could with Ori & the Blind Forest). Fortunately, some controls are redundant. The SHIFT key and right mouse button both switch on your radio. Left-clicking and scrolling the mouse wheel both manipulate what frequency your radio is set to. Clicking the middle-mouse button and the left CTRL both bring up a map.
The primary fulcrum of this game is dialogue. Your character (Alex) will be given three responses to choose from, which are available only for limited time, meaning you have to think fast about how you wish to contribute to a conversation. A forth option is to make no choice, where which Alex will remain silent. There are times where saying nothing is a better choice than running your mouth. In some cases, your dialogue choice will wait until another character has finished their lines before Alex begins responding. In other cases, she'll interject. This dynamic may put some people off, who like orderly, turn-based dialogue, but I found the whole setup very natural. The voice acting is very well done.
The secondary fulcrum of the game is your radio. There is a TON of sound floating around the airwaves in Oxenfree, including actual broadcasts from US history, even what sounded like Mel Blanc doing Bugs Bunny. Some transmissions are in-game informative (take notes if your memory isn't up to snuff), other broadcasts are sinister, and others still... well, you can see for yourself.
The story is engrossing. Think Twin Peaks, or Stranger Things. The characters feel natural, and the way you're able to interact with them equally so.
It only took around 8 HRS to complete one play-through, and some of that was idle time, so adjusting for that, I'd say more like 6.5 - 7 hrs. However, having beaten Oxenfree, I find my thoughts lingering on the journey, the ramifications of my choices, the story that preceeds the game, and follows after it concludes. The art design fits perfectly with the narrative, like an old cartoon (before they were all mind-numbing, or CG).
6.5-7 hrs is a bit on the short side, but considering what kind of game this is, it avoids feeling padded. If Oxenfree resonates with you, you're going to be going back for another romp.

Well,
looks all stylish like recent indie games do - but somehow it doesn't work.
Even for a mystery game the story lacks plausability, not in a scientificly-it-makes-all-sense-way but narratively. It's simply not well told. Normal teenagers, who went through a tragedy (or even any person who gets teleported by using a radio on an creep island) wouldn't react like the people in this game. This kills a lot credibility from the beginning. Why should I care about the the protagonists feelings (which deal with death in the family, a seriouse matter) if that protagonist acts totally generic and cliché on mindblowing, supernatural events?
Also the pace doesn't fit the theme the story is trying to tell. It starts promising but stumbles into the mystery part too fast and clumsy leaving the player with a big question mark on the back story which is needed to care.
You lose interest in a possible good story too fast. You feel there might be a nice ending to this but you also quickly start not to care that much to climb all the unnecessary rocks and ledges on the way.
This also has a lot to do with the point-and-click-feel but instead WASD-mouse interaction of the game. 30% of the time is stretched due to unnecessary complicated controls and obstacles. It is not a good (and never was a good) gameplay element to swirl the mouse around to get something triggered - it's just annoying and trivial.
The short time frame for reacting to conversations isn't helping either. And why does interaction stop the dialog? The game is about conversation. It transports a big chunk of the story in it.
Looks like the time developing this went into admittedly good looking graphics but not into finding out what to do with it. It tries too hard to be a fresh, cool, different approach. In the end Oxenfree is nothing new, nothing special and not worth 20€ and the time to spend in it's annoying loops. It's not even bad or good, it's just petty.

If I have one main complaint about this game, it is about its inconsistent tone. The gameplay is balls-to-the-walls action, with an on-screen avatar capable of carrying a dozen guns, shooting an almost-endless wall of bullets and missiles, and made invulnerable by nigh-magical health-kits and armor-pickups. The bad-guys are all unredeemably evil, a mix of robot and Nazis; the setting is cheesy and fantastic, ranging from Nazi moon-bases to ancient Atlantean strongholds. There are bombastic explosions and heads bursting in almost-comic showers of blood. And then there are the cut-scenes, where the hero contemplates in a quiet voice all the things he has lost in the war, his dashed hopes, the horrors of the seemingly unending conflict, his desire for nothing more than to be held in the arms of the woman he loves.
Wait, what?
It even has slow sex scenes (note: this is not a game for the kids, although the "exploding heads" thing probably should have given that away). The mood of story is so contrary to the tone of the actual gameplay it is almost risible in comparison, and this opposition detracts from both. On the one hand, the game presents you with all the tools to indulge in a male-power fantasy, indulging in gore and violence and saving the world from the Forces of Evil (tm). On the other hand, it then chastises you for enjoying it. I mean, the game puts you in a Nazi death-camp; how can anyone have fun with a reminder of man's cruelty hanging over their head?
Beyond that, the game is fairly forgettable. The gameplay is passable but unexceptional for the genre; the levels are fairly linear and scripted, and the challenge is minimized by the small number of enemies on the screen at once. I also wished that the ammo pool had been larger for all the weapons since it seemed my guns all ran dry after only three or four seconds of firing. A few puzzle sequences helped keep things fresh, although these were fairly simplistic and too many of these revolved around finding optional collectibles. There was a stealth feature, but its use was fortunately optional as well.
Not a bad game, but one better enjoyed if I just skipped the cut-scenes.

There's so much to say, but I'll try to keep it short:
- You will be angry how you emptied that mag into someone but he killed you with 2 hits;
- You will be angry how confusing everything is for the first 20 hours;
- You will be angry how there's always bullets (or lazors) flying into you from random directions;
And you will be angry, frustrated, confused about a lot of things,
BUT
Once you get past all that, it's an amazing game. Almost everyone can find their "thing" - some want to be medics, some want to be pilots, tank drivers, spawn point supports, flanking light assaults etc. There's so much freedom (which can also be a bit confusing at first - not knowing what you're supposed to do). I'm sorry, but I have to compare it to Dark Souls - you start out as a confused player with a bunch of good equipment, you start out constantly dying to everything, but slowly you figure out how the game works and you actually feel your skills progressing. It's the same with Planetside.
I definitely recommend you give it a try - and don't give up on the few hours of frustration. You will learn positioning and enemy movement and it will get easier. Also, joining an outfit (the equivalent of a guild in PS2) is almost required. The high-level players are almost always helpful on answering newbie questions.
Few more points:
- No, the high-level decked-out enemies aren't much stronger than you. Beginner gear is very good, the other guns you can buy are not upgrades - they're meant for different playstyles, but the beginners are good all-rounders.
- Getting cert points is very slow at first, don't be fooled by the first 15 levels where you get 100 for every level-up. Levels 15-40 will be a painful cert grind, but don't let that discourage you. For me I usually do better if I forget about grinding certs and just play for fun.
- Almost noone is a hacker, they're just really good.
- Game is not Pay 2 Win, money can just speed up your progress towards new guns or upgrades (don't) or get you some really cool cosmetic items (do if you can afford it, please support the company for this amazing game).
- You will probably play it off and on again, which is completely fine, most of us do. It's a game you almost always return back to.
- It's pretty heavy. Find graphical and performance tweaking guides online.
TL;DR - try it for a few hours, you won't regret it.

If you're looking for a game to scratch your Mario Kart itch on the PC, and want a game in that vein that isn't completely dependent on luck and rubber-banding, Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing Transformed is it.
The PC port of this game is very technically proficient (I can run it at 2560x1440 at 60 FPS with my 560Ti), has 360 pad support, and has good netcode so that no random teleporting or other lag-related nonsense ever happens when you play online. Which is accomplished by *forcing* clients to always have their state properly sync'd, and would rather have players lose control of their kart for a split-second as their game tries to sync in the event of a network de-sync. The result is that when something happens in the game, it happens. No nonsense. And from my personal experience, this very, very rarely ever happens - and I think it's a good trade-off.
The reason I'm giving so much emphasis on the netcode is because I think Transformed is inherently a game that is meant to be played with others, and a sane, consistent online experience is paramount to that.
And I have to say that despite growing-up with Kart racers (namely, Mario Kart on the SNES, N64, and GameCube), Transformed is easily my favourite Kart racer of all time, due to the good online experience, and its focus on skilled driving and item-use. No connection and luck-based nonsense here.

A textbook example of how one man's ineptitude and greed can kill an otherwise highly successful title.
TL;DR Avoid this game if you haven't played it for 4+ years.
Freejam's CEO, Mark, took their almost-universally well-liked and flourishing game that routinely sat in the top-5 of steam player stats into a hot mess of terrible design choices,
It started with megabots. Mega-weapons and movement systems; hugely powerful items that could only fit on the most elite of players bots. The cost to power ratio made them balanced in the tiers you fought them in. Then megabots took the stage. A single player with a greatly expanded part allotment with an entire team to back them up. It was high times for Robocraft. The game routinely hit #4-5 in the concurrent players list. Balance and variety in the parts were coming along smoothly, exploits like Mega Heavy Machine Gun were getting patched quickly..
And then Mark lost a match against a better designed megabot. (Atleast, how it's gone down into legend) The next day the entire game mode was scrapped. Then, because Mark's new bot got killed by a player in a hover SMG T10 triforced boat repeatedly, he decided it was time to eliminate the tier system so all players would be able to fight any other player at any time. (Moreso he just wanted to stop playing against the same 20 veterans who sat in T10 queue instead of T9.)
They were hemmoraging players, the aspects that protected players from getting into highly one-sided matches was gone. (It still could happen with seal clubbers, but wasn't as common as people made it out to be.) The mode most people enjoyed the most was scrapped, and their bots rendered useless due to changes in part scaling, and 'streamlining'. So Freejam did the only reasonable thing anyone could do.
They removed the tech tree, the in game currency, redesigned the flow of the game, and made it so new parts could only be aquired through their new Gatcha boxes (Which conveniently is now the only thing on which to spend real money on), which have a 99% chance of giving you either 50 basic cubes you can't do anything with, or a 1% chance to get a shiny legendary weapon which will always be locked behind a paywall.
Fast forward to today. Now, major exploits can take weeks to get patched, if they even bother; part balance has gone out the window; (If you don't have a shotgun, don't bother queuing.) and games went from 12 v 12 elimination, to 8 v 8 tower strife, to the exciting 5 v 5 caputre and hold on poorly designed maps.
Freejam finally has taken notice of their players. (Rather the lack of money they were shoveling into their faces.) Robocraft no longer even lists in the top 100 games of steam in the PM hours. So, to try to figure out why people aren't shoveling money at them, they've taken to performing unannounced and unfair control-group studies. They gave 50% of new accounts a permanent (It was meant to be a 7-game) buff that doubled all of their stats, HP, ATK, DEF... This was done to test "Does winning a game make you want to play that game?" Or more easily "Do people like fun?"
Well, the answer is yes. But when you neglect to tell your playerbase, and your staff what you are doing, you have two weeks of people sending in thousands of hacker reports for these new accounts popping up out of nowhere who are seemingly invulnerable, and no one being able to give an answer as to why. What few players they did have left over the years, and they've managed to pick up along the way were disgusted. Another mass exodus occured. Now, Robocraft rarely sees more than 5000 players online, compared to the half-million it had four years ago.
Finally, Mark came clean. He explained what he did, and how it was a monumentally bad idea (in hindsight only) and decided they'd be more open about their testing. So, again, to find out why people aren't shoveling money at them, they did a new test. 25% of new accounts were unaffected. 25% got 30 brand new starter bots to experiment with. (Which amounted to enough money to recycle and buy a mega-weapon with, since there's only one good starter.) 25% got 7 days premium, and the last quarter got premium and the bots.
Turns out people don't pay for premium when they already have premium, and then promptly quit as soon as the time ran out because they aren't invested enough to keep playing. Shocker. Also, people like building their own bots, instead of playing with some hastily constructed crapshoot that dies in one plasma volley.
Summing everything up though, Robocraft used to be a great game. It was the picture of how someone should design a game, it was going great, and then Mark up and kicked over the Jenga tower because he wasn't making enough money from his already pay-to-skip-progression game.
Update: Nov. 2017
Hacking's gotten worse, servers are more unstable, cosmetic items were removed from the crafting system so you have to hope you get them out of the already problematic loot crates, and game balance is even more out the window than it was then.
On the up side, you can now build a bot with so much HP it takes three people over 20 seconds to kill you while you laugh at them and strip all their guns with t1 lasers. I guess that's a good thing.

When making a robot, you have to choose between firepower, and size.  For example, a big robot can't fire guns as long as a small one, and they sacrifice movement speed as well.  Using powerful guns will cause you to deal more damage, but they can only be fired in short bursts unlike small guns.  Because the balancing mechanics are so diverse, there is a very high skillcap.  Past updates tended to give and take what you have in terms of content, but the game seams to be nearing completion.

Portal 2 takes the Portal 1 formula we all know and love and does it again, only better and with more content! The gameplay is a refined version of the first game, only now you can see an outline of were you placed your portal(s) through walls, and you can zoom in the camera, allowing more precise aiming. The voice cast is also fantastic, in every sense of the word. Ellen McLain returns as 'GLaDOS' (and portrays another new character added in the lore, which I will not spoil). Stephen Merchant Voices the all new character 'Wheatly' (A ""loyal"" robotic ""friend""), and I don't know who donsent like J.K. Simmons (voice of Cave Johnson, The founder of 'Apperture Science'). Oh and there's also Joe Micheals (yeah, I don't know who that is either...) who voices the announcer. Also the soundtracks is just as good, if not better than the first games. The last thing I want to mention is that Portal 2 is about 3-5 hours long (depending on your skill), This is excellent, as my only compliant about the first game was it's short length. As well as that, I find that Portal 2 is significant more challenging than the first installment (A good, fair sort of challenge). Overall, Portal 2 is simply incredible.
9.6/10: I cannot stress enough how good Portal 2 is. Do yourself a favor, and buy it (especially when it's on sale)
Extra point: I fell as if this is a good time to mention the portal bundle, which comes with the first and second game, for £1.49 (on sale), you really can't go wrong. I'd even consider buying it off-sale for a full £14.99. You might want to wait for it to go cheap, though.

I've lost count of the number of hours that I've spent on the original 1997 classic. Even to this day it's considered by many to be the best pinball game ever made. The ball physics are spot on and it's the only pinball game that I've played which actually feels like a real table. All the others just feel like computer games next to this.
This Ultra HD remake plays identically to the original game but with much improved visuals. The pre-rendered graphics and lighting effects are virtually photo realistic and look better than the 3D graphics in other pinball games. The graphics scale well too and it runs super smooth on my seven year old PC which has a first generation Core i5 processor, 4GB of RAM and a HD5850 graphics card (a tip for people using low powered computers is switch the vsinc option off as this has a big hit on the frame rate).
£10 for one table may not sound like good value but this table is such a gem it's worth every penny. There's more depth and replay value in this one table than there is in all of the Pinball FX and Pinball Arcade tables put together.
The only minus point that I can think of is when I rotate my monitor by 90 degrees to play the game in portrait mode the screen has black borders at the top and bottom. Hopefully a future patch will sort this out so that I can play in full screen when the monitor is oriented vertically. Other than this minor issue there are no bugs in the game.

is an independent First Person Shooter style Action Simulator by developer EmkeyGame (Mykhail Konokh), who was responsible for 2014's
. Unlike that physics-based puzzler, this new outing finds you doing what we all find to be one of the most frustrating events in our lives: Killing a fly that somehow got inside. It's a small game that has been picked up by KISS Ltd. for digital distribution in March of this year. But is this follow-up outing worth the price, or is it far more infuriating than the real thing happens to be?
First of all, yes, there is a bit of a story to
. You just came back from travelling abroad to an empty home. As you reminisce and realize how long its been since you have seen any sort of family, you are interrupted by the obnoxious buzzing of a fly that somehow followed you indoors. What else is there to do but kill it and wreck the apartment in the process? This story is essentially fleshed out across the three stages, the later two being in an office and a castle. Along with your interrupted thoughts, you are given a decent
-esque score that helps amp up your adrenaline a bit in order to keep you destroying or on the hunt for the winged ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spawn of Satan that continues to elude the projectiles that are your personal belongings and décor.
There are three different locations to explore and destroy throughout the course of
. The last two, however, are locked from the start. In order to access these new stages, you need to complete a number of objectives during the level prior. Many of these are just hitting a specific score or killing a certain number of flies. Other than that, there are some mystery objectives you need to earn. One such mission is to unlock the "Rockstar" goal by throwing your television out the window in the first stage, as well as finding hidden objects in each level. The latter of these are a lot easier to find while in Free Play mode thanks to the lack of a timer and fly to distract you.
And, really, the latter two objectives is where the game actually excels over its core concept. Taking your time to go on a scavenger hunt or just do random things in the restrictive sandbox stages does encourage you to explore the levels more than just race from one destructive object to the next in order to kill the fly that never sits the hell down long enough for you to try to kill it within the allotted length of time. In a way, it's soothing and adds a casual element to something that would better suit the more hardcore First Person Shooter gamers that might be interested in this title. Of course, just running around destroying everything to rack up points is always a plus, but those two types of game play are met by a few very detrimental flaws.
One of the most frustrating elements of
is the lack of consideration to physics other than what you can pick up. Given the developer's previous game, this is the most shocking downfall of the game. A pillow from a couch can cause as much damage as throwing a bottle, lamp, stereo speaker, chair, table, or even a television to name some of the lighter heavyweight objects you're able to toss around gleefully. While it aids in trying to kill the fly and earn as many points as possible, it'd be nice to have a little variety in damage ratios, even in a common sense way, between certain objects, thus allowing another layer to the game and possibly increase playability.
This isn't to say that all logic and science is flawed. Thankfully there is an obvious restriction on what you can pick up on throw. While everything seems to do about the same amount of damage, you're not going to be able to pick up obviously overweight items like a refrigerator or couch, let alone use them as flying weapons of mass destruction. At best, you will need to desatroy these things and hope that you can still use the debris, which, in most cases, you are.
The other problems are not so scientific, as they are a break in the system. On many occasions I found that, after doing enough damage, the game would not pick anything up, even if it wasn't touched or broken in the first place. This is probably some break in the code somewhere, but it does leave you either restarting the level, or sitting there waiting for the stage to end so all you've done is counted towards the objectives. The other gripes are merely cosmetic decisions that don't quite work out. If you move your mouse fast enough, any object you're holding will automatically be thrown in the direction you made the camera turn to, not to mention the key to throw said object is set to "f", which would have been better suited to the "E" key, or even the right mouse button that seems to serve no purpose. There's also no auto-lock, so those accustomed to
-style targeting will definitely be let down a bit. Yes, it would destroy the point of the game, but considering there is an option to highlight said fly, it'd be nice to have a choice of difficulty that might impose some restrictions as far as how to progress further for the sake of automatically locking onto a target, and removing those options at a harder difficulty for those striving for realism.
There isn't anything much else to say about this game, really. One moment you're hunting a fly, the next you're tearing the roof down for a ball or destroying the walls to get to the plunger that somehow found its way into the pipes. It's an interesting game that, pending skill and amount of time you sink into it, can keep the player invested for a decent amount of time, but not quite worth the full ten dollars (US) that is being asked for it on Steam. If you see this go on sale for a decent price, even half off, and enjoy silly games like the
or
crossed with the visual aesthetics of
, then
is something worth checking out.

The full review
This is a decent game but very short. You can and likely will finish a single play through in 4 hours or less if you play in one sitting. It's story driven with your choices being taken with dialog options (speech bubbles that you can pick from) that effect the final out come with the ending credits and minor story aspects.
The first 30 minutes of this game... Wow, nothing less then amazing! It actually gave me goosebumps and really got me on the edge of my seat, being highly invested in what happens next with Clarissa. Is she, isn't she? What's going on?

Unfortunately the game starts to go down hill after this peek. The game holds your hand an aweful lot and choices start to feel forced onto you rather then you picking how you want things to go. Your told often by your traveling companion to go to point B from point A for example and shown a basic map. However the map can't be recalled so you wonder around trying to find where you need to go. Extremely frustrating if you spend a little time away from the game and forget where your meant to be going and what your meant to be doing.
As the game goes on you get the feeling you don't really matter and any choice you pick from the speech bubbles has little to no effect on what's going on making it feel flat and stale as your choices no longer seem important. I got the impression that the story was forced and pushing you down one path with a set party member. I remember being given a choice of who to travel with only for that choice to be rejected and being forced to go with Jonus even know my character said to the other potential party members that I did not want to go with him and if I spent more time with him I would scratch his eyes out. Yet I'm still paired with him anyway and the story goes on.
The frequency scanner is the only real puzzle you'll have to deal with and you'll need to make sure you take your time scanning or you'll miss the frequency you need and have to scan the whole frequency band again. When you upgrade the scanner this only added to the feeling of disapointment as your upgrade feels more like a downgrade due to even more bandwith to scan through. Even with these problems this is a fun game to play. The ambient sound is excellent and the voice acting top notch, both rasing the games over all quality and enjoyment factor. The game is smooth and solid with not a single crash.
Bought at 75% off for £3.74 I feel I got a fair amount of enjoyment from the game. I would of been disappointed if I had paid the full asking price. If you like story driven games then you should definitely pick this game up while it's on sale.

Dark Messiah of Might & Magic is a first-person hack 'n slash game based on the Source engine and placed in the world of Ashan - the same one where Heroes of Might & Magic V takes place. This game is basically what would happen if you mixed Half-Life with Elder Scrolls - an on-rails first-person fantasy adventure.
The game is a little bit old, but the graphics aren't very weary. I would say that even today they look very good, with details put both into enemies and weapons alike. The location design is also great - most of the time you'll spend in dark, moody catacombs and dungeons of sort, which can strike a bit of fear into your heart considering you don't really know what lies further ahead.
The plot is good enough to be interesting, but somewhat predictable, actually. The dialogues is what makes it stand out - the voice acting is good, and Xana has to be one of the most interesting Mission Control-type characters in video games. Mostly thanks to her sarcastic remarks for most of the game.
Gameplay-wise, it focuses almost entirely on exploration and combat. There is a lot of options you are given for fights - whether you want to kick your enemies into pits, spikes, sneak in and backstab them, sling magic spells, or just get out your sword and hack them to bits, it's all up to you. There is also a skill point system where you can buy new abilities - you'll get enough to buy most of the more useful skills, so it's all up to you whether you want to be a standard fighter, archer, mage, stealthy assassin, or a hybrid of any (getting a healing spell early on makes the game a lot easier).
The game also has a multiplayer mode with a few different gamemodes - most of which are focused on team battles with five classes: Warrior, Archer, Assassin, Priestess and Mage.
Unfortunately, since the game is old and based on Source engine, you can expect it to have hiccups here and there. I got framerate problems once and the game crashed a few times during combat, but nothing too painful.
Overall, this game is a very good first-person hack 'n slash. I recommend it to anyone who liked games like Might & Magic or even Half-Life, if they don't have anything against swapping out guns for swords.

If you're looking for a game to scratch your Mario Kart itch on the PC, and want a game in that vein that isn't completely dependent on luck and rubber-banding, Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing Transformed is it.
The PC port of this game is very technically proficient (I can run it at 2560x1440 at 60 FPS with my 560Ti), has 360 pad support, and has good netcode so that no random teleporting or other lag-related nonsense ever happens when you play online. Which is accomplished by *forcing* clients to always have their state properly sync'd, and would rather have players lose control of their kart for a split-second as their game tries to sync in the event of a network de-sync. The result is that when something happens in the game, it happens. No nonsense. And from my personal experience, this very, very rarely ever happens - and I think it's a good trade-off.
The reason I'm giving so much emphasis on the netcode is because I think Transformed is inherently a game that is meant to be played with others, and a sane, consistent online experience is paramount to that.
And I have to say that despite growing-up with Kart racers (namely, Mario Kart on the SNES, N64, and GameCube), Transformed is easily my favourite Kart racer of all time, due to the good online experience, and its focus on skilled driving and item-use. No connection and luck-based nonsense here.

Summary:
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a well-deserved modern addition to the original Wolfenstein game series. The game is entirely a singleplayer campaign, and is based around a timeline where Nazis create very powerful weapons, stalling the end of the second World War. You play as BJ Blazkowicz, an American soldier. The gameplay is first-person, and revolves around both shooter and stealth mechanics.
Pros:
Amazing story, very captivating and thought provoking
Dual-wielding of rifles and other weapons, a very interesting concept I think was done well
Incredible art and visuals

Its been almost a year since i wrote this review so im updating it, partially because so much has changed and partially because there is a forums badge i can earn :D My original review was posted 6/6/2016, it is 3/28/2017 as of this edit.
To start:
The game has come a long way over the last year. They converted it from java to c++, it has undergone two or three texture reworks, sound rework, creature reworks, ui reworks, performance changes, resource distribution reworks, and so on.
They added inverted slopes and the cave systems are a lot more interesting and explorable. There is no longer two creatures with two models. There are Four creatures types, some with a few differeing models some with differing skins depending on tier/type.
When I started there were like 40 planets you could travel to at will. Now there are 12 planets that seem to exist within the same universe. Traveling between them may require you to pick a point on a planet in the sky then build a warp to it, or finding a portal that has been created by players.
Originally there were no portals. Just menu > select planet > done. Now, players can build warps (single transfer) or portals (duration based planetary access points) and maintain them as working junctions. You can see what is happening on the other planet through the portal in real time.
When i started you could only craft (from what i remember) crafting tables and maybe the work bench. Now we have several machines which are used to produce different types of blocks/tools.
In the near future, we will see the first implementation of an official 'Race' as well as a long awaited skill tree.
There arent really any quests as there are no npcs but there are 'objectives' that you can complete such as kill x amount of x creature, or build x machine.
You start the game with a beacon, a block that gives you a protected ownership of a plot of blocks. As you mine, build, craft etc. you gain xp, and each level awards you an amount of coin and plots to add to your beacon. Coin can be spent traveling from world to world through your own warps, or used to trade with players. Oh that reminds me, trading wasnt in game for the longest time. There is also a friend system, and you can warp to your friends locations to meet up with them if you're in different locations by selecting their location from the warp ui.
There is still quite a bit of balancing to be done and content to be created, but considering the small group of developers working on it the pacing is pretty good. They are devoted people who keep the community informed with weekly developer updates and every week or two some content is added or stuff fixed/tweaked.
There is also a considerable community.
Im not too familiar with other block based crafting games, but from what i gathered from the few minecraft clips ive seen here or there, they exist on a flat plane that has borders that lead into nothing. In Boundless the worlds are wrapped so that they are basically a round planet and you can run around the planets in any direction fully.
There is soon to be a guild system. And in the near future, large settlements with the most activity will earn the title of capital and get special markers for others to see when theyre viewing planets orbiting around them.
While the progression hits a stopping point once you hit the end of the crafting roadway (i.e. all machines and such) it boils down to your creatitivity and imagination. Building stuff is pretty much the main focus at this point.
I do recommend the game, if you like early access and watching a game grow, Or if you like to build build build (as i do).
If youre an impatient player, you may hold off on this one for another 6 months then check back to see what progress has been made.

Just finished all endings (TP only, no DLC).
One more time - it would be better to have some scale, like 1-5 stars or something to really evaluate. 0/1 is not really fair... I'd give 4 out of 5 stars. Or 2 out of 3. Why?
My attitude towards the game was changing, I would not be able to finish it in one shot (playing only this game until I finish). Initially I was very enthusiastic, liked the idea, style of the puzzles, and also - criticized by some - philosophical threads dealing with mysticism, religion, AI, meaning of life etc. Then after some time I felt a bit tired of doing similar puzzles and just needed some time away. But then come back was again very entertaining, until I was tired... and so on. I finished the game in such sinusoid-like cycles. Why was like that?
One of the reasons is annoying lack of 'save anywhere' option. I did not like that I had to repeat large part of some more complex puzzle because I 'died' and was forced to redo the puzzle from start. After some second/third "not again!" I was leaving the game as I do not like silly repeating. It should be possible to preserve any progress done.
Fortunately most puzzles are free from this issue and only few are fillled with killing machines in this annoying way.
Puzzles are entertaining and well balanced, in rare cases the difficulty is raised just by hiding something a bit too much - second reason for taking a break...
Relation between the puzzles and storyline is limited, but unlike others - I do not see it as a problem. I just enjoyed both.
The storyline built from pieces of text heard or available in computer systems is a mixture of philosophy, science and religion from ancients to some futurisms. Of course all could be heard here and there, but still I find it a lot deeper than what's found in most games and makes to think a bit about things detached from our materialistic bullsh-t world. It nicely diverts from just solving puzzles.
The good:
- the artwork - music and graphics are very pleasant and well corresponds to "storyline"
- generally good puzzles - with few minor annoyances
The bad:
- lack of "save anywhere" - death results in resetting the puzzle (annoying in few cases)
PS. I saw that there are some codes for god mode etc. Do not use it with this game! (it is not an unbeatable FPS...) Just have some patience and think. Or take a break... ;-)

There is just no other game like Planetside 2...
Basically it's a MMO FPS, a game where thousands of players fight each others to capture bases in battles involving infantry, vehicles and aircrafts. You can do so many things in this game... You want to massacre dozens of poor infantery ? Grab a tank and ask for a teammate to be your gunner. You want to get rid of these nasty tanks ? Spawn as an engineer and drop tank mines or spawn as an heavy assault or a MAX and equip some anti-vehicular weapons. You can be a medic healing/revivng soldiers, an engineer repairing stuff and supplying mates with ammo. You can be an infiltrator using cloak to stab ennemies behind front lines or using a sniper rifle and go for fun headshots. So much potential fun, from dropping claymores to jumping on roof tops with light infantery's jetpack, dogfighting with your aircraft...
So why isn't everybody playing this game ? Here are some cons :
- The population is not what it used to be
Quite normal for a 5 years old game. At the beginning there were fights quite everywhere on the map (and the map is huge and splitted accross multiple continents). The typical mistake for a new player is to spawn randomly and wander on the map. All the players are gathered on a couple of battle spots (it has to do with game mechanics and how the bases are linked to each other), the good approach is to use the "Join Combat" feature on the map and the game will teleport you to a place where people are actually fighting.
- The graphics are outdated
Again it is a 5 years old game. Personally I always drop the Gfx Quality on shooters to boost my FPS. That doesn't bother me and the game still looks great but that can be a huge drawback to some.
- The cert points are too hard to get
That one is a really hard one. Cert points are used to unlock weapons, weapons accessories and class boost. You earn them by killing people or helping people (heal, revive, supply, repair...) and they are not that easy to earn. For example : 1 kill is 100XP and 1 cert comes with each 250XP, given that most weapons cost 1000 certs... you see the problem.
But you can make things easier : you have 100 cert per level for the first 15 levels, you have 5 dailies a day (ribbons) each giving you 1 cert. You can farm XP with medic or engineer (heal/repair gives XP) or you can kill lots of people if you are skilled with tanks. Without a premium access, you can expect to farm 100 cert/hour with not too much issues if you focus on maxing your XP gain.
- It is scaring to unlock the wrong stuff
There is a training area where you can try anything without unlocking it. There are many vids on YT with advices about what you should unlock first.
I played many FPS but I always get bored at some point, I'm not into performance, I don't play for the best rank or the best K/D ratio, I like PvP, tactics, finding the weak spot, the breach in the opposing force ... Planetside 2 is the only game offering this kind of fun.

I recently purchased the lifetime premium for this game.  Normally I don't enjoy "Pay to Win" games, but it seems with a 1-2 weeks of grinding you can build a bot that is highly competitive, I just didn't want to do the grind and I enjoyed the game enough to give the developers some money.
The game is not without its frustrations... placing shields and weapons can be difficult while crafting the shape of robot you want.  I feel like shielding should be a shell over individual blocks, but with a cost, as opposed to unwieldy plates.  Some weapons are overpowered, and some weapons are underpowered... standard balance stuff.
Another flaw in my opinion is how the game deals with flying craft.  I have found it very difficult to create a flyer using standard ideas... instead good flyers have an odd configuration of hover parts and opposite pointed jets to compensate for the games lack of yaw control.  The lack of yaw control is pretty horrible.
The true enjoyment from the game comes from seeing your Robot's design impact the battle in equal amounts to your gaming skill, and tweaking your design for better performance.  The build system is very easy.
Overall I am excited to see where the developers take this game, but if it remains unimproved in a year regarding the things I listed, I might change my review.

What happens when you crashland 3 people on a strange and alien world with naught more than some basic resources and leave them to fend against the local flora and fauna as well as a myriad of trials and tribulations? Well then you get a game called Rimworld.
Start from scratch and build a home on a world that's out for your blood. Repel tribal raids, repair broken cooking stoves, experience the drawbacks of solarflare and stock up because
. A game of Rimworld is never the same and will test your nerves as its storyteller don't have the world easy in their vocabulary. Much like any sandbox these days you can modify the game to a high degree and the workshop makes for even more possibilities with extra furniture (if you like building sprawling bases), more fauna (if you fancy yourself an agricultural person), more weapons or even more storytellers. Your destination is space, your goal is survival, your biggest hurdle being random events. For a game listing itself as Pre-Alpha this game is currently good enough to keep you occupied for far more hours than you would like..... If you like sandbox games that provide a true challenge then you should've bought Rimworld yesterday.
Pro's
* Pre alpha but this game puts others in this category to shame with being VERY complete and VERY playable
* Hardly, if any, bug are present and bugs you encounter are usually as a result of community created mods but NOT because of the core game
* Extreme freedom and no pressure; you decide how (fast) to play this game
* Low end graphics which ensure you don't need a monster-rig to enjoy this game
* Active and friendly community

Let's rock and roll!
Well, where else can you find a good cartoonish racing game that's as fun as this? Game's been optimized for real, even my low end machine can play smoothly without lag - except internet problem during multiplayer - on medium-high settings. Graphic settings in-game allow you to fine tune the game to suit your preferences and rig. There's a major netcode weakness though- if you RTO twice in a row, bye bye multiplayer session and you'll earn a loss. Pretty weird since many multiplayer games have tendency to tolerate lags/delays (even in Dota 2 you can reconnect easily if you DC). Use of good and stable connection and playing with host in the same region are recommended. Moreover, this game implements peer to peer, so can't expect much stability when playing as it depends also on the host player. A shining MP game when it works.
Now the gameplay, with many track selections in place, you won't get bored. From air battle to water fight, you name it all. The learning curve is incredibly steep as the differences among tracks are too great, you won't even be able compete effectively without any knowledge at all. Basically, it's a matter of skills, understanding of environment, and luck when it comes to rolling the weapons. Keep on repeating the same tracks until you understand what's the best choice to race in it. And of course you'd need to train the character you choose to play with. Each character comes with different allstars weapons, and different traits in race. Handling Sonic who is an all around racer, as opposed to AiAi's excelling when turning/braking would be a massively different style.
Being a racing game, playing with controller is highly recommended. Can't recommend DInput as the button mappings are all wrong, but XInput or using XInput wrapper should be more than enough. F310 and Rumblepad 2 (with x360ce wrapper) work amicably with this game - XBOX360 is not even questionable. If you play with keyboard, drifting and jumping at the same time will prove to be quite problematic for the fingers. I'm not even sure how to perform both without being awkward.
Single player experience has tons of stuffs to be done and unlocked. There's a world map split into smaller zones. Each zones has its own stage that give challenges in three categories - racing against bots/AIs, Ring Race (pass thru rings while flying within time allocated) and Time Attack (pass thru checkpoints when evading obstacles). Each challenge completion earns you a star, depending on your performance. With more stars collected you can get character mods, unlock more tracks and areas to play. Not to mention than doing Single Player is essential to improve your skill for multiplayer.

Just finished all endings (TP only, no DLC).
One more time - it would be better to have some scale, like 1-5 stars or something to really evaluate. 0/1 is not really fair... I'd give 4 out of 5 stars. Or 2 out of 3. Why?
My attitude towards the game was changing, I would not be able to finish it in one shot (playing only this game until I finish). Initially I was very enthusiastic, liked the idea, style of the puzzles, and also - criticized by some - philosophical threads dealing with mysticism, religion, AI, meaning of life etc. Then after some time I felt a bit tired of doing similar puzzles and just needed some time away. But then come back was again very entertaining, until I was tired... and so on. I finished the game in such sinusoid-like cycles. Why was like that?
One of the reasons is annoying lack of 'save anywhere' option. I did not like that I had to repeat large part of some more complex puzzle because I 'died' and was forced to redo the puzzle from start. After some second/third "not again!" I was leaving the game as I do not like silly repeating. It should be possible to preserve any progress done.
Fortunately most puzzles are free from this issue and only few are fillled with killing machines in this annoying way.
Puzzles are entertaining and well balanced, in rare cases the difficulty is raised just by hiding something a bit too much - second reason for taking a break...
Relation between the puzzles and storyline is limited, but unlike others - I do not see it as a problem. I just enjoyed both.
The storyline built from pieces of text heard or available in computer systems is a mixture of philosophy, science and religion from ancients to some futurisms. Of course all could be heard here and there, but still I find it a lot deeper than what's found in most games and makes to think a bit about things detached from our materialistic bullsh-t world. It nicely diverts from just solving puzzles.
The good:
- the artwork - music and graphics are very pleasant and well corresponds to "storyline"
- generally good puzzles - with few minor annoyances
The bad:
- lack of "save anywhere" - death results in resetting the puzzle (annoying in few cases)
PS. I saw that there are some codes for god mode etc. Do not use it with this game! (it is not an unbeatable FPS...) Just have some patience and think. Or take a break... ;-)

I have played this game since I was four years old. I have so many fond memories of playing Age of Kings (which we called the "red CD") with my brother and my father back in '99 and '00 and then the "blue CD" (the Conquerors expansion). I don't have any competitive experience but this is the only game I have always come back to.
When I learned in 2013 that they would release an HD edition compatible with the new and recent operating systems it was the happiest news I received for years and made up for some of the sorrow I still felt for the loss of our wonderful Ensemble Studios, the awesome people who brought this game to life, back in 2009.
It is a very solid RTS and I would still prefer it to any other I have played (AoE3, SC2, WoC, etc). And with the scenario editor you can create your own maps and shape them how ever you like (well you can't choose the shape, it will always be a square on the tip but you can choose whichever terrain and elevation you want). Plus you can publish your own maps or scenarios on the workshop and share them!
With the Rise of the Rajas expansion released recently, the game offers more civs than I ever dreamed possible. The campaigns (especially the first ones from Age of Kings and the Conquerors) are well-made and the voice acting is wonderful!
The game even offers a mini encyclopaedia on the Main Menu for both civs, mechanics, and history.
The game community is wonderful and I recommend you follow Resonance22, ZeroEmpires and Spirit of the Law (to name a few) on youtube for good insight on both in-depth analysis of mehanics and civs as well as upcoming community events, streams, expert gameplay and tournaments.
The developers have been slacking off the earlier part of 2016, leaving a buggy and relatively unstable game on the same patch for many months. Out-of-sync have been a common issue. But it seems they've gotten a thumb out and fixing stuff now in the autumn.
If you already own AoC on CD, you can play on voobly instead which is arguably more balanced and stable (but the average skill level is much higher and people are more competitive there in my experience and you will miss out on all the neat new expansions they're making now)

Escape Goat is a fun puzzle platformer that feels like it came straight out of the original NES days.  Many of the puzzles in the initial game are simple enough with a few challenging levels here and there that can be completed without being killed too terribly much and the first set can be completed within a couple of hours tops.  Once you've completed this fun set of levels, you unlock the extreme difficulty set of levels in another zone.  These appear to be designed more toward the crowd that likes rage games as the difficulty takes a massive spike upward for these.  Expect to die nearly non-stop on the extreme levels.  I have no idea if there is a third set of levels past the second group as the second group feels nearly impossible to complete, and I'm a veteran gamer.
The music is pretty great and goes well with the game.  This is a good thing since you'll be hearing the same tracks a lot once you reach the extreme difficulty.
Controls feel a little floaty at times, especially when you're trying to make precision jumps to small platforms.  It gives you a tendancy to either fall short of your jump or slide past it.  This can lead to some minor frustration in the easy levels and be downright infuriating in the extreme levels.
Level design is really good.  It feels like they could have included an intermediate set of levels to help smooth the transition along to the extreme levels.  That's assuming the extreme levels aren't actually the intermediate ones, though I can't imagine how that would be possible given how incredibly hard the game got after the easy set.
Overall this is a great little 2d platform puzzle game that everyone should at least give a try.  Unless you're a completionist or masochist, I wouldn't recommend doing more than taking a cursory look at the extreme difficulty levels once you're through the easy set as you'll be beating your head against the game for what feels like hours just to complete a single room at that point.

I found Oxenfree to be a very interesting little game, if you can call it that at least. I think the term visual novel would be better because gameplay wise it's very basic. There are no puzzles of any kind and you don't really interact all that much with objects besides a radio that you receive at the start. You basically walk around, following the storyline and talk to your fellow characters in the game, make choices during the dialogue and that's about it.
If this sounds boring to some I can't really blame you, this is definitely not for everyone. The story presented here isn't bad but since it's advertised as being a thriller/mystery I did expect more from it in terms of tension or atmosphere.
That said though, the game looks nice with an original looking graphical style to it. The voice acting is also very well done and will keep you interested in the characters throughout the story. I just wish the story itself would be a little better. I find it difficult to recommend this for the full price as it's only 3 hours long or so and doesn't have much re-playability unless you want to explore the alternative endings. Yet on a discount like I bought it, I think it's worth it, especially if you are into visual novels.

Oxenfree ist ein kurzes, ziemlich interessantes und storylastiges Indiespiel mit Thrillerelementen.
Vorweg sollte ich sagen, dass das Spiel soweit ich weiß noch keine deutsche Übersetzung hat - daher sollte man zumindest gute "Schulenglisch-Kenntnisse" haben um das Spiel im vollen ausmaß zu genießen.
Man schlüpft in die Rolle von Alex, einer Schülerin, die mit ihren Freunden einen Partyausflug auf die naheliegende Insel Edward's Island macht. Im Verlauf der ersten 20 Minuten bekommt man schon ein grobes Bild von den Charakteren, was sich im Spielverlauf noch vertieft - es werden Details über die Vergangenheit der Charaktere offenbart und man puzzelt sich viel zusammen.
Nach einiger Zeit passieren auf der Insel paranormale Dinge, die ich nicht weiter spoilern werde, worauf Alex dann durch nutzen ihres Taschenradios regieren muss - ich rate hier zum benutzen eines Controllers, da dieser mit rumble-Funktion etc das Spiel deutlich stimmiger gestaltet. Das Spiel ist nicht zwingend ein Horrorspiel, aber hat einen düsteren/verstörenden Hintergrund.
Die Grafik ist simplistisch gehalten, sieht aber soweit gut aus, und auch an der Preformance hatte ich jetzt nix zu meckern.  Die Musik und Vertonung ist treffend und sorgt dafür, dass man sich sehr schnell in das Spiel einfühlt. Oxenfree glänzt durch eine gute Story, tiefe und realistische Charaktere - und lässt sich auch ab und zu mit Life is Strange vergleichen - denn es werden auch viele wichtige Entscheidungen getroffen,  das Spiel hat dort viel Potential.
Daher rate ich Leuten, die an Spielen mit realistischen, tiefen Charakteren interessiert sind, oder die sich einfach mal mit nem ruhigeren und etwas düsteren Titel entspannen wollen stark zum Kauf von Oxenfree!

I've been playing pinball, off and on, for over 50 years, and I've played hundreds of tables. I've played every table by both major companies on Steam to the tune of many thousands of games, but all that is pretty much in the past, because I have discovered Pro Pinball Ultra's "Timeshock" table. Most days it’s the only pinball I play.
In the 35 days since Timeshock was released 0n 1/27/16, I've recorded over 1,200 games. And I've yet to even BEGIN to be bored with playing the same table, mostly because Timeshock has so much depth and challenge. It's hard! I would go so far to say that even with its "novice" mode, it's not a table for beginners, but it IS the table to strive toward playing, no matter one's skill level, or the amount of time one has to devote.
With Timeshock's many challenging modes, including a 4-level video mode that really adds tremendously, there is no clue when a game begins if it will end with a score of 3 million, or 300 million....or much more. I tend to have a short attention span and often get frustrated fairly easily, but at least for me, Timeshock is pretty much rage-proof, because it's just so MUCH fun to play! (And I’m really only an average pinball player.) The challenge of some shots is the very source of the tremendous feeling of success I sometimes get, and I can honestly say that with time comes much greater proficiency, and tremendous personal satisfaction.
Timeshock offers a very complex story about time travel, and the acquisition of artifacts from the varying periods visited.  The table guide I typically use, by Jens Goering -
, is 32 pages of valuable information and graphics, very well written and structured. Clearly, this is no simple table to be mastered overnight, but rather a commitment than might require years of pure joy.
Not only is the Timeshock table itself interesting and challenging, there are numerous varying methods of play to choose from, each adding its own dimension of fun. As well, each has its own leaderboard to track progress against players the world over. It even has an unusual “glass removed” feature that allows the player to investigate the table actions in great detail (but does not count on leaderboards.) If a player had done well on the first three balls during any regular game, Timeshock offers the opportunity to extend the game by up to three additional balls for what offers the possibility of REALLY high scores for the best players. And Timeshock has my ALL-TIME favorite score in pinball; Lucky!, a 5 million point shot when you almost lose the ball down the left outlane. (Admittedly, I haven’t personally accessed many of the high-score features, so please forgive and notify if errors have been made in this review.)
At first glance it might seem that Timeshock is more expensive than most single computer pinball tables, and I really bought it because I had heard so much about it for so long. (It is a truly legendary pinball table, perhaps the MOST renowned single computer pinball table available.) But while I paid about $15US, after a little over a month it comes to just over a penny a game, a pittance I’m grateful didn’t prevent me from THE pinball experience of my lifetime.

Squad - where do I begin?
An incredibly tough game - it punishes the lone wolf and rewards the team oriented play.
Spotting enemies is what this game is all about. If you are constantly on the move - in a hurry to get somewhere - you will take fire and die 9 out of 10 times with that lucky once in a while to be in the right spot at the right time and see them first.
Squad size is up to 9 soldiers - and most should be on high ground spotting. You can chat via Microphone to your entire squad - or to those within earshot - Squad Leaders can talk to eachother and coordinate 18, 27, 36 soldiers if you're playing on a pro server. You can also text chat the same way - even to all players in the game (text only for that one).
Snipers - SAW gunners - Grenadiers - Medics - Anti-Tank Soldiers - Riflemen - you need to work together to survive and win. This game is extremely challenging - but the rewards are fantastic when you get in a squad that works together and accomplishes missions. In 2 battles our 9 man squad had actually bonded and we covered each other, called out enemy locations, provided medics with supressing fire while they patched buddies and split a 4 man fire-team to flank enemy positions while the remaining five engaged at medium range.
The Squad Leader placed .50 cal emplacements at our F.O.B. (Forward OperatingBase) and we used entrenching tools to build sandbags and barbed wire to secure locations, then went through hell together trying to hold that position (depends on the map/mission).
Rally points to respawn, FOBs to dig in and resupply at - vehicles with arms and armor - even though in Alpha this game is amazingly complex and can be quite rewarding, and very frustrating.
Bottom line: Not for the loner who doesn't like to use a microphoine. Looking for a game where communication is the norm and teamwork expected? Fire fights occur at medium to long range unless it's CQB in town? Pick up Squad and set your 2 hour timer. But I doubt you'll be refunding this game - it's just that damn good.

In the historical development of designing pinball machines and video games, TimeShock! continues to stand the "test of time". When it was originally developed using actual CAD and pinball engineering software, it was WAY ahead of even real pinball machines. It used too many feature lamps on the matrix, actual accurate switch location design was not really considered, and the physical mechanics were not directly feasible (Time Crystal, ramp alignment, etc) based on what was included in the virtual game among other factors. It is an absolute classic that although has taken FOREVER to get to this stage, is still worth the time and money.
If you want to complain about this only being one table, go play Pinball Arcade by Farsight Studios.  The ball physics of this table, however, are much more accurate and the detail of the table is refined.
My credentials for assessment review of this pinball simulation are direct and simple.
I restore pinball machines as a collector, technician, and operator and have done so for well over a quarter century.  I still maintain a large "stable" private collection of machines.
I am not a millenlial gamer.
I was involved the Bally/Williams pinball department in the 1990s.
I am intrinically aware of the challenges and design of pinball machines at both an electronic and physical level.
Currently, this simulation is being developed as a sample prototype machine by Silver Castle Pinball.  Scheduled for demonstration at Pinball Expo in Chicago in 2016.

An immaculate update to an all-time classic.
The original 1997 Timeshock! still looks and runs great today, despite being almost 20 years old, but the much improved reflections, dynamic lighting and the support for larger resolutions and modern operating systems makes this £10 update completely worth it. Those familiar with the original game will feel right at home, because although the ball physics are vastly improved, the table still feels exactly the same.
Glass-Off mode is a welcome addition too, as it lets you practice tricky shots and combos, and allows you to advance through difficult missions just by clicking the ball and flicking it where it needs to go (great for when you're curious about some of the later missions but lack the skill to reach them legitimately!).
Performance is excellent; I've never dipped below 60 FPS, even during intense multiballs. The game generally hovers at around 120-150 FPS on an FX 8350 and HD7970 at 1440p and 4x MSAA when a single ball is in play. I've seen it go as low 75 FPS when there are seven balls on the table.
In the future I'd like to see options added for table tilt, flipper strength and level of wear (some of my favourite features to play with in Big Race USA), and of course, more tables! I'd be very excited to see The Web, Big Race USA and Fantastic Journey recieve the same treatment as Timeshock! Maybe a brand new table as well? Fingers crossed.

It's early to write a review for 'Pro Pinball Ultra,' as it's not finished, so I'll write a small one for Timeshock instead.
One of the best pinball tables ever designed I'd say; I think that's fair. As far as virtual/digital pinball goes, I think it is only beaten by one table: Fantastic Journey. FJ had the last and best physics that Barnstorm created, but I think a lot of the rubber on the table was firmer too (less bouncy) and maybe that's why I prefer it.
Writing a review is tricky here: I'd give the original Timeshock 10/10. The score would be due to the table design AND the implementation (the physics, the views given, the virtual DMD, the soundtrack, everything about it). But lots of that stuff in not done for this version of Timeshock yet, and the physics will be changed (note that it was stated that there would be an option included to allow play with the original physics; not sure how leaderboards will deal with this though).
So it's tricky to review 'Pro Pinball Ultra' you see.
Personally, I expect Barnstorm to put in all the time needed to make it as good as it can possibly be: I have that faith. I feel safe recommending the game that will be, but as I write this review the original 'finished' Timeshock is better.

Timeshock is still the very best pinball game for PC. If you like pinball or are just even slightly interested in it, buy it now.
This is a graphically updated version of the excellent pinball simulation Timeshock from 1997. The Pro Pinball series was the absolute top of PC pinball back then and has not been surpassed since. This updated version does the game justice. The updates include higher resolution, better lighting and portrait mode, which of course works great for pinball.
The table itself is unchanged, which is a good thing. It remains one of the best tables I have ever played virtual or real. The table design is perfect, the shots have exactly the right difficulty and feel very satisfying. The ruleset is very deep, there are an incredible number of modes, super modes, wizard modes, frenzys, manias, video mode... etc. which will keep all but the most seasoned pinball veteran occupied forever. (I have played this table for almost 20 years and never reached the super wizard mode in normal play.) The modes and table elements all interact to form a path and a story. Still, the table keeps a simple elegance and is not overwhelming, even for beginners.
The updated graphics are gorgeous, the light show at the beginning of the time travel mode is one of the best in any pinball machine. The sound and music were not upgraded, but still do the job nicely. The guitar music soundtrack is a matter of taste, I personally like it a lot. There are different tracks for different game situations and modes and they fit very nicely.
This is a simulation of a real world pinball table, there even is an operator's menu to tweak the internal settings of the machine. That also means it is quite difficult, especially compared to the more arcady games like Pinball FX and Pinball Arcade. The table is unforgiving, but never unfair. Through the operator's menu the game can be made easier, but for me the standard settings work well.
There are a few things that are still missing: UI to change default controls, controller support and more table views. I was the most disappointed that they have not improved the physics to at least the level of the later Pro Pinball games „Big Race USA” and “Fantastic Journey” yet, I hope this is coming soon. The current physics model is from the original game. It is by no means bad and feels very real. It is in every way superior to other games like Pinball Arcade. But the physics of the later Pro Pinball games are even better and I was hoping that 20 years later and with superior hardware, this could have been taken up another notch.
These things are promised, unfortunately Barnstorm Games has not exactly convinced with speed on what is a mere upgrade and has struggled through 2 years of development. I hope they can improve their development process and dedication to the PC platform, implement the missing features soon and hopefully even upgrade the other old tables and design new ones.
While the price of this game is higher than other tables on the market, it is absolutely justified by the superior simulation. The table design is on a completely different level than Pinball FX tables and the realism and graphics easily and clearly surpass Pinball Arcade. This table makes these other pinball games look bad by comparison. It would be amazing if the Pinball Arcade developers could reach the same level of detail and realism. The table design can absolutely compare to some of the best real tables out there, so it is not surprising that there is a company working on a real world version of Timeshock.
I have been playing the original for almost 20 years and I know I will play this for at least as long. For an early access game it is already very much playable and I can recommend it highly to both pinball experts and beginners.
